For one who has great desires, while remaining within the sphere of desire, manifests the virtues present in oneself—such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and the ascetic qualities (*dhuta-dhamma*).
In such a person, there is also a lack of moderation in receiving alms. It is with reference to this that they say: "The manifestation of existing virtues and a lack of moderation in receiving alms."
“This is the characteristic of great desire. Furthermore, this great desire comes down precisely by way of such passages as: “Here, someone being faithful desires, ‘May people know me as faithful’;
being virtuous, he desires, ‘May people know me as virtuous.
A person endowed with that [desire] is difficult to satisfy; even his own mother and father cannot win over his mind.
He is unable [to satisfy them]. Therefore, this is said:
“The mass of fire, the ocean, and the person of great desire—these three cannot be satisfied even if they were given provisions by means of a cart.”
He says, "by association with groups and by association with defilements," meaning that it is a gathering together, a comingling, with beings and with defilements.

"And he is followed by indolence" means he is followed by the state of being indolent; the state of one who is indolent is *kosajja*. Regarding the phrase "by the fulfillment of the eight grounds of indolence":
here, one who sinks (*sīdati*) in what is base (*kucchita*) is "indolent" (*kusīta*), [the change from] *da* to *sa* [being a phonetic shift].
Having added the letter *ta*. That state by virtue of which a person is called "lazy" is here expressed by the word *kusīta*.
For even without a word explicitly denoting an abstract state (*bhāva*), the meaning of that state is understood—as in the expression "the whiteness of the cloth.
Therefore, the meaning is "the bases for the state of laziness"; what is meant is "the causes of indolence. For it is thus:
“I have work to be done, and while doing this work my body will become weary; what if I were to lie down?

Thus he lies down and does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized—this is the first ground of laziness. “I have indeed work...”
"I have performed work, and while performing that work my body became weary; well now, I shall lie down...
[as before] ...I must travel along a road, and while traveling along that road my body will become weary; well now, I shall lie down...
[as before] ...I have indeed traveled along a road, and while traveling along that road my body has become weary."
"Come now, I shall lie down... [as before] ...While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain sufficient or complete food, whether coarse or refined;
my body is weary and unfit for work, so come now, I shall lie down...
[as before] ...While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did obtain coarse..."
Or after eating as much of excellent food as I desired until full satisfaction, my body became heavy and unwieldy, as if covered with fat;
"Well now, I shall lie down... [as before]... "This slight ailment has arisen in me;
it is appropriate for me to lie down; well now, I shall lie down... [as before]... "I have recently recovered from illness and have not long been free from sickness."
“‘My body is weak and unfit for work; come now, let me lie down,’ he thinks, and he lies down;
he does not arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.

This is the eighth ground of indolence. Thus, these instances of despondency occurring with the thought, “Come now, let me lie down,” are called the eight grounds of indolence because they successively cause laziness. The meaning is that [the practice] leads to the fulfillment of those [grounds].
"Easy to support and easy to satisfy" means that he can be supported and nourished with ease by his own attendants.
For some, established in restraint, are easy to support and easy to satisfy even for themselves; others are so even for their attendants.
How so? It is one who, having received whatever food—whether coarse or refined—eats it with a contented mind and then goes to the monastery.
One who performs his own duties is easy to support for himself.

But one who, having received from others a gift—whether small or great, coarse or refined—consumes it right in their presence with a cheerful mind and a serene face, is easy to support for his attendants.
Seeing this, people become exceedingly confident, thinking, "For us..."
The Venerable Subhara is easily supported; he is satisfied with even a little. "We ourselves shall support him," they promised, and so they supported him.
*Appicchatā* means the state of being devoid of desire. Here, the phrasing (*byañjana*) seems as if it has something remaining, but the meaning (*attha*) is complete.
It can be understood that the word *appa* here has the sense of "absence" (*abhāva*), as in such expressions as "I perceive freedom from illness" (*appābādhataṃ*).

For that very reason, it says: "the state of being free from craving. Regarding "satisfaction of threefold distinction": this is stated by way of the commonality of satisfaction such as "according to what is obtained" (yathālābha) and so forth;

however, since there are three types of satisfaction for each of the four requisites, satisfaction is twelvefold. How so? In the case of robes, there is satisfaction with whatever is obtained and satisfaction according to one's capacity.
Contentment according to suitability is threefold. It is likewise with regard to alms-food and the other requisites.
This is its detailed explanation: here, a bhikkhu receives a robe, whether beautiful or ugly; he makes do with that alone and does not long for another, nor does he accept one even if it is offered.
This is his contentment with whatever robe is obtained (*yathālābhasantosa*). Furthermore, if he is naturally weak...
Or he may be afflicted by illness or overcome by old age; when putting on a heavy robe, he becomes exhausted.
By exchanging it with a fellow monk of similar status and making do with a light one, he is indeed content. This is his contentment regarding robes according to his strength.
For heavy robes do not bring comfort to those who are naturally weak and the like, but rather cause physical distress.
By means of purpose—namely, by way of having no excessive desire and so forth—one transforms those [robes]; thus, the use of light robes is not in contradiction with contentment.
Another person obtains superior requisites; having received one of the costly robes such as a fine cloth robe (*paṭṭacīvara*), or many robes, he thinks:
"This is suitable for the elders who have long been gone forth; this is appropriate for those of great learning."

Having given [the robes], thinking, "May this be for the sick, may this be for those who have little gain," even when he has made a *saṅghāṭī* from old robes or scraps gathered from rubbish heaps and wears it, he remains content.
This is his contentment with robes as they are appropriate. For even having obtained a costly robe or many robes, he—
Giving up one thing and taking up another according to what is appropriate does not contradict contentment, because it is established in accordance with what is suitable.
In this case, however, a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined;

he subsists on that alone and does not long for anything else, nor does he accept more even when it is offered. This is his contentment with whatever almsfood is obtained (*yathālābha-santosa*). But as for him who...

If he receives almsfood that is contrary to his natural constitution or contrary to his illness—such that by consuming it he would experience discomfort—he should give it to a fellow monk who is of a similar temperament. Having received suitable food from that monk’s hand and eaten it, even while performing the duties of a recluse, he remains truly contented.
This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another...
Even if he receives abundant and choice almsfood, he gives it away like a robe to those who have been long ordained, to the learned, to those of little gain, or to the sick;
or else, having given what remains to them, he goes for alms himself and eats mixed food. Even so, he remains contented.
This is his contentment with almsfood as is appropriate.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives a lodging that is either pleasing or unpleasing;
he gives rise to neither gladness nor repulsion because of it, but is content with whatever he has received, even if it is merely a spread of grass.
This is his contentment with whatever lodging is obtained. However, as for that which is contrary to one's own nature or contrary to one's illness...
He receives a lodging where he dwells uncomfortably; having given that to a fellow monk of like standing, even though he dwells in the suitable lodging belonging to that other, he remains contented.
This is his contentment with regard to lodgings according to his strength.
Another person of great merit receives many excellent lodgings, such as caves, pavilions, gabled houses, and so forth; he [remains contented] with those...

Just as with robes and other requisites, he remains content wherever he dwells, having given [his preference] to those who have been long ordained, those who are learned, those who have little gain, and those who are ill.
This is his contentment with a dwelling-place that is appropriate to him. Furthermore, he thinks:
"An excellent dwelling-place is a ground for negligence; sloth and torpor descend upon one sitting there, and for one overcome by sleep, upon waking again..."
Having reflected thus, "Evil thoughts become manifest," he does not accept even such a lodging as has come to him;
having rejected it, he remains content even while dwelling in the open air, at the foot of a tree, and so forth.
This too is his contentment with a lodging that is suitable.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives medicine, whether coarse or refined;
he is content with whatever he receives and does not long for another, nor does he take it even when receiving it. This is his contentment with what is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine.
However, one who needs oil and receives molasses gives that to a fellow bhikkhu of similar status and [uses] its...
Even if he takes oil from someone’s hand or seeks out something else entirely to prepare medicine, he remains content.
This is his contentment with the requisite of medicine according to his strength. Another person of great merit receives abundant and excellent medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses;
he gives these away like a robe to those who have been long ordained, to the learned, to those of little gain, or to the sick. To them...
He is content even when subsisting on whatever has been brought to him by anyone at all. Furthermore, suppose someone were told:
"Venerable sir, take whichever you wish—here is myrobalan in urine placed in one vessel, and here is the fourfold sweet [mixture] in another.
If his illness were to be cured by either of these, he would choose the fourfold sweet mixture, thinking: "The myrobalan in urine is merely praised by the Buddha and others."
Having rejected [other medicines], he is supremely content making medicine with only the *muttaharītaka* (urine-soaked myrobalan) alone.

This is his contentment with what is suitable regarding the requisite of medicine. Thus, it should be understood that the threefold contentment—beginning with "whatever is obtained"—becomes twelvefold by way of the four requisites.
The three unwholesome types of thought by way of thoughts of sensual desire (*kāmavitakka*), thoughts of ill will (*byāpādavitakka*), and thoughts of cruelty (*vihiṃsāvitakka*).

The three wholesome types of thought by way of thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*), thoughts of non-ill will (*abyāpādavitakka*), and thoughts of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsāvitakka*). "By means of the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) which consists in the diminution of all defilements" means by means of the element of Nibbāna, which is the cause for the diminution of all defilements such as lust.
"By the fulfillment of the eight bases for the arousal of energy" means of the eight...
For the sake of fulfilling the causes for the arousal of energy. For indeed, the initial exertion that occurs in whatever manner serves as the cause for the subsequent arousal of energy.

It should be understood that the eight bases for the arousal of energy are either the acts of exertion accompanied by appropriate reflection, or reflections rooted in those acts of exertion. For it is thus:
“I must perform some work; however, while I am performing that work, it will not be easy for me to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas.
Come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized.
I have indeed performed this work; yet, while I have performed this work...”
While doing so, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas; well then, let me arouse energy...

"I must travel along a road; while traveling along a road, it is not easy for me to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas; well then, let me arouse energy... ... "I have indeed traveled along a road; while on the road..."
"Furthermore, while traveling, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas; well then, let me arouse energy... [as before]...
While wandering for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain as much coarse or refined food as I required for full satisfaction;
consequently, my body has become light and pliant; well then, let me arouse energy... [as before]..."
"While wandering for alms in a village or town, I obtained as much of coarse or refined food as I required for my full satisfaction;
therefore, my body is strong and fit for work. Come now, I shall arouse energy...
[as before] ...This slight illness has arisen in me, but it is possible that this illness might..."
"It might increase; let me, then, arouse energy... I have recently recovered from illness and am not long emerged from my sickness.
It is possible that my affliction might recur;
let me, then, arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized."
The eight bases for the arousal of energy (*vīriyārambhavatthu*) consist of the efforts accompanied by a review of what has thus proceeded, or the reviews based on that [effort].
Regarding the phrase "suitable thereto" (*tadanucchavika*) and "conducive thereto" (*tadanulomika*), the word *ta-* (that) refers both to what is yet to be stated and to what has already passed;
therefore, he says: "the training rule which he will now lay down," and so forth. For all pronouns refer even to words that are yet to be spoken.
There are also words concerning those who have departed. "Connected with restraint and abandoning" means connected with both the fivefold restraint and the fivefold abandoning.
For restraint is fivefold: restraint of virtue, restraint of mindfulness, restraint of knowledge, restraint of patience, and restraint of energy.
Abandoning is also fivefold: abandoning by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*), abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), and abandoning by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).
“Abandonment by subsiding” and “abandonment by escape.
Therein, the restraint of the Pātimokkha—referred to in such passages as “He is endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha, fully endowed”—is called the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*);
and in its actual meaning, it is the non-transgression of body and speech. “He guards the faculty of the eye...”

"Restraint regarding the faculty of the eye"—thus it is said; this guarding of the faculties is restraint by mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*), and in its actual meaning, it is simply mindfulness occurring in that manner.
"I call it the restraint of the streams; by wisdom these are closed up"—thus it is said;
this is restraint by knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*). For here, after stating "I call it the restraint of the streams," the statement "by wisdom these are closed up" is made.

The knowledge that completely eradicates the defilements—craving, views, misconduct, ignorance, and so forth—associated with the ear is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) in the sense of closing [the door].
Endurance as it occurs in such passages as “He is patient with cold and heat” is the restraint of patience (*khanti-saṃvara*);

and in terms of its actual meaning (*attha*), this consists of the aggregates functioning in that way, or non-hatred (*adosa*). Some say it is wisdom (*paññā*), but that should not be accepted. “When [an unwholesome thought] has arisen...”

"Virtue as restraint of energy" (vīriya-saṃvara) is precisely that energy which functions by way of dispelling sensual thoughts and so forth, as it has been handed down in the passage: "One does not tolerate a sensual thought.

And this entire restraint consists in the non-arising of misconduct of body and speech—termed immorality—which ought to be restrained according to its respective type, or of negligence termed forgetfulness, or of covetousness and the like, or of impatience.
It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because it restrains, covers, and conceals ignorance and negligence. It is called "restraint" because it restrains;
the meaning is that it covers, prevents, and does not allow [unwholesome states] to proceed.

For here, "restraining" refers precisely to the non-arising, in various ways, of bodily misconduct and so forth, which would otherwise be liable to arise when the necessary conditions coincide. Thus, first of all...
Restraint should be understood as fivefold.
The abandoning of each respective unwholesome factor by means of its corresponding wholesome factor is "abandoning by way of substitution" (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

For, through the determination of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*)—just as darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp—the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is abandoned because it stands in opposition to the insight-knowledges (*vipassanāñāṇa*) such as the discernment of name-and-form.
By the discernment of conditions, the views of no-cause and irregular cause are abandoned; subsequently, by the overcoming of doubt, the state of being a sceptic is abandoned;

by the comprehension of groups, the grasping at "I" and "mine" is abandoned; by the determination of what is the path and what is not the path, the perception of a path where there is no path is abandoned;
and by the vision of arising, the view of annihilationism is abandoned, while by the vision of passing away, the view of eternalism is abandoned.

The abandoning of each respective unwholesome factor by means of its corresponding insight-knowledge—according to the method beginning with "perceiving fear in what is fearful" and so forth—should be understood as *tadaṅga-pahāna* (abandoning by substitution of opposites).

Furthermore, that which occurs through concentration, distinguished by access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*), functions to arrest the process of arising; like the striking of a pot against the surface of water, it effects the abandoning of those various factors such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
This is called abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*). Suppression itself is the abandonment; thus it is "abandonment by suppression.

Because of the cultivation of the four noble paths, within the continuum of one who possesses those respective paths, there occurs the absolute non-arising of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination—which was described by way of the formula beginning with "for the abandoning of the various types of views" (*diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāya*)—and so forth.

This is called abandonment by cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*). Furthermore, that state of the defilements being subsided and calmed at the moment of the fruit (*phala*) is called abandonment by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhippahāna*).

That Nibbāna, which has abandoned all conditioned things because it is dissociated from all the conditioned, is called abandonment by escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*). And all of this is also called "abandonment" in the sense of relinquishment (*cāga*).
Thus, the teaching of the Dhamma associated with these aforementioned restraints (*saṃvara*) and abandonments (*pahāna*) should be understood as "associated with restraint and abandonment.

"Not bound to the Suttantas" means not fixed within the Suttantas; the meaning is that it has not been included in the Canon (*pāḷi*). For a miscellaneous teaching of the Dhamma does not enter into the compendium.
Explaining this very point, he said, "excluded from the Canon" (*pāḷivinimutta*). Alternatively, [the text continues:]
"Unbound by the Suttas" is said with reference to the fact that it has not ascended into the Sutta or Abhidhamma Piṭaka;
"freed from the Piṭaka" is said with reference to the fact that it has not ascended into the Vinaya Piṭaka.

A "dhamma-teaching by way of penetration" (okkantika-dhammadesanā) is a teaching of the Dhamma delivered in the midst [of a discourse] after having entered into it with knowledge; it is intended for rejection, like that of the Elder Bhaddāli. Because it is to be understood...
Because one must go there after passing away, it is called *samparāya*, the world beyond. That which pertains to that is *samparāyika*.
"Threatening with the fear of the round of existence" means threatening them by saying, "In this way, those who are immoral encounter suffering in the hells and other realms. [The question is:
"How did the Blessed One deliver such a vast teaching on the Dhamma in a single moment, in a single instant, even as long as the *Dīghanikāya* or the *Majjhimanikāya*? [The answer follows:]...
It should not be said that [the Blessed One] does not speak. For while the worldly masses speak one word, the Elder Ānanda speaks eight words;
and while the Elder Ānanda speaks one word, the Blessed One speaks sixteen words.
By this method, at the moment a worldly person utters one word, the Blessed One [speaks] one hundred and twenty-eight words.
He speaks. Why? Because the Blessed One’s tongue is supple, his lips are well-kissed, his speech is unhesitating, and his habituation to the life-continuum is light;

therefore, even if one bhikkhu asks about body-contemplation, another about feeling-contemplation, another about mind-contemplation, and another about dharma-contemplation, he does not think, "When this one has been asked, I shall ask. Rather, he speaks.

He does not look at even one [of them]; yet, even though this is so, for those monks the turn of questioning—such as "this one asked first, this one second," and so forth—is discernible by one possessed of such wisdom, because it is possible to perceive subtle internal distinctions.

However, the turn of the Buddhas' teaching is not discernible by others at all, because within a moment as brief as the snap of a finger, the occurrence of many thousands of millions of mental states is possible.

Before the arrow shot by a skilled archer with a firm bow could even pass beyond the shadow of a palm tree by a span or four finger-breadths, the Blessed One had already taught the fourteen-fold contemplation of the body, the nine-fold contemplation of feelings, the sixteen-fold contemplation of the mind, and the five-fold contemplation of phenomena. Or let it be: [let the arrow pass].

If these four were to ask questions regarding the four right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eight factors of the path—and there were yet other four [groups]—the Blessed One would explain those as well.
Let alone these eight; if there were thirty-seven other people [to ask] concerning the factors conducive to enlightenment...
If they were to ask questions, the Blessed One would explain them at that very moment.
It should be understood that "root," "support," and "foundation" are synonyms for each preceding term in relation to each succeeding one.

In this context, "foundation" refers to the state of being a basis by way of association (*sampayoga*) and by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). For those things comprised under the training (*sikkhā*),...
The remaining wholesome states may serve as a foundation either by way of association with the abstinence from sexual intercourse, or by way of being its decisive support (*upanissaya*).

For this very reason, he said, “The restraint from sexual intercourse,” and so forth. By the phrase “in accordance with the meaning stated,” he means by way of the method for attaining that foundation.
Desiring to show that the volition of abstinence and the states associated with it, as specified in the analysis of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga*), constitute the training rule itself—
He said: "And this meaning is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*.

For in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*, the factors such as abstinence (*virati*) and so forth are called "training rules" (*sikkhāpada*) both in the primary sense and in a figurative sense. Indeed, it is said there:
"In that regard, what is the training rule of abstinence from sexual misconduct? At whatever time one [abstains] from the sensual sphere..."
When a wholesome state of mind has arisen, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge,
for one abstaining from sexual misconduct— whatever at that time constitutes abstention, desisting, refraining, abstinence, non-doing,
non-performance, non-transgression, not overstepping the limit, and the destruction of the bridge regarding sexual misconduct— this is called [abstention] from sexual misconduct.
The training precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct. The remaining factors are associated with this abstention.
In that regard, what is the training precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct?
At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, [and directed] toward sexual misconduct—
At the time of abstaining, whatever volition, intention, and state of intending there is—this is called the training precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct.
The remaining phenomena are associated with that volition.
In this context, what is the training precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct? At whatever time one [engages in] the sense-sphere realm...
“When a wholesome state of mind has arisen, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge, for one abstaining from sexual misconduct—whatever at that time is contact...
[and so on] ...exertion, non-distraction: this is called the training precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct.”
For here, since it is not only abstinence (*virati*) that is a training precept (*sikkhāpada*), but volition (*cetanā*) as well,
the second method was stated in order to demonstrate this. Furthermore, since it is not only these two factors that are training precepts,
but also the fifty-odd states associated with volition, because they constitute the categories to be trained in, they too are indeed training precepts.
Therefore, the third method has been shown. For the training rule (sikkhāpada) is twofold: the literal training rule (nippariyāya-sikkhāpada) and the figurative training rule (pariyāya-sikkhāpada).
Therein, abstention (virati) is the literal training rule; for it is this that is stated in the Canon as "abstaining from taking life" (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī), and not volition (cetanā).
One abstains from various things by means of that very [abstention], and not by means of volition; yet volition also—
Having brought them forth, it displays them; likewise, it displays the other states associated with volition (cetanā).
Therefore, it should be understood that both volition and the remaining associated states constitute the "training rule" (sikkhāpada) in a figurative sense.
Now, it is not only the factors such as abstinence (virati) here that are the training rules, but rather the formal designation (paññatti) which illuminates their meaning.

Showing this, he says “Furthermore,” and so forth. They say: “That which there is called ‘the group of names’ (nāmakāya) and ‘the group of phrases’ (padakāya) is what is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
The “group of names” is a collection of names, that is, merely designation by name (*nāmapaññatti*).

Words, etymologies, and phonemes are synonyms for “name,” as in such passages as “name, naming-act, and etymology of names. The “sections of training” (*sikkhākoṭṭhāsa*) are simply the abstentions and so forth.
The statement that even the words which illuminate that meaning constitute a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is indeed applicable here as well.

Regarding the phrase "for a specific purpose" (*atthavasena*), it refers to a particular kind of growth or a particular kind of benefit (*ānisaṃsa*). Since these are the reasons for the proclamation of those training rules, he said, "for ten reasons" (*dasa kāraṇavase*);
the meaning is "for ten specific reasons. Therefore, he said, "for a specific benefit" (*hitavisese*). It is simply the goal itself.

Or, "for the sake of the goal" (*atthavaso*); that is to say, ten goals mean ten reasons. Alternatively, *attha* is the fruit (*phala*), and since it has mastery (*vaso*) over that [fruit] because its existence depends upon it, it is called *atthavaso*;
thus, it should be understood here as meaning "cause" (*hetu*). "Very well, O King"—this was spoken in the training rule concerning entry into the royal palace:
"For those who think my words should be heard and believed, may that be for their welfare for a long time."
Because it was said, "for happiness," it was further stated: "And for whoever accepts the word of the Tathāgata, that leads to their welfare and happiness for a long time.

Having shown the disadvantage in not accepting [the teaching]—as in the Bhaddāli Sutta—it follows that since there is no dwelling in happiness for one who does not accept it, even co-residence is itself a dwelling in happiness.
It has been said. "Happy dwelling" (*sukhavihāra*) refers to the well-being of the four postures. "Humiliation" (*maṅku*) means the state of being devoid of luster.
Regarding the terms "in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammena*) and so forth: "Dhamma" is the factual basis; "Vinaya" is both the formal accusation and the subsequent reminder;
"the Teacher’s instruction" (*satthusāsana*) is the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana*). "Of those of dear virtue" (*piyasīlānaṃ*)...
[It is] for those who desire training; for indeed, virtue is dear to them. For this very reason it was said: "striving for the fulfillment of the three trainings.
"Sandiṭṭhamānā" means falling into doubt. "Ubbāḷhā hontī" means they are oppressed. "Saṅghakammāni":
although both the Uposatha and the Pavāraṇā are acts of the Saṅgha, according to the maxim of the "ox and the bullock," [the term refers specifically to] the Uposatha and the Pavāraṇā.

It should be understood that this refers to the inclusion of the formal acts (*saṅghakamma*) of the Saṅgha, such as those involving *upasampadā* (ordination) and *saṅghādisesa* (formal offenses requiring suspension). The state of being united is *sāmaggī*.

In the passage, “Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma solely for the restraint of taints (*āsava*) pertaining to the present life,” it is the defilements (*kilesa*) that constitute the root of dispute which are referred to as “taints. [And in the verse:
“By which one is reborn as a god, or becomes a Gandhabba, or a bird that flies through the air...”
"By which I might go to the state of a *yakkha*, or fall back into the human state—those taints (*āsava*) of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.

Here, this refers to karma pertaining to the three planes and all remaining unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*). However, in this context, it refers specifically to reviling others, remorse, execution, imprisonment, and so forth.

And because there are various kinds of calamities that constitute the suffering of the states of deprivation (apāya), he said: "By one who stands in non-restraint, [these] are to be experienced in that very same personal existence," and so forth.

For if the Blessed One had not laid down the training rules (sikkhāpada), then those various kinds of misfortunes pertaining to the present life—such as the reproach of others—which would arise on account of indulging in unrighteous conduct, taking what is not given, killing living beings, and so on, as well as those [misfortunes] which have that very [indulgence] as their cause...

The various misfortunes experienced as great suffering—such as being subjected to the fivefold fetters and punishments for those reborn in the hells and other realms—are what is intended here when it is said:
“for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life and for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives.
“Present life” (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to one’s own manifest personal existence; that which exists therein is “pertaining to the present life” (*diṭṭhadhammika*).
Therefore it was said: “to be attained in that very same personal existence. Disgrace (*akitti*) is censure in one’s presence; infamy (*ayasa*) is censure in one’s absence.
Alternatively, it should be understood that disgrace is censure both in one’s presence and in one’s absence, while infamy is the loss of one’s retinue.
“For the purpose of blocking the path of arrival” means for the purpose of burning down the door through which [the fire] arrives. “Because of being departed” means having passed away (*pecca*).

Because it is something to be gone toward, it is called the "future world" (*samparāya*), or the "other world" (*paraloka*); thus he said, "in the future world, in the hells and so forth. Sexual intercourse and the like are bases for passion;
killing living beings and the like are bases for hatred.

The fourteen *khandhaka-vattas* (observances of the Khandhaka) are those stated in the *Vattakkhandhaka*: the observance for newcomers, for residents, for those departing, for the expression of thanks, for the meal-hall attendant, for the alms-collector, for forest-dwellers, for the lodging-attendant, for the bathhouse attendant, for the latrine attendant, and the observances for the preceptor, the co-resident pupil, the teacher, and the resident student.

These are the fourteen observances (*vatta*). Beyond these, there are eighty-two major observances that must be practiced only at certain times, such as when one has been subjected to a censure act (*tajjanīya-kamma*), and not at all stages; therefore, they are not included among the fourteen observances of the *Khandhaka*.
These, however, begin with the words, "I shall prescribe the observance for monks who are on probation (*pārivāsika*"), and continue with "not... [and so forth].
"One should grant full ordination... [and so on] ...one should not walk the meditation path while another is walking the meditation path on the ground"—these sixty-six rules end with that statement.

Following that: "Monks, a monk who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) should not, together with a monk who is senior to him in the duration of his probation, or one who is subject to being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), or one who is subject to the trial period (mānattāraha), or one who is practicing the trial period (mānattacārika), or one who is subject to rehabilitation (abbhānāraha)..."

The observances stated in such passages as “one must dwell in a residence with another bhikkhu under the same roof,” and so forth, are not counted separately because they are identical to those practiced by one of normal status (*pakatatta*).

Rather, since they must be observed toward other types of persons—such as those on probation (*pārivāsika*) or those senior in standing—they are grouped together according to those categories and counted individually;
thus, there are seventy-one observances. This includes the observances for those subjected to an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*).
It is said: “One should not accept the salutation or rising up for a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu... nor the rubbing of the back during bathing.
This non-acceptance of salutation and so forth constitutes one rule; and there are ten others, such as “A regular bhikkhu must not be accused of failure in virtue,” and so on.
Thus, these are the eighty-two rules of conduct (vatta). Among these very rules, some are rules concerning formal acts of censure (tajjanīya-kamma) and the like.
By including those [rules] such as the *pārivāsika* duties through the method of "including what was not previously mentioned," there are exactly eighty-two;
however, elsewhere in the *Aṭṭhakathā-padese*, it is stated that "there are eighty *khaṇḍhaka*-duties," because in that context, even a slight deficiency or excess does not affect the count.

*Saṃvara-vinaya* refers to the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), the restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*), the restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇa-saṃvara*), the restraint of patience (*khanti-saṃvara*), and the restraint of energy (*vīriya-saṃvara*).
The fivefold restraint is called "restraint" (saṃvara) because it restrains those things that ought to be restrained and those things that ought to be disciplined, such as bodily misconduct;
and it is called "discipline" (vinaya) because it disciplines them.

As for "discipline as abandonment" (pahānavinaya), it consists of abandonment by way of its own nature (tadaṅgappahāna), abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanappahāna), abandonment by eradication (samucchedappahāna), abandonment by subsiding (paṭippassaddhippahāna), and abandonment by escape (nissaraṇappahāna).

Since all five kinds of abandonment are "abandonment" in the sense of relinquishing (*cāga*), and "discipline" (*vinaya*) in the sense of disciplining (*vinayana*), they are therefore called "discipline as abandonment.
"Discipline as settlement" (*samathavinaya*) refers to the seven methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*).

"Discipline as formulation" (*paññattivinaya*) refers to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) itself; for since a training rule can only come into existence when its formulation is present, discipline as formulation is also supported by the formulation of the training rule.
Now—“That which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha; that which is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of refractory persons;
that which is for the restraint of refractory persons is for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus. That which...
For the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus; that which is for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life is for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives;
that which is for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives is for the inspiration of those without faith; that which is for the inspiration of those without faith...
That which leads to confidence leads to the increase of those who have confidence; that which leads to the increase of those who have confidence leads to the endurance of the true Dhamma;
that which leads to the endurance of the true Dhamma leads to the support of the Vinaya.
"That which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha; that which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of difficult persons."
For the restraint [of the wicked], that which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus;

that which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life; that which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives;
that which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the inspiration of those without faith; that which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for [the increase of] those with faith.
For the increase [of the Saṅgha], that which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the endurance of the true Dhamma; that which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the support of the Vinaya.
"That which is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of refractory persons;

that which is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus; that which is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life."
That which is comfortable for the Saṅgha leads to the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives; that which is comfortable for the Saṅgha leads to the inspiration of those without confidence;
that which is comfortable for the Saṅgha leads to the increase of those with confidence; that which is comfortable for the Saṅgha leads to the endurance of the true Dhamma;
that which is comfortable for the Saṅgha leads to the support of the Vinaya; that which is comfortable for the Saṅgha leads to the well-being of the Saṅgha.
“That which is for the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct... [and so on] ...that which is for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus...
[and so on] ...that which is for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life... [and so on] ...that which is for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives...

[and so on] ...that which is for the inspiration of those without confidence... [and so on] ...that which is for the increase of those with confidence... [and so on] ...that which is for the endurance of the true Dhamma... [and so on]”...
That which supports the Vinaya is for the welfare of the Saṅgha; that which supports the Vinaya is for the comfort of the Saṅgha;
that which supports the Vinaya is for the restraint of difficult persons;
that which supports the Vinaya is for the ease of living of well-behaved bhikkhus; that which supports the Vinaya is for the [abandonment of] taints pertaining to the present life.
That which is for the sake of restraint is for the assistance of the discipline; that which is for the assistance of the discipline is for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives;
that which is for the assistance of the discipline is for the inspiration of those without confidence; that which is for the assistance of the discipline is for the increase of those with confidence;
that which is for the assistance of the discipline is for the endurance of the true Dhamma.
“Eight hundred on the states, one hundred on the phenomena, two hundred on the definitions,
and four hundred on the knowledges— these are the eight purposes in this treatise.
In order to show what was thus stated in the Parivāra, he said, “Moreover, here,” and so forth.
In this context, with reference to what was stated in the sequence beginning, "That which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha;

that which is for the comfort of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of difficult persons," it is called the "linked method" (saṅkhalikanaya) because the successive words are joined with each immediately following word, resembling the binding of a chain. This is the linked method.

"Having made" (*katvā*) is the connection. With reference to what was stated—namely, having joined each single phrase among the ten points (beginning with "What is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the comfort of the Saṅgha;

what is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of difficult persons") with the remaining nine phrases each time—it is said: "having performed the joining ten times, based on each single phrase."

Regarding the passage beginning with "one hundred and eight meanings" (*atthasata*), first, according to the *saṅkhalika* (linked) method, one hundred phenomena (*dhamma*) should be understood by way of each preceding term, and one hundred meanings (*attha*) should be seen by way of each succeeding term. How so?

Although in the *Parivāra* it is stated that in the *saṅkhalika* method there is only a "partial wheel" (*khaṇḍacakkam*)—beginning with "What is beneficial to the Saṅgha is comfortable for the Saṅgha"—nevertheless, by that very same method...

The method for the "bound wheel" (baddhacakkha) has also been given; therefore, having stated, “What is beneficial to the Saṅgha is comfortable for the Saṅgha,” and so forth, one should apply it by saying, “What is for the assistance of the Vinaya is beneficial to the Saṅgha,” and thus construct the bound wheel.
Likewise, having stated, “What is comfortable for the Saṅgha is for the restraint of difficult persons,” and so forth, [one should likewise apply it]. What is for the assistance of the Vinaya...

Having joined them thus: "That which is good for the Saṅgha is that which is beneficial to the Saṅgha; that which is beneficial to the Saṅgha is that which is comfortable for the Saṅgha," one should construct the "bound wheel" (*baddhacakkam*).
When the remaining phrases are joined in this sequence, there are ten bound wheels according to the method of linked chains (*saṅkhalikanaya*).
Within each of those wheels, there are ten qualities based on each preceding phrase and [ten] based on each succeeding phrase.
According to the method of the linked series (*saṅkhalikanaya*), there are ten for each [of the ten bases], thus resulting in one hundred meanings and one hundred teachings.
However, in the method of the single root (*ekamūlakanaya*), a single phrase—such as "What is beneficial to the Saṅgha is comfortable for the Saṅgha;
what is beneficial to the Saṅgha is for the restraint of difficult persons"—is joined with the remaining nine phrases. Thus, for the first phrase...
In the method of the single root, there is only one *dhammapada* and exactly nine *atthapadas*.

Therefore, when ten times the application is made by taking each of the ten phrases as a root according to the method of the single root, based on the *dhammapadas*, there are ten *dhammapadas* and ninety *atthapadas*;
thus, neither a hundred meanings nor a hundred *dhamma*s are achieved. Therefore, in the method of the single root...

In the Saṅkhalika method, rather than taking one hundred meanings and one hundred phenomena according to the stated method, all that is described there as one hundred phrases—by way of ten phrases of phenomena and ninety phrases of meanings—is taken as the "one hundred phenomena.

Then, by way of illustrating their meaning, the phrases of meaning such as "being beneficial to the Saṅgha" and so forth, which are stated in the commentary, are taken as the "one hundred meanings. When it is understood in this manner:
One hundred meanings and one hundred phenomena are thus accomplished. In this way, first, one hundred meanings and one hundred phenomena are to be understood.

Regarding the phrase "and two hundred etymologies": here, one hundred etymologies are to be understood by way of etymologies that illuminate the meaning (*atthajotika*), and another hundred etymologies by way of etymologies that consist of the phenomena themselves (*dhammabhūta*); thus there are two hundred etymologies.

"Four hundred kinds of knowledge": there is one hundred kinds of knowledge regarding the hundred meanings, one hundred kinds of knowledge regarding the hundred phenomena, and two hundred kinds of knowledge regarding the two hundred linguistic expressions; thus, there are four hundred kinds of knowledge.
And as for the phrase "And so, monks," the word "and" (*ca*) here should be construed by breaking the order of the sequence; thus he said, "you should recite."
"And ‘and’ (ca). But how is it that when “you should recite” is said here, meanings such as “you should master” and so forth are possible?
To this he says: “For the word ‘and’ (ca) here has the sense of bringing in something additional. Bringing in a meaning not already stated is “bringing in something additional” (*atirekānayanam*);
that which has this as its meaning is “having the sense of bringing in something additional,” meaning it has the sense of including what was not previously mentioned. Thus it is said.
[The word] “becomes” [is used]. Because it was stated as “non-cohabitation,” it was stated as “having made firm.
Thus ends the Discussion on the First Proclamation in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya-ṭīkā.
The commentary on the section concerning Sudinna is finished.
Commentary on the Story of the Monkey: 40.
Explanation of the Non-Obvious Terms (*anuttānapadavaṇṇanā*): "Obvious" (*uttāna*) means manifest; its opposite, "non-obvious" (*anuttāna*), means unmanifest.
"Scanty" (*appacura*) means difficult to understand. "Commentary on the obscure words" (*anuttānapadavaṇṇanā*) refers to the explanation of those words that are not clear.

The term "obscure" (*anuttāna*) is used because there is no purpose in commenting on words that are already clear. "One who practices frequently" (*pacurapaṭisevī*) means one who practices extensively;
the meaning is that one practices continuously day after day. For the word is used in the sense of frequency, meaning "at all times."
Even in the absence of actual usage, the present tense is employed by way of general application, as in such expressions as "here the Mallas are fighting.
"Āhiṇḍantā" means wandering about. "In others too" means among other monks as well.

"Seized together with the goods" (sahoḍḍhaggahito) means seized along with the merchandise. By one's own false apprehension or by a slight pretext (lesaoḍḍanena), even that which has a full meaning...
While altering the first formal rule, he said: "And that too [must be] with a human woman, not with one belonging to the animal realm.
"Looking" means looking with passion. "Grasping" means grasping with the hand by way of passion alone.
"Touching" is merely touching her body with one's own body; "contacting" is doing so more firmly than that.
"Contact" (*saṃphusana*) means touching; making it even firmer than that, it is the touching of one body with another.
"All of that" (*taṃ sabbaṃ pi*) refers to all [actions] such as seeing and so forth.
"He made the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) firmer" means the strengthening of the training rule through a supplementary enactment (*anupaññatti*) within this context.
Desiring to show, by way of analysis, how the relaxation [of the training] follows as a consequence, he said: "For the training rule (sikkhāpada) is twofold," and so forth.
Therein, that training rule which involves a conscious state (*sacittaka*) and where the mind is exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*) is a "worldly offense" (*lokavajja*).
That which belongs to the category involving both conscious and unconscious states, as well as the unconscious category, is such that in its conscious aspect, the mind is exclusively unwholesome.
In order to show this point—that even [acts] such as drinking liquor are "worldly offenses" (*lokavajja*)—it is said:

"That for which, in the case of being with consciousness (*sacittakapakkhe*), the mind is exclusively unwholesome, that is called a worldly offense. For this expression "in the case of being with consciousness" was stated with reference to those who are without consciousness (*acittaka*);
for it is not the case that for one who is definitively with consciousness, the term "in the case of being with consciousness" applies.

There is a purpose for this qualification. Furthermore, in the phrase "on the side of one with a conscious mind" (*sacittakapakkhe*), it should be understood as referring to the state of mind that recognizes the transgression of the physical basis (*vatthu*), not the state of mind that recognizes the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*).

For if even a mind that recognizes the formal rule—thinking "it is not permitted"—were to have an unwholesome state of mind regarding the side of one with a conscious mind in respect to a particular training rule, then one would have to say that even such a case constitutes a worldly offense (*lokavajja*).

Otherwise, all training rules (sikkhāpada) prohibited by convention (paṇṇattivajja) would also become offenses prohibited by nature (lokavajja), because even for those prohibited by convention, an unwholesome state of mind (akusalacitta) necessarily arises when one transgresses them, knowing that "it is not permitted.
For indeed, no wholesome state of mind (kusalacitta) arises in one who tramples [the rule] while knowing it is the Blessed One’s command;
rather, due to disrespect, only a mind of aversion (paṭighacitta) arises.

Furthermore, from the statement here, “In the case of one with consciousness, the mind is exclusively unwholesome,” it is understood that there is no such fixed rule as “in the case of one without consciousness,
the mind is exclusively unwholesome” by way of not knowing the physical basis (vatthu) while without consciousness.
For if, even in the case of one without consciousness, the mind were to be exclusively unwholesome, then the qualification “in the case of one with consciousness” would be purposeless.

It may be so. If it were stated merely that "whatever mind is unwholesome is a worldly transgression," then because an offense would arise even without an unwholesome mind for a person drinking liquor while unaware of its nature as such,
or for nuns applying perfumes, pigments, and the like while unaware of their nature as such,

one must set aside the training rule regarding intentional (sacittaka) acts— which is exclusively unwholesome— and [distinguish] the training rules regarding unintentional (acittaka) acts, such as drinking liquor.

In order to include those [cases] as well—so that there would be no lack of worldly transgression—it is said: "That for which, on the side of having consciousness, the mind is exclusively unwholesome, that is a worldly transgression.
For this very reason, it is stated in both the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*:
"For one who lies down in that very place thinking, 'I will kill this being,' and kills another [being] because of the commonality of life..."
"Just as there is the offense of taking life when one kills with the perception that it is a living being, so too, for one drinking another kind of intoxicant while thinking,
'I shall drink this intoxicant,' unwholesome karma certainly occurs because of the presence of the common characteristic of intoxicants. However,

just as there is no taking of life for one who kills a snake with the perception that it is a stick, so too there is no unwholesome karma for one who drinks an intoxicant with the perception that it is coconut water."
However, some say: "For a novice monk who drinks liquor without knowing it, there is no *pārājika* offense, though there is unwholesome karma (*akusala*).
This is merely their own opinion. [The correct view is: "Even for a bhikkhu who drinks intoxicants starting from the seed without knowing them, there is a *pācittiya* offense;
whereas a novice monk who drinks knowing them incurs a breach of virtue (*sīlabheda*), not one who drinks without knowing."
For this much alone is stated in the commentary: "But it is unwholesome," whereas it is not stated that [the drinking] does not occur. Others further say:

"Even for a stream-enterer who drinks without knowing, liquor does not enter his mouth, because it can only be drunk with a volitional state of mind that has reached the level of a course of action (kamma-patha).
That too is not correct. It is like the case of the Bodhisatta’s mother’s virtue while the Bodhisatta was in her womb.

Indeed, this too should be understood as established by the very nature of things (*dhammatā*) for noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*). For that very reason, it is said in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* on the *Kūṭadantasutta*:
"Even in another existence, a noble disciple does not kill a living being nor drink liquor even for the sake of his life.
Even if they were to mix liquor with milk and put it into his mouth, only the milk would enter, not the liquor. How is this so?"
"Just as, when water mixed with milk is present for cranes, only the milk enters [their mouths] and not the water—is this established by reason (*yonisiddha*)?

This too should be understood as established by the nature of things (*dhammatāsiddha*). If this is so, then in the commentary on the training rule regarding the drinking of intoxicants, it says: "And here, the state of being without intention (*acittakatā*) should be understood as resulting from the lack of knowledge of the substance."
"Why was it said, 'It is a worldly offense because it must be committed with an unwholesome state of mind'? This is not a fault.
For this is the intended meaning here: in the case of those involving the mind, it is a worldly offense because it must be committed with an unwholesome mind.

It is precisely for this reason that, even regarding other worldly offenses among the training rules that do not involve the mind, only the presence of an unwholesome mind is mentioned, and not the involvement of the mind itself.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*:
“The Giraggasamajja, the Cittāgāra, the Saṅghāṇi, female ornaments, scents and cosmetics, scented sesame paste,
and the rubbing and massaging by bhikkhunīs and others— these ten training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are unintentional, offenses against the world, and unwholesome states of mind.”
The intended meaning here is as follows: they are "without consciousness" (*acittaka*) because they can be committed even without consciousness;
however, when consciousness is present, they are "worldly offenses" (*lokavajja*) and "unwholesome consciousnesses" (*akusalacitta*) because they can only be committed with an unwholesome mind.

Therefore, the three training rules concerning drinking liquor, gambling, and going to the battlefield found in the *Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga*, and those concerning mountain-top festivals and so forth found in the *Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga*—

It should be understood that the qualification "in the case of the *sacittaka* [offenses]" has been made for the purpose of showing that these thirteen training rules (*sikkhāpada*) involving no mental state (*acittaka*) are offenses by worldly convention (*lokavajja*).
However, since in the case of an offense by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), when there is a mind that does not recognize the transgression of the objective basis (*vatthu*),
the mind in the *sacittaka* category may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, therefore, in its case, in the *sacittaka* category—
"There is no fixed rule that the mind is exclusively unwholesome"; thus it is said that the remainder [of the factors] are "excepted by the formal precepts" (*paṇṇattivajja*).
"They obstruct" means they obstruct transgression. "They close the door" means they close the door to the stain of transgression.
"Cutting off the stream" means cutting off the stream of successive transgressions. Alternatively, "they obstruct" [means...]
“Blocking the stain of non-offense” means blocking the door to the stain of non-offense.
“Cutting off the stream” means cutting off the stream of non-offense; what is meant is that one is actually committing an offense.

But is it not the case that when a supplementary rule (anupaññatti) arises regarding a worldly offense (lokavajja), it arises as something that makes [the discipline] lax? Therefore, regarding a worldly offense—
Regarding the statement, "A supplementary rule (anupaññatti), when arising... pe ... arises making [the offense] more grave," why was this said? He replied:

"Except for overestimation (adhimāna) and except for dreaming," and so forth. For this supplementary rule, "except for overestimation," the reason given is "because there is no transgression" (vītikkamābhāvā);
for "except for dreaming," the reason is "because it is a matter of common knowledge" (abbohārikattā).
The reason has been stated. Therein, "due to the absence of transgression" means due to the absence of transgressions such as being "one who desires evil" or "one overcome by desire.

For regarding superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), one becomes subject to a defeat (*pārājika*) when speaking falsely with the intention of deceiving, according to the statement: "One who desires evil, overcome by desire, claims to possess a superhuman state. However, this [person] perceives himself as having attained [the state] through overestimation (*adhimāna*).

Having offered the oblation, he speaks out; he does not wish to transgress the training rule. Therefore, this supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*), "except in the case of overestimation," arose and became non-offensive because there was no transgression. Regarding "being indeterminate" (*abbhohārikattā*):
it is because even though the volition exists in a dream, and there is a desire to transgress, it is indeterminate. For although in a dream there is the volition of taking pleasure in emission—
It exists; sometimes there is even an effort, yet because it is overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, that consciousness is not reckoned [as an offense].
Because the consciousness is not reckoned, the volition that would lead to the performance of the effort is also not reckoned.
For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "There is this volition, monks, but it is not reckoned. Therefore...
“Except in a dream”: this is a subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) which, because it is not subject to conventional usage (*abbhohārikattā*), results in there being no offense.
Regarding “when no transgression has been committed,” this refers to cases such as “fearing wrongdoing, they did not eat,” where no actual transgression has taken place.

“They make it loose” means: having first released the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) that was bound in a general sense, they act so as to cause there to be no offense within their own respective domains.
They are making it loose. "Giving the door" means giving the door in a way that constitutes no offense. For this very reason, it says:

"Even by doing so repeatedly, one is creating non-offense. But is it not the case that in the Sañcaritta-sikkhāpada, when the supplementary rule (anupaññatti) stating "even for a single moment" arises, it gives rise to an offense?
So why is it said here that "it arises as one who is creating non-offense"?

He said, "At the very least, even for that moment," and so forth. Because it was formulated in the case of the monk Udāyin’s falling into the offense of matchmaking for that very moment, it is stated, "when the transgression has been committed.
It follows the same category as the original formulation; thus, it is included within the primary rule itself.
The commentary on the discussion of the monkey incident is finished.
The Section on Recitation:
Commentary on the Case of the Vajjiputtakas. 43.
Because their residence is Vesālī, they are called "Vesālikas"; thus he says, "those who dwell in Vesālī. They are those dwelling in the country of the Vajjis.
He says, “Vajjins, sons of the Vajjis, Vajjiputtakas,” meaning “sons of the clans in Vesālī in the Vajjī country.
“Calamity for kinsmen” (ñātīnaṃ byasanaṃ) means the destruction of kinsmen. That destruction of kinsmen occurs due to causes such as royal punishment;
therefore he says, “by way of royal punishment, disease, death, and separation. “Calamity for wealth” (bhogabyasanaṃ) means the destruction of wealth.
And because there is destruction by royal punishment and the like of those objects of enjoyment and use, such as gold, bullion, female slaves, male slaves, and so forth, he said:
"This same method applies to the second phrase as well. "We do not revile the Buddha" means we do not revile the Buddha by saying things such as "the Buddha is not omniscient.
"We do not revile the Dhamma" means we do not revile the Dhamma by saying things such as "the Dhamma does not lead to liberation."
"Not censuring the Saṅgha" means we do not criticize the Saṅgha by saying, "The Saṅgha has practiced wrongly," and so forth. Regarding "among the thirty-eight objects":

since the two—namely, the light-kasiṇa and the space-kasiṇa—are not included among the forty meditation subjects listed in the Canon (consisting of the ten kasiṇas, ten foulness subjects, ten recollections, four divine abidings, four immaterial states, the analysis of the four elements, and the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment), [they are added here].

This is stated having set aside [certain factors] and taken the remainder. "Wholesome states analyzed" refers to the sublime wholesome states, such as the first jhāna and so forth, together with access concentration, which are analyzed in this way: "In this object, this arises.
"Those very same states" refers to those very wholesome states. The middle watch of the night is for the purpose of dispelling the fatigue of sleep for the bhikkhus.

He said, "The first watch and the last watch," meaning that it was not already included. Awakening—that is, the knowledge of the path of arahantship—is called *bodhi* because one awakens to and penetrates the Truths (*sacca*).
Because they are on the side of that [awakening] by way of being its benefactors, they are called *bodhipakkhiya*. Thus he said:
"Of those that exist on the side of awakening, that is, of those that are benefactors of the knowledge of the path of arahantship. These are the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) are: the four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and the noble eightfold path (*ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo*).

The phrase "having abandoned the impediment of household life and the impediment of dwelling" is stated because the severance of these two specific impediments is extremely difficult to accomplish. "Appropriately engaged" (*yuttapayuttā*) means properly engaged.

They "lie down" (āsayanti) upon their underlying intention (*adhyāśaya*). By permitting the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of those Vajjiputtakas who had practiced sexual intercourse while remaining in the state of a monk without having renounced the training, the Blessed One was, as it were, overturning the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) thus prescribed: "He is one who has committed a defeat (*pārājika*);
he is not in communion. Therefore it was said: "If indeed the Blessed One... [and so on]... were to overturn what has been prescribed."

However, because it is stated, “But whichever monk...,” one who permits full ordination for someone who has already renounced the training and engaged in sexual intercourse does not indeed abolish [the offense].
For he does not engage in it while being a monk. Because of the statement, “When he has returned, he should not be ordained,” the status of a novice (sāmaṇera) is permitted;
thus he says, “But standing on the level of a novice,” and so forth. The supreme goal (uttamattha).
[It is] either Arahantship or Nibbāna itself.
The commentary on the account of the Vajjiputtakas is finished.
Commentary on the Fourfold Discourse on the Vinaya.
45. "Having extracted" means having extracted from the teaching (sāsana). For it is said: "O Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should not be interrogated.
With which five? He does not know the Sutta; he does not know what is in accordance with the Sutta," and so forth.

Having thus extracted the Sutta and what is in accordance with the Sutta from the teaching of the Higher Doctrine (pariyatti), they proclaimed: "In this way, there is no offense; such is the learning of our teachers."
In the case of the passage beginning with "He grasps by means of inquiry," they extracted and proclaimed the Teacher's word from the scriptural tradition (*pariyatti-sāsana*).

In the case of the Bhārukacchaka episode, where it says, "The Venerable Upāli said: 'Friends, there is no offense in the case of a dream,'" they extracted and proclaimed their own opinion (*attanomati*) from that very same scriptural tradition.
For it was by virtue of that personal opinion that the Elder attained the position of being foremost (*etadagga-ṭṭhāna*).
“Vuttaṃ” means spoken by the Elder Nāgasena. A “pada” (word) is that by which a meaning is reached;

an “āhaccapada” (direct word) is a word spoken by the Blessed One specifically, having touched upon the source of the articulation of sounds such as the throat—it is the very speech of the Blessed One himself.
Therefore he said: “By ‘āhaccapada,’ a Sutta is intended. [As for the passage: “Monks, whatever—without making a distinction such as ‘this is allowable’ or ‘this is not allowable’—”

"The general characteristic stated in such passages as, 'This was not prohibited by me with the thought, "this is not allowable"; yet if it conforms to what is unallowable and opposes what is allowable, that is not allowable for you,' is intended here by the term 'flavour' (rasa). Thus he said: "Flavour is conformity with the Suttas.
This refers to the tradition of the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā-tanti) brought down through the succession of teachers beginning from the compilers of the Dhamma (Dhammasaṅgāhaka).
Here, it is intended in the sense of "the lineage of teachers" (ācariyavaṃsa); thus he says, "The lineage of teachers means the teaching of the teachers.
Since the determination of the Vinaya is the subject here, he states—showing a sutta appropriate to that—"A sutta is the Pāḷi in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.
"Great authorities" (mahāpadesā) means great opportunities; they are the great bases for the establishment of the Vinaya.
The Vinaya established upon these [authorities] is adjudicated without doubt. Alternatively, "great authorities" (*mahāpadesā*) refers to great reasons;
what is meant is that they are the great reasons for the adjudication of the Vinaya. However, they say: "In terms of meaning, the very Pāḷi spoken by means of 'Bhikkhus, whatever...
and so forth, together with its underlying intention (*sādhippāyā*), constitutes the great authorities. For this very reason, he said: "Those which were spoken thus by the Blessed One," and so on.
These Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*) are recorded in the *Khandhaka*; therefore, their detailed exposition will be clarified in that very place and is not discussed here.

Furthermore, although the various incidental teachings delivered by the Blessed One in this or that context constitute the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary), it was nevertheless compiled by the Reciters of the Dhamma (*dhammasaṅgāhaka*) only after they had first recited the Three Piṭakas, in accordance with the explanation of their meaning.
Because it has been set down as a path of recitation, it is called the "Teacher’s Word" (*ācariyavāda*), in the sense that the teachers speak and comment upon the Canon by means of it.
Therefore he said: "The Teacher’s Word is... the lineage of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathātantī*).

Furthermore, the very path of discourse consisting of the commentary on the meaning of the Buddha’s word, which was established during the three councils, was brought [to Ceylon] by the Elder Mahāmahinda.
It was brought to Tambapaṇṇidīpa and subsequently established in the Sihaḷa language by the Great Elders of Tambapaṇṇi for the purpose of avoiding the confusion of the tenets of other schools.
Although one’s own opinion is formulated only after being compared with the Suttas and other authorities, nevertheless, it is not specifically pointed out within the Suttas and so forth;
thus he says, "setting aside the Suttas, the Suttas’ conformity, and the teachers' doctrines. Regarding the phrase *anubuddhiyā*:
"By means of a comprehension that follows the suttas and so forth" means by grasping the method (naya) obtainable from the suttas and other sources.
Having first shown his own opinion in general terms with the words "Furthermore," he now speaks beginning with "Moreover" in order to demonstrate that very same opinion in detail.
Now, showing the manner in which one should proceed therein, he says: "But by one who, having adopted that personal opinion, explains [it]," and so forth.
"By the meaning" means by the meaning perceived by oneself. "Should be brought down into the teacher’s doctrine" means it should be introduced into the teacher’s doctrine by means of knowledge.
"Extremely weak" refers to the fact that it is merely the individual's own inspired intuition (*paṭibhāna*).
Showing that there may sometimes be a failure to reconcile [the text] with the Sutta according to the teacher’s doctrine due to a careless reading, he says: "That should not be accepted."
He said: "The teacher's statement... [etc. ...must be accepted as equal.
By saying "it must be accepted as equal," he shows that meanings should be extracted from the great authorities (mahāpadesa) in such a way that they accord with the Sutta.

Although a teaching in conformity with the Sutta (suttānuloma) is but a portion of the Sutta, it is spoken with definitive authority—delimiting what is allowable and what is not allowable—just like the Sutta itself.
He said, "There is nothing [to contradict it]," because "the Sutta itself is more authoritative than that which conforms to the Sutta.
"Irreversible" means unopposable. "Similar to the Saṅgha of those who performed the recitation" means similar to the Saṅgha of the compilers because of its authority.
By the phrase "similar to the time when the Buddhas were present," it is meant that since it was spoken by the Buddhas themselves, it is similar to the time when a Buddha is actually living.

For when a sutta is rejected, it is the Buddha himself who is rejected. "The proponent of his own position takes up a sutta and speaks"—this means the proponent of his own position expresses himself by taking up a sutta from his own tradition.
"The opponent speaks in conformity with a sutta"—this means one who follows another Nikāya speaks by taking up what is in conformity with a sutta within their own Nikāya.
"Without casting contempt or censure"—that is, without saying, "What is the use of this? and thus expressing contempt.
Or, without censuring [the opponent] by saying, "What is this fool saying?", one should apply the meaning as follows:

"In accordance with the Suttas" means that what has been stated by the opponent accords with the Suttas in another Nikāya. "It should be brought down into one's own Suttas" means it should be verified against the Suttas of one's own school.

"One must stand firm within the Suttas themselves" means one must remain steadfast within one's own Suttas. The application of the meaning should be made in the same way for the remaining sections. This is [the method].

The proponent of our own school (*sakavādī*). "The other" (*paro*) refers to one who propounds a different Nikāya; the same applies to the remaining cases. But was it not stated above that "in accordance with the Suttas, the Sutta itself is more authoritative"?

Why, then, is it said here that "the Sutta must be brought into conformity with the Sutta," and so forth? There is no contradiction here. [For] "in accordance with the Suttas, the Sutta itself... [is what was meant].

For this statement, "more powerful," was spoken specifically with reference to that very same sutta. For therein, referring only to the sutta and so forth included within one's own opinion, it is said:
"One's own opinion is the weakest; the teacher’s doctrine is more powerful than one's own opinion;
that which accords with the sutta is more powerful than the teacher’s doctrine; and the sutta itself is more powerful than that which accords with the sutta."

This has been stated. However, here, with reference to a sutta brought forward by an opponent from another Nikāya, it is said: "A sutta should be brought down into conformity with a sutta," and so forth.

Therefore, the method explained here is this: having brought down the sutta and other texts brought forward by an opponent into one's own conformity with the sutta, the teachers' tradition, and one's own reflection, only that which is consistent should be accepted, while the other should not be accepted. This is the principle stated here.
There is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
"External suttas" refers to the suttas of those dwelling in the Mahāsaṅghika school, such as the *Guḷha-vessantara* and others, which were not included in the three councils (*saṅgīti*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Vedalla, etc.," it should be understood that the *Guḷha-ummagga* and other such texts are included; the remainder refers to the "censurable suttas."

"It should not be accepted; one should simply abide by one's own judgment"—by this, he shows that even when a sutta is brought from another school, one's own judgment within one's own school is indeed more authoritative.

By stating, "The proponent speaks having taken up a sutta, and the opponent likewise [speaks] having taken up a sutta," and so forth, the sequence is not stated according to those of the same class; rather, it is the application of a sutta to a sutta itself.
It does not appear as if it were separate, and it can be connected in the very manner already stated.

Now, showing the procedure to be followed when a dispute arises between one’s own school (sakavādin) and an opponent (paravādin) concerning what is allowable (kappiya) and what is unallowable (akappiya), etc., he said:
“But if this person, taking it to be allowable, speaks,” and so forth. In that regard, [it concerns] the Sutta and that which is in conformity with the Sutta (suttānuloma).
"And it should be brought down" means that the proponent himself should bring it down into his own suttas and into what is in conformity with the suttas.
"The other finds no reason" means that the opponent does not obtain a reason.
"He shows much reason and determination from the suttas" means that the opponent brings forward and demonstrates much reason and determination from his own suttas. "Excellent! [is said].

By the statement, "Having accepted it, one must remain in what is improper," the proponent of our own side (sakavādī), who does not find such a sutta or similar authority within his own school, asserts that one must remain according to the words of the opponent (paravādī).

"The shadow of a reason for both is seen" means that a semblance of a reason—serving as a proof for the status of being either allowable (kappiya) or unallowable (akappiya)—is seen for both the proponent of our own side and the opponent. If for both...
The shadow of the cause is seen; why, then, did he say, "One must stand only in what is allowable"?
He said, "Having reached the Vinaya," and so forth. To make the meaning already stated even clearer, he said, "By resorting to the investigation of what is allowable and what is unallowable.

Regarding the words "it should be obstructed" and so on, when there is a state of allowability or unallowability that is difficult to discern in a legal decision, the grasping [of it] as allowable— [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence.]
It must be restrained; the grasping of what is unallowable (*akappiya*) must be made firm. The stream of grasping allowable things that continues from one instance to another must be cut off;
the meaning is that it must remain precisely in the state of unallowability, which is characterized by its gravity.
"By many reasons for determining the Suttas" means by many Suttas themselves and by the reasons for determination derived therefrom.
