"And: 'One's own taking is not to be relinquished' means that the proponent of one's own position (sakavādin) must not relinquish his own taking [of the position] as being unallowable (akappiya).

Now, concluding the very point just stated, he says 'Evaṃ' and so forth. Therein, 'yo' (whoever) refers to anyone among the proponents of one's own position or the proponents of the opposing position.
However, some say: 'Only whoever among the proponents of one's own position is intended here. If that were the case, then..."

In all such instances as "having taken it up as allowable, he speaks," both [parties] would be proponents of their own position (sakavādin), because terms such as "thus" (evaṃ) are stated by way of a conclusion for what was already explained above; therefore, that [interpretation] should not be accepted.

Regarding the phrase "it obtains an additional reason" (atirekakāraṇaṃ labhati): here, among the Suttas and so forth, each preceding one is called an "additional reason" (atirekakāraṇa). As for that which...
Or, when one obtains a greater number of reasons among the four—such as the discourses (sutta) and so forth—one is said to obtain "excessive reasons" (atirekakāraṇa).
It is "well-functioning" (suppavatti) because its occurrence is excellent, or it is well-functioning by nature. Therefore he said:
"Suppavattī means 'well-occurred'. That which has emerged through speech is "vācuggata"; it is well-grasped by means of speech.
This has been stated. The explanation of the term “from the Sutta” is “from the Pāḷi.

And here, since it is said that “Sutta means the entire Vinaya Piṭaka,” one should understand that the “Pāḷi” referred to as the source of meaning is a different [textual] Pāḷi that illuminates its meaning.
The explanation of the term “from the Anubyañjana” is “from the Paripucchā and from the Aṭṭhakathā. This is because the meaning is clarified by following the Pāḷi through its phrasing (byañjana).
"Anubyañjana" refers to both the "paripucchā" (inquiry) and the "aṭṭhakathā" (commentary), as it is said that they are from the point of view of elucidation.
Here, since the *aṭṭhakathā* is mentioned separately, "paripucchā" is stated to mean the "Theravāda" (the doctrine of the Elders).

"Saṅgharājī" is a designation for the quarrel that occurred prior to a schism in the Saṅgha. "Kukkuccako" means one who, by way of seeing danger even in the slightest faults, possesses "kukkucca" (remorse or scrupulousness).
"Bringing it forth. "Without contradicting that" means without altering the text (pāḷi).
"Not overstepping" means not transgressing. "Snorting" means snorting without seeing the meaning. "Quivering" means trembling.
"Unable to settle" means unable to remain established in a single meaning. Therefore he said: "Whatever is spoken by another, that..."
“He allows it. “He adopts the opponent’s argument” means: when an opponent says, “In sugarcane, the pulp is for life-long use;
the juice is for seven days; and apart from those two, there is no such thing as sugarcane itself; therefore, even sugarcane is permitted at the wrong time,” he adopts that view as well.
“A single hair” is said with reference to grey hair. “In whom” means in which person.
“Exhaustion” (*parikkhaya*) and “termination” (*pariyādāna*) are one in meaning.
Regarding the phrase “the succession of teachers has been well-learned by him”: here, “succession of teachers” (*ācariyaparamparā*) refers to the lineage of the teachers’ analytical interpretations.
For this very reason, he will say: “Just as the teacher and the teacher’s teacher [have transmitted] both the text (*pāḷi*) and the interrogation (*paripucchā*).”
“They say so; it is fitting to know it thus. Regarding the connection between what precedes and what follows:

this means that one understands according to the sequence of what comes before and after, thinking, “This is the preceding statement, this is the subsequent statement, and this is the connection. Regarding the lineage of teachers (*ācariyaparamparā*): this is a synonym for the “Theravāda-division” (*theravādaṅga*);
the meaning is the succession of elders (*therapaṭipāṭi*). “Two or three rounds” (*dve tayo parivaṭṭā*) means two or three successions.
"By these three characteristics" refers to the three characteristics mentioned below, beginning with "The Sutta is well-received by him.
Here, by the first characteristic, the state of the Vinaya having been thoroughly mastered is stated;
by the second, its immovability and firm establishment once mastered are stated; and by the third, that which [is found] in the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā...
And since that [ability] does not exist, it is stated as the capacity to determine even by means of the teacher’s word.
"When the matter has been brought forward" means when the matter—consisting of either an accusation or a transgression—has been brought into the midst of the Saṅgha; the meaning is "having entered.
Clarifying exactly what was said, he states: "when what is to be said has been spoken by both the accuser and the accused. However, some...
They connect it thus: "When the matter has been brought forward by the accuser and stated by the accused. Others, however, connect it as:
"When it has been stated by both the accuser and the accused, and must be spoken by the Vinaya-expert.
But it should be understood that this very connection—namely, "when it has been stated by both the accuser and the accused, and must be spoken"—is more excellent. The matter (*vatthu*).
“Should be examined” means that the basis (*vatthu*) for each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*) should be examined. For this [rule]—“If anyone should come with grass or leaves... [etc.

...there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)”—was laid down in connection with the basis of the training rule concerning requesting from one who is not related regarding the forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Because the offenses of a grave transgression (*thullaccaya*) and of improper speech (*dubbhāsita*) do not appear in the summary table (*mātikā*), [the text says]: “Of the five... [and so forth].

"Any one of the offenses," it is said. Regarding "any one offense," this is stated with reference to the *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) that has been handed down in such passages as: "If it is the right time, but one perceives it as the wrong time, there is an offense of wrongdoing; if it is the right time, but one is uncertain, there is an offense of wrongdoing.
"In between the training rules" means within each individual training rule, including the specific case of its application (*vinītavatthu*) therein.
"Sukhumā" (subtle) is said because the mind—which is difficult to discern even for oneself and which changes rapidly—possesses a swift rate of change.
Therefore, it is said: "lightness of mind. Those for whom the mind is light and changes swiftly are "those with light minds" (*cittalahuka*). "Those" refers to those who transgress.
"Based on that" (*taṃvatthuka*) means that those transgressions of taking what is not given and of sexual misconduct have that as their basis or foundation.
"Based on that" (*taṃvatthukaṃ*) means having that as its cause. "Having purified the virtues" means:
without attending to the basis upon which the remorse arose, one purifies the remaining virtues. It is said, "First, attend to the thirty-two aspects," because they are evident and easy to handle.
However, for one who has already practiced another meditation subject, one should attend to that very same one.
It should be done. "It joins with the meditation subject" means that it joins with the mind for a long time as its object, without showing any gaps in between.
"The formations appear clearly" means that if one is a practitioner of insight (vipassanā), the formations appear clearly to him.
If he should have committed an offense involving defeat (pārājika), [the formations would not appear clearly].
Even though he has no desire to remember it, because it presents itself again and again by way of being a basis for remorse, he does not find one-pointedness of mind.
Therefore it is said: “He does not apply himself to the meditation subject,” and so forth.
“He knows by himself” means he knows by his own self; this is an instrumental case used in the sense of identity, meaning that the self knows. And another...
"Deities know" means that deities other than the protective deities (*ārakkhadevatā*), who are knowers of the minds of others, also know.
The commentary on the fourfold discussion of the Vinaya and the commentary on the characteristics and so forth of one who holds the Vinaya are concluded.
Commentary on the Analysis of the Terms for a Bhikkhu:
"Tasmā" means because he spoke only the word "yo" (who), which indicates a person without restriction, having removed the word "pana.
"Ettha" means in this word "yo. Since the word "pana" is merely a particle, [the author] explains the meaning of the word "yo" itself.
"‘Whoever’ means it is said: ‘anyone whatsoever. “‘Whoever indeed’ means that whether it be this person or that person, it is called ‘whoever.
“‘Devoted to the duty of dwelling’ means devoted to the duty of insight (*vipassanā*). “‘In the precepts’ means in the natural [precepts].
“‘He begs’ means he asks. “‘Whether obtaining or not obtaining’ means whoever begs, seeks, or searches for alms.”
Whether he obtains it or not, he is nevertheless called a *bhikkhu* because he begs; this is the intended meaning here. "By means of noble begging" refers to the noble begging described as:
"The Noble Ones stand having designated [the gift] for themselves; this is the begging of the Noble Ones," and not to the begging that proceeds with the words "Give!
Give! like that of the wretched, the travelers, the mendicants, or the supplicants. "The practice of begging" (*bhikkhācariya*)...
"Living by gleaning" (*uñchācariya*). "Because of having undertaken it" means because of having practiced it. "Food brought in baskets" (*kājabhatta*) means food brought by means of baskets.

"By way of difference in value, touch, and color" means by the abandonment of their previous natural state (*pakati*), such as value and so forth; for here, "difference" (*bheda*) is intended to mean the abandonment of the previous natural state.
"Stain" (*mala*) is that which has the nature of being impossible to wash away or remove; likewise, [the opposite] is that which has the nature of being possible to remove.

*Jallikā*. The etymological explanation (*nibbacana*) "one who wears tattered robes" is given because the term *bhikkhu* is conventionally established (*nirulhatthā*) for one who wears tattered robes.
"Endowed with the proximate cause" (*upanissayasampanna*) means endowed with the proximate cause of having previously given the eight requisites, or at least the bowl and robe.

For whoever [gives] the eight requisites beginning with the robe, or even just the bowl and robe, to a noble one such as a stream-enterer, or even to an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) endowed with virtue...
Having given it, he made this aspiration: "May this gift of requisites be a condition for the state of 'Come, monk' (ehibhikkhu) in the future.

It should be understood that, provided there is success in his spiritual practice (adhikārasampatti), this leads to the acquisition of supernaturally produced (iddhimaya) requisites when he is in the presence of the Buddhas.
"Brahmaghosa" means the supreme sound, or a sound resembling the voice of Brahmā.

"Brahmacariya" refers to both the brahmacariya of the Dispensation (*sāsanabrahmacariya*) and the brahmacariya of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*). It should be construed with the phrase "for the complete ending of suffering.
"Bhaṇḍu" means one who is shaven-headed. "Vāsī" means an axe for cutting tooth-sticks. "Bandhana" means a waist-band.
"Yuttayoga" means one who possesses application to the practice of development; thus, it refers to one who is devoted to the practice of development.
This has been stated. To clarify his perfection in the modes of deportment (iriyāpatha), it is said, "like the Elder Saṭṭhivassika.
One whose teacher for both the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā) is the Buddha alone is called "one who has the Buddha as teacher" (buddhācariyaka).
Since there were no other full ordinations at all during the very first period of the First Enlightenment, he says, "at one time during the First Enlightenment."
“The five bhikkhus of the group-of-five” means there were five bhikkhus of the group-of-five. “Three hundred” means three hundred;
the change in word order was made for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition. “And one elder” is said with reference to the Elder Aṅgulimāla.
“Not mentioned” means not mentioned in the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). “Therein” means in the Vinaya Piṭaka.
While seated in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) at the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana, the Blessed One,
knowing that the Elder Mahākassapa had gone forth specifically for his sake, went out to meet him alone, traveling three gavutas of the road; then,
sitting cross-legged at the foot of the Bahuputta Nigrodha tree, he waited as Mahākassapa approached his presence.

Having displayed the highest degree of humility, and having declared his status as a disciple three times—saying, "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am a disciple. Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am a disciple"—the Elder Mahākassapa stood there.
To illustrate the greatness of that elder’s humility and his own great majesty, [the Buddha spoke] to another who did not know it at all, saying, "I know."
"Kassapa, if a disciple of an outside teacher who has made such a claim were to perform such supreme service with his whole heart and with a confident mind,
his head would fall from his neck like a ripe palm fruit severed at its stalk,
or it would split into seven pieces," [the Blessed One said], showing this by saying: "Whoever, Kassapa, with his whole heart..."

“Kassapa, if one who does not know were to say ‘I know,’ or if one who does not see were to say ‘I see,’ his head would surely split into seven pieces. But I, Kassapa, knowing indeed say ‘I know,’ and seeing indeed say ‘I see.
Having said this, for the purpose of abandoning the intoxication with birth, the intoxication with pride, the intoxication with wealth, and the intoxication with beauty, he gave three exhortations.
While instructing the Elder Mahākassapa, he said, "Therefore, Kassapa, in this regard...
and so forth. Therein, "therefore, in this regard" (*tasmātiha*) means simply "therefore" (*tasmā*);

the sense is: because I say "I know" only when I actually know, and I say "I see" only when I actually see, therefore [it is so]. The syllables *ti* and *ha* are particles. Alternatively, *iha* means "in this."

In the *sāsana*, the letter *ta* has come [into the text] by way of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). "Thus it should be trained in" means it should be trained in the manner that is now being stated.
"Intense" (*tibba*) means thick or great. "And moral shame and moral dread" (*hirī ca ottappañca*) refers to shame and dread.
"It will be present" (*paccupaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati*) means it will be established even prior to approaching [the object]. For when that is so:
In their presence, a sense of reverence and deference is established.
For when one approaches the elders and others having established shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*), the elders and others likewise approach him with shame and dread of blame;

this is the benefit herein. "Associated with the wholesome" (*kusalūpasaṃhita*) means dependent on the wholesome; the meaning is that it is dependent on blameless phenomena (*anavajjadhamma*). *Aṭṭhiṃ*...
"Having made [it] a bone" means having made oneself a bone by means of that Dhamma, or having made that Dhamma a bone [thinking], "This is my Dhamma.

"Having attended to it" means having established it in the mind. "Having applied the whole mind" means having applied it with a mind of total attention, not allowing the mind to go even slightly outward. "With ear pricked up" means...
"With ear applied" means with the ear directed toward the Dhamma. "In this way you should train yourself":
having applied both the stream of knowledge and the stream of confidence, thinking "I shall listen attentively to the Dhamma taught by me," in this way you should train yourself.

"And may mindfulness directed to the body be accompanied by pleasure" means that it is associated with pleasure by way of the first jhāna, both in regard to the foul (aśubha) and in breath-meditation (ānāpāna).
Mindfulness directed to the body. Furthermore, this threefold instruction was itself the Elder’s going-forth and his full admission.
The fine-material-sphere jhāna having a kasiṇa as its object is "perception of form. Here, jhāna is expressed by way of its factor of perception;
and that very jhāna is called "perception of the bloated" because its counterpart object is the bloated corpse. That novice Sōpāka was [instructed] by the Blessed One...

When asked, he replied: "These two are identical in substance as states belonging to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*); only the phrasing is different. "One whose mind is won" (*āraddhacitta*) means one whose mind has been gratified.
The full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the acceptance of the heavy rules (*garudhamma*) and so forth will be explained in detail later by himself.
Regarding the phrase "virtuous worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) and so forth": here, because various types of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and other such views have not yet been destroyed...

One who generates [defilements], or one who has been generated by them, is a *puthujjana*; and since he is both "excellent" (*kalyāṇa*) and a *puthujjana*, he is an "excellent *puthujjana*" (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*).
Those for whom he is the first—namely, the stream-enterers and so forth—are the "excellent *puthujjana*s and others. By the inclusion of the term "excellent" here, the blind *puthujjana* is excluded.
For there are two kinds of *puthujjanas*: the blind *puthujjana* and the excellent *puthujjana*. Indeed, this has been said:
“Two types of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
one is a blind worldling, and the other is a noble worldling.
This should be connected with “by auspicious wisdom” and “by auspicious liberation. Regarding the phrase beginning with “by virtue,” “virtue” (sīla) refers to the fourfold purification of virtue.
"Concentration" refers to the eight attainments that serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*).

"Wisdom" refers to mundane and supramundane knowledge. "Liberation" refers to the liberation of the noble fruit (*ariyaphala*). "Knowledge and vision of liberation" refers to the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).

The application [of these terms] here should be understood according to what is possible: for a wholesome worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*), only the three beginning with virtue (*sīla*) are possible; whereas for the noble ones (*ariya*), [all five are possible].

However, all [virtues] beginning with morality (*sīla*) are included. Since it is said that even "the core monk" (*sāro bhikkhu*) refers to noble ordinary persons (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) and others, he says, "by those very things—the core of morality, etc.

Alternatively, from the non-figurative standpoint, only one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) is called a "core monk"; thus he says, "or because of the absence of the 'sapwood' of defilements," and so forth.
This also applies to the noble ordinary person who fulfills the practice in accordance with the truth, is perfected in morality, and guards the doors of the sense faculties.

One who dwells knowing the proper measure in food, devoted to the practice of wakefulness, and devoted to the practice of developing the qualities conducive to enlightenment during the first and last watches of the night, thinking, "Today or tomorrow I shall attain one of the fruits of recluseship"—he too is called a trainee (*sekha*) because he trains;
thus it was said [in the commentary], "together with the virtuous worldling. The seven noble ones (*ariya*) are as follows:

The four who stand on the path and the first three who stand in the fruition—these seven are noble ones (*ariya*). The three trainings are the three trainings beginning with higher virtue (*adhisīla*).
One is a trainee (*sekha*) because one is born into the trainings; for a noble person (*ariyapuggala*), being born through noble birth, is born into the trainings, not into a [biological] womb.
Or, one is a trainee because it is their nature to train; or, in a discourse focused on the person, [it refers to] the trainee.
The qualities of the threefold path and fruit, which are not shared by others, are spoken of in the sense of the trainee (sekha).

And as for the term "adept" (asekha), this is a negation where there might be a suspicion of the state of being a trainee; thus, it should be understood that mundane states and nibbāna do not fall under the category of being an adept.
For the trainings—consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom—are purified because they are liberated from their respective opposing defilements.
Because they do not even become objects for the secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*), it is appropriate to call them "trainings" (*sikkhā*);

they exist in all eight paths and fruits. Therefore, just as one who possesses the four paths and the three lower fruits is [a trainee], so too one who possesses the fruit of Arahantship is born into those trainings.

Consequently, if that Arahant who possesses them were to have the status of a trainee (*sekhatta*) like the others, the expression "this belongs to a trainee" (*sekhass' ayam*) would apply to him just as it does to the others.

One might say that a person "possesses training" (*sikkhā*) as their virtue (*sīla*), and thus should be called a "trainee" (*sekha*); it is for the purpose of excluding such a person that the negation of the aforementioned state of being a trainee is made by the term "non-trainee" (*asekha*).
The training that proceeds from the fruits of Arhatship does not perform the function of training because the duties of training have been fully completed;
it proceeds solely by way of being the fruit of training. Therefore, those [fruits] do not deserve the designation "training."
Nor does one who possesses that [fruit] deserve to be called by the term "learner" (sekha), nor is he of a nature to train, nor is he "born into the trainings.

However, in the case of the lower fruits, the trainings do perform the function of training because they serve as the decisive support (upanissaya) for the insight and so forth pertaining to the path of the once-returner; thus, they deserve the designation "trainings," and those who possess them deserve the designation "learners" and are of a nature to train.
They deserve to be called "born in the trainings" because it is shown that those whose training is not yet completed are "trainers" (*sekha*) by the definition "they train, thus they are trainers.
By the phrase "he does not train, thus he is beyond-training" (*asekha*), one who has completed the training is shown, not one who is devoid of training.
Thus it was said: "Having transcended the states of a trainer... one whose taints are destroyed is called 'beyond-training'. This refers to one whose training has reached its full development.

Or, regarding the term "one beyond training" (*asekha*): in this sense, does it mean that for some noble one (*ariya*) established in the very qualities of those in training (*sekhadhamma*), there is the attainment of the state of being beyond training—that is, because the factors of the path to Arhatship have reached growth, they are designated as "in training" according to the aforementioned meanings, and thus the state of being beyond training is attained by one who possesses them while standing on the supreme path? No;
because that designation is applied to those similar to them. [This is] from the *Arahattamagga*.
Indeed, with the exception of the fruit of arahantship—which lacks differentiation—these [states] perform the function of full understanding and possess the nature of fruition;
therefore, it can be said that those very trainees have attained the state of the Dhamma of the supreme fruit.

Furthermore, since the bliss of fruition is more refined than the bliss of the wholesome due to its greater tranquility, and since these states have reached growth, one who possesses them is called "one beyond training" (asekha).
"In every way" means by the ultimate limit. It is said "to be performed by a group of five" because it pertains to the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*).
A "group of five" (*pañcavagga*) is a collection of five; or, a group consisting of the measure of five is a "group of five.
An act to be performed by such a group is "to be performed by a group of five. "As many bhikkhus as... [is the phrase].

"As many bhikkhus as there are. "Those who have reached the stage for the formal act" means those who are eligible for the act—those who have not committed a *pārājika* offense and have not been suspended.

Since the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā*) is to be performed by a quorum of five, exactly five bhikkhus are "those who have reached the stage for the formal act," because the act is accomplished even with that many;

the others are merely "those entitled to give their consent. Regarding the phrase "by a motion followed by three proclamations" (*ñatticatutthena*): although the motion (*ñatti*) is spoken first, of the three...

However, because there is no difference in meaning or phrasing among the proclamations (*anussāvana*), the motion (*ñatti*)—which differs in both meaning and phrasing—is called "the fourth" in relation to them;
thus it is termed "a formal act consisting of a motion as the fourth" (*ñatticatuttha*). It is for this very reason, in accordance with the phrasing, that the Commentary states:
"by three proclamations and one motion. But according to the sequence of the occurrence of the meanings, it is said: "by one motion and three proclamations."

It should be stated. Regarding the phrase "because it is endowed with the perfection of the subject matter (*vatthu*), the motion (*ñatti*), the proclamation (*anussāvana*), the boundary (*sīmā*), and the assembly (*parisa*)," here "subject matter" refers to the person seeking full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Excluding those under twenty years of age, the final offense (*antimavatthu*) previously committed, and the eleven types of persons incapable of ordination (*abhabbapuggala*) such as eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and others, this is how it should be understood. For these thirteen types of persons, beginning with those under twenty years of age, [are ineligible] for full ordination.

This is not a valid basis (*avatthu*). However, when there is another person seeking full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*) other than these [excluded ones], the formal act of ordination (*upasampadākamma*) is said to be "endowed with the perfection of the basis" (*vatthusampattisampanna*).
First, there are five defects of the motion (*ñattidosā*): the failure to specify the basis, the Saṅgha, the individual, the proclamation (*ñatti*), and the subsequent establishment of the motion.
Among these, the failure to specify the basis is the non-mentioning of the person seeking ordination by name, as in: "This person named so-and-so."
Regarding the term *nāma*: in the phrase “Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs,” to speak thus without mentioning the word “Saṅgha” is called *saṅgha-aparāmasana* (omission of the Saṅgha).
To fail to announce the preceptor by saying “The one seeking full ordination is so-and-so” is called *puggala-aparāmasana* (omission of the person).
To fail to recite the motion (*ñatti*) in its entirety is *ñatti-aparāmasana* (omission of the motion).
Having completed the first formal motion (*kammavācā*) and said, "This is the motion," one then says, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha.

This subsequent proclamation of the motion is called the "establishment of the motion" (*ñatti-ṭṭhapana*). Thus, a motion that is free from these faults is said to be "endowed with the perfection of the motion" (*ñatti-sampatti-sampanna*).
The five defects of the proclamation (*anusāvana*) are: omitting the matter, the Saṅgha, or the individual; omitting the proclamation; and proclaiming at an improper time.

Among these, the omissions regarding the matter and so forth are exactly as described in the case of the motion (*ñatti*). However, among the three proclamations, if there is an omission of any of these at any point, it is indeed an omission;
yet, [if the omission occurs] entirely throughout the entire formal act (*kammavācā*), [it is a more serious defect].
Or, it may be merely the failure to proclaim the motion (*ñatti*) four times.

Alternatively, within the course of the formal act (*kammavācā*), the non-utterance or the faulty utterance of a syllable or a word constitutes what is called "omitting the proclamation" (*sāvanāya hāpana*).

Performing the subsequent proclamations (*anussāvanā*) without first establishing the motion in the proper place for proclamation is called "proclaiming at the wrong time" (*akāle sāvana*). Thus, by these faults—
When the proclamation for the formal act of liberation has been completed, it is called "accomplished by the perfection of the proclamation.
When, however, the formal act is performed within a boundary that has transcended the characteristics of a defective boundary, it is called "accomplished by the perfection of the boundary.
[Furthermore, there is] the non-arrival of as many monks as are entitled to participate in the formal act, and the non-bringing of the consent of those who are entitled to give their consent.

"Protestation in the presence [of those present]"—these are the three defects of an assembly; when an assembly is free from these, what it performs is said to be "endowed with the perfection of the assembly.
The word of the Blessed One, consisting of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) for full ordination (*upasampadā*), is the cause for the performance of the ordination ritual.

The "proper occasion" (*ṭhāna*) refers to that which is appropriate to the situation and, as instructed by the Blessed One, has been performed accordingly—namely, the motion (*ñatti*) and the proclamation (*anussāvana*) as previously described, being complete and without deficiency—and that which is not stated out of order yet is fit for the occasion.

For if it is not performed exactly as the Blessed One has declared it should be performed, it does not constitute a valid cause for the act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*); therefore, such a case is not "fit for the occasion."
Therefore he said, "by means of the most excellent cause and the most excellent teaching of the Teacher.

By this, the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the proclamation (*anussāvana*) should be understood as being stated. By the phrase "by a united Saṅgha," the perfection of the assembly (*parisa*) is indeed stated.

By the phrase "unshakeable" (*akuppa*), it should be understood that the perfections of the matter (*vatthu*) and the boundary (*sīmā*) are stated by way of elimination (*pārisesato*). However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), the characteristic of being unshakeable is...
In order to show [the meaning] by combining them into one, the meaning of the term *akuppena* (unshakeable) is stated as:
"Because it is endowed with the perfection of the subject matter, the proclamation, the boundary, and the assembly, it has reached a state that is not to be shaken and not to be rejected.

However, some say that in this context, "ṭhānāraheṇa" refers to the Teacher’s instruction, such as "one whose hands have been cut off should not be ordained," and so forth, as being the "ṭhāna" (proper ground).
Regarding the phrase “by a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation,” having introduced it here as a relevant digression from this section,
[the author], wishing to show that the definition of a formal act— which has been elaborated upon in all the commentaries— is to be understood exactly where it is found [in the Vinaya],
states “standing at this point,” etc., in order to demonstrate the purpose of not mentioning it here and of mentioning it there.
Among the eight modes of full ordination (*upasampadā*), those ordained by way of the "Come, monk" ordination,
the ordination by going for refuge, the ordination by receiving instruction, and the ordination by answering questions are incapable of transgressing the training rules regarding worldly offenses;
therefore, there are the ordinations by acceptance of the heavy rules (*garudhamma*), by messenger, and by the eightfold verbal formula.

Since these three types of full ordination (*upasampadā*) were prescribed only for bhikkhunīs, it should be understood that one ordained by means of the formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*) is here intended.
For indeed, the "Come, Bhikkhu" (*ehibhikkhu*) ordination was for those in their final existence;
the ordination by going for refuge was for those who were pure; and the ordination by answering questions on the acceptance of exhortation was for Mahākassapa and Soreyya.

Furthermore, they are incapable of committing a *pārājika* or other offenses that are "worldly transgressions" (*lokavajja*); moreover, the acceptance of the heavy rules (*garudhamma*) and so forth were authorized only for bhikkhunīs, and this person is a bhikkhu;
therefore, it should be understood that in this context, only one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) by means of the motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*) is included.
However, regarding the training rules concerning conventional offenses (*paṇṇattivajja*), others as well—such as those ordained by the "Come, monk! (*ehibhikkhu*) formula—are also included.
They do indeed go; for they too incur an offense that is a breach of the formal rules (paṇṇattivajja), such as sleeping together and so forth.

If this is so, why is it stated that even regarding training rules (sikkhāpada) that are breaches of formal rules, one who has been fully ordained (upasampanna) by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma) is intended here as a "monk" (bhikkhu)?
Because he is capable of transgressing all training rules and because [the status] pertains to all times. This refers to those such as the "Come, monk! (ehibhikkhu) ordination and others.
For indeed, not all training rules (sikkhāpada) are subject to transgression, nor are they all of universal application.

Thus, among the eight ways of full ordination (upasampadā), only these three—the ordination by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma), ordination by messenger (dūtena), and ordination by eight verbal declarations (aṭṭhavācika)—are stable (thāvara);
the remaining ones occurred only while the Buddha was still living. And for that very reason, even in the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga, it says: "In this regard, whichever..."

"A bhikkhunī who has been fully ordained by a unanimous dual Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), which is irreversible and fit for the occasion—
this is the bhikkhunī intended in this context. Thus, having included those ordained by means of a messenger and those ordained by means of eight proclamations,
[it refers to] a bhikkhunī who has been fully ordained by a dual Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations.

She was ordained by means of the acceptance of the eight *garudhammas*, not by the ordination through the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*), because that [former] ordination was personal (*pāṭipuggalika*) and was not available at all times. For the ordination by the acceptance of the *garudhammas* was permitted only for Mahāpajāpatī herself and was thus personal;

therefore, she was subject to the transgression of all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) until her ordination by the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations, which is available at all times.
It should be understood that all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were laid down specifically with reference to one who has already received full ordination (*upasampanna*).

If this is so, how is it to be understood that those ordained by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu*) and others are also included within the training rules that are not prohibited by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*)? It is because they have, in fact, entered into them by their very nature.
For it is said: "Two persons are incapable of committing an offense: the Buddhas and the Paccekabuddhas; two persons..."

Because it is stated generally that "both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs are capable of committing an offense," even those who have received full ordination through the "Come, bhikkhu" formula and others may commit offenses such as sleeping in the same bed, which are classified as *paṇṇattivajja* (offenses of formal rule) when committed unintentionally or through lack of mindfulness and are thus *acittaka* (without mental fault). Therefore, the essential point here is that they are indeed said to have "committed" [the offense] in this sense.
As for whatever has been elaborated by others in a manner different from this, it should not be accepted as the core meaning.
"By way of etymology" means by way of derivation. "By way of expression" means by way of conventional usage.

"When the formal act (kammavācā) has not yet arisen" means when the formal act consisting of the motion followed by three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kammavācā) has not yet arisen. "By way of qualities" means because of being endowed with various specific qualities such as virtue (sīla) and so forth.
And here, the etymological derivation of "bhikkhu" should be understood as: one who "breaks" (bhindati) evil, unwholesome states (dhamma).
The commentary on the analysis of the terms for the bhikkhu is finished.
Commentary on the analysis of the terms for training and livelihood:
"To be trained in" means to be practiced. "Supreme" means distinguished. Even though higher virtue and so forth exist, [it is distinguished] by virtue and the rest.

It must be so. For just as a sunshade or banner that exceeds the measure of a smaller one is called "an oversized sunshade" or "an oversized banner," so too here, in relation to ordinary virtue (*anukkaṭṭhasīla*), one must possess "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*);
likewise, in relation to ordinary mind and wisdom, one must possess "higher mind" (*adhicitta*) and "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*).
Having taken virtue and the rest to heart, desiring to analyze them according to their specific nature, he said, "But what herein is virtue? and so forth.
Since the eightfold virtue is included within the tenfold virtue, it was not mentioned separately; thus, only "the fivefold and tenfold virtue" was stated.
Furthermore, the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha is twofold—by way of what is to be practiced and what is to be avoided—and is contained within the Vinaya Piṭaka.

The virtue of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-sīla*). For that which protects and guards one is called *pātimokkha*, because it liberates (*mokheti*) or causes one to be liberated (*moceti*) from the sufferings of the states of woe and so forth.
Restraint is *saṃvara*; it is the non-transgression by body and speech. The very *pātimokkha* as restraint is *pātimokkha-saṃvara*.
That itself, in the sense of "steadying" (*sīlana*), is virtue (*sīla*); thus it is the virtue of *pātimokkha*-restraint (*pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla*).

Another method: He is a *pātī* because he is prone to falling frequently into the states of misery (*apāya*), owing to the powerful nature of his defilements, the ease with which he performs evil deeds, and the difficulty with which he performs meritorious deeds.

Alternatively, he is one whose nature is to go (*gamana-sīlo*) because, due to impermanence, he is cast by the force of karma into various existences and wanders about without stability, like a potter’s wheel.
It falls (*pāti*); or, by way of death, it is that which has the nature of falling away from its selfhood within this or that class of beings, thus it is *pāti*.
It refers to the continuum of a being, or simply to the mind. Because it releases (*mokkheti*) that which falls (*pātinaṃ*) from the suffering of *saṃsāra*, it is called *pātimokkha*.

For it is said that "through the liberation of the mind, a being is liberated. Indeed, it is stated: "Through the purification of the mind, they are purified," and "without clinging, [one is freed] from the taints."
and "the mind is liberated.
Alternatively, it is called *pāti* because by means of causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*), one falls into, goes toward, and proceeds within *saṃsāra*.
For it is said: "Of beings hindered by ignorance (*avijjānīvaraṇa*) and fettered by craving (*taṇhāsaṃyojana*), who run and wander through [existence]. Of that being who falls (*pātino sattassa*)...

It is called *pātimokkha* because by means of it there is liberation (*mokkha*) from the threefold defilement beginning with craving (*taṇhā*). Its formation as a compound should be understood in the same way as in such terms as *kaṇṭhekāḷo* (“black-necked”).
Alternatively, it is a *pāti* because it causes one to fall (*pāteti*), that is, to fall into suffering; for it has been said: “The world is led by the mind, it is dragged about by the mind.

It is the *pātimokkha* because by means of it there is liberation (*mokkha*) for that which falls (*pāti*), namely, the mind. Or else, one falls (*patati*) into the suffering of the states of misery (*apāya*) by means of it.

The "protection" (*pāti*) against the suffering of *saṃsāra* is the corruption of craving (*taṇhā-saṃkileso*). For it has been said: "Craving gives birth to a person; craving is the companion of a person," and so forth.
That which protects one from that [craving] is the *Pātimokkha*.
Alternatively, the "protection" (*pāti*) is that wherein one falls; namely, the six internal and external sense bases (*āyatana*). For it has been said: "In the six, the world..."
"Once arisen, it forms intimacy with the six. Therefore, because it is liberation from what is designated as the six internal and external sense bases, it is the *pātimokkha*.
Alternatively, that which has *pāti*—meaning "falling down" or "destruction"—namely *saṃsāra*, is its characteristic; thus, because it is liberation from that, it is the *pātimokkha*.
Alternatively, the Blessed One is called *pati* because he is the Lord (*adhipati*) of the entire world and the Master of Dhamma (*dhammissara*). That by which one is liberated is *mokkha*.
Since it is prescribed as the liberation of the Master (*patino mokkho*), it is the *pātimokkha*.

Or else, because it is the root of all virtues, it is the *pati* in the sense of being supreme; and since it is liberation in the sense already stated, it is the *patimokkha*. Thus, it is the *pātimokkha*.
The *pātimokkha* is indeed the *pātimokkha*. For it has been said in detail: “*Pātimokkha* means this is the mouth (*mukha*), this is the foremost (*pamukha*).

Alternatively, *pa-* is a prefix meaning ‘in various ways’ (*pakāre*), and *ati-* is a particle used in the sense of ‘excessively’ (*accantatthe*); therefore, it is called *pātimokkha* because it liberates (*mokkheti*) excessively (*accantaṃ*) in various ways (*pakārehi*).
Indeed, this virtue (*sīla*), when accompanied by concentration and wisdom through its own intrinsic nature as a factor of the path, [acts] by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
It is called *pātimokkha* because it liberates by means of absolute release through complete eradication (*samuccheda*).
Alternatively, it is *patimokkha* in the sense that there is liberation (*mokkha*) for each individual (*pati-pati*);

the meaning is that it brings about liberation from each respective fault of transgression. Thus, *pātimokkha* is simply *patimokkha*. Or else, *mokkha* is Nibbāna; it is so called because it is the counterpart (*paṭibimba*) of that liberation.
The *pātimokkha*. For the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) is like the rising of the sun; it is the dawn of Nibbāna and its counterpart, because it extinguishes the defilements as appropriate.
Thus, *patimokkha* itself is *pātimokkha*. Alternatively, it is called *patimokkha* because it turns toward liberation (*mokkha*).
Since it is the very *patimokkha*, it is *pātimokkha*. In this way, the meaning of the word *pātimokkha* should be understood here.

It is called *saṃvara* because one restrains (*saṃvarati*) or closes off (*pidahati*) by means of it; thus, the *pātimokkha* itself as restraint is *pātimokkhasaṃvara*. That very thing is virtue (*sīla*), hence *pātimokkhasaṃvarasīla*.
In terms of its actual meaning, however, it consists of both abstinences (*virati*) and volitions (*cetanā*) from various things that ought to be transgressed against.

It is called "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*) because it is a superior and distinguished virtue due to its state of being a complete restraint of body and speech, and because it serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the virtue of the Path. [The word] *pajjotānaṃ*...
Of lights. But surely even Paccekabuddhas possess the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha by way of natural law (*dhammatā*);
this being so, why was it stated with such restriction that "it occurs only when a Buddha has arisen, not without the arising of a Buddha"?
To this he says: "For it is not by lifting up that formal rule (*paññatti*)," and so forth. Although Paccekabuddhas are indeed endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha...
The intention is that [the training] exists, yet it does not proceed by being expanded out according to those [specific instances].
The designation—“In this matter, in this transgression, this specific name applies”—is beyond the scope of others;
it is the domain of the Buddhas alone, for it is the power of the Buddhas. Thus he said, “But only the Buddhas,” and so forth. Regarding the state of mundane virtue as *adhisīla* (higher virtue):

By the phrase "in a figurative sense" (pariyāyena), it is stated—"even more than the restraint of the Pātimokkha, it is precisely the virtue associated with the Path and its Fruits that is 'higher virtue'"—in order to show that this is indeed the non-figurative (nippariyāya) sense.
For one who has attained that [Path] is not called a "bhikkhu" [in the primary sense], because among householders, stream-enterers (sotāpannas) may still transgress against their wives;
for they continue to dwell in the household together with their sons and wives.
"Encouraging others and undertaking oneself" means encouraging others and undertaking it oneself.
"It is called 'higher mind'" (adhicitta) because it is the foundation for the concentration of the Path (maggasamādhi). "Not without the arising of a Buddha":
although even Paccekabuddhas certainly possess the eightfold meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) that serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*), they do not [possess them] in that regard...
The intention is that it does not proceed by way of those [others] who are able to cause others to undertake [the practice], for that reason it is not expanded upon.

Regarding the establishment of "higher wisdom" (adhipaññatā) even through insight-wisdom (vipassanāpaññā), it should be understood that the statement "not without the arising of a Buddha" was spoken with this very same intention.
As for the mundane mind being "higher mind" (adhicitta), that is only figuratively; in the direct sense, it is not so.
In order to show this, he said: "Furthermore, the mind of the path and fruit is itself 'higher mind' (adhicitta).

However, by the statement in the Commentary that "that [mind] is not intended here," it is understood that the training in higher mind (adhicittasikkhā) pertaining to mundane (lokiya) consciousness is what is intended here.
For it is by means of that mundane higher mind that a bhikkhu who has attained meditative absorption does not engage in sexual intercourse. And by this [statement], the mundane higher mind...

"One who has entered [a meditative attainment] engages in sexual intercourse" refers to one who has fallen into [an offense]. Furthermore, in the exposition of higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*), it is stated:
"And even there, only the wisdom of the path and its fruit is 'higher wisdom'"; yet, because it continues, "But that is not intended here;
for a bhikkhu who has entered that [attainment] does not engage in sexual intercourse," it follows that by way of mundane wisdom (*lokiya-paññā*), the training in higher wisdom is also intended here.
It is understood from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) that for one who has entered that [attainment], the practice of sexual intercourse is permitted.

However, all of this does not accord with the following canonical text (*pāḷi*): "In this context, that which is the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is the training intended. For this canonical text indicates that it is specifically the training in higher virtue that is intended here, and not the other [trainings].
Therefore, the intention of both the Canon (Pāḷi) and the Commentary should be understood as follows:

for one who has attained mundane higher consciousness (adhicitta) and higher wisdom (adhipaññā), if the thought "I shall engage in sexual intercourse" arises based on such conditions, then falling away from that higher consciousness and higher wisdom becomes possible;
thus, it is not possible for one who has attained those two to engage in sexual intercourse.
"To have practiced" refers specifically to the training in higher virtue (*adhisīlasikkhā*) as stated in the Pāḷi.

For as long as one does not commit a transgression, one remains as if possessed of concentration; for the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is not said to be broken by a mere arising of thought.
However, in the Commentary, it is stated that even if a bhikkhu falls away from mundane higher consciousness (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*), [he remains so]...
One might wonder whether the practice of sexual intercourse could ever occur [for one who has attained the supramundane path].
Since that dyad (the attainment of the path and its fruit) is of an unshakable nature, it is impossible for a monk who has entered that state to fall away from it and engage in sexual intercourse;
therefore, it should be understood that the prohibition applies specifically to the supramundane higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*).
By this [passage] beginning with, “There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed,” etc., it is shown:
“In that regard, what is the knowledge of the ownership of kamma? ‘There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered;
there is the fruit and result of good and evil deeds; there is this world, there is the other world... [and so forth].

‘There is a mother; there is a father; there are beings of spontaneous birth; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known’—such wisdom as this, such understanding...
non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view: this is called the knowledge of the ownership of one’s actions (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*).
"Excluding the knowledge that accords with truth, all wholesome wisdom associated with the taints is the knowledge of the ownership of kamma"—this is how he includes this passage from the *Vibhaṅga*.
Therein, in the phrases "there is what is given" and so forth, the meaning should be understood by way of the principle: "there is a fruit by reason of what has been given."
"Given" (*dinna*) refers to giving by way of the category of "things to be given. "Sacrificed" (*yiṭṭha*) means a great sacrifice, the sense being a great gift common to all.
"Offered" (*huta*) intends a sufficient honorarium. "There is a mother, there is a father" states the arising of the results of right conduct, wrong conduct, and so forth, toward one's parents.
"This is called... refers to the knowledge that "this action is one's own; this is not one's own."
He knows; this is what is called "the knowledge of one's own karma as one's own property"—this is the meaning.
In that regard, the threefold misconduct of body, the fourfold misconduct of speech, and the threefold misconduct of mind are not called "one's own karma";
rather, all ten types of good conduct across the three doors are called "one's own karma. Whether it belongs to oneself or to another, all of it—
Unwholesome action is not what is called "one's own karma. Why? Because it destroys one's welfare and produces harm.
Whether it belongs to oneself or to another, all wholesome action is indeed "one's own karma. Why? Because it prevents harm and produces welfare.
Standing firm in this knowledge of being the owner of one's own karma—which is capable of such understanding—one should give much in alms and observe moral discipline.

There is no limit to the number of beings who, having observed the Uposatha and undertaken its precepts, have experienced happiness upon happiness and prosperity upon prosperity, and have thereby attained Nibbāna—provided one sets aside the knowledge that conforms to the Truths (saccānulomika-ñāṇa).

This insight-knowledge is called "conforming to the Truths" because it conforms to both the Path Truth and the Ultimate Truth (paramattha-sacca). Excluding this, there is no counting the number of those who have reached liberation.
The meaning is that all remaining wholesome wisdom associated with the taints (*sāsavā*) is precisely the knowledge of the ownership of kamma.

"Delimiting the modes of the three characteristics" means that which cuts through the modes such as non-existence by way of the three characteristics, namely impermanence and so forth. It is called "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*) because insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is the foundation for the wisdom of the Path (*maggapaññā*).
"A doer of good reaps good; a doer of evil reaps evil."
"He experiences this pair; he follows after the doer.

Thus, by way of discerning the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the past and the future, the wisdom of self-agency (*kammassakata-paññā*), which serves as a condition for the longing for liberation through its quality as a basis for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega-vatthu*), is also called "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*). Regarding the status of mundane wisdom (*lokiya-paññā*) as "higher wisdom":

Regarding the phrase "by way of a method" (*pariyāyena*), it is said that "even more than that, the wisdom of the path and its fruit is indeed higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*) in order to show that very point directly (*nippariyāya*).
As for the term *sājīva*—meaning "that wherein they live together"—it refers to all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*); thus he says:

"All [the training rules]... therefore it is called *sājīva*. In this context, "training rule" (*sikkhāpada*) refers to "the body of names, the body of phrases, the body of terminology, and the body of phonemes."
The training rule (sikkhāpada) spoken by the Blessed One, which is designated as his word.
"Those of similar conduct" means those whose way of life is the same, whose behavior is identical; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "one trains in that":

since the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) requires something to be placed within it, he asks what it is that is expected to be placed there, and thus states: "having made that training rule the locus for the mind."

The meaning is: having made that training rule known as the "mode of livelihood" (sājīva) the basis for the mind—which is contained within it—by way of its occurrence in the form, "Do I train according to this training rule, or do I not train? because it has the training rule as its object.
But is it not the case that, when providing the word-commentary for the phrase "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood," [it says]: "Whatever training..."?
One might have said: "Having entered upon both the training and the livelihood, he trains in them;

therefore it is said, 'one who has entered upon the training and the livelihood,'" but instead of saying that, why was only this much said—"He trains in that; therefore it is said, 'one who has entered upon the livelihood'"?
Addressing this objection regarding what is omitted within, he says: "And this is not only in this... and so forth.
"And of that training" means of that training known as the higher virtue (*adhisīla*).

"Fulfilling the training" means fulfilling the restraint of virtue; the sense is that he causes within himself both the volition associated with abstinence by way of the virtue of avoidance (*vāritta-sīla*) and the volition dissociated from abstinence by way of the virtue of performance (*cāritta-sīla*). And not transgressing that rule of training...

"He trains" means that, without transgressing the training rule consisting of the Blessed One’s word—namely, "the body of names, the body of phrases, the body of terminology, and the body of phonemes"—he trains in that aforementioned training rule; this is the meaning.
The intention here is that these two alone constitute what is called "training": the fulfillment of the restraint of virtue and the non-transgression of the proper mode of livelihood. In that regard:

Not transgressing the way of life (ājīva) is a condition for the fulfillment of training. For it is through not transgressing the way of life that the fulfillment of training extends as far as the Path.

Furthermore, in this context, by the phrase "he trains while fulfilling the training," the time when the restraint of virtue—consisting of abstinence and volition—is specifically active within the continuum is indicated;
whereas by the phrase "he trains without transgressing," even the time when it is not so active is included.
For even when one causes the training to proceed within oneself by way of fulfilling it, and does not cause it to proceed due to sleep and so forth,
one is nevertheless said to "train without transgression" because there is no transgression.
The commentary on the word-analysis of the training and livelihood is finished.
Commentary on the Analysis of the Renunciation of Training (*Sikkhāpaccakkhāna-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā*):
The reading “appaccakkhāya appaccakkhātāya” (without having renounced, [even though] not renounced) is stated in both ways in all three *gaṇṭhipada*s.

“Even when weakness has been manifested” means even when a state of weakness has been made known by such statements as, “What if I were to renounce the Buddha,” and so forth. Regarding the training (*sikkhā*):
"But when it has been renounced" means when the training has been renounced by saying, "I renounce the Buddha," and so forth.

Since the preceding and following words are joined together when the expression "two nights" is used, but not when it is not used, he says, "for the sake of the smoothness of the phrasing (*byañjanasiliṭṭhatā*)," meaning that the purpose is merely the smoothness of the verbal expression. "For the sake of being present in the mouth" means...
The meaning is: "because such a statement has entered the mouth of the world.

Regarding the phrase "he perfects the phrasing" (*byañjanaṃ sampādeti*): since that [phrasing] has no separate meaning of its own, he "perfects the phrasing" by illustrating the very meaning already stated through another word.
He says, "For [it is] devoid of accompanying words," and so forth, in order to analyze that very meaning already stated by means of a reason.
A word that illuminates the meaning is an "atthapada" (meaning-word).
Regarding "the renunciation of the training": this refers to the statement of renouncing the training, such as "I renounce the Buddha.
In passages such as "I renounce the Buddha," it is said: "In this way, monks, there is both a manifestation of weakness and a renunciation of the training."
Because it has been stated that both [occurs], he said: "In some cases, there is the meaning of the disclosure of weakness.

Although the word-meaning of the disclosure of weakness does not apply to the verbal expression of renouncing the training, such as "I renounce the Buddha," nevertheless, when one says "I renounce the Buddha," the disclosure of weakness regarding the fulfillment of the training is also implied.
It is said: "There is a partial disclosure of weakness regarding the renunciation of the training.
With reference to this means with reference to that which constitutes the disclosure of weakness.
Regarding "the specific and the non-specific": herein, that by which there is only a disclosure of weakness and not a renunciation of the training—therein...
There is a distinction between the renunciation of training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*), weakness (*dubbalya*), and disclosure (*āvikamma*).
However, it should be understood that where both the renunciation of training and weakness occur together, there is no distinction between them.

Because the root *kaṭh* is listed among the roots meaning "to live with difficulty," it is said: "one who has reached a life of hardship" (*kicchajīvikappatto*). *Ukkaṇṭhanā* means dissatisfaction; [it refers to] a life of hardship.
“Distressed because he has come from there” means: “from there,” that is, from that place or from that monastery.

“There” refers to the region he wishes to go to. Oppressed by discontent, with a distracted mind, lifting his head and looking upward, he wanders about glancing here and there; thus it is said, “dwelling with his neck held up.”

Regarding the term *aṭṭīyamāno*: here, because one behaves as if distressed (*aṭṭa*), one is "distressed" (*aṭṭīyati*). Since the word *aṭṭīya* contains an inherent comparison where the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is the self (*attā*), it is transitive by virtue of that very self which serves as the object of comparison, and not by way of the state of being a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*).

Therefore, he said: "‘The state of being a monk’ means ‘by way of the state of being a monk. For he does not behave as if distressed toward the state of being a monk; rather, [he is distressed] toward himself. Therefore...

"One should understand the meaning here as ‘being distressed by oneself through the state of being a bhikkhu acting as the instrument’; thus he said, ‘The accusative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.

But regarding the phrase ‘one would be distressed by [something] clung to the throat,’ he said, ‘It is expressed by the instrumental case according to its grammatical definition,’ because in this instance the instrumental case is used in the sense of the instrumental itself. Or alternatively, the accusative case is used in the sense of the agent."
He said, “It is to be seen,” beginning with the words, “by that state of being a bhikkhu,” etc.;
the meaning is: by that state of being a bhikkhu which has become the agent. Regarding this matter, however, one should understand the formation of the word *aṭṭīyamāno* as follows:

having derived the word *aṭṭīya* from the sense of “he suffers” (*aṭṭaṃ karoti*) or “he is distressed” (*aṭṭīyati*), and then adding the suffix *māna* in the sense of the object, the form is established. For this very reason he said: “suffering being produced... (*aṭṭo kariyamāno*).
"Being oppressed. But when this is connected with the word "disgusted" (*jigucchamāno*), it is in the accusative case in the sense of the object, namely "the state of being a bhikkhu";
thus he says, "feeling disgust for it as if it were impurity," meaning "feeling disgust for that state of being a bhikkhu.
"If I" (*sacāhaṃ*) means "if I."
"Expressed by way of renunciation" means they are expressed in connection with the mode of renunciation because of the statement, "one should renounce what is to be renounced.
"By way of the mode of alternative states of being" means that because it has come down as "it would be, it would be," it refers to the mode of alternative states of whatever one wishes to become;
the intention is that it refers to the mode of alternative states of being other than the state of a bhikkhu.
50. "I am not able" shows the absence of energy in himself regarding this or that matter.

"I am not capable" shows the state of being unbearable for him regarding things such as eating only one meal a day. "I do not delight" shows that "there is no happiness for me rooted in the going-forth.
"I do not rejoice" shows the absence of personal contentment with the going-forth.
Now, while standing at the section on the renunciation of training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*), this analysis should be understood:

therein, by the phrases beginning with "desirous of falling away from the state of a recluse" (*sāmaññā cavitukāmo*), he shows the restriction of the mind (*cittaniyama*). By the phrases beginning with "the Buddha, the Dhamma," he shows the restriction of the field (*khettaniyama*).
For just as in the world the place where crops grow is called a "field," so too is this [the Triple Gem] the field for the renunciation of training.
Because it is a place where [grain] grows, it is called "field" (*khetta*). By the words "I renounce; hold this in mind," he shows the restriction of time.

By the word "speaks," he shows the restriction of application (*payoga*). Furthermore, by means of [phrases such as] "Enough for me with the Buddha," "What use have I for the Buddha?," "I have no need for the Buddha," and "I am well-freed from the Buddha," there is also renunciation by way of time that is not explicitly mentioned.
This shows that [the act] occurs. By the term “makes known,” it shows the necessity of comprehension (*vijānana*).
By such statements as “one who is insane renounces the training” and “one renounces the training in the presence of one who is insane,” it shows the necessity of the person. [And by the statement:
“An Ariyan renounces the training in the presence of a non-Aryan, yet he does not comprehend it; it is as if the training has not been renounced.”
By such statements as “the training,” etc., he shows that even when there is a restriction regarding the person and so forth, a restriction regarding the act of understanding is impossible.

By such statements as “He renounces the training for the sake of sport; the training has not been renounced,” he shows that it does not apply because there is no restriction of the mind, even when there is a restriction regarding the field and so forth.
By this [statement], “Though desiring to announce it, he does not announce it; the training has not been renounced,” [he shows] even in the case of a restriction of the mind...
This shows that [the act] does not take root because there is no restriction regarding the application (*payoga*).

By the phrases, “he makes it heard by one who does not understand, but not by one who understands,” it is shown that even though there is a restriction regarding the mind, field, time, application, and person who understands, the act takes root only through the hearing by the specific person for whom he makes it heard, and not by anyone else.
Or, “if he does not make it heard at all, [it does not take root] when it is not directly witnessed.”
The statement, “the training has been relinquished,” is said for the purpose of showing that the training is relinquished only through the restriction of the mind and so forth,
and not otherwise. Therefore, having understood the relinquishment of the training by way of the restrictions concerning the mind,
the field, the time, the application, and the person, one should understand its non-relinquishment by the absence of those [restrictions].

How so? For the renunciation of the training occurs only with a mind that desires to fall away from the state of one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), not for one who speaks out of jest or in jest. Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs through the power of the mind, not in its absence.
Likewise: "I renounce the Buddha; I renounce the Dhamma; I renounce the Saṅgha;

the training; the Vinaya; the Pātimokkha; the recitation; the preceptor (*upajjhāya*); the teacher (*ācariya*); the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*); the resident pupil (*antevāsika*); those with the same preceptor (*samānupajjhāyaka*)."

Of these twenty-two: the fourteen beginning with the Buddha who were addressed thus, "I renounce my common teacher and my fellow-celibate," and the eight beginning with the householder who were addressed thus, "Regard me as a householder;

regard me as a lay follower (upāsaka), an attendant (ārāmika), a novice (sāmaṇera), a member of another sect (titthiya), a disciple of another sect (titthiyasāvaka), one who is not a recluse (assamaṇa), or one who is not a son of the Sakyans (asakyaputtiya)."

Regarding the fields, for anyone who speaks by means of any synonymous term whatsoever, and even if one wishes to say anything at all concerning those [fields], there is a renunciation of the training;
it does not occur when one renounces the training after taking the name of a specific tree or the like.
Thus, the renunciation of the training occurs by way of the field, and not in the absence thereof.
In this context, there is that present-tense expression which was spoken as “I renounce” (*paccakkhāmi*) and “hold me [in mind]” (*maṃ dhārehi*);

and there are those statements expressed by way of the verb, without specifying a tense, such as “Enough for me with the Buddha,” “What need have I of the Buddha?,” “I have no use for the Buddha,” and “I am well-liberated from the Buddha,” which were spoken in conjunction with the preceding fourteen phrases.
The four phrases beginning with “Enough for me” constitute the renunciation itself by way of those very synonyms;

it does not occur for one who speaks words of past, future, or hypothetical construction, such as “He has renounced,” “He will renounce,” “Do you hold [this] for me? “Will you hold [it] for me? or “What if I were to renounce? Thus...
The renunciation occurs by way of both the present time and the unspecified time, but not by way of their absence.
Furthermore, the formal act (*payoga*) is twofold: physical and verbal.

In that regard, by making a vocal utterance in any language whatsoever according to the formula "I renounce the Buddha," etc., the renunciation occurs through the verbal formal act alone; it does not occur through the writing of syllables.
or making a physical effort such as showing hand gestures; in this way, the renunciation occurs through verbal action alone, not in its absence.
Furthermore, the person is twofold: he who renounces and he to whom one renounces. Therein, he who renounces...
Thus, provided that he is not one who is insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by pain;
and provided that the person to whom he renounces the training is of human birth, is not one who is insane or otherwise [as previously mentioned], and is present before him—
because a declaration made through a messenger or by letter does not take effect for one who is not present— in this way, by way of the persons already described...
There is a renunciation, not by way of their absence.
Consciousness (*vijānana*) is also twofold, according to whether it is restricted or unrestricted.

In that regard, for one who, having restricted [the object], says, "I announce this to him" or "I announce these to them," if those people, having heard the words as they normally do in the world, at the moment of mental advertence (*āvajjana*)—
If they know— immediately after his speech, through any means whatsoever, whether by thinking "this person is dissatisfied" or "he desires the state of a householder"—
that he has renounced the training, then the training is considered renounced. However, if later on,
after considering "What was said by him?", they come to know, or others know it, [only then] is it not yet renounced.

There is the training. However, for one who declares it without specifying [the person], if anyone belonging to the human race understands the meaning of the words in the manner described, the training is indeed renounced.
Thus, the renunciation occurs by way of such understanding, not merely by the absence of those factors.
Therefore, it should be understood that the renunciation of the training occurs only through these aforementioned types of consciousness and so forth, and not otherwise.

51. Regarding the phrase "speaks" (*vadati*), since the word "makes understood" (*viññāpeti*) is stated immediately after it demonstrates the application of vocal articulation, what is intended here is the making known of one's intention by that very vocal articulation, and not by any other means; thus he says, "by that very vocal articulation.
"Having reversed the order of the words" means having transposed the sequence of the words. And this refers to the employment of the words...

It was stated because of the lack of fixed order. For just as in the world, the communication of a meaning is seen through an indefinite application of words such as "bring the bowl" or "bring the bowl," so too here, the communication of that same meaning occurs through an indefinite application of words such as "I renounce the Buddha" (*buddhaṃ paccakkhāmi*) or "I renounce the Buddha" (*paccakkhāmi buddhaṃ*);
this is the intended sense. "I renounce the Buddha" (*buddhaṃ paccakkhāmīti*).

This exposition is primarily concerned with the meaning (attha), not primarily with the sound (sadda); thus he said, "One might state that meaning in any of the non-Aryan languages (milakkhabhāsā) or in another language.
All languages remaining other than the Māgadhī language—such as those of the Andhas, Damilas, and so forth—should be understood as non-Aryan languages.
Even if one who intends to speak a particular field-term (khettapada) were to speak something else, [it would still be valid] because it is included within the category of field-terms.
Showing that one has indeed renounced the training, he said: “Intending to say, ‘I renounce the Buddha,’ and so forth.

Even if, while unwilling to say “I renounce the Buddha,” one mentally rejects that [intention] and, desiring to say something else, should again by mistake say that very same thing—nevertheless, as long as there is a mind desiring to fall away from the Dispensation (sāsana), [the offense is incurred].

Because it is stated as a "field-phrase" (*khetta-pada*) and because the fulfillment of the factors (*aṅga*) is thereby possible, it should be understood that there is indeed a renunciation of the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*).
"He has descended into the field itself" means he has descended into the very field that serves as the locus for the growth of the renunciation of the training.

Because the present tense—expressed by the words "I renounce; hold [this]"—is intended to be emphasized as the primary factor, [the meaning is not established] by means of expressions referring to the past or the future.
Showing that there is no such thing as a formal renunciation of the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*), he said: “But if they should renounce the Buddha,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “he speaks, he makes known”: here, because the act is restricted by the word “speaks,” it is shown that the renunciation of the training occurs only through one’s own verbal expression in the presence of another, and not through means such as sending a messenger or a message.
He said: “Or he sends a messenger,” and so forth. Therein, “or he sends a messenger” is stated by way of a verbal message, [meaning] “Speak to him of my state of having renounced the training.
“Or he sends a communication” is stated by way of sending [a message] written on a leaf.
“Or he carves a letter” is stated by way of carving characters on trees and the like to show them.
"He announces that matter by means of a hand-gesture" is said with reference to the communication of intention by means of the hand.
For a movement of the hand that communicates intention is a "hand-gesture" (*hatthamuddā*).

And here, the word "hand" (*hattha*) should be understood as referring to the fingers, which are parts of it, just as in such expressions as "I will not put my whole hand into my mouth. Therefore, by means of that which communicates intention...
The meaning here should be understood as follows: he makes that matter known by means of a hand-gesture, such as the contraction of the fingers.
"Associated with the mind" (*cittasampayutta*) means associated with the state of mind desiring to renounce.

Now, showing that the renunciation of the training should be understood as twofold—determined and undetermined—by way of the act of making it known, he says: "If only this person should know," and so forth.

And this distinction should be understood as obtained through the following method: "Because 'speaks' and 'makes known' have the same object, it is intended that the person to whom one speaks is the very same person who understands, not someone else.
For the meaning—that one makes known someone other than the one to whom one speaks—is not possible.
By the restriction "he alone knows," it is implied that while he does not know, another [does].
He rejects the act of knowing. For this very reason it was said: “Now, if he does not know, but another standing nearby knows, the training has not been renounced.

Therefore, if one makes a specific restriction, saying, “Let this person alone know,” and then declares [the renunciation], even if that person knows and another also knows, the renunciation of the training still takes place because the act of knowing occurs by virtue of the specific restriction made toward the one restricted.
It should be seen that [the rule] is unrestricted by the thought, "Let no one else know.

The phrase "having restricted both" is said with reference to an announcement made after such restriction as: "Let either two or one know; I shall announce it to these two alone. For this very reason, he says:
"Even when one knows, or even when two know. Therefore, [one should think]: "Let only two know; let not one know."
Thus, having made a restriction between two people, it is said that the renunciation of training occurs only when both know [of the act], not when only one knows.

"In common" means among those who are trustworthy. "Suspecting" means fearing, "If they were to find out, they would stop me. "One who knows the occasion" means one skilled in the conduct of the Dispensation;
however, here, one is called "one who knows the occasion" merely by knowing the intention behind it.
It happens. For this very reason it was said: “He knows: ‘This one is dissatisfied… he has fallen away from the Dispensation.

Therefore, even if one understands the meaning of “I renounce the Buddha,” if one does not know whether “this person wishes to fall away from the state of a bhikkhu or wishes to become a householder,” the training remains unrenounced. However, if [one knows]: “I renounce the Buddha”—
Even if one does not understand the meaning of the words, if one knows the intention—thinking, "He is weary and wishes to become a householder"—the training is indeed renounced.
