It is said, "But at that very moment, it is difficult to discern as neither before nor after," because the apprehension of the sound occurs in the cognitive process of auditory consciousness at one moment, while the understanding of its meaning occurs in the cognitive process of mental consciousness at another moment. For it is not...
Hearing the sound and the cognition of its meaning can occur at one and the same moment.
For instance, when someone says "pot" or "cloth," one takes up the present sound *gha* (or *pa*), and a single process of ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇavīthi*) arises and ceases;
immediately thereafter, a single process of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇavīthi*) arises, taking up that very same [sound] as it has passed.
Thus, regarding the words spoken by him, as many syllables as there are, taking each single syllable both as present and as past,
after they have arisen and ceased through the process of ear-consciousness and the process of mind-consciousness,
at the conclusion, those syllables are combined; having grasped the collection of syllables, a single process of mind-consciousness arises and ceases.
Immediately thereafter, after another mental consciousness process has arisen and ceased by way of grasping the designation of a name—

thinking, "This collection of syllables is the name for this"— it becomes possible for the subsequent mental consciousness process that arises immediately after it to naturally cognize the meaning of that [name], thinking, "This is its meaning."
“By the time of adverting” (*āvajjana-samaye*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of a locative; the meaning is “at the time of attending to the object.
Now, explaining that very time of adverting, he says: “Just as by nature... [they] know.
Because it is the communication of the intention through that very vocal expression which is intended here, for one who later wonders, “What was said by this?”—[it serves as the answer].
The understanding of one’s intention may occur after some time through some other means as well, not solely through a verbal expression;

thus he said: “Then, at a later time... the training is not renounced. When one says, “I shall become a householder,” there is a difference in meaning and a difference in time, and therefore the training is not renounced. For [the phrase] “Bear it” refers to this person’s...

The meaning and the time [of the vow] do not apply to the thought "I shall become [a monk]. However, when one says, "I am a householder," there is indeed a difference in meaning, but no difference in time, because the word "am" (homī) refers to the present time alone.

In the cases of "I have become a householder" (*gihī jāto'mhi*) and "I am a householder" (*gihīmhī*), because both the meaning and the time differ, the training is not renounced. As for the phrase "from today onwards" (*ajja paṭṭhāyā*):
Although it was stated in that way, it was said having completed [the explanation] because of the nature of the fault.

By saying "Hold it," he shows that since this exposition has the meaning as its primary focus, there is indeed a renunciation of the training even through synonymous expressions; thus he says "Know it," and so forth.
For these words—"hold it," "know it," "perceive it," and "attend to it"—are identical in both meaning and time.

52. "The former fourteen" refers to those beginning with the Buddha and ending with his fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*). Regarding the phrase "let it be," he says, "Let it be; the meaning is 'it is sufficient,'" indicating that this too is merely a rejection [of further elaboration]. 53. "The *Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna*"—the Mahāsaṅghikas say this is a single discourse (*sutta*) that illuminates the qualities of the Buddha. Regarding the "Upāli verses": "Dhīrassa vigatamohassa... [and so forth]... 54. "The *Saddhammappajotikā*. This is the name of the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*. It was composed by the Venerable Dhammapāla, who dwelt in the Mahāvihāra monastery in the island of Laṅkā. It is called *Saddhammappajotikā* because it illuminates the True Dhamma. It is called a "commentary" (*aṭṭhakathā*) because it explains the meaning of the text. It is called a "sub-commentary" (*ṭīkā*) because it clarifies the commentary. It is called a "word-explanation" (*padavaṇṇanā*) because it explains each word. It is called a "purification of the text" (*pāḷi-visodhanī*) because it purifies the text from errors. It is called a "clarification of the meaning" (*atthavibhāvanī*) because it clarifies the meaning. It is called a "lamp of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammappajotikā*) because it illuminates the True Dhamma. It is called a "treasury of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammaratnākara*) because it is a mine of the True Dhamma. It is called a "jewel-lamp of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammaratnapradīpa*) because it is a lamp made of the jewels of the True Dhamma. It is called a "guide to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammanettī*) because it leads one to the True Dhamma. It is called a "bridge to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammasetaṅga*) because it is a bridge for crossing over to the True Dhamma. It is called a "raft to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammakulla*) because it is a raft for crossing over to the True Dhamma. It is called a "boat to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammanāvā*) because it is a boat for crossing over to the True Dhamma. It is called a "vehicle to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammayāna*) because it is a vehicle for reaching the True Dhamma. It is called a "path to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammamagga*) because it is the path leading to the True Dhamma. It is called a "door to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammaduvāra*) because it is the door for entering the True Dhamma. It is called a "stairway to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammasopāna*) because it is a stairway for ascending to the True Dhamma. It is called a "ladder to the True Dhamma" (*saddhammaladduka*) because it is a ladder for climbing to the True Dhamma. It is called a "palace of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammapāsāda*) because it is a palace of the True Dhamma. It is called a "city of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammanagara*) because it is a city of the True Dhamma. It is called a "kingdom of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammarājya*) because it is a kingdom of the True Dhamma. It is called a "sovereignty of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammādhipateyya*) because it is the sovereignty of the True Dhamma.

It is called a "supreme state of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammavarapada*) because it is the supreme state of the True Dhamma. It is called a "nirvana of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammanibbāna*) because it is the nirvana of the True Dhamma. It is called a "liberation of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammavimutti*) because it is the liberation of the True Dhamma. It is called a "peace of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammasanti*) because it is the peace of the True Dhamma. It is called a "bliss of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammasukha*) because it is the bliss of the True Dhamma. It is called a "joy of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammapīti*) because it is the joy of the True Dhamma. It is called a "rapture of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammapassaddhi*) because it is the rapture of the True Dhamma. It is called a "equanimity of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammupekkhā*) because it is the equanimity of the True Dhamma. It is called a "mindfulness of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammasati*) because it is the mindfulness of the True Dhamma. It is called a "concentration of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammasamādhi*) because it is the concentration of the True Dhamma. It is called a "wisdom of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammapaññā*) because it is the wisdom of the True Dhamma. It is called a "vision of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammadassana*) because it is the vision of the True Dhamma. It is called a "knowledge of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammañāṇa*) because it is the knowledge of the True Dhamma. It is called a "insight of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammavipassanā*) because it is the insight of the True Dhamma. It is called a "enlightenment of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammabodhi*) because it is the enlightenment of the True Dhamma. It is called a "awakening of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammabujjha*) because it is the awakening of the True Dhamma. It is called a "realization of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammabhisamaya*) because it is the realization of the True Dhamma. It is called a "attainment of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammapatti*) because it is the attainment of the True Dhamma. It is called a "fulfillment of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammaparipūraṇā*) because it is the fulfillment of the True Dhamma. It is called a "perfection of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammapāramī*) because it is the perfection of the True Dhamma. It is called a "pāramitā of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammapāramitā*) because it is the pāramitā of the True Dhamma. It is called a "great compassion of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammamahākaruṇā*) because it is the great compassion of the True Dhamma. It is called a "great loving-kindness of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammamahāmaitrī*) because it is the great loving-kindness of the True Dhamma. It is called a "great sympathetic joy of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammamahāmuditā*) because it is the great sympathetic joy of the True Dhamma. It is called a "great equanimity of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammamahaupekkhā*) because it is the great equanimity of the True Dhamma. It is called a "fourfold foundation of mindfulness of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammacatuṛṛipasmṛti*) because it is the fourfold foundation of mindfulness of the True Dhamma. It is called a "fourfold right effort of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammacatuṛṛisamyakprahāṇa*) because it is the fourfold right effort of the True Dhamma. It is called a "fourfold base of psychic power of the True Dhamma" (*saddhammacatuṛṛirddhipāda*) because it is the fourfold base of psychic power of the True Dhamma. It is called a "fivefold faculty of the True Dhamma" (*
Of one whose taints are destroyed, who has conquered victory,
who is free from distress, whose mind is perfectly balanced,
whose virtue is mature, and whose wisdom is excellent—
I am a disciple of that Blessed One, who is stainless and free from the stain of craving,
who is beyond doubt and dwells in the Tusita realm.
For the person who has vomited up the bait of worldly gain, who is joyful,
who has performed the duties of a recluse,
and who is a man in his final body.
“I am a disciple of that Blessed One, who is incomparable, free from passion,
and beyond doubt. “Of the one who is skillful and free from doubt...”
To the charioteer who removes the defilements,
to the unsurpassed one of radiant Dhamma,
to the one free from doubt, the illuminator.
Of that Hero who has cut off pride,
I am a disciple of that Blessed One—
of the Bull-like One, the immeasurable.
Of the profound one who has attained silence,
the teacher of security,
the upholder of the Dhamma, and the self-restrained.
I am a disciple of that Blessed One, who has transcended attachments and is liberated—
a Naga dwelling in the forest solitude.
To one whose fetters are destroyed, who is liberated,
who has transcended all bonds, who is washed clean,
whose banner is lowered, and who is free from passion.
Of the Tamed One, free from conceptual proliferation;
I am a disciple of that Blessed One.
Of the Seventh Sage, the guileless one;
Of one possessing the threefold knowledge, who has attained the state of Brahmā;
of one who is purified, a master of the verses;
of one who is tranquil, who has known what is to be known.
Of Sakka Purindada;
I am a disciple of that Blessed One.
Of the Noble One whose self is cultivated;
Of one who has reached the further shore of exposition,
who possesses mindfulness and insight,
who is neither attracted nor repelled.
I am a disciple of that Blessed One, who has attained mastery over the mind and is free from agitation,
a meditator who has risen above all.
For one who is consistently devoted, pure,
unattached, beneficial,
secluded, and who has attained the summit.
Of him who has crossed over and is ferrying others across—
that Blessed One, I am a disciple.
Of him who is peaceful and possessed of vast wisdom...
Of the one of great wisdom, free from greed;
of the Tathāgata, the Sugata;
the peerless one, the incomparable.
Of the confident and subtle one—
I am a disciple of that Blessed One,
the Buddha who has severed craving.
To the one from whom smoke has vanished, the unstained,
the one worthy of offerings, the spirit-like being,
the supreme person, the incomparable.
“I am a disciple of that Blessed One who has attained great fame”—
thus were the verses recited by the householder Upāli in the *Upāli Sutta*.

"According to the literal expression" (*yathārutaṃ eva*) means exactly as it was stated; the intention is that it is precisely as it appears in the canonical text (*pāḷi*). This is because "the Perfectly Enlightened One," "one of infinite wisdom," "one of peerless wisdom," and "enlightenment-intelligence" are the names recorded in the *Vaṇṇappakaraṇa* (The Section on Praise), whereas "the Wise One" (*dhīra*) and so forth are the names recorded in the verses of Upāli.
In this context, "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) refers to omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), [and the term "Buddha" is applied] because that [omniscience] is the cause for his realization.

He possesses wisdom regarding this, thus he is the Blessed One, the "Wisdom-Enlightened" (*bodhipaññāṇa*). He who takes up, or cultivates, with his intellect—that is, with wisdom—is called "wise" (*dhīra*).

Because all the stakes of the mind have been utterly severed, he is one "who has broken the stake" (*pabhinnakhīla*). They have conquered, are conquering, and will conquer all worldlings; thus they are "victors" (*vijaya*). Who are they?
The Māra of Death, the Māra of Defilements, and the Māra of the Son of a Deva. These are the "victories" (*vijayā*) because they have been conquered.

By this [phrase], the Blessed One is "one who has conquered the victory. It should be understood that by the very conquest of the Māra of defilements and the Māra of death, the Māras of the aggregates of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārakkhandha*) are also necessarily conquered here.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*):
it is because he has made manifest the holy life (*brahmacariya*) which is meaningful, possessed of both letter and spirit, complete in its entirety, and utterly pure.
The Dhamma is well-expounded (*svākkhāta*); or, it is "well-expounded" because its meaning is free from perversion.

For the meaning of the Dhamma of other sectarians falls into perversion: because the things described by them as "obstructive" lack the quality of being obstructive, and the things described as "leading out" lack the quality of leading out; therefore, those other sectarians have indeed ill-expounded Dhammas.

The meaning of the Blessed One’s Dhamma does not undergo perversion, because the nature of those things described as "these things are obstructive" or "these things lead to liberation" does not transcend their actual state. Thus, first of all, the Dhamma of the scriptures is well-expounded.

Furthermore, the supramundane Dhamma is well-expounded because the practice has been expounded in accordance with Nibbāna, and Nibbāna has been expounded in accordance with the practice. As it is said:
“Moreover, the path leading to Nibbāna well-expounded by that Blessed One for his disciples converges with Nibbāna; the path and Nibbāna are in harmony.

Just as the waters of the Ganges converge and flow together with the waters of the Yamunā, even so the path leading to Nibbāna well-expounded by that Blessed One for his disciples converges with Nibbāna; the path and Nibbāna are in harmony.”
And herein, the Noble Path is well-expounded because it is declared as the "Middle Way" precisely by way of being the Middle Way that does not fall into either of the two extremes.
The fruits of recluseship are well-expounded because they are declared as "having subsided defilements" precisely by way of having defilements that have subsided.
Nibbāna is well-expounded by way of its nature as eternal, deathless, a refuge, a shelter, and so forth, precisely because it has the nature of being eternal and so on.
Because it has been well-expounded, it is "well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*); thus, even the supramundane Dhamma is well-expounded.

It is "visible here and now" (*sanditthika*) because it must be seen personally by a noble person (*ariya-puggala*) within their own continuum—who, by means of the Noble Path, effects the absence of lust and other defilements—thinking, "By the Noble Path, my lust and so forth have been abandoned," and thus it must be seen by oneself without depending on another.

"Visible here and now" (*sandiṭṭhika*) means being visible right now. Furthermore, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is "visible here and now" because whichever noble disciple has attained it, having abandoned the need to rely on another's faith, must see it for himself through direct knowledge (*paccakkha-ñāṇa*).
Alternatively, "visible here and now" (*sanditṭhi*) refers to a praiseworthy view; that which triumphs by means of such a view is "visible here and now."

Thus, here the Noble Path conquers defilements by means of the "visible" (sanditthi) associated with it; the Noble Fruit, by means of the visible as its cause; and Nibbāna, by means of the visible as its object.

Therefore, just as one who wins by means of a chariot is called a "charioteer," so too the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is "visible" because it conquers by means of the visible. Alternatively, "seen" (diṭṭha) refers to seeing (dassana).
*Diṭṭhaṃ* (seen) is the same as *sand-iṭṭhaṃ* (seen here and now); the meaning is "that which shows.

It is called *sandiṭṭhika* because it deserves to be seen (*sand-iṭṭhaṃ arahati*). For the supramundane Dhamma, when being seen through the realization of cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*) and the realization of direct experience (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*), puts an end to the fear of saṃsāra.
Therefore, just as something that deserves its basis is called *vatthika*, so too, that which deserves to be seen is called *sandiṭṭhika*.
With reference to its giving of its own fruit, there is no time that must be awaited for it; thus it is "timeless" (*akāla*).

For while mundane wholesome states have a time to be awaited for the giving of their fruit—such as "upon rebirth" (*upapajja*) or "in subsequent lives" (*aparāpariya*)—this is not the case for this [Dhamma];

such is the meaning. Being timeless (*akāla*) itself, it is "timeless" (*akālika*); it does not give its fruit after wasting time divided into periods of five or seven days, etc., but rather [gives its fruit] of its own accord.
However, it is said that [the fruit] arises immediately after its occurrence.

Alternatively, it is "kālika" (belonging to time) because it has reached, arrived at, or been brought to a remote and distant time for the giving of its own fruit; thus, it is one that gives fruit at another time. What is this? It is mundane wholesome dhamma.

But this [path] is not "kālika" because it gives its fruit immediately after [its occurrence]; therefore, it is called "akālika" (timeless). Indeed, it is with reference to the path alone that this term "akālika" was stated.
It is called *ehipassiko* because it deserves the method of "Come and see this Dhamma.
Why does it deserve that method? Because it exists in the ultimate sense and because it is utterly pure.

For even if one were to say, "There is gold or bullion in an empty fist," one could not say, "Come and see this. Why? Because it does not exist. But this Dhamma is otherwise. Therefore, it deserves the method of "Come and see. Thus it is *ehipassiko*.

Because they do not exist. Even if excrement or urine were actually present, one could not say, "Come and see this," for the purpose of gladdening the mind by proclaiming their pleasant nature; rather, it must simply be covered over with grass or leaves. Why?
Because they are impure. But this ninefold supramundane Dhamma exists by its very intrinsic nature.
It is like the full orb of the moon in a cloudless sky, or like a natural gem placed upon a white woolen cloth;
it is thus utterly pure. Therefore, because it exists and because it is utterly pure, it deserves the method of "come and see" (*ehi-passa*);
hence it is called *ehi-passiko*. It is to be brought near (*upanetabbo*), thus it is *opanayyiko*. Herein, this is the analysis: bringing near is *upanaya*; [it is like] a garment on fire...
Or, even after disregarding [the world] like lead, it is "worthy of being brought near" (*opanayyika*) because it merits being brought into and produced within one's own mind by way of meditation.
This applies to the conditioned supramundane dhamma; however, the unconditioned is "worthy of being brought near" because it merits being brought near as an object within one's own mind.
The meaning is that it merits being adhered to by way of realization. Now...

The Noble Path is "to be led" (upaneyya) in the sense that it leads one to Nibbāna as a noble person; the phenomena of the fruit and Nibbāna are "to be led" in the sense that they are to be brought to realization.
That which is indeed to be led is "leading" (opanayika).
By all wise persons—beginning with those who understand through a condensed statement—it is known: "The path has been developed by me; the fruit has been attained; [Nibbāna] has been realized."
"Cessation" is to be experienced within oneself; thus it is said, "to be personally realized by the wise.
For the defilements of a co-resident disciple are not abandoned by the path developed by his preceptor;
he does not dwell in comfort through the preceptor’s attainment of the fruit; nor does he realize the Nibbāna realized by him. Therefore, this [cessation] does not reside upon the head of another.
It should be regarded as an ornament; however, it should be regarded within one’s own mind alone—it is meant that it is to be experienced by the wise.

"Unconditioned" (asaṅkhata) means not made or produced by a coming together, a meeting, or a combination—that is, by the gathering of conditions characterized by the convergence of requisite factors. "Deathless" (amata) means that there is no death (mata) in this.
Or, when this has been attained, there is no death for the person; thus it is "deathless" (*amata*).

Although in all instances here the application of the word *dhamma* is shown through such expressions as "I renounce the well-expounded *dhamma*," nevertheless, even when stated without joining it with the word *dhamma*, it is not that there is no renunciation;
thus [it is said] "I renounce the well-expounded," and so forth.
It should be understood that even when this is said, there is indeed a renunciation of the training.

Furthermore, it should be known that the application of the word *dhamma* in the phrase "the well-expounded Dhamma" (*svākkhātaṃ dhammaṃ*) and so forth is intended to show that the words "well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*) and the others function as qualifiers of *dhamma*.
Regarding the expression "even for a single dhamma-aggregate," here [it refers to] "the first dhamma-aggregate, the second dhamma-aggregate..."

The names of the *dhammakkhandhas* (sections of the Dhamma) should be understood through such passages as, "the section of the Dhamma consisting of questions" and "the section of the Dhamma consisting of answers.
"Well-practiced" (*suppaṭipanna*) means well-practiced because one has practiced according to the instructions within the well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya.
It is so called because, by practicing via the Middle Way without falling into either extreme, one abandons the faults of crookedness, curvature, and tortuousness of body, speech, and mind.
Because he has practiced correctly, he is "one who has practiced straightly. *Ñāya* is said to be Nibbāna, because it is understood, penetrated, and realized by means of the Noble Path and so forth;
because he has practiced for that purpose, he is "one who has practiced according to the method.

Because he has practiced in such a way that others, out of appreciation for his virtues, perform respectful services toward him such as rising from their seats, he is "one who has practiced with propriety."
In terms of pairs, the one standing on the first path and the one standing in the fruit constitute one pair; thus there are four pairs of persons (*purisayuga*).

Here, however, it should be understood that although one ought to say "the Saṅgha consists of the four pairs of persons," the designation was made without eliding the case-ending, saying "four" instead. For [the term] *catupurisayuga* means "that in which there are four pairs of persons."

The Saṅgha is what is spoken of. "Eight persons" (aṭṭhapurisapuggala) means that, by way of individual persons, there are exactly eight persons according to this method: one standing in the first path and one standing in the fruit, and so on.
That wherein these eight persons reside is the "eight-person Saṅgha. And here, the words "person" (purisa) and "individual" (puggala) are synonymous.
However, this was said with reference to those who are to be converted (*veneyya*).
Regarding the terms such as *āhuneyya*: "that which is to be offered after having been brought" is *āhuna*;

this is a designation for the four requisites that should be brought even from afar and given to those possessed of virtue. One is "fit to receive that offering" because of making it yield great fruit.
The Saṅgha is worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya*). Alternatively, it is *āhavanīya* because even from afar one comes and offers all one's possessions therein;

or it is *āhavanīya* because it is worthy of being offered to by Sakka and others. Furthermore, this is the "offering-fire" (*āhavanīyo aggi*) of the Brahmins, according to their doctrine, wherein what is offered bears great fruit.
If it is called *āhavanīya* because of the great fruitfulness of what is offered, then it is the Saṅgha alone.
The Āhavanīya fire. For an offering made to the Saṅgha is of great fruit. As it is said:
"Though a person might tend the sacrificial fire in the forest for a hundred years, yet if one were to honor for even a moment one whose self is cultivated..."
“That very worship is better than a hundred years of sacrifice.
In another Nikāya, the word *āhavanīyo* is found; here, it is identical in meaning to the word *āhuneyyo*, though there is a slight difference in their phonetic form (*byañjana*).
Furthermore, regarding the term *pāhuneyya*, the word *pāhuṇa* refers to dear and agreeable kinsmen and friends who have arrived from the cardinal and intermediate directions.
There is the guest-offering prepared with honor for the sake of [the Sangha].
Setting aside even such [offerings] intended for those dear friends and relatives who have arrived as guests, it is proper to give them to the Sangha alone; the Sangha alone is fit to receive them.
For there is no guest equal to the Sangha. Indeed, he (the Buddha) appears only once in the interval between two Buddhas, and [his appearance] is uninterrupted.
One who is endowed with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) which produce what is dear and agreeable is thus worthy of being given hospitality to, and worthy of receiving hospitality;
hence, he is "one worthy of hospitality" (*pāhuneyya*).
It is called a "sacrificial gift" (*dakkhiṇā*) because by means of it, beings increase with the intended attainments and [proceed] to the next world.
The gift that should be given with faith is worthy of that offering; or, because it purifies through the production of great fruit, it is "worthy of offerings" (*dakṣiṇeyya*).

Because he is worthy of the act of joining the palms in reverential salutation performed by the entire world, having placed both hands upon his head, he is "one to whom the añjali is made. He is called "the unsurpassed field of merit," being peerless for the whole world.

It is a place for the growth of merit. Just as the place where a king’s or a minister’s rice or barley grows is called a "king’s rice field" or a "barley field," so too the Saṅgha is the place for the growth of all the world’s merits.
For it is by depending on the Saṅgha that the various kinds of merits leading to welfare and happiness grow for the world.
Therefore, the Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

Here too, the application of the word *saṅgha* in all instances—such as in the phrase “the well-practiced Saṅgha”—is made for the purpose of showing that words like “well-practiced” (*suppaṭipanna*) function as qualifiers of the Saṅgha.
Consequently, it should be understood that even when one says, “I renounce the well-practiced [Saṅgha],” it constitutes a renunciation of the training (*sikkhā*).
Regarding the synonyms for training (*sikkhā*), however, the words *bhikkhu* and *bhikkhunī* by themselves—without the word *sikkhā*—are not designations for training;
therefore, it is only when one says "the training of a bhikkhu" (*bhikkhusikkhā*) or "the training of a bhikkhunī" (*bhikkhunīsikkhā*) that the primary meaning is established.

But since the higher training in virtue (*adhisīla*) and so forth are themselves training, the primary meaning is established even when one says "I renounce the higher training in virtue" (*adhisīlaṃ paccakkhāmi*) and so on.
Thus it is said. By the phrase "the first *pārājika*," etc., one should understand that this refers specifically to the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), not to the offenses (*āpatti*).

Among the synonyms for preceptor (*upajjhāya*), the statement "he who ordained me" and so forth is said with reference to one who, having been a preceptor, both conferred the going-forth (*pabbājesi*) and the full admission (*upasampādesi*).
"On whose account" means on whose basis, by whose primary influence, or by whose causal agency.
Or: that which has "root" (mūla) as its state of being the primary factor or its state of being the cause is "yassamūlikā," namely, going-forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā).

Although the word *mūla* here possesses a sense of expectancy, it should be understood as a derivative formation (*taddhitavutti*) because it is always expectant and thus conveys the meaning [of the compound].

Among the synonyms for "preceptor" (*ācariya*), however, one who ordains someone while acting solely as a preceptor without having first granted the status of a "teacher" (*upajjhāya*) is the "officiating preceptor" (*kammavācā-ācariya*).

Having offered the sacrifice, he ordained him; it is with reference to this that it is said, "He who gave me the going-forth, he who instructed me. By these two statements, both the preceptor for the going-forth (*pabbajjā-ācariya*) and the preceptor for full ordination (*upasampadā-ācariya*) are shown.
By the words, "The one depending on whom I live," the teacher of dependence (*nissaya-ācariya*) is shown.
Furthermore, by the phrase, "The one from whom I receive instruction," and so forth, the teacher of the Dhamma (*dhamma-ācariya*) is mentioned.
In that context, "I cause [him] to recite" means I cause him to recite the text. "I question thoroughly" means I question thoroughly about the meaning of the text already learned.
The meaning regarding the synonyms for *saddhivihārika* (co-resident) and so forth should be understood according to what has been stated.
Regarding the phrase "at his root," however, the meaning here should be understood as "in his presence."
"Okallaka" is a designation for those wretched people who are beset by the sufferings of hunger, thirst, and so forth; whose happiness is exhausted;
and who are deprived of bodily care such as bathing. "Moḷibaddha" means one with a topknot tied, or one who has removed his crown.
Although a lay follower (*upāsaka*) defined by two formulas could only have existed during the First Enlightenment, nevertheless, [the Buddha] spoke using the name current at that time.
It is stated as "a two-statement lay follower" (*dvevāciko upāsako*) in order to show that even when [the formula] has been spoken, there is indeed a renunciation of the training.
However, it should be understood that "two-statement" is merely a synonym here;
therefore, even when only so much is said—"Hold me to be a two-statement one"—it constitutes the head [of the matter]. The same applies to the remaining cases as well.
A *kumārakoti* is a very young novice, still in the stage of a child. A *cellaka* is a slightly older, junior novice.
A *ceṭaka* is one of middle age. A *moḷigalla* is a senior novice. However, *samaṇuddesa* is a general term for any novice.
It should be understood that terms such as *nigaṇṭhupaṭṭhāka* are synonyms for followers of other sects (*titthiya*).

“Immoral” (*dussīla*) means devoid of virtue, lacking in moral conduct. “Of evil nature” (*pāpadhamma*) means that, precisely because of his immorality, he possesses a base disposition and a lowly character.

“Of impure and suspicious conduct” (*asucisaṅkassarasamācāra*) means that, being impure due to the lack of purity in his bodily actions and so forth, his conduct is such that it must be regarded with suspicion.
For an immoral person, upon seeing anything inappropriate, becomes an object of suspicion for others, thinking, “This must have been done by such-and-such a one.”
[It] exists. Seeing monks consulting together for some business or other, one thinks, "Are they perhaps consulting because they know of the deed I have committed?
Thus, due to one's own suspicion, one's conduct becomes something that must be concealed. "One whose actions are concealed" means one whose actions must be hidden because they are shameful.
"Not a recluse" (assamaṇo) means not a true ascetic. In matters such as the taking of voting sticks (*salākā*), [one thinks], "I too am a recluse."
One who claims to be an ascetic through false profession; one who is not a celibate due to conduct that is not supreme;

one who claims to be a celibate through false profession by saying "I too am a celibate" on the Uposatha days and so forth; one who is internally rotten because of the entry of moral failure through putrid actions;
and one who is leaking because of the constant oozing of defilements such as lust from the six sense-doors.

Because it is covered with the refuse of lust and other defilements, and because it must be discarded by those possessed of virtue, it is "corrupt" (*kasambujāta*). "Worthless" (*koṇṭha*) is a designation for one who is immoral.
Regarding the statement, "Or whatever other synonyms for 'Buddha' there may be," and so forth, he says: "By those aspects...

by the synonyms for the Buddha and the others," because the pronoun *taṃ* (that) refers back to the same things referred to by the pronoun *yaṃ* (which), namely the synonyms for the Buddha and the rest.
But how are they expressed by terms such as "ākāra" (form) and so forth? To this he says: "For they are synonyms," and so on.

Let it be granted that for those things possessing shape, such as the Buddha and others, there is the indication of their shape; but how is it for those things devoid of shape, such as the Dhamma and the training (sikkhā)?
To this he says: "Or rather, because of the very shape of the renunciation of the training. For the synonyms are of the nature of the renunciation of the training.

“They are called ‘the formal acts of renouncing the training. Regarding the phrase “in this way indeed,” he said “just so” (*evameva*) to indicate that the particle *kho* here has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇatthe*).

54. “Overcome by fainting” means overcome by a swoon. To show a non-human being (*tiracchānagata*) capable of understanding the meaning of words, the passage beginning with “of the young Nāga” was stated. “With a three-root rebirth-linking” is stated by way of the majority of cases.
For not all deities possess rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) based on three roots (tihetuka), since there is also the possibility of those with two roots (dvihetuka).
"They know very quickly" is said because the deities' dwelling in the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is not as slow-witted as that of humans.
"Of one of the same class" means of a male; "of a different class" means of a female. "A non-Ariyan" refers to one other than the Magadhan mode of expression.

“*Davā*” means hastily. “*Ravā*” means having faltered. One should connect it thus: when one says something else intending to say something else, thinking, “I shall say another thing,” yet says, “I renounce the Buddha,” that is what is meant.
Alternatively, because of not understanding the proper timing of syllables or due to a lack of perfection in articulation, being unable to speak what should be spoken, one speaks otherwise;
this is called “speaking *ravā*. In both cases, it refers to one who intends to say something else.
Since it is the same as "speaking of something else," he asks: "What is the distinction from the former?
"He causes to recite" means that while reciting the text, he causes [the student] to learn something else; thus he causes to recite.
"He questions thoroughly" means that while questioning the meaning of the text, he questions the text itself. "He learns" means that he learns the text in the presence of another. "Recitation..."
"Does" means he recites the text he has mastered. "Describes" means that while commenting on the meaning of the text, he describes the text itself.
It is said to be "like a figure on a cloth" because the old man knows nothing or because his faculties are unperceived;
the meaning is that it is like a figure made of clay. "Of dull intelligence" is said because there is an absence of swift engagement with objects.
"Of slow progress" means one whose wisdom is heavy; that is to say, one of dull wisdom.
By the phrase "in every way," he shows the absence of the arising of such a thought as, "I shall cause this person to hear: 'I renounce the training.
For when such an arising of thought is absent, one cannot, by any means, produce such a vocal expression.
What is called "proclaiming" (sāvana) is not possible at all; therefore it was said: "In such cases as 'I renounce the Buddha,' etc. ... having made a vocal utterance, one does not proclaim it.
The commentary on the analysis of the renunciation of training (sikkhā-paccakkhāna-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) is finished. Commentary on the original formulation (mūla-paññatti-vaṇṇanā).
55. “Of that which is to be demonstrated” means of that which is to be uncovered and made manifest.
“By defilements” means by defilements such as shamelessness (*ahirika*) and so forth. “From here onwards” means from the word *duṭṭhulla*.

“Of that action” refers to the action consisting of the practice of sexual intercourse. “Seeing,” and so forth, is exactly according to the method already stated. “Of it” refers to sexual intercourse.
Because they are to be entered by pairs, it is called "the attainment of pairs" (*dvaya-dvaya-samāpatti*); thus he said, "because they are to be entered by two and two.

Because these beings have reached a state of similarity through the obsession of lust, they are "couples" (*mithuna*); this very thing is "sexual intercourse" (*methuna*), and that which is the nature of sexual intercourse is "the practice of sexual intercourse" (*methuna-dhamma*).
Thus he said, "of both who are impassioned," and so forth. In that context, "impassioned" means impassioned by the lust for sexual intercourse.

"Sārattānaṃ" means those who are excessively impassioned by that very lust. "Avassutānaṃ" means those who are soaked by the lust for sexual intercourse arising from intimacy with worldly pleasures and friends.
"Pariyuṭṭhitānaṃ" means those whose minds are enveloped by the arising of lust for sexual intercourse.
"Sadisānaṃ" means those who are similar [to one another] in their impassioned state and so forth.
Since the phrase "he indeed practices" (*paṭisevati nāma*) does not exist in the matrix (*mātikā*), he said, "He would practice... [etc.
...the matrix phrase," in order to show the reason for anyone who might wonder, "Why was 'he indeed practices' extracted?
This phrase "by means of a woman's sign" (*itthiyā nimittena*) is to be understood like "he goes by way of the path" (*maggena gacchati*). For just as in the case of "he goes by way of the path"...
When it is said, "he goes on the path" or "he goes in the path," this meaning is obtained;
likewise, when it is said, "he inserts by means of the female sign," this meaning is obtained: "he inserts the female sign" or "he inserts in the sign.
And this is stated for the most part to show the male's activity. In terms of its actual referent, "sign" (nimitta) and "genital organ" (aṅgajāta) are one and the same.
"Insertion" does not mean merely touching the outside; thus it is said: "in a place not touched by wind, which is not open space.
For one who causes [the object] to enter within is said to "insert," not one who touches it from the outside.
And "within" refers to a place not touched by wind, belonging to a sign that was originally completely closed off.
Now, in order to burn away every last trace of a place for defilement (*lesokāsa*), he says, "In the female organ there are four corners," and so forth,
showing the specific parts found in both the female and male organs that are capable of mutual contact at the time of entry.
For if one were to enter by touching with even a single part anywhere in a space not touched by the wind— that is, in a non-worldly space (*allokāsa*)— [the meditation would fail].
"It is called 'inserts. "In the middle" refers to the lower surface of the female organ when an opening has been made, such that one inserts [the member] without touching the four sides;
however, regarding the male organ, "in the middle" is said with reference to the tip.
"Above" refers to the region above the tip. And this [is measured] by the middle.

For one who inserts [the organ] after bending [the fingers], this is said with reference to the middle part of the upper side of the sexual organ, which resembles the back of the middle phalanx of a finger when one inserts it while having bent the middle phalanx of a finger.
"Inserting from below" means inserting while touching with the lower part of the female organ (*itthinimitta*). "Inserting by the middle" means...
Entering by touching the inner surface with the middle part. For one who inserts [the organ] without touching it in some places and then withdraws it, there is no *pārājika* offense;
however, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense, just as in the case of the severed head, for one who inserts and withdraws it without touching it when the mouth has been made round.
"Entering while touching with the middle part" means touching with the tip of the [organ].
“Inserting”: the connection is with “with the fingers bent on the back of the middle phalanx. Alternatively, it should be construed as:
“as if inserting [the finger] with the fingers bent on the back of the middle phalanx. “Having contracted” means having pierced it with the middle of the sign.
“With the upper part” means with the tip of the upper part of that which has been contracted. Now, regarding the male sign among those mentioned below...
Regarding the phrase "in six places above," having separately taken four sides according to the immediately preceding statement, he says "therein" (*tattha*) and so forth,
showing the tenfold division of places in the male sign. However, below, without taking those [sides] separately,
but rather by taking some of them that are obtainable individually through the commonality of the expression "four sides," [he speaks of] six.
The positions have been stated. "For one inserting it like a balance-beam" means for one inserting it straight.
"Arisen in the sign" means arisen in one's own [sexual] sign. "A leather peg" refers to the very skin that has protruded at the sign; they also call it an "eruption.
Since even what is born in the sign, such as a leather peg, is indeed the sign itself, he said, "there is an offense of pārājika. "One whose bodily sensitivity is impaired."

The statement "having lost the bodily sensitivity" (*naṭṭhakāyappasāda*) is for the purpose of showing the non-existence of the state of being clung-to (*upādinnabhāva*). For this very reason, it says:

"either a dead hide or a dried pustule. For if there were still a state of being clung-to, even when the bodily sensitivity is destroyed, there would be an offense of defeat (*pārājika*), just as in the case of a sense base where the faculty has been impaired;
however, [this is not so] in the case of a dead hide or a dried pustule.

An offense involving what is not clung-to (anupādinnaka) against that which is clung-to (upādinnaka) is indeed a *pārājika* offense. For this very reason, it says, "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
It is stated as a *dukkaṭa* because it is impossible to claim there is no offense for one acting in such a manner;

however, even when the female characteristic has perished, if its state of being clung-to remains, it is still a *pārājika* offense. This is because it is stated that there is a *pārājika* offense when [the body] is dead, or when it is mostly decomposed.
By the phrase "through the gratification of sexual intercourse," bodily contact with passion is excluded. For if there were bodily contact with passion, it would indeed be a *saṅghādisesa* offense;
however, since even the seeds do not count as a "sign" (*nimitta*), it is stated that it is merely a *dukkaṭa*. For it is said: "He inserts a sign into a sign."

Now, because this talk of sexual intercourse is unseemly, he spoke the words beginning with "And this talk of sexual intercourse" in order to instruct that those who speak or listen to such a topic should practice in this way.
Because talk of sexual intercourse is a cause for the increase of lust and is a subject for laughter,
[he teaches] the application of attention to repulsiveness and so forth in order to avoid both of these.
He applies himself. For by means of attention to repulsiveness, lust is turned back; and when perceptions such as that of being a recluse are present, laughter is turned back.
"Out of compassion for beings" means for the sake of protecting beings from the sufferings of the states of misery and so forth.
"Out of sympathy for the world" means out of sympathy directed toward the world of sentient beings.
"Having covered the mouth" means having closed the mouth. If, through some negligence, one should ever smile even slightly, then the dignity [of the teacher] might be disturbed;
therefore, at such a time, for the sake of not violating that state of dignity, one should sit with the mouth covered by a cloth—this is the intended meaning.
Alternatively, "having covered the mouth" means having closed the mouth.
The meaning is this: one should not sit with the mouth covered by a seed-vessel (bījaka) while laughing; this is the intended sense here.
*Dantavidaṃsakaṃ* means showing the teeth and opening [the mouth] wide. *Gabbhitena* means without falling into contraction, that is, with a spirit of enthusiasm.
For if one were to fall into contraction, thinking, "I am speaking such unseemly words," [the rule would not apply].
The exposition of the meaning would not otherwise be possible; therefore, the intention is that it should be spoken by one who has generated such enthusiasm, thinking:
"If even a Perfectly Enlightened One like him spoke in this way, how much more so should I?
"By one who is a counterpart to the Teacher" means by one who is like the Teacher, resembling the Teacher—this is the meaning.
The commentary on the original formulation (*mūlapaññatti*) is concluded. The commentary on the subsequent formulation (*anupaññatti*):
"Among animals" (*tiracchānesu gatāya*) means arisen among animals. For those known as animals include even those that are extremely small.
There are those for whom even the insertion of a sesame seed is not possible within their vaginal passages; therefore, not all female animals constitute an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*).
Thus, specifying those female animals that are encountered as being capable of such insertion, he said: "And here, it is only those that constitute an offense involving defeat," and so forth.
The verse beginning with "The snake and the fish" is an *apadāna* (illustrative example).
These were established by the ancients for the purpose of showing the lower limit of the grounds for defeat (*pārājika*).

In that context, regarding the term "snake" (*ahi*), since all species of serpents are included by way of this designation of genus, it is said: "By the inclusion of 'snake'... [and so on]... the long-snouted species (*dīghajāti*) is included.
In that context, "bull-snakes" (*gonasa*) are a specific kind of snake, upon whose backs large circular markings are visible. The inclusion of "fish" (*maccha*)...
He said, "The phrase 'of the water-born class' is a defining characteristic," thus stating: "By the inclusion of fish... [etc. ...the water-born class is comprised.
For that very reason, although frogs and turtles possess feet, they are included because they belong to the water-born class.
"Shape of the mouth" means the shape of the skin of the lips. "It goes into the category of wounds" means it is subsumed under the classification of wounds.
The intention is that [the penis] is included within the nine openings of the body.

Regarding the grave offense (*thullaccaya*) in the case of a wound, it should be understood by way of this passage: "If one inserts [the penis] into a non-path through a non-path, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
For in that sutta, it is stated that there is a *thullaccaya* for one who, having inserted [the penis] into one of two mixed wounds, withdraws it through the second.
And it will say: “In accordance with this sutta, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is to be understood everywhere in the summary of the wound.
The mention of the cock is an indicative term for all species of birds; thus he said: “By the mention of the cock... [etc.
...the species of birds is included. The mention of the bear should also be regarded as an indicative term for the species of quadrupeds.

Therefore he said: "By the inclusion of marrow and blood... four-footed animals are comprised. They say that what are called "tree-dogs" are squirrels (*kalandaka*). *Maṅgusa* means *naṅgula* (a type of lizard).
The word *parājita*, having undergone the strengthening of the prefix and the change of the letter *t* to *k*, becomes *pārājika*.

It is said that it has been defined: “‘Pārājika’ means one who is defeated. Regarding the statement, “In some instances it refers to an offense—as in ‘one should accuse another with a *pārājika* offense,’ and so forth;
in other instances it refers to a training rule (*sikkhāpada*)—this should be understood by looking at this [passage],” it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*.
It is called *pārājika* because it causes defeat (*parājayati*). Furthermore, by the word *pārājika* used as an agent-noun (*kattusādhana*), it refers to the training rule.

Showing that "offense" (āpatti) is what is being spoken of, he said: "He who transgresses it," and so forth. Showing, however, that the person (puggala) is expressed by the term *pārājika* through a karmasādhana derivation, he said:
"Because the person is defeated," and so forth. Indeed, it is with reference to this very meaning [that it is said]: "The person who has fallen into that offense is defeated, having incurred defeat."

It is with reference to this meaning [that it was said]. For by the passage beginning "fallen, defeated," etc., the sense that the person who has committed that offense has fallen, is defeated, and has met with defeat is understood;
however, it is not the case that the person becomes what is called "one who has undergone a pārājika" (a defeated one).

It is with reference to this meaning that [the statement] should be understood. Indeed, even in the *Parivāra*, the verses are not intended merely to show the derivation of the word *pārājika* as applied to a person.
This has been stated because it was explained in the context of analyzing the etymological divisions of the terms *pārājika* and so forth among the rules for offenses (*āpatti-vutti*).
For this is the meaning of the verse from the *Parivāra*:

regarding what is called an "offense that is a *pārājika*" (*āpatti-pārājika*) among persons, offenses, training rules, and *pārājikas*, a person who commits such an offense is defeated (*parājita*), has fallen into defeat, has fallen away from the true Dhamma, and is ruined.
He is defeated and excluded; once that person has been removed, there is no further communal living with him—such as the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremonies—and for that reason, it is said:
"for this cause, this is called an offense involving defeat (āpatti-pārājika).
This, however, is the summary of the meaning here: because one is defeated by this, therefore it is called a Pārājika.
*Paribhaṭṭho* means fallen away from the Dispensation; the meaning is "deprived. *Chinno* means cut off in the middle.
*Saddhiṃ yojanāya* means together with the word-connection (*padayojanā*). "The fourfold Saṅgha-kamma" refers to the fourfold formal act by way of *apalokana* (announcement) and so forth.
*Sīmāparicchinnehi* means by those included within a single boundary. Those called *pakatattā* (of normal status) are those who have not committed a *pārājika* offense.
"Neither fallen nor suspended. "Even fivefold" means even that which is fivefold by way of the enumeration of the origins (*nidāna*) and so forth.

With the exception of those specifically permitted—such as for those who were previously barbers—all remaining training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are stated to be "because they must be trained in equally by all modest persons," since they are not to be transgressed by any modest individuals whatsoever. "Equally" (*sama*).
"Simultaneously" means either together or all at once. "Because it is to be trained in" means because it is to be trained in by way of not transgressing, through study, interrogation, and so forth.
Regarding the training precepts of the ascetic life, because one must not think, "This is not to be trained in by you," it is said:
"Not even a single thing is seen outside of that. This connects with the phrase "that which was stated."
56. By the phrase "not only the sign of a woman," it is shown that the sign of a woman alone is not the basis for a *pārājika* offense;
rather, the signs of those with both sexual organs (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*), and men are also bases for a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, by the phrase "and not only of a human woman," it is shown that the sign of a human woman alone is the basis for a *pārājika* offense.
This shows that even the sign of a non-human female, a female animal, a hermaphrodite human, and so forth, is not a basis for a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the statement, “‘It is not even a basis’—this rejects [the case of] gold, silver, and so forth, which arose in connection with the mention of a non-human female,” this is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries; however, it does not appear to be reasonable. For from this...

Previously, there was no mention of taking hold of non-human women (*amanussitthi*), by which such a contingency might have arisen. For it was only now, with the statement beginning "three women," etc., that the taking hold of non-human women was mentioned;
and yet, a contingency involving objects made of gold, silver, and so forth, is not appropriate through the taking hold of non-human women.
Having classified [sentient beings] into three types according to their birth—human, non-human, and animal—the sentient beings who constitute the basis for a *pārājika* offense...
Because by means of the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), the possibility of [the offense applying to] objects made of gold, silver, and so forth is excluded.
For thus, in the matrix (*mātikā*), without specifying anyone among women or men, or humans or non-humans, it is stated only in this general way: "one should engage in sexual intercourse.
And in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for that, the matrix-word "he engages in" (*paṭisevati*)—

Having extracted [the meaning], the manner of practice alone is shown by the statement: "Whoever inserts a sign into a sign, or the male organ into the male organ—even if only as much as a sesame seed—that person is said to 'practice'";
however, the bases for the offense of defeat (pārājika), namely human, non-human, or animal beings;
females, males, eunuchs, or hermaphrodites; and the specific supports for the signs, have not been definitively specified.
Therefore, there might be doubt as to whether the basis for an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) is the sign of a woman alone, or whether it belongs to others as well;
furthermore, the conventional term "sign" (*nimitta*) is indeed applicable to images made of gold, silver, and so forth. For this very reason, in the cases of the Vinaya rulings, it is said:
"He touched the sign of a painted image with his organ," and "He touched the sign of a wooden doll with his organ."

It has been stated; therefore, because of the commonality of the "sign" (*nimitta*), someone might have the suspicion: "Is the sign of things made of gold, silver, and so forth a ground for a *pārājika* offense, or is it not?
For this very reason, it is said: "He had scruples (*kukkucca*) regarding objects such as paintings on plaster.
Therefore, in order to dispel that suspicion and to define the sentient being as the specific ground for a *pārājika* offense, [the following is stated].

Having divided beings into three categories— human, non-human, and so forth— according to their class (*jāti*), the Blessed One analyzes and demonstrates those beings who constitute the basis for a *pārājika* offense.

Therefore, it must be stated that by means of the commonality of the "sign" (*nimitta*), he excludes signs made of gold, silver, and so forth, which are included under the general category of "not being the [proper] basis."

The word *magge* is used in the locative sense; thus he said, "The meaning should be understood as 'in the three paths'. By the phrase "in all cases" (*evaṃ sabbattha*), it is indicated that even in the case of the expression "two paths," the meaning should be understood as "in two paths.
The commentary on the supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) is finished.
The commentary on the first tetrad discussion.
57. Regarding the phrase "assā" (of it), he says "hoti" (it is) in order to show that it is a verbal form and to demonstrate its meaning.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, an alternative interpretation is also presented, stating: "The word 'assā' refers to the person, and the remainder of the statement is shown as 'hoti'.

This is not the more excellent interpretation. For if the remainder of the statement were intended, one should have simply said "hoti"; by that very [fact of saying "assā"], [the sense is already conveyed].
The phrase "there is another alternative meaning" is used as a remainder of the statement.
Regarding the expression "only for one who consents," "consenting" here means the arising of a mind desiring to engage in sexual intercourse; thus he says, "for one possessing the mind of engagement.
"They strive against [the defilements]" refers to those monks who desire training.
"In the *Gaṇṭhipada* it is said: 'They seek out [and assist] someone who is the opposite of the state of immorality.
However, the meaning here should be understood as follows: they seek out and search for some enemy who is the opposite of their own hostile person.
For adversaries, wishing to destroy their own enemy, [seek] some enemy who is the opposite of that [enemy]."

They desire one who approaches as a companion. Since the enemies of kings and so forth will be discussed later, he spoke thus—“enemies of monks are monk-enemies”—in order to show the meaning in accordance with that context.
However, if it were stated as “enemies of a monk are monk-enemies,” then kings and others who are enemies of a monk would also be included here.
"They are grouped together" means that enemies of the king and so forth would not need to be mentioned separately;
however, in other contexts, the meaning "enemies of a monk" (*bhikkhu-paccatthikā*) is certainly obtained, just as in the expression "enemies of the Dispensation" (*sāsana-paccatthikā*).
"Possessed by envy" means overcome by envy, which is characterized by an inability to endure the gains, honor, and so forth of others. "Without resistance" means...
"Free from agitation" means having grasped it in such a way that it is unable to move or turn.
"Joining together" means connecting it with the urinary passage.
"At that moment" refers to the moment of insertion; the time of insertion is from the tip down to the base.
It is said [thus]. "Consenting" means the arising of a mind intent on indulgence; therefore, it is said: "he brings to presence a mind intent on indulgence. At the time of entry:
at the time when the male organ has entered without remainder as much of the place as is capable of admitting its entry.
The time of remaining is the interval between the beginning of the extraction of that which has thus entered and the moment it is fully withdrawn. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*...

The phrase "at the time of the emission of semen" is said with reference to the moment when, having reached the emission of semen, one has completely desisted despite striving in every way and remains so.
"Extraction" (uddharaṇa) refers to the time of drawing it out to the tip; thus he says:
"he establishes the intention for enjoyment at the time of extraction. "A pit of embers" means a heap of embers. Non-consent at such a time [is required].
He said, "This [state] is not the object for everyone," beginning with the words, "For this one who has thus begun insight," and so forth.
"By eleven fires" means by the eleven fires consisting of lust, hatred, delusion, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
For lust and the others are called "fires" in the sense of burning; they indeed consume whoever possesses them.
And they become great fevers difficult to extinguish. Furthermore, since the Blessed One indeed desires the restraint of persons who are difficult to manage, he said:
"While thwarting the desires of his adversaries. "Of him" (assa) means of one who, as previously described, possesses those qualities and does not consent [to their misconduct].
The commentary on the first tetrad is finished.
Commentary on the two hundred and sixty-nine tetrads: 59–60.

Regarding the phrase "unexplained signs," he says: "They are expressed by the word 'unexplained' through the elision of the latter member [of the compound], as in the case of ‘fox-jackal’ (*soṇasiṅgāla*) and so forth."
"Unexplained sign": that which has an unexplained sign is "unexplained-sign.
Because they lack qualifying adjectives such as "they are awake," they are called "pure tetrads.
"Teachers of the same school" refers to the resident pupils of a single teacher. "In the great terror" means during the terror caused by the Brahmin Tissa.
The region beyond the Ganges is "Aparagaṅgā. *Vata* is a particle used in the sense of censure.

To the question of what should be done by one who does not relinquish [the offense], he says: "It should be listened to at all times," and so forth. By the phrase "those who hold the Vinaya in high esteem," the reason for the necessity of honoring the legal determination (*vinicchaya*) that will be stated below is expressed.
"Having encompassed everything" means having included the entire domain of offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*) without exception.
"Having taken. "Having cut off the stream" means having cut off the stream of transgression within the sphere of a *pārājika* offense.
It is said, "But here the shadow of a *pārājika* is not seen," because it has not been formally laid down as such and because there is an absence of logical consistency (*yutti*).

Some, however, say, "He did not lay down a *pārājika* rule for that case because its state of being half-chewed is difficult to determine"; but that is not a valid reason, for difficulty of determination is not [an obstacle to the establishment of a rule].
The reason for not making a formal rule (apaññatti) regarding "mostly gnawed" and so forth is that these cases are equally difficult to determine.
For if something is gnawed by even slightly more or slightly less than half, it is still reckoned as "mostly gnawed" rather than "not gnawed";
thus, like "half-gnawed," "mostly gnawed" and the others are likewise difficult to distinguish.
Furthermore, if even half-cut [wood] were by its very nature a field for a *pārājika* offense, the Blessed One would not have prescribed that a *pārājika* is difficult to judge in such a case.
Now, having supported the judgment already made by the Elder, he shows another reason for that matter:
He said, “Moreover,” and so forth. He spoke thus to show that if even a tiny streak of flesh remains in the sign (nimitte), it is still considered “mostly consumed” (yebhuyyakkhāyita);
however, once the sign has been entirely consumed, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Furthermore, he stated, “Beyond that, there is no grave offense (thullaccaya).
Alternatively, what is called “mostly consumed” refers to the anus, the urinary passage, and the mouth.
It should be understood that eating [meat] having passed two portions and continuing up to the end of the third portion constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
furthermore, eating beyond the third portion and continuing up to the end of the fourth portion must also be understood as an object of wrong-doing.
This is to be understood specifically in regard to a dead body, based on the statement: "The dead [body] is for the most part unexposed," and so forth.
"In the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: 'Even the passage beginning with "If the sign appears entirely...
and so forth, all refers specifically to a living body. However, someone has written: 'That should be examined and understood. What is there to examine here?
For since this is an addition concerning only the living body, the determination [of the sign] that applies to a dead body is not included."
And because it will be explained separately later. For that very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* as well, it says:

"If, on a path of the kind already described, even when the skin and so forth of a living body have been completely severed without remainder, only the mere configuration of the sign remains apparent—therein, even in the case of the genitals, [if there is] a bone or a sensitive part of the body..."
Even for one who inserts a boil or a piece of skin-callus, if there is the intention of sexual intercourse, it is a *pārājika* offense;
for one who inserts a withered boil whose bodily tissues have perished, or a dead piece of skin, or a hair, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If the entire path has been completely torn open without leaving even the mere shape of the sign, then by reason of the effort made therein, it is a *thullaccaya* according to the classification of a wound.
The analysis as previously described was shown specifically regarding a living body.
"Completely devoured" means that the skin and hide situated on the outside of the area of the sign have been entirely cut away and made to resemble what has been eaten by dogs, jackals, and the like;
for this very reason, it says, "there is no skin or hide. However, within the flesh of the sign...
Because the skin and hide still exist, it is said that "the shape of the sign is discerned. For this very reason, it says, "entry occurs.
Regarding the phrase "without leaving behind the shape of the sign": this means without leaving behind the skin, hide, flesh, and so forth, which remain in the form of the sign.
Having shown the specific characteristics found in a living body, [the text now] shows the specific characteristics found in a dead body.
Showing this, he said, “But in the case of dead bodies,” and so forth.
However, by the statement “in the case of living human bodies,” etc., it is understood that even the eyes and other parts fall under the category of a wound;

thus, treating them as identical to a wound, a *thullaccaya* offense is stated for damaging the eyes and so on as well. And their inclusion in the category of a wound is [stated in the passage]: “The nine doors...”

This is to be understood according to such suttas as "The great forest" (*mahāvaṇa*). However, regarding the *dukkaṭa* offense for [cutting] the eyes, ears, or sores of animals, one must accept it based on the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

For just as there is no difference among humans, non-humans, and animals in terms of the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth being grounds for a *pārājika* offense, so too there is no difference between the eyes and other [parts] in their being grounds for a *thullaccaya* or other [offenses].
There must be a distinction [between the cases]. Regarding the wound, the *thullaccaya* offense is stated in general terms as:
"If one inserts it where it should not be inserted, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*"; however, there is no specific qualification such as "of human beings.
And if there were to be no *thullaccaya* for wounds of animals, then [in the case of] a frog with the mouth of a moth...

Regarding the shape of the face, one should not say that there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) based on a mere summary of the wound; for this has been stated [elsewhere]. Therefore, the teachers of the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentaries) are the authority in this matter.
Indeed, the teachers of the *Aṭṭhakathā* understand the intention of the Blessed One. For this very reason it was said:

"The Dhamma and the Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha, and they are understood exactly so by his sons," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of human beings" (*manussānaṃ*), it refers to women, men, eunuchs, and those with both sexual organs.
This has been stated by way of generality. "In the bladder-sheaths" means in the bladder-pouches and in the sheaths of the male organs.
A "fresh body" should be understood as one that has not yet begun to putrefy through states such as bloating (*uddhumātaka*). Therefore he said:

Regarding the phrase "she abandons," the meaning here should be understood as she abandons both the status of being a ground for a *pārājika* offense and the status of being a ground for a *thullaccaya* offense.
The connection is with the words "of dead animals.
Since it was stated that a *thullaccaya* occurs for one who inserts [the organ] into the vaginal opening out of lust for sexual intercourse, he said, "without inserting it into the vaginal opening."
"Not inserting into a woman" means not inserting into the female organ. By saying "not inserting," he shows the absence of the intention to insert.

However, for one who touches [the organ] from the outside with the intention to insert, since it constitutes a preliminary act (*pubbapayoga*) to sexual intercourse, there must necessarily be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"If he touches organ with organ, it is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*)"—this [refers to the case where], "And not... [as follows].
This was stated by way of this sutta: “Monks, with a lustful mind, the genitals should not be touched; whoever should touch them, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
And therein, showing the method for an alternative interpretation of the meaning for some, he said:

Although it was stated [in some sources] as "the body," nevertheless, in order to show the absence of the expression "with the mouth through lust for sexual intercourse" in the other commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it was said, "But in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*... Because it was not stated as "with the genitals," it was said, "without distinction.
Now, demonstrating the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* in harmony with the canonical text (*pāḷi*), he said, "As for what was stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*," and so forth.

"Otherwise, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that for one who touches [the body] by way of the natural opening, there would be an offense of wrong-doing, just as in the case of grasping the horns and so forth.

Regarding “an offense of wrong-doing due to the lust for physical contact”: for one who touches [her] with the lust for physical contact, whether by way of the sign or by way of the natural opening, there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing.

Commentary on the analysis of the fourfold group concerning the spread rug (saṇṭhata-catukka): 61–2.
“Of one who has entered the path” means of one who has initiated insight (vipassaka). “Appropriated” is said with reference to the body-faculty (kāyindriya).

"He touches with what is clung-to" (*upādinnakena phusatī*) means "he is touched by, or struck by, what is clung-to. Thus, the meaning should be understood in the passive sense through the elision of the *ya*-suffix.

thus the meaning should be seen here. "They will cast a hint" (*lesaṃ oḍḍessantī*) means they will give rise to a hint.

"It will imagine" is what is meant. In the phrase "of the spread" (*santhatāya*), a term for the whole is applied to a single part, as in expressions such as "the cloth is burnt. For indeed, even when it is only one part of the cloth...

When a cloth is burnt, people say, "The cloth is burnt. In the same way, when a woman has spread [a garment] over any part of her body, such as the vaginal passage, she is called "one who has spread [a garment].
Therefore he said, "One who has spread [a garment] (santhatā)," and so forth.

Regarding the term "having wrapped around," this refers to binding after placing garments and the like outside without inserting them inside. This is by means of applying the designation for the whole to a single part.

Since even a monk is called "one who has been rubbed," he said, "What is meant by 'rubbed' (santhata)," and so forth. "When it has entered to whatever extent" means when it has entered even to the size of a sesame seed.
Even when the eye and so forth are rubbed, it remains exactly as it was in its original state; therefore he said, "In the case of a field for a thullaccaya offense, there is a thullaccaya;

However, if he touches the post itself—which has entered slightly inside—with his penis, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
"Its surface" refers to the inner surface of the bamboo, reed, or similar opening.

In the *Vinītavatthu*: "At that time, a certain bhikkhu went to a charnel ground and, seeing a headless corpse, inserted his penis—which was not touching—into the mouth which had been turned upward. He became anxious... [as before] ...It was said:

“It is said: ‘If, having made it go into the air, one inserts it and then withdraws it, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Regarding ‘outside the stump’:

this refers to a bamboo joint or the like that has been inserted inside but protrudes outside. Commentary on the Section on Offenses and Non-offenses (Āpattānāpattivāra-vaṇṇanā): 66. "There is no making of a formal admission" means that there is no need for questioning.

For one who has committed an act of defilement does not deserve to be questioned in this manner: "With what state of mind did you commit the transgression? Did you do it knowingly, or rather unknowingly? "Right there" refers to Vesālī.

"In the great forest" (mahāvane) means exactly that. By the word "etc. in "trembling of the body, etc.," one includes the yellow color of the eyes and so forth. "Situated in the gall-bladder" refers to the heart and lungs.
It is situated within the body, resting upon the liver flesh, inside a gall-bladder that resembles the pod of a large *kosātaki* gourd.
"Agitated" means having moved out from the gall-bladder and emerged externally.

Desiring to throw him out, they manifest a terrifying personal form with a white face, a blue belly, deep red hands and feet, a massive head, and blazing eyes; or they let out a terrifying sound;
or, while he is still speaking, they thrust their hand into his mouth and crush the flesh of his heart, whereby that being becomes insane.
One whose mind is deranged. For this very reason, it says: "or by showing terrifying objects," and so forth.
In that context, "terrifying" means capable of producing fear, trepidation, and horripilation in beings merely by being seen.
"He is constantly insane" refers to one from whose gall-bladder the bile has moved and issued outwards.

It has been said. However, it should be understood that one whose bile, having become disturbed, remains within the gall-bladder itself and does not exit externally, regains consciousness from time to time and does not remain constantly insane.

*Pakiṇṇaka* refers to the method of miscellaneous topics. *Samuṭṭhāna* means the cause of arising. The mention of "action" (*kiriya*) and so forth is merely illustrative;
