For it is the offense itself that is spoken of under the heading of "training rule.
Indeed, the origins and so forth pertain to the offense, not to the training rule. Among these six origins, the first three...
The former [offenses] are without thought; the latter are with thought. Among them, offenses arise through one, two, three, four, or six origins;
there is no such thing as an offense that arises from five origins. In that regard, an offense arising from one origin arises through the fourth, fifth, and sixth origins, but not...
By another [method]. Those with two origins arise from the first and fourth, the second and fifth, the third and sixth, and the fourth and sixth origins, and not from others.
Those with three origins arise from the first three origins and the last three origins, and not from others. Those with four origins...
It originates through the first, third, fourth, and sixth origins, and through the second, third, fifth, and sixth origins, but not through any others.
That which has six origins originates through all six.
Regarding the statement, "There is a training rule that has six origins," it should be understood that here too, the offense is spoken of by way of the heading "training rule."

For this very reason he will say: "All of this is applicable to an offense, but in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the teaching has been set forth under the heading of training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
"Arising from six" means arising by way of the six [bases] such as the body, or that which has six origins; thus it is called "six-origin.
There is also that which has four origins: namely, body, body-and-speech, body-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind.
These four—namely, speech, body-and-speech, speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind—or these four origins belong to this [offense], thus it is "originating from four" (*catusamuṭṭhāna*).

There is also that which originates from three: either these three—body, speech, and body-and-speech—or these three origins—body-and-mind, speech-and-mind, and body-speech-and-mind—belong to this, thus it is "originating from three" (*tisamuṭṭhāna*).
Showing both those originating from two sources and those originating from one source by way of the headings of their origins, he said: “There is an origin consisting of the *kathina*,” and so forth.

For there are thirteen headings of origins: the origin consisting of the first *pārājika*, the origin consisting of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), the origin consisting of acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*), the origin consisting of formal admonition (*samanubhāsana*), the origin consisting of the *kathina*, the origin consisting of wool (*eḷakaloma*), and the origin consisting of the purification of feet (*padasodhamma*).

[The offenses] originating from traveling on a journey, originating from a caravan of thieves, originating from teaching the Dhamma, originating from reporting what has actually occurred, originating from causing a thief to leave [the community], and originating from not being authorized.

In that context, by the phrase "there is that which originates in six ways," the offense originating from acting as a go-between is stated. By the phrase "there is that which originates in four ways,"...
By this, however, the originations from travel (*addhānasamuṭṭhāna*) and the originations from what is not permitted (*ananuññātasamuṭṭhāna*) are included.

For that which originates by means of the first, third, fourth, and sixth [rules] is an origination from travel; whereas that which originates by means of the second, third, fifth, and sixth is an origination from what is not permitted.

By the phrase "there is an origination from three," the origination from taking what is not given (*adinnādānasamuṭṭhāna*) and the origination from speaking of reality (*bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhāna*) are included.
It is included. For that which originates from the three origins involving the mind is the origin of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*).
However, that which originates from the three origins not involving the mind is the origin of announcing [the robe] as already finished (*bhūtārocana*).
By the phrase "there is the origin of the Kathina," etc., he includes both the two-origin and the one-origin offenses under the general heading of the remaining origins. For it is thus:

That which originates through the third and sixth [factors] is called "origination by means of the kaṭhina. That which originates through the first and fourth [factors] is "origination by means of sheep’s wool.

That which originates through the sixth alone is "origination by means of relinquishing the burden" (*dhuranikkhepa*); it is also known by the name "origination by means of formal admonition" (*samanubhāsana*).

Furthermore, among those included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are the origins of the first *pārājika*, the *padasodhamma*, the theft of a needle, the teaching of the Dhamma, and the instigation of thieves.
That which originates from both body and mind is the origin of the first *pārājika*.
That which originates from the second and the fifth is the origin of the *padasodhamma*.
That which originates from the fourth and the sixth is the origin of the *theyyasattha*. That which originates from the fifth alone is the origin of the *dhammadesanā*.
That which originates from the fifth and sixth [categories] should be understood as the "origination by way of causing a thief to rise.

Having thus shown all the training rules (sikkhāpada) in thirteen ways by way of their mode of origination (samuṭṭhāna), he now says, "In that regard, some originate from action (kiriyā)," etc., showing them in five ways by way of action.
Therein, "some" (kiñci) refers to the heading of the training rules.

One speaks of an offense. Therefore, that which occurs for one who transgresses by means of body or speech—as in the case of digging the earth and so forth—is said to "originate from action" (*kiriyato samuṭṭhāti*).
That which occurs for one who fails to do what ought to be done by body or speech—as in the case of the first *kaṭhina* offense—is said to "originate from non-action" (*akiriyato samuṭṭhāti*).
That which occurs both for one who does it and for one who does not do it—as in the case of [approaching] a woman who is not a relative...

That which arises from both action and non-action—such as the offense incurred by a nun’s receiving a robe from the hand [of a man]—is said to originate from both *kiriya* (action) and *akiriya* (non-action).

That which may occur whether one is acting or not acting—such as the offense of receiving money—is said to originate sometimes from *kiriya* and sometimes from *akiriya*. That which occurs whether one is acting... [or not acting].
And for one who does not perform [the action], there is an offense, just as in the case of the offense of having a hut built; this is said to "originate from both performance and non-performance.
Now, showing that all training rules (sikkhāpada) are divided into two types by way of perception (saññā), he says:

"In that regard, there is release through perception," and so forth. The compound *saññāvimokkha* should be understood as a *majjhepadalopa-samāsa* (a compound with the middle term elided), meaning "that which has release by means of perception" (*saññāya abhāvena vimokkho assa*).
Because one is released through the absence of the perception of transgression, this is called "liberation by perception" (*saññāvimokkha*).
"It certainly obtains the mental factor" means that it arises only through origins associated with consciousness, such as the body and mind.
By the restrictive term "certainly obtains," he shows that it does not fail to obtain it. Therefore, regarding the mental factor which it both obtains and does not obtain:
That which was called "the other" [in the previous verse] refers to the object of contrast implied by the word *itara*.
Again, showing that all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are twofold according to the mind, he said: "Again, there is that which involves the mind," and so forth.
"That which is committed together with the mind" means that which is committed through a mental origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) alone, and not through one that is without the mind.
By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even without," it is shown that one incurs [the offense] even with the mind.
For that which sometimes originates through a mindless origination and sometimes through a mindful origination is called "mindless.
Furthermore, it should be understood that here the dyad on perception is stated by way of non-offense, while the dyad on the mind is stated by way of offense; this is the distinction between them.
Since the characteristics of the *Lokavajja-duka* (the category of offenses involving worldly transgression) have already been explained above, they will not be analyzed here.

Now, in order to show that all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are twofold by way of action (*kamma*), and threefold by way of being wholesome and so forth, as well as by way of feeling (*vedanā*), [the author] says:
"By way of action, wholesomeness, and feeling," and so on. In this context, although bodily action (*kāyakamma*)—according to the method handed down in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*)—is...
"Vocal action" (vacīkamma) was stated as a dyad by way of the types of action; however, it is appropriate to show it as a triad.
For indeed, every training rule (sikkhāpada) is threefold: because it may be committed through the door of body, through the door of speech, or through both the doors of body and speech.
Therefore, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "All [rules] are [threefold] by way of bodily action, vocal action, and both."

They are threefold. Therein, that which is to be committed at the door of the body is called bodily action (kāyakamma); that which is to be committed at the door of speech is called verbal action (vacīkamma);
and that which is to be committed at both is called bodily and verbal action (kāyakammavacīkamma).
For this very reason, in the training rules concerning taking what is not given and so forth, it is shown as "bodily and verbal action" by way of those two.

By the passage beginning "But is there a training rule that is wholesome," it is shown whether one who incurs an offense does so while possessing a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind; however, it does not mean that there is such a thing as a wholesome offense.
For there is no such thing as a wholesome offense; [as it is said: "An offense-formal-proceeding may be unwholesome or it may be indeterminate."

Because of the statement: "There is no unwholesome offense-offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). The ten sense-sphere functional consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-kiriya-citta*) consist of the eight great functional consciousnesses together with the smile-producing and the determining consciousnesses.

The fact that the two types of direct-knowledge consciousness (*abhiññā-citta*) originate offenses should be understood in cases such as the transformation of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbanā*) for one who does not know the formal rule (*paññatti*). It should be understood that this classification alone is applicable— namely, that some [states] are exclusively unwholesome consciousness, some are twofold by way of being wholesome or indeterminate, and some are threefold by way of all [three types]— and no other. Furthermore,

It should be understood that when questioned by the Blessed One, he reported this matter to the Blessed One, saying, "It is true, Blessed One. However, in the case of the Vajjiputtaka episode,
having engaged in sexual intercourse without renouncing the training and without disclosing his weakness,
and having subsequently left the order, those who approached the Elder Ānanda for re-ordination and full admission—
It was with reference to those who made such requests that it was stated in the *anupaññatti* (subsequent rule):

"Ānanda, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that the Tathāgata would rescind a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) on a matter of defeat (*pārājika*) already laid down for his disciples on account of the Vajjis or the Vajjiputtakas," and so forth.
However, as for those who, without having left the order, remained in their own robes and became troubled by remorse toward the Blessed One...
They reported this matter; with reference to them, it was said here: "Bhikkhus, you have committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).

However, some, not understanding this underlying intention, say: "The case of the monkey and the case of the Vajjiputtakas are entirely different cases that appear among the cases for disciplinary training (vinītavatthu)."
"Having tied with *kusa* grass" means having tied it with *kusa* blades. "With hair" means with human hair. "That lust" refers to lust for bodily contact.

"Knowing" means having understood by oneself. If [the offense] was committed through lust for bodily contact, why is it not mentioned here among the cases explained (*vinītavatthu*) under the training rule on lust for bodily contact, but is instead stated here?
It is said in reply: although that [offense] was indeed through lust for bodily contact...

It was said; however, because that bhikkhu had made an effort within the scope of a *pārājika* offense, he experienced remorse regarding the matter of a *pārājika*, thinking, "Have I fallen into a *pārājika*?"—this is what is stated here. For this very reason it was said:
"There is no offense, bhikkhu, for a *pārājika*; there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*."
68. "Exceedingly beautiful to behold" (*atidassanīya*) means that it is highly worthy of being seen because it never satiates those who look upon it even for a whole day.
Regarding the phrase "by the excellence of complexion" (*vaṇṇapokkharatāya*): here, *pokkharatā* refers to the state of being beautiful; the excellence of complexion is *vaṇṇapokkharatā*.
By that *vaṇṇapokkharatā*, the meaning is "by the perfection of complexion. However, the ancients say that *pokkhara* refers to the body.
"Vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇameva. According to their opinion, "vaṇṇapokkharāni" refers to both the color and the lotus;
the state of these is "vaṇṇapokkharatā," and therefore "vaṇṇapokkharatāya" means by means of both a perfectly pure color and the excellence of bodily form.
Alternatively, "vaṇṇapokkharaṃ" is a lotus endowed with color; here, there is an elision of the latter member of the compound while retaining the former member.
It is to be seen; its state is "beauty of complexion" (*vaṇṇapokkharatā*). By that beauty of complexion—meaning by the possession of a body endowed with beauty.
"He surpassed" means he overcame. But how did she sit without consenting? He says: "With the intention of unrighteousness... like a stump. "Does not smear" means does not adhere.
"In sensual pleasures" refers to both sensual objects and the defilements of sensual desire. This is what is meant: just as...
"A drop of water does not remain on a lotus leaf, nor does a mustard seed rest upon the point of a needle;
even so, in one who is not smeared by the two kinds of sensual desire within, sensual desire finds no footing. Him I call a brahmin.
(69) By showing the non-arising of fruit when there is no production of seeds, [it is shown that] the male form has disappeared and the female form has arisen.
It should be understood that even the cause is said to be "without arising. For when the male faculty (*purisindriya*) is lost, the male form disappears;
when the female faculty (*itthindriya*) arises, the female form becomes manifest. Thus, it is asked:
"Does the male faculty arise in one in whom the female faculty arises? "No. Or rather: "In one in whom the male faculty..."

Because it is stated in the *Yamaka-pakaraṇa* that "when the life-faculty arises, does the female faculty arise?"—the answer being "No"—it is impossible for these two faculties to function simultaneously within a single continuum;

therefore, at the moment the female faculty manifests, from the seventeenth consciousness prior to that point onward, the male faculty does not arise. Regarding those [consciousnesses] that arose prior to that:
And when the male faculties, together with the co-nascent material phenomena, have ceased in succession within that continuum,
the female faculty arises therein. Then, after the karma-born material phenomena— which had been occurring in the form of a male shape—
and the remaining material phenomena have persisted for some time and ceased, a continuity of fourfold material phenomena proceeds in the form of a female shape.
It is said that the male form disappears and the female form appears. This same principle should be understood to apply when a woman manifests the male characteristic as well.

By the statement "the male characteristic is superior and the female characteristic is inferior," the superiority of the male faculty (*purisindriya*) and [the inferiority of the female faculty (*itthindriya*)] are indicated.
And it should be understood that the state of being inferior has been stated [with respect to the faculty].
For without the inferiority or superiority of the faculty, the inferiority or superiority of the gender-mark (liṅga) which is its support cannot occur.

By such statements as "the male gender-mark disappears through powerful unwholesome [kamma]," it should also be understood that the non-arising of the faculty itself has been stated. For when the faculty is destroyed or arisen, [the state of the mark] depends upon it.

The disappearance and the establishment of the gender-signs are also possible. But how is it that here the male sign disappears through powerful unwholesome [kamma], while the female sign is established through weak wholesome [kamma]? It is said:

First, at the moment of rebirth-linking, there is strong wholesome kamma capable of producing the male faculty, with its potency unimpaired, which brings about the male faculty itself for as long as the life-span lasts.

It produces [the faculties]. However, if its capacity has been impaired by some intervening powerful unwholesome kamma—such as adultery or other acts—and that same wholesome kamma which was to provide rebirth-linking becomes weakened, it fails to produce the male faculty (*purisindriya*) and instead produces the female faculty (*itthindriya*) during the course of existence (*pavatta*) according to its own remaining capacity. But when, at the very moment of giving rebirth-linking...
When the capacity to produce the male faculty (*purisindriya*) is impaired by some acquired condition— such as the unwholesome karma of adultery or similar acts—
that weakened wholesome karma fails to produce the male faculty and instead produces the female faculty (*itthindriya*) at the very moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Therefore, "the male sign disappears through powerful unwholesome [karma], and the female sign..."
"It is said that one is established by weak wholesome [kamma].

Regarding "it disappears through weak unwholesome [kamma]": when there is the weakness of a powerful unwholesome kamma—such as adultery—that obstructs the arising of the male faculty, the female characteristic (*itthiliṅga*) which was disappearing is said to "disappear through weak unwholesome [kamma]."

For instance, because a woman’s rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) consciousness has been excluded by powerful unwholesome kamma such as adultery, her weak wholesome kamma— which is capable of producing the female faculty (itthindriya)— is rendered incapable of producing the male faculty (purisindriya) at rebirth.

This occurs when that weak wholesome kamma has had its capacity suppressed by powerful wholesome kamma accumulated through the practice of celibacy (brahmacariya), the avoidance of sexual misconduct, or through the aspiration for masculinity during the course of existence (pavatti).

When one has not produced the capable female faculty (*itthindriya*) but produces the male faculty (*purisindriya*) corresponding to one's own capacity, then, provided that the powerful unwholesome karma which was an obstacle to the production of the male faculty has become weak, that female faculty disappears; thus it is said:
"The female characteristic (*itthiliṅga*) disappears through weak unwholesome [karma]."

It is said: because the male faculty (*purisindriya*) is produced by a powerful wholesome kamma in the manner already described, it is said that "the male characteristic (*purisaliṅga*) is established by powerful wholesome [kamma].
This same principle should be understood even in the case of one who was previously female, when the male faculty arises at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Both [characteristics] disappear through unwholesome [kamma] and are obtained through wholesome [kamma]. This...

This was stated with reference to a happy rebirth; however, it should be understood that in the case of an unhappy rebirth, the arising and destruction of both [the male and female] occurs solely through unwholesome karma.

Furthermore, there is an offense of lying down together for both [monks and nuns], because it is said: "Whichever monk should lie down together with a woman, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Whichever nun should lie down together with a man, it is an offense of expiation."
For both [of them], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) by virtue of sharing a bed. "Suffering" (dukkhī) means suffering due to being possessed of mental suffering.
"Dejected" (dummano) means one whose mind is corrupted by hatred, or whose mind is disfigured because it is overwhelmed by mental distress (domanassa).
Having said, "He should be comforted," he stated, "Let it be; do not worry," and so forth, in order to show the method of comforting. "Unobstructed" (anāvata) means unforbidden.
"Dhamma" refers to the Triple Dhamma consisting of the threefold categories of the scriptures (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha).
"Saggamagga" means both heaven and the path, or the path to heaven; it is the practice that brings about rebirth in heaven.
Showing that the offense incurred in traveling a journey by prior arrangement with a bhikkhunī must be avoided, he says: "having avoided the making of an appointment."
He said: "There is no offense because there was no prior agreement, such as saying, 'We are going to such-and-such a place,' and then [the other] saying, 'Come, we will go together,' and so forth.

"Outside the village" means outside the village where one is residing. There is no offense regarding the offenses for staying apart at night between villages, crossing a river, or being left behind by the group;
this is because it corresponds to the characteristics of non-offense stated in passages such as, "The companion nun has departed," and so forth.
It has been said. "Capable" means capable of winning over the mind. "Having offended them" means having abandoned them. Regarding the phrase "those who possess a sense of shame... it is possible":

this was stated specifically by way of inclusion, thinking, "In the absence of such support, she might become dissatisfied and leave. Regarding the phrase "those who lack a sense of shame... it is possible":
this was stated because, due to their shamelessness, they would side with those who are unvirtuous. Regarding the phrase "those who are not related... it is appropriate": [the same applies].
However, they say that this was permitted in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) by treating it as a unique case for her.
"Even in the state of a bhikkhu" means even during the time he was a bhikkhu. "One who frequents assemblies" refers to one who, having been an upajjhāya or an ācariya, attends upon assemblies.

"Dependence (nissaya) must be taken in the presence of another" means that those who have received full ordination (upasampadā) from him [must take dependence] from someone other than him, [namely] his saddhivihārikas.
"Dependence (nissaya) must be taken from a teacher. This is said with reference to those living in dependence upon him.

"A preceptor (upajjhā) must be taken" means that for the purpose of full ordination (upasampadā), a preceptor must be taken; what is meant is that one should receive full ordination in the presence of another.
"A formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma)" is said with reference to the assignment (vikappana). "Must be done again" means it must be assigned again. Again...

It is stated [in the text] for the purpose of showing that what has been received again on the seventh day—even if it contains food—is permissible, based on the words: “I allow you, monks, having had the stored-up food of the nuns received by monks, and the stored-up food of the monks received by nuns, to consume it.
Regarding the phrase “on the seventh day,” this refers to the *nissaggiya* (offense involving forfeiture).
This is stated for the purpose of showing that it is permissible to use [the item] again for another seven days even without having forfeited it.
Furthermore, since what is subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) by a nun is permissible for a monk, and what is subject to forfeiture by a monk is permissible for a nun,
therefore, even on the eighth day, if there is a change of gender, it is permissible to use it within the seven-day period without having forfeited it.
"It is permissible," they say. "He who is of natural status protects it" means that one whose gender has not changed protects it by not relinquishing the act of receiving;
the intention is that because there is no formal distribution, the act of receiving is not relinquished.

"Having taken it himself, he should set it down" means that after having received it, he should set it down himself. "There is an offense for one using it" refers to the case where, upon a change of gender, the act of receiving is relinquished.
Furthermore, there is an offense for one who, having accepted [the food] again, consumes it.

Regarding the phrase "by returning to the lower state," the *Tīsupi Gaṇṭhipadesu* states: "By returning to the lower state means by one who has committed a *pārājika* offense proceeding to the state of a householder.
That is well said. For it is not the case that for one who has not committed a *pārājika*, saying "I shall disrobe" without having formally renounced the training [constitutes such a return].

The status of a bhikkhu is destroyed merely by the assumption of the layman’s outward signs. However, one who has committed a *pārājika* offense remains a bhikkhu as long as he does not acknowledge it;
until then, his status as a bhikkhu still exists, and he is not reckoned among those who are no longer ordained (*anupasampanna*).

For in that case, even if he consents to living in communion (*saṃvāsa*), he does not become a "one who lives in communion by theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*), nor does he incur an offense such as sharing a sleeping place with him.

It does not produce [a *pārājika* offense], but it does produce a *pācittiya* for abusive speech (*omasavāda*). For this very reason, regarding the statement: "A person who has committed one of the *pārājika* offenses is impure;

if, while maintaining a view of his own purity, he asks for permission and speaks with the intent to abuse, there is an offense of abusive speech," a *pācittiya* for abusive speech is thus stated. For if monkhood were non-existent...
There would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); furthermore, for one who still possesses the status of a monk, it is improper to relinquish the acceptance of what has been accepted.

Therefore, because the status of a monk is entirely absent, the assumption of the layman’s marks after having committed a *pārājika* offense and thus entering the state of a householder is what is intended here by the term “returning to the lower state,” and not merely the assumption of the layman’s marks by one who remains a regular monk (*pakatatta*).

For that very reason, because it shares the same destination as the renunciation of the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*) in certain instances, they do not count "returning to the lower state" (*hīnāyāvattana*) separately.

Since the abandonment of the acceptance [of the precepts] has already been mentioned through the renunciation of the training, there is no need to speak further regarding one who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense, because by entering the state of a householder, his status as a monk is entirely non-existent. For thus it was said by the teacher Buddhadatta:
Regarding the determination of one’s own discipline:
“From forfeiture regardless of concealment,
from the abandonment of training, from death, and from the change of gender;”
"By means of that gift, both for himself and for the other who is without a monk [to receive it], all receiving comes to utter destruction.
Thus much was said. Likewise, by the Elder Dhammasiri as well—

It is said: “By the signs of training and death, by relinquishing without regard, by cutting off, and by giving to one who is not fully ordained—there is the loss of acceptance and the loss of formal authorization.
And if, for a regular monk (*pakatatta*), the acceptance [of an offering] were lost merely by his taking up the marks of a householder, then those...

The teachers might say that this too was stated separately, yet it was not; from that, it is understood that "merely taking up the marks of a householder" is not what is intended here by "returning to the lower state.
However, because a bhikkhunī has no formal renunciation of the training (sikkhā-paccakkhāna), she loses her status as a recipient [of offerings] even by merely taking up the marks of a householder.
“By giving away without regard” means: by giving away without expectation—either because one has no further need for it, thinking, “There is no use for this;
I will not use it now,” regarding the objects themselves, or thinking, “I will receive them again and use them,” regarding the act of receiving—or by having them taken away by thieves and the like.
“By taking after they have been seized” means: by taking [them back] after they have been seized by thieves and others.

"In this place" means in the monastery of the bhikkhus. "Planted trees" refers to the trees and shrubs planted by him. "In the thirteen formal appointments" (sammuti) refers to the thirteen formal appointments known as:

the appointment of the meal-designator, the assigner of lodgings, the storekeeper, the receiver of robes, the distributor of robes, the distributor of rice-gruel, the distributor of fruits, the distributor of solid food, the dispenser of trifles, the one who causes the *sāṭiyaga* to be taken, the one who causes the bowl to be taken, the supervisor of monastery attendants (*ārāmika*), and the supervisor of novices (*sāmaṇera*).
Granted, the taking of lodgings during both the earlier and later periods of the rains residence naturally ceases [at the end of the period].
However, since it is possible to go elsewhere once the taking of lodgings during the first period has ceased,
he has separately shown the cessation of the taking of lodgings for the first period; whereas,
since it is not possible to go elsewhere once the taking of lodgings during the second period has ceased, he now shows the duties to be performed by the monks in that regard.
He said, “If, during the later period (pacchimikā), a dwelling has been taken,” and so forth.
Only the *mānatta* penance for a fortnight (*pakkhamānatta*) should be given, because even for a concealed offense of nuns, only the practice of *mānatta* was permitted.
Again, only the *mānatta* penance for a fortnight should be given, because there was no prior practice of *mānatta* during the time they were monks. By the nuns...

"The act of rehabilitation (abbhāna-kamma) should be performed" is stated because it is considered that one who has practiced the *mānatta* penance during the time as a monk is likewise accounted as having practiced the *mānatta* penance during the time as a nun. "If [the offense] results in unwholesome rebirth... pe...

the *mānatta* penance itself should be given for six days"—this is stated because the case concerns a change of gender while one is undergoing the *mānatta* penance. However, if [the offense occurred] during the time as a monk...
If the gender of one who is undergoing probation for a concealed offense common to both orders changes before the probation has been formally undertaken,
and while he is practicing the half-month *mānatta* penance during his time as a nun, when the unwholesome result has been exhausted and his gender has changed back,
they say that probation should be granted to him again; and once the probation has been completed, a six-night *mānatta* penance should be granted.

"An offense of misconduct" (sañcaritta-āpatti) is stated for the purpose of showing that it is a common offense. "There is no granting of probation" (parivāsa-dānaṃ natthi) because it was not concealed during the time he was a bhikkhu.
However, they say that even if it was confessed during the time he was a bhikkhunī, if it was not confessed during the time he was a bhikkhu, it remains as though concealed.
"When the bhikkhus have not yet granted the trial period" (mānatte adinne) refers to when the trial period has not been practiced.
"When there is a change of gender (liṅgaparivatta): the connection is that even for one remaining in the state of a bhikkhunī, those [offenses] are indeed well-allayed.
'The offenses which were previously allayed' refers to those non-common offenses which were previously allayed while in the state of a bhikkhu.
For one who has committed a pārājika offense, when there is a change of gender, because of the unity of the mental continuum (santāna), he does not [need] the ordination again."

They say: "Just as one who has renounced [the order] does not receive re-ordination when there is a change of gender (*liṅgaparivatta*), so too a nun who has renounced does not receive re-ordination when there is a change of gender.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of non-appropriated things" (*anupādinnakesu*): it is stated in both the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada* that because of the governing context, the same principle applies to appropriated things (*upādinnaka*) as well;
however, that is poorly stated. For [the rule] does not apply to one who makes an effort toward a sign (*nimitta*) consisting of appropriated things.

An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is seen [to apply]. For likewise, it is stated that for one who makes an effort outside without inserting the sign into the clung-to parts, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya);
because it was said: "Monks, the genitals must not be touched with a lustful mind; whoever should touch them, there is an offense of grave wrongdoing.
And whatever is to be said here, all of that has already been explained in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
It has already been considered. "Only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" is said because of the absence of lust for emission.
"In the same way" refers to the meaning: "whether he emits or not.
"Outside his range" is stated because it is difficult to avoid consent in such a situation. [This refers to] the woman's words.
"Having accepted" means having accepted the words spoken such as, "I shall exert myself; you need not exert yourself. The offense occurs through the exertion of both parties;
it was said, "you need not exert yourself," because of that perception. 73.
To show the meaning of "in a hollowed-out [space]," he said, "when open. "Only while remaining in the air out of fear of a *pārājika* offense..."

They say that if, while performing the acts of insertion and so forth, one suddenly touches the palate, the eye, or the generative organ, it is only a *dukkaṭa* offense because of the absence of lust for sexual intercourse;
this must be understood after careful investigation. "Well-covered" (*suphusitā*) means well-shut.
"There is no space inside the mouth" means that because the teeth are well-shut, there is no room to insert [the organ] inside the mouth.
There is none. However, when the flesh of the lip has been torn away and one makes an effort against the teeth themselves, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense);
this is a *thullaccaya* by way of a summary of the wound, similar to the shape of the mouth of a grasshopper-faced frog.

Or, because it shares the same characteristic as the rule: "If, with lust for sexual intercourse, one touches organ to organ without inserting [the penis] into a woman, it is a *thullaccaya*," there is a *thullaccaya* here.
It has been stated. This same principle applies even to those whose teeth or tongues have protruded outside.
Regarding the offense of *thullaccaya* when there is no emission, it is because of the statement: "If one intends and makes an effort, but there is no emission, it is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "those such as the *nijjhāmataṇhika*," the inclusion of *petas* such as those suffering from hunger and thirst should be understood.
"One cannot even touch them" means that because their bodies are constantly ablaze with flames of fire arising from the pores of their skin due to the burning thirst (*nijjhāmataṇhika*),
and because their bodies— consisting of nothing but bones and skin— are extremely repulsive, deformed, hideous, and perpetually afflicted by hunger,
thirst, and so forth, they cannot even be touched. Regarding the phrase "they enjoy prosperity like devas," *yāsaṃ* here is a genitive plural form.
The word *yāti* should be construed by changing it into the singular form (*paccattavacana*), as in: "the deity who experiences such prosperity. Regarding seeing and so forth:
"seeing" refers to the bhikkhu’s seeing of them; "grasping" likewise refers to the bhikkhu’s grasping of their limbs and members.
However, touching and the other acts are the functions belonging to those deities. In that context, "touching" means [the contact] of the bhikkhu’s body with his own body.
"Touching" (*āmasana*) is merely the act of touching; "contact" (*phusana*) is touching more firmly than that;
"striking" (*ghaṭṭana*) is striking the body with the body even more firmly than that.
"Having rendered unconscious" means having acted in such a way that she does not perceive even the effort made. Although touching and so forth are her own actions, nevertheless, by that very [act]...

Since it is stated, "having rendered that person unconscious," without mentioning non-offense, if one consents after knowing [the act] while not having rendered them unconscious, it is indeed a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, for a bhikkhu, there is no such thing as "non-consent" when seeing and taking hold occur;
thus, when seeing and taking hold are manifest, no exemption from offense is mentioned. However, if first seeing and taking hold occur, and subsequently...
If, having rendered the person unconscious, she performs acts such as touching and departs after fulfilling her own desire, there is no *pārājika* offense.

"One whose bodily sensitivity is impaired" (*upahatakāyappasāda*) refers to one whose bodily sensitivity has been damaged by wind, bile, and so forth, either by way of rendering it incapable of producing body-consciousness even though the physical tissue (*kāyappasāda*) itself is not destroyed.
"An offense by way of the intention to pursue" (*sevanacittavasena āpatti*) means, for example, by way of the sign of what is already spread out (*santhatanimitta*).
Even for one who does not experience tactile contact (*upādinnaphassa*), there is an offense by virtue of the intention to engage in sexual intercourse;

likewise here, even for one who does not feel it because the physical sensitivity (*kāyappasāda*) has been impaired by bile, wind, or other humors, there is an offense by virtue of the intention to engage in sexual intercourse.
But is it not the case that regarding the matter of mere touching, [the Buddha said]: "‘I shall practice the act of sexual intercourse’—having merely touched it, he felt remorse"?

Since it is stated, "it has occurred," there ought to be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the preliminary effort (*pubbapayoga*) of sexual intercourse; so why then is it stated, "there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*"?
Having taken this internal objection into consideration, the following passage beginning with "who [engages in] sexual intercourse" is commenced in order to resolve it.
In that context, "the head" refers to the insertion of the organ into the organ. For that [is the culmination] of the efforts...
Because it resembles the head, it is called “the head,” as there is no further application [of the term] beyond that.

“They stand in an offense of wrong-doing” means they generate an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For those applications such as grasping by the hand, which generate an offense of wrong-doing, are said to “stand in an offense of wrong-doing” because they do not proceed toward the generation of any other offense.
74. "Of clusters of *jāti*-flowers" means of clusters of *sumana* jasmine flowers. "Due to their abundance" means due to their great quantity.
"In the vicinity" means in the nearby area. "By that support of wind" refers to the support of wind described thus:

"the limbs and members become stiffened by wind. By this, the cause for falling asleep is stated. "Of a single flavor" means uninterrupted by the consciousnesses of the cognitive process, such as adverting and so forth.

76. “A monk who is like a warrior at the head of battle”: because he has not been overcome by the enemies that are the defilements (*kleśa*) but has defeated them, the monk is thus like a warrior at the front of a battle.
77. “When the matter has arisen”: when the matter of sexual intercourse has arisen. “Only a door suitable for turning back”:
a door capable of being turned this way and that by means of closing and opening. “The tree-peg and thorn door”: the tree-peg door.
And the "thorn-gate. Alternatively, the reading is "the tree-spindle gate" (*rukkhasūcidvāra*), which is the same as the "thorn-gate.
That which they construct by planting wooden posts on both sides, piercing them there, and inserting two or three tree-spindles in the middle—that is the tree-spindle gate.
That which is removable at the time of entering or exiting and is suitable for bolting—[that is the thorn-gate].
That which is made with one or many thorny branches is a "thorn gate" (*kaṇṭakadvāra*).
A "gate equipped with a wheel" (*cakkalakayutta-dvāra*) is a large gate constructed by attaching a wheel beneath it, which cannot be closed or opened by a single person.

"Having secured" (*gopphetvā*) means having tied it with ropes. Regarding the phrase "only one cloth-curtain gate," it should be understood that a mat-curtain gate (*kilañja-sāṇi-dvāra*) is also included therein.
In order to show the procedure to be followed where it is not possible to lie down after closing the door, it is said:

“If there is a place used by many,” and so forth. Even in a place not used by many, it is indeed permissible to lie down after having asked permission from one person. Then, as for the passage beginning with “the bhikkhus... were seated,” this refers to the bhikkhus there.

This was stated for the purpose of demonstrating the state of being present (*sannihita-bhāva*). It is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Whether he be sitting or lying down, if he is present there in whatever posture he may have, it is permissible to direct one's attention (*ābhoga*).
However, some [hold that] because of the expression "they are sitting," if they are lying down, [one should not direct one's attention].
If they say, "It is not proper to apply attention [to the object]," that is not correct.
For if it were improper to apply attention when one is lying down because of the statement "they are sitting," then it would also be improper to apply attention when standing or walking.
Indeed, the word "sitting" does not exclude only the state of lying down; therefore, this phrase "they are sitting" [is intended] therein—
This is for the purpose of indicating their mere existence, not for the purpose of excluding the possession of the other modes of deportment (*iriyāpatha*).
Even so, it is our view that one who is lying down and sleeping is not entitled to mental application (*ābhoga*), because he stands on the side of non-existence.
Indeed, precisely because he stands on the side of non-existence, there is no offense when one is sitting in private or lying down and sleeping.
"It does not do so" is what was stated. Regarding "closing the doors," this refers to preventing the entry of bhikkhunīs and others; thus he said:
"It is not permissible to ask permission from a bhikkhunī or a woman. Some say:
"It is not permissible to ask permission from a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka) or a female paṇḍaka. [This concerns] the state of a woman being situated within the inner chamber.
There is no offense for one who, having understood this, lies down after performing the procedure as previously described at the door.
"Having raised a ladder" means that it is permissible to lie down even after raising it to the upper floor, dismantling it and dropping it to the ground, or cutting it down.
Regarding the statement "both doors must be attended to": here, if there is no door-panel on one door, [the procedure] is according to the method stated below.
If it is impossible to close [the door], it is permissible to lie down even without closing the other door.

"Having turned back from the alms-round" means having desisted from wandering for alms. "Of the doorkeeper" refers to one who stands at the gatehouse, at the main entrance, or at the base of a ladder, guarding the door.
"The burden of those following behind" refers to those coming in single file as a continuous succession.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). It should be connected as follows: "in the inner chamber when the doors are not secured" and "outside" means outside of the chamber.

Regarding the statement, "Even at the time of lying down... it is indeed permissible," they say: "Because the door-keeper is dependent on him [the monk], it is indeed permissible for the monk to exercise mindfulness even without considering whether the door-keeper is present or absent there at that time."
"Enclosed by anything whatsoever" means enclosed by a wall, a fence, or by whatever else.
They say that "the measurement of the height of the enclosure should be understood according to the method stated regarding what is sufficient for sleeping together.
However, if in one part the enclosure is lower than the stated measurement, it is permissible. "It is a large compound" means it is large.

It is a courtyard. The statement that it is "like the courtyard of the Mahābodhi and the courtyard of the Lohapāsāda" is said for the purpose of showing that there is much movement [of people], not for the purpose of showing a large physical extent. "He rises when the dawn has broken; there is no offense":
for one who lies down with a pure mind and falls asleep exactly as the dawn breaks, there is no offense by virtue of being under the influence of sleep. Having awakened, again...

"Sleeps, there is an offense": even if one wakes at sunrise, if one does not recognize the rising of the sun and continues to sleep without rising, there is an offense for one who sleeps with that same continuity of sleep.
Even for one who wakes before sunrise, if they do not recognize it and continue to sleep with that same continuity of sleep, there is likewise an offense once the sun has risen.
"One emerges exactly according to the limit" means precisely when the sun has risen.

He rises. Regarding the phrase "there is an offense for him": because he lay down with an impure mind, even though he was sleeping, when the sun has risen, there is an offense rooted in daytime seclusion (*divāpaṭisallāna*).

Since it is stated, "One who lies down in this manner is not exempt from the *dukkaṭa* offense of disrespect," one who lies down with an impure mind—whether they rise before sunrise or do not rise—is [considered to have committed the offense] at the very moment of lying down.
One incurs a *dukkaṭa* for disrespect; however, one incurs the *dukkaṭa* based on daytime seclusion only when the sun has actually risen.

As for what is stated here in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "If one lies down after closing the door at night, and even though the door is open at the time of sunrise, one still lies down, there is an offense for him because he lay down having closed it in a place that is not a [proper] enclosure. At the time of sunrise..."

Even when the door is open, if one closes the door at night thinking, "I will lie down," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for disrespect at the time of lying down because it was not done in a proper place;
furthermore, when the sun has risen, there is the root-offense of wrong-doing for lying down.
This applies even if the door was closed at night—whether the door was actually closed or not—at the very moment the sun rises, regardless of whether the door is now open or closed.
Furthermore, as for the statement, “Moreover, having opened [the door], there is no offense because the field was closed due to its being shut,” that does not accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is shown that an offense occurs at the rising of the dawn for one who has lain down without closing the door during the night;
therefore, whether the field is enclosed or unenclosed, we hold that in this case, the act of closing itself is the determining factor.
"He lies down on account of sleep" means that, being overcome by drowsiness, he lies down on one side;
however, it is stated that there is no offense for one who, while thus lying down, does not actually remain in that position.

"While sleeping leaning against something" means while sleeping leaning against a pillar or the like, without allowing even a small portion of the space between the hips and the middle of the back to touch the ground.

"He suddenly wakes up" means that he wakes up abruptly, as if having stumbled and fallen. "He lies right there and does not wake up" means that, being overcome by sleep while sleeping, he does not wake up;
it is not because he is possessed by a swoon. For that very reason, it was not stated that "no offense is seen because it is outside the scope [of the rule]."
"By breaking one side" means by the breaking of one flank; it is said that, without lifting the foot from the ground in the manner described below, he broke one flank, bent it, and lay down.
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, the connection is with what was stated by the Elder Mahāpaduma: "Because he fell down in a swoon, no offense is seen, as it was outside the scope [of the rule]."

It has been stated [thus]. However, the teachers do not say there is no offense on the grounds that one who has fainted and fallen lies down for some time while unconscious because of a lack of self-control, just as one seized by a spirit, having been bound and laid down, is under the power of another.
This is the position of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* regarding the case of one seized by a spirit and one who has been bound and laid down.
Only that which follows [the Sutta] should be accepted as authoritative. And thus he will say:
"In all cases, whichever statement of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) or the Thera-vāda is stated last, that alone should be regarded as authoritative.

Furthermore, it should be understood that by the mention of one "possessed by a yakkha," one who has lost consciousness is also included. However, one who lies down on only one side is not considered "lying down" in the technical sense.
Regarding the phrase "he is indeed released": according to the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā tradition, it should be understood that he is not at fault.

For one who has restrained himself during the day and lies down, there is no offense even if the door is opened by someone else, because he lay down having already restrained himself at the time of lying down.
If, after restraining himself during the day, he lies down near the door and subsequently opens the door himself, this is also permissible.
And this offense is one without consciousness (*acittaka*), and it is both an act (*kiriya*) and a non-act (*akiriya*).

Having said, "As if making a footprint where there is no footing," he spoke again, "As if showing a footprint in the sky," in order to clarify that very same point. "This is the foremost" means this is the best. "Namely, this which... refers to that which is here. The rest is self-evident in meaning.
The commentary on the narrative of the disciplinary case (*vinītavatthu*) is concluded.
The passage beginning with "Tatridanti" has already had its meaning explained above.
Thus ends the commentary on the first *pārājika* in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a sub-commentary to the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
2. The Second Pārājika:

Since the turn has now come for the commentary on that second Pārājika which was proclaimed by the Peerless Conqueror, therefore, setting aside everything that is easy to understand and all that was previously explained, [we shall now treat] this second one.
"This is the commentary" is the connection [of the sentence].
Regarding the "Commentary on the Story of Dhaniya":
at Rājagaha, because it is endowed with the excellence of being a difficult terrain, a specific location, and so forth, it is designated as "Rājagaha" by kings in its preeminent sense.
Regarding the statement, “It is taken and possessed, thus it is called Rājagaha,” [the text says]: “Mandhātu... is so called.

In this context, since what was possessed by the Great Being Mahāgovinda was indeed possessed by Reṇu, the mention of Mahāgovinda is made. For the proclamation of possession by Mahāgovinda serves as a characteristic mark of its being possessed at that time by Reṇu, the King of Magadha;
for he (Reṇu) had him (Mahāgovinda) as his domestic priest. “Mahāgovinda” means...
"Of great power, ancient, and the sole king of Magadha," say some. "Because it was taken possession of" means because it was taken possession of as a royal capital.
It is called *gaha* (a seizing) because it is seized; "the seizing of kings" is *Rājagaha*. This neuter designation is used in view of the word "city. There are other explanations here as well:
"It is Rājagaha because all the seizing (*gaha*) was caused to be done by the king who entered the city; and because it is surrounded by Gijjhakūṭa and other peaks..."
Rājagaha is so called because its dwellings are as if surrounded by kings of mountains; it is Rājagaha because it is a dwelling that is "kingly" due to its magnificent palaces;
it is Rājagaha because it has become a "house" (a place of confinement) for rival kings who have approached it with harmful intent, owing to its well-ordered protection;
and it is Rājagaha because it has become the "house" of those kings who, having seen it, established it properly.

“Rājagaha”: it is so called because it shines (*rājate*) with the beauty of its groves and parks, or because it is grasped and possessed by beings through the sense of "mine" due to the happiness of dwelling there and other such qualities.
That region, being a specific location, is enjoyed by exalted beings; thus he says, "But as for that," and so forth.
In this context, the phrase "during the time of a Buddha and during the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch" is stated according to the general rule (*yebhuyyavasena*).
It has been said. "Of them" means of the *yakkhas*. "Dwelling forest" refers to a grove that serves as a place of recreation. It is called *Gijjha* because vultures (*gijjha*) are found there;
it is a peak (*kūṭa*). That [peak] belongs to this [mountain], thus it is *Gijjhakūṭa*. Alternatively, it is called *Gijjha* because it is like a vulture; it is a peak.
That [peak] belongs to this [mountain], thus it is *Gijjhakūṭa*, the mountain. Or, *Gijjhakūṭa* is a compound with the middle term elided, meaning "a peak resembling a vulture."
As in the expression “Sākapatthava,” [this refers] to that Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa). Therefore he said, “Vultures,” and so forth.
Following that, “the Saṅgha” refers to three persons, because they have attained the status for formal acts (kamma) such as those requiring a quorum of four (catuvaggakaraṇīya).
Having assembled on that mountain, they pass their time in meditative attainment (samāpatti), [having gone] for alms to a place suitable for them.
Having performed their alms-round and finished their meal, they would return to the interior of the shrine-chamber;

as if opening the great twin-doors of the cetiya, they split that mountain in two and entered within. Having established places for standing by night and by day, they spent their time there in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
When, then, did they dwell there? It is said that in the past, before the appearance of the Tathāgatas, near Bārāṇasī, in a certain...
In a certain village, there was a daughter of good family who was guarding a field.
While she was parching rice in her field-hut, about five hundred large, beautiful grains of puffed rice, as big as *mahākarañja* flowers, sprouted there.
She took them and placed them in a large lotus leaf. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha [arrived] at her...

He was walking not far from the field boundary for the sake of gathering alms. Seeing him, her mind filled with serene faith, she took a large, fully blossomed lotus flower, placed parched grain within it, and approached the Paccekabuddha.
Having offered the lotus flower along with five hundred grains of parched grain, she paid homage to him by prostrating at his five points and said, "To this..."
“Venerable sir, by the power of merit, may I obtain five hundred sons endowed with great majesty,” she thus prayed for five hundred sons.

At that very moment, five hundred deer-hunters who had gathered their provisions and whose knowledge of individual enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*) was fully matured, gave sweet meat to that same Paccekabuddha and made this aspiration: “May we become her sons.”
Because she had come to them as their son during many past births, it was so for them. Having lived out her full lifespan, she was reborn in the world of the devas;
passing away from there, she was reborn within the calyx of a lotus in a lake of birth.
A certain ascetic saw her and looked after her. As she walked about on foot, lotuses sprang up from the ground at every step she took.
They were born. A certain forest-dweller saw them and informed the King of Bārāṇasī. The King brought her back and made her his chief queen, and she conceived a pregnancy.

Prince Mahāpaduma remained in the mother’s womb, while the others were produced through moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) birth, depending on the impurities of the womb that had been cast out. Some say they were of apparitional (*opapātika*) birth. When they reached maturity—
While sporting in the lotus pond in the park, they each sat upon a lotus flower and, having established the contemplation of decay and fall, they realized the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*.
This was the verse of their prophecy:
“Here is a lake-born lotus, with its petals fully blossomed, frequented by swarms of bees;”
“Having understood this impermanence and its passing away, one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn.

At that time, they dwelt there. Then the name “Isigili” arose for that mountain. These are the seers (isi); these are the Paccekabuddha-seers. It is called a “name” (samaññā) because it is known through it; the meaning is “designation. By omitting the middle term in the compound *tiṇacchadanakuṭiyo* (grass-roofed huts), or by applying the designation of the whole to a part— [The verse continues: “Having understood this impermanence and its passing away, one should wander alone like the rhinoceros horn. At that time, they dwelt there. Then the name “Isigili” arose for that mountain. These are the seers; these are the Paccekabuddha-seers.

It is called a “name” because it is known through it; the meaning is “designation. By omitting the middle term in the compound *tiṇacchadanakuṭiyo*, or by applying the designation of the whole to a part—
“They were called ‘grass huts. Since it is said, ‘They entered the rains retreat,’ one should understand that these were huts with doors and bolts, as they were fit for entering the rains retreat;
thus he says, ‘Huts with grass roofs and doors and bolts. ‘By one entering the rains’ means by one entering the rains residence.
‘The path of Nālaka’ refers to [the teaching] beginning with, ‘I shall teach you moneyya (monkhood),’ etc., by the Teacher.”

The practice of the way of the sages (*moneyya-paṭipadā*) taught to the Elder Nālaka is that which should be practiced by not giving rise to a defiled mind from the time one is still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Having heard that practice, the Elder Nālaka became moderate in his desires in three respects:
in seeing, in hearing, and in questioning. Indeed, at the conclusion of the teaching, with a heart full of confidence, he paid homage to the Blessed One.
He entered the forest. Furthermore, he did not give rise to a longing state of mind, thinking, "O, that I might see the Blessed One again";
this is his fewness of desires regarding seeing [the Buddha]. Likewise, he did not give rise to a longing state of mind, thinking, "O, that I might hear the teaching of the Dhamma again";

this is his fewness of desires regarding hearing [the Dhamma]. Likewise, [he did not give rise to a longing state of mind], thinking, "O, that I might again ask about the practice of the way of the sage (moneyyapaṭipadā)."
He did not give rise to a state of longing; this was his fewness of desires regarding the question.

Being thus few in desires, he entered a mountain foot and did not dwell for two days in a single grove, did not sit at the root of a single tree for two days, and did not enter a single village for alms for two days.
Thus, wandering from forest to forest, tree to tree, and village to village, and practicing the appropriate course of conduct, he established himself in the highest fruit.
During the time of a single Blessed One, only one person can fulfill this;
for a bhikkhu fulfilling this way of the sage (moneyya-paṭipadā) in its highest form lives for only seven months, while fulfilling it in its medium form [he lives] for seven...
[Others] fulfilled [the training] for sixteen years, having made it easy; but this Elder fulfilled it by making it difficult.

Therefore, after remaining for seven months and knowing that his own life-faculties (*āyu-saṅkhāra*) were exhausted, he bathed, put on his lower robe, fastened his waist-band, donned his double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), and with palms joined in the five-point prostration toward the One of Ten Powers (*dasabala*), [he passed away].
Having paid homage to him and raised his hands in reverential salutation, he attained final Nibbāna by the element of Nibbāna without residue while still standing beside the Hiṅgulaka Mountain.
Knowing that he had attained final Nibbāna, the Blessed One went there together with the community of bhikkhus;
having performed the funeral rites for the body and caused the relics to be collected, he established a cetiya.
He arrived. Even by one who has entered upon such a practice, when entering the rains residence, he must enter a place that is sheltered and provided with a door-securing device.
The phrase "even by one who has entered upon the Nālaka practice" is stated to show that even on account of fewness of desires, there is no transgression of the training rule.
"Of the five kinds of roofing" means of the five kinds of roofing known as grass, leaves, brick, stone, and plaster.

They say: "The prohibition—'Monks, one who does not have a dwelling should not enter the rains residence'—was made with reference only to entering the rains residence by making a formal verbal declaration, not with reference to entering it by way of establishing a temporary abode (*ālaya*). Thus it is stated in the Pāḷi.

However, because there is no distinction [in the rule] and because it is stated emphatically and without qualification in the Aṭṭhakathā—beginning with the words, “even by one who has entered upon the Nālaka practice”—it is our conviction that for one who does not possess a lodging, staying elsewhere apart from a boat or such is not permitted.
For it is specifically regarding those cases excluding boats and caravans that it is said: “Monks, I allow you to enter the rains residence on a boat,” and so forth.

Since the entering upon the rains residence has been separately authorized whether or not there is a lodging, this prohibition—"Monks, one should not enter upon the rains residence without a lodging"—does not apply there;
therefore, it is stated that even in the absence of a lodging, one may enter upon the residence in boats and so forth by way of taking them as one's abode.
"In accordance with the Dhamma" means the proper conduct (*vatta*). By the word "etcetera" in "night-stations, day-stations, etc.,"...
It includes the places for excrement and urine in the cow-pen and so forth.
By establishing both the *katika-vatta* (formal agreements) and the *khandhaka-vatta* (monastic rules), the Dhamma of the scriptures establishes the threefold True Dhamma;
therefore, recite it carefully, cause it to be recited, and perform its rehearsal.

While residing in the meditation hall, without causing any disturbance, sit within the vihāra and recite, cause others to recite, engage in study, and ensure that the hearing of the Dhamma flourishes. When ordaining, ordain only after purifying [the candidate];
when conferring full admission, confer it only after purifying; when granting dependence, grant it only after purifying. For even a single son of good family, through ordination and full admission—
Having received the entire teaching, he establishes it. According to your own strength, undertake as many ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) as you are able;

during this rainy season retreat, you must remain heedful throughout the whole day and during the first and last watches of the night, and you must exert energy. Even the great elders of old [abandoned] all worldly attachments...

Having completed the rains retreat, they fulfilled the duties of solitary wandering. Knowing the proper measure in speech, it is appropriate to deliver discourses on the ten bases, the ten kinds of foulness, the ten recollections, and the thirty-eight objects of meditation.

It is appropriate to perform the duties for newcomers and to grant leave to those who have gone on business for seven days after informing them. [One should avoid] contentious, slanderous, and harsh speech.
Do not speak; day after day, remain intent on mindfulness, frequently reflecting upon the precepts and never neglecting the four protections.
While worshipping a shrine or the Bodhi tree, or offering perfumes and garlands, or putting alms bowls into their bags, you must not converse;
nor should you engage in talk concerning requisites with people within the village.
Having undertaken the formal observances (*katikavatta*) and the *Khandhaka* observances by means of such instructions as: "One should not engage in talk that is discordant;
one should keep the sense faculties guarded; and one should fulfill the duties of the *Khandhakas* and the duties of the training rules (*sekhiyavatta*)," [the monks should observe them].

Then, regarding the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) for those who have completed the rains residence, [the Buddha said]: "Monks, I allow those who have completed the rains residence to perform the invitation ceremony in three ways."
Because this sutta has been authorized, from the time the dawn breaks on the day of the *pavāraṇā* onwards,

even those who have not yet performed the *pavāraṇā* are called "those who have completed the rains residence" (*vuṭṭhavassa*). Although, by virtue of the statement "I enter the rains for these three months," that day is included within the three-month period,
as long as they have not yet performed the *pavāraṇā*, they are indeed still considered "dwelling in the rains."

Nevertheless, even though it did not rain on that day except in one part, it is said to have "rained" because it was considered to have rained in view of the portion where it did rain—just as the conventional expression "done" or "not done" applies to a whole collection in view of the portions that were done or not done.
For whatever is left incomplete is called "done-and-not-done. "Monks, I allow the kaṭhina-cloth for those who have completed the rains residence."

However, by way of this sutta, in order to show that according to the non-figurative (nippariyāya) sense those who have performed the *pavāraṇā* on the Great *Pavāraṇā* day are called "those who have completed the rains" (*vuṭṭhavassa*) starting from the first day of the month (*pāṭipada*), it was said: "having performed the *pavāraṇā* on the Great *Pavāraṇā*," and so forth.
For, as stated in the *Parivāra*, the spreading of the *kaṭhina* robe is permitted during the last month of the rainy season starting from the first day of the month.
Because it is stated, “The month for the spreading of the *kaṭhina* must be known; it is to be known as the last month of the rains,” [it follows that this refers to the end of the rains].
Furthermore, the phrase “they have been invited at the Great Invitation” is merely an indication of the natural state of those who entered the rains residence during the first period (*purimikā*);
even if they have not been invited due to some obstacle, they are still called “those who have completed the rains.”
Having stated, “She should ask for permission,” he now explains the procedure for asking permission by saying, “If this hut...,” and so forth.
“Or she does not obtain a caretaker” means that because it was built on the outskirts of the monastery, she does not obtain a caretaker.
“But those monks set out on a journey through the countryside” is the grammatical connection. In the Teaching, the term *cārikā* (journey) refers to traveling along a road.

It is conventional (*nirūḷha*). Although this term "wandering" (*cārikā*) is applicable only to Buddhas for the purpose of gathering the great masses of people, it is nevertheless applied to disciples as well by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsadda*) following the Buddha—just as the designation "palmyra fan" is applied even to fans made of reeds and the like.
"Having gathered together" means having made a heap in one place. Now, showing that very method of gathering:
He said, “And just as it was placed,” and so forth. *Anovassakaṃ* means “it does not get rained upon”; here, the suffix *-aka* should be understood in the sense of the object (*kamma*).
The meaning is: “Just as it was placed, it does not get rained upon, it does not get soaked.
Regarding *anavayo*: here, *vaya* means decline, as in “increase and decline” (*āyavayo*) and similar expressions. There is no decline in one’s own craft for this person.
"Deficiency" (*ūnatā*) means "incompleteness"; thus he said, "one who is not deficient and whose craft is perfected. "The teacher's work" (*ācariyaka*) means "the work of the teacher";
thus he said, "in the teacher's work. "A wooden frame" (*piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa*) refers to the door-posts; "woodwork" (*kaṭṭhakamma*) refers to pillars and so forth.
"With oil, lac, and clay" means with clay mixed with oil and lac.

85. *Kuṭikāya karaṇabhāvan* means the state of having been made as a hut. Since those learned in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*) desire the future tense when used in conjunction with the word *kiṃ*, it is said: "Its definition should be sought from the science of grammar.

*Mettāpubbhāgaṃ* means that which constitutes the preliminary stage of the meditation on loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*), consisting merely in the pervasion of all beings with benevolence. But why was this stated?
Is it not the case that the word *anuddayā* occurs in the sense of compassion (*karuṇā*)? True, this is so;

however, this word *anuddayā*, when occurring by incorporating the meaning of "protecting" (*anurakkhaṇa*) within itself, occurs in the sense of both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion. Here, it is stated as occurring in the sense of loving-kindness;
therefore, it is well said: "By this, he shows the preliminary stage of loving-kindness. [The phrase] "the preliminary stage of compassion" refers to...
It is merely a feeling of compassion toward sentient beings that constitutes the preliminary stage of the meditation on compassion (*karuṇā-jhāna*). "Mud" refers to clay;

its "kneading" is the act of rubbing it with the hands and so forth after pouring water upon it. "Of loving-kindness and compassion" refers to those states of loving-kindness and compassion that have reached absorption (*appanā*).
Although the Elder did not intentionally harm even the smallest or most minute living beings with the intent to kill, nevertheless...
Because he acted without compassion, failing to consider that "if this were done, these living beings would perish," he rebuked the Elder.
He said "the mass of people" (*janatā*) because it is a collection of people; thus he said "the last mass of people. "The state of being drinkable" means the state of being destroyed.
By saying "of those committing the taking of life," he shows the manner of observation by others even when the taking of life was not performed by the Elder himself.
"Following his view" means following after his opinion. "To be struck" means to be rubbed or destroyed;
that is the meaning. "One should not think thus" means one should not think in the manner done by the Elder.

From the statement, "Lest later generations fall into the habit of drinking blood from living beings," it follows that a monk [should refrain] regarding such things as baking bricks, baking bowls, building huts, having monasteries constructed, sweeping monasteries, setting fire to grass, digging wells, lotus ponds, and so forth.

This shows that where one knows, "There will be injury to small and minute living beings," even if one speaks a formal declaration of what is allowable (*kappiya-vacana*) in such a place, that action must not be performed.

Regarding the phrase "the offense stated in each respective case": this refers to the offenses such as *pācittiya* mentioned in the contexts of digging the earth, destroying a grove of living beings (*bhūtagāma-pātabyatā*), and so forth.

"Because he is a first-offender, there is no offense" means there is no offense on account of building a hut. "Having transgressed the training rule" means having transgressed the training rule stated thus:
"Monks, a hut made entirely of clay must not be built; whoever should build one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If there were to be no offense for one who dwells there after obtaining it as built by another, [then this would be so].

“The Blessed One would not have had that hut demolished,” [the opponent] says; [the Buddha] replies: “Even for those who dwell there after it has been built, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“Whether in this way or that, let it be mixed”: by whatever means it may be mixed—such as with clay below and building materials above—and so forth.
“In the manner of the Giñjakāvasatha”: here, *giñjakā* refers to bricks (*iṭṭhakā*); [it is so called] because of the bricks.
Thus was the Āvasatha, the Giñjakāvasatha, constructed. This is a designation for a dwelling made of bricks.
It is said that they built and covered that dwelling using only bricks, such that there was no need for plastering;
however, the beams, crossbeams, door-panels, and planks were made of wood. "Scattering" means making them into a powder or dust.

"Kissāti" means for what reason. "There is also work of construction (*vayakamma*)" means that there is also work of construction performed in such things as the fashioning of door-panels and so forth.
It is called "the banner of the heretics" because it is unsuitable for monks and because it conforms to the practices of the heretics.
Having established two of the reasons intended by himself among those stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, [he then presents] other reasons also stated therein.
Showing this, he said: “In the commentary, however, other reasons are also stated,” and so forth.
Therein, “out of compassion for beings” means out of compassion for those beings who would perish because of the construction of such a hut.
Since a hut made entirely of clay is easy to break, the bowl, robes, and other belongings placed therein remain unprotected from thieves and the like.
It is possible to take it away. Therefore it was said: "for the purpose of protecting the bowl and robes.
"For the purpose of prohibiting an abundance of lodgings" means for the purpose of prohibiting a multiplicity of lodgings;

or rather, for the purpose of prohibiting monks from becoming constantly preoccupied—having abandoned other duties such as teaching and interrogation—in the preparation of such lodgings. "Without fault" means...
One should not speak after having attributed a fault.
Regarding the commentary on the decisions outside the text (*pāḷimuttakavinicchaya-vaṇṇanā*):

among those decisions outside the text, the passage beginning with "And furthermore... [omitted] ...not for the sake of making it beautiful" refers to the grasping of the umbrella handle, the tally-sticks, and the weaving of the cage.
They say this with intentional meaning. "In all respects" means in every part of the handle of the umbrella.
"With the tip" means with the point of the socket. "It may be carried even after breaking the knob or the animal-head ornament":
if one obtains such an unallowable umbrella, it may be carried after breaking and cutting away both the knob and the animal-head ornament. Or else, the handle must be wrapped with thread.
It should be wound [around the handle] in such a way that no lines are visible on the umbrella-staff.

"At the base of the staff" (*daṇḍabunde*) means at the bottom part of the umbrella-staff. "The small circle within the umbrella" (*chattamaṇḍalikaṃ*) refers to the small circular area inside the umbrella. "Having sprinkled" (*ukkiritvā*) means having raised it up.
"That is permissible" (*sā vaṭṭati*) means that even if they do not bind it with cords, it is permissible because it is a suitable place for binding.
"By various strips" means by strips of various colors. This is stated for the purpose of showing the manner of making it for those who do so;
however, it is not even permissible to sew it in the aforementioned manner using a strip of a single color.
"At the edge of the cloth" means at the tip of the cloth-strip. This is said with reference to the place where two cloth-strips meet. "At the border."
"At the edge of the robe": this is said with reference to the wind blowing against the robe. "Veṇi" (braided seam) refers to sewing in the shape of a *varaka* flower-head.

"Saṅkhalikā" (chain-seam) refers to sewing in the shape of a cat's chain-fastening. Here, the term "veṇiṃ saṅkhalikaṃ" is in the accusative case, dependent on the verb "karonti" (they make), which expresses the action of doing.
"Agghiya, gaya, muggara, etc."—here, "agghiya" means [a design] in the shape of a cetiya (stupa).
*Siṃbanaṃ*: sewing by making the stitches thin at the base and wide at the tip in the shape of a club; *muggaro*:
