sewing by making the stitches uniform at both the base and the tip in the shape of a mallet. "They carve out crab-eyes" means that having bound the edge of the toggle-straps and the loops with thread, they raise them into the shape of crab-eyes;
the meaning is that they fashion them so. "Corner-thread-blisters... [text continues].
"The ends of the threads drawn out from the corners of the loops and strips"—this is stated in all three sections on the knots (*gaṇṭhi*).
But how are those pincushions (*piḷaka*) to be made so that their form is difficult to discern?

By making them difficult to discern in nature by either tying a knot once at the ends of the threads drawn out from the corners, or by sewing them back after turning them over, [one prepares] the ends of the threads.
Having shortened it, it should be cut. However, the Elder Dhammasiri stated:
"The corner-sutras and the pustules are indeed difficult to discern in the *kappara*.
Likewise, the Elder Ācariya Buddhadatta also said:
It is said: “The cords and the bosses therein are explained as being difficult to discern.
Therefore, according to their opinion, the meaning here should be understood as follows: the corner-cords and the bosses are “corner-cord- and-bosses.
By “jewel” (*maṇi*) is meant a stone such as emerald (*masāragalla*) and so forth. “Should not be rubbed” means it should not be ground; [this refers to] the shoulder-straps and the waist-bands.
However, it is permissible to rub [the cloth] with conch shells and the like. "It should be tied after making a loop" means it should be tied at the time of dyeing;

at other times, it should be untied and kept [loose]. "On a knot" refers to a knot made of ivory or similar materials. "Pustules" refers to pustules that should be raised by forming small drops [of dye] here and there.
"‘Of such a color’ is said with reference to a color appropriate for a recluse; however, it is said that if one obtains a bowl of jewel-like color made by another, it is permissible to use it.
Regarding "bowl-rings": these are bowl-rings made of tin, lead, or other such materials. [The Buddha said:
"Monks, variegated bowl-rings, covered with figures or decorated like wall-paintings, must not be worn."
Because it was stated [in the Vinaya], it was said: "Wall-painting is not permitted.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to carve a *makaradantaka* (crocodile-tooth pattern)," it was said:
"But the *makaradantaka* is permitted. "*Makaramukha*" means shaped like the mouth of a crocodile. "*Deḍḍhubhasīsa*" means shaped like the head of a water-snake (*deḍḍhubha*). "*Acchīni*" means eyes.

[The robes] are shaped like an elephant’s trunk. Regarding the waist-band (*rajjukakāyabandhana*), it is permitted that there be only one; thus, when fastening the band, it is permitted to tie it as a single strand.
It is not permitted to split it in the middle and tie it as a double strand.
However, without making it double, one may even fold a single strand back and forth a hundred times or more and then tie it.
It is permissible. "Not even one [loop] is permissible" means it is not permissible to tie it together even by making a single loop.
Regarding the phrase "many cords... is permissible," this was said with reference to the waistband (*kāyabandhana*), not with reference to the hem-fringe (*dasā*).
For such a waistband is permissible to tie. For this very reason, it was stated by the Elder Master Buddhadatta:
“The waistband made of a single cord was taught by the Sage;
even one shaped like five tassels is not permitted.
Having joined many cords together into one, [it is not allowed].”
"For it is permissible to bind [the waistband] after wrapping it continuously.
However, a *muraja* (drum-shaped) waistband is not permitted, because it has been stated:

"Monks, various types of waistbands must not be worn—namely, the *kalābuka*, the *deḍḍhubhaka*, the *muraja*, and the *maddavīṇā*. Whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)."
But then, if one were to take many cords together, wrap them around [an object] continuously with a single [piece of cloth], would it not count as a *muraja*?
Yes, it does not count. For what is called a *muraja* is made by wrapping various colored threads around the shape of a *muraja*-frame.
However, some say that a *muraja* is made by gathering many cords together and [binding them] with a single cord.
If they say, "It was made by wrapping it with many cords," that should not be accepted.

For if this were a *muraja* (drum-like belt), one could not say, "Many cords were brought together, wrapped continuously with one [of them], and thus made of many cords"; otherwise, the statement "that is allowable" would be contradicted.
However, for a *muraja* and for one shaped like a *pāmaṅga* (waist-belt), it is allowable at the ends (*dasāsu*). This applies to the waist-band.
"Frays wear out. Monks, I allow the *muraja* drum and the *maddavīṇā* lute," because it was said thus. For that very reason he will say:
"Monks, I allow the *muraja* drum and the *maddavīṇā* lute"—this was permitted specifically regarding frays.
Regarding the waistband: "The end of the waistband wears out. Monks, I allow a *vidha* (waistband)."

Because it is stated [in the Vinaya], one should make decorations made of ivory, horn, or other materials at the base of the fringe on the side of the waistband (*kāyabandhana*) for the sake of its stability. They say:
"The eight auspicious signs (*maṅgala*) are the conch, the wheel, the full water-jar, the elephant, the *sirīvaccha* (palm-tree cluster), the hook, the banner, and the *sovatthika* (swastika).
"Merely a boundary line" means merely a decorative border-line that should be made at both ends.
Because it is stated, “only straight,” anything with curved lines such as a four-sided shape is not permitted.
They say that “umbrella handles, Dhamma-wheels, collyrium tubes, and those made with various colored lines are not permitted.
Regarding *ārakaṇṭaka*: it refers to long-pointed knives made for the purpose of preparing books and the like. *Vaṭṭamaṇika* means...
A bubble that must be raised at the tip of a turned lathe; or, by the phrase "another smooth color," this includes pustules and the like.
A "jewel" (*maṇika*) is a single-spiraled gem. A "pustule" (*piḷaka*) is a small, mustard-seed-sized mark with many circular lines resembling the streaks on a peacock's tail.
They say: "Since it is not mentioned in this specific context, any smooth-colored object suitable for a pen is acceptable."
“Valitakaṃ” means having raised a fold in the middle. “Maṇḍalaṃ hoti” means it becomes a rounded surface for the purpose of inserting the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi).
Although only a small chisel for cutting tooth-sticks is mentioned here, even a large chisel is not permitted.
The connection is: “to tie it straight. The ellipsis is: “on both sides or on one side. [It is tied] to the tip of a small staff (kattarayaṭṭhi).
"Bracelets" refers even to rings which, through their mutual friction, produce a sound.

"In a vessel made of *āmaṇḍa*" means in a container made from *āmalaka* fruit. "A floor-covering" refers to coverings such as painted mats (*cittakaṭa*) or painted rugs (*cittattharaṇa*) that are spread upon a prepared floor.
"A water-jar" includes by this term even small flasks (*kuṇḍika*) and bowls (*saraka*).

He gathers [them]. He causes them to be sown in a four-cornered sowing bed. "Everything... is permissible" means that among the aforementioned items such as beds and chairs, everything—including floral designs, vine-work, and so forth, provided they are polished and colored—is permissible for a bhikkhu, with the exception of female figures.
Regarding the lodging, there is nothing to be prohibited except for a "disputed lodging. Herein, this is the intended meaning: among the requisites for a lodging—

There is nothing whatsoever that must be prohibited; however, a conflicting dwelling-place (viruddha-senāsana) must be rejected by oneself. "Others" refers to those who are the masters of the boundary (sīmasāmika).

Those who are favorites of the king—whether belonging to another school (paranikāyika) or the same school (ekanikāyika)—who cause obstacles to the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies, who are shameless (alajjina), and who are attached to royal families, are called [those to be excluded].
"A circle of the conscientious" (lajjiparisā) refers to the assembly of those masters of the boundary.
The assembly of the Lajjis is capable of becoming a faction and providing support.
"Well-done indeed" means that even what has been done regarding the property of others is considered well-done if it was performed according to the procedure prescribed within one's own boundary.
The commentary on the determination independent of the canonical text (*pāḷimuttakavinicchaya*) is finished.
86. *Devena gahitadārūni*: wood taken by the king; that is to say, wood belonging to the king. *Khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ karonto*: making it into small and large pieces. 87.
One who has great *matta*—that is, measure (*pamāṇa*)—in terms of lineage, wealth, sovereignty, and so forth, is a *mahāmatta*. Therefore he said: “endowed with great sovereign power.
88. *Avajjhāyanti*: they look down upon [it], or they think [it] thus. Therefore he said: “disregarding,” and so forth.
"They think of it as inferior" means they think of it as lowly.
"They speak of it" means they say to one another, "What is this?
What is this? But how, in this context, does the plural form "logs" (*dārūni*) come to be connected with the singular form "not given" (*adinnam*)?
He said: "‘He will take what is not given’—this is for the purpose of censuring,” and so forth.
Since censuring has as its object the taking of what is not given, it is stated that the taking of what is not given is the purpose of the censure.

Furthermore, although the wood was actually given by the keeper, because it was taken indirectly rather than directly, the Elder should be understood as having “taken what was not given. “In the distinction of speech-forms” means in the distinction between the singular and plural numbers.

“Sabbāvantaṃ parisam” means a retinue possessing all its parts, such as monks, nuns, and so forth. It is called “sabbāvantā” because the entire assembly (pajā) comprised of the fourfold retinue exists therein.
“Seniko” means one who possesses an army; “seniyo” is simply another form of “seniko.
“Bimbisāra” is his name; herein, “bimbī” means gold, and thus [he is so called] because of his complexion resembling the finest gold.

It should be understood that he is called Bimbisāra. By the statement "a fourth part is to be understood as a *pāda*," it should be seen that this implies that in all regions, a twentieth part of a *kahāpaṇa* is a *māsaka*.

It should be understood that the blue *kahāpaṇas* produced were endowed with the characteristics in accordance with the ancient teachers. That which was produced by Rudradāma is called a *rudradāmaka*.
It is said that it is worth one-third of a blue kahāpaṇa. They say that even in a place where blue kahāpaṇas do not exist,
one should take goods that circulate at the same value both in places where blue kahāpaṇas are used and in places where they are not, and make the valuation in terms of blue kahāpaṇas themselves.
The commentary on the story of Dhaniya is finished.
Its meaning... [as follows] ...should be understood in the same manner as previously stated;
by this it is shown that "this training rule was thus laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus, and this other incident also arose"—thus, in the commentary on the first *pārājika*.
The meaning of that should be understood according to the method already stated. By saying, "Now, in order to show that other matter which had arisen, he said:
'Then at that time,' etc.," he demonstrates that the connection with the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) is to be understood there in the very same manner as previously explained.

90–91. It is called a *rajakattharaṇa* because dyers spread [their goods] there; thus, it is said that a *rajakattharaṇa* refers to a dyer’s ford (*rajakatittha*). Therefore, he says, “having gone to the dyer’s ford. Explaining the meaning already stated, he says, “For in that place,” and so forth.
Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis (Padabhājanīya) 92.
A newly settled village consisting of a single hut or the like is so called until people have entered and established their residence.
They say that it does not count as a village; therefore, there is no requirement to ask for permission to enter it, nor any other such duties.
"Possessed by a yakkha" is said in the sense of being subject to affliction, or it includes a city of yakkhas and the like.
Even a city of yakkhas counts as a village when shops and such are visible, but it does not so count when they are not visible; therefore, even a city of yakkhas—
They say that when entering [the village], if shops and such are visible, the entire procedure for entering a village must be performed; if they are not visible, it need not be performed.
Furthermore, by the phrase "desiring to come back," he shows their state of having expectations regarding that place.
However, when they depart having become free from expectation, that [place] does not count as a village; therefore, in that case—
There is no need for the formal inquiry regarding entering a village and so forth.
One might object: "But isn't it stated in the *mātikā* simply as 'from a village or from a forest'? Therefore, after showing the characteristics of a village, one should have shown only the forest;
why then was it said, 'The vicinity of a village,' and so on? To this he replied: "'The vicinity of a village,' etc."

It is said, "for the purpose of showing the delimitation of the forest. For when the vicinity of the village (*gāmūpacāra*) is shown, one can show the delimitation of the forest by stating that, excluding both the village and its vicinity, the remainder is called the forest.

And this was stated in order to show the village and its vicinity without confusion. However, it should be understood that in the *mātikā*, the vicinity of the village is included by the mention of the "village" itself.

For in the world, the vicinity of a village (*gāmūpacāra*) is indeed reckoned as part of the village itself. By establishing it thus, the inclusion of the entire location for taking [an object] is accomplished in the *Mātikā*.

"The threshold-stone" (*indakhīla*) means the door-sill. It is reckoned as belonging to the forest because it is stated in the *Abhidhamma*: "Having gone out beyond the threshold-stone, all this is the forest.
It is called specifically the "middle" threshold-stone because it serves as the representative point for the threshold-stone.
Even when there is no gatepost (*indakhīla*), it is nevertheless called the "middle" (*vemajjha*) in that same way.

However, where even the doorposts do not exist, one must understand the term "gatepost" to refer to the middle point between the two ends of a fence or a wall, because that location serves as the functional equivalent of a gatepost.
"Uḍḍāpento" means causing to fly away; "luṭhitvā" means having rolled over.

“Of a man of medium size” means of a man of medium strength. By this statement, however, it should be understood that even the throwing of a pestle with a mortar is performed by way of demonstrating strength.

In the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated with the intention that “the village is the vicinity of the house” that “the throw of a clod for one standing in the vicinity of the house is the vicinity of the village. “At the door” [is the phrase].
This was said with reference to the interior from the point where water falls off the eaves.
And "inside the house" was said specifically with reference to the interior of the front porch.
By the phrase "enclosed," it is meant that the area demarcated around the entire house constitutes what is called the "vicinity of the house. Regarding a house where cattle [wander] all around—

A surrounding enclosure made of walls, fences, and so forth is established for the purpose of preventing entry; in that case, that very enclosure constitutes the vicinity of the house (*gharūpacāra*).
However, it should be understood that the definition of the boundaries such as the water-ditch and so on refers to a house that is not so enclosed.
This is the measure here, for the sake of a clear determination that prevents confusion between the village and the vicinity of the village in cases such as entering a village at an improper time.

Because it must be understood [in this way]. For, according to the method stated in the *Kurundi* and other commentaries, since a "village" (*gāma*) is defined as the vicinity of a house (*gharūpacāra*), there would be a confusion between the house, the vicinity of the house, the village, and the vicinity of the village.
By the phrase "thus in all cases," he shows that even prior to this point, the latter position alone possesses authority.
Some, however, say that this was stated with reference to the doctrine that will be explained from here on; that should not be accepted.
He says this with reference to the characteristic of the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*). "Therein" means in that taking of the village precinct.
"For the purpose of showing the boundary of that [unenclosed] village" means for the purpose of showing the boundary of that village which lacks a boundary;
such is the meaning. If this is so, then having cited the phrase "what is called a village," [the text continues]: "In the case of an unenclosed village, within the precinct of the houses..."
Why was it not stated, "the distance of a stone's throw for a man of medium height"?
They say: "Although 'village' is not explicitly mentioned here, it is understood by virtue of the context. Others, however, say:
"By the phrase 'the vicinity of a village' (*gāmūpacāro*), the inclusion of both the village and its vicinity should be seen. How so? [The vicinity] of the village..."

Regarding the phrase "the vicinity of a village" (*gāmūpacāro*): when this is analyzed in this way, the definition of the vicinity of an enclosed village is shown by the statement, "the range of a stone’s throw by a man of medium height standing at the gate-pillar (*indakhīla*) of an enclosed village.
However, if it were understood as "the vicinity consisting of the village itself is the village-vicinity," then [it would apply] to an unenclosed [village].

"By the phrase 'the range of a clod thrown by a middle-sized man standing at the vicinity of a house within a village,' it can be understood that the boundary of an unenclosed village is shown. [He replied:
"If, by the phrase 'the range of a clod thrown by a middle-sized man standing at the vicinity of a house,' the enclosure of even an enclosed village is [measured] beyond the range of that clod—"
They say that the boundary of the village should be understood as extending only as far as the range of a clod-throw.
"In the same manner as previously stated" means in the same manner as stated regarding an enclosed village.
"It becomes mixed" means it is intermingled. "Therein" refers to within the individual courtyards of houses and the general vicinity of the village. "Entering a village at an improper time..."
Since it has been stated, "For one crossing the boundary of an enclosed village, there is an offense of *pācittiya*;
for one entering the precinct (*upacāra*) of an unenclosed village, there is an offense of *pācittiya*," the non-confusion of the village and its precinct must be maintained;
therefore, he said: "And here, the determination should be understood according to their non-confusion in cases such as entering a village at an improper time."

And here, some say: "For one who crosses the enclosure of an enclosed village, or for one who crosses the place where the enclosure would be for an unenclosed village, there is an offense of entering a village at an improper time. This should not be accepted; however, the word-commentary states:
"For one who crosses the enclosure of an enclosed village, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); for one [crossing] an unenclosed [village]..."
Because it is stated: "For one entering the vicinity (*upacāra*) of a village, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

It should be understood that for an unenclosed village, an offense occurs upon entering the village vicinity, which is defined as the distance of a second stone-throw starting from the vicinity of the houses.
For this very reason, in the commentary on the training rule regarding entering a village at an improper time, it says: "The vicinity of an unenclosed village..."
"It should be understood in the same manner as explained regarding taking what is not given," it is said. In the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary on the Schedule) it is also stated:
"The offense in cases such as entering a village at an improper time should be delimited by way of that 'vicinity' (*upacāra*) which was shown for an unenclosed village.
If this is so, does it not contradict the rule: "One should not enter a village at an improper time"? No.
It is contradicted because the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*) is also included by the mention of the "village" (*gāma*).

Therefore, one must conclude that an offense for entering a village at an improper time occurs when one crosses the boundary of an enclosed village, or when one enters the precinct of an unenclosed village.
In the phrase "entering a village at an improper time, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes [entering] the interior of houses, their precincts, and so forth.
It gathers for those who remain such things as the alms received and the vessels.
"Having gone out beyond the threshold" (*nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā*) means having gone out from outside the threshold. And here, according to the Vinaya method, it is stated:
"With the exception of the village and the vicinity of the village, the rest is forest"; according to the Sutta method:
With reference to a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, it is stated: "A dwelling place called 'forest-dwelling' (āraññaka) is one that is at least five hundred bow-lengths distant from the last village.

Both the Vinaya and the Suttanta are indeed teachings by way of a methodological approach (pariyāya-desanā), whereas the Abhidhamma is a teaching not by way of a methodological approach (nippariyāya-desanā).
And since, according to the non-methodological approach, a place detached from a village is simply "forest" (arañña), [this definition] is according to the Abhidhamma method.
To show this, it is said: "having gone out beyond the threshold.

Regarding the "teacher’s bow," they say it is nine spans in measure when held in the ordinary hand, but four cubits in measure when the string is drawn up. It is for the purpose of excluding any possibility of doubt [regarding where the theft occurred], [thinking]:
"I have not taken it either in the village or in the forest; nor was it in a house, or in the vicinity of a house, or in the vicinity of a village, or in any such place."
This means: "Let him not be allowed to speak.

It is stated as "suitable" (*kappiya*) by way of propriety. However, even that which is unsuitable (*akappiya*), if it has not been formally accepted, falls under the category of what has not been given (*adatta*).
Even if the act of relinquishment and so forth has not been performed, and one does not know "this belongs to me," it remains the property of another.
It is like the property of infants lying on their backs, belonging to their parents after the latter have passed away.
That by means of which a person is called a "thief" is "theft"; thus he said, "This is a designation for the intention to misappropriate.
The word *saṅkhā* is seen in the senses of knowledge, a portion, a designation, counting, and so forth—as in such passages as, "Having reckoned, one partakes of one [thing]."
For it is seen in the sense of knowledge (*ñāṇa*); in such passages as “the conceptual proliferations of perception (*papañcasaññāsaṅkhā*) are active,” it refers to a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*);

in such passages as “the designation (*saṅkhā*) and conventional term (*samaññā*) for those respective phenomena,” it refers to a description (*paññatti*); and in such passages as “it is not easy to calculate (*saṅkhātuṃ*),” it refers to enumeration (*gaṇanā*).
Therein, with reference to the word *saṅkhā* in the sense of a constituent part, he said: “‘Saṅkhā’ and ‘saṅkhāta’ are one in meaning.”
Therefore he said: “This is a designation for a portion. “Proliferations” (*papañca-saṅkhā*) refers to the portions of proliferation consisting of craving, conceit, and views.

“A single mental portion” means that among those [mental states]—namely, the mind that occurs at the beginning with the thought ‘I shall carry it away,’ the mind that occurs in the middle accomplishing the going and so forth, or accomplishing the grasping and so forth, and that which accomplishes the application of moving from one place—the latter alone is this single [portion].

Some say that "the final mental factor" is intended here. However, in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "Among the mental factors involved in taking less than a māsaka, one māsaka, less than five māsakas, or five māsakas, there is one mental factor.

In both the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "Because the mind has many divisions, it is called 'one mental factor'. This alone is more excellent here: [that which is] designated as the "thieving mind."
Because it is said, "one factor of consciousness. By what is reckoned as theft means by the factor of consciousness consisting of the intention to steal acting as the instrument;
it does not mean by the factor of consciousness occurring in the taking of something through trust, for a limited time, and so forth—this is what is meant.
By way of legal action means by way of a lawsuit. "He brings a charge" means he accuses; the meaning is that he institutes a lawsuit. "The place imagined" means...
A place imagined by way of imagining a specific location. "Toll-house" (*suṅkaghāta*): here, "toll" (*suṅka*) is a designation for the portion to be given to kings;
it is called a "toll-house" because it is struck [with punishment] by those who pass through without having paid.
It is a designation for a place demarcated by signs such as trees or mountains with the instruction: "Toll must be paid by those who have entered here."

Commentary on the Discussion of the Twenty-five Modes of Conduct: “Confused” means crowded. “Agitated” means stirred up. “In some places” means in one commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). One pentad has been shown:
“It is possessed by another, one perceives it as possessed by another, and the requisite is of great value.”
"Whether it be five māsakas or more than five māsakas, if the intent to steal is present, and one touches it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one moves it, there is an offense of grave wrongdoing (thullaccaya). If one removes it from its place, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
Thus, the five factors of theft mentioned here are shown as one set of five. Two sets of five have been shown; [the next begins with] "in six ways... [as follows].
For one who takes what is not given, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).

If he does not perceive it as his own, nor takes it in trust, nor takes it temporarily, and if the article is of great value—worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas—and if the intention to steal is present, then upon touching it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Upon moving it, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
Having removed one from the six points stated as, “He causes [her] to fall from her position;
there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika),” and having shown that the remaining five points constitute one pentad, two pentads are thus demonstrated by including the pentad mentioned below.
Herein, “in the case of one taking what is not given in five ways,” etc., refers to all these points. By all the points...

By the phrases beginning with “and it is possessed by another,” etc., [it is meant]. “The pentads that are actually obtainable” refers to the pentads obtainable among the twenty-five types of theft (*avahāra*).
A “pentad” (*pañcaka*) is a collection of five types of theft. “With one’s own hand” (*sahattha*) means by one’s own hand; that which is produced by means of that [is *sahatthanibbatta*]. Of that...
Or, "that which is connected" is *sāhatthika* (taking by hand); this is the taking away (*avahāra*).

The designation "the pentad of *sāhatthika*" for the pentad beginning with *sāhatthika* should be understood as being obtained through the first term, just as the expression "wholesome triad" is used for the triad beginning with the wholesome.
By this same method, the pentad beginning with prior effort is called the "pentad of prior effort," and the pentad beginning with fraudulent taking is called the "pentad of fraudulent taking."
"It should be understood" means: regarding the third and fifth pentads—that is, the pentad of "by one's own hand" (*sāhatthika*) and the pentad of "by theft" (*theyyāvahāra*).

"By way of the terms found [in the rules]" means that it should be applied by way of the term "involving forfeiture" (*nissaggiyāvahāra*) found in the pentad of "by one's own hand," and by way of the term "involving scheming" (*parikappāvahāra*) found in the pentad of "by theft. This is the meaning.
*Āṇattika* (by command): An act committed by means of a command is *āṇattika*. *Nissagga*: The act of relinquishing;
it refers to the casting out of goods outside [the boundary] while standing at a customs house or in a designated place. *Nissaggiya*: That which is itself a relinquishment.

It is called *atthasādhaka* (accomplisher of the object) because it accomplishes the objective—namely, the offense of defeat (*pārājika*)—even prior to the completion of the physical action. "When you are able, [take] such-and-such a person's goods..."
For an instigation such as "then take it away," or the act of depositing sandals and so forth with someone who must inevitably drink a foot-measure of oil from another's oil-jar,
accomplishes the matter designated as an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) even prior to the taking of the goods by the one commanded and the drinking of the oil by those [who receive the sandals].
The same applies to the instigation involving direct physical contact (*sāhatthika*).
For it is said that one who accomplishes such a purpose is called an "accomplisher of the aim" (*atthasādhaka*).
Indeed, this is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "One called an 'accomplisher of the aim' is one who commands: 'When you are able, then steal such-and-such a person's goods.
In that case, if the other person, being free from obstacles, steals it, there is a *pārājika* offense for the commander at the very moment of the command."

"Or, if one puts oil worth a *pāda* into another person's oil-jar, or puts sandals or other items that must necessarily be worn into it, at the very moment they leave the hand, it is a *pārājika* offense.
"Laying down the burden" (*dhuranikkhepa*) means the relinquishing of the responsibility.
In cases such as making claims regarding a monastery, or in the giving and receiving of gifts by oneself and others—
The state of becoming devoid of effort. "Steals with his own hand" means he takes it with his own hand.
Regarding "he commands another, saying, 'Steal such-and-such a person's goods,'" here too the offense of the commander should be understood as occurring at the very moment of the command.
If this is so, what is the distinction between this [offense] and that which accomplishes the purpose? It is the act of enjoining [the other] to take [the object] at that very moment.
The distinction between these two is as follows: the *āṇattika-payoga* (instigation by command) is an instigation for the purpose of taking possession at a later time;
it is a means of accomplishing the objective. For this very reason it was said: "He commands: 'When you are able, then steal such-and-such a person's goods.

And here, it is shown that only the act of commanding is the means of accomplishing the objective; however, the means of accomplishing the objective by way of one's own hand (*sāhatthika*) will be explained further below.
Furthermore, the "laying down of the burden" (dhuranikkhepa) should be understood by way of the goods deposited; this is merely an illustration.
The same principle applies even in cases such as a formal challenge to a monastery (ārāmābhiyuñjana), where there is no giving of goods on loan or as a gift.
Because it is stated that "the preliminary effort (pubbapayoga) is to be understood by way of the command," for one who takes [the goods] without interruption, [it refers to] "of so-and-so..."

Commanding "Steal the goods" is a preliminary effort (*pubbapayoga*) because it precedes the actual seizing of the goods. Stealing that occurs simultaneously with the effort is simultaneous effort (*sahapayoga*).
Stealing after having made an agreement and deliberated, thinking "We shall steal such-and-such a good," is stealing by agreement (*saṃvidāvahāra*).
"Making a signal" (*saṅketakamma*) refers to the act of making an appointment by way of delimiting a time, such as the morning and so forth.
“Giving a sign” (*nimittakamma*) means making a sign, such as winking the eyes, for the purpose of arousing recognition.

As for the phrase “concomitant action by way of causing displacement from one’s place,” this should be regarded as merely an illustration; concomitant action should also be understood to exist in cases such as crossing a threshold, even in the absence of displacement from one’s place.
For this has been stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: “By way of causing displacement from one’s place...”
"Having transferred [the property] from waste-lands and so forth, it should be understood as a concurrent application by way of taking fields and so forth.
Theft (*theyya*) is called "thief" (*thena*); its state is "theft" (*theyya*). Taking away by means of that is "taking by theft" (*theyyāvahāra*).

For one who, having committed breaking into walls and so forth, takes away while remaining invisible, or who takes after deceiving with false weights, false measures, or counterfeit coins and the like—
For one who takes in this manner, it is "taking by theft" (*theyyāvahāra*). Taking after having overcome and subdued [the victim] is "taking by force" (*pasayhāvahāra*).

For when one takes what belongs to others by force through physical compulsion—such as village-robbers and the like—or when one takes more than what is rightfully one's own by means of stated methods, such as royal officials and the like, the taking of one who takes in this way is "taking by force."
Stealing after having devised a plan based on the nature of the goods and the circumstances is "stealing by design" (*parikappāvahāra*).
Hiding a finger-ring or similar object with grass, leaves, and so forth, and subsequently stealing it while it is thus concealed, is "stealing by concealment" (*paṭicchannāvahāra*).
Stealing after shifting the attention [of the owner] is "stealing by diversion" (*kusāvahāra*).

“Having weighed” means having examined. “Proper conduct” (*sāmīcī*) refers to the formal duties (*vatta*); the intention is that there is no offense. “A great crush of people” means a great commotion of people.
“When the crowd has departed” means when the multitude of people has gone away.
For what reason did he say, “Make this saffron robe your own property and give it to this very bhikkhu”? It was because the owner of the robe had abandoned his responsibility.
Therefore, it is not permissible to take what has not been given by him.
Even the thief, from the moment remorse arises, wanders about seeking the owner of the robe, thinking, "I shall give it back.
And when the owner of the robe says, "This is mine," the thief also relinquishes his attachment; that is why he spoke thus. If this is so, [then] the owner of the robe alone...
Why was it not said, “Take what belongs to yourself”? It was for the purpose of removing the remorse of both parties.
How so? Remorse might arise in the thief, thinking, “I did not give this with my own hand;
this is merely a commodity to be paid for. Remorse might also arise in the other, thinking, “Having first relinquished my responsibility, I later took what was not given.”

"It depreciates what is of little value. "It fulfills the purpose of the wood" means it accomplishes whatever task is to be done with the wood. The entire passage beginning with "While I am present" was spoken by the king out of his favor; one should not think, however, that "the Elder acted inappropriately.

As for this depreciation of value mentioned regarding the cutting of tooth-sticks and so forth on a single day, all of that was spoken with reference specifically to what has been purchased and taken by the owner of the goods.
Furthermore, all of this must be accepted according to the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā* masters.

“Stone and gravel” means stone-gravel. The passage beginning with “whether it be an offense or no offense” is the explanation of the phrase “the wise person should carry [it] for the sake of its purpose.
The commentary on the discussion of the twenty-five modes of taking is finished.
Regarding the term *akkhadassā*: here, it is said that by the word *akkha*, the hall of legal adjudication (*vinicchaya-sālā*) is meant.
Because they sit there and see what is blameworthy and what is blameless, those who investigate the Dhamma are called *akkhadassā*. Regarding the phrase *haneyyuṃ*:
here, "killing" (*hanana*) consists both of striking with hands, feet, and so forth, and of cutting off the head and so forth; thus he says: "‘They would kill’ means they would strike and..."

"And they might cut [him]. For this very reason, the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*) states: "They might strike him with a hand, or a foot, or a whip, or a cane, or a short staff, or by means of cutting.
In that context, "with a short staff" (*aḍḍhadaṇḍakena*) means with a short mallet measuring two cubits in length, or with a bamboo splinter.
"By means of cutting" (*chejjāya*) means by the cutting off of hands, feet, head, and so forth. "They might carry him away" (*nīhareyyun*):...
They would lead him out from the village, town, or other such place. Regarding the words "You are a thief...
you are a bandit," one should understand the meaning by supplying the word "they would revile" (*paribhāseyyun*); thus he says, "Having said 'You are a thief' and so forth, they would revile him.
93. The connection is with the phrase "that property which was shown. "Wherever it was situated" means on the ground or in whatever other location.

"Where it is situated": "In whatever manner the taking proceeds" means that even if there is no grasping at all, the goods situated on the ground or elsewhere approach a state of being taken in whichever manner [the taker intends].
Commentary on the Discussion of Goods Situated on the Ground.

94. Regarding the statement, "If one makes oneself throb, it is always an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)": here it should be understood that it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing even for one who, having made oneself throb with the thought, "I shall rise," subsequently does not rise but remains lying there;
and it is also an offense of wrong-doing for one who rises in a single effort without making any part of the limbs or body throb.
Or, in the case of something else that does not assist in going, such as when closing a door, [it is an offense] regarding the act of going to the place where the pot was kept.
There is no offense because it is of no assistance; likewise, there is no offense for bodily or verbal actions that do not assist in going elsewhere.
"Word by word" means by each individual word, as indicated by the phrase *ekekatthadīpikā*. "Apprehended" means known.

Regarding the phrase "and we shall perform meritorious deeds," in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated: "For one who says, 'Having committed false speech, we shall perform meritorious deeds,' there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense."
What has been stated contradicts the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā* regarding this very point. For it will say:

"Whatever word is false, in each such case there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)," and "Indeed, in the preliminary stage of taking what is not given, there is no such thing as an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in place of an offense of expiation.
However, if it were stated in that way, it would not contradict [the following]: "Having committed a falsehood..."
"For one who says, 'I shall perform meritorious deeds,' there is a *dukkaṭa* offense together with the *pācittiya*.
For it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: "For those digging unallowable earth, there are *pācittiya* offenses together with *dukkaṭas*";
and he will further say: "And just as here, so everywhere in the place of a *pācittiya*, one is not exempt from *dukkaṭas*. But if...
A person with a wholesome mind says, "We shall perform meritorious deeds," and there is no offense;

for it will be stated that "there is no offense if one generates a wholesome state of mind thinking, 'We shall perform an offering to the Buddha, an offering to the Dhamma, or a meal for the Saṅgha,' and there is no offense in going with a wholesome mind," and likewise,
"as here, so everywhere, there is no offense for one whose mind is free from theft."
"It should be understood as 'written by oversight'" means it should be understood that it was written after having been omitted at the time of being transcribed into a book later on.
Since only this pair— "a hoe or a basket"— is mentioned in the Canon and in the remaining commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*),
while the axe and adze are not mentioned, [the author] states the following in order to show that those two are also found in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* and other works.
It is said: “In the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* and in the *Mahāpaccarī*, however,” and so forth. Because it was committed with a thieving mind, it is stated:
“Together with the *dukkaṭas*, there are *pācittiyas*. Following that, “in all actions” means in all actions to be performed after the taking of seeds.
“Everything according to the previous method” means that up until the conclusion of the Piṭaka, there is a *dukkaṭa* for every hand-movement and foot-step.

"Shown by the Elders": this was shown by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma after synthesizing [the rules] for the sake of avoiding confusion regarding the preliminary and concurrent offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

They say: "Since all *dukkaṭa* offenses must be subsumed within these very eight, it should be classified as a Vinaya *dukkaṭa* alone, being distinct from the other seven types of *dukkaṭa*. The tenfold jewel:
The ten kinds of gems mentioned as follows: “pearl, mani-jewel, beryl, conch, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and masāragalla. Also:
“mani-jewel, pearl, beryl, and conch...”
“Stone, coral, silver, and gold; ruby, and emerald—
the wise one knows these ten as jewels.”
Thus it was said.
"Seven kinds of grain" refers to these seven types of grain: rice (*sāli*), paddy (*vīhi*), barley (*yava*), millet (*kaṅgu*), wild millet (*kudrūsa*), beans (*varaka*), and wheat (*godhuma*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "weapons and goods and so forth," musical instruments, female forms, and the like are included. [These are] things not to be touched.

Regarding the basis, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); [there is] an offense of wrong-doing for touching what should not be touched. “An offense of wrong-doing through bad practice” (*durupaciṇṇadukkaṭa*):

because one has done what was forbidden by thinking, “This should not be done,” it is a bad habit or conduct; thus it is “bad practice. An offense of wrong-doing in that regard is an offense of wrong-doing through bad practice.

An offense of wrong-doing prescribed in the Discipline (*vinaya*) is an offense of wrong-doing in the Discipline. Having heard that someone is striving for a schism in the Saṅgha, for the purpose of preventing that...
If one does not speak when the matter is known, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for knowing. The eleven formal admonitions (*samanubhāsanā*) consist of:

five in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha—namely, the four *saṅghādisesa* offenses that require a third formal act and the Ariṭṭha training rule—and six in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha—namely, the one *pārājika* offense that requires a third formal act, the four *saṅghādisesa* offenses, and the Caṇḍakāḷī training rule. [The rest includes] the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsa*), etc.
For one who has given a promise but does not fulfill it, there is the *dukkaṭa* offense pertaining to the promise,
known as the *paṭissava-dukkata*. [This applies] in the case of prior preparation,
in improper conduct involving physical contact, in the Vinaya, in what is known, in a formal motion (*ñatti*), and in a promise.
These eight offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) have been declared in the Vinaya by the one who knows the Vinaya.
And herein, it is said, "then, without laying down the burden," and so forth, because the preceding offenses cease from the point of the preliminary action (sahapayoga) onwards.
In that context, because it is stated "without laying down the burden" (dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā), [it refers to] the laying down of the burden.
It should be understood that for one who digs after having [already] done so, the previous offenses do not cease.
The statement that "the dukkaṭa of shifting [the earth] ceases and one stands guilty of the dukkaṭa of uprooting" is said in order to show the sequence as it appears in the Pāḷi.
However, if, after uprooting the soil, one digs again while still maintaining the same resolve, the dukkaṭa of uprooting ceases.
It stands as a transgression of digging.
Since "that which is done" (*kataṃ*), "doing" (*karaṇaṃ*), and "action" (*kiriyā*) are identical in meaning, he said, "That action is improper.
Now, demonstrating this very point by means of the *Parivāra* text, he said, "And this has also been stated," and so forth. In that context, "failed" (*aparaddhaṃ*) means "missed" (*viraddhaṃ*).
"Khali" is a synonym for everything that is called "dukkaṭa" (wrong-doing) here;
for whatever is badly done or deformedly done is "dukkaṭa. Furthermore, this is "aparaddha" (failed) because it was not done as taught by the Teacher;
it is "viraddha" (missed) because it proceeded by missing the wholesome; and it is [a failure] regarding the practice of the Noble Lineage.
It is called "transgression" (khalita) because it has not been ascended to. "Whatever a human being does" is the illustration of the simile here. Its meaning is as follows:

just as whatever evil a person in the world commits, whether openly or in secret, they proclaim that to be "misdeed" (dukkaṭa), so too this is evil by virtue of its base nature, which is censured by the Buddha; therefore, it should be understood as "misdeed."

Just as that which is painful or base is called a "bad destination" (*duggati*) when it ought to be called a "painful or base destination," and just as that which has a bitter fruit is called "bitter-fruited" (*kaṭukapphala*) when it ought to be called "having bitter fruit," so too here,

in order to show that it is called a "grave offense" (*thullaccaya*) when it ought to be called a "grave transgression" (*thūlaccaya*) because of its grossness and its being a transgression, [the text says] "in the future life... (*samparāye*).
And he said, "and miserable rebirths," and so forth. However, when a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) is formed, the shortening of the vowel following the conjunct is already established;
bearing this in mind, it was stated merely as "the state of being a conjunct should be understood. "In the root of one" means in the presence of one.
"There is no transgression equal to that" means among the transgressions leading to instruction, there is no transgression as grave as that. Therefore, this...
Regarding the phrase "it is so called": because the offense is grave (*thulla*), it is called a *thullaccaya*; this is the meaning.
"In all cases, a *dukkaṭa* occurs for touching and a *thullaccaya* for causing to move; these occur separately for one who performs the act of touching and causing to move with a mind of theft.
However, for one who takes [the object] in a single continuous effort, [the offense arises] upon its removal..."
“They say it is indeed a *pārājika*, and not *dukkaṭa* or *thullaccaya* offenses.
Regarding the phrase “without having engaged in the preliminary effort,” it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:

“Because there is no cessation of the offenses committed during the preliminary effort, even if one has engaged in the preliminary effort, one who has fallen into a state of shame must confess the offenses committed during that preliminary effort. This is the word of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

However, the inclusion of the phrase "but when [the act] has been performed" indicates that even for those offenses committed during the preliminary application (*pubbapayoga*) along with the actual performance (*sahapayoga*), there is a cessation of the offense;
otherwise, this qualification—"but without performing it together"—would be entirely purposeless. Furthermore, as stated below:
"But if, even when grass, trees, creepers, and so forth growing there have been cut, a sense of shame (*lajjidhamma*) descends upon him, restraint (*saṃvara*)..."

"...arises; having confessed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) on account of the cutting, one is released"—this too indicates the subsiding of the offenses committed during the prior application once the simultaneous application has been performed, because it is stated that the confession is for the wrong-doing incurred specifically on account of the cutting during the simultaneous application.
And the phrase "starting from the simultaneous application" refers to what occurred prior to that point for one who has reached the simultaneous application.
This indicates the subsiding even of those offenses committed through prior preparation (*pubbapayoga*). By this, the following meaning is understood:
"As long as one does not reach the stage of actual performance (*sahapayoga*), there is no subsiding of the offenses previously committed;
however, from the moment one reaches the stage of actual performance, there is subsiding even of those [prior offenses]. Therefore, it is well...
Having investigated, one should accept that which is more appropriate.
Regarding the statement, "Even if there are many offenses, one is freed by confessing only one," this is the intended meaning:

if ten offenses were incurred for each of the acts of digging, sorting, and removing, one is freed from them by confessing ten offenses for the act of removing, as it constitutes a dissimilar action (*visabhāga-kiriyā*).

"Because the preceding offenses have been pacified. However, by taking the offenses committed through the same action as being one due to their commonality of origin, it is said, "having confessed only one";
therefore, by this statement from the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā as well, it supports only the pacification of the preceding offenses as previously stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, and not—
There is a difference in meaning between the two commentaries. Furthermore, they describe another aspect here:
"Even in the case of identical actions, the offenses incurred due to each successive moment of digging subside upon reaching the subsequent moments;
with this intention, [it is said]: 'And when a sense of shame arises during the digging of soil, etc.'"
"Even if there are many offenses, one is released by confessing only one," so it is said in the Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā.
But if that were the case, the phrase "even if there are many offenses" would not need to be stated; yet it has been stated.

Therefore, it must be understood that only after reaching an action of a different category (visabhāga-kiriya) does one desire the subsiding of the previous offenses, and thus, even among many offenses, one is released by confessing only one.
They also say: "In this passage, a distinct sequence of teaching is shown.

This is their intention: just as here the subsiding of previous offenses is accepted according to the authority of the Aṭṭhakathā masters, so too, the statement that one is released by confessing even a single offense among many is likewise based solely on the authority of the Aṭṭhakathā masters.
This should be understood. Just as in the Pāḷi it is shown that even where there is a *pācittiya* offense,

here a specific distinction of offenses is presented by treating it as a *dukkaṭa*, so too the specific distinction regarding the subsiding of previous offenses and the specific distinction regarding the confession have been shown by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā.
“Sinking down from below” means: thinking, “When the owners have come and gone without seeing me, I will take it,” one sinks it into the ground below with a thieving mind.

“With the base” means: with the lower surface of the pot. Thus, the connection is that the removal from its place of a pot standing in one location is to be understood through six modes. “He draws out the handle; [this is] a Pārājika.”
If one does not let it go into the air but drags it out by rubbing it, then at the mere moment it is dragged out from the cut edge, there is a *pārājika* offense.
"He moves it here and there" means that while still rubbing it, he moves it without letting it go into the air.
"At the mere moment of being cut, there is a *pārājika*" means that if it necessarily falls, there is a *pārājika* at the very moment it is cut. "The limit" refers to [the value of] five māsakas.
"Or more than five māsakas"—this is the limit of the number mentioned.
"Shifting aside" means dividing with the hand into two parts while thinking, "I will take what is standing below. "In a half-pot" means in a pot that is half-full.
But why should one not accept even what is stated in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* and other texts, according to the authority of the masters of the commentaries?
He said: "When a grave matter concerning the adjudication of the Vinaya has arisen, one must stand firm.

"The nature of the Vinaya" (*vinayadhammatā*) means the natural disposition of those who hold the Vinaya in high esteem. For those who revere the Vinaya stand firm when a grave matter concerning the adjudication of the Vinaya arises.

Here, the word "Vinaya" is used specifically to denote one who values the Vinaya, for the purpose of expressing that state of valuing the Vinaya; or else, it is the "nature of the Vinaya" because the domain of the Vinaya is the object of their profound respect.
Now, showing that what is stated in the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries does not agree with the *Pāḷi*, he said, “Moreover,” and so forth.
“Vessel” (*bhājana*) refers to a vessel such as a bowl. For one who takes [food] without filling the bowl, the limit is the rim even before it is lifted;
however, for one who takes it after filling it, the limit occurs at the time of lifting. Therefore, he said: “Or by the limit of the rim.”
"Or by means of a scoop. However, when it is impossible to take [oil] from a jar of oil and the like because the oil is not abundant, then it is done only by the limit of the rim.
"Cikkanam" means stiff. "Suitable for pulling back and forth":
here, pulling toward oneself is "ākaḍḍhanam," while pulling away is "vikaḍḍhanam."

“Dragging away”: to drag away from one’s own vessel. “An offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) at the mere moment it is released from the hand” is because the preliminary effort for seizing what belongs to another with a thieving mind has been performed. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* itself:
“Even if, having made the boundary weak, [one takes] the water-outlet of a dry pond or the water-drawing bucket...”
Because it is stated that "if one covers [the water] or blocks the path for its exit elsewhere,
or straightens a dry channel, then when rain falls later and the water comes, it breaks the boundary; in all such cases,
there is an offense requiring the payment of goods," it is said that "this, however, is contradicted by the legal decision regarding the straightening of a dry channel in a dried-up pond."
The characteristic of theft (*avahāralakkhaṇa*) refers to even a single instance among the twenty-five types of theft;
or it is simply the application of moving [an object] from its place. "Removes" (*uddharati*) means when even as much as a hair’s breadth is removed from the spot touched by the cooking-pot.

"Appropriate" (*yutta*) means it is appropriate because of the presence of the application of moving [the object] from its place. "For the sake of protection" (*saṅgopanatthāya*) indicates a state of pure mind. "Will obstruct" (*palibujjhissati*) means he will prevent [it].
"An offense entailing defeat (pārājika) by the very method already stated" means that it is an offense entailing defeat at the very moment [the object] leaves the hand.
"He removes it with a pure mind" means that even before pouring the oil into the pot, he sets it down with a pure mind, and afterwards he removes it with a pure mind.
"It is not a theft" because the preliminary effort of stealing with a thieving mind has not been performed. This is because it was his own vessel.
However, the statement "not the neck" means that only the absence of an offense was stated; the intention is that it was not analyzed in this manner.

Alternatively, by the phrase "only the absence of an offense was stated," he establishes the position of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā previously cited as "not the neck," because the word "neck" does not occur there, even according to the Kurundi doctrine shown later.
The argument of the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*) alone is established. Regarding "one's own goods":
it refers to the yellow oil placed in one’s own jar with a pure mind prior to the pouring of the oil. "A point of confusion" means a point of confusion by way of determining the offense.
"It is called 'gone outside'" means that from that moment on, because the oil no longer has its proper place and because it is turned downward, it is considered to have gone outside.
It is so called. When a hole is made starting from the inside, the oil, having emerged, goes to whatever place it reaches, and that very place comes to be counted as a separate vessel;
thus he said: "When it has flowed out to the extent of one *pādagaḷanaka* from the outer edge, it is a *pārājika* offense.
"Made in whatever way" means made starting either from the outer edge or from the inner edge. "A hole made by placing [the tool] in the middle" means in the middle.

Having set down a skull fragment, when one cuts it afterwards, the breach is made by that cut. In the case of cutting a boundary: one standing inside and cutting outwards must be dealt with according to the inner edge;
one standing outside and cutting inwards must be dealt with according to the outer edge;
and one who cuts both inside and outside, having established the center, and cuts through it, [is dealt with] according to the middle.
Because it is stated that [the offense] "must be made amends for," it is said that "it corresponds to the breaking of the boundary of a reservoir. What is appropriate here is this:

if the breach was made starting from both the inside and the outside, it must be made amends for by way of the middle; if it was made starting from the inside, it must be made amends for by way of the outside edge;
and if it was made starting from the outside, it must be made amends for by way of the interior. This threefold method applies here to a breach made in a place where there is no obstruction.
It is appropriate. Because there is no application [of effort] in water, it is said: "because of the absence of an application that causes displacement from its place.
When it says "stated in the Commentary," it means stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the eating of solid food and the drinking of liquids such as ghee and so forth by one who is firm [in his resolve], he says: "he makes it something not to be eaten or not to be drunk. How?
But because one acts in that way, he says, "Feces or urine," and so forth. Why, however, is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) mentioned here? He says:
"Because there is no displacement from the original position, it is a *dukkaṭa*. "The first two" refers to breaking and discarding.
Why does it not coincide [with the previous rule]? He says: "For that," and so forth. "By making a water-jar worn out" means by making a full water-jar worn out.
"By straightening the water-channel" means by making the water-channel, which was full of water, straight.

"A single characteristic" means that breaking [the vessel] by crushing it like a jar and discarding it by straightening the water-channel share one and the same nature, because the method of removing [the object] from its place is present in both.
"But the latter two," however, refer to burning and making it unusable.
"Regarding the phrase 'here they state the decision thus': here, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, certain teachers state the decision thus.

As for the statement 'this was said with reference to the latter two': since the decision regarding the former two can be understood according to what has been stated below, nothing further is said there;
rather, [the decision is given] with reference to the latter two, because there is no displacement from one's position."

“An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)” means this is what was stated; such is the intended meaning. “With a thieving mind” means with a mind of theft that has arisen through the desire to do so for oneself or for another.
“With the intention of destroying” means with the mere intention of destroying, like one who would cut off hands, feet, and so forth.
Regarding the first two [cases], he asks: “What happens? With what intention is nothing said? and thus he says: “But in the first two... pe... [etc.]”

“Pārājika. In this context, the meaning is: for one who breaks it or discards it according to the method stated there—that is, for one who breaks it by striking it with a mallet, or for one who removes it by pouring water or sand over it. And as for the word “inappropriate” (*ayutta*):
since only a *dukkaṭa* offense was mentioned in the first two clauses of the Pāḷi, [the commentary states]: “In the first two... [etc. ...pārājika. This—
“If it were yours,” means “if it should belong to you. Having refuted the possibility of its being inappropriate, he states the reason for that:
“because the meaning must be understood otherwise. To the question, “How then should the meaning be understood here? he says, “For in the Pāḷi,” and so forth.
Since the meaning is not contradicted even in the case of the desire to destroy [the object], according to the method explained below, he specifies, “in the case of the intention to steal.”

It has been said: “Thus they speak of the determination. From this point onward, because everything that has been stated constitutes a single statement, it is stated by way of conclusion as “thus some say.
Now, when the meaning of the text is understood according to what has just been said, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, [it is stated] generally regarding all four...

Since there would be no distinction in the statement that "this was said with reference to the latter two," and because it would follow that there is no distinction between the phrases "he discards" and "he makes unusable" among the four points stated in the Pāḷi, [the commentator],
desiring to demonstrate the meaning by himself harmonizing the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā in another way, says: "But here..."

He said, "The essence," and so forth. Since it is stated in the *Vinītavatthu* that "he burned a heap of grass belonging to the Saṅgha with a thieving mind," by this very [example] of one who burns grass in the *Vinītavatthu*, it should be understood that here too, the phrase "desiring to move [the object] from its place" implies "desiring to move it from its place with a thieving mind. It means "only desiring not to discard it."
Here too, it should be connected with the phrase "with a thieving mind.

For this was stated with reference to the category of the thieving mind, since the category of the desire to destroy will be explained later. Therefore he said, "But in the case of the desire to destroy," and so forth.

"It is also appropriate in the other way" means that even for one who wishes to move [the object] from its place due to the absence of a thieving mind, a *dukkaṭa* offense is appropriate; this is what is meant.
The commentary on the *Bhūmaṭṭha* is finished.
Commentary on the *Ākāsaṭṭha*: 96.
In the commentary on the *Ākāsaṭṭha*, "with the tip of the mouth" means with the front of the mouth; "with the tip of the tail-feathers" means with the cluster of tail-feathers.

"By the tip. "He extends" means he extends it for the purpose of grasping. "Or without having grasped" means either by striking with a clod of earth or the like, or by way of leading [the animal] without having grasped it.

Although the determination of what is situated in space (ākāsaṭṭha) is being stated, in order to avoid confusion regarding the fact that even when something situated in space has entered the state of being situated in the air (vehāsaṭṭha), etc., as a consequence of that, it was said:
"In whichever limb it settles," and so forth. "Within the enclosure" refers to an enclosed dwelling.
“Inside. “Within the village” means inside a village that is enclosed by a boundary wall.
However, in the case of an unenclosed site, the very place where one stands within the village is considered the location. “He makes it face the forest” means he makes it face toward the wilderness.

“He protects” means he protects it because the person’s desired destination has not been reached by that particular course of action. This refers to one who is walking upon the ground; regarding the second step...
Thus it was said. "Of one who has gone out from a village" means of one who has gone out from an enclosed village. A *kapiñjala* is a species of bird.
The commentary on the section concerning what is situated in the air is finished.
The commentary on the section concerning what is situated in the open air.

97. However, in the *Vehāsaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated with the intention that "the transgression of the aforementioned area occurs through the pulling of a robe placed on a robe-stand by even a mere one or two finger-breadths" that "there is a *pārājika* offense by the mere pulling of one or two finger-breadths.
And this was said with reference to such a robe-stand pole that is not very large; in the case of a large one...
However, it may occur simply by pulling [the robe] out further than that.
"Having tied it with a cord" means having tied the robe with one end of a cord and the robe-stand with the other end, and then leaving the robe thus placed.
Because it is of a nature to fall immediately upon being released, it is stated: "Upon release, there is a *pārājika* offense."
"An offense involving defeat (pārājika) occurs when even a single person has passed through the space of a touch" is stated because [the bed] was placed without touching the wall.
"Placed leaning against a wall" means it was placed after being hung upon pegs or similar supports set up in a row, so that it actually touches the wall.
"Placed by hanging it onto the leaves of a tree" is said with reference to something placed by others.
The commentary on the section concerning what is situated in the air is finished.
Commentary on the section concerning what is situated in water: 98.
Regarding the commentary on what is situated in water, he says "in water that does not flow" because what is placed in flowing water does not remain [static].
"An offense" (*anāpatti*) is stated with reference to the absence of the *dukkaṭa* offense regarding hand-movements and foot-movements.
"Pulls" (*kaḍḍhati*) means draws down from below. Regarding "lotuses and so forth" (*uppalādīsu*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *paduma*, *puṇḍarīka*, and others.
A red lotus is the *paduma*; a white one is the *puṇḍarīka*. Or, a white lotus is the *paduma*; a red one is the *puṇḍarīka*. Alternatively, [the phrase] "red or... [is used].
Whether it be a white lotus with a hundred petals or a white water-lily (*puṇḍarīka*) with fewer than a hundred petals—“the basis is fulfilled” means that the basis for a *pārājika* offense arises.
“At the mere moment of cutting it, it is a *pārājika*” refers to the cutting from a place above the water, that is, from the part of the plant released from the water.
“The basis which fulfills” refers to whichever flower fulfills the basis for a *pārājika* offense.
“Handako had made a bundle with ten flowers; having made a large bundle, it was tied so as to be a heavy load.

Regarding the phrase “having spread grass over the ropes”: here, “having placed two ropes on the surface of the water, having spread grass across them from side to side, and then—whether tying or not tying [the flowers] upon them—the flowers [are arranged] only across [the grass].”
"Excluding the two ropes that have gone below, they lift [the water] up and place it upon the flower," so they say.

"It moves even by the measure of a hair's breadth from its original position" means that it moves the space touched by the far end [of the staff], while moving the space at the near end by the measure of a hair's breadth.
"The entire water" means all the water located in the space touched by the staff. Not...
“Water is not a place” because the place made by oneself is not a [valid] place. “Both of these”: here, “without having released the bond... [etc.
...an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika)” is the first; “the first bond... [etc. ...the delimitation of the place” is the second.
“In a lotus grove” means in a cluster of lotuses. “Uprooted” means uprooted by others for one’s own sake.
"Placed outside" means placed outside of the water.
"Bound" refers to being tied in bundles, having been made small by way of hand-measures. "Root" means a bulb.
"Or leaf, or flower"—this is said with reference to what stands having entered within the mud. "The entire water" means all the water contained within reservoirs and the like.
“Niddhamanatumba” means the outlet for the water from a pond. “Udakavāhaka” means a large irrigation channel (mahāmātikā).
He says, “It is not theft,” because this is not the same as the previous case, adding: “Why? … For such was the agreement made there.

“There is no theft” because it was taken from a place held in common by all, where there is no private ownership. “Having diverted the channel” means having diverted a small irrigation channel (khuddakamātikā).

Having placed [the fish] on it... [and so on]... "They remain": here they say that since those dead fish are indeed the property of those [fishermen], there is no theft for one who takes them while they are still alive.
The commentary on the discussion of water is finished.
Commentary on the Boat Sutta (Nāvaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā) 99.
In the Boat Sutta, however, by the phrase "one who does not move from his place as soon as he is released from the bond," it rejects the case of a boat tied up in a violent current.
"In that case, it is an offense of wrong-doing" refers to the rule: "If one releases the bond, there is an offense of wrong-doing."
This was said with reference to the *dukkaṭa* offense prescribed for one who is thus releasing [the semen]. Regarding the statement, "There is also a *thullaccaya* and there is a *pārājika*":
it should be understood that if it is released without first moving it from its place, there is a *thullaccaya*; if it is released after first moving it from its place, there is a *pārājika*.
As for the phrase, "Like a pig bound in a snare," and so forth, he says, "The reasoning therein has already been stated above."

"Vippanaṭṭhā nāvā" means that having met with destruction due to adverse winds and so forth, and having sunk into the water, it refers to a ship that has come to rest in mid-water without reaching the ground below.
For this very reason it is said: "For one who is sinking it... [etc.
...when the rim of the mouth [of the vessel] has merely passed over the area touched by the ship's keel, it is a pārājika offense. "Opilāpentassa" means for one who is causing it to sink.

"At the mere moment of having passed beyond" means at the very moment the space has been transgressed. "The same method applies" indicates that it is a *pārājika* offense at the mere moment of being released.
Because it is a large rope suitable for pulling a boat, the entire length starting from the end of the rope is called "the place.
It is said that "it causes it to catch the wind" because it is positioned in such a way that it catches the wind even when there is no wind. It is powerful.
And by the phrase "and the wind having come," it is shown that this application was made when there was no wind. For that very reason it is said: "There is no theft for the person.
However, when the wind is present, the application made is indeed an application for moving from its place;
thus, as in the case of straightening a dry furrow, it should be understood that theft does exist. It is not an application for moving from its place in the case of straightening a dry furrow.
This is because, in the absence of wind, it has been employed [as a boat]. "But it is liable for damages" means that the owner of the boat is liable for damages.
The commentary on the Boat Kammaṭṭhāna is finished.
The commentary on the Vehicle Kammaṭṭhāna.
100. In the *Yāna-aṭṭhakathā*, "yoked with two" means yoked with two oxen. "Unyoked" means not yoked with oxen.
"Made fit" means made so that it stands level on two parts [of the ground].
"Three or four places" refers to three places by way of the supports for what is not made fit, and four places by way of what is made fit.
"Places" (*ṭhānāni*): this connects with "three places for that which is placed upon the earth in such a manner.
"That" refers to what is placed upon a plank or a log, as well as what is placed directly on the earth. "With two axle-tips" means with two ends of the axles.
"Of that which is placed upon two logs" means having suspended it by two axle-ends above two logs within a wagon-shed.
Of that which has been placed [there]. "Of the lower part" means of the lower portion of the carriage-pole as it stands touching the ground.
The remainder is similar to what was stated regarding the boat; by this [it is meant]:

"But if, while it is thus moving, one cuts off its natural course and leads it to another direction, it is a *pārājika* offense. Even if it reaches some village of its own accord, without moving it from its place..."
The method is clearly indicated by the statement: "If one goes after selling [the goods], there is no theft (*avahāra*), but there is an obligation to pay for the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*).
The commentary on the eight cases concerning vehicles (*yāna*) is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the eight cases concerning loads (*bhāra*).
101. In the *Bhāraṭṭhakathā*, "the upper end of the throat" (*purimagale galavāṭaka*) refers to the upper opening of the throat.

"In the middle of the chest-limit" (*uraparicchedamajjhe*) means in the center of the boundary of the chest. "Because there was no instruction" (*anāṇattattā*) means because there was no instruction such as, "Take it to such-and-such a place.

"And this which was stated regarding the head-load" (*yo cāyaṃ sīsabhāre vutto*) refers to that legal determination which was stated concerning a load carried on the head. Or, "let it be taken by the head, etc. (*sīsādīhi vā gahito hotūti*).
The connection [is as follows]. "Such" means capable of concealing that [fault].
The commentary on the eightfold burden is finished.
The commentary on the eightfold monastery.
102. In the commentary on the *Ārāma* [offense], "binding" refers to the place where the stalks of the flowers are fixed.
"Brings a charge against" means to accuse or to institute a lawsuit. "As an application of taking what is not given" refers to the preliminary act (*payoga*) performed upon the object itself;
for it is by way of this preliminary act that this constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. "Devoted to legal decisions" means appointed to legal adjudication. "Harsh" means...
“Dāruṇo” means cruel. “Dhuraṃ nikkhipatī” means he abandons his effort; the meaning is that he becomes devoid of exertion regarding the making of the property his own.
Even for one who commits a fraudulent gambling debt, if he does not abandon his burden, there is no offense of theft;
thus it is said: “If he himself also abandons the burden. “Himself” refers to the accuser as well. “Abandons the burden” means: “Now [I shall not do it].”
“I will give this to him”—thus he has laid down the burden of giving. Regarding “the state of being one who assents to ‘What shall I do?’”:
one who wanders about assenting to whatever is asked, saying “What shall I do? What shall I do? is a *kiṅkārapaṭissāvī*;
the state of such a person is *kiṅkārapaṭissāvibhāvo*. In that [state], it is said, “the state of being under one’s own control.”
"Having given a bribe" means having given a gift. "Of those who decide falsely" refers to those who are appointed to make false decisions, namely the Vinaya-holders.

Even if one does not say "Take it," but speaks by way of a circuitous expression such as "This is the owner of what has no owner," because they have determined the ownership and then uttered their words, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense for both those who make the false decision and the false witnesses.
Even though there is no actual displacement from the place here, it is precisely the laying down of the burden by both parties that constitutes the "displacement from the place" in this context.
Regarding this laying down of the burden: when an act is performed with the intent to cause doubt in the owner regarding a *pārājika* offense, there is a *thullaccaya*;
when that very act of laying down the burden is brought to completion, there is a *pārājika*. Thus, the one who acts as the fraudulent gambler incurs defeat.
The commentary on the meaning of *ārāma* is finished.
**Commentary on the Meaning of *Vihāra*** 103.
In the commentary on the meaning of *vihāra*, it is said that a *vihāra*, a *pariveṇa*, and an *āvāsa* are all reckoned simply as a *vihāra*.

He said: “A monastery (*vihāra*),” and so forth. Therein, “monastery” refers to a great monastery (*mahāvihāra*). “Cell” (*pariveṇa*) refers to a distinct area within a great monastery, demarcated by its own wall.
“Dwelling” (*āvāsa*) refers to a single residence. It is said, “the attempt does not succeed,” because even when an attempt is made, the theft cannot be accomplished.
However, in the case of property belonging to a community (*gaṇa*), because the ownership is restricted [to that specific group],...
Thinking that it might be possible to make them lay down their burden, he said: "But as for a group consisting of long-reciters and others.
Here too, if even a single person does not lay down his burden, [the offense] is still averted. For it is only through the laying down of the burden by all of them that there is a *pārājika*.
