The commentary on the discussion of the monastery is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Field (Khettaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā) 104. Regarding the phrase "seven kinds of grain" in the Discourse on the Field:

there are seven kinds of grain by way of rice, paddy, barley, millet, wild rice, fine wheat, and common wheat. In the expressions "having pounded," etc., the word "of one who takes" (*gaṇhantassa*) should be applied to each [verb] individually.
In that context, "grasping after crushing" means grasping with the hand exactly as it stands after cutting off the tip of a rice stalk, pulling it out, and taking only the seed.
"One by one" means each individual rice stalk. "Or having uprooted" means having pulled out beans, peas, and so forth.
"In whichever seed," etc., refers to the sequence corresponding to "grasping after crushing" and the other methods.
It should be applied as follows: for one who takes [the grain] by crushing the rice-heads and so forth, it is when the substance fills the seed;
for one who takes it by cutting each one with the hand, it is when the substance fills the head; for one who gathers it by pulling with the teeth, it is when the substance fills the fist;
and for one who pulls out many at once, it is when the substance fills the fruit, such as a mung bean or a māsa bean.

"The basis is fulfilled"—thus it should be understood here according to the sequence. From the statement, "As soon as that [plant] has been released from its bond," it should be understood that when that seed or other [part] has been released from its bond, even if it has not yet been removed from there, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
"Being severed" means having become severed and remaining so. "Entangled" means those that have been cut and are entangled with those that are uncut.
The meaning is "they exist. *Abhusanti* means together with straw; *abhusanti* means devoid of straw. By "a stake" (*khīlena*) is meant by a wooden post (*khāṇukena*).
And here, in the cases of staking a field and so forth, both are possible: simultaneous use and the relinquishing of the burden.
For when one makes a portion of another's fields and so forth one's own by means of staking it and so forth, [both apply].
In that case, even though the owners have already relinquished their responsibility, it does not occur without the simultaneous application of actions such as moving a boundary-stake;
therefore, it is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) precisely through that simultaneous application. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"The simultaneous application should be understood by way of moving the stakes and so forth from their place, and by way of taking possession of the field and so forth. However, when...

When no relinquishment of responsibility (*dhuranikkhepa*) has occurred, but merely the crossing of a boundary-stake (*khīla*) and so forth has been performed, then since it does not happen without the relinquishment of responsibility, the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) occurs only through that relinquishment.
For this very reason, it is stated here: "And that [occurs] by the relinquishment of responsibility on the part of the owners.
The phrase "in all cases" extends the aforementioned principle to the crossing of a rope (*rajjusaṅkamana*) and other such instances.
“Yaṭṭhin” means a measuring-stick. Regarding the statement, “If it has not yet reached one [unit], there is a thullaccaya; when it has reached that, there is a pārājika”:
here, if he intends to take it by burying the wood [in the ground] and taking exactly that much, the pārājika occurs at the final piece of wood.
If he intends to take it by also making an inclusion for a branch there, it should be understood that the pārājika occurs at the final branch. By that much...
"Unable" means being unable to construct a fence by driving stakes into the wood.

"Field boundary" is stated to clarify the same meaning already mentioned; it is expressed as "the embankment of a rice paddy. "He makes it wide" means he makes the existing boundary wider than before.
"Or he establishes one not yet made" means he establishes a boundary that did not exist previously.
The commentary on the section concerning fields is finished.
Commentary on the section concerning sites (Vatthuṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā):
Regarding the phrase "of three walls" in the commentary on sites, it refers to three types of walls made of brick, stone, and timber.

“By this same method” indicates the matter already stated [in the previous section]: “Having cleared the ground alone... or without fencing it. **Commentary on the Discussion of Villages (Gāmaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā)** 106.
In the *Gāmaṭṭhakathā*, the phrase “what is called a village” is not mentioned in the Pāḷi because the definition of a village has been stated in its entirety previously.
Commentary on the Discourse on Forests (Araññaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā) 107.

Regarding the phrase "what is called a forest" in the Commentary on Forests: here, "forest" is intended not merely by virtue of meeting the previously stated definition of a forest, but rather that which is a forest by its own characteristic of a forest and is not claimed by another.
This is stated in order to show that the forest intended here is that which exists [in such a manner]. By the word "that" (tena), it refers again to the mention of "forest.

The state of being unappropriated is not the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a forest; for if the state of being unappropriated were the characteristic of a forest, one would have said only this much:
"A forest is that which is unappropriated by humans"—this is the intended meaning. "Which" (yaṃ) [refers to the aforementioned].
He said, "But that which is a forest by its own characteristic of a forest," referring to the very same forest characterized as previously stated.
"Having pierced straight through" means having pierced directly. "Or a leaf" refers to a leaf such as a palm leaf (*tālapaṇṇa*) and so forth.

"Even though it has been there for a long time" means even if it has remained right there for a long period. "It should not be taken" refers here to that which [has been taken] from the hands of others who are the owners of the forest.
Having bought it and cut it down, if it is left right there, it must not be taken even if permitted by the forest owner.
It is said that taking it with the perception of "rags from a dustheap" (paṃsukūla) is permissible on the grounds that it has been discarded by the owners.
"Even of one whose marks have been cut off" refers to the identification mark made by those who took it after buying it from the hands of the forest owners. "Covered with bark."
By the word "hoti" (is), he illustrates the owners' lack of concern. Therefore it is said, "it is permissible to take.
If there is concern on the part of the owners, it is not permissible.
"Those [buildings] are built and inhabited" means those houses and so forth are completed and occupied by people. "Even the timber" refers to that of the houses and so forth.
"Because of what has been done" means because of the remaining logs from that [work]. "Of these" means of these aforementioned logs.
"Their place of protection" means the place where those forest-keepers are stationed. Regarding the phrase "when told 'give,' it must indeed be given":
here, when told "give," because there is the presence of the mental application (ābhoga) thinking "I shall give," one cannot depart without giving even if not told "give."
"It is indeed permissible. "Give leave to go" means grant permission to depart. "He goes without seeing [the owner]" refers to one who goes with a pure mind;

there is no debt for the goods. Even in the case of timber that has been carried off anywhere, since it remains the property of the forest owners, it is said that even if one departs with a pure mind, if one subsequently goes while conceiving a thieving intent, it is a *pārājika* offense.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Forest is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Water (Udakakathā): 108. In the Discourse on Water, a large-mouthed water-jar is a *udakamaṇika*. It is also said: "A jar with a rim is a *udakamaṇika*."
They say: "Therein" means in those vessels. "Water for draining off" refers to the water released from one side of a reservoir for the purpose of protecting it, with the thought:
"When the great flood comes, let it not break the embankment of the tank.
"A spout for discharging" is the outlet for water for the sake of crops and so forth. "Having made the embankment weak" means necessarily...
This was stated for the purpose of demonstrating that the integrity [of the water] has been severed, and for the purpose of demonstrating the scope of what must be returned as compensation.

Even if a boundary has not been established, when the aforementioned application of force is carried out, one must indeed be dealt with according to the offense of theft (avahāra) in proportion to the value of the water that has flowed out after the boundary was broken.
"Without having emerged" means remaining in the water within the tank itself, without having gone out. "Even before arriving" means having already emerged from the tank...
"Remaining in the great channel itself": "not having emerged" means the water has not emerged from the reservoir. "Well-bound": the intention is that there is no obligation to pay for the goods.
Therefore he said, "If bound after emerging, it is an obligation to pay for the goods. This means:
if, having emerged from the reservoir and not yet reached the mouth of another small channel, the water remains in the great channel itself and is bound, it is an obligation to pay for the goods.
The meaning is as follows: “If [the water] has not been drawn out, what is bound is well-bound;
if it has been drawn out, what is bound is liable for restitution”—these two cases have been stated in sequence according to the two alternatives mentioned below.
Regarding the statement “there is no theft,” some say: “There is no theft, but there is liability for restitution,” because the water contained in a reservoir is common property to all.
That appears improper, and it does not accord with this statement from the Aṭṭhakathā: “When [the owner] has not departed, what is bound is well-bound.
Regarding the phrase “The object... does not accord,” the intended meaning here is that because water in a reservoir is common to all, the object in this case is unenclosed.
The commentary on the Discussion of Water is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of Tooth-sticks (109):
Regarding the discussion on tooth-sticks, from that point onward there is no forfeiture; thus, "the Saṅgha of bhikkhus may use them as they please."

Because it is set aside for use at one’s pleasure with the words “let him enjoy it,” because it is not to be divided by the *vassa* (rainy-season) period, because it is not to be guarded [as a private possession], and because it is common to all, it is not like other property belonging to the Saṅgha;
thus, even for one who takes it with a thieving mind, there is no offense of theft (*avahāra*).
The duties (*vatta*) refer to the duty regarding the taking of tooth-sticks. Now, that very duty—
Showing this, he said, beginning with “For whoever...”. It should be construed as follows: “Some elders might say, ‘Novices will bring it again’.
The commentary on the discussion regarding tooth-sticks is finished.
The commentary on the discussion regarding forest trees.

110. Regarding the discourse on the forest tree (*vanappati*): they say that the statement "it stands upright" is spoken with the intention that it indeed falls from its place because it has been shaken slightly by the weight of the tree itself.

"It clears the opening for the wind" means that, just as the wind comes and fells the tree, so too [the tree] stands obstructing the path by which the wind arrives, with its branches, thickets, and so forth.

It is purified by cutting away and removing [the impurities]. Regarding the "frog-thorn," some say it is "the thorn situated at the tip of the tail of a frog," while others say it is "a single uneven fish-thorn.
The commentary on the discussion of the forest-tree is finished.

Commentary on the Story of the Robbery (Haraṇakakathāvaṇṇanā) 111. Regarding the story of the robbery: "The robbery" (*haraṇaka*) means that which is being carried away. "Dragging toward oneself" (*ākaḍḍhana*) is pulling [the object] directly forward; "dragging away" (*vikaḍḍhana*) is dragging it in the other directions.
As for the statement, "If it is worth one *pāda*, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense," here I do not take [the value of] the whole [coin] into account.
Because he did not perceive it within, thinking "I shall take it," even though it was only a portion of a cloth that had been perceived, a *pārājika* offense is stated.
"Together with the carrier of goods" means together with the person carrying the goods. "Having intimidated" means having intimidated him with a bow or other weapons.
"He" refers to the carrier of goods. "Uninhabited" means unclaimed; the meaning is that it has no owner.

Regarding the phrase "it should be made to be brought back": here, because it is stated that even those who have abandoned their burden and departed without attachment may have their belongings brought back, local residents hold that it is permissible— even by force—
to have monks' own requisites brought back when they have been seized by others after the monks themselves relinquished their responsibility over them.
The teachers say this, but some teachers dwelling on the island of Siṃhala do not accept it. For that very reason, it is stated in both the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*:
"But for us, that is not pleasing. Regarding the phrase "in others," it refers to the *Mahāpaccarī* and so forth.
The statement "there is no investigation" means that since there is no rejection [of the view] even in those texts, this is indeed the intended meaning.
The commentary on the story of the theft is finished.
Commentary on the story of the deposit:
In this story of the deposit, regarding "goods placed in one's own hand for the purpose of protection" in a secure location...

They say: "Even if no other act of taking back has been performed apart from the formal application of taking back, at a time such as a political upheaval, if both parties—sitting each in their own place—renounce their responsibility, thinking, 'I will not give it to him now,' and 'He will not give it to me now,' it is indeed a *pārājika* offense because the application of taking back has been carried out.
This is because [the object] has been placed in one's own hand.
The intention here is that there is no theft, because from the moment the object is placed in one's own hand for the purpose of safeguarding it, it remains dependent upon that [hand];

because the person stands in the position of the owner of the goods due to the act of guarding; and because the place [of the object] is subject to that [guardian], it is impossible to displace it from its location.
Thus, there is no theft.
"Having caused [him] to recite the Dhamma" means having caused [him] to speak the Dhamma. "The same method applies" means that there is a *pārājika* offense precisely for the removal [of the robe].
Why? Because it is stated as a distinctive mark (*abhiññāṇa*) not shared by others. When one says, "It is appropriate when he takes another exactly like it," this is a sign;
and because the location has been specified by the speaker himself as "in such-and-such a place," [the offense occurs] in that very place.
"In the three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated that this was said with reference to another similar bowl placed there later after the one standing [there] had been removed.
This is because, even though the thief did not actually seize the bowl he had noticed,
his intent to steal (*theyyacitta*) was present toward that similar object situated in that same place, thinking, "I shall take this by stealing it."
It is appropriate for one who takes another [bowl] of a similar kind; thus, the theft of a thief is demonstrated.

"By the track of the foot" means by the track of the foot of the thief as he goes after taking the bowl that was brought out and given by the Elder. It is appropriate for one who takes something not of a similar kind;
thus, having realized, "This bowl is not mine," or "This bowl was not mentioned by me."

This is stated because there is the presence of theft for one who takes with a thieving mind, and for one who takes after having generated a thieving mind regarding the object itself, thinking, "I will take this by stealing.
"The village gate" is merely a conventional expression appropriate for ascetics; it means simply "inside the village. In the manner already described...

"An offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) for the elder": because he took what belonged to another with a mind of theft, the elder incurs an offense entailing expulsion at the very moment of taking it away.
"An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the thief": because he took it with an impure mind, the thief incurs an offense of wrong-doing at the time of taking it.

"An offense of wrong-doing for both in the manner already stated": since the thief was given [the goods] by the owner, there is no offense entailing expulsion for him; however, because he took it with an impure mind, [he incurs an offense of wrong-doing].

There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because of taking [the bowl]; however, for the elder, there is an offense of wrong-doing even regarding what belongs to himself due to his impure state of mind.

Regarding the phrase "because it was taken by command": here, when the elder has given the command, saying, "Take the bowl and robes; let us go to such-and-such a village and wander for alms," from the boundary of the monastery's exterior precincts onwards...
The intention is that everything beyond the precincts of that village is considered a field.
Regarding the phrase "having stepped off from the path," it should be understood here that even the space between two cart-track paths is indeed a path.

Regarding "without standing or sitting," this refers to one who, having entered a monastery, stands or sits without having set down the burden on the ground from their head or other parts of the body.
Or, having rested until the thought of theft has subsided, if he goes again after generating the thought of theft, he should be dealt with according to the value of what was taken.
If, however, having placed it on the ground, he picks it up again and goes, he should be dealt with according to the value of what was taken. Why?
Because the duty that must be performed by virtue of the commander’s command has already been completed. Some, however, [say] regarding the first case...
They say that even if the intent to steal has not subsided, one who goes after resting must be made to pay according to the value of the theft by the *pāduddhāra* or *uddhāra* method.

They also say that if one says, "We will enter the village," without specifying which particular village, then the entire range of villages within the monastery’s vicinity constitutes the field of theft. As for the rest...

"Everything such as setting out on the path, entering the monastery, and so forth" means that even though it was taken without prior instruction, because it was taken after informing the owner, it is stated that everything—including the vicinity of the monastery mentioned below—is indeed "field," since it is similar to what preceded.
"In the same manner" refers by extension to the method described in the passage beginning with "having conceived a thieving mind on the way. Regarding the "sign": [text continues].
"Or having made a sign" means: when a sign has been made such as, "My robe is soiled; who indeed will dye it and give it back to me? "In the same manner as stated" means:
in the very same manner as stated in the section concerning going with an elder who has not been instructed, taking his bowl and robe.
"On one side" means: living on one side of the monastery, not revealing oneself due to its great size. With a thieving mind.

"Consuming while wearing it out": when a thought of theft has arisen, if one consumes [the robe] by means of the very manner of wearing and putting on it that was used previously, without moving it from its place, one wears it out.

However, for one who moves it from its place while possessing a thought of theft, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*), just as in the case of shifting a load from the head to the shoulder and so forth.
"It may be lost in some way or another" means by fire and the like, or by ants and the like.
"Or it is eaten, or it is lost;
or someone else [takes it]"—by this phrase, it should be understood that the person by whom it was placed is also included.

In the case of lying, such as "I have obtained your coarse cloth," there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because it is an attempt at taking what is not given. For one who takes the other [item], there is a defeat (*pārājika*) upon its removal.

In this context, because it is released from being a deposit by the very statement, "Having entered, take your cloth," and because there is still an attachment to one's own cloth even when taking the other for the owner, a *pārājika* offense is stated regarding the removal [of the cloth].
"They do not know" means they do not know because they have not heard the words spoken by him. "The same method applies here" means that even if they know [the truth],...
"They do not accept with the mind"—this same method should be understood [to apply here as well]. "They reject":
it should be understood that here the mental rejection is also included. Regarding the phrase "whether requested or unrequested":
if they accept even mentally when requested, there is liability for loss. However, if they are unrequested, even if they accept mentally, there is no liability.
"He takes it and puts it down": here, even if he moves it and places it back in that very same spot, if it is lost, he is liable for the value.
"While the vicinity exists" means while there exists a place for excrement and urine in the vicinity of the storehouse. "If I die and the lodging of the Saṅgha is ruined":
here, even if one opens it with the sole intention, "Let not the lodging of the Saṅgha perish," [it is not an offense].
"It is indeed permissible," they say. "One must have companions" means that something or other should also be given by them.
"This is the proper conduct" refers to this duty for those residing in the storehouse.
"The Elder Lolamahāthera" refers to an elder who is dull-witted, bewildered, or prone to laughter and play. [In] their respective dwelling cells...
It should be construed as: "storing the requisites of the bhikkhus who belong to the same community. "By the others" means by the other bhikkhus residing in that very same cell.
A *vihāravārika* is one appointed for the duty of the monastery; having taken his turn, he is the guardian of the monastery. "Provisions" refers to food and wages.
"When they had gone out on the road" means that, having learned of the approach of bandits, [they went] even earlier than usual.
Thinking, "Let us go and make a noise," they went toward the thieves.
"Tending to their own dependents" means that while supporting their respective dependents through the practice of training, they also have those dependents tend to the monastery.

The reading "asahāyassa adutiyassa" (of one without a companion, of one who is not second) is appropriate; the latter is merely a synonym for the former. Or, "asahāyassa" may mean "of one who has oneself as a companion."
However, regarding this reading, some say that because what brought by one person is not sufficient for two, the turn for even one who has himself as a companion is prohibited;
this should be examined, as it does not accord with the statement: "For whom there is no fellow monk to bring and give food.
One who subsists [on alms] must remain so; thus, even for one who dwells in the open air or at the foot of a tree, the cycle of cooked food [must be maintained].

One who lives in dependence [upon a monastery] must remain when it is the turn of the monastery's watch in order to protect the bowl and robes. "They inquire" means they ask questions regarding the answers to those questions or the *aṭṭhakathā* (commentaries).
"Twofold" means they say that even without being assigned by seniority (*vassaga*), one is placed in two sections.
"By way of the fortnight" means by way of the half-month period.
The commentary on the Discourse on Deposits is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Customs House Collector: 113.
Regarding the phrase "they strike them from there" in the Discourse on the Customs House Collector: they strike them as they bring [goods] out from there. "There" refers to the customs house.
“From which” means from whichever object being carried out. “Royal” means dependent upon the king. Since that too is indeed fit for the king, he said, “This is the meaning.

“From this” means from this object. Regarding the phrase “he steps across the second foot,” they say here: “Having placed the first foot outside the boundary, as soon as the second foot is lifted, it is a *pārājika* offense”; having thus lifted [the foot]—
Because even though it is placed outside, it is considered as being "standing outside.
They say that wherever an offense is to be determined according to the sequence of steps, this same method applies in every such case. "Outside the customs house" means beyond the customs house.
"Necessarily falling" means necessarily falling outside the customs house. "In the very manner previously stated" means necessarily...
It means "as soon as it is released from the hand. The intention of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* statement, "it enters back inside again," is clarified by the *Kuruṇḍi-saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā*.
It protects [the bowl] when it goes out after having stood inside, because the momentum of the monk's movement has subsided right there inside. Having turned it over, [one places] the inner [side]...
"He places it outside" means that having turned over a packet situated inside, he places it outside.
And here they say: "In this case, when the inner packet has merely been released from the ground, it is a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the phrase "while the vehicle is moving... he places it," [this refers to] placing it outside without having entered the customs station (*suṅkaghāta*). In all three [cases], [the offense is established].

It is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that it is "placed outside the customs station" because it will be explained [later]. However, the Teachers (Ācariyā), having proposed the reading "standing outside the customs station," explain:

"Even when vehicles and so forth have already entered the customs enclosure, if they are placed [there] first and subsequently carried out together with the vehicle, it is 'standing outside the customs station'; yet it has not been taken away by that [vehicle]."

They speak thus. This, however, is their intention: since a monk’s goods placed on vehicles and such that have entered within the toll-station are removed by another even without the monk’s instigation, there is no *pārājika* offense;
and because it was said, “Let them take the toll from whatever has entered here,” there is also no obligation to pay the toll for the goods standing outside that were removed by another.

And this same method appears even more appropriate when it accords with the statement: "Even that which was placed inside with the thought, 'It will go out after turning,' or 'Another will turn it,' goes outside while turning by itself later or being turned by another;
it certainly guards [the boundary]. This applies even to one who enters within the toll-station and returns again.
If, for one who crosses the boundary by that side, they still collect a toll from those passing through even beyond it, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense upon crossing the boundary.
"In the *Hatthisutta* and so forth" means in the *Hatthisikkhā* and other such texts.
"In this instance" refers to the manner described regarding the aforementioned vehicles and so on.
Regarding "removing": "There is no offense" means that because of the word "with one's own hand" used there, there is no offense for one who has another remove it.
"Here" refers to this training rule on taking what is not given. "There" refers to that training rule on wool. "They are" (honti):
here the word *iti* has the sense of a reason; because wool is an article to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*), therefore it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
The meaning is as follows: "There is no offense here" means that there is no offense because there is no act of theft in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

"The vicinity" (*upacāra*) refers to the area within two *leḍḍupāta* (the distance of a stone's throw) all around the boundary of the customs house (*suṅkaghāta*), which is known as the vicinity near the enclosure wall.
Since there is a disadvantage in entering such a vicinity and carrying [the goods] away, a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is stated. "In this place" refers to the customs house.
"In the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* it is stated: 'The rule regarding "two throws of a clod" is handed down through the lineage of teachers.
The commentary on the discussion of toll-gates is finished. The commentary on the discussion of living beings begins.
114. Regarding the discussion on living beings (*pāṇakathā*), since it is impossible for a being belonging to the animal realm to have its value determined solely by the price of its feet, he said:

"Showing a living being that is sufficient to constitute theft (*avahāra*) in every respect. There is no theft for one who carries off a free person (*bhujissa*), because such a person lacks the status of being owned by another. A "free person" (*bhujissa*) means one who is not a slave.
"Entrusted" (*āṭhapita*) means [entrusted] by parents who, while taking a loan... [until... *yāva* (as far as).

“Let this debt be with you,” he said, and it was handed over to the creditors. Since parents are not masters of their children in the same way that slaves are masters of their children, and even those to whom the debt was entrusted are masters only of his manual labor and not of him himself, he said, “There is no forfeiture.
However, as for the wealth, it increases in the place where it has gone; regarding this, [he said] after having entrusted it...
"The property taken, together with its interest, is the debt of the thief"—thus it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.

Regarding the passage "one born in the house... there is theft": here, by virtue of the practice in that particular region, it should be understood that even for one who steals a person who has entered into slavery by offering themselves up of their own accord, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense. [This applies to] one born from the womb of a female slave of the house.
"Born of a slave" (dāsassa jāto) is stated by taking what is possible, as this too is possible. However, even one born of another in the womb of a female domestic slave is included here.
"Brought from a place of execution" (karamarānīto) means one seized for imprisonment. Therefore he said, "having been brought from a foreign land," and so forth.
In that context, "having been brought from a foreign land" refers to those who plunder foreign lands.
"Having been sent from another country by great thieves such as royal ministers and high officials.

"There is no offense against the Pārājika rule" means that if one does not increase the momentum beyond what was said by that person, there is no offense. "By a circuitous way" means by a roundabout statement.
Since it is stated regarding the category of human beings, "or he should praise the beauty of death," one is not exempt even from speech that is merely circuitous.
But here, because it is stated specifically as "one should take what is not given, which is reckoned as theft," one is exempted by way of figurative discourse.
The commentary on the section concerning living beings is finished. Now begins the commentary on the section concerning footless creatures.

In the discourse on footless creatures (*apadaka-kathā*), "by name" means either by its own name or by the name given by its owner. "A basket-lid" (*karaṇḍapuṭa*) is the cover of a box. "Having struck" (*āhacca*) means having hit it.
Commentary on the Discourse on Four-Footed Creatures (116):
In the discourse on four-footed creatures, "a young *bhiṅka* bird" refers to one that has received this name because it makes the sound "bhiṅka-bhiṅka."
"A young elephant. "Within the precincts" means within the enclosed precincts.
"In the royal courtyard" refers to the royal courtyard outside the gate of the walled city. "The place where the elephant stall stands" refers to the area inside the water-trough.
"Standing outside the city" is said with reference to a walled city; [the same applies] in the case of an unwalled city.
However, even for one standing within the city, the location is indeed the place where he stands. "Broken door" means a door broken by oneself.
"Bent branch" means a branch that has been bent. "Two for one who is lying down" means two together with the act of binding.

Regarding the term "causes to be killed," the teachers say: "For one who causes [a person] to perish with a mind of theft, there is only *dukkaṭa* because it is a simultaneous application of effort, not a *pācittiya*."
The commentary on the Discourse on the Four-Footed Animals is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Protector of Deposits:
In the discourse on the protector of deposits, *oṇi* means that which has been brought near; the meaning is "brought forward" (*ānīta*). "Goods placed in the presence of a protector of deposits..."
They say that because it was placed there not for the purpose of concealment like a deposit, but for the purpose of looking at it for a moment,
the offense of *pārājika* is produced merely by its removal from that place.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning theft by prior agreement (*saṃvidāvahāra*).

In this discussion on theft by mutual agreement, because it is stated without qualification in the Pāḷi that "if many have agreed together and one person steals the goods, there is an offense of pārājika for all," the offense for those who give the orders occurs at the moment of ordering;
as for the thief, the meaning should be understood by applying [the rule] to the act of stealing according to what is possible, as in the discussion on ordering: "He steals that goods..."
In passages such as "the offense for all is a pārājika," it is stated that the offense of the one who gives the command occurs at the very moment of the command.

And so he will say: "Now, when that property is inevitably lost—which was previously stated to be an offense of pārājika for all—then for this person, the pārājika occurs at that very moment. This is [the meaning].
“Reasoning should be understood everywhere. Furthermore, in the case of the *saṃvidāvahāra* (agreement-based taking), one cannot say that “there is no formal command,” because of the statement:
“For each of the pupils, there is one māsaka given by hand; [thus] there are five instances of commanding.
And when a command exists, the offense of the commander should be accepted at the very moment of the command, not at the time of the actual taking.
If this is so, why was it said: "If one among them steals the goods, when they are recovered, there is a *pārājika* offense for all"?

This is not a fault. For here, in order to show that an offense applies to all of them, he stated, "when they are recovered, there is a *pārājika* for all," while demonstrating the occasion for the arising of the offense even for the thief;
however, it does not mean that for the commanders (*āṇāpaka*) as well, the offense occurs only upon recovery.

The meaning should be understood as follows: "for the purpose of revealing the offense. In such passages as, "When several people command one [person], saying, 'Go, bring this,' there is a *pārājika* offense for all of them upon his recovery," the meaning is to be understood in exactly the same way.

Alternatively, in the case of stealing by prior agreement (*saṃvidāvahāra*), the offense for the commanders occurs only upon the recovery [of the object], not at the moment of the command; thus, according to the authority of the commentators on the *Aṭṭhakathā*, this is a unique characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*).

It should be accepted; or otherwise, in a manner different from this, it should be accepted after investigation such that there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

"Having made an arrangement" means having made an agreement. By virtue of that command, for them there are offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) and formal offenses (*āpatti*), including the offense of defeat (*pārājika*).
This was said because [the other] is impossible. For if those who were commanded necessarily carry it away, only a *pārājika* offense is to be seen for them, not a *dukkaṭa* offense.
A direct (*sāhatthika*) act is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*) of a commissioned (*āṇattika*) act, nor is a commissioned act a constituent factor of a direct act;
because they pertain to different times, they are not constituent factors for one another. Thus, with one's own hand...
For one who steals, there is an offense at the moment of moving [the object] from its place; however, for one who gives an order, it is at the very moment of the command.
Thus, the offenses to be incurred through personal action and through commanding differ in their timing.
The commentary on the discussion of stealing by prior agreement is finished.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Act of Appointment (Saṅketakammakathāvaṇṇanā) 119. Regarding the phrase "in the same manner as stated concerning the spies" in the discussion on the act of appointment, it refers to the method stated in the passage beginning with "certainly, when the goods are being carried away.
In the Pāḷi, the expression "that appointment before or after" (*taṃ saṅketaṃ pure vā pacchā vā*)—here, *taṃ saṅketaṃ* is used in the sense of the genitive case (possessive).
It should be understood as a statement of application; the meaning is "of that convention. Alternatively, the construction here should be understood as:
"either before reaching that convention, or after having passed beyond that convention. For this very reason, he said:
"Having passed beyond that convention determined by 'today,'" and so forth. [The phrase] "before or after that sign" follows.
Here too, the meaning should be understood by this same method.
The commentary on the discussion of the act of convention is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the act of signs.
120. Regarding the discussion on preparatory acts (*nimittakamma*): preparatory acts such as winking the eyes are light and of short duration;
therefore, it is impossible to steal that property at that very moment. For instance, some property may be distant, or some may be heavy;
by the time one has gone to take it or exerted oneself to lift it, the preparatory act [has already ceased].
It occurs later. Even so, because one has begun to take it from the moment the sign was made, one is said to steal by means of that very sign.
If this is so, does the position that "this is merely a preliminary act before the meal" become authoritative? It does not.
For the making of a sign should not be viewed in the same way as the making of a convention; for in that case, there is a limitation of time.
"It exists here; it does not exist there. For the "act of agreement" (*saṅketakamma*) is stated by way of time, while the "act of sign" (*nimittakamma*) is by way of action;

this is the distinction between them. However, the statement, "If he steals that goods either before or after that sign, there is no offense for the one who was the original owner," is said with reference to one who takes the goods on his own initiative, without having begun to take them when that act of sign had been performed by the other.
The commentary on the discussion of the preparatory act (*nimittakamma*) is finished. Commentary on the discussion of the command (*āṇattikathā*): 121.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of non-confusion" in the discussion of the command: because one who performs a conventional act (*saṅketakamma*) or a preparatory act (*nimittakamma*) is a single person...
Or, having seen [someone] scratching their eyes and so forth before the meal, he says, "Take it";
or one person, having made a reference to a specific object to be taken, says, "Before the meal, take an object of such color and shape";
or one person gives orders according to a sequence of individuals, saying, "Tell so-and-so; let him tell another," and so forth. Therefore, by way of time...
This is for the purpose of avoiding confusion regarding these acts of convention and acts of signs— whether they are enjoined by way of action, by way of goods, or by way of persons—

and whether they are conventional or non-conventional. "Having made a perception of the sign" means having made a mnemonic mark (*saññāṇa*) that serves as a sign for grasping [the object] by way of its color,
shape, and so forth, thinking, "The goods are of such-and-such a kind."
"If it goes according to the intention" means that if they speak in this sequence—the second [informing] the third, and the third the fourth—then it is so stated.
However, if the second informs the fourth, the instruction has not reached its intended destination;
therefore, there is no *thullaccaya*, and there is only the *dukkaṭa* mentioned first. "It is that very same [offense]" means...

The meaning is that since it is accomplished merely by the acceptance of the message alone, without the taking of goods, that itself constitutes a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), not a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) nor a *pārājika* (defeat). "In all cases" means in all such instances.
"For them too, a *dukkaṭa*" means a *dukkaṭa* due to the act of reporting. Regarding the phrase "merely upon having accepted": here, if one necessarily accepts [the message],...
Therefore, it should be understood that prior to that, the teacher committed a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), but not one for "accepting" [the gift].
Why, then, is it a *thullaccaya*? He says: "For by him, the great multitude was incited to evil.

As for the *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) of the one who is the root-cause, this is first the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary); however, the Teachers [say] that it is precisely because of the lack of consensus...

Regarding the phrase "for one who is the primary offender" (*mūlaṭṭhassa*): since this is not stated in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), it is said that the *dukkaṭa* offense applies only to the one who receives [the food].
By this very principle, it should be understood that in the preceding sections as well, the *dukkaṭa* offense for those receiving [food] occurs at the moment of reception;
however, they say that because there was no room for it there, it was not mentioned then, but is stated here.
Furthermore, it is stated that even by such an instruction, there is only an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), because at that time there is an absence of the accomplishment of the objective.

"An offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) occurs at the very moment of the instruction" means that, like the fruit immediately following the path, one becomes defeated at the very moment of the volition of the instruction that accomplishes the objective.
"Because of deafness" means that even while speaking loudly, one does not make oneself heard due to deafness. Regarding the phrase, "I have been instructed by you": [The rest of the passage follows.]
Furthermore, because it cannot be revoked and because it lacks the capacity to accomplish the purpose, there is no *pārājika* offense for one who has merely the intention (*mūlaṭṭha*).

Regarding this, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "If one writes, 'Theft must be committed,' on a leaf, a stone, or anywhere else, and leaves it there, there is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
However, that [statement] is released from the charge of theft by way of figurative speech (*pariyāyakathā*).
Therefore, it should be accepted after investigation. However, if one writes on a letter, "In such-and-such a place, such-and-such an article is kept;
steal it," and sends it to someone, and that person steals the article, then because it was stolen by means of an order, it is logical that the sender incurs a *pārājika* offense.
The commentary on the discussion of commands is finished.
Commentary on the classification of offenses: 122.

"In this and that" refers to those situated on the ground, on dry land, and so forth. It should be construed as "and showing the factor. "By way of the difference in the subject matter" (vatthubhedena).
By way of the distinction between heavy and light objects to be taken away. "Distinction of offenses" means the classification of offenses according to *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, and *dukkaṭa*.
"Possessed by another" (*parapariggahita*) means that which is owned by another person who has become human.
By the phrase "nor perceiving it as one's own," the object possessed by another is described. "Nor taking it through trust," [is also mentioned].
By the phrase "not for the time being," the perception that it is owned by another is expressed.

"Not taken on trust" means the state of not having been taken through a relationship of trust. "Not taken as a temporary loan" means the state of not having been taken with the intention that it must be returned later.
"Not inhabited" refers to forest trees, grass, leaves, and so forth, which have not been occupied by way of the appropriation [of ownership] thinking, "This is mine."
"Abandoned" means discarded in forests and such places by wood-gatherers and others because they have become too heavy or because they no longer need it.
"Severed at the root" means lost; it is "severed at the root" because its root—consisting of attachment—has been cut after being sought out.
"Ownerless" refers to property that is ownerless in the three ways shown, beginning with "not inhabited. "Both" refers to the characteristics as previously described.
[It is] ownerless and one's own property.
The commentary on the classification of offenses is finished.
The commentary on the classification of non-offenses.
131. That bed upon which one passes away is called the "bed of non-exertion" (*anuṭṭhānaseyyā*).
To clarify the meaning already stated—that "he accepts it with the mind"—it is said that "he says nothing.
"To make it as it was originally" means that whatever was taken or consumed must be returned in its entirety.
"Paṭidassāmi" (I shall give back) means that one will give back either that very same thing which was taken, or something else of a similar kind.
Because it is impossible to obtain permission from the Saṅgha regarding property belonging to the Saṅgha, and because no such object can be permitted [for personal use], it is said:
"However, it is proper only to give back what belongs to the Saṅgha."
"Even though they were reborn in that very same physical form" means even though they arose within that very dead body.
In the *Vinītavatthu*, this should be understood as being like a hungry ghost (*preta*) reborn in that very dead body due to craving for the cloth.

Regarding the statement "there is nothing at all to be said about the cloth caught on trees and so forth," this was said with reference to [a cloth] not claimed by people. However, if it is guarded by protectors...
"It has been taken possession of; it is not permissible to take it.
The commentary on the analysis of non-offenses is finished.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis is finished.

In the commentary on the miscellaneous discourse (*pakinnakakathāvaṇṇanā*), regarding the case of the log (*dārukhaṇḍa*) and so forth— where it is said, "This is heavy; you lift one side, I shall lift the other"—

the phrase "by means of one's own hand and by command" (*sāhatthikāṇattika*) is stated with reference to the displacement of a single object from its place through the combined effort of both parties.
And this has been stated merely to show that body and speech function as constituent factors (*aṅga*) in such a situation.

However, the offense should be determined by way of that volition (*cetanā*) which, having given rise to an application (*payoga*)—whether manual or by command—effects the displacement from one's position as the primary factor.
Otherwise, manual action does not constitute a constituent factor for a command, nor does a command [constitute one for manual action].
Or else, this contradicts [the rule] "by means of one's own hand.
The commentary on the miscellaneous discussion is finished.
Commentary on the bases of the training rules (*vinītavatthu*).
132. In the *Vinītavatthu*, "runs about" means he runs well. "Runs in various ways" means he runs in diverse and manifold manners.
"Even without the distinction of doors of body and speech" means even without physical movement or vocal expression.
"By the power of reflection" means by the power of contemplating the danger in such an arising of consciousness.

135. *Pucchāsabhāgena* means in accordance with the question. *Niruttipatha* is the path of language itself; [it refers] to that path of language. Therefore he said: "merely in conventional expression. 137.
By the phrase *yathākammaṃ gato* (gone according to his karma), he shows that [the person] has passed away.
By the word *abbhuṇhe* (fresh), in order to clarify what was already stated by way of a synonym, he said *allasarīre* (on a fresh body). *Visabhāgasarīre* means on a female body.
Because the body is of a different sex, one must not come too close; thus he said, "on the head," and so forth.
"It is allowable" means that even with regard to a body of a different sex, it is allowable to perform the procedure prescribed for oneself and to take hold of the cloth.
However, some say: "Although there is no offense under this training rule, there is nevertheless an act of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who touches a female form."
138. "Having exchanged the *kusa* measure" means having traded the *kusa* measure.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "false measures, false coins, etc.," it includes false scales, false weights, deception, and so forth. In that context, false measures are threefold:

by way of the breach of the heart (*hadaya*), the breach of the crest (*sikhā*), and the breach of the cord (*rajjubheda*). Therein, the "heart" refers to the interior of measuring vessels such as the *nāḷi*; its "breach" is the making of a hole therein.
The breaking of the heart occurs at the time of measuring ghee, oil, and the like.
For when one who is taking these measures says, "Pour slowly," using a measure with a hole at the bottom, they take it after causing much of the liquid to flow out into the vessel;
whereas when giving, they close the hole and give it quickly once it is full. The breaking of the crest occurs at the time of measuring sesame, rice, and the like. For these...
When taking [the measure], one takes it slowly after raising the tip; when giving, one gives by filling it quickly while cutting off the tip.
The breaking of the cord occurs at the time of measuring fields and lands.
For those measuring fields and so forth, they measure even what is not large as large, and what is large as not large. A counterfeit coin is well known indeed.

Deception by the scale (*tulākūṭa*), however, is fourfold: deception by the form (*rūpakūṭa*), deception by the parts (*aṅgakūṭa*), deception by the grasping (*gahaṇakūṭa*), and deception by concealment (*paṭicchannakūṭa*).
Among these, "deception by the form" means making two scales look identical: when taking [the goods], one uses the large scale; when giving [in exchange], one gives using the small scale.
"Deception by the parts" means that when taking, one presses down on the scale with the hand at the rear part; when giving, [one does so] at the front part.
He oversteps. "The deception of taking" means that when taking, one holds the rope at the bottom, but when giving, one holds it at the top.
"The deception of concealment" means having made a hollow scale and filled it inside with iron filings, one places it at the rear when taking, but at the front when giving.
"Kaṃsa" refers to a golden bowl; deception by means of that is "the deception of the kaṃsa. How so? Having fashioned a single golden bowl...
They fashioned two or three copper basins that appeared golden in color;
then, having gone to the countryside and entered some wealthy household, they said, "Buy these golden vessels. When asked about their price, they wished to give them at a very high cost.
Then, when those people asked, "How can we know whether these are gold? they replied, "Examine them and then take them."
Having rubbed a golden bowl against a stone and given away all their bowls, they depart.
Deceit (*vañcanā*) means deceiving others by various means. Here is one such instance:
it is said that a certain hunter was coming along, having captured both a deer and a fawn. A certain rogue asked him, "Sir, how much is the deer worth?"
“What is it, a fawn? he asked. When it was said, “A deer is two kahāpaṇas;
a fawn is one,” he gave one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, and after going a short distance, turned back and said, “Sir, I have no need for the fawn;
give me the deer. “Then give me two kahāpaṇas,” [the other] said. He replied, “But, sir, did I not first—”
“Was one kahāpaṇa given? “Yes, it was given. “Take this young deer;
thus, that kahāpaṇa and this young deer, worth a kahāpaṇa, will become two kahāpaṇas.
Perceiving that he was speaking reasonably, he took the young deer and gave him the deer.
"By force" means by means of strength. By the mention of "waylayers," both snow-thieves (*himaviparāmosaka*) and bush-thieves (*gumbaviparāmosaka*) are included.
Among these, those who, being concealed by snow during the time of a snowfall, steal from people traveling on the road, are snow-thieves.
Those who, being concealed by bushes and the like, steal from people, are bush-thieves.

“It is indeed a *pārājika* offense to lift [the cloth]”: this is because the intention “if it is a garment, I will take it” has arisen as a mental calculation (*parikappa*), and because a garment is actually present there.
“It must be dealt with according to the steps taken”: this is said because he examined it without having set it down on the ground.
“Obsessed” means being pursued [by the thought]. By the phrase “because it was taken after seeing it, no application of the mental calculation is seen,” [it is shown that the offense is established].
By showing the impossibility of the application of a hypothetical interpretation (*parikappāvahāra*), he clarifies the unsuitability of what was stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries.

However, by stating "In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*" and so forth, he clarifies both the possibility of the application of a hypothetical interpretation and its consistency with the canonical text (*pāḷi*), thereby demonstrating that what was stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* alone is well-stated. For this very reason, it is also said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
Only the method of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* has been shown.

"Some" refers to certain teachers within the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* itself. As for the word "but" (*pana*) in the phrase "but in the *Mahāpaccarī*," it serves to indicate the distinction between the view of "some" and the view of the *Mahāpaccarī*.
By this, it is shown that the view of "some" does not even accord with the view of the *Mahāpaccarī*.
[The author] shows this. Furthermore, he clarifies that the method of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* (Great Commentary) alone is more appropriate because it accords with the *Mahāpaccarī*.
"Ornaments" (*alaṅkārabhaṇḍa*) refers to ornaments such as finger-rings and the like.

"Having laid down *kusa* grass" means having laid down any kind of *kusa* grass used as a marker, whether made of reeds or palm leaves. "Of lesser value" (*samagghatara*) means of less worth (*appagghatara*).
Even when the grass has been pulled out from its surrounding sections, the turning over of the grass has not yet occurred; therefore it is said, "he protects it during the uprooting.
*Siveyyaka* means born in the kingdom of Sivi. 139.
Regarding the matter of the sauna (*jantāghara*), because the Elder Ānanda knew that there was no offense in that case, therefore—
It is not stated that "he felt remorse. And because he did not inform the Blessed One himself, the singular form "he informed" (*ārocesi*) is not used.
140. *Vighāsa* means what remains after eating or leavings. *Kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā* means having had it cooked. *Attaguttatthāya* means for the sake of protecting oneself.
For the purpose of protecting oneself from the calamities caused by that [animal].

For lions and other such creatures, overcome by hunger, might even do harm to those who seize them while they are being eaten. "Out of compassion for others" means out of sympathy for other beings, such as lions and the like.
For if one were to seize [the animal] after making it flee from those [beings] who would eat it in order to dispel their own hunger, [one would incur no fault] toward them.
"Compassion will not exist.

(141) This is stated because it is common to all forms of lying, as in the case of the story of the rice gruel with three kinds of sugar. "By those commanded" means by those authorized who have been commanded.
"By one commanded" means by one commanded by the owners. "Give a portion to another," having pointed out a person who does not exist.
Because it was taken, it is called "the value of the goods" (*bhaṇḍadeyya*). "By another" means by someone other than the four mentioned above, such as one who has been authorized (*sammatādi*).
Even when told, "Give me another portion," because it belongs to the Saṅgha, it is still considered baseless (*amūlaka*) as it was taken;
therefore, it is said that "he should be made to pay the value of the goods" (*uddhāreva bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo*). "Being given by the others" refers to [those] authorized or commanded by him.
"Being given": thus, for one who takes by saying "Give me another portion as well," or by counting false years.

"Sudinna" (well-given): when something belonging to a householder is being given by the owner below, or by one authorized by him, if one takes it by saying "Give another person's portion," because there is no other person [to whom it belongs], it remains the property of the owner; therefore, it is "bhaṇḍadeyya" (an object to be returned).

It is established. However, in this case, when they are giving [the robe] in such a manner, because it was said, "Give another portion as well," or "Give it to one who takes by counting false years," it constitutes merely a request from a stranger;
thus, setting aside the offense of a *pārājika* or the duty to restore the goods (*bhaṇḍadeyya*), it is indeed considered properly given.
142–3. What is the difference between the requisites mentioned under the heading of "requisites" (*parikkhāra*) and the articles mentioned below?
That which is established according to its own nature, without being fashioned into something suitable for use such as an ornament, is an "article" (*bhaṇḍa*).
However, that which is fashioned accordingly and established in a form suitable for use, such as an ornament, is a "requisite."
It should be understood as "requisites.
144–146. "Having transferred" means having removed from the place where it was standing. "A bag" refers to any kind of bag, such as a sandal-bag and so forth.
Regarding the "value of the goods" when they are being brought back, because of the statement, "He is satisfied when it has been taken," [this applies] to one who is not satisfied.
It is stated that even if something has already been taken as a gift, it must be given back.

Because of the statement, “It should be distributed among those who are present,” it follows that the goods to be shared reach only those standing within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*); thus he says, “It is permissible to take [the goods] only from one standing within the precinct boundary.
(148–9) “‘Goods to be given’ (*bhaṇḍadeyya*) means: when there is a sense of longing in both parties, whether for the thief or for the owner, [it belongs to] whoever arrives.”

"It is permissible to give it to anyone," they say. "The same method applies" means that for an item taken with the perception that it is a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), it is a forfeiture offense (*bhaṇḍadeyya*);
however, if taken with the intention to steal, it is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).

"In villages" refers to the people who live in the villages; here, by the mention of "village," those residing in the village are meant. "While they are departing" means while they are abandoning the village and fleeing. "When they dwell again in the countryside" [is the phrase].
Furthermore, regarding those from the countryside who have come and are residing there:
it is stated "without distinction" means it was spoken in general terms without grasping at the specific qualification of "whether with effort or without effort.
For the intention here is this: when even a few are without effort, the property does not cease to be "belonging to the Saṅgha" and become "not belonging to the Saṅgha."
"It is only my own authority that is the standard" is said because it has been delimited by its owners.

"From there" means from what belongs to the community (*gaṇa*) or from what belongs to an individual (*puggala*). "Designated for the purpose of lodgings" is merely an illustration; the same principle applies even if it has been designated for any of the four requisites.
"By virtue of ownership" means either after having asked another for permission...
There is no obligation to give without having asked permission; this alone is the standard here—thus [he acts] out of his own sense of ownership.
"He is to be dealt with according to the value" means he is to be dealt with by an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) or a serious offense (*thullaccaya*) in accordance with the value.

"The fine belongs to him who uses it out of a sense of ownership" means that the fine applies not only in this case, but also in the previous instance where he acted out of a sense of ownership for the sake of maintaining the family.

Or even when it has been given, it is [the responsibility of] the neck alone. "Easily obtained" means that it was easily obtained because the prescribed procedure—such as sitting within the monastery and striking the bell—has been performed.

For regarding property belonging to the Sangha that is subject to distribution, whether it be inside the monastery or outside the boundary, it is not permissible for those standing outside the boundary to divide it without having obtained formal consent (*apaloketvā*). However, even if it is situated in both places, [it remains] within the boundary...
It is indeed permissible for those who are present to distribute [the goods] after obtaining their consent. For that very reason, it is stated in all three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:

“Because it was done while sitting right there in the monastery, it is said to be ‘easily consumed. And this meaning will be clarified in the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) on the *Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka*. 150.
Regarding the items mentioned in the *Vuttavādaka-vatthu*, in the Canon (*Pāḷi*), *yugasāṭaka* means a pair of garments. A *tula* is one hundred *palas*. A *doṇa* is...
"Only sixteen nāḷis. "Having made a limit," however, means having made a limit according to whatever is desired, whether by value or by the requisite of robes and so forth.
"Criticism" refers to the attribution of fault, such as saying, "The venerable ones speak without having made a limit."
153. *Chātajjhattaṃ* means a mental continuum afflicted by the suffering of hunger. *Dhanukaṃ* means a small bow.
*Baddho hoti* means it is bound crosswise. *Sunakhadaṭṭhaṃ* means seized by a dog released by its owners.
*Yaṭṭhiyā saha pātetī* means that even before the pig arrives, [one casts it] there for the purpose of striking it.
He causes it to fall. "Going while intoxicated" means that one must pay compensation for the value of a single pig as restitution for the goods.
For not all the pigs traveling along that path are caught by that snare; only the one who goes first is caught.
Therefore, compensation for the value of a single pig must be paid. "Going afterwards" means...
By that method he has employed, it goes by itself later without having been brought. This same principle applies to such cases mentioned below as well.
"Having picked up and discarded" means having picked it up and discarded it beforehand.
"In the vicinity of the monastery" means in a forest area near the monastery. "Having requested protection" means having gone into the presence of kings, royal ministers, and so forth.
"Having requested protection for a specific purpose.

"The mouth of a fish-trap (*kumīnamukha*)" means the entrance through which fish enter into the trap. "He throws it into the water; it is a fine to be paid for goods" means that a fine for goods must be paid according to the value of the fish that were to have entered the trap.
156. "A place with a limited number of monks" means a place where there are monks defined by a limit of twenty, thirty, and so forth. "Of the elders..."

Of the newly arrived elders (*āgantukatthera*). "Of them too" means of the resident monks (*āvāsikabhikkhu*) as well. "For the purpose of use" means for the sake of using [the property] by way of communal use belonging to the Saṅgha.
"In the taking" is to be understood as a remainder of the text (*pāṭhasesa*). "Where" means in whichever monastery.
"The presence of others" means the presence of other visiting monks (*āgantukabhikkhu*). "Therein" means in such a monastery. Having divided [it].
"They eat" means that they distribute and eat even for those guests who have arrived.
"They properly provide for the four requisites" means that by selling mango fruits and such, they properly provide for the four requisites, beginning with robes.
"Given as designated for the purpose of robes" means: "By selling the fruits of these trees, [the proceeds] are to be used for robes alone."
“[These things] must be brought [to the newcomers]; they must not be eaten after being divided”—having thus made this restriction, they were given.

Even among those [items], the newcomers have no authority [to divide them], because they were given with the restriction that they be used as requisites; therefore, they have no authority to eat them after dividing them.
“They should not stand among them...pe... [they should not remain]”: here, according to the method explained below for the newcomers, they should be eaten after being divided.
The intention is as follows: "One must abide by their agreement" means that when the residents have made an agreement—

such as "it shall not be eaten after dividing it up," or "we shall take fruit from only so many trees," or "we shall take only so many fruits," or "we shall take them within so many days," or "we shall not take anything at all"— one must abide by that agreement.

The newcomers must remain [there]. The very meaning indicated by the word "non-authoritative" (*anissara*) in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* is shown in detail in the *Mahāpaccarī* by the passage beginning with "of the four requisites" (*catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ*). Regarding the phrase "only by way of use" (*paribhogavaseneva*), the particle *eva* here is used out of place;
it should be construed as "having divided that very [matter] by way of use. "In this" (*ettha*) means in this monastery.
Or in the country. "Requisite of lodging" means both the lodging itself and that which has been set aside and designated for its purpose.
"From the lowest limit" means beginning with what is low; it is said, "starting from inferior lodgings.
Even regarding the lodging, items such as grass and so forth must be assigned starting from the lowest limit, and even the requisites for the lodging must be assigned starting from the lowest limit.

Regarding the question, "What is meant by the statement, 'Having cut off the root and the foundation, one should not bring [the matter] forward'?"—first, in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, this is stated:
"It is meant that not all lodgings (*senāsana*) are to be relinquished.
However, we do not accept the interpretation that the meaning expressed is that even when relinquishing down to the lowest limit, the grounds of the lodgings themselves must not be relinquished.
Having reflected, one should take whatever is pleasing.
Regarding whether it is appropriate to perform an offering to the Buddha with what belongs to the Dhamma, or to perform an offering to the Dhamma with what belongs to the Buddha:
"Vāseṭṭha, this is indeed a designation for the Tathāgata, namely 'the Dhamma-body'. And so forth.
Some say it is permissible because of the statement: "Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma, he sees me. Others, however, say:

"If that were the case, then based on the statement, 'Bhikkhus, whoever would attend upon me, he should attend upon the sick,' it would follow that it is appropriate to provide medicine for the sick using what belongs to the Buddha; therefore, it is not permissible."

They say that this is not the reason. For by the statement, "Bhikkhus, whoever would attend upon me, he should attend upon the sick," it is not said that there is an identity between oneself and the sick person, nor that the attendance upon them yields equal fruit.
This is the meaning here: "Whoever would attend upon me by carrying out my advice and instruction, he should attend upon the sick; by carrying out my advice..."
"A sick person should be attended. One should not, however, take the meaning here to be that attending upon the Blessed One and attending upon a sick person are exactly the same.

Therefore, because of the statement: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya which have been taught and laid down by me shall be your teacher after my passing," [it follows that] "Now I alone am advising and instructing; in my absence..."

Furthermore, because it was said, "When [the Buddha] has attained final Nibbāna, these eighty-four thousand Buddhas will exhort and instruct you," and because the Blessed One praised the learned bhikkhu,
saying, "He who is learned is not merely called your disciple;
he is indeed the Buddha, O Cunda," and because of his profound respect for the Dhamma, it is our conviction that the former method alone is more highly esteemed by the Tathāgata.
"Having posted a notice" means having posted a notice stating, "Only so many trees are to be taken from so many [trees]";
it is the same as saying "having written it. "Having made a sign" means having established a convention.
"Children" refers to their sons, grandsons, and other children; it includes all those who are cowherds. In all these cases, it refers to the giving of cows by householders to cowherds.

One should take as much as the cowherds give; however, since it is explained that in the case of property belonging to the Saṅgha, one must take only according to the designated limit, it is said to be "identical in meaning.

"From that" means from the collection of timber set aside for the purpose of constructing the aforementioned Uposatha hall and so forth. "Having asked permission" refers to [asking] the performing Saṅgha.
"Having asked for permission. "Having brought all of that" means having brought it back even without asking for permission, as a temporary loan. "Causing it to be brought":

in this case, it must indeed be given even if he does not cause it to be brought. "This very bhikkhu is the owner" means that the place where it belongs to one bhikkhu is precisely from that very lodging that it should be given to him; nor should he be made to rise from there—this is what is meant.
“Water-worship (*udakapūjā*) means sprinkling at shrine sites (*cetiya-ṭṭhāna*); thus it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*.
“By way of duty (*vattasīsena*)” means solely out of faith, not for the sake of wages or the like. “Together with its base (*savatthuka*)” means together with the ground.

Why, then, is it said that “only a blade of grass should be given”? Is it because that [grass] is not a heavy object (*garubhaṇḍa*)? It is not so. For in a place that is unprotected and unguarded, by virtue of its being subject to destruction—
There is no heavy furniture remaining; therefore, it was said with reference to such [a case]: "but even a mere blade of grass should be given.
"Having tended" means having tended it year after year.
"Wall" means the wall of a house. "Rampart" means a surrounding enclosure wall. "From there" means from the abandoned monastery. From there...

"Having brought [materials], the lodging has been prepared": this means that after bringing timber and other materials from a monastery abandoned by monks residing in a neighboring village, the lodging has been constructed.

157. "Mixed with a fourth part of water": mixed with one-fourth part water. "In the case of the matter concerning the distribution of rice": in the case of the matter arising when someone says, "Give a portion to another."
159. "The noble ladies do not perform even what is appropriate for them to do; they are exceedingly stubborn," [thinking thus], he broke his confidence and became agitated in mind.
Therefore it is said: "For the sake of guarding his confidence. "He withdrew his psychic power" means he relinquished his psychic power.
"He stood right where he was" means that because the psychic power had been relinquished, even though he did not resolve, "Let the palace come back! [it returned].
He himself came and stood in his own place. Because he had previously resolved, saying, "As long as the children ascend the palace,
let the palace remain near them," and because he had made a resolution with a temporal limit—
considering that after that time the supernatural power (*iddhi*) would be withdrawn— it is said, "The Elder withdrew his supernatural power."

It should be understood that the Elder acted in this way because those children did not belong to those who had taken them away, and because by such a means they could not be said to have been brought back by the Elder. For this very reason he said, "By way of worldly convention," and so forth.
To see elephants and other things externally without abandoning one's own natural form is what is meant by "having been one, he becomes many."

And because it is accomplished by way of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), that which is described as "having arrived, he abandons his natural form and displays the form of a youth, or the form of a nāga... [and so on]... or he displays various military arrays" is called supernormal power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*).
Supernormal power of transformation (*vikubbaṇiddhi*) is so called because it proceeds by way of the alteration of abandoning one's natural form. Oneself...
It should be understood that even showing elephants and so forth externally without revealing oneself is included in this very category.
For what is called "abandoning one's natural appearance" means not being seen by others in one's own natural form; it does not mean the total cessation of that form.
And having established this, [the statement] "even showing elephants and so forth externally without revealing oneself is included in this very category" [is justified].
This does not contradict the root phrase stated as "having abandoned the natural appearance.
The commentary on the *Vinītavatthu* is finished.
Thus, in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā*, the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā...
The commentary on the second *pārājika* is completed.
Commentary on the Discourse of Instruction:
"By one whose defilements are defeated" means by producing the state of non-arising again within the mental continuum together with the four path-knowledges.
"By one whose latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been severed and all defilements (*kilesa*) eradicated. "Here" means in this teaching (*sāsana*).

It should be construed thus: "There exists no other training rule (*sikkhāpada*) equal to that [specific] training rule, which is interwoven with manifold methods and possesses a profound analysis of meaning (*atthavinicchaya*).
"Meaning and analysis" are *atthavinicchayā*; that which has profound analyses of meaning is "possessing a profound analysis of meaning" (*gambhīratthavinicchayaṃ*).
"In the matter having descended" means when the matter of the charge has descended into the midst of the Saṅgha;

it is said that this occurs either when one person has been charged by another, or when one has come forward of their own accord and declared the transgression they have committed. "In this" refers to when the matter has thus descended.
To show what must be done by one making a legal decision (vinicchaya), without hastily saying "it is a pārājika," he says "the Pāḷi," and so forth.

“Legal decision” (*vinicchaya*) means the decision regarding an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*). “Without having said” means without having said, “You have committed an offense involving defeat.
“Even when the object is allowable” means even when it is allowable to take, such as an object belonging to one’s mother or father.
“Moving quickly” means moving swiftly due to the arising of a thieving mind. “A venomous snake” [is so called] because it [stings] the entire body very rapidly.
The poison capable of pervading [the body].
The commentary on the discourse on instruction is finished.
The commentary on the first part of the Pārājika-khaṇḍa-ṭīkā is completed.
3. The Third Pārājika.
"By three" means by way of the doors of body, speech, and mind. "Expounded" (vibhāvita) means made manifest; it is said to be taught and laid down.
This is the commentary on the introduction to the first laying down of the rule.
162. "By increasing the enclosure of the rampart three times" means by expanding the city grounds with a rampart enclosure three times over.
"Because it had become spacious" means because it had expanded by one *gāvuta* at a time.

It is said that a fetus was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī; having realized this, she informed the king, and the king provided her with the necessary care for the pregnancy.
She gave [it] away. Being properly cared for, she entered the birth-chamber when her pregnancy had reached maturity.

For those possessed of merit, the delivery of the fetus occurs at dawn; she was one such, and therefore at dawn she gave birth to a lump of flesh resembling a coating of lac or a bandhujīvaka flower. Then [the thought occurred]:
"Other queens give birth to sons resembling golden images, but the chief queen..."

Thinking, "If this piece of meat were to appear before the king, my reputation would suffer," and out of fear for that ill repute, he placed the piece of meat in a vessel, sealed it, and having affixed the royal seal, he caused it to be cast into the current of the Ganges.
As soon as the people had discarded it, deities established a protective guard over it. And there, upon a golden tablet—
