Having written, "The offspring of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī," with vermilion, they bound it [to the vessel].
Then that vessel, unassailed by dangers such as waves, was carried along by the current of the Ganges.
At that time, a certain ascetic was dwelling on the bank of the Ganges, supported by a family of cowherds. Early in the morning, he...
Having entered the Ganges and seeing that vessel coming toward him, he took it up with the perception that it was a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*).
Then, having seen the strip of writing and the royal seal-mark upon it, he released it and saw that piece of flesh.
Upon seeing it, this thought occurred to him: "There might be an embryo, for there is no foul stench or putridity in it. Even though it had come by means of the flow of the water...
Thinking, "Indeed, warmth does not depart; and such warmth would indeed exist in a state endowed with consciousness, so there might be an embryo," she reflected.
Furthermore, due to her merit, there was no foul odor, nor any putrefaction resulting from the process of decay.
Having thought thus, she led her to the hermitage and placed her in a clean spot. Then, after the lapse of half a month, two lumps of flesh appeared.
They were thus. Seeing this, the ascetic set them down even more carefully.
Then, after another half-month had passed, for each single piece of flesh (*maṃsapesī*), five swellings arose on the hands, feet, and head.

Then, after another half-month had passed from that, one piece of flesh became a boy resembling a golden *bimba* fruit, and the other became a girl. In them, the ascetic felt the affection of a father for his children.
He was born, and due to the children’s supportive power of merit (*puññupanissaya*), milk issued from his thumb.
From that time forth, he received milk-rice. After the ascetic had eaten his meal, he would pour milk into the mouths of the children.
Whatever entered their bellies appeared as if it were contained within a crystal vessel (*maṇibhājana*). In his final existence...
Because the skin of the Bodhisatta’s mother was so clear and translucent when the Bodhisatta was in her womb, they likewise became "Nicchavī" (skinless) in that same way.
Others say: "Their skin became so closely adhered to one another as if it had been sewn together.
Thus, because of their lack of skin or because of their closely adhering skin, they were known as "Licchavī."
While supporting the children, the ascetic would enter the village for alms after sunrise and return only when it was well past midday.
Knowing this activity of his, the cowherds said, "Venerable sir, raising children is an obstacle for those who have gone forth.
Give the children to us; we will raise them, while you attend to your own duties. The ascetic replied, "Very well."
He agreed. On the second day, the cowherds leveled the road, scattered flowers upon it, raised banners and flags, and arrived at the hermitage while musical instruments were being played.
The ascetic said, "These children possess great merit; let them grow with diligence.
Once they have grown, let them marry one another, and having satisfied the king with the five products of the cow, [obtain] a plot of land..."
"Take them and build a city; there, consecrate the boy as king," he said, and gave the children to them.

They replied, "Very well," and taking the children, they raised them. When the children had grown up and were playing, they would strike other cowherd boys with their hands and feet at points of contention, and those boys would cry. Their parents would ask, "Why are you crying? and so forth.
They said, "These people, who have no parents and are raised by ascetics, strike us excessively.
Then their foster-parents also said, "These children harass and cause suffering to other children;
they should not be welcomed, they must be shunned. From that time on, it is said, that region was called "Vajjī," measuring one hundred yojanas in extent.
Then the cowherds, having gratified the king, took possession of that region. Having established a city there and consecrated the prince, who was sixteen years of age, they made him king.

Because he had performed the deed that bestows the attainment of sovereignty, and because he was born into an unbroken royal lineage, the deities—urged by the power of the prince’s merit and possessed by his majesty—acted [on his behalf].
Some [people], having arranged a marriage between a boy and a girl, made an agreement: "No girl is to be brought from outside;
no girl from here is to be given to anyone. Through their first union, two children were born—a daughter and a son.
In this manner, sixteen times they had two children each born. Then, of those children, in due order...

As the city expanded and could no longer contain the prosperity of their monasteries, gardens, residences, and retinues, they surrounded it three times over with walls at intervals of one *gāvuta* each.
Because it was made increasingly spacious (*visālīkata*) in this way, it came to be known by the name "Vesālī.
Therefore it is said: "Because it became spacious through the threefold expansion of its wall enclosures..."
“It is called Vesālī.
This indicates that this city is not only Rājagaha and Sāvatthī.
In this context, “the Great Wood,” and so forth, is the common commentary of both the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya and the Saṃyutta Nikāya. For in the Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā...
In the *Saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated according to this very method. However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it says:

"At Mahāvana: there is a self-grown forest situated outside the city, forming a single continuous expanse with the Himalayas, which is called 'Mahāvana' precisely because of its great size; in that Mahāvana. At the gabled hall: in that forest grove."

They established a monastery (saṅghārāma). There, having joined together the rafters and constructed upon the pillars a palace resembling a celestial mansion (devavimāna) in the form of a gabled hall (kūṭāgārasālā), the entire monastery came to be known as the Gabled Hall from that point on.

It is said that because it was built in the middle of a forest, it is called "in dependence on the forest" (vanaṃ nissāya). "In the monastery" (ārāme) means in the monastic community’s residence (saṅghārāme).
“By means of the swan-wheel covering” means by that which is covered by a swan-wheel; the meaning is: in the form of a circle of swans.
Regarding the phrase “in many ways,” the word *pariyāya* here signifies a reason; thus he says, “by many reasons.
This body, whether devoid of consciousness or possessed of consciousness, is impure in this way and impure in that way—meaning it is impure through various kinds of reasons.

The meaning is as follows: "Proceeding by way of demonstrating the aspect of foulness" means proceeding by way of seeing the aspect of foulness in every respect there, by means of [the parts] beginning with head-hairs.
"A discourse for the purpose of creating revulsion for the body" means a discourse that produces revulsion toward one's own and another's body made of kamma-born matter.
By the words "urine," and so forth, he shows the unattractiveness of the body by way of contrast.
Therein, first, by means of the first three phrases, he shows its lack of beauty and its corelessness; in the middle, by four phrases, its foul odor;

and at the end, by one phrase, the absence of even a trace of loveliness. Then, with the words "But indeed" (*atha kho*) and so forth, there is a demonstration of its unloveliness through positive correlation (*anvaya*) and by way of its actual nature.
"Desire" (*chanda*) is weak lust; "lust" (*rāga*) is powerful lust. "Hair, body hair, etc. is stated in brief.
In order to demonstrate the meaning already stated through analysis, the passage beginning with "Those who too... was spoken.
They are called "impure" (*asubha*) because they are devoid of any adventitious beauty. They are "unclean" (*asucina*) by their very own nature.
They are "repulsive" (*paṭikūla*) because they are loathsome, like a place of filth for a city-dweller.
Showing that these hairs are repulsive in terms of their color, shape, smell, habitat, and location, he said:
"And this should be understood by them through five reasons.
For even when seeing something the color of hair in a bowl of pleasant rice gruel or a bowl of cooked rice, people feel disgust and say, "This is mixed with hair; take it away!"
Thus, hair is repulsive by way of its color. Even those who use it at night feel such loathing upon touching its texture—whether it be hemp or silk—that it is likewise repulsive by way of its shape.
Furthermore, the odor of hair that is devoid of preparations such as oil-anointing, flowers, and incense is extremely foul; it becomes even more foul when cast into the fire. Thus, hair is repulsive.
For although these things may not be repulsive in terms of their color and shape, they are indeed repulsive by way of their odor.
For example, the excrement of a young child is yellow in color like turmeric and its shape is like a lump of turmeric;
likewise, the bloated carcass of a black dog discarded in a rubbish heap is the color of a ripe palm fruit in terms of color, and is rounded in shape.
The shape of the discarded *mudiṅga* fruit and his fangs, which resemble jasmine buds—both of these might be non-repulsive in terms of color and shape;
however, they are indeed repulsive by their odor. In the same way, even the hair might be non-repulsive in terms of color and shape, but it is indeed repulsive by its odor.

Just as vegetables grown in a place of filth through the seepage from a village become repulsive and unfit for consumption to city-dwellers, so too these hairs are repulsive because they are produced by the seepage of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so forth;
this is their repulsiveness by way of their source (*āsayato paṭikkūlatā*). And these so-called hairs are like a tuft of grass growing on a heap of dung.

They are produced within a mass of thirty-one parts; because they are born in an impure place—like vegetables growing in a cemetery or a rubbish heap, or like lotuses and water-lilies growing in a ditch—they are supremely disgusting.
This is their repulsiveness by way of location (*okāsato paṭikkūlatā*). And just as with the head-hairs, so too for all the parts, by way of their color, shape, smell, habitat, and location...
"One should understand the fivefold repulsiveness" is what he meant by saying, "thus of the body hair and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by way of fivefold divisions," this should be seen as a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning "that which has five divisions each";

thus, it is called "fivefold division. "Expounding" means explaining in detail. "In the foul" (*asubhāya*) refers to the matrix of foulness (*asubhamātikā*). "Counter-practice" (*phātikamma*) means frequent cultivation. "Abandoned of the five factors."

Regarding the phrase "endowed with five factors": here, the state of being "abandoned of five factors" should be understood by way of the abandoning of these five hindrances, namely: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
For as long as these are not abandoned, jhāna does not arise; therefore, they are called the "factors of abandoning. Indeed, at the moment of jhāna...
Other unwholesome states are also abandoned, yet these [five hindrances] specifically obstruct the jhānas.
For a mind enticed by various objects through sensual desire does not concentrate on a single object;
or, a mind overcome by sensual desire does not enter upon the path for the abandoning of the sense-sphere realm. And by ill-will, the mind is struck against its object.
It does not proceed uninterruptedly; overcome by sloth and torpor, it becomes unwieldy; possessed by restlessness and remorse, it wanders about without being calmed;
and impaired by doubt, it fails to ascend the path that accomplishes the attainment of jhāna.
Thus, because these specifically act as obstacles to jhāna, they are called the factors for abandoning.
Since initial application (vitakka) applies the mind to the object and sustained application (vicāra) follows after it,
joy (pīti) causes swelling and bliss (sukha) causes nourishment for the mind whose effort has been accomplished through those two for the sake of non-distraction;
thus, by means of these— application, following, swelling, and nourishment— it [the mind], together with its associated states, [becomes concentrated].

Supported by these factors, one-pointedness is applied evenly and correctly toward a single object; therefore, the possession of five factors should be understood by way of the arising of these five—namely, applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*).
For when these five have arisen, the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) is said to have arisen; thus, these five are its constituent factors.
Therefore, one should not conclude that there exists some other thing called "jhāna" distinct from those [factors] with which it is endowed.
Just as an army is called "fourfold" or music "fivefold" and the path "eightfold" by virtue of its constituent parts alone,
so too this [jhāna] is called "fivefold" or "endowed with five factors" by virtue of its constituent parts alone.
Or it should be understood that this is what is being said.
Although these five factors are present even at the moment of access concentration (*upacāra*), they are nevertheless stronger than the natural mind during access;
here, however, they are even stronger than access, having reached the moment of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). In this regard—
For applied thought (*vitakka*) arises placing the mind upon the object in a very clear manner; sustained thought (*vicāra*) intensely rubs against the object;
and rapture and bliss pervade the entire body. For this very reason it is said:
"There is nothing of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and bliss born of seclusion. One-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) also...
It arises with great smoothness toward the object, like the upper lid of a casket meeting the lower lid of a casket.
This is their distinction from the others; therefore, the phrase "endowed with five factors" is stated specifically to distinguish absorption concentration (*appanā-jhāna*).
Regarding the description "beautiful in three ways and possessed of ten characteristics," this refers to the beginning, middle, and end of the jhāna.
The state of being good in three ways should be understood as the possession of ten characteristics by virtue of those very beginnings, middles, and endings.
Furthermore, he himself will explain the method of detailed exposition here.
Because it cannot be overcome by the thieves of the defilements, meditation is called the "jewel casket of the mind. "Depending on" means making it a foundation.
Since the threefold excellence is also revealed by the very exposition of the ten characteristics, he first shows those ten characteristics, saying: "In this regard, these are...

and so forth. Therein, the meaning of such phrases as "purification of mind from obstacles" will be made clear in the commentary on the canonical text itself, introduced by the words: "In this regard, here is the text... and so forth. *Tatra* means "in that."
In the exposition of the ten characteristics: "Purification of the way" (*paṭipadā-visuddhi*). It is called the "way" (*paṭipadā*) because one proceeds (*paṭipajjati*) by means of it;

it refers to the method of development belonging to the prior stage, culminating in the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*). Purification (*visuddhi*) is cleansing from obstacles; purification of the way is *paṭipadā-visuddhi*.
Since this is obtained at the moment of the arising of jhāna, it is therefore said: "purification of the way."

“Ādi” means: “The intensification of equanimity” (*upekkhānubrūhanā*) refers to the intensification through the accomplishment of the function of the equanimity of onlooking (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) included within the jhāna, because there is an absence of the need for purification and so forth.
Since this [equanimity] is especially obtained at the moment of the stability (*ṭhiti*) of the jhāna, it is therefore said:
“The intensification of equanimity is in the middle. “Encouragement” (*sampahaṃsanā*) refers to that which accomplishes the non-overstepping of factors therein, etc.

Purification occurs by way of the accomplishment of the function of knowledge. Since that [purification] becomes manifest at the conclusion of the jhāna, it is said: "Encouragement is the conclusion. These three characteristics are:
the mode of the mind’s purification from obstacles, the mode of proceeding toward the middle sign of serenity (samatha), and the mode of leaping forward into that [sign].
These three are the characteristics of the attainment of absorption (*appanā*) at the initial moment of the arising of jhāna.

Because there is no attainment of absorption without these modes, and because they are absent when absorption is not present, it is "good in the beginning" due to being a path of purification, and it is "endowed with the three characteristics" because it possesses the aforementioned characteristics.
In this same manner, the application of the characteristics of the middle and the end should be understood.

However, some explain that "purity of the way" refers to access concentration together with its requisites, "intensification of equanimity" refers to absorption, and "encouragement" refers to reviewing;
but that is not correct. For if that were so, it would be as if the qualities of one meditative state were being described by means of the factors of another meditative state.
Indeed, one level of existence (bhūmi) does not belong to another level of existence.

This contradicts the Canon (pāḷi). For it is said in the Canon: “The mind that has attained unity (ekattagata) both leaps forward by means of purification of the way (paṭipadāvisuddhi) and is nourished by equanimity (upekkhā), and is gladdened by knowledge (ñāṇa).

Herein, “the mind that has attained unity” refers to that which has reached unity in accordance with the single-flavored state of the faculties and the attainment of the pinnacle of one-pointedness (ekaggatā).

The consciousness accompanied by the factors [of jhāna] that has reached absorption (appanā) has been described; immediately following that, its progression through the purification of the way (paṭipadā-visuddhi) and so forth is now being explained.

Therefore, since the purification of the way and the other stages are stated in the text as occurring within a single moment of the absorption-consciousness, the purification of the way occurs right within the absorption itself by way of the arrival at the preliminary work (parikamma). Through equanimity regarding the middle (tatramajjhattupekkhā)...

The intensification of equanimity should be understood by way of its function; and the encouragement should be understood by way of the accomplishment of the function of purifying knowledge through the establishment of the state of non-transgression regarding phenomena. How so?
In whichever session absorption arises, in that [session], whatever group of defilements consisting of the hindrances...
This is an obstacle to jhāna; therefore, the mind becomes purified. Being purified, it becomes free from hindrances and enters upon the middle sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*).
The "middle sign of serenity" is precisely the absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) proceeding evenly.
It is "middle" because it does not fall into either of the two extremes known as dullness (*līna*) and agitation (*uddhacca*); it is distinguished by its [overcoming] of adverse states.

It is called "tranquillity" (*samatha*) because of its quality of pacifying; it is considered a "sign" (*nimitta*) because it serves as the cause for the specific types of bliss experienced by the yogi.

Furthermore, the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhū-citta*), which acts as the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for that absorption consciousness (*appanā-citta*),—despite the distinction between the limited and the sublime states, and despite the distinction between the condition and the conditioned—is termed "the transformation within a single continuity" (*ekasantatipariṇāmanayena*), because it undergoes transformation within one and the same continuum.
When it approaches the state of being concentrated by means of absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*), it is said to "enter upon" the intermediate sign of calm (*samathanimitta*).
Because it has entered upon it in this way, it is said to "launch into" that [sign] by approaching the state of suchness (*tathattūpagamana*).
For at the very moment it enters upon the intermediate sign of calm—that is, suchness—at that same moment, by approaching the state of suchness...

By means of absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*), through the attainment of a state of composure, one is said to "launch into" that [object]. Thus, first, the modes of purification from obstacles,
the middle way of serenity (*samatha*), and the launching [into the object], which exist in the preceding change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhū-citta*) and are accomplished by way of arrival,
constitute the "purification by the way" (*paṭipadā-visuddhi*) at the very moment of the arising of the first jhāna.
These very aspects, when produced at the moment of jhāna through specific conditions, are called "purification by way of the path" (*paṭipadā-visuddhi*).
Since that mind, thus purified, has no further need for cleansing, one does not exert effort toward purification but rather "looks on with equanimity" at the purified mind.
This occurs for one who has entered into serenity (*samatha*) by means of attaining the state of serenity.
Furthermore, when one does not exert effort toward further concentration, one is said to "look on with equanimity" at that which has entered into serenity (*samatha*).

And because it has entered into serenity, having abandoned contact with the defilements and being established in unity, when one does not exert effort toward the further establishment of that unity, one is said to "look on with equanimity" at the establishment of unity.
Thus, by way of its function, [equanimity] is called "the equanimity of middle-state neutrality" (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
The cultivation of equanimity is to be understood.

Furthermore, when that jhāna-consciousness has been thus cultivated with equanimity, there arise within it the factors known as concentration and wisdom—these twin-yoked states—which proceed without one surpassing the other;
and there are also the faculties such as faith and the rest, which [are freed] from various defilements.
Because they are liberated, they proceed having become of a single flavor through the taste of liberation.
And as for that energy which he exerts, which is appropriate to those [factors] that have reached that state— possessing a nature of a single flavor in not overstepping one another—

and as for the cultivation (āsevanā) that occurs at that moment, all these modes [of practice] are such because, through knowledge, having seen the respective danger and the respective benefit in both defilement and purification, [he proceeds] in such and such a way.

It is said that because [the mind] has been gladdened, purified, and cleansed, it is accomplished; therefore, gladdening should be understood as the accomplishment of the function of the purifying knowledge by means of establishing the state of non-transgression regarding phenomena and so forth.
Now, why is it that gladdening alone is called the "conclusion," and not the intensification of equanimity? Because in that [state]...
In the mind of development, knowledge becomes manifest through the influence of equanimity; therefore, encouragement—which consists in the function of knowledge—is called the "conclusion.

For at the time of absorption, because development proceeds evenly and the opposing factors have been well abandoned, no effort such as exertion needs to be made; thus, there is only pure looking on. With reference to this:
It is said: “At the appropriate time, there is equanimity regarding the mind; he looks on with equanimity at the purified mind,” and so forth.
This equanimity, moreover, occurs through the accomplishment of the function of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), because the operation of absorption (*appanā*) is specifically achieved by means of knowledge.
Therefore, encouragement (*sampahaṃsanā*), which constitutes the function of knowledge, is called the “conclusion. Thus, by means of this threefold purification of the way (*paṭipadāvisuddhi*).
When the threefold intensification of equanimity has been attained, the fourfold encouragement is accomplished through the preeminent state of the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*).
Thus, by way of the function of knowledge regarding the equanimity that has arrived, all ten aspects are to be understood as occurring within the jhāna itself.
In this way, the phrases beginning with "the mind has reached a threefold state" are words of praise for that very mind. Therein, thus...

"Attained to the threefold state": thus it has reached a threefold condition by way of the purification of the path, the launching into equanimity, and the intensification of knowledge, according to the method already described.
"Endowed with applied thought": because it is free from the agitation of defilements, it has attained a state of excellence through applied thought (*vitakka*).
"Endowed with the mind's resolution": [this refers] to that very object, by means of what is termed the uninterrupted occurrence of the mind.

It is endowed with resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and is not deficient. Just as the occurrence of jhāna is called "resolution" because it is under the mastery of resolution, so too here, "resolution of the mind" is appropriately understood as one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*). For by that [one-pointedness], the mind is resolved upon a single object and does not waver therein.
However, because it is stated separately as "endowed with concentration" (*samādhisampanna*), [it refers to the specific factor of concentration].

It should be understood in the manner already stated. Alternatively, because concentration itself is included among the factors of jhāna, it is described by way of the five jhāna-factors as "endowed with the mental basis of the mind.
It is described by way of the five faculties as "endowed with concentration," because concentration is included among the faculties.
"Cultivated by the perception of foulness" means that the jhāna is accompanied by the perception that arises regarding the entire body as foul.
The perception of foulness, when cultivated and developed by that [perception]. "By the mind" means by the consciousness. "Abundantly" means frequently.
"Dwells" means for one who dwells; the meaning is: for one who is abundant in the attainment of the foul.
"By way of engaging in sexual intercourse" means because of being possessed of sexual intercourse. "Contracts" means it shrinks away to one side; it becomes as if hidden.
"Contracts" means it shrinks. "Turns away" means it retreats. "Does not stretch out" means it does not spread;
the meaning is that it does not leap forward due to a lack of delight. Alternatively, "draws back" means it shrinks because it remains fixed there due to its repulsiveness.
"Contracts" means it withdraws and does not approach. "Turns away" means it retreats from there.
"Thus he does not wander about. *Nhārudaddula* means a piece of sinew or a scraping of sinew.
*Addhamāsaṃ* is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection.

*Paṭisallīyituṃ* means to cause the mind to settle day by day, for the aforementioned period, in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and in reflection on the Dhamma. *Payuttavācaṃ* means speech connected with the [four] requisites.
The statement beginning with, "In these days the Buddhas do not go for alms, but sit only in the monastery; what is given to them is of great fruit," refers to such words.

"By way of a wholesome supporting condition" means by way of the supporting condition for the going forth (*pabbajjā*). Regarding the phrase "they say of others," the particle *kira* indicates a lack of approval.
Therefore he said, "But this is merely a wish. This refers to the state of one who reports the discovery of conduct, as well as the prohibition regarding what is already known.
This is merely their wish, but not the actual reason; such is the meaning. Others, however, say:
"It is said that during this half-month there was no one who could be converted by the Buddha. Therefore, the Teacher thought:
'I shall spend this half-month in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Thus, there will be a dwelling in happiness for myself, and for future generations..."
“The Teacher too, having abandoned his following, dwelt alone; how much more so should we?
Thinking, “He will follow this example, and that will lead to his welfare and happiness for a long time,” he spoke thus for this reason.
“No one at all approached the Blessed One” means that, apart from the one who brought almsfood, no one else approached the Blessed One.
The community of monks, having accepted the Teacher’s word, assigned one monk [to him].
That monk would perform all his duties— such as sweeping the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber, providing water for rinsing the mouth, and offering tooth-sticks—
at their respective times, and then depart.
Regarding the phrase "mixed with many causes": here, the impurity, foul odor, loathsomeness, and repulsiveness of the body constitute the "many causes.
"By nature fond of adornment" means having the inherent disposition for ornamentation. Some, though young, are not youthful;
some, though youthful, are not by nature fond of adornment—such as those whose nature is tranquil or who are overcome by sloth, vice, and so forth. But here, [the subject] is both young and...

A young man who is fond of ornaments is intended here. "First youth" refers to the period from fifteen years up to thirty-two years, or from sixteen years up to thirty-three years. "Corpse" means a dead body;
"snake-corpse" means the corpse of a snake. The others are to be understood in the same way. And herein, because of their nature as being exceedingly repulsive and loathsome—

It should be understood that these three alone are so described. For people even consume the carcasses of other animals, such as rabbits and pigs, after preparing them with pungent condiments and the like;

yet they feel disgust even for the fresh carcasses of these [creatures], let alone when they have become putrid through the passage of time. And their state of being extremely loathsome and disgusting is exceedingly great.
They say that foul odor arises from the body due to the excessive heat of snakes and the accumulation of boiled rice and sour gruel by dog-like humans.
"A sham ascetic" (*samaṇakuttaka*) means one who performs the duties of an ascetic; it is said that he performs the duties of an ascetic by means of wearing saffron robes and so forth.

Therefore he said, "one who wears the guise of a recluse. "They did everything" means that ordinary worldlings (puthujjana), perceiving even what is blameworthy there as blameless, did everything—including the acts themselves, the instigating of others, and the consenting thereto.
Regarding "blood-red," here they also read "having become blood" (*lohitagata*). "Vaggū" means those considered beautiful;
"puññasammatā" means [those] esteemed as meritorious by reason of producing for beings the fruits of becoming worthy of honor.
By means of this purification, it is considered "merit. "I shall carry away" means I shall cause to go; the sense is "I shall purify.
(163) "The realm of Māra" refers to the phenomena of the three planes. According to the etymology of the word, however, it is the *dheyya* (domain/abode) of Māra, hence *māradheyya*.
*Dheyya* means a place, a site, a dwelling, or a range of activity. Alternatively, it is so called because Māra dwells, stands, and operates therein.
Regarding "the realm of Māra" (*māradheyya*), here "Māra" is intended to mean the *kilesamāra* (the Māra of defilements);

it is precisely through the power of the *kilesamāra* that the *devaputtamāra* (the Māra who is a son of the gods) exercises sovereignty over the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*). "Thinking, 'He will not transcend the domain of Māra'" means:
"Having thus attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he might even transcend the domain of Māra; however, when I have spoken thus, he will quell the urgency that has arisen."
"Thinking, 'He will not transcend the realm of Māra,' [she speaks]. 'The dual expression' means speaking twice; it is said to be a reduplicated statement.

Regarding the word 'inciting': here, this blind and foolish deity, having thought, 'If this person were to practice the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) rooted in such arisen spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he might even transcend the realm of Māra,'—out of her own ignorance, [she says] 'dead [to] saṃsāra'..."
It should be understood that although she held such a view, she did not examine the fact that those monks who were dead were being liberated from *saṃsāra* according to their own respective views;
rather, she directed them toward that [practice] based on her own conviction.
Furthermore, even though the Blessed One, when speaking on the discourse of foulness (*asubha-kathā*), acted in such a way that those monks would not experience fear of death...

It will come to pass; for because it was taught in such a way, and because the bhikkhus, having heard that discourse on the Dhamma, have through their application to the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā) become free from desire and lust for the body, they have no fear due to their longing for death.
However, with reference to the fear arising in other bhikkhus upon seeing him wandering about with a sword in hand, [the Buddha said]: "There certainly is..."

They say that [the phrase] beginning with "out of fear" was stated [in this context]. Because it is said, "They deprive themselves of life, and they also deprive one another of life," it should be understood that the statement, "He deprived all those five hundred bhikkhus of life," was made by way of the majority.
For a small deficiency or excess does not affect the count.

“Five hundred” is what was said. Therefore, it should be understood that—with the exception of those who themselves took their own lives and those who took one another’s lives—he deprived all the remaining ordinary monks (*puthujjana-bhikkhu*) as well as all the noble ones (*ariya*) of life.

164. Regarding the phrase “emerged from seclusion” (*paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito*): here, “seclusion” (*paṭisallāna*) means having turned away from those various conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) [of sentient beings].
“Having withdrawn” means the hiding away, the seclusion, of the arrows; it is said that there is a state of solitude through body and mind, which is their being separate from those [arrows].
Therefore he says, “from solitude” (*ekībhāvato*), the meaning of which is “from seclusion” (*pavivekato*). For “solitude” (*ekībhāvo*) is stated to be the seclusion of body and mind.
“Emerging” (*vuṭṭhito*) refers to the arising of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) from that twofold seclusion, through its association with formations such as visible objects and so forth.

And it is free from the gathering of beings such as householders and those gone forth. "They learn the recitation and the interrogation" means they learn them in the presence of their respective teachers.

Granted that mindfulness of breathing is already included by the inclusion of the ten recollections, nevertheless, it is suitable and beneficial for many among the monks assembled there; therefore, it is mentioned again.
For the Blessed One taught that very same meditation subject to those bhikkhus.
It should be understood that the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is similar to the meditation subject on the foul, whereas the four formless attainments are unsuitable for beginners;
therefore, they are not included here.
"Dependent upon Vesālī" means having made the city of Vesālī their alms-resort village (*gocaragāma*). "In the assembly hall" means in the Dhamma hall (*dhammasabhā*).
"In just a moment" is said with reference to the fact that immediately after the words of the monks who had approached out of reverence for the Teacher and the True Dhamma, they rose up.
It is said that during the time of the Buddha, the monks would receive the Blessed One’s message with their heads bowed in homage.
They dwell with their ears attentive. "Of which" means of that which ought to be done. "Time" he says with reference to the time of teaching.
The commentary on the introduction to the first formulation is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the discourse on the concentration of mindfulness of breathing.
165. "For the attainment of arahantship" means for the purpose of attaining arahantship. "Another method" means another cause for the realization of arahantship.
"Explaining" means teaching preceded by praise; and the praise is for the purpose of providing encouragement by generating delight in that [method].
Having heard that, the bhikkhus [thought], "The Blessed One praises this concentration in many ways..."
Thinking, "This concentration is indeed noble, sublime, delightful, and a blissful dwelling;
it causes evil states to vanish on the spot," those who have conceived a sense of interest and developed enthusiasm believe that they must apply themselves with diligence and practice accordingly.
Regarding the sequence of the meaning and the application: the Blessed One [described] the concentration that was directly experienced by himself.
By the power of his teaching, making it near and evident even to those monks, he spoke the words beginning with “This too,” by way of summary.
“Grasping the in-breath and out-breath” means grasping the in-breath and out-breath by delimiting them according to their specific qualities such as long and short;
the meaning is that it occurs with reference to them.
Now, explaining the aforementioned meaning by means of the canonical text (pāḷi), he said, "For it has been said," and so forth.
Therein, "neither out-breath nor in-breath" expresses that same meaning by way of negation for the sake of distinction. "By way of the in-breath" means having made the in-breath the object;
the same method applies here to "by way of the out-breath. "Establishment is mindfulness" refers to the state of non-forgetfulness.

The meaning is that mindfulness is so called because it stands having approached that very in-breath and out-breath. Up to this point, the meaning of "mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassati*)—that is, mindfulness regarding the in-breaths and out-breaths—has been stated.
Now, wishing to describe the person by way of mindfulness itself, it is said:
"It is established for him who breathes in; it is established for him who breathes out. He who breathes in...
The meaning is: for one who breathes in, mindfulness remains having approached the in-breath; for one who breathes out, mindfulness remains having approached the out-breath.
"Engaged" means associated. "In mindfulness of breathing" means in mindfulness of breathing that has become a condition.
For in the first sense, by the mention of association, the state of being a co-nascent and other conditions of concentration by means of mindfulness is stated; in the second [sense],...

Furthermore, there is also the state of being a decisive support (*upanissaya*). For mindfulness accompanied by access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) is a decisive support for absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*);
thus, he demonstrates the conditionality [of mindfulness] by way of all seven conditions, such as co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth.
“Furthermore, Udāyi, the practice for my disciples has been declared by me; practicing accordingly, my disciples [attain] the four...”
In such passages as "developing the foundations of mindfulness," it is called "development" (bhāvanā) in the sense of producing and increasing;

thus, showing the meaning according to both of these, he said: "Developed means produced and increased. In that context, it is "developed" (bhāvita) because it has gone from this [state] to being (bhāva), i.e., existing;
the meaning is that it has been produced merely as something acquired. But when it has arisen and gained practice, it is "developed" (bhāvita).
"Made proficient" means it has been developed; "practiced frequently" means it has been made to occur repeatedly.

By this, he expresses the attainment of mastery over the preliminary mental advertence (*āvajjana*) and so forth. For that which has attained mastery can be entered into at any desired moment and will therefore occur again and again.
Hence it is said: "done again and again. As it is said: "Right here, monks, is the ascetic, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... (MN 2).
In such cases as these, the word *eva* mentioned in the first clause is indeed understood in the second and subsequent clauses as well;
thus he says, "In this case too, the restriction (*niyama*) is to be understood by means of the word *eva* in both places.
To show the benefit obtained through the restriction of both terms, he says, "For this... and so forth. [The term is] "the meditation subject of the foul" (*asubha-kammaṭṭhāna*).

He speaks of jhāna having the foul (asubha) as its object. For that is called the "foul meditation subject" (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) because it constitutes the practice of yoga regarding foul things, and because it serves as the cause for the specific types of happiness for the yogi.
By the word "only" (kevalaṃ), he excludes other objects. "By way of penetration" (paṭivedha-vasena) means by way of the penetration of jhāna;
for jhāna, when accomplished through a specific mode of cultivation, penetrates its own objective domain.
It is called "penetration" (*paṭivedha*) because it occurs according to the true nature [of things] and is penetrated. "Because of its coarse object" means because of its loathsome object.
"Because of its repulsive object" means because of its object that should be felt with disgust. "By way of a method" means by way of a reason or by way of a different approach.
"Even by way of the continuity of objects" refers to the extreme subtlety of the object reached through successive stages of discernment.
He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For when the object is peaceful and settled, the state (*dhamma*) that occurs taking it as its object is itself also peaceful and settled.
Therefore he said: "peaceful, stilled, extinguished" (*nibbuto*); the meaning is that all feverish distress (*pariḷāha*) has been extinguished.

The peacefulness of the states that take that [object] as their object due to the peacefulness of the object is to be illustrated by the reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*) cognitions that have supramundane states as their objects.
It is "unadulterated" (*asecanaka*) because it possesses no admixture that could bring about a state of agitation; because it is unadulterated, it is "unmixed" (*anāsittaka*);

because it is unmixed, it is "uninterrupted" (*abbokiṇṇa*), meaning it is not blended with preliminary exercises (*parikamma*) and so forth; for that very reason, it is "distinct," "separate," "individual," and "exclusive.
All of this is stated to show its state of peace (*santabhāva*) by way of its own intrinsic essence (*sarasa*), or else [to show] the preliminary exercise as the cause of that state of peace.

"Preparation" (*parikamma*) refers to the process beginning with the creation of the *kasiṇa* and ending with the arising of the sign; the intention here is that such a thing does not exist [in this case].
For at that time, because the meditation subject lacks flavor, it would be non-existent and unabsorbed.

Or, the construction is: "There is no continuity here even by way of access. Just as at the moment of access, through the disappearance of the hindrances and the manifestation of the factors, for others...
It is continuous, but not so for this [meditator]. However, the construction is: "He brings it to mind from the beginning... and it is sublime.

The phrase "some say" refers to those residing in the Uttaravihāra monastery. "Unsprinkled" means not sprinkled with a condiment; therefore he said "rich in essence," meaning similar to that which is rich in essence. "Sweet" means desirable. It leads to the attainment of mental pleasure by way of the threefold and fourfold jhānas.

Alternatively, it should be understood that [the attainment] leads to the acquisition of bodily pleasure for everyone because of the state of peace inherent in equanimity (*upekkhā*) and its quality of being a happy destination.

However, the phrase "leading to the acquisition of bodily pleasure" should be seen as referring to the body being touched by the sublime matter produced by meditation (*jhāna-samuṭṭhāna-panīta-rūpa*), and this occurs specifically at the time of emerging from the meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
In this interpretation, the locative case in the expression "at every moment of absorption" (*appita-appitakkhaṇe*) should be understood as denoting the cause (*hetumhi bhummavacana*).
"Unsuppressed" means not removed from one's own continuum by means of jhāna, that is, not abandoned.
"Born of unskillfulness": unskillfulness is called ignorance (*avijjā*); [the defilements] are born from that. For all evil states have ignorance as their precursor.
"In an instant" means in the very moment of its own occurrence. "Causes to disappear": here, causing to disappear is destruction. And that...
Because it is the one who practices meditation (jhānakattuka) who is intended here, he says "he suppresses" (vikkhambheti), meaning there is the abandonment of the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna).
"He pacifies" (vūpasameti) means he pacifies specifically. Since specific pacification is indeed thorough pacification, he says "he thoroughly pacifies" (suṭṭhu upasameti).
But surely other types of concentration also cause opposing states to disappear and subside at the very moment of their own occurrence;
why, then, is this specific concentration described with such distinction? Because from its preliminary stage onward, it possesses the quality of suppressing various discursive thoughts (*vitakka*).

For it has been said: "Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) should be developed for the cutting off of discursive thoughts. Furthermore, this [is the case] for one of sharp wisdom whose knowledge is supreme.

The meditation subject and the abandonment of defilements by one who has knowledge as the supreme goal are superior to those of others, just as one who has attained right view is superior to those resolved through faith;
therefore, with reference to this distinction, it is said that "it makes [the defilements] disappear and pacifies them immediately.
Alternatively, because when the sign appears, the manifestation of the factors occurs in an instant, this very concentration—

"It makes [the defilements] disappear and pacifies them instantly" means that it is like the instantaneous subsiding of dust and mud on the earth when the downpour from a great, untimely cloud arises. For this very reason, he said:

"Bhikkhus, just as if a great, untimely cloud had arisen," and so forth. The development of jhāna by one belonging to the Dispensation is for the most part conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) alone.
He said, "Because it partakes of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiyattā*). For the Buddhas, however, it partakes exclusively of penetration.
Indeed, by developing this very meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones attain Perfect Enlightenment.
This concentration, being the foundation for the Noble Path, gradually increases and eventually reaches the state of the Noble Path.

"It seems as if it were so," he said, "having gradually attained the growth of the Noble Path. However, this meaning is correctly applicable by way of the contemplations of fading away (*virāga*), cessation (*nirodha*), and relinquishment (*paṭinissagga*). How so?
This is a phrase intended to clarify the manner of the question; and here, the question is posed by way of a desire to explain [the matter] to others.

Because it is impossible [to describe each one individually], and because that [practice] serves as a touchstone for all the various specific modes that have been introduced in the subsequent teaching—showing this meaning, he said: "How... pe ... the inquiry out of a desire to explain in detail.

Regarding the phrase "how is it cultivated," here too the term "concentration through mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*) must be supplied and connected. In that context, "how" refers to the cultivation of concentration through mindfulness of breathing.

The question arises from a desire to explain in detail in various ways. The statement "concentration through mindfulness of breathing when practiced frequently" is an indication of the dhamma asked about;
this meaning is shown by the phrase "the same method applies," which serves as an illustration.

Showing the meaning already explained below at length in a summarized form for ease of grasping, he says: "But here is the summary of the meaning," which means it is the condensed meaning (*piṇḍattha*).

"Tamatthan" means that object which was stated briefly by way of the question, "How is it developed? and so forth. In such passages as "Here, the Tathāgata arises in the world," the word "here" (idha) is used with reference to the world. In such passages as "Standing right here," it refers to a place. In such passages as "Bhikkhus, here I would have been one who has eaten and is invited," it serves merely to complete the meter. "Here... [The text continues:]... "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... and so forth, the word "here" is used with reference to the Dhamma. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is virtuous," it is used with reference to a person. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is practicing the way," it is used with reference to the practice. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered final Nibbāna," it is used with reference to Nibbāna. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has attained the fruit of stream-entry," it is used with reference to the fruit. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has attained the fruit of once-returning," it is used with reference to the fruit. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has attained the fruit of non-returning," it is used with reference to the fruit. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has attained the fruit of arahantship," it is used with reference to the fruit. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the path of stream-entry," it is used with reference to the path. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the path of once-returning," it is used with reference to the path. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the path of non-returning," it is used with reference to the path. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the path of arahantship," it is used with reference to the path. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is a stream-enterer," it is used with reference to the person. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is a once-returner," it is used with reference to the person. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is a non-returner," it is used with reference to the person. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is an arahant," it is used with reference to the person. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry," it is used with reference to the practice. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning," it is used with reference to the practice. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning," it is used with reference to the practice. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship," it is used with reference to the practice. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has abandoned the fetter of sensual lust," it is used with reference to the abandonment. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has abandoned the fetter of ill will," it is used with reference to the abandonment. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has abandoned the fetter of conceit," it is used with reference to the abandonment. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has abandoned the fetter of ignorance," it is used with reference to the abandonment. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has destroyed the taints," it is used with reference to the destruction. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a non-returner," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a stream-enterer," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a once-returner," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a non-returner," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of an arahant," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a paccekabuddha," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a Buddha," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a disciple," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a teacher," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a wheel-turning monarch," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a universal monarch," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a noble one," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a worldling," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a deva," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a brahmā," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a human being," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a beast," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having heard that a certain person has entered the state of a hungry ghost," it is used with reference to the state. In such passages as "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu
In passages such as "the bhikkhu masters the Dhamma," however, it refers to the Dispensation (sāsana).

Here too, in the phrase "Here, bhikkhus, bhikkhus," he shows that it is indeed the Dispensation, saying, "Bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, bhikkhus. Then, in order to make that same meaning clear, he said, "For this...
and so forth. Therein, "of one who produces concentration through mindfulness of breathing in all its modes" means:
The inclusion of "all modes" refers to the sixteen modes. For these exist only within this very teaching;
outsiders, even if they know them, know only four modes from the beginning.

Therefore he said, "the negation of such a state in other teachings," which means the negation of the status of being a support for the person as previously described. By this, [he explains] "here, monks."
This shows that the word *eva* is included within [the compound]. For there are even single words that function as exclusives (*avadhāraṇa*), such as "one who subsists on air" (*vāyubhakṣa*).

Therefore he said: "Right here, monks, is the ascetic," and so forth. For one who possesses the qualities that constitute a complete ascetic is a producer of concentration through mindfulness of breathing in all its modes.
"The doctrines of others" (*parappavāda*) refers to those of other sectarians (*aññatitthiya*).
The various types of doctrines are the sectarian tenets.
The passage beginning with “For this person... is stated in order to show that forest dwellings and the like are suitable lodgings for meditation.
A “bull of a beast” (*kūṭagoṇa*) is an untamed ox that has not submitted to training. Just as milk does not flow from its udders at all, so too...

A deceptive cow is one that obstructs the milking. "Of the cowherd" means of the owner of the cow. The "taste of the object," such as visible forms and sounds, refers to the gratification arising in dependence upon visible forms, sounds, and so forth.
"An object previously practiced" means an object familiarized prior to going forth, or throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
It should be understood that one "sits near" by way of access concentration (*upacāra*) and "lies down near" by way of absorption (*appanā*).

*Idha* means in this teaching. *Nibandheyya* means he should bind [the mind]. *Satiyā* means by means of mindfulness that proceeds through the correct observation of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

*Ārammaṇe* means on the object, which is the meditation subject. *Daḷhaṃ* means firm; the meaning is that he should make it stable so that the concentration—distinguished as access and absorption—of one who practices with mindfulness may succeed.
"Muddhabhūtaṃ" means it is like a crest because it possesses distinguished qualities such as continuity (*santati*) and so forth, and because it has been cultivated by noble ones such as the Buddhas;

the meaning is "supreme. It is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for the attainment of distinction and for the pleasant abiding in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) for all Buddhas, some Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddhas.
And it is the proximate cause for the dwelling in happiness in this very life for those who have attained distinction through other meditation subjects.
The Blessed One is like a teacher of the science of sites (*vatthuvijjā*), because he points out suitable places of residence to yogis.
A bhikkhu is like a leopard, because by dwelling alone in the forest, he achieves his desired goal by crushing opposing forces. "The supreme fruit" means...
He spoke of the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*). "A ground suitable for the speed of exertion" means a ground that serves as the basis for the speed of energetic application in meditation.
"In those [places] characterized as thus stated" refers to those characterized according to the method of the Abhidhamma and the method of the Suttas.
"Near a tree" means to the extent that at midday the shade spreads all around, and leaves fall in the absence of wind—to that extent...
The phrase "the foot of a tree" refers to the area situated near a tree as it has been described. The remaining seven types of lodgings are those described as:
a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a forest thicket, an open space, and a heap of straw.

These are suitable for the three seasons, for the three temperaments of the elements, and for the three temperaments of the mental dispositions—namely, the three seasons beginning with summer, the three elements beginning with phlegm, and the three temperaments beginning with delusion.

And it is also favorable. For instance, during the summer season, the forest is favorable because of its gentle coolness; in winter, the foot of a tree is favorable because it wards off the falling snow;
and in the rainy season, an empty dwelling is favorable because it provides shelter from the rain.

For one whose constituent element is phlegm (semha) and whose natural temperament is phlegmatic, the forest is favorable, as the phlegm is pacified by wandering for alms after traveling a long distance.
The foot of a tree is favorable for one of bilious temperament (*pittadhātu*) because it gives rise to the contact of cool breezes;
an empty hut is favorable for one of windy temperament (*vātadhātu*) because it wards off the wind. A forest is favorable for one whose character is dominated by delusion (*mohacarita*);

for in a great forest the mind does not shrink, owing to its open and spacious nature. The foot of a tree is favorable for one whose character is dominated by hatred (*dosacarita*) because of its inspiring and pleasing quality.
For one of lustful temperament, an empty dwelling is suitable because it prevents the entry of discordant objects.

"Favorable to neither sluggishness nor agitation" means it is conducive to neither contraction nor distraction. For lying down is conducive to indolence, while standing and walking are conducive to agitation;
sitting is not so. Precisely for that reason, it possesses tranquility. The firmness of the sitting posture is achieved by folding the legs in the cross-legged position (*pallaṅka*).
He shows the ease in the occurrence of the inhalation and exhalation by straightening the upper body, and the means for grasping the object by fixing mindfulness "in front.
"The cross-legged posture" (*ūrubaddhāsana*) refers to sitting with the thighs bound together; it is the placing of the lower body in a non-erect position.

"It is understood by the word 'sitting' itself. Regarding "the body straight," he says—"having placed the upper part of the body straight"—because here the word *kāya* refers specifically to the upper body. To show that placing [the body] straight both in its essential form and its purpose, it is said:
"eighteen," and so forth. "Not bending" means not inclining. "Not falling over" means...
It does not depart from the path nor does it overstep it; rather, through the arising of successive distinctions, it attains growth and expansion.
Here, the prefix *pari-* has the same meaning as the prefix *abhi-*, which is why he says "facing the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānābhimukha*);
the meaning is that, having turned back from external, manifold objects, one keeps the meditation subject alone before oneself. *Parī-*...
The sense of "embracing" (*pariggaha*) is as in the phrase "the guide" (*pariṇāyikā*), and so forth. The sense of "issuing forth" (*niyyāna*) is the sense of emerging from its opposite;

therefore, "with mindfulness embracing the issue" means having established mindfulness that is in every way grasped without confusion and has abandoned confusion, that is to say, having established supreme mindfulness and circumspection.
"Mindful" (*sato*) means being endowed with mindfulness, breathing in only while being mindful.
The meaning is that there is no occurrence of an inhalation devoid of mindfulness for him.

Regarding the phrase "mindfully breathing out," here too the word *eva* (only) should be supplied, so that it means "mindfully only breathing out. "One who acts mindfully" means one who, being mindful only, is either a doer of what ought to be done by means of mindfulness, or one whose habit is to act with mindfulness.

"By way of thirty-two aspects" means by way of the thirty-two aspects beginning with long inhalation and ending with the out-breath that contemplates relinquishment—these being stated by dividing into two the sixteen terms, such as long and short, which appear in the four tetrads, according to the modes of inhalation and exhalation.
This is what is stated in the *Vibhaṅga* commentary on the passage: "Mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out."
Now, why is it that, instead of saying simply "he breathes in and breathes out," it is said "he acts with mindfulness"?

It is because of the desire to give a teaching of uniform flavor (*ekarasa*). For in the first tetrad, only two terms are presented according to the present tense, while the others are according to the future tense;
therefore, in order to provide a teaching of uniform flavor, the term "acting with mindfulness" (*satokāri*) is used throughout.
It has been stated. "By way of long inhalation" means by way of a long inhalation; this is a designation formed by eliding the case-ending (*vibhatti*).

Or, it is by way of the inhalation spoken of as "long" by the Blessed One. "One-pointedness of mind and non-distraction": because it is the opposite of distraction, it receives the name "non-distraction";
for one who understands this state of one-pointedness of mind, mindfulness becomes established, having approached the object.
"It is established" means by that mindfulness and by that knowledge—that is, by the aforementioned mindfulness and the aforementioned knowledge.

This is what is meant: when one understands with full awareness (*sampajañña*)—either through non-distraction or through non-delusion—the long inhalation which has become the object, mindfulness is indeed established therein; for one who understands it, [mindfulness] is established by way of making that [breath] the object.

Or, clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) occurs by way of non-delusion; through mindfulness and clear comprehension dependent upon that, the practitioner endowed with them is called "one who acts with mindfulness.
Regarding the phrase "by way of inhalation while contemplating relinquishment": it means being one who contemplates relinquishment by way of the inhalation.
Alternatively, the reading is "by way of inhalation while contemplating relinquishment" (*paṭinissaggānupassī-assāsavasena*); for one who contemplates relinquishment...
The meaning is: by way of inhalations that are mindful of relinquishment.
Inhalation (*assāsa*) is the movement arising within; exhalation (*passāsa*) is the movement arising outside. Thus he said: "Inhalation is the wind going out," and so forth.

However, in the *Suttanta-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that inhalation is the movement from outside to inside, even though it arises outside; and exhalation is the movement from inside to outside, even though it arises inside.
It is stated in reverse order by taking the exhalation (*passāsa*) as being "outside" [the body].

Alternatively, according to the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, the wind of the breath first goes outside immediately upon emerging from the mother’s womb—having had no opportunity to exit while still in the womb—and thus it says, "In the beginning, the inhalation (*assāsa*) is the breath. For this very reason, he said: "Of all..."

“Of those lying in the womb,” and so forth. However, in the *Suttanta-aṭṭhakathā*, because one first draws the breath of the nose inward at the time of beginning the development during its occurrence, and subsequently emits it outward, the inward-moving wind is described as "inhalation (*assāsa*)" according to the sequence of its occurrence, stating:
"Inhalation is the breath at the beginning. And herein, the method of the Suttanta itself [is followed] regarding the beginning, middle, and end of inhalation.

This accords with the following canonical passage: "For one who follows [the breath] with mindfulness, if the mind is distracted internally, both body and mind become agitated, perturbed, and trembling;
for one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath with mindfulness, if the mind is distracted externally, both body and mind become agitated, perturbed, and trembling."
They say: “It is more excellent because, at the commencement of its cultivation, it is desired that the sequence of occurrence [be established] first.
“It is extinguished by striking the palate” means it ceases by striking the palate. It is said that a newborn infant makes a spitting sound with that [tongue].
“Thus far,” etc., is the conclusion of the meaning as previously stated. Some [explain]: “‘Thus far’ refers to this sequence of occurrence...”
They say that the intention is that "in-breath" (assāsa) should be understood as the air exiting outward.
"By way of duration" (addhānavasena) means by way of the duration of time (kāladdhāna). For this word *addhāna* denotes both time and space.
Having shown there the duration of space by way of an illustration, [the text now treats] the in-breaths and out-breaths by way of the duration of time.
To clarify their length, the passage beginning with "Just as" (*yathā hi*) was stated. Therein, "the extent of the space" (*okāsaddhānaṃ*) means the extent that constitutes the space.
"Having pervaded" (*pharitvā*) means having spread out. Even when reduced to powder, they exist in the form of many clusters;
thus, "a long extent" (*dīghamaddhānaṃ*) refers to a long location. Therefore, because they proceed slowly and possess a long continuity, they are called "long. In this context:

It should be understood that the length and shortness of the in-breaths and out-breaths in the bodies of elephants and so forth, as well as in the bodies of dogs and so forth, are spoken of solely by way of the duration of time (*kāla-addhāna*), distinguished by location (*desa*).
This is because of the statement: "Having filled [the body] slowly, they exit slowly; having filled it quickly, they exit quickly.
Regarding the phrase "among humans": this refers to human bodies even when they are of equal size.
"Breathing long" means causing a long series of inhalations to proceed;
the same method applies here for "breathing out. The construction is: like dogs, hares, and so forth, they breathe in and breathe out short.
This long and short inhalation and exhalation, however, should be understood as the natural characteristic of the bodies of those beings.
“Of them” means of those beings. “Those” refers to the inhalations and exhalations. “A short duration” means a brief period of time.

“By way of nine modes” refers to the three modes mentioned first by way of mere duration for one who is devoted to the development of meditation but has not yet attained any further distinction between what precedes and what follows;
and indeed, one person clearly observes the inhalation, another the exhalation, and another—
“Both of these” refers to the three types of persons mentioned above.
However, some say that the expression “breathing in and breathing out” is stated as a single unit in order to show that the development proceeds without interruption.
[The breaths are contemplated] in the same three ways as before by way of desire (*chanda*), and likewise by way of gladness (*pāmojja*); thus, by these nine modes.

Although in this context only three modes are actually found for a single individual, it is stated, "In this case, the bhikkhu [proceeds] by nine modes," because all [nine] have been included in the Canon according to their respective systems and because the preliminary work must be performed according to them.
"Thus understanding" means understanding the in-breaths and out-breaths in the manner just described; therein—
While applying attention (manasikāra). "By one mode" means by one of the four modes beginning with long inhalation, or by one of the three [sets] among the nine. For he will say:
"The inhalation is long and short..."
And the out-breath is likewise;
the four colors proceed right at the tip of the bhikkhu’s nose.

Having established that "this is the development of the contemplation of the body as in-breaths and out-breaths," it was said: "the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body succeeds.
Now, in order to show those nine aspects and the method of development according to the scriptural tradition itself, the passage beginning with "As it is said" is commenced.
In that context, he asks "How does he understand? out of a desire to explain the method of understanding. [He understands] "a long in-breath," etc.
The long inhalation has the characteristics already described. "In what is reckoned as a duration" (*addhānasaṅkhāte*) means in a long time that has come to be reckoned (*saṅkhāta*) as a duration;
the meaning is "a long moment. Alternatively, the word *saṅkhāta* is a synonym for "part" (*koṭṭhāsa*), as in expressions such as "reckoned as theft" (*theyyasaṅkhāta*).
Therefore, "in what is reckoned as a duration" means in a portion of space that constitutes a part of a duration. "A desire arises" (*chando uppajjati*).
Because they bring about successive excellence in meditation, one attains a sense of satisfaction;
thus, a wholesome desire (*kusalacchanda*) characterized by an exceptional eagerness to act arises therein. "By way of desire" means:

for one who applies himself to the special development of meditation through such arisen desire, and for whom the meditation subject reaches growth and expansion. "More subtle than that" refers to the occurrence of the aforementioned desire.

It becomes more subtle than before. For, through the power of meditation, because the distress and feverishness of the body have been stilled, the inhalations and exhalations proceed in a more subtle manner.

"Joy arises" means that joy arises because the object has become more peaceful due to the subtlety of the inhalations and exhalations, and because the meditation subject has entered its proper course.
Joy accompanied by the mind of development arises as "minor rapture" (*khuddikā*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the mind turns away":

some say that because the inhalations and exhalations gradually reach an extremely subtle state and cease to appear, the mind turns away from them as they have reached a state where they must be investigated.
However, when the inhalations and exhalations have reached a subtler state through the power of meditation...
Therein, when the counterpart sign has arisen, the mind turns away from the natural in-breaths and out-breaths.

"Equanimity becomes established" means that once that counterpart sign—consisting of the types of concentration known as access and absorption—has arisen, there is a state of looking on with indifference because there is no further effort required for the production of the jhāna;
this equanimity, moreover, should be understood as the equanimity of specific neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
"By these nine aspects" means occurring by way of these nine modes as previously described. "Long in-breaths and out-breaths are the body":
although the in-breaths and out-breaths are broken down into minute particles, they are called a "body" (*kāya*) in the sense of being a collection.
Here, the sign that arises dependent upon the in-breaths and out-breaths is also spoken of by way of the commonality of those breaths. "Establishment is mindfulness" refers to that [mindfulness].

"Mindfulness is called 'establishment' (upaṭṭhāna) because it stands having approached its object. "Insight is knowledge of contemplation" means that by way of serenity, there is the contemplation of the sign;

and by way of insight, there is the contemplation of name-and-form after one has defined the in-breaths and out-breaths, along with the body which is their support, as "form," and the mind and the mental states associated with it as "non-form."

Knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is the comprehension of things as they truly are. "The body is the foundation" (*upaṭṭhāna*): that body is called a foundation because mindfulness (*sati*) stands upon it by approaching it through the act of making it its object.

And here, by the statement "the body is the foundation," other bodies are also included, since the mode of practice consisting of full comprehension (*sammasanacāra*) is intended here as well. "Not mindfulness": that body is not itself mindfulness.
It is not merely a name. Mindfulness (*sati*) is both a presence (*upaṭṭhāna*) and mindfulness itself, in the sense of remembering and in the sense of being established.

"By that mindfulness" means by the mindfulness already described. "By that knowledge" means by the very knowledge already described. "That body" refers to both the body of the in-breaths and out-breaths themselves and the material body which is their support.
"Contemplates" means by means of the knowledge associated with jhāna and by means of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
He contemplates each [body]. Therefore it is called "the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body in the body.

By means of that contemplation, this is called the development of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body in regard to the body as already described—that is, in regard to the body of inhalations and exhalations and the "karma-born" body which serves as its support. This is what is meant:
whatever this [contemplation] is in regard to the aforementioned body of inhalations and exhalations and the karma-born body which is its basis, it is simply the body...

Contemplation (*anupassanā*) is not the contemplation of permanence and so forth in the body whose intrinsic nature is impermanence and so forth—just as there is no contemplation of water in a mirage that is devoid of water;
rather, it is the contemplation precisely of the states of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness, as appropriate to each case.
Alternatively, because there is nothing whatsoever in the body to be grasped as "I," "mine," "woman," or "man," one does not contemplate it in such a manner.
