Contemplation of the body alone is *kāyānupassanā*; mindfulness itself, which is associated with that contemplation of the body, is the foundation (*upaṭṭhāna*), thus it is *satipaṭṭhāna*;
the cultivation and increase of that is "the cultivation of the foundation of mindfulness through the contemplation of the body.
The same method applies: the procedure stated by the words "by way of nine aspects" and so forth is extended to the abbreviated terms. "In this" means in this [context].
As shown in the method of the Pāli text that comes down as “How, breathing in long,” and so forth; here, in the method of the Pāli text that comes down by way of short terms.
“He” refers to the practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*). “By way of duration” means by way of a long period of time.
“By way of brevity” means by way of a limited period of time. “By these modes” means by these nine modes.
"Such-like" (*tādiso*) means long and short. "The four colors" (*cattāro vaṇṇā*) refers to the four modes, which are precisely those beginning with long.

The phrase "on the tip of the nose, O Bhikkhunī" is stated using the short vowel for the sake of metrical ease in the verse. In the expression "on the tip of the nose" (*nāsikagge vā*), the word *vā* has the sense of non-restriction;
by it, the upper lip is included.
"Sensing the whole body" (*sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī*) means one whose nature is to feel and know each and every part of the entire body correctly;
or, it means one for whom there is a correct individual feeling of that [body], or one who is correctly feeling each and every part of it.
In this context, by the inclusion of the term "all" (*sabba*), the body—beginning with inhalation—is taken in its entirety without remainder.

Even though [the term] is established, the inclusion of the prefix *paṭi-* is for the purpose of showing that there is awareness of all its constituent parts, because it consists of a collection of many components;
and the inclusion of the prefix *saṃ-* is for the purpose of showing the state of one who acts with thoroughness (*sakkacca*) therein.

Demonstrating this point, he says: "of the whole," and so forth. In that regard, just as in the case of inhalation and exhalation, which are common to all, there is a specific method of practice for the yogin...
It should be understood that a separate teaching was given to show that each [practice] must be undertaken with due care;
likewise, although the meaning is the same, a separate commentary on the meaning of the two phrases beginning with "of the whole" was provided in order to illuminate that very point.
"Making manifest" means making clear, the sense being "making it entirely evident."
Showing that making [the breath] manifest and discerning it occurs through the engagement of those very knowledges that do not become confused regarding them, he said:

“Making it known thus,” and so forth. In this context, “therefore” means: because one causes the in-breath and out-breath to proceed only with a consciousness associated with knowledge, and not with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge;
therefore, being such, one thinks: “I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body.”

The construction is: "It is said by the Buddha and others that one trains [thinking], 'I shall breathe out. "Spread out into fine particles" means spread out in the state of being pulverized due to having many constituent parts.
"The beginning becomes manifest" because of the occurrence of previously formed volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*) by way of mindfulness and knowledge.
"One should become like that" means one should become similar to the fourth type of person; how much more so, then, with mindfulness.
The intention is that, having established knowledge, one should proceed with a consciousness associated with knowledge in all three stages.
"In this way" means by way of experiencing the whole body as previously described. "Exerts" means he strives;
"makes an effort" means he applies mental attention. "Of one who has become thus" refers to one who is developing mindfulness of breathing.
"Restraint" (*saṃvara*) means either mindfulness (*sati*) or energy (*vīriya*). "By that mindfulness" means by that mindfulness which has proceeded having taken *ānāpāna* as its object.
"By that attention" (*manasikāra*) means together with that attention consisting of cultivation which is preceded by mindfulness therein;

this is the intended meaning. "He cultivates" (*āsevati*) means that when the "three trainings" are mentioned, he cultivates the wholesome states (*adhikusaladhamma*). For it is the cultivation of those [wholesome states] that is meant here.
"Training" is what is intended. "In the former method" means in the former method of development; the intention is that this refers to the first two stages.

Even there, although the arising of knowledge is certainly obtained because of the presence of the realization of the long and short states of the in-breaths and out-breaths as they truly are, nevertheless, since that consists merely in grasping them as they occur, the application of the present tense is used therein.
This, however, is difficult to perform, being like a man walking upon the edge of a razor;

therefore, it is shown that there must be an extraordinary degree of prior mental preparation (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*) here. To demonstrate this point—that the application [of the term] refers to the future time—it is said, "In that regard, because...

and so forth. Therein, in the phrase "in the arising of knowledge, etc.," the word "etc. includes the subsiding of the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*), the experiencing of rapture (*pīti*), and so on.
He includes [them]. Some, however, say here that it is "the inclusion of the undertakings of restraint.

"Bodily formation" refers to inhalation and exhalation. For although it is mind-originated, it is called a "bodily formation" because its activity is bound up with the physical body (*karaja-kāya*), and thus it is formed by that body. As for what is called "bodily formation" and "vocal formation":

The bodily formation that has arrived in this way, characterized by volition, is designated by the "body-door" (kāyadvāra) because it occurs predominantly and frequently there, despite its arising through other doors as well; however, that is not what is intended here.
In the phrases beginning with "calming" (passambhento), each subsequent term is a synonym for the preceding one. Therefore, "calming" (passambhana) means:

"Tranquillization" should be understood as the non-arising of gross bodily formations—which would otherwise arise if such application were absent—through the successful application [of effort]. "Therein" refers to the phrase "tranquilizing the gross bodily formation.

"At a time when it is not yet taken hold of" means at a time when the meditation subject has not yet been commenced; for that very reason, it is also a time when both body and mind have not yet been taken hold of.
For by the phrase, “He sits having folded his legs crosswise and set his body erect,” the encompassing of the body is stated;
and by the phrase, “having established mindfulness before him,” the encompassing of the mind is stated. Therefore it was said: “Both body and mind are encompassed.
“Body” here refers to the physical body composed of the four great elements. “With fever” means with a burning sensation. And that state of theirs being “with fever” is due to its heaviness.
Because it is invariably concomitant with grossness due to its similarity to it, he says, "gross. "Stronger" means powerful and thick.
"They become peaceful" means that when the mind, having become one-pointed through the absence of outward distraction, proceeds by grasping the meditation subject, it becomes peaceful and tranquil;
and for that very reason, the material phenomena originating from it attain a state of lightness, softness, and wieldiness.

The remainder of the material form of the three continuums exists in conformity with that; thus, while the mind and body are proceeding in a state of tranquility, the inhalations and exhalations dependent upon them proceed by gradually becoming calmer, more calm, and most calm.
Therefore it was said: "But when his body also... and so forth. "I calm" refers to the first application of attention (*āvajjanā*). *Ābhoga* is the act of directing the mind.
"Right and successive bringing together" (*samannāhāra*) is the repeated application of attention toward that very same object;
"attention" (*manasikāra*) is the mental orientation toward that same object, its placing within the mind; "investigation" (*vīmaṃsā*) is reflective examination.

"Agitated" (*sāraddha*) means with distress (*sadaratha*) and with feverish excitement (*sapariḷāha*). "Excessive" (*adhimatta*) means powerful and gross; [this is expressed] by a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
It has been stated. For it is the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) that is intended. The phrase "it proceeds in an excessive manner" is an adverbial qualification of the action.
The same principle applies here to the term "subtle" (sukhuma). In the expression "in the body," one must supply the words "and in the mind" and connect them accordingly.
The preliminary work (parikamma) for the second jhāna, which involves different advertings (nānāvajjana), is performed after emerging from the first jhāna; [this refers to] the first jhāna.

Considering that its opposite has been cast far away, the bodily formation originating from it is described as "coarse" in the first jhāna and in the access concentration (upacāra) of the second jhāna;
this same method applies to the other two access concentrations as well.
Alternatively, for the yogin who is striving to attain the second jhāna and so forth, and who is fatigued by the painful path of practice (dukkhāpaṭipadā) and so on:

The grossness of the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) in the access stages of the second jhāna and so forth should be understood by way of the agitation of applied thought (vitakka) and the rest, and by the state of the mental process being accompanied by vibration due to physical fatigue and mental distress.
"Exceedingly subtle" means that the bodily formation found elsewhere becomes even more subtle in the fourth jhāna; its state of subtlety is [even greater] there.
How could there be grossness? Because it does not occur. Therefore he said, "He reaches non-occurrence itself.

Regarding the one who possesses this [attainment], the Majjhimabhāṇakas—referring to the acquisition of all jhānas in a single sitting at the time of entering the successive attainments (anupubbasamāpatti)—[state that] even in the access (upacāra) to each higher jhāna from each lower jhāna...
They desire something more subtle. For therein, for those jhānas accompanied by access (sopacārānaṃ), there may arise both a progressive distinction and a continuity;
or rather, this was said with reference to the single adverting (ekāvajjana) as the access.
Thus, the non-contradiction of this doctrine with the statement made previously is established, because their respective scopes are different. "Of all" refers to both types. Since...

All of them, according to the method already stated, desire tranquility alone. The statement that "the bodily formation active during the period when [the breath] is not yet grasped subsides during the period when it is grasped" is said because of the similarity of the continuum;
for it is not those same gross in-breaths and so forth that become subtle. Rather, the manner of their subsiding has already been explained below.
“Subtle in the discernment of the primary elements” is said with reference to the application of insight by way of the four elements.

It is subtle in the discernment of all material phenomena because it becomes increasingly refined through successive stages of meditation. For this very reason, he says: “It is subtle in the discernment of both the material and the immaterial.
By “insight having the characteristics as its object,” he means the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*). From the contemplation of disenchantment...

From that point onward, insight (vipassanā) is strong; prior to that, it is weak. "By the method stated previously" means by the method stated in the section on serenity (samatha), beginning with the words "at the time of non-apprehension.

It should be understood that the subsiding (paṭippassaddhi) is also to be applied to the method of insight (vipassanā) by way of the passage: "The bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) occurring during non-apprehension subsides upon the apprehension of the great primary elements (mahābhūta)," and so forth.
"Assā" refers to this phrase, "calming the bodily formations. "By means of interrogation and clarification" means by means of questions and their respective resolutions.

"In this way" means in the manner that will now be stated. "How" means: how, in what manner, does the calming of the bodily formations and the training of the yogin occur, as it was said: "Calming... [etc. ...he trains"?

Having asked out of a desire to explain, the passage beginning with “What are the bodily formations? is commenced in order to show the bodily formations according to their specific nature, their relative coarseness and subtlety, their subsiding, and through the presentation of questions and answers.
In this context, *kāyikā* means existing in the material body (*rūpakāya*). *Kāyappaṭibaddhā* means dependent upon the body.
They exist when the body exists and do not exist when it does not; for that very reason, they are not originated by anything other than the body.
They are called "bodily formations" (*kāyasaṅkhārā*) because they are conditioned by means of the body. "Calming" means calming them progressively, from the coarsest to the coarsest.
The remaining two terms are synonyms for that same process. For one who causes the coarse bodily formation—which has an uncalmed nature—to settle down is said to be "calming it";
one who brings about its non-arising and cessation is said to be "ceasing it"; [and one who brings it to] a state of perfect peace...
"Leading [the mind], they cause it to be stilled.
"By such kinds" means by what sort. "Bodily formations" means by gross bodily formations. "Bending forward" (*ānamanā*) is the bending of the body toward [the object].
"Bending aside" (*vinamanā*) is the bending as one looks from side to side. "Bending down completely" (*sannamanā*) is [bending] thoroughly from all sides.
Or *ānamanā* (bending forward). *Paṇamanā* is bending backward. *Iñjanā* and the others are synonyms for *ānamanā* and the rest;
or else, the intense movements toward the front and so forth are *ānamanā* and the rest, while the weak ones are *iñjanā* and the rest.
"Calming the bodily formations" means calming the gross bodily formation that serves as the cause for such bending and the rest. For in that [state],...
When [the bodily formations] have become tranquil, even the inclining and so forth become tranquil.
"Peaceful and subtle": by means of such bodily formations as are the cause for the body's lack of agitation, there is no inclining and so forth;
thus, due to the absence of distress, they are peaceful, and due to their non-coarseness, they are subtle. [The phrase] "tranquilizing"…
He speaks thus, treating "bodily formations" as a single category in general. Alternatively, having successively stilled grosser and grosser bodily formations,
and having produced those that are subtler and even more subtle which serve as the cause for the body's lack of movement,
and having stilled even those, he stills that bodily formation which has reached the ultimate limit of extreme subtlety.
It was said with reference to that: “He tranquillizes the bodily formation that is peaceful and subtle.
The words beginning with “itī” (thus) are the challenger’s statement. Therein, “iti” is a particle used in the sense of manner;
“kira” indicates lack of approval, meaning “even if it were so. This is the intended meaning here: “If, in the manner described, he were to tranquillize even the most subtle bodily formation.”
"‘Evaṃ sante’ means when this is so, that is, when the manner described by you is obtainable. ‘Vātūpaladdhiyā’ means through the apprehension of wind.

The word ‘ca’ has the sense of conjunction. The intention is that there is no production, generation, or occurrence of a mind having inhalation and so forth as its object, and those [breaths] must be tranquillized by it. And regarding ‘the production of inhalation and exhalation,’ [this refers to] the coarse [level]."
By suppressing inhalation and exhalation through meditation, there is no further development of those subtle [breaths], because both of them must be suppressed by that means.

Furthermore, there is no occurrence of mindfulness directed to breathing (*ānāpānassati*)—that is, of mindfulness having inhalation and exhalation as its object—due to the absence of inhalation and exhalation.
For that very reason, there is also no concentration associated with that mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*).
There is neither manifestation nor production [of that attainment]. For never do states possessing an object (sārammaṇa-dhammā) arise without an object.

And as for the word "naṃ," here "naṃ" is a mere particle. The construction is: "The wise, the possessors of wisdom, neither enter into that aforementioned attainment, nor do they emerge from it. Thus the challenger [speaks] in every respect.
He urges [the opponent] with the intention that "tranquility" means the bringing about of non-existence.
The phrase beginning with "Puna iti kira" (Again, it is said... is the response to the aforementioned challenge.

In this context, "kira" is a particle used in the sense of "yadi" (if). Thus, "iti kira sikkhati" means "if he trains in the manner stated by me. "Evaṃ sante" (this being so) [is explained as follows].
Thus, when there is subsiding, "there is manifestation" means that even if the gross bodily formations have subsided,
the subtle ones still remain; therefore, by way of their gradually reaching a state of extreme subtlety,

the manifestation of the sign, of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), and of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*) is indeed accomplished— this is the intended meaning.
"How is it? means: how should that aforementioned method be regarded? The intention is that there is some simile for correctly establishing its meaning.
Now, in order to show the simile, "Just as" (*seyyathāpi*) and so forth was said. Therein, *seyyathāpi* is a particle used in the sense of a simile.
"In bronze" (*kaṃse*) means in a bronze vessel. "The sign" (*nimittaṃ*) refers to the sign—that is, the mode of occurrence of those sounds.
The meaning is as follows: this is the accusative case used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī-attha*). "Because they were well-grasped" means because they were thoroughly apprehended.
"Because they were well-attended to" means because they were properly established in the mind. "Because they were well-retained" means because they were correctly reflected upon and observed.
"Subtle sounds" refers to reverberations; those that are slight. For here the particle *ka* has the sense of "slight. "And because they have subtle sounds as their sign and object" means...
The subtle sound itself is the sign; thus it is called "the sign of the subtle sound. What is meant is that [the mind] has that as its object.

Granted, at that time even the subtle sounds have ceased; nevertheless, because the sign of the sound was well grasped, the mind continues to proceed by taking as its object the sign of an even subtler sound.
For from the very beginning, the sign of each respective sound that has ceased has been maintained by one who is undistracted.
As he investigates with the mind, eventually, even taking the extremely subtle sign of sound as his object,
the mind continues to proceed. The mind does not become distracted because of the presence of concentration upon that sign as it has appeared.
The passage beginning with "When this is so" (*evaṃ santa*) is stated as a conclusion to the very meaning already explained.

Therein, having extracted that sutta passage for which the meaning was stated along with the objection and its resolution, the words beginning with "calming the bodily formations" (*passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ*) are spoken in order to show the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) of body-contemplation in detail.
In that context, "calming the bodily formations" refers to the aforementioned inhalations and exhalations.
The construction should be understood as "the body. Alternatively, in the phrase "calming the bodily formations" (*passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ*), the meaning should be seen as follows:

here, "body" refers to the inhalation and exhalation. This is because, when explaining the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*) in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, it was stated specifically in the first tetrad;
and likewise in the *Ānāpānassati Sutta*: "Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu, breathing in long..."
And because it is said: "He understands: ‘I am breathing in long’... [and so on] ...he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
On that occasion, monks, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body," it is therefore stated:
"of the first tetrad taught by way of the contemplation of the body."
"By way of the meditation subject for a beginner" is said with reference to the meditation subject for serenity (*samatha*);

however, the meditation subject for insight (*vipassanā*) is indeed obtainable even in the other tetrads. "In this" refers to the first tetrad. "Together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*)" is merely an illustration;

for those who possess merit and are endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), even the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) are accomplished. "Fourfold" is by way of the restraint of the Pātimokkha and so forth.
It is fourfold. "Non-transgression" means not committing any one of the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).
"Emergence from what has been committed" means emergence by performing the appropriate remedy for an offense that requires remediation;

specifically, it is said to be emergence through confession for an offense leading to confession, and emergence through the performance of disciplinary acts such as probation (*parivāsa*) for an offense leading to emergence.
For since there is emergence from an offense committed even through confession (*desanā*), that too is included within "emergence" itself.

And "not being oppressed by defilements" means not being oppressed by evil states such as anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, aggression, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, and negligence; what is meant is the non-arising of these.

The connection is: "That which is called the morality of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*). Regarding the phrase "the eighty-two duties of the Khandhakas and the fourteen kinds of great duties (*mahāvatta*)," here the "great duties" refers to the fourteen duties taught in the Khandhaka section on Duties (*Vattakkhandhaka*):

the duty for newcomers, the duty for residents, the duty for those departing, the duty of thanksgiving, the duty regarding the meal-hall, the duty for those going on alms-round, the duty for forest-dwellers, the duty for those using the bathhouse, the duty for those using the restroom, the duty for preceptors, the duty for co-resident pupils, the duty for teachers, and the duty for resident students.
Other than these, however, there are duties that must be practiced only at certain times, such as when a formal act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*) has been performed.
The eighty-two *khaṇḍaka-vattas* are not to be practiced in all circumstances; therefore, they are not included among the *mahāvattas*.
Therein, beginning with the words, "I shall prescribe the duties for monks who are on probation (*pārivāsika*)," there are sixty-six duties stated as: "One should not confer full ordination...
[and so on] ...one should not walk on a walking-path while those walking on the ground are walking. Beyond that—

“Monks, a monk who is on probation (pārivāsika) should not dwell under one roof in a residence with a monk who is senior to him in the duration of his probation, nor with a monk who is subject to sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), nor with a monk who is subject to the trial period (mānattāraha), nor with a monk who is undergoing the trial period (mānattacārika), nor with a monk who is subject to rehabilitation (abbhānāraha).

Since these [offenses] are stated in such passages as these, they are not counted separately because they are not distinct from those [rules] to be observed by one in good standing (pakatatta). Among those such as the one senior in probation...
Because they are to be practiced toward other persons, when condensed according to those persons and calculated by making each one a single unit, there are seventy-one rules (vatta).
Regarding the rules for those subjected to an act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma), it is stated under the heading of the establishment of the rules: "One must not accept the salutation... [etc. ...
nor the back-massage from a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu during bathing. This refers to the salutations and so forth.
There is one on non-acceptance, and ten beginning with “A regular bhikkhu must not be accused of failure in virtue,” making eighty-two in total.
Among these, some are rules for formal acts such as the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*), while others are rules for those undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*);
thus, by including all that has been mentioned, there are exactly eighty-two. However, in other places, according to the *Aṭṭhakathā*, there may be slight deficiencies or excesses.
Or, because it does not fall under the category of counting, it is called "the eighty khandhaka-vattas. Regarding the term *ābhisamācārika-sīla*:
here, *abhisamācāra* means "excellent conduct"; *ābhisamācārika* is that which is itself excellent conduct, or that which is prescribed with reference to excellent conduct;
and that very thing being virtue (*sīla*), it is called *ābhisamācārika-sīla*. [This refers to] that which is included within the khandhaka-vattas...
This is a designation for virtue (*sīla*). In such passages as "I guard virtue;

what is the use of the *ābhisamācārika* [virtue]?", "virtue" should be understood as referring exclusively to that which is included within the two *Vibhaṅgas*, because that which is included within the *Khandhaka* observances is already covered by the term *ābhisamācārika*.
"Fulfills" means having made complete, or it has the sense of "having fulfilled."
"Beyond that" means after the purification of virtue as previously described. "Abode" refers to the impediment of an abode (*āvāsa-palibodha*).

The same method applies to "clan" (*kula*) and the other terms as well. In this context, "abode" may refer to even a single room, a single courtyard (*pariveṇa*), or an entire monastic complex (*saṅghārāma*).
This, however, is not an impediment for everyone; rather, it becomes an impediment for one who falls into zeal for building works and the like within it.
Or if there is a great accumulation of goods, or for whatever reason he has expectations and a mind bound by attachment, that itself becomes an impediment for him, and not for the other.

"Family" means either a family of kinsmen or a family of supporters; for some, even a family of supporters [becomes an impediment] through such thoughts as, "When they are happy, I am happy," and so forth.
For one who dwells in close association with householders according to worldly custom, there is an impediment;

such a person does not go even to a neighboring monastery to hear the Dhamma without his family members. For some, however, even parents do not constitute an impediment, as was the case for the young bhikkhu, the nephew of the elder residing at Koraṇḍaka Vihāra.
"Gains" refers to the four requisites. How do these become obstacles? For when a meritorious bhikkhu goes from place to place, people provide him with requisites along with a large retinue;
as he expresses his thanks to them and teaches the Dhamma, he finds no opportunity to practice the ascetic life.
From dawn until the first watch of the night, there is constant contact with people.

It is interrupted; yet again, at the very time of the strong dawn, alms-collectors who live in abundance arrive and say, "Venerable sir, such-and-such a lay follower, a female lay follower, a minister, or a minister’s daughter wish to see you.
He thinks, "Take the bowl and robes, friends," and is ready to go; he is constantly busy, and these very requisites become obstacles for him.
[They] exist. Therefore, having abandoned the group, he should wander alone in a place where they do not know him;
in this way, that impediment is severed.
"Group" means a group of Suttantikas or a group of Abhidhammikas. [It refers to] whoever [gives] him a recitation or an interrogation.
If he gives [himself] over to the duties of a recluse, he finds no opportunity; thus, the group becomes an impediment for him.
He should sever that connection in this way: if those monks have done much and little remains, he should finish it and then enter the forest.
If they have done little and much remains, he should not go more than a league away, but within the limit of one league—
One should approach another leader of a group and say, "Venerable sir, please look after these people with recitations and so forth.

If one still does not obtain this, one should leave the group, saying, "Friends, I have a certain task to attend to; you may go to whatever places are convenient for you," and then perform one's own duty.
"By work" means by the obstruction of work (*kamma-palibodha*). There is also a reading: "And work is the fifth. In that context, "work" refers to new construction (*navakamma*).
One who performs it must know what has been obtained or not obtained from carpenters and others; he must exert himself regarding what has been done and what remains to be done.
Thus, in every respect, it is an obstruction. It should be severed in this way: if only a little remains, [it may be abandoned].
It must be completed. If it is extensive and belongs to the Saṅgha, the new construction work must be handed over to the Saṅgha or to monks who are capable of carrying the burden.
If it belongs to oneself, it must be handed over to those capable of carrying one's own burden.
If such persons cannot be found, one should relinquish it to the Saṅgha and depart.

"Journeying" means traveling on a road. For one who is seeking ordination somewhere, or for whom some requisite is to be obtained—if, failing to obtain it, he is unable to endure [the delay]—then even for one who has entered the forest and is practicing the duty of a recluse, the "mind of one going away" is difficult to dispel; therefore, having gone...
Only after completing that duty should one exert oneself in the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).

"Relatives" refers to those in the monastery—such as preceptors (*ācariya*), teachers (*upajjhāya*), co-residents (*saddhivihārika*), pupils (*antevāsika*), those with the same preceptor, and those with the same teacher—as well as those at home, such as mother, father, and brothers.
When they are ill, they become an obstacle (*palibodha*) for him; therefore, that is an obstacle.

Having attended to them, [the duty] should be terminated by restoring them to their normal state. In this regard, first, if a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) who is ill does not recover quickly, he must be nursed for as long as he lives;

likewise for the teacher of the going-forth (*pabbajjācariya*), the teacher of full ordination (*upasampadācariya*), a co-resident student (*saddhivihārika*), a pupil ordained or gone-forth under one’s care (*antevāsika*), those with the same preceptor, the teacher of dependence (*nissayācariya*), the teacher of recitation (*uddesācariya*), the pupil dependent on one, the pupil receiving instruction, and those with the same teacher.

However, they must be looked after for as long as the period of dependence (*nissaya*) and instruction (*uddesa*) have not been terminated. Even beyond that, one who is able must continue to look after them.
One should look after one's mother and father just as one would an *upajjhāya*.
For even if they are established in royalty and expect service from their son, it must certainly be performed. Now, regarding their medicine:
If [the brother or sister] has nothing, one’s own property should be given. If that is lacking, it should certainly be given after seeking it through wandering for alms.
However, in the case of brothers and sisters, one should give only after setting aside what belongs to them. If they have nothing, one may lend one’s own property temporarily;
if it is later recovered, it should be taken back, but if it is not recovered, they should not be pressured. [This applies] to one who is unrelated.
It is not permissible for a sister to prepare medicine for her husband’s sake, nor to give it to him;
however, she may give it to him after saying, "Give this to your husband. The same rule applies to a brother's wife as well.
But since their children are indeed his own relatives, it is permissible for him to prepare medicine for them.
“Sickness” refers to any kind of disease. When it afflicts one, it becomes an impediment; therefore, it should be severed by administering medicine.
However, if it does not subside even after taking medicine for several days, one should reproach one’s own person, thinking:
“I am not your slave, nor your hireling; yet while supporting you in this way, I have fallen into suffering throughout the beginningless round of saṃsāra.”
The duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) must be performed.
"The book" refers to the preservation of the scriptures (pariyatti). That is an impediment only for one who is constantly occupied with recitation and so forth, not for another.

"By means of psychic power" means by way of the impediment of psychic power (iddhipalibodha). There is also a reading: "‘Psychic power’ refers to those ten [bases]. In that context, "psychic power" refers to that of worldlings (pothujjanika).
Supernormal power (*iddhi*). For this is difficult to manage like a child lying on its back or like young grain; it is broken by even a slight [distraction].
Moreover, it is an impediment to insight (*vipassanā*), but not to concentration (*samādhi*), because concentration is to be attained after reaching concentration itself.
Therefore, one who seeks insight must sever the impediment of supernormal power, while for others it remains as it is. [This concludes] the cultivation of the meditation subject.
It is called a *palibodha* because it binds (*paribandheti*), obstructs (*uparodheti*), and does not allow [the mind] to proceed;

the letter *r* has been changed to *l* in this expression, and its meaning is "obstacle" (*paripantha*). It is "to be cut off" (*upacchinditabba*) means it must be restrained through attainment (*samāpatti*) and inclusion (*saṅgahaṇa*);
the meaning is that it must be made free from obstruction (*apalibodha*).
One who is devoted to a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is a *kammaṭṭhānika*; one who is intent upon mental development (*bhāvanā*).
By that *kammaṭṭhānika*. "Having delimited" means having delimited them thus: "all the bhikkhus in this monastery. "Of those living together" means of the bhikkhus living together.
"He generates a gentle state of mind" means he produces a gentle state of mind within himself. And this [is] for those living together...

The purpose of generating gentleness of mind and so forth is to be illustrated by the Discourse on the Benefits of Loving-kindness (*mettānisaṃsasutta*), which proceeds in the manner beginning with, "He becomes dear to human beings.
"He is not of shrinking disposition" means that he is not one whose conduct is retracted from right practice, nor one of inferior energy; the meaning is that he is one who has aroused energy.
The intention is that this applies even to divine objects, let alone others. "In all respects" means in every way.

"In what is to be done by a recluse" (samaṇakaraṇīye) means either in all applications of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). "Should be attended to" (atthayitabbaṃ) means it should be attended to by way of prior cultivation.
"Application to yoga" (yogānuyoga) is the engagement in the development of yoga; that itself is "work" (kamma) in the sense of being something to be done.
"Because it is the proximate cause" (padaṭṭhānattā) means because it is the cause for its accomplishment.
Having included the light-kasiṇa within the white-kasiṇa, and the limited-space-kasiṇa within the space-kasiṇa derived from the removal of the kasiṇa disk,
[the commentary]— since the text explicitly mentions only eight kasiṇas, such as the earth-kasiṇa and others, which have material jhāna as their object—
excludes both the space-kasiṇa and the light-kasiṇa, following the method stated in the text: "among the thirty-eight objects."
Thus it was said. According to the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, when the space-kasiṇa and the light-kasiṇa are taken separately, there are exactly forty meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Among these, the forty meditation subjects are as follows: ten kasiṇas, ten foulness subjects (*asubha*), ten recollections (*anussati*), four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), four formless attainments (*āruppa*), one perception (*saññā*), and one analysis (*vavatthāna*).

In that regard, the ten *kasiṇas* are: the earth-*kasiṇa*, water-*kasiṇa*, fire-*kasiṇa*, air-*kasiṇa*, blue-*kasiṇa*, yellow-*kasiṇa*, red-*kasiṇa*, white-*kasiṇa*, light-*kasiṇa*, and the limited-space-*kasiṇa*. [The ten foulness objects are:
the bloated, the livid, the festering, the fissured, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the mutilated and scattered, ... [the bleeding].
The bloated, the festering, and the skeletal—these are the ten foulnesses (*asubha*).

The recollection of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, the deities, death, mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of breathing, and the recollection of peace—these are the ten recollections (*anussati*).
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—these are the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). The base of infinite space...
The base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these are the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
The perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is one perception. The analysis of the four elements is one analysis.

Regarding the phrase "whatever is suitable to one's temperament": first, for one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*), there are the ten foulness meditations and mindfulness occupied with the body, making eleven.
The meditation subjects suitable for those of a hateful temperament are eight: the four divine abidings and the four colored kasiṇas;
for those of a deluded temperament and those of a discursive temperament, there is only the single meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing;
for those of a faithful temperament, the first six recollections; and for those of an intellectual temperament, mindfulness of death, the recollection of peace, and the analysis of the four elements.
The perception of repulsiveness in food consists of four [meditation subjects]. The remaining kasiṇas and the four formless attainments (āruppa) are suitable for all temperaments (carita).

Among the kasiṇas, it should be understood that any limited (paritta) one is suitable for one whose temperament is characterized by applied thought (vitakkacarita), while an immeasurable (appamāṇa) one is suitable for one whose temperament is characterized by delusion (mohacarita).
The phrase "by the method already stated" refers to the meaning: "because they are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the practice of yoga."

Regarding the statement, "By means of this very meditation subject... it should be learned," it is said that one who desires to take up a particular meditation subject should, by means of that very subject, develop the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, and having increased insight which has jhāna as its proximate cause, learn it in the presence of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and who has attained the destruction of the taints.
The phrase "for the Arahants, etc. refers to those among the khīṇāsavas who have reached a certain stage.
This was undertaken to show that one who is well-versed in the scriptures is superior in the giving of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Like one leading out a great elephant's path" means as if showing the ground of the meditation subject by making it like a great elephant's track.

"Having delimited what is suitable and what is unsuitable" means having determined, through the investigation of reasoning, whether a particular meditation subject is beneficial or not beneficial for the person to whom it is being explained.

Now, one going to the presence of the giver of the meditation subject should not go with feet washed and rubbed, nor wearing sandals, nor carrying a sunshade, nor having oil-tubes, honey, molasses, and so forth carried for him, nor surrounded by a retinue of pupils.
Rather, having fulfilled the duties of one setting out on a journey, he should take his own bowl and robes himself; and along the way, whatever...

He enters the monastery; at all times when entering, he fulfills the duties of a guest, and at the time of departing, the duties of one going away—thus, by showing this meaning in brief, [the text says]: "one who lives with few possessions and is endowed with the conduct prescribed by the Vinaya.
One should go about with very light requisites, living a life of supreme austerity.
He said: "But having gone thus, one entering that monastery must, while still on the way, have a tooth-stick made allowable and take it with him before entering;

he must not enter another cell to rest for a moment, wash his feet, apply ointments, or the like, thinking, 'I will go to the presence of the teacher. Why? Because if, while he is there, the teacher..."

The monks there might be of a different disposition; having asked the reason for his coming and proclaimed dispraise of the teacher, they might cause him remorse by saying, "You are ruined if you have come into his presence," whereby he would turn back from that very spot.
Therefore, having asked for the teacher’s dwelling place, one should go straight there.
Regarding the teacher of the kind described:
“He is dear, venerable, and inspiring; he instructs and is patient with what is said;
he delivers profound discourse and does not urge one toward what is improper.”

A "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*) teacher is one who possesses the aforementioned qualities such as faith, who is solely intent on others' welfare, and who stands on the side of progress. Regarding the phrase "having pleased the mind through the performance of duties":
if the teacher is younger, one should not accept his bowl or robes and so forth; if he is older, having approached the teacher...
One should stand after having paid homage. When told, "Friend, set aside your bowl and robe," they should set them aside.
When told, "Drink some water," they may drink it if they wish. When told, "Wash your feet," they should not wash them yet;
for if the water had been brought by the teacher himself, it would not be appropriate. [If told,] "Wash them, friend, it was not brought by me..."
However, when it is said, "brought by others," one should wash the feet while sitting in a concealed place where the teacher cannot see, or even at the edge of an open-air dwelling.
If the teacher brings the oil tube, one should stand up and receive it respectfully with both hands. For if one were not to receive it, [the teacher might think]: "This..."
If the teacher were to think, "From this moment on, the bhikkhu is breaking off our communion," it would cause a change in his disposition.
Therefore, when taking [the oil], one should not first smear the feet. For if that were the teacher’s body-anointing oil, it would be improper;
thus, having first smeared the head, the shoulders and other parts should then be smeared. [One should consider: "This is oil for all purposes."
When told, "Friend, rub my feet," he should rub them; then, saying, "Venerable sir, I am setting down this oil tube," he should hand it over when the teacher takes it.
From the day he has departed, he must not say, "Venerable sir, please teach me the meditation subject. This [rule] applies from the second day onward.
From that point on, if the teacher has a regular attendant, one should perform the duties after requesting him;
if he does not grant permission even when requested, they should be performed as soon as an opportunity arises.
While performing them, three types of tooth-sticks—small, medium, and large—should be offered. Likewise, two kinds of water for rinsing the mouth and bathing—cold and warm—should be provided.
It should be prepared. Then, exactly the same kind of food as that which the teacher consumes for three days must be constantly provided;
or, for one who consumes whatever is available without restriction, whatever is obtained should be offered to him. What is the use of saying more?
As it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, a resident pupil should conduct himself properly toward his teacher."

In this regard, the proper conduct is as follows: having risen early, removing one's sandals, arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, one should provide a tooth-stick, provide water for rinsing the mouth, and prepare a seat.
If there is rice-gruel, one should wash the vessel and offer the gruel. This and other such rules of conduct prescribed in the Khandhaka have been laid down.
Everything should be done. Thus, it should be understood that one who practices according to the method just described delights the mind with the performance of duties (*vatta*).
"Five-jointed" means having five sections; the meaning is "five parts. "The learning of the meditation subject" refers to the manual of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānagandha*).

"Acquisition" (uggaha) is the learning of the meditation subject; "inquiry" (paripucchā) is the questioning regarding its meaning. Alternatively, "acquisition" is the learning of the meditation subject both from the text and from the meaning, while "inquiry" is the questioning about doubts therein.
"Appearance of the meditation subject" refers to the appearance of the sign (*nimitta*); thus, for one who is devoted to development, [it is the realization]: "In this way, this sign appears."
Sustained bearing; likewise, the absorption of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhānappanā) is described as "thus one enters jhāna.
The characteristic of the meditation subject is the perfection of establishing [the mind] after having intensified its cultivation by means of counting, following, and touching;
or else, it is the discernment of the essential nature of the meditation subject, which is the reaching of the summit by means of discerning and so forth beyond that point.
Therefore he said: "It means 'the upholding of the intrinsic nature of the meditation subject.
One does not weary oneself because one learns the meditation subject specifically;

for that very reason, one does not trouble the teacher, since one brings the practice of the Dharma to its ultimate consummation through development. "Therefore" means for that purpose, by way of not wearying oneself and not troubling the teacher.

"Little by little" means in small increments. "There" means where the teacher dwells. "It is suitable" means that through obtaining what is suitable for the dwelling and so forth, there is ease of attention and conformity to meditation.
By the phrase "at most a league," a distance of four *gāvutas* or two-and-a-half leagues (*aḍḍhayojana*) is also included.
For one of duller wisdom, even while living at a distance of four *gāvutas*, two-and-a-half leagues, or a single league, [the meditation subject]...
If, at any point, doubt or forgetfulness should arise regarding mindfulness, one should perform the duties of the monastery early in the morning,
wander for alms along the way, and upon the conclusion of the meal, go to the teacher’s dwelling.
Having clarified the meditation subject in the presence of the teacher that day, one should pay homage to the teacher on the following day and depart.
Having wandered for alms along the way, he will be able to reach his own dwelling place without even becoming weary;

therefore it is said, "one of dull wisdom, having gone at most a league. If one of keen wisdom does not find a comfortable place within that league, he should, by means of that [journey], cut through every knot in the meditation subject and become purified, being bound to the act of adverting.
Having made a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), it is permissible to go even as far as a league; thus he said, "one of sharp wisdom, having gone even a long distance.

"Free from the eighteen faults of a lodging" refers to: greatness, newness, dilapidation, proximity to a road, a drain, leaves, flowers, fruits, desirability, proximity to a city, and proximity to timber.

It is free from these eighteen faults of lodgings: dependence on fields, the presence of persons of a different class, dependence on a town, dependence on a border region, dependence on a royal boundary, unsuitability, and the lack of acquisition of good friends.
For a lodging possessed of any one of these eighteen faults is unsuitable for meditation.
Why? Because in the Mahāvihāra, many people with diverse inclinations assemble;
due to their mutual opposition, they do not perform the duties, so that the Bodhi-tree courtyard and other areas remain unswept, and drinking water and washing water are not set out.
Even one who has gone forth there, having taken up bowl and robe with the thought, "I will go for alms in the village for alms-food," [finds these conditions lacking].
If he sees that his duty has not been performed, such as the water-jar being empty, then he must perform that duty;
he must provide drinking water. If he does not do so, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of duty. If he performs it, the time passes;
having entered [the village] too late, he receives nothing once the alms-round is finished. Even when he has gone into seclusion, [he must attend to] the novices and junior monks...

One is distracted by loud noises and by formal acts of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*). However, one may dwell even in a great monastery where all the proper duties (*vatta*) are performed and there is no other disturbance.

In a new monastery, there is much building work; people complain if one does not participate. But one should dwell in a place where the monks say, "Venerable sir, please practice the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma*) as you wish; we shall do the building work. In such a place, one should reside.

In an old monastery, however, there is much that must be looked after; even those who do not look after their own individual lodging as little as possible are criticized. For one who does look after it, his meditation subject suffers decline.
In a large monastery situated on a main road, visitors gather day and night.
Having given one's own lodging to those who arrive at an improper time, one must live at the foot of a tree or on a stone slab; and on the following day as well...
In such a case, there is no opportunity for the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). However, one should dwell where there is no such crowding of visitors.
A "soṇḍī" is a stone lotus-pool. There, the great multitude gathers for the purpose of drinking water;
the disciples of the resident monks who are supported by the royal family come there to do dyeing work, bringing with them their vessels, wooden troughs, and so forth.
When people ask him, he must point out, "In such and such places. Thus, he is constantly occupied at all times.

Furthermore, in a place where there are various kinds of vegetable leaves, even when he has taken up his meditation subject and is sitting for his midday rest, women bringing vegetables may sing as they pick the leaves nearby; thus, the clash of these discordant sounds creates an obstacle to his meditation subject.
Furthermore, wherever there are various kinds of flowering creeper-groves in full bloom, there too is such a calamity.
Wherever there are various kinds of fruits such as mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits, those seeking fruit come and beg;
if one does not give, they become angry, or they take them by force. And while walking in the middle of the monastery at the time of evening, [one encounters this].
Seeing them, when asked, "Lay followers, why are you acting thus?", they reviled him as they pleased and even strove to drive him away.

But when people saw him dwelling in monasteries such as Dakkhiṇagiri, Hatthikucchi, Cetiyagiri, and Cittalapabbata— places highly desirable and esteemed by the world— they honored him, thinking, "This one is an Arahant," and flocked from all sides, desiring to pay him homage.
Therefore, he does not find comfort there. However, for one for whom it is suitable, he should go elsewhere during the day and stay there at night.
When staying near a city, discordant objects enter the range of perception: even water-carriers pass by clashing their jars together;
they descend [into the road] and do not yield the way; and even persons of high status sit in the middle of the monastery, having screened themselves with a cloth curtain.

Regarding dependence on timber: where there are logs and trees suitable for building materials, wood-gatherers cause inconvenience just as the gatherers of vegetables and flowers mentioned previously do.
If there are trees in the monastery, people come and cut them down, thinking, "We will build houses by cutting these down. If, at the time of evening, one has gone out from the meditation hall...
While walking in the middle of the monastery, he saw them and asked, "Upāsakas, why are you doing this?
They reviled him as they pleased and even attempted to drive him out.
However, in a place situated near a field and surrounded on all sides by fields, people [behave] right there in the middle of the monastery.
Having threshed the grain, they trample it; they sleep in prominent positions and cause many other inconveniences as well.
Even where there is great property belonging to the Saṅgha, they block the cattle of the monastery attendants' families and obstruct the water supply.
Taking ears of rice, people show them to the Saṅgha, saying, "Look at the work of your monastery attendants' families!"
For various reasons, one must go to the doorways of kings, royal ministers, and great officials; this too is included under the heading of "dependence on fields.
Furthermore, there are places where monks who are mutually incompatible and hostile dwell together;
when they engage in quarrels and are being restrained with the words, "Venerable sirs, do not do this," they say, "Ever since this refuse-rag wearer arrived, we have been ruined."

Furthermore, if it is situated near a port on the water or a port on land, people arriving frequently by ship or caravan there cause disturbance and discomfort, clamoring, "Give us space! Give us water! Give us salt!
However, if it is situated near a border region, the people have little faith in the Buddha and the others.
If it is situated near a frontier between kingdoms, there is fear of kings; for one king thinks of that territory, "It does not remain under my control."

It strikes; the other also thinks, "He does not remain under my control. In this regard, this bhikkhu sometimes wanders in the realm of this king and sometimes in that of another; then, thinking "This is a spy," they bring him to ruin and disaster.
"Unsuitability" means unsuitability due to the convergence of discordant objects such as visible forms, or because of being possessed by non-human beings.
This is the story: It is said that a certain elder lived in the forest. Then a certain female spirit (yakkhinī) stood at the door of his leaf-hut and sang.
He went out and stood at the door; she went to the head of the walkway and sang. The elder went to the head of the walkway;
she stood on a precipice a hundred fathoms deep and sang. The elder turned back, and then she [rushed] toward him with speed.
Having gone and seized him, he said, "Venerable sir, it was not just one or two like you that I have devoured.

Where it is impossible to find a teacher or one equal to a teacher, a preceptor or one equal to a preceptor, or a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta), there this lack of spiritual friends is indeed a great fault. Therefore, of these...
A lodging possessed of any one of these eighteen faults should be understood as unsuitable for meditation.
And this has been said in the Commentaries:
"A large dwelling, a new dwelling, an old dwelling, and one on a main road;..."
The trunk, the leaf, the flower, and the fruit that has been desired.
A city made of wood, a field, a port with dissimilar [inhabitants],
and a border region where no suitable friend is found.
“Having understood these eighteen points, a wise person should avoid them from afar, just as one would a path beset with dangers.

Endowed with the five factors of a lodging means being endowed with the five factors of a lodging, such as not being too far from nor too near a village, and so forth. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“And how, bhikkhus, is a lodging endowed with five factors? Here, bhikkhus, a lodging is not too far and not too near, which has a good path for coming and going;
it is little frequented by day, with little noise and little clamor at night;
it is free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping things. And in that lodging...”
While he dwells there, robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick arise for him without difficulty.
Furthermore, in that monastery dwell elder bhikkhus who are learned, of inherited knowledge, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā;
having approached them from time to time, he questions and inquires: "This..."

“Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this? Then those venerable ones reveal what was undisclosed to him, clarify what was not made clear, and dispel his doubt regarding various points that might give rise to uncertainty.
“In this way, monks, a lodging is endowed with five factors.”
And herein, "not too far, not too near, and convenient for coming and going" constitutes one factor;
"little crowded by day, with little noise and little clamor at night" constitutes one; "free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping things" constitutes one;
"for one dwelling in that lodging... [and] the requisites" constitutes one; and in that regard... [the rest].
"The elders [resolve their doubts] regarding the lodging... [etc.]... thus they dispel doubt"—this is one [factor]. In this way, the five factors are to be understood.

Regarding the phrase "by cutting off the minor impediments": here, by one who cuts off the minor impediments, the long hair of the head, nails, and body-hair must be shorn; and in the case of worn-out robes, strengthening work must be done by means of patching, darning, and so forth.
Or he should perform needlework, such as mending threads, or dye dirty garments.
If there is grime on the bowl, the bowl should be cleaned; beds, chairs, and so forth should be swept.
"Having dispelled the drowsiness caused by food" means having removed the fatigue resulting from eating; for as soon as food has entered the stomach, it acts as a foreign substance.
For there might generally be some fatigue of the body; having allayed that, [one should proceed], for if it were not allayed, the mind would not attain one-pointedness due to bodily exhaustion.
It is called "learning" (*uggaha*) because it is to be learned; it refers to the entire method of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), not merely the learning mentioned previously.
"Learning from a teacher" (*ācariyuggaha*) means learning from a teacher; from that [source]. "Even a single word" (*ekapadam-pi*) means even a single portion.
"Following" (*anubandhanā*) means the continuous proceeding of mindfulness by way of following after the in-breaths and out-breaths.

"Touching" (*phusanā*) refers to their touching the location of the tip of the nose and so forth, for one who has withdrawn the counting while counting the in-breaths and out-breaths, and who places the mind in such a way that absorption (*appanā*) occurs as they follow them with mindfulness. Furthermore, because...
There is no separate mental attention (manasikāra) by way of contact and so forth as there is by way of counting and so forth;
rather, it is shown that counting should be performed only at the very place touched. Demonstrating this by stating "contact is the place touched," he said: "Contact is the place touched.
"Fixing" (ṭhapanā) means stabilization. For that is the proper placing or fixing of the mind upon the object.
For concentration is defined as "the steadiness and stability of the mind. Since absorption (*appanā*) has concentration as its dominant factor, it is said:
"Establishing is absorption. Insight (*vipassanā*) is "clear observation" because it clearly observes impermanence and so forth.

The Path (*magga*) is "turning away" because it turns away from both the occurrence [of defilements] and the sign [of the object]. It is so called because of the state of the complete subsiding of all defilements.
"Complete purity" (*sabbaso suddhi*) refers to the fruit of purification (*pārisuddhi-phala*). "Of these" (*tesam*) refers to the purifications of turning away (*vivaṭṭanā-pārisuddhi*).
"Contemplation" (*paṭipassanā*) means seeing again and again, looking closely; thus he said "reviewing" (*paccavekkhaṇā*).
"Fragment" (*khaṇḍa*) refers to the breaking up by way of counting, such as one, three, five, and so forth. He says "in a place" (*okāse*) with reference to the method of counting.
This refers to one who relies on counting rather than on the meditation subject itself. The phrase "Has it reached the peak?
is said with reference to one who attends to the counting for a longer period; for such a person might think so based merely on the non-distraction he has attained in that way.
The phrase "taking that which appears among the in-breaths and out-breaths" refers to whichever [breath] appears among the in-breaths and out-breaths.
It is said with reference to that which appears first as the one [breath]. However, for one to whom both appear, both should be taken and counted.

Furthermore, by the phrase "whichever appears," it should be understood that this also indicates the meaning that whichever of the two nostril-winds is more manifest should be taken. "As it occurs, as it occurs" means...
By means of the repeated word, he shows the continuous discernment (*upalakkhaṇa*) of the inhalations and exhalations.

The meaning is: "having discerned them in the manner thus described. He says, "the inhalations and exhalations become manifest," because even when they appear one by one at first, for one who counts after having discerned them, both eventually become clear. By that, [he indicates] "only after discerning them..."
Regarding the phrase "it should be counted," this statement—"for one counting in this way... they become clear"—should be understood as the explanatory reason (*kāraṇavacana*).
In that context, "they become clear" means that by means of counting, they become distinct due to the absence of distraction toward external objects.

The "threshold pillar" (*palighatthambha*) is the pillar at which they place the crossbar (*paligha*) for turning back. "For three nights and days" (*tiyāmarattiṃ*) denotes continuous duration (*accantasamyoga*).

This is the statement on the method of application. "By the previous method" means by rapid counting; the meaning is "by the cowherd’s method. The sequence "one, two, three, four, five" is the demonstration of the procedure for counting.
Therefore, even in cases such as "eight," and so forth, one must reach each number—eight and the rest—starting from one.
Having stated, "It must be counted very rapidly indeed," the reason and illustration for this are given.
He shows this by the words beginning with “in that which is bound to counting,” and so forth. In that context, *aritta* is that by which one steers;
it is the steering oar (*pājanadaṇḍo*). Support by means of the oar is *arittūpatthambhana*; it is by way of that [support].
Since, in the non-figurative sense, uninterrupted occurrence belongs only to the stage of *ṭhapanā* (establishment), he said, “as if occurring uninterruptedly.”
By attending to it as it enters within, one is said to cause the mind to enter within. The same method applies when withdrawing the mind from outside.
"Struck by the wind" means that for one who attends extensively to the wind gone inside, that place appears as if struck by the wind and as if filled with fat;
it manifests in that way. "Withdrawing" refers to the area touched [by the breath].

[This refers to] one who releases [the breath] and draws it out. However, as the mind wanders among various objects by way of following the course of the wind as it is drawn out in that manner, he said: "The mind is distracted by a multiplicity of objects.
"This" refers to this set of inhalations and exhalations. "Following" means by way of making the inhalations and exhalations, as they occur, the object of attention.
It is the following along with mindfulness, the tracking after [the breath]. For this very reason it was said: “And that is by way of following the beginning, middle, and end.
The navel is the beginning because it is where [the breath] first arises there. For here, the consideration of the beginning is by way of its first arising, not merely by way of its occurrence.
For indeed, from the navel up to the tip of the nose, they arise everywhere. Wherever...

They arise and break up right there and then, because there is no movement of phenomena. However, the conventional term "going" (gati) is applied to their arrival at another location according to conditions.
"The heart is the middle" means that the region near the heart, specifically its upper part, is the middle.
"The tip of the nose is the end" means that the location of the nose is the end of the in-breaths and out-breaths.

Because that [limit] serves as the boundary for the conventional designation (*samaññā*). For these [breaths] are described as mind-originated (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*), and there is no occurrence of mind-originated phenomena outside [the body].
Therefore he said: "The tip of the nose, etc., for the wind entering within.

It should be understood, however, that the manner of entering and exiting is stated merely by way of similarity to that [wind]. "Distracted" (*vikkhepagata*) means having approached distraction; it is distracted (*vikkhitta*).

The meaning is "unconcentrated. "Of one who is agitated" means because of a state of agitation (*sadaratha*). "For the sake of wavering" means for the wavering of attention toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"By a mind that has reached distraction": the instrumental case is used here either to express the cause or as a characteristic mark of the state attained.
"Agitated" means full of longing. "Wavering" means those who waver, those who move; likewise, "quivering."
“By way of the beginning, middle, and end” means that it should not be brought to mind by way of following the beginning, middle, and end;

this is the connection. To explain the intention behind the statement, “One who brings it to mind by way of following should bring it to mind by way of touching and by way of fixing,” he said, “Just as in the case of following by counting,” and so forth. Therein:
"There is no separate attention" means that there is no attention to the meditation subject by way of mere touching and placing in their respective order, without counting and following.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, just as there is no attention by way of placing without touching, there is likewise no attention by way of counting without touching? [Reply: Even if there is none, counting nevertheless—just as...
Because attention to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-manasikāra*) is its root, it should be grasped as the primary factor;
thus, following [the breath] is the basis for fixing [the mind], since fixing is impossible without it.

Therefore, even though there is no immediate proximity in the case of touching, he says—showing that the others are absent because counting and following are the primary factors due to their being the root—"by way of counting and following..."
"For there is no separate attention by way of touching and placing, as it were.
If this is so, why are they taken separately in the summary (uddesa)? He says: "Only at the place touched," and so forth.
Therein, by the phrase "counting only at the place touched," he shows that touching is a factor of counting. Therefore he said: "By counting and by touching..."
"And he brings it to mind. "Right there" means right at the very place touched [by the breath].
"Following them with mindfulness" means following the method of counting and binding them with mindfulness; the meaning is that he examines them continuously right at the location touched.
"Fixing the mind by way of absorption" means fixing it in such a way that absorption occurs, according to how it has been established.
"Fixing the mind on the sign" means concentrating it. Regarding the phrases "by way of following," etc., the construction is:
"one attends by way of following, by way of touching, and by way of fixing. This is the meaning:
that which was stated as, "counting only at each point touched, withdrawing the counting right there, and following those [breaths] with mindfulness"—that is this meaning.
That which does not measure and does not determine absolutely is "near to conceit" (*mānassa samīpa*); this is an analogy such as "a *gavaya* is like a cow.
"Lame" (*paṅgula*) means one who is a cripple. "Swing" (*dola*) means a swing. "Of those playing" (*kīḷatan-ti*) means of those who are playing.
"Of mother and son" (*mātāputtānan-ti*) means of one's own wife and son. "Both ends" (*ubho koṭiyo*) refers to the front end for one coming toward [the swing] and the back end for one going away.
"Two ends" refers to the two extremities. "The middle" means the middle of the swing-board itself. "Like a supporting pillar" means like a pillar used for support;
it refers to the tip of the nose or the point of the mouth. Having stood near its base—that is, in its vicinity—how does one stand?
By means of mindfulness (*sati*). For the practitioner of yoga stands there, establishing mindfulness well upon that object.

It is called by the name [of its parts] because the whole must be designated by means of the properties of its components. "In the sign" (*nimitta*) means in the sign of the tip of the nose and so forth.
"Seated with mindfulness" (*satiyā nisinno*) means sitting by way of mindfulness. For it should be stated as in the passage beginning, "For mindfulness is there," just as in the case of a place.
"There" (*tattha*) means at the place touched. "Those" (*te*) refers to the people who have gone inside and outside the city, and their gathering (*saṅgaha*).
"Come into one's hand": from the beginning means starting from the point where the meaning of the simile is shown.
In the verse, "the sign" (nimitta) refers to the sign for anchoring. "Not the object of a single consciousness" means it is not the object of one consciousness;
the sense is that they do not become objects. And "not knowing the three things" refers to the sign, the breath-in (assāsa), and [the breath-out].
"Exhalation": this refers to one who does not find these three things—the sign and so forth—as objects of focus.
The word *ca* (and) is used in the sense of exclusion. "Development" means the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).
"Is not obtained" means it is not found or does not succeed; such is the meaning of this verse of objection. The second verse, which provides the reply, is indeed easy to understand.
How is it that there is an inquiry out of a desire to speak in order to explain the meaning of those verses concerning the objection and its resolution?
Regarding the phrases beginning with "These three things," the explanation of the meaning together with the construction of the words is as follows:

how is it that these three things—namely, the sign and so forth—do not become the object of a single consciousness? And even if they do not possess the status of being objects, why is it that these three... [are not so]?
The phenomena (dhammas) are unknown; and how is it that they are not unknown? For if they were unknown, how could the mind avoid distraction?
And how could the exertion—the energy that brings about the development [of the path]—be manifested?
Furthermore, [how could there be] the application known as devotion to development, which truly brings about concentration and suppresses the hindrances?

"How does the yogī accomplish this? How does he attain successive distinctions, both mundane and supramundane?"—it is to establish this point by means of the simile of the saw that the passage beginning with "Just as" (*seyyathāpi*) was spoken.
For if a tree is unstable due to the unevenness of the ground, the act of cutting it would not be easy; and if that were the case, the movement of the teeth of the saw would be difficult to discern.
He said: "On a level patch of ground. "With a saw" means with a small, coarse-toothed blade. Therefore he said: "A man.
"By way of the teeth of the saw that have been touched" means by way of those teeth of the saw that have repeatedly come into contact.

By this, he shows that mindfulness is established for the man only at those very places touched by the teeth of the saw. Therefore he said: "He does not attend to the teeth of the saw as they come or go."
When the saw is being pulled toward the man, the teeth are said to have "come" as they proceed facing him; when it is being pushed away, they are said to have "gone" as they depart from there.
Yet, neither the coming nor the going of the saw-teeth remains unnoticed, because mindfulness is established at all times;
for there is no absence of saw-teeth as they move forward and backward, since they do not fail to touch the place where the wood is to be cut.

"Exertion" (*padhāna*) is the effort of cutting down a tree. "Application" (*payoga*) is the act of cutting that very tree. In this simile, the phrase "he attains distinction" (*visesam adhigacchati*) does not appear in the canonical text (*pāḷi*);
however, it should be supplied and explained. For this very reason, in the *Visuddhimagga*, even within the simile, the phrase "he attains distinction" is stated by way of such a supply.
And in its commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*), it says: "'Distinction' means the attainment of various states; and by that..."
The meaning stated is: "the specific purpose to be accomplished. The passage beginning with "Just as a tree...
is the correlation of the simile. It is called *upanibandhanā* (binding) because by means of it the mind is bound to the object;
thus, it is the sign for the observation of the in-breaths and out-breaths, which is the sign of binding (*upanibandhanānimitta*), namely, the tip of the nose.

Or for the sake of the face. "In this very way" means: just as that man, while cutting a tree with a saw, even though he does not attend to the teeth of the saw as they pass back and forth, knows the teeth of the saw as they come and go by establishing mindfulness precisely on the points where they touch, and thus, without missing a single thread of the line, accomplishes his purpose—just so [it is]. On the tip of the nose.

"By means of the sign of the mouth": for one with a long nose, [it refers to] the upper lip, which has received the name "sign of the mouth" because the mouth—the act of eating—is covered or closed by it.
"This is the exertion": by means of this application of energy, the body and mind of the practitioner who has initiated energy become pliant.
"It becomes capable of the work of meditation and fit for the work of meditation" means that this energy is the "exertion"; thus, he shows the cause by means of its fruit.
"The defilements are abandoned" means that the hindrances, which are the defilements of the mind, are abandoned by way of suppression.
"Thoughts are stilled" means that, for that very reason, wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth are brought to pacification.

They proceed; or, having shown the attainment of the first jhāna through the abandoning of the hindrances, he speaks of the attainment of the second jhāna and the others by means of the subsiding of applied thought (*vitakka*).
"This is the application" (*ayaṃ payogo*): this engagement with the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), which serves as the cause for the attainment of jhāna, is the application.
"The fetters are abandoned": the ten fetters are abandoned by way of their total eradication according to the sequence of the paths.

They are abandoned. "The underlying tendencies (anusaya) come to an end" means that likewise, through the production of the state of non-arising, even the mere destruction of the seven underlying tendencies becomes entirely and completely gone. And here, the abandoning of the fetters (saṃyojana) occurs precisely through the cessation of the underlying tendencies;
furthermore, it is for the purpose of showing that once the fetters are abandoned, not even a trace of the underlying tendencies will remain, that [the text says] "fetters..."
"It is said: 'The underlying tendencies (anusaya) are abandoned and brought to an end. This is the distinction:

the meaning is that this sequence beginning with the abandoning of the fetters (saṃyojana), which is obtained gradually by relying on this concentration, is the specific excellence (visesa) of this concentration.
'Yassa' means 'by whom. 'Anupubbaṃ' means 'gradually. 'Paricitā' means 'cultivated. This, then, is the summary of the meaning here."
— Just as mindfulness of breathing was taught by the Buddha, the Blessed One, so too,
when it has been gradually cultivated and well-developed through the method beginning with long and short breaths, and thus fulfilled by the completion of the sixteen bases and entirely perfected,
that bhikkhu illuminates this world of his own aggregates and so forth with the radiance of wisdom. Just as...
What [is it like]? It is like the moon released from clouds; that is, like the moon, the king of stars, when freed from the defilements such as clouds.

For in the explanation of the phrase "like the moon released from clouds," since mist and so forth are also mentioned, it should be understood that the word "etc. (*ādi*) has been elided here. "Here" (*idha*) refers to the simile of the saw.
"His" (*assa*) refers to the practitioner (*yogī*). Alternatively, "here" (*idha*) means in this place, and "his" (*assa*) refers to that which serves as the simile.
