Of the saw. Just as that man had no further concern for the saw because of its coming and going, so too the purpose of bringing about the mere non-attention to the in-breaths and out-breaths by way of their coming and going is fulfilled.
"Not long thereafter" is said with reference to one who has performed the preliminary work.

"The sign" refers to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*). "Adorned with the remaining jhāna factors" means adorned with the remaining jhāna factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.
They say this; however, strictly speaking, one should say "sustained thought and so forth," because initial application (vitakka) lacks the state of absorption (appanā).

For in the Canon, it is defined as "absorption and directed application" (byappanā); or else, because of its association with that [initial application], the usage of the Commentary is that "jhāna is absorption.
Furthermore, among the factors of jhāna, concentration (samādhi) is predominant. Therefore, showing that it is absorption, [the text says]: "Adorned with the remaining jhāna-factors..."

"and the fixing known as absorption (appanā) is accomplished," he said. Regarding the phrase "for some, however, from the very time of attention by way of counting," here only this much of the text—"in due order...
like reaching [the goal]... as if it were a bowl"—has been lost;
yet in some old manuscripts, that passage remains written exactly as it was.
In some person whose body is agitated, it bends down due to the sagging of the waist-cloth and so forth. It "twists" means it makes a sound.
It "wrinkles" means it becomes wrinkled here and there. Why? Because one whose body is agitated is heavy.
The cessation of coarse inhalation and exhalation, which is accomplished together with the subsiding of bodily distress, is [explained] by way of contrast.
It is stated as if it were its proof. "By means of the cessation of gross in-breathing and out-breathing" refers to the proof of that meaning by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

When bodily agitation has subsided: the lightness, malleability, and wieldiness of the remaining material phenomena of the mental continuum—which arise from mind—are here intended as the "lightness of the body. This [lightness] occurs because of the lightness, etc., of the mind.
Without [the body], it does not exist; therefore it was said: "Both the body and the mind become light.

The passage beginning with "when the gross in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased" is introduced to show the method of investigating the bodily formation that has reached the stage of being analyzed according to the manner explained below.

"Becoming more and more manifest" means they become increasingly clear through the power of meditation. "From the location" means from the location of contact as it normally occurs, that is, from the place previously determined by one's own mode of contacting.

In order to clarify the meaning by combining together the investigation from the perspective of place—asking “Where is it not?”—and the investigation from the perspective of person—asking “For whom is it not?”—the passage beginning with “inside the mother’s womb” was stated.
Therein, “just as for one submerged in water the inhalations and exhalations do not occur because the space has ceased, so it is inside the mother’s womb; just as for the dead... [and so forth].

"Because of the absence of a motivating consciousness, [it does not arise] in those who have thus become unconscious, in those overcome by fainting, or in those born among the non-percipient beings, as well as in those who have attained the cessation attainment"—thus it was stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.

In the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*, however, the reason given is: "because of the feebleness of the activity of consciousness in those overcome by fainting. This applies to those who have attained the fourth jhāna.
Their non-arising occurs simply by way of natural law (*dhammatā*), as it does for those possessing existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms. Some, however, state the reason:

"Because of the attainment of subtlety through successive stages, for one who has entered the fourth jhāna, and because of the subtlety of both material phenomena and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) in the fine-material realm, there are no [breaths] for those possessing existence in the fine-material realm. Yet, those in-breaths and out-breaths do indeed exist.
"By way of elimination" (pārisesato) is the intended meaning; for there is no place outside the seven aforementioned locations where inhalation and exhalation could arise.
"By way of the natural point of contact" (pakatiphuṭṭhavasena) means by way of the location touched in the ordinary course.
"The sign should be established" means that a firmer mental mark (saññāṇa) should be produced by mindfulness so that it may proceed with ease therein. It is the basis for a firm perception.
"Indeed, it being so. "This very one" means the method of establishing this very bodily formation that has not yet been established, by way of extracting a thorn.
"The purpose" means the cause; for the effect is the purpose (*attha*), and that by virtue of which something proceeds is called the "purpose" (*atthavasa*).
"Of one who is unmindful" means of one whose mindfulness is destroyed. "Of one who lacks clear comprehension" means of one devoid of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).

The intention is that for one who lacks the mindfulness and wisdom capable of investigating the inhalations and exhalations as they fail to appear in succession during meditation—so as to determine "these are those" and to know them correctly—this is another meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Heavy" means burdensome. Its heaviness consists in the fact that its cultivation is extremely difficult; thus he says, "heavy cultivation."
Having stated that "mindfulness and wisdom must be powerful, very clear, and courageous" because they must reach a state of ever-increasing peace and subtlety, the passage beginning with "Just as...
was spoken to show that in order to accomplish a subtle object, one must also become subtle oneself.
Now, he shows the method for searching for the in-breaths and out-breaths when they are not appearing.
He said, “And by those,” and so forth. Therein, “step by step” (*anupada*) means following each word. “Having practiced” (*caritvā*) means having taken up the range of activity.
“In that very place” means in the place known as the sign for anchoring (*upanibandhananimitta*). “Having yoked” means having yoked it through mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Or, the phrase “having bound it with the rein of mindfulness” expresses the same meaning as “having yoked it in that very place. For indeed—

The points of application for the binding of the object of comparison (*upameyya*) are found separately. "The sign" (*nimitta*) refers either to the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*) or the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*);
both are stated here together. For while the three similes beginning with the tuft of cotton are applicable to the learning sign, the remainder applies to both.
"Some" (*ekacce*) refers to certain teachers.
"Like the form of a star" means like the radiant form of a star. Similes such as "a bead of crystal" and so forth apply to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga*).
But how is it that this single meditation subject appears in many forms? To answer this, he says: "And furthermore, this... and so on.
"Sutta" means a single discourse. He speaks thus with reference to its uninterrupted flow due to its state of being well-mastered, and its vast range of application.
“Like a great mountain river. In that regard, because of its perfection of phrasing, the discourse is entirely auspicious;
like a forest grove beautiful on all sides and in full bloom, he said, “like a single row of trees.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “As if upon a forest thicket in full flower at its peak,” containing various connections, various elaborations, and manifold skillful methods.
He said, “Like a tree with cool shade...,” meaning that those who desire it should properly approach the Sutta, which is the gateway to many kinds of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
“Due to the diversity of perceptions” means due to the various states of the perceptions that occurred prior to the appearance of the sign (*nimitta*).
“Perception-born” refers to the mere act of perceiving by means of the perception of cultivation (*bhāvanā-saññā*), which is produced by that very perception of cultivation.
For there is no arising from anywhere for that which lacks intrinsic nature. Therefore he said: "It appears as manifold"; what is meant is that it is merely the mode of appearance.
"These three things" refers to these three things: the in-breath, the out-breath, and the sign.

"There is not" means that, by way of being an object of attention as a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), it does not exist and is not found. "Not even access" means that it does not even reach the stage of access concentration (*upacāra*).

The intention is that it is even more so for one who has attained absorption (*appanā*). As for the phrase "but for whom," this should be understood according to the existing alternative, following the method already stated.
Now, in order to support the meaning just explained, the verse beginning with "the sign" (*nimitta*), which appears in the *Kakacūpama Sutta*, is cited.
"The sign" refers to the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) as previously described. "It becomes thus" refers to one devoted to meditation (*bhāvanā*).
It occurs thus; therefore, he should be told: "Apply your mind in this way again and again. He might fall into complacency, thinking:
"The sign is difficult to produce, yet this has been obtained; well then, I shall now bring about a distinction whenever the time is right.
Or he might become despondent, thinking: "For so long a time I have been devoted to meditation..."
One might fall into despondency, thinking, "Not even a sign has arisen; I am surely incapable of attaining distinction.

When it is said, "This is the sign for one who has entered upon this practice with the thought, 'By means of this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death,'" how could there be any occasion for discouragement? On the contrary, one would only increase one's effort all the more.
Therefore, the Majjhimabhāṇakas say: "This is the sign... [and so on]... it should be stated thus. Thus.
By fixing the mind of development upon the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) itself in the manner described.

"From this point on" means starting from the arising of the counterpart sign. Regarding what was stated previously—that one "attends by way of following, touching, and fixing"—therein, having relinquished following and touching, it should be developed solely by way of fixing.
He said: "Development occurs by way of establishing.
Showing that this meaning was stated by the ancients, he recited the verse beginning with "In the sign. Therein, "in the sign" means in the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*).
"Establishing the mind" means placing the mind of development; the sense is that one attends to it by way of establishing. "Various aspects" (*nānākāra*)...
“‘The four castes’—this refers to the various forms thus described. This is expressed in the singular by way of their commonality of form.
‘They discern’: making clear, causing to disappear. For from the moment the sign arises, those various forms become, as it were, disappeared through non-attention.
‘In-breath and out-breath’: discerning that variety which exists in the in-breath and out-breath, [one discerns] that which has arisen from the in-breath and out-breath...”
Or [it means] "on the sign. "He binds his own mind" means that by means of that very same placement (*ṭhapanā*), he fastens his own mind;
the meaning is that he settles it. Some, however, explain the meaning as "they clarify, making it clear, making the known manifest";
that would be appropriate from the perspective of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*). This, then, is the meaning here: because he is endowed with fortitude (*dhiti*), he is wise (*dhīra*).
The yogi, discerning the various modes in inhalation and exhalation, understanding them according to those various modes, and making them manifest in what has been known,
either by calming or pacifying the coarse and more coarse aspects of those various modes, fixes his mind upon whatever sign (nimitta) is obtained therein;
thus, step by step, he binds and settles his own mind.
When the faculties beginning with faith (saddhā) proceed very clear and sharp, then, due to the distancing of states such as lack of faith (assaddhiya),

the factors of absorption belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara)— namely, applied thought (vitakka) and the rest— become numerous and manifest, having gained support from the seven powers (bala) that have attained an exceptional degree of strength.
For this very reason, the hindrances such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda), which are their direct opposites, [are suppressed].
Together with the evil states associated with them, they become distant from the arising of the counterpart sign;
taking that as their object, access concentration arises. Therefore it was said: "From the moment the sign appears, the hindrances are indeed suppressed," and so forth.
In this context, *sannisinnāva* means they have sat down properly, that is, they are truly tranquil.
The meaning [of the compound] is as follows. By the restrictive phrase "only when suppressed do they sit still," he shows that an effort must be made for that purpose.
"In two ways" means by these two causes: the distancing of the factors opposed to the jhāna states and the attainment of stability.
Now, in order to show those causes by way of their stages, he says: "On the level of access (upacāra-bhūmi)," and so forth.

It has been said. Therein, "on the plane of access" (upacārabhūmiyaṃ) means in the state of access. For although at that time the jhāna factors do not arise in their more distinct form or reach the state of loftiness (mahaggata), the mind nevertheless becomes concentrated through the suppression of those states that are their opposites.
Therefore, he said: "by the abandoning of the hindrances. "On the plane of acquisition" (paṭilābhabhūmiyaṃ) means in the state of the attainment of jhāna.
For at that time, the mind becomes concentrated through the arising of the dhammas of jhāna that have reached absorption (*appanā*). Therefore, he said:
"by the manifestation of the factors. In access concentration (*upacāra*), the factors are not yet firmly established;
because the factors lack firmness, just as a young child, when lifted up and set down, falls back to the ground again and again, even so the mind, when access concentration has arisen—
At one time it takes the sign as its object, and at another time it descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Therefore it is said:
"Access concentration, having impelled through the wholesome cognitive process, descends into the life-continuum. In absorption (appanā), however, the factors are firmly established;
because of their firm establishment, just as a strong man might rise from his seat and remain standing even for a whole day, so too does the mind remain fixed in absorption.

In the same way, when absorption concentration (appanāsamādhi) has arisen, the mind cuts off the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) once and remains for the whole night or the whole day, proceeding solely by way of a succession of wholesome javanas. Therefore it was said: "Absorption concentration...
does not descend into the life-continuum. As for "by its appearance": it means by the appearance as it presents itself, like a mass of wool, a star, or a form.

"By way of characteristics" means by way of its intrinsic nature such as hardness, or by way of its intrinsic nature such as impermanence. "That sign is to be protected" is the grammatical connection.
"Loss of what has been gained" refers to the loss of access jhāna that has already been attained. When the sign does not perish, the jhāna having that as its object remains unlost;
however, when the sign perishes due to a lack of protection, even the jhāna that has been attained again and again [is lost].
It perishes because its existence is dependent upon that. Therefore he said, “In guarding,” and so forth.
Now, with the words “This is the means of guarding therein,” etc., [he says]:
“Dwelling, range, speech, person, food, and climate;”
“Regarding the modes of conduct, one should avoid the seven things that are unsuitable.
One should cultivate the seven things that are suitable;
for one who practices in this way, absorption will arise before long.”
Thus he explains in brief the method of protection. Herein, this is the detailed account:
that dwelling where, for one living there, a sign that has not yet arisen does not arise, or one that has already arisen perishes;
where unestablished mindfulness does not become established, and an unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated—that is unsuitable. Where the sign...
When [the mind] both arises and becomes stable, mindfulness is established, and the mind becomes concentrated—this is suitable.
Therefore, in a monastery where there are many dwellings, one should stay for three days in each one;
then, wherever the mind becomes one-pointed, there one should remain.

As for the village as a resort (*gocaragāma*): that which lies neither too far from the lodging—within one and a half *krośas* to the north or south—and where alms-food is easily obtained and abundant, is suitable;

the opposite is unsuitable. As for talk: talk included among the thirty-two kinds of base chatter is unsuitable, as it leads to the disappearance of the sign (*nimitta*) of concentration. Talk based on the ten topics of discourse is suitable, and that should be spoken in moderation. As for the person:
one who avoids base chatter and is endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) is suitable, depending upon whom an unconcentrated mind may become concentrated.
That which is suitable is such that one becomes concentrated, or the concentrated mind becomes more stable.
However, one who is full of bodily rigidity and given to frivolous talk is unsuitable; for he makes the mind turbid, just as muddy water makes clear water turbid.
By relying on such a person, even the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of a young monk living at Koṭapabbata was lost, let alone the sign (*nimitta*).
However, for some, sweet food is suitable, while for others, sour food is suitable. Likewise, for some, a cool temperature is suitable, while for others, a warm one is suitable.

Therefore, whatever food or temperature brings comfort to one who partakes of it, or by which an unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, or a concentrated mind becomes more stable—that is the suitable food and that is the suitable temperature.
Food is unsuitable, and the climate is unsuitable.
Among the postures as well, walking may be suitable for one person, while for another, one of the others—lying down, standing, or sitting—is suitable.
Therefore, having examined that dwelling for three days just as one would examine a residence, in whichever posture the mind is not concentrated...
That which causes one to concentrate, or makes what is already concentrated more stable, should be understood as suitable;
the other is unsuitable. Thus, having avoided these seven kinds of the unsuitable, one should cultivate the suitable.
For one who practices in this way and frequently cultivates the sign, absorption (*appanā*) will arise before long.
But for one who does not succeed even while practicing in this way, it must be shown that he should perfect the ten kinds of skill in absorption (*appanā-kosalla*); thus, the text says:
"The act of making the basis pure," and so forth. Therein, "making the basis pure" means making the internal and external bases clean.
For when his hair of the head, nails, and body hair are long, or when his body...
When the seat is not properly grasped, then the internal basis is unclear and impure.
But when his robe is worn out, soiled, and foul-smelling, or the lodging is dirty, then the external basis is unclear and impure.
For when both the internal and external bases are unclear, regarding the consciousness and mental factors that have arisen—
Knowledge is also impure, like the light from the flame of a lamp that has arisen depending on an impure lamp-stand, wick, and oil.
And for one who contemplates formations with impure knowledge, the formations do not become clear;
and for one who devotes himself to the meditation subject, the meditation subject does not reach growth, increase, or expansion. [It is] pure...

Furthermore, when consciousness and mental factors arise with respect to internal and external objects, knowledge becomes clear and purified, like the radiance of a lamp-flame arising from pure oil in a clean lamp-socket.

And for one who comprehends formations with such purified knowledge, the formations become manifest; likewise, for one devoted to the meditation subject, the meditation subject itself becomes manifest.
It attains growth, increase, and abundance.
"The balancing of the faculties" means making the faculties, such as faith and the rest, equal in strength.
For if his faculty of faith is strong while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy must perform the function of exertion, and the faculty of mindfulness...
The faculty of concentration cannot perform its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom cannot perform its function of seeing.
Therefore, that [hindrance] should be discarded by reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena, or by not attending to it in whatever way its power arose when one was attending.
The story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration of this. If...

However, when the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) is powerful, then the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is unable to perform its function of resolution, nor can the others perform their respective functions.
Therefore, that [excess] must be diminished through the cultivation of tranquility (*passaddhi*) and the other [factors]. In this regard, the story of the Elder Soṇa should be cited.
Likewise, in the case of the remaining [faculties], when one is predominant, the inability of the others to perform their own functions should be understood.
In particular, however, they praise here the balance of faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy.

For one who has strong faith but weak wisdom has blind confidence; he places his trust in what is not a true ground. One who has strong wisdom but weak faith sides with the "fraudulent" faction (the heretics);
like a disease arising from medicine, he becomes incurable. Through the balance of both, [one trusts] only in what is a true ground.
It becomes settled. However, when concentration is strong but energy is weak, because concentration belongs to the side of indolence, indolence overcomes it;
when energy is strong but concentration is weak, because energy belongs to the side of agitation, agitation overcomes it.
But concentration joined with energy does not allow one to fall into indolence, and energy joined with concentration [does not allow one to fall into agitation].
One cannot fall into agitation. Therefore, both of these must be made equal; for absorption (appanā) occurs through the balancing of both.
Furthermore, for one whose work is concentration, even strong faith is appropriate. For by believing and resolving in this way, one will reach absorption.
However, for one whose work is concentration, strong one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is required in both concentration and wisdom.
In this way he attains absorption; for one engaged in insight (vipassanā), wisdom must be strong.
In this way he attains penetration of the characteristics; however, absorption also occurs through the balance of both.
But mindfulness must be strong in all cases, for mindfulness restrains the mind from faith, energy, and wisdom when they lean toward restlessness.
By means of it, one is protected from falling into agitation through its own nature, and from falling into indolence through concentration associated with indolence.
Therefore, like salt seasoning in all curries, or like a minister for all affairs in all royal duties,
it is desirable in every respect.

Skill in signs (*nimittakusalatā*) means: skill in producing a sign for one-pointedness of mind—such as the earth-kasiṇa—that has not yet been produced; skill in developing one that has been produced; and skill in protecting one obtained through development. This is what is intended here.
How does he restrain the mind at the time when it ought to be restrained?

When his mind becomes agitated due to over-exertion of energy and so forth, then he [cultivates] the three factors beginning with the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*).
Having abandoned [the former], he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility and the others. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, suppose a man wished to extinguish a great mass of fire;
he would throw dry grass into it, he would throw dry cow dung into it, and he would throw dry wood into it.”
"and were to throw [grass] into it, blow upon it with his mouth, and not sprinkle it with dust—would that man be able to extinguish that great mass of fire? "Certainly not, Bhante.
"In the same way, monks, when the mind is agitated, that is the wrong time for the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment."

For the cultivation [of these factors]. It is the wrong time for the cultivation of the enlightenment factor of energy... it is the wrong time for the cultivation of the enlightenment factor of rapture.
Why is that? Because, monks, the mind is agitated; it is difficult to pacify with these states.
"Monks, at whatever time the mind is agitated, that is the time for the enlightenment factor of tranquility."
For the development of [the factors]. It is the time for the development of concentration... pe ...it is the time for the development of the equanimity factor of enlightenment.
Why is that? Because, monks, a restless mind is easily pacified by these states.
Just as if, monks, a man wishing to extinguish a great mass of fire were to throw wet grass into it;
“If one were to throw wet cow dung, throw wet wood, provide water and wind, and sprinkle it with dust—would that man be able to extinguish that great mass of fire? “Yes, venerable sir.
And here, the cultivation of the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility should be understood according to their respective nourishment. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“There is, monks, tranquility of body and tranquility of mind;

the frequent application of wise attention to these is the nutriment that leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility if it has not yet arisen, or to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has arisen. Likewise, monks, there is...”
The sign of serenity is the sign of non-distraction;

frequent and thorough attention directed toward it is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration... Likewise, monks, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
Regarding those phenomena, frequent and thorough attention is the nutriment that leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity if it has not yet arisen,
or to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment if it has already arisen.”

In this context, "appropriate attention" (yonisomanasikāra) regarding the three stages refers precisely to the attention that proceeds by way of producing those factors—such as tranquility (passaddhi) and the rest—after having observed the manner in which they previously arose. Furthermore, "the sign of serenity" (samathanimitta) is a designation for serenity itself;
and in the sense of non-distraction, it is the "sign of non-agitation" (abyagganimitta) for that very same serenity.
Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility:
the use of refined food, the use of a pleasant climate, the use of a comfortable posture, the practice of equanimity, avoiding persons with agitated bodies,
associating with persons whose bodies are tranquil, and being intent upon that [tranquility].
Eleven things lead to the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor: clarity of the basis, skill in the sign, balancing of the spiritual faculties,
restraining the mind at the proper time, exerting the mind at the proper time,
gladdening the dispirited mind by means of faith and a sense of urgency, and maintaining equanimity toward the mind that proceeds evenly.
Avoiding persons who are unconcentrated, associating with persons who are concentrated, reviewing the jhānas and liberations, and being intent upon them.
Five things lead to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor:
neutrality toward beings, neutrality toward formations, avoiding persons who are partial toward beings and formations, associating with persons who are neutral toward beings and formations, [and]...
"Being intent upon that. Thus, by means of these modes, one who causes these states to arise is said to "develop" the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*).
In this way, at whatever time the mind should be restrained, at that time he restrains the mind.
And how is it that at whatever time the mind should be exerted, at that time he exerts the mind? When for him—

When the mind becomes sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and other such factors, one should then develop the three beginning with the enlightenment factor of tranquility (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*), and not develop those beginning with the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (*dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga*). For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, suppose a man wished to kindle a small fire, and he were to [place] wet... [pieces of wood] there..."
"Suppose one were to throw grasses into it... and sprinkle it with dust. Would that man be able to kindle that small fire?

Certainly not, Bhante. In the same way, monks, when the mind is sluggish, that is not the time for the development of the tranquility enlightenment factor; it is not the time for concentration... [and so on].
It is not the time for the cultivation of the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because, monks, a sunken mind is difficult to arouse by means of those states.
But, monks, at whatever time the mind is sunken, that is the time for the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.
It is the time for the cultivation of energy... [and so on] ...it is the time for the cultivation of the enlightenment factor of rapture.
Why is that? Because a sluggish mind, monks, is easily stirred up by these states.
Just as if, monks, a man wishing to kindle a small fire were to throw dry grass into it... [and so on] ...
"And if one were to sprinkle it with dust, would that man be able to kindle that small fire?"—"Yes, venerable sir.

In this case too, the development of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor and the others should be understood according to their respective nutriment. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"There are, bhikkhus, wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, inferior and superior states, dark and bright states with their counterparts."

Regarding these phenomena, frequent and thorough mental attention is the nutriment that leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena if it has not yet arisen, or to its increase, expansion, development,
and fulfillment once it has arisen. Likewise, monks, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of perseverance.

In this regard, frequent and thorough mental attention is the nutriment that leads to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor if it has not yet arisen, or to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment once it has arisen.
Likewise, monks, there are states conducive to the joy enlightenment factor; in these, frequent and thorough mental attention [is the nutriment].
“This nutriment leads to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture.
In this context, the attention that proceeds by way of penetrating the specific and general characteristics is wise attention directed toward the wholesome and so forth.

...is called "name. Attention that occurs by way of the arising of the element of initiative (*ārambha-dhātu*) and so forth is what is meant by "wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) toward the element of initiative and so forth.
In this context, the "element of initiative" refers to the first kind of energy (*vīriya*). The "element of exertion" (*nikkama-dhātu*) is stronger than that, because it has emerged from indolence.
The "element of perseverance" (*parakkama-dhātu*) is even stronger than that, because it advances to ever-higher stages.
"States conducive to the enlightenment factor of rapture" is a name for rapture itself;
the attention that produces it is called "wise attention.
Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena: being a questioner, ... [and so forth].

Purification of the basis, balancing of the faculties, avoidance of persons of poor wisdom, cultivation of persons possessed of wisdom, reflection on the conduct of those with deep knowledge, and devotion thereto.
Eleven things lead to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor: reflecting on the fear of the states of misery and so forth; ... [and so on].
It is the vision of the benefits of attaining the distinctions of both the mundane and supramundane states which depend upon energy;
the reflection on the path of travel, thinking, "The path traveled by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples must be traveled by me, and that cannot be traveled by one who is indolent";
the honoring of alms-food by making it bear great fruit for the donors; and the thought, "My Teacher is a proponent of the praise of the arousal of energy."
"His teaching is not to be transgressed, he has been very helpful to us, and he is truly honored when his practice is honored, and not otherwise"—
thus is the reflection on the greatness of the Teacher. "The great inheritance known as the True Dhamma must be taken up by me,
and that cannot be taken up by one who is indolent"— thus is the reflection on the greatness of the inheritance.
The dispelling of sloth and torpor by means of attending to the perception of light, changing one’s posture, frequenting open spaces, and so forth;
avoiding persons who are indolent; associating with persons who have aroused energy; reviewing the right exertions;

and being intent upon that—these eleven things lead to the arising of the joy enlightenment factor: recollection of the Buddha, and recollection of the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, and the devas.
Recollection of peace, avoidance of persons who are coarse, association with persons who are gentle, reflection on discourses that inspire confidence, and devotion thereto.
Thus, by arousing these states through these modes, one is said to develop the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor and the others.
In this way, at whatever time the mind is to be exerted, at that time he exerts the mind.
How does one gladden the mind at the time when it should be gladdened?

When the mind becomes dispirited due to a deficiency in the application of wisdom or because the bliss of tranquility has not been attained, then one should stir it by reflecting upon the eight grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
These are called the eight grounds for spiritual urgency.
There are four: birth, aging, sickness, and death; the suffering of the states of deprivation is the fifth; there is suffering rooted in the round of existence in the past;
suffering rooted in the round of existence in the future; and suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present.
Furthermore, he generates confidence by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Thus, at whatever time the mind should be gladdened, at that time he gladdens the mind.
How does he, at the time when the mind is to be looked upon with equanimity, look upon the mind with equanimity? When, by practicing in this way,
his mind becomes unflagging, unagitated, free from distaste, proceeding evenly toward the object, and has entered the path of serenity (samatha),
then he adopts a state of non-activity regarding its further exertion, restraint, or encouragement, just like a charioteer.
And when the horses are proceeding evenly. Thus, at whatever time the mind should be looked upon with equanimity, at that time he looks upon the mind with equanimity.
"Avoidance of persons who are not concentrated" means avoiding those who have never previously ascended the path of renunciation and are preoccupied with many worldly duties.
The abandonment from afar of persons whose hearts are distracted;
"associating with persons who are concentrated" means approaching from time to time those persons who have attained concentration and who have entered upon the way of renunciation;

"being intent upon that" means being intent upon concentration—that is to say, having respect for concentration, leaning toward concentration, inclining toward concentration, and tending toward concentration.
In this way, these ten kinds of skill in absorption (appanā-kosalla) must be accomplished. Therefore he said: "By one who does not abandon these ten skills in absorption.
In that context, the method by which one becomes skilled in absorption is itself the tenfold skill in absorption, or the knowledge produced thereby.
For one accomplishing these ten kinds of skill in absorption, regarding the sign (nimitta) thus acquired:
Absorption arises. For this has been said:
“For one who accomplishes it in this way, this skill in absorption occurs;
once the sign has been acquired, absorption proceeds.”

"Yoga is to be practiced": even for one who is perfecting skill in absorption (*appanā-kosalla*), if absorption does not arise, he should not abandon his application to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Instead, having observed the manner of movement of bees and so forth among pollen and the like, and having freed the mind from states of sluggishness and agitation, he should practice yoga again and again by applying himself to the balancing of energy (*vīriya-samata*). For this has been said:
“If, for one practicing in this way, that [insight] does not arise, even then the wise man should not abandon his application; he should simply exert himself further.
For by abandoning right effort, O youth, one surely attains no distinction.”
One will not attain even the slightest [result]; such a state does not exist.
Therefore, the wise person, observing the mode of the mind's activity, should repeatedly apply himself to the balancing of energy alone.
“If the mind is sinking even slightly, one should uplift it;
having restrained it when over-exerted, one should cause it to proceed with evenness.
As with dust on a lotus petal, a thread, a boat, or a balance scale...”
Just as the activity of bees and so forth has been correctly described:
“Having completely freed the mind from states of dullness and agitation,
one should thus direct the consciousness toward the sign.”

For just as an unskilled bee, having perceived that "a flower has blossomed on such-and-such a tree," springs forward with sharp speed and, overshooting it upon its return, reaches the spot where the pollen has already vanished;
whereas another unskilled bee, springing forward with slow speed, reaches the spot where the pollen has indeed vanished; but the skilled one, springing forward with even speed—
Having reached a heap of flowers with ease, he takes as much pollen as he desires, prepares honey, and enjoys the honey.
And just as when a pupil of a surgeon is learning surgery on lotus leaves placed in a water basin,
one who is unskilled, striking with the knife too hastily, either cuts the lotus leaf in two or causes it to sink into the water;
Another, being unskilled, does not even dare to touch a saw for fear of cutting himself or being pierced;

but a skilled man, by means of an even application, having shown the stroke of the saw there and becoming one whose craft is purified, performs his work in such places and gains profit. And just as it is said: "He who brings a spider’s thread measuring four fathoms..."
When the king said, "Thus one receives four thousand [pieces]," one unskilled man pulled the spider’s thread with great force, cutting it here and there;
another unskilled man did not even dare to touch it for fear of breaking it;
but the skilled man, starting from the end, wound the stalks evenly using a balanced technique and brought them back.
He gains profit; and just as an unskilled pilot, while filling the sails in a strong wind, causes the ship to go astray, whereas another unskilled pilot,
lowering the sails in a light wind, leaves the ship right where it is, but a skilled pilot,
having filled the sails in a light wind and then half-filled them in a strong wind, reaches the desired destination in safety.
And just as when a teacher tells his pupils, "He who fills the tube without spilling any oil gains the prize," one unskilled pupil, greedy for the prize, fills it too quickly and spills the oil;
another unskilled pupil, out of fear of spilling the oil, does not even dare to pour it in;
but the skilled one, filling it with a balanced application, gains the prize—just so.
One bhikkhu, when the sign has arisen, exerts intense energy, thinking, "I shall reach absorption very quickly.
Because his mind possesses over-exerted energy, it falls into agitation, and he is unable to reach absorption.
Another, seeing the fault in over-exerted energy, thinks, "What use have I for absorption now? and relaxes his energy; his...
The mind falls into indolence because its energy is too slack, and thus it cannot reach absorption (appanā).

However, he who releases the mind even slightly from its state of sluggishness and from agitation, and directs it toward the sign (nimitta) with balanced application, reaches absorption; one must become such as that.
Now, showing the occurrence of absorption (*appanā*) for one who has practiced in this way, he said: "For one thus devoted," and so forth.

Therein, the statement beginning with "first the preliminary work" (*parikamma*) is stated by way of including what has not been mentioned; however, by way of including what has already been mentioned, all designations apply to all without distinction.
For indeed, because they are the preliminary work for absorption and because they perform the act of reflection, all of them are also called "preliminary works."

Just as the area near a village or the like is called "the vicinity of the village" (*gāmūpacāra*) or "the vicinity of the house" (*gharūpacāra*), so too these are called "access concentrations" (*upacārāni*) because they are near to absorption (*appanā*) or because they conduct one in its proximity.
Furthermore, they are called "conformities" (*anulomāni*) because they conform to the preliminary tasks (*parikamma*) that precede them and to the absorption that follows them.
And that which is the very last among them is so called because it overcomes the limited lineage (*parittagotta*) and develops the exalted lineage (*mahaggatagotta*).
And it is also called "the lineage" (*gotrabhū*). For "lineage" (*gotta*) means that which protects the "limited" (*paritta*);
it is called the "limited lineage" because it protects both the name and the cognition currently occurring by way of their having a single object.
For just as cognition does not function without an object that serves as its referent, so too the name does not function without the thing to be named; therefore, it protects those two.

It is called "it protects. Furthermore, that [state] should be understood as the unique materiality (rūpa) of sense-sphere phenomena, which is devoid of the sublime and the unsurpassed and serves as the objective domain for craving for sensual pleasures.
The meaning should also be understood in this same manner regarding the "sublime lineage" (*mahaggatagotta*).
Thus, because it overcomes such a limited lineage (*parittagotta*) and because it brings about and generates the sublime lineage, the final [stage] is also called "change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*).
It is said: "The fourth itself is called the fifth" because this is stated with reference to those of quick higher knowledge (*khippābhiñña*) and those of sluggish higher knowledge (*dandhābhiñña*).
For the fourth [jhāna] enters into absorption for one of quick higher knowledge, while the fifth enters for one of sluggish higher knowledge.
But why does it enter the fourth or the fifth, and not the sixth or the seventh? To this he says: "Because of the proximity to the falling back into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). Just as...
For just as a man running toward the edge of a precipice is unable to stop and plant his foot on the rim even if he wishes to stand,
and instead falls right over the precipice, so too one is unable to attain the sixth or seventh jhāna because it is too close to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Therefore, it should be understood that absorption occurs only in the fourth or fifth jhānas.

Because it is stated that “preceding wholesome states are a condition for succeeding wholesome states by way of the condition of repetition (āsevanapaccaya),” he said: “Wholesome states become powerful through the condition of repetition.

Just as the first impulsion (javana), having not yet acquired repetition, does not produce the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) due to its weakness, but [the subsequent ones] having acquired repetition...
Because of its strengthened state, it produces either the second or the third change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*);

thus, through the strength gained by repeated practice, it enters the sixth or even the seventh [jhāna]—this is the Elder’s intention. Therefore he said: "Therefore, it enters the sixth or the seventh.
"That" refers to the Elder’s statement. "Refuted" means [refuted] by means of the Suttas, the Suttas’ conformity, and the teachers’ doctrines.
Because it was not supported [by other evidence], it was rejected with the statement: "This is merely the Elder's own opinion.
However, the Sutta passage, "The preceding wholesome states," is not a decisive reason for the strength of the condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), because that is not invariably the case.

For instance, even a first volition that has not received repetition may be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), whereas a second volition that has received repetition may also be so.
Up to the sixth consciousness-moment, volition is to be experienced in a subsequent life (aparāpariya-vedanīya).

If the sixth and seventh moments are weak because their impetus has been exhausted and they lack strength through the condition of repetition (āsevana-paccaya), how can the seventh javana-volition be both to be experienced upon rebirth (upapajja-vedanīya) and an immediate (ānantariya) deed? This distinction does not arise from attaining strength through the condition of repetition; rather—
By way of the distinction of the stages of action (*kiriyāvatthā*). For the stage of action is threefold according to its beginning, middle, and end.

In this context, it should be understood that at the final stage, because of its nature as a decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*), there is the state of being experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) and so forth, but not by virtue of its strength.
Likewise, [it is so] by virtue of being the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) for the stream of result (*vipākasantāna*) which arises immediately after rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
And they say it is "because of being conditioned"; therefore, because the sixth and seventh [moments of consciousness] are facing toward the precipice, their loss of momentum cannot be prevented.
"Preparatory thoughts" refers to three or four moments of consciousness.
"In this" means in this mindfulness of the body. "Desiring to attain purity" means desiring to reach, or desiring to enter into, [that state].
And therein, it should be connected thus: "one who desires to attain by way of both discerning and expanding, and one who desires to enter by way of discerning.
Regarding the passage beginning with "adverting and entering... [and so on] ...attaining mastery," the five kinds of mastery should be understood as follows:

when, having emerged from the first jhāna, one adverts to the initial applied thought (*vitakka*), immediately after the adverting consciousness that has arisen following the interruption of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), [the first mastery occurs].
Four or five impulsion moments (javana) arise with the applied thought (vitakka) itself as their object; after that, two life-continuum (bhavaṅga) moments occur;
then, an adverting consciousness (āvajjana) occurs with the sustained thought (vicāra) as its object, followed by impulsion moments in the same manner as previously described.

When one is thus able to direct the mind continuously through the five jhāna factors, then mastery over adverting (āvajjana-vasī) is achieved for him. This, however, is [mastery] interrupted by two life-continuum moments.

Mastery reaching the peak is obtained by the Blessed One during the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*), or by others such as the General of the Dhamma (*dhammasenāpati*) and so forth, at the time when they produce the mastery of adverting with greater ease, arising again and again. However, that [mastery] is temporary and of limited duration;
it does not possess a long-lasting continuity like that of the Teacher’s Twin Miracle. For instance, that—
This has been stated as not shared with other disciples. Beyond this, there is no such thing as mastery over adverting that is swifter.
However, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s capacity to enter attainment swiftly—such as in his taming of the Naga kings Nanda and Upananda—is called mastery over attainment (*samāpajjana-vasī*).
And herein, immediately after the desire to attain [jhāna], when two moments of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) have arisen, [the mind adverts].
The ability to attain [jhāna] swiftly is the capacity to enter attainment immediately after the adverting consciousness that has arisen following the interruption of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
And this mastery in attaining, which has reached its peak, is found in the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma; it was with reference to this that it was said:
"Then, Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very discourse, right there, in that very [moment]..."
“Upon the sign of concentration, I settle the mind within myself, I compose it, I unify it, and I concentrate it;
by means of this, I indeed dwell for all time. There is nothing swifter than this so-called mastery of attainment (samāpajjanavasī).
The capacity to establish jhāna for the duration of a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps is mastery of determination (adhiṭṭhānavasī).

Likewise, the capacity to emerge from jhāna after having been possessed of jhāna for a brief moment—whether lasting only a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps—is called "mastery of emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna-vasī*).
Here, "emergence from jhāna" refers specifically to the occurrence of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*).
And in this context, just as one might previously prepare by thinking, "I shall maintain the jhāna for only this much time," [so too does one master its emergence].

Mastery over resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-vasī*) is the capacity for resolution. Likewise, mastery over emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-vasī*) should be understood as the capacity for emergence through prior preparation, such that one thinks: "Having been possessed of jhāna for exactly this much time, I shall emerge from jhāna";

this is what is called skill in emerging from attainment (*samāpatti-vuṭṭhāna-kusala*). Mastery over reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa-vasī*), however, is simply a form of mastery over adverting (*āvajjana-vasī*).
...are stated. For in that case, it is only the reviewing javanas that follow immediately after the adverting consciousness.
Just as the mastery of adverting is established, so too should the mastery of reviewing be understood to be established.
Or, preceded by the immaterial [attainments]...pe... "He initiates insight"—this is the meaning stated in brief; now, [it is explained] in detail:

The passage beginning with “How? was stated in order to show this. Therein, “having discerned the jhāna factors” means having discerned the jhāna factors—such as initial application (vitakka) and so forth—and the states associated with them, by way of their specific characteristics, functions, and so on.
For the phrase “jhāna factors” is merely an illustration; one who sees the jhāna factors also sees the states associated with them. Of these...
"Regarding the heart-basis as the support: just as a man, having seen a snake inside his house and pursuing it, sees its lair;
even so this practitioner of yoga, while examining those immaterial phenomena and searching, 'Upon what support do these phenomena proceed?', sees the heart-basis as their support."
“Jhāna factors are immaterial”: here it should be understood that this includes the states associated with them as well.
Having shown the discernment of materiality preceded by the immaterial, he now says “Or else,” etc., showing the discernment of the immaterial preceded by materiality.
Regarding the phrase “having discerned the parts beginning with head-hairs... and the materiality dependent on them”: here... [text continues].
First, in the case of the head hairs, the characteristic of hardness should be discerned as the earth element;
right there, the characteristic of cohesion as the water element; the characteristic of maturation as the fire element; and the characteristic of distension as the air element.
In this way, within each and every component, the four great elements are to be discerned.
Then, when the elements have been made manifest by him according to their true nature and specific characteristics, first, regarding that which is produced by kamma—such as the hair:

there are ten material phenomena by way of the body-decad (*kāyadasaka*), namely, those four elements possessing the aforementioned characteristics, along with the color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, life-faculty, and bodily sensitivity dependent upon them;
and in that very same place, because of the presence of the state [of being], there is the state-decad (*bhāvadasaka*).
The ten material qualities, the nutritive-essence octad produced by nutriment, the temperature-produced, and the consciousness-produced—these are another twenty-four.
Thus, among the twenty-four sections within the fourfold origination, forty-four material qualities are to be discerned.
However, as for sweat, tears, spittle, and snot, these are included within the two nutritive-essence octads produced by temperature and consciousness among those four [originations].

By way of these [four], there are sixteen material phenomena for each. Regarding the four things produced by temperature—undigested food, excrement, pus, and urine—one should discern eight material phenomena for each, consisting of the nutritive essence (*oja*) as the eighth, which itself is produced by temperature.
This, first of all, is the method regarding the thirty-two aspects.
Furthermore, when these thirty-two aspects have become manifest, another ten aspects become manifest: four portions of fire and six portions of air.

In that regard, within the portion of fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*) which matures what is eaten and so forth, there are nine material phenomena: the octad of nutritive essence (*ojā-aṭṭhamaka*) and vitality (*jīvita*).
Likewise, in the portion of air born of consciousness (*cittaja*), consisting of inhalation and exhalation, there are nine material phenomena: the octad of nutritive essence and sound.
Thus there are nine; in the remaining eight [bases] arising from the four origins, thirty-three material phenomena each—namely, the life-nonad and three nutritive-octads—are to be discerned.

Thus, when these primary and derived material phenomena have become evident in detail by way of forty-two modes, there are the five decads beginning with the eye-decad, according to the bases and doors.
The "heart-basis decad" (*hadayavatthudasaka*)—thus another sixty material phenomena are to be discerned.
However, if, while discerning the immaterial by means of that or that door after having discerned matter, the immaterial does not appear because of its subtlety, he should not abandon his task;
rather, he should repeatedly contemplate, attend to, and discern matter alone.

It must be defined. For in whatever way matter becomes well-washed, stripped of its tangles, and thoroughly purified, in that same way the immaterial phenomena having that as their object become manifest of their own accord.
Just as, for example, when a man with good eyesight looks at the reflection of his face in an unpurified mirror, the reflection—
"It is not perceived" does not mean that one discards the mirror; rather, one polishes it again and again.
When the mirror is purified, the reflection becomes manifest of its own accord.
In the same way, that bhikkhu, without laying down the burden, must repeatedly comprehend, attend to, discern, and define form itself.
For just as his material form becomes well-cleansed, free from tangles, and perfectly pure, so too do the immaterial states that have that form as their object become manifest of their own accord.
When he has thus discerned the material form with full purity, the immaterial states appear to him in three ways:
either by way of contact, or by way of feeling, or by way of consciousness.

How so? First, for one who discerns the elements in the manner beginning, “In the head-hairs there is the earth element characterized by hardness… in the in-breaths and out-breaths there is the earth element characterized by hardness,” the initial impact is contact (*phassa*);

the feeling associated with that is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*); the perception is the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*); and volition together with contact is the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
The aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) and consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) appear as mind. Thus, immaterial phenomena appear by way of contact (*phassa*).

For one person, the feeling that experiences the taste of that object—[thinking] "the earth element in the head-hairs has the characteristic of hardness... [and so on] ...the earth element in the in-breaths and out-breaths has the characteristic of hardness"—is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*); associated with that [feeling]...
Perception is the perception aggregate; the contact and volition associated with it are the formations aggregate;
and the consciousness associated with them is the consciousness aggregate—thus they appear. In this way, immaterial phenomena appear by way of feeling. For another person, [they appear thus]:
"In the head hairs, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness... pe ...in the in-breaths and out-breaths, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness."
The consciousness aggregate is the discerning of the object; the feeling associated with it is the feeling aggregate; perception is the perception aggregate;
and contact and volition are the formations aggregate—thus they appear. In this way, immaterial phenomena appear by way of consciousness.
By this same method, [one contemplates] "in hair produced by kamma, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness," and so forth.
By way of this method, among the forty-two groups of elements, by means of each set of four elements, and likewise for the remaining ones,
one who discerns them according to their bases and doors— taking the heart-base as the support-characteristic for the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element,
and the eye and so forth as the sensitivity-characteristic of the primary elements capable of being struck by material form— [should proceed].

The first moment of impact is contact (*phassa*); the feeling associated with that is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*), and so forth—in these three ways, immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) appear by way of contact and the rest. Therefore it was said:
"One sees consciousness together with its associated states, having as its object the material form as determined, or having as its object the doors and bases of the material forms as determined."
Now, showing another way of discerning the immaterial preceded by the material, he says, “Or else,” and so forth.
Therein, the passage beginning with “For just as” is a demonstration of how the body and the mind are the origin of the in-breaths and out-breaths.
“A smith’s bellows” refers to the bellows used for blowing the fire in a smith’s furnace. “While being blown” means while emitting smoke, or causing the wind to enter.
The meaning is as follows: "Tajjanti" means "they strike" in accordance with that. "Evamevaṃ" (in this very way):
here, the body composed of the four elements (*karajakāya*) should be regarded as being like the blacksmith's bellows, and the mind (*citta*) as being like the wind.
Although inhalation and exhalation are mind-originated, they are said to be "dependent upon both body and mind" because they do not occur without the body composed of the four elements.

“Of that” means of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). “He seeks the condition” means he seeks, investigates, and grasps the conditions beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), according to the formula: “With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form,” and so forth.
“He overcomes doubt” means he transcends and abandons the sixteen-based perplexity that proceeds in such a manner as: “Did I exist in the past? and so on.
“Whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present,” and so forth—this is the comprehension by groups (*kalāpasammasana*) proceeding in such a manner.

“In the prior stage” means when it has arisen prior to the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*), which is included within the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi*).
“The illumination and so forth” refers to: illumination, knowledge, rapture, tranquility, bliss, resolution, exertion, equanimity, and establishment.
"Craving" refers to these ten things beginning with illumination.

Among them, "illumination" is the illumination of insight (*vipassanā-obhāsa*). This consists of both the radiant matter (*pabhassara-rūpa*) produced by the continuity of the mind of insight and that produced by temperature (*utu-samuṭṭhāna*).
Therein, that which is produced by the mind of insight is radiant only within the body of the practitioner.
"Having sacrificed" means that [the light] remains after abandoning the body of mind-born matter because it does not proceed outside of it;
whereas the other [light], having abandoned the body, spreads out in all directions according to the power of knowledge, and that is perceived by him alone.
One should investigate whether he sees even the material form in the place touched by that light by means of eye-consciousness or by means of mind-consciousness.
They say this. Like those who have attained the divine eye, it appears as though it is appropriate to say that this light is cognizable solely by mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*).
Now, this light arises for some monk illuminating only the area where he sits cross-legged;
for some, it illuminates the interior of the room; for some, even the exterior of the room; for some, the entire monastery; or a *gāvuta*.
It extended for half a *yojana*, one *yojana*, two *yojanas*, or three *yojanas; for some, it created a single expanse of light from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world.
But for the Blessed One, it arose illuminating the ten-thousandfold world-system.
When that had arisen, the practitioner [thought]: "Indeed, never before has such a radiance arisen for me; certainly..."
Thinking, "I have reached the path; I have reached the fruit," he takes what is not the path to be the "path" and what is not the fruit to be the "fruit.
For one who thus takes what is not the path to be the "path" or what is not the fruit to be the "fruit," the course of insight (vipassanāvīthi) is said to have been lost.
Abandoning his own original meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he sits taking delight in the mere illumination (obhāsa) alone.

"Knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). It is said that as one weighs and examines material and immaterial phenomena, there arises a knowledge that is sharp, keen, and exceedingly clear, with an unimpeded force like a released thunderbolt.

"Rapture" (pīti) refers to the rapture of insight (vipassanā-pīti). It is said that at that time, this fivefold rapture—namely, minor rapture, momentary rapture, showering rapture, uplifting rapture, and pervading rapture—arises filling the entire body.

"Tranquility" refers to the tranquility of insight (*vipassanā-passaddhi*). It is said that at that time, for him while sitting in his night-quarters or day-quarters, there is neither distress nor heaviness, neither rigidity nor unwieldiness, nor sickness, nor crookedness of body and mind;
rather, his body and mind are tranquil, light, and pliant.

They become workable, very clear, and indeed straight. At that time, with his body and mind assisted by these factors beginning with serenity, he experiences a delight called "superhuman. With reference to this, it was said:
"For the bhikkhu who has entered an empty place, whose mind is peaceful..."
There is superhuman delight for one who clearly sees the Dhamma with right insight.
"From whatever point one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and joy; that is the deathless for one who understands."
Thus, as he accomplishes this superhuman delight, there arises tranquility associated with lightness and the other [characteristics].
"Bliss" refers to the bliss of insight (vipassanā). It is said that at that time, an exceedingly refined bliss arises, suffusing his entire body.
"Resolution" refers to faith. For at that moment, there arises a powerful faith, which is an extraordinary clarity of the mind and mental factors associated with insight.
"Exertion" is energy (*vīriya*). For him, there arises energy that is well-exerted—neither lax nor over-tense—and which is indeed associated with insight (*vipassanā*).

"Establishment" is mindfulness (*sati*). For him, there arises mindfulness that is well-established, firmly grounded, fixed, immovable, and like the king of mountains; it is indeed associated with insight. Whatever object he adverts to or attends to...
He attends to it and reviews it; having entered into and leaped upon each respective state, it appears to his mindfulness as the world beyond does to the divine eye.
"Equanimity" here refers both to equanimity of insight and to equanimity of adverting. For at that time, regarding all conditioned formations...
Equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*), having become balanced, arises powerfully, as does the advertence-equanimity (*āvajjanupekkhā*) at the mind-door.
For when he adverts to this or that object, it flows forth with a sharp intensity, like a loosened thunderbolt,
or like a red-hot iron arrow leaping into a leaf-cup.

“Craving” (*nikanti*) here refers to craving for insight (*vipassanā-nikanti*). Thus, as he forms an attachment to that insight adorned with the aura and so forth, there arises a subtle and peaceful form of craving which is not even possible to identify as a “defilement” (*kilesa*).
And just as with the aura, when any one of these has arisen, the practitioner thinks:
“Indeed, never before has such knowledge, such rapture, such tranquility, such bliss, such resolve, or such exertion arisen in me.”
When he takes what is not the path for "the path" and what is not the fruit for "the fruit"—thinking, "Service has been rendered; equanimity has arisen; attachment has arisen before;

indeed, I have attained the path, I have attained the fruit"—then for him who takes the non-path as "path" and the non-fruit as "fruit," the course of insight is said to have gone astray. Having abandoned his own original meditation subject, he...
He sits relishing attachment itself.
And here, illumination and the rest are called "defilements" because they are the basis for defilement, not because they are unwholesome;
however, attachment is both a defilement and the basis for defilement. These ten are so numbered by way of their bases, but by way of their modes of grasping—
There are thirty. How so? For one who grasps [the light] thinking, "A radiance has arisen for me," there is the grasping of views (*diṭṭhiggāha*);

for one who grasps it thinking, "Ah, what a pleasing radiance has arisen," there is the grasping of conceit (*mānaggāha*); and for one who relishes the radiance, there is the grasping of craving (*taṇhāggāha*).

Thus, regarding the radiance, there are three graspings by way of view, conceit, and craving. The same applies to the remaining [signs]. In this way, by way of these graspings, there are thirty defilements (*upakkilesa*).
By means of these, an unskilled and incompetent practitioner wavers and is distracted by the illumination and the other signs;
he regards each one among the illumination and the rest as "this is mine, this am I, this is my self. Therefore the ancients said:
"He wavers in regard to the illumination, And in regard to knowledge, And in regard to rapture;..."
“Through tranquility and through pleasure, the mind trembles;
it wavers in resolution, exertion, and establishment;
and it wavers in the adverting of equanimity, in equanimity itself, and in attachment.”
When illumination and the like have arisen, the skilled, wise, proficient, and intelligent practitioner of yoga discerns and examines them with wisdom, thinking:

"This illumination has indeed arisen for me; moreover, it is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Then...
Or else he reflects thus: "If the radiance were the self, it would be right to grasp it as 'self';

however, this which is non-self is grasped as 'self. Therefore, in the sense of being subject to lack of mastery, it is non-self; in the sense of not existing after having come to be, it is impermanent;
and in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, it is suffering. And just as with the radiance, so too with the rest.
Having investigated in this way, he regards the illumination thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
He regards knowledge... [and so on] ...regards inclination thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Regarding it in this way, he does not waver or tremble regarding the illumination and the rest. Thus spoke the ancients:
“He who has fully mastered these ten points through wisdom is skilled in the agitation regarding the Dhamma and does not fall into distraction. Thus,
not falling into distraction, he disentangles that tangle of thirty kinds of defilements, [beginning with] illumination and so forth.
“Phenomena are not the path; rather, insight-knowledge that is free from defilements and has entered the right course is the path.
Thus he defines what is not the path as the path. It is with reference to this that it was said:

“Having abandoned the ten imperfections of insight, such as illumination and so forth, and having defined the knowledge of the way—which is free from imperfections—as the path. “Having abandoned arising” means...
Having relinquished the arising of formations grasped through the contemplation of rise and fall,

and having reached the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution by contemplating their very breaking-up, one becomes disenchanted through the contemplation of disenchantment preceded by the contemplation of danger.

At the conclusion of the practice of the knowledges of desire for deliverance, reflective contemplation, equanimity towards formations, and conformity, immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage has arisen—
By means of the path-knowledge that has arisen, he becomes dispassionate toward and liberated from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
For at the moment of the path, the noble one is said to "become dispassionate" and "be liberated. Therefore it was said: "having reached the four noble paths in their proper order.
[This refers to the knowledge] which is nineteenfold, distinguished by the objects to be reviewed—namely, the defilements abandoned through the paths and fruits, and those remaining.

For an Arahant, because there are no remaining defilements, there are nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). "Assa" means for one whose meditation subject is mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānika*).

It is said that there is no separate method for the development of the meditation subject because it was taught by way of the contemplation of feelings, mind, and mental objects for one who has attained jhāna by means of the first tetrad. "Tesaṃ" refers to the three tetrads. "Experiencing rapture" (*pītippaṭisaṃvedī*)...
One who has the nature of experiencing rapture thoroughly and repeatedly, or one for whom there is such thorough and repeated experience of it,

or one who experiences it thoroughly and repeatedly. In this context, while the state of having understood rapture with care is indeed already indicated by the inclusion of the term "experiencing" (*saṃvedana*),
[the author] shows the specific modes by which its experience is intended:

The inclusion of the word *paṭi* [in the compound] is for the purpose of [explaining] "one who experiences each [object] is an experiencer (*paṭisaṃvedī*). Therefore, he said, "by two modes," and so forth.
In that context, "How is joy experienced by way of the object? is the interrogative statement.
"He attains the two jhānas accompanied by joy" means that he attains, in succession, the first and second jhānas associated with joy. "Of him... [refers to the practitioner].
By that [word]. For this genitive case ending has the sense of the agent (kattū), with reference to the word "clearly experienced" (*paṭisaṃviditā*).

"At the moment of attainment" means at the moment of having entered [into absorption]. "By the acquisition of jhāna" means by way of being endowed with jhāna. "By way of the object" means by way of the object;
the joy included in the jhāna that takes that as its object is clearly experienced because the object is clearly experienced.

What is meant by this? Just as when someone wandering in search of a snake has identified its lair, the snake itself is also effectively identified because it is easy to capture with the power of mantras and medicinal charms;

so too, when the object which serves as the abode of rapture is identified, that rapture is effectively identified by way of its specific characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*) and its general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).
"And that grasping is easy to apprehend.
Having brought this forward, it should be connected [to the question]: "How is joy experienced through non-delusion?

At the moment of insight (*vipassanā-khaṇe*) means at the moment of seeing the object by means of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) proceeding with sharp and clear activity. "By the penetration of the characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedhena*).
By means of penetrating both the specific characteristic and the general characteristic of rapture.

For when whatever is the specific and general characteristic of something is known, that thing itself is known exactly as it is. Therefore he said: "Rapture is clearly experienced through non-delusion."
Now, in order to clarify that meaning by means of the text itself, he said, "For this has been said," and so forth.

Regarding that, whatever needs to be said concerning the phrases "by way of long inhalation" and so on has already been stated below. Furthermore, in that previous context the text was presented by way of showing mindful performance (*satokāritā*), whereas here it is by way of being experienced as rapture (*pītippaṭisaṃviditā*).
And the experience of rapture has indeed already been analyzed according to its meaning. Moreover—
This is the meaning in brief here: “By way of a long inhalation” means that for one who understands by way of the long inhalation which has become the object, that rapture is experienced;

this is the connection. “Understanding the unification and non-distraction of the mind” means understanding the unification of the mind—which has acquired the name ‘non-distraction’ when included within jhāna—and [the rapture] associated with it.
For one who understands with wisdom. For just as rapture is experienced by way of the object, so too are the states associated with it experienced by way of the object.

"Mindfulness is established" means that mindfulness associated with the jhāna, through long inhalation, is established upon its object; thus, by way of the object, it is said to be established in the jhāna as well.

"By that mindfulness": by means of that mindfulness established in this way, and because the object has been well-penetrated by the aforementioned knowledge, that joy is experienced through its influence upon that object.
The meaning in the phrases "by means of long inhalation," etc., should also be understood according to this same method.

In order to show, by way of analysis, the experience of rapture (*pītippaṭisaṃvedanā*) as presented through the first tetrad—both in terms of its object and its non-delusion—the passage beginning with "for one who adverts" (*āvajjato*) was stated.
Therein, "for one who adverts" means for one who is adverting to the jhāna. "That rapture" refers to the rapture included within that jhāna.
"For one who knows" means for one who knows by way of the object at the moment of attainment. Of that...
The connection is: "that rapture is clearly experienced. "Seeing" means seeing after emerging from jhāna by means of knowledge that consists of vision.
"Reviewing" means reviewing the jhāna. "Resolving the mind" means resolving the jhāna-consciousness with the thought, "I shall remain possessed of jhāna for this long a time.
Thus, regarding the mastery over these five [powers]...
By means of the knowledge of jhāna through the door of discernment, the experience of joy from the perspective of the object has been shown.

Now, in order to demonstrate the experience of joy by way of those factors—such as faith and the rest—which include both the jhānas and insight, whether they are comprised within jhāna or comprised within the path of insight, it is said: "of one who resolves with faith," and so forth.
