In this context, "resolves" means for one who has faith; the intention is that this occurs by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). The same method applies to the phrases "exerts energy," and so forth.

"To be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) means to be known by means of highly distinguished wisdom (*paññā*). "Directly knowing" (*abhijānato*) means knowing by means of the wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*), which is preceded by the wisdom of insight.

"To be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) refers to the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), which is fully understood through the full understanding of investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*) and the wisdom of the path.

"To be abandoned" refers to the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*), which is abandoned by one who abandons it through the full understanding of abandonment (*pahānapariññā*) and the wisdom of the path (*maggapaññā*).
For one who develops and realizes, there is the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) to be developed and the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) to be realized.

However, some here extract the factors to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth based on rapture (*pīti*) alone; that is incorrect, because what is intended is the extraction of rapture from the aggregate of jhāna and the other factors.
And here, by means of the first tetrad beginning with "by way of long inhalation," the experience of rapture through the object is stated;
likewise by the five terms beginning with "by adverting. However, by the terms beginning with "by directly knowing what is to be directly known," it is stated through non-delusion;
and by the terms beginning with "by resolving with faith," it is stated both ways—briefly, by way of serenity and by way of the object.
It should be understood that the "experience of rapture" is mentioned here by way of non-delusion through insight (vipassanā).
Why, however, is feeling taken up under the heading of rapture in this contemplation of feeling, rather than being presented in its own form?

It is in order to show the fourfold contemplation of feeling by dividing feeling according to its planes and so forth. Furthermore, it is while demonstrating the meditation subject of feeling that [this is stated].
Because rapture (*pīti*) is gross, the Blessed One shows the pleasure associated with it under the heading of rapture for the purpose of identifying that pleasure.

By this same method, the remaining terms—“experiencing pleasure” (*sukhapaṭisaṃvedī*) and “experiencing mental formations” (*cittasaṅkhārappaṭisaṃvedī*)—should be understood in meaning according to the method already given for the term “experiencing rapture. For it is possible [to understand] that “pleasure is experienced in two ways.”
By substituting terms such as "pleasure" (*sukha*) for "rapture" (*pīti*) in passages beginning with, "It is experienced through the mental formations;
it is experienced by way of its object," one understands the meaning through such statements as, "He attains three or four jhānas accompanied by pleasure.
Therefore, he said, "By way of the three jhānas," and so forth. In the phrase "feeling and the rest" (*vedanādayo*), the word "and the rest" (*ādi*) includes perception (*saññā*).

[They] have been taken up. Therefore he said, "two aggregates. For the purpose of showing the plane of insight (vipassanā), that is, for the purpose of showing the plane of insight by way of the comprehension of miscellaneous formations, it was said, "pleasure:
two kinds of pleasure," and so forth; because in serenity (samatha) there is an absence of bodily pleasure.
"He" refers to that cessation spoken of by way of the method of tranquilization. By the passage beginning, "For at the time when this bhikkhu has not yet grasped [the object]," etc.
It was explained in detail regarding the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*); therefore, it should be understood according to the method stated therein.
The only difference there is that it was presented by way of the bodily formation, whereas here it is by way of the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*).
Having thus shown the subsiding of the mental formation by way of extended application (*atidesa*), whatever else remains to be said regarding this tetrad—

To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apicā*) was stated. Therein, regarding the phrase “the section on rapture” (*pītipade*), it refers to the specific portion taught by the words “experiencing rapture” (*pītippaṭisaṃvedī*).
The intention is that feeling (*vedanā*) is expressed by way of the heading “rapture”; thus, by the designation “rapture,” the feeling associated with it is meant, not rapture itself.
The reason for this has already been explained above. Regarding the two phrases “mental formations” (*cittasaṅkhāra*): [“experiencing mental formations”].
"Calming the mental formations (*cittasaṅkhāra*)" refers to the two passages associated with the mental formations.
Because of the statement, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) [arises]," they are bound to the mind, thus they are "mind-bound.

For that very reason, although they are indeed formed by the mind, they are called "mental formations," such as perception (*saññā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth; however, in this context, these are merely illustrative examples, for here it is specifically perception and feeling that are intended.
“Intended” means he said, “feeling associated with perception.
Regarding the phrase “experiencing the mind,” here it is experienced in two ways: by way of the object and by way of non-delusion.
How by way of the object? One attains the four jhānas; at the moment of attainment, through the acquisition of the jhāna, and so forth.
Since everything is easily understood according to the method already stated, he said: “It should be understood as the discernment of mind by way of the four jhānas.

“Gladdening the mind” means either gladdening the mind associated with jhāna through the joy associated with it, or gladdening the insight-mind that has arisen taking that joy as its object, by means of that very joy which serves as its object.
The words beginning with "rejoicing" (*pamodento*) are synonyms for that very [state],

because they are expressions for *pīti* (rapture). "It gladdens the mind through associated rapture" means that through the rapture of absorption— characterized by elation, which is a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) associated with the absorption-mind—
it gladdens that very absorption-mind by way of the co-nascent and other conditions, as well as by way of the condition of absorption (*jhāna-paccaya*).
And by nourishing it and manifesting a state of extreme joy, he gladdens and rejoices.
"Making it the object" means that the insight-consciousness (vipassanā-citta) proceeding by making sublime joy associated with jhāna its object—
the practitioner, manifesting a state of extreme joy through that very joy which has become the object, is said to "gladden and rejoice."
"Placing it evenly" means placing it by way of absorption (appanā) so that it does not lean even slightly toward either the side of dullness or the side of agitation;

rather, it is neither depressed nor exalted, and is perfectly established through the balanced practice of the faculties or through the attainment of imperturbability (āneñja) by reaching the pinnacle of concentration. "By penetration of the characteristics" means...
By means of piercing through each characteristic, such as impermanence, there is an awakening moment by moment.

"Momentary one-pointedness of mind" is concentration that lasts for only a single moment. For even this, proceeding uninterruptedly in a single mode toward its object and remaining unoverpowered by opposing states, places the mind immovably as if it were absorbed.
Therefore it is said: "When it has arisen in this way," and so forth.
"Separating" means separating by way of liberation through suppression; the meaning is that he abandons the hindrances.
"At the moment of insight" refers to the moment of contemplating dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*). For dissolution is indeed the ultimate limit of impermanence;
therefore, the practitioner who contemplates dissolution through that [moment] sees the entire range of conditioned phenomena as impermanent by way of the mind.

He contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent; because that which is impermanent is suffering, and because that which is suffering is non-self, he contemplates that very thing as suffering, not as pleasure, and contemplates it as non-self, not as self.

Furthermore, since that which is impermanent, suffering, and non-self is not to be delighted in, and that which is not to be delighted in is not to be craved, therefore, by following the observation of its dissolution—
When one sees the conditioned state as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," one becomes disenchanted with it, not delighted;
one becomes dispassionate, not impassioned. Thus becoming disenchanted and dispassionate, by means of mundane knowledge alone, one brings about the cessation of lust and does not cause its arising;
this is the meaning. Alternatively, he is thus dispassionate regarding what has been seen.
That which has become conditioned formations, when seen thus by one’s own knowledge, ceases and does not arise;
the meaning is that one attends only to its cessation, not to its arising. One who practices in this way relinquishes and does not grasp—this is what is meant.
For this contemplation of impermanence and so forth involves the complete abandoning of the defilements along with the formative activities of the aggregates.
Because one sees the defects of the conditioned and, by inclining toward its opposite, Nibbāna, leaps into it, this is called both "renunciation as relinquishing" and "renunciation as leaping.

Therefore, the practitioner endowed with that [insight] relinquishes the defilements and leaps into Nibbāna in the manner described. Hence it was said: "At the moment of insight, through the contemplation of impermanence..."

“Liberating and releasing the mind from the perception of permanence... [and so on] ...liberating and releasing the mind from grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment, he breathes in and breathes out.

In this context, the contemplation of what is impermanent as “impermanent” is the *aniccānupassanā* (contemplation of impermanence). It is the impermanence of the phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.

This is the name for insight that has been set in motion after having been grasped. "Perception of permanence" refers to the false perception that occurs regarding conditioned phenomena as "permanent" and "eternal.
By means of the term "perception," the inclusion of mind and views should also be understood. This same method applies to the perception of pleasure and so forth.
"Contemplation of disenchantment" refers to the contemplation that proceeds by way of becoming disenchanted with the formations (*saṅkhāra*).
"From delight" means from craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*). "By the contemplation of fading away" means by the contemplation that occurs in the manner of fading away;
thus it is said, "liberating from lust. "By the contemplation of cessation" means by the contemplation of the cessation of formations (*saṅkhāra*);
or rather, it is the contemplation such that formations simply cease and do not arise again in the future as renewed existence.
Contemplation of cessation. For this desire for deliverance has now reached the stage of strength; therefore, it is said: "while liberating from arising.
Contemplation that occurs in the mode of relinquishing is the contemplation of relinquishment (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*).
"From grasping" should be understood here as grasping by way of permanence and so forth, or as grasping at rebirth-linking.
Regarding the phrase "contemplating as impermanent" (*aniccanti anupassī*), or "one whose habit is to contemplate the impermanent," meaning "one who contemplates impermanence" (*aniccānupassī*):
here, one must clarify the fourfold set—what is impermanent, how it is impermanent, what is the contemplation of impermanence, and for whom there is the contemplation of impermanence.
To demonstrate this, he said, "Impermanence is to be understood," and so forth. In that context, "permanent" (*nicca*) means constant (*dhuvam*).

Eternal like Nibbāna; not permanent, thus impermanent, possessing arising and passing away, and in its essential nature being conditioned phenomena—thus he said "impermanent," referring to the five aggregates. Why? Because of the states of arising, vanishing, and change; the meaning is because of the presence of arising, vanishing, and change.
Therein, the arising of conditioned phenomena by means of causes and conditions is their coming into being, their manifestation, and their acquisition of selfhood after having not existed.
Arising is the appearance of things that have arisen; their momentary cessation is destruction or passing away; and alteration through aging is changeability.

For just as there is no difference in the substance when the state of arising has passed into the state of dissolution, so too there is no difference in the substance during the state known as "stability," which is the phase facing dissolution.
Wherever the conventional term "aging" applies, therefore, there is [no difference] even for a single phenomenon.

Aging is joined [to the entity], which is called momentary aging. Furthermore, one must necessarily accept that there is no difference in the substance throughout its states of arising and dissolution;
otherwise, it would follow that "one thing arises and another dissolves.
It is with reference to this momentary aging that he says "alteration."
Because those three characteristics exist within the aggregates, there is the conventional designation "impermanence" for them;
and because impermanence is the conventional designation for that triad of characteristics, it was said: "Impermanence is their very arising, passing away, and change.

Having stated this, [the author] says "or non-existence after having been" and so forth, in order to show specifically that the term "impermanence" is used for the momentary cessation of phenomena. In that context, because it is preceded by arising...
The apprehension of non-existence as having been [previously] existent. By this, he shows that the state of destruction is preceded by the state of manifestation.
"In that very mode" means in the mode of production. "By momentary dissolution" means by momentary cessation.

"Of that impermanence" refers to the impermanence characterized as momentary dissolution. "By that contemplation" refers to the aforementioned contemplation of impermanence. "Endowed with" means the practitioner has become possessed of it.

“Destruction” (*khaya*) is the dissolution of formations (*saṅkhārā*). “Fading away” (*virajjana*) is their very crumbling; fading away is destruction, thus it is “destruction-and-fading-away,” which is momentary cessation.
“Absolute fading away” (*accantavirāga*) means that when this [state] is attained, formations fade away and cease absolutely;
it is Nibbāna. Therefore he said: “‘Destruction-and-fading-away’ is the momentary breaking up of formations. ‘Absolute fading away’...”

"...Nibbāna. It occurs by way of seeing both: its occurrence as insight should be connected with the contemplation of destruction and fading away, and its occurrence as the Path with the contemplation of absolute fading away.

Alternatively, it occurs as insight by way of the contemplation of destruction and fading away from the perspective of the object, and by way of the contemplation of absolute fading away due to being inclined toward that [object].

Furthermore, its occurrence should be understood by way of the contemplation of destruction and fading away through non-delusion regarding the path, and by way of the contemplation of absolute fading away with respect to the object.
By the phrase "the same method applies," since the commentary on the meaning—beginning with "there are two kinds of cessation:
cessation as destruction and absolute cessation"—is indicated according to the method stated under the term "contemplating fading away," therefore...

By substituting the term "cessation" for the term "dispassion," its commentary on the meaning should be understood here according to the method stated in the passage beginning, "The destruction of formations, their vanishing.

Relinquishment (*paṭinissajjana*) is the abandoning or giving up of what is to be abandoned, either by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*) or by way of complete eradication (*samuccheda*). This is relinquishment as renunciation (*pariccāga-paṭinissagga*).
Likewise, "launching out" (pakkhandana) refers to the relinquishing of one's own self into the unconditioned (visaṅkhāra), which is the relinquishment of all acquisitions (upadhi);
or, because it is inclined toward that and has that as its object, it is the launching out into that state. Regarding the phrase "by way of its specific factor" (tadaṅgavasena):
first, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) abandons the perception of permanence by way of abandoning through its specific factor; while so abandoning, it...

And by means of its non-occurrence in that way, one relinquishes—by way of making them not to occur—all those defilements which would arise in the future through the apprehension [of things] as "permanent," along with the volitional formations rooted in them, and the resultant aggregates rooted in both;
likewise for the perception of suffering and so forth. Therefore he said: "For insight, by way of its specific factor (tadaṅga), together with..."

“By means of the formative activities of the aggregates, one abandons the defilements. By “seeing the fault in the conditioned” is meant seeing the faults such as impermanence in the conditioned states belonging to the three planes of existence.
“The opposite of that” refers to [the state] characterized by permanence and so forth. “Inclination toward that” means being intent upon that.
“Enters” means it penetrates; it is as if it were penetrating. Together with the formative activities of the aggregates, the defilements...

"He relinquishes" means that when the defilements have been relinquished by the path, through the production of the state of being subject to non-arising, the volitional formations and the aggregates rooted in them become "relinquished" in the sense of being incapable of arising; thus it is said that the path relinquishes all of them.
"Both" refers to insight-knowledge and path-knowledge. For even path-knowledge [is the relinquisher] of change-of-lineage knowledge.
It is called "contemplation" (*anupassanā*) because it occurs subsequently to the seeing of Nibbāna.
This fourth tetrad is stated solely by way of pure insight (*suddha-vipassanā*), whereas the preceding three were stated by way of both serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*).
Thus, the development of mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases should be understood by way of these four tetrads.
Thus, it should be understood that this mindfulness of breathing, when developed by way of these sixteen bases, is of great fruit and great benefit.
Furthermore, its great benefit is shown by such passages as, "Bhikkhus, when concentration through mindfulness of breathing is thus developed," by way of the state of peace and so forth.
Its great benefit should also be seen in its capacity to cut off discursive thought (*vitakka*).

For this [mindfulness of breathing], by virtue of its peaceful, sublime, and refreshing state of blissful abiding, cuts off the mind’s wandering hither and thither due to applied thoughts (*vitakka*) that act as obstacles to concentration, and makes the mind face exclusively toward the object of the breath.
Therefore it is said: "Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of applied thoughts. For the fulfillment of true knowledge and liberation (*vijjā-vimutti*).
Furthermore, its great benefit should be understood even in its fundamental nature. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness;
the four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven factors of enlightenment..."
“When cultivated and frequently practiced, it fulfills true knowledge and liberation.
Furthermore, its great benefit should be understood from the fact that it brings about the full comprehension of even the final in-and-out breaths. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Rāhula, when mindfulness of breathing has been thus developed and thus frequently practiced, even those final in-and-out breaths cease only when they are fully known, not when they are unknown.”
In this context, by way of cessation, there are three types of "final" (carimaka): final in respect to existence (bhava), final in respect to jhāna, and final in respect to death (cuti).

For among existences, inhalation and exhalation occur in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) but do not occur in the fine-material or immaterial existences (rūpa- and arūpabhava); therefore, they are "final in respect to existence.
Among jhānas, they occur in the first three jhānas but do not occur in the fourth; therefore, they are "final in respect to jhāna."

However, those [mental states] which arise together with the sixteenth consciousness prior to the death-consciousness and cease along with that death-consciousness are called "the final ones at death" (*cuti-carimaka*).
These are what is intended here by the term "final" (*carimaka*).
It is said that these become manifest to a bhikkhu devoted to this meditation subject when the object of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) has become well-mastered.
Because they have been grasped. For when one adverts to the arising of the sixteenth consciousness immediately preceding the death-consciousness, its arising becomes clear to them;
when one adverts to its presence, its presence becomes clear to them; and when one adverts to its dissolution, its dissolution becomes clear to them.
This is for one who has attained Arahantship by developing this meditation subject other than that [previously mentioned].

For a bhikkhu’s lifespan may be either limited or unlimited; however, for one who has attained Arahantship by developing this mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases, the lifespan is indeed limited.
Knowing, "Only this much of my life-process will now proceed, and no further," he—by his own natural law—performs the maintenance of the body, such as dressing and robing, and so forth.

Having completed all his duties, he closed his eyes, like the Elder Tissa who dwelt at Koṭapabbata Vihāra, like the Elder Mahātissa who dwelt at Mahākarañjiya Vihāra, like the Elder Piṇḍapātika who dwelt in Devaputtaraṭṭha, and like the two brothers, the Elders who dwelt at Cittalapabbata Vihāra. Herein, this is an illustration by way of a single instance:
it is said that on the day of the full-moon Uposatha, one of the two brother Elders [recited] the Pātimokkha.
Having been reinstated and surrounded by the community of monks, he went to his own dwelling place.

Standing on the walking path, at the hour of dusk during the bright fortnight, he saw the vault of heaven as if being drenched on all sides by streams of milk and the surface of the earth as if covered with sand, resembling a sheet of silver;
and seeing this, he thought: "How delightful indeed is this time and place, so suited to my own disposition!"
“How long must this burden of suffering be carried? Reflecting thus upon his own life-faculties (*āyu-saṅkhāra*), he addressed the community of monks:
“How have you previously seen monks passing into final Nibbāna? Thereupon, some said:
“We have previously seen them passing into final Nibbāna while still seated on their seats. Others said: “We have seen them in the air, having crossed their legs...”
“...sitting with legs crossed. The Elder said, “Now I shall show you my final passing away while walking in the meditation path (caṅkama).

Then, having drawn a line across the middle of the walkway, he said, “Having gone from this end of the walkway to the opposite end and returning, I shall attain final nibbāna upon reaching this line,” and having descended onto the walkway, [he went] to the far side.
Having gone and returning, at the very moment he stepped upon the writing with one foot, he attained final Nibbāna.
The commentary on the discussion of concentration through mindfulness of breathing is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the first formal proclamation.
167. Even though the Noble Ones neither took their own lives nor caused one another to take their lives,
nor did they approach Migalaṇḍika the false ascetic and incite him [to do so], nevertheless,
because Noble Ones were also included among those who died by the three aforementioned modes, it is said that [the assembly] was "mixed with noble persons."

For the Noble Ones (ariya) have neither committed the taking of life, nor incited others to do so, nor approved of it. Alternatively, since there are indeed Noble Ones who, while still ordinary worldlings (puthujjana),
caused their own death by developing insight (vipassanā) at the moment of death and thereby attained the Noble Path (ariyamagga),
the same principle applies to the taking of one's own life.
Because noble ones (ariya) are also present and thus the assembly is mixed with noble persons, the term "foolish men" (moghapurisa) was not used.
Regarding the phrase "those bhikkhus," it was stated as "How indeed, bhikkhus, could those bhikkhus deprive even themselves of life?"— here,
instead of saying "foolish men," it is said "those bhikkhus."
Commentary on the Discussion of Subsequent Rules (Anupaññatti-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 168.
"Having minds bound to women" means being inflamed by desire and lust, having a state of longing; thus he said, "inflamed and longing.
The praise of the virtues of death is preceded by seeing the danger in life; thus he said, "in life..."
"Having shown the danger," [it continues]: "What is the use of this evil, wretched life for you?"—this is the demonstration of the danger in living.
However, "Death is better for you than life," and so forth, should be understood as a praise of the virtues of death.

Because greed and the other [defilements] are exceedingly predominant, an act committed impulsively without careful reflection is called a *kibbisa* (sinful transgression); thus he said: "A *kibbisa*..."
“Hasty action is the surging of defilements such as greed. Why is this said? Because this statement refers specifically to the group of six (Chabbaggiyas).
The word *mata* (dead) is a term for a state (*bhāva*), as in the case of words like *gata* (gone); thus he says, “your death. *Katakāla* means the time for death has been made.
Alternatively, *kāla* is a synonym for death; therefore, *kata-kāla* means one whose death has been brought about.

This is the meaning. For this very reason, he said: "having passed away, having died. "Celestial" (*dibba*) means existing in the heavens; thus he said: "by those reborn in the world of the gods" (*devaloka*).
"Endowed" (*samappita*) means joined. "Possessed" (*samaṅgībhūta*) means having properly attained a state of oneness.
Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis (*Padabhājanīya-vaṇṇanā*)
172. "Ussukka-vacanaṃ" (the word for prior effort) refers to a statement concerning an action performed at a prior time.
For this is the etymological designation for a statement concerning a prior action among statements concerning prior and subsequent actions when the agent is the same.

Regarding the word "sañcicca," in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it has been formulated according to the letter by way of prior actions as follows: "having known, having fully known, having intended, and having resolved."

Instead of stating it thus, having established the person as the subject by saying "knowing and perceiving," and because the act of taking life—namely, "having willed and deliberated, there is transgression"—is explained for that specific purpose, it is said: "without paying attention to the phrasing.
Although "knowing" is stated without qualification, [the full meaning is] "one should intentionally deprive a human being of life."
Because it has been stated that "knowledge here has living beings as its object," he says, "knowing 'it is a living being' (pāṇo)," which means knowing "a sentient being (satto) goes" (ayati).
For in conventional usage, "living being" (pāṇo) refers to a sentient being, whereas in the ultimate sense, it denotes the life-faculty (jīvitindriya).

By saying "knowing 'it is a living being'" instead of saying "knowing 'it is a human form,'" he indicates that [the offense occurs] even when one does not know "this is a human," but acts solely with the perception of a sentient being.
This was stated in order to demonstrate that even for one who is killing [a human], there is the status of a *pārājika* offense.

For this very reason, in the "Fourfold Case of the Sheep" (*eḷakacatukka*), it is shown that for one who kills a human being while perceiving them as a sheep, there is an offense of *pārājika*. Therefore, instead of saying "one who has the form of a human," it is stated without qualification as "knowing it to be a living being."
Regarding the term *sañjānanto*, he states that here the prefix *sam-* has the same meaning as the word *saha* (together with):
"knowing together with that very mode of cognizing the living being. The meaning is: "knowing 'I am depriving of life together with that very mode of cognizing the living being.

Even though it is impossible for a single consciousness to have both [the living being and the act of killing] as its object simultaneously, [it is said so] because of the cognition "this is a living being" together with [the intention to take] life...
The cognition "I am depriving [him]" cannot occur in a single moment; rather, it is said "knowing together with that very [person]...

and so forth" with reference to the cognition "I am killing," while not having abandoned the perception that it is a living being. Therefore, "together with" (saddhiṃ) means "without having abandoned" (avijahitvā).

Some, however, [say]: "In phenomena whose intrinsic nature has been seen through full comprehension by knowledge (ñātapariññā), the three characteristics [are discerned] through full comprehension by scrutiny (tīraṇapariññā)."
They say that, having applied [the mind], one knows it simultaneously with its own intrinsic nature—such as "form is impermanent"—just as one knows the characteristics of impermanence and so forth;
likewise, one knows [the object] simultaneously with one's own action, thinking, "I am killing this living being.
However, other teachers do not speak thus even in that case.
"Having intended by way of murderous intention" means having thought with a murderous intention, "I shall kill this person.
"Having planned" means having delimited it with the mind thus, "I will kill. "Having resolved" means having made a firm determination.
For this reason, he said, "having dispatched a mind free from hesitation. "By way of an effort" means by way of an effort such as that performed with one's own hand (sāhatthika), and so forth.
"Of one proceeding thus" means of one proceeding according to the method already described.
Although the transgression is entirely completed by the phrase "should deprive of life," which expresses an action occurring at a subsequent time—
since the word "intentionally" (*sañcicca*) is an incomplete term— nevertheless, even an incomplete transgression is expressed by the word "intentionally."
The word-commentary “transgression” (vītikkama) is stated in order to show [the offense] having reached its conclusion. Therefore it was said:
“This is what is meant by the sense of the word ‘intentionally’ (sañcicca) reaching its ultimate limit.
“From the beginning” means from the moment of the kalala-materiality that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa). They themselves...
"Herein" (*ettha*) means "in a bed. Those for whom the womb—designated as the mother's belly—is their bed are "womb-bedders" (*gabbhaseyyaka*); these are the egg-born and the moisture-born.

The passage beginning with "whatever [is done] in the mother's womb" was stated for the purpose of showing the most subtle state of existence among those womb-bedders, not for the purpose of defining the specific basis for a *pārājika* offense.
For even humans who are spontaneously born (*opapātika*) or moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) are subject to the same basis for a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, it is not possible to deprive this human being of life at the very first moment.

For thirty types of materiality born of kamma arise simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*); and while those [materialities] remain, sixteen moments of life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*) arise and cease.
Within this interval, for the child who has taken rebirth-linking, or for his mother...
Or rather, there is no obstacle for him; this is indeed what is called "not the occasion for death.
For within a single period of sixteen mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*), there is no death for the child, because at that time the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) is impossible.

Nor is it possible for the mother to die during that same interval and then immediately thereafter conceive again, because she is subject to passing away (*cavanadhammā*) right after that moment. By the very mention of "mind" (*citta*),...

Because the remaining immaterial phenomena are included through their inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), and because the mental body (*nāmakāya*)—supported by the material body—exists only in the fivefold plane of existence (*pañcavokāra*), it is said:
"The entire rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) of the fivefold plane has been shown.
In that context, "the entire rebirth-linking of the fivefold plane" means the complete and unabridged rebirth-linking of the five aggregates, beginning with form.
The meaning should be understood in this way: it is not that every rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) within the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokārabhava) [is meant].
For that very reason, he said: “Therefore, that first consciousness... [and] the kalala-materiality—this is the very first human formation.
Regarding the phrase “the wool of a sheep born on that same day is ‘birth-wool’ (jātiuṇṇā),” some say: “Birth-wool is the wool of a high-quality sheep born in the Himalayan region.”
Others say: "There are indeed certain sheep in the Himalayas that have very fine wool. Others say: "The wool obtained by splitting open the womb of a sheep is 'jātiuṇṇā' (wool from birth).
This was stated according to the opinion of the Khuddakabhāṇakas, as they hold that [it refers to] "beings dwelling in the womb. Thus: "Of beings dwelling in the womb..."
"At the moment of rebirth-linking, the five aggregates appear simultaneously, neither before nor after one another.
At that moment, the continuity of material form known as the *kalala*—which has appeared—is minute, being only as much as could be taken up by a single effort of a small fly.
Having said this, he spoke again: "That is too much; it is like the oil that drips from the tip of a fine needle when it is withdrawn after having been immersed in it."

It was said: "the amount of a drop remaining at the tip. Having rejected that as well, it was said: "the amount of a drop remaining at the tip of a single hair after it has been extracted from oil and taken out. Having rejected that too, it was said:
"In this country, when human hair is split into eight parts, the measure of one such portion is the size of a hair of those in Uttarakuru; of that [hair]..."
It is said: "Just a drop remaining at the tip of a wick drawn out from clarified sesame oil. Having rejected even that, the Khuddakabhāṇakas say:
"Jātiuṇṇā is a fine [wick]; having placed a single strand of it into clarified sesame oil, it is just a drop remaining at the tip of the wick as it is drawn out and drips down.
However, the Saṃyuttabhāṇakas say: "With three strands of jātiuṇṇā..."
They say that the *kalala* is the size of a drop of oil resting on the tip of a blade of kusa grass.
The word “clear” (*accha*) clarifies the aforementioned meaning by means of a synonym as “limpid” (*vippasanna*).
“Cream of ghee” (*sappimaṇḍo*) refers to clarified ghee. The word “just as” (*yathā*) should be brought here and connected to this as well; for even the cream of ghee...
Only that which is the size of a drop of dew is intended here. "Having such a resemblance of color" means delimited by the aforementioned size and shape.
Alternatively, "having such a resemblance of color" means having such a color and such a shape.
Or, *paṭibhāga* means "resemblance," in the sense of sharing a likeness or attaining similarity. Such a resemblance of color, in terms of both color and shape, is [the counterpart sign].
"And because it has a resemblance to this, it is called 'having a similar appearance' (*evaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ*).
"It is called *kalala*" means that the personal existence (*attabhāva*), which consists of primary elements and derived matter and proceeds by way of a continuum, is designated as *kalala*.
"Of one with a lifespan of one hundred years" is merely an illustration, since there are also humans whose lifespans are less or more than that.

"Even in the *kalala* stage" refers to the personal existence designated as *kalala*, which occurs by way of a continuous stream within the first seven days, and it is with reference to this that he speaks—namely, that it is possible to deprive such a being of life.

"Or after that" is said with reference to those who have reached the state of *abbuda* and so forth during the second week and subsequent periods. But is it not the case that arisen phenomena cease only through their own inherent nature (*sarasanirodha*)?
Since it is impossible to effect an interruption in the midst of what is ceasing, why was it said: “Therefore... [he] cuts off and obstructs the life-faculty”?
To this he says: “It is called ‘obstructing’ because it obstructs the continuity of the life-faculty.
And how is this meaning to be understood? To this he says: “This meaning,” and so forth.
Here it is asked: among conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), which cease in every moment by their very nature, who is the slayer and who is slain?

If it is the continuum of mind and mental factors (*cittacetasika-santāna*), then because it is formless (*arūpa*), it is incapable of being disturbed by means of cutting, breaking, and so forth, nor is it susceptible to such disturbance.

If, on the other hand, it is the continuum of material form (*rūpa-santāna*), then because it is insentient (*acetana*), like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, there can be no cutting or the like therein.

Taking life occurs, as in the case of a dead body. The application for taking life—the aforementioned striking with a weapon and so forth—might occur either in past formations, or in future ones, or in present ones. In this regard, it cannot occur in the past or the future because they no longer exist;
nor can it occur in the present, because formations are momentary and by their very nature cease as soon as they arise.

When [the body] is already facing destruction, the effort [of striking] would be purposeless; and since destruction is devoid of a cause, death is not caused by the effort of striking with a weapon or similar means.

Furthermore, because conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are inactive, to whom does that effort belong? And because of their momentariness, since the action terminates at the very moment it arises simultaneously with the intent to kill, to whom is the bond of the kamma of taking life attached?
It is said: A mass of formations (saṅkhāra) designated as a "being," accompanied by the volition to kill, kills.

By means of that [volition], the collection of material and immaterial phenomena—which has lost its vitality-consciousness (jīvitindriya), which is the basis for the conventional usage of the term "dead," and which would otherwise be subject to arising had the aforementioned murderous application not been performed—is killed;
or else, the mere continuum of mind and mental factors is killed, even though it is not the actual object of the murderous application.

In the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokārabhava), because its continuity depends upon the continuity of material form (rūpasantāna), when that continuity is disrupted by an effort applied by another to sever the life-faculty (jīvitindriya)—

an effort which brings about the arising of dissimilar material forms that obstruct the production of those [original forms]— then a cessation occurs. Thus, there is no impossibility of the taking of life (pāṇātipāta),
nor is the taking of life causeless, nor is the effort devoid of purpose with respect to present formations (saṅkhāra).
Because of the non-arising of the aggregate of formations—which is due to arise immediately thereafter by virtue of the application already performed—there is no causeless death;

for momentary formations are not intended here as "death" in the sense of momentary death, and because, according to the method already stated, the death of the continuum possesses a cause. Nor is there an act of taking life that is devoid of an agent.
Because the designation of "agent" is established for causes that— though themselves inactive— are helpful by their mere presence and are determined to produce their respective fruits,
as in the expressions, "the lamp illuminates" or "the moon, the maker of night, shines. Furthermore,
it is not intended that the mere aggregate of mind and mental factors, coexisting with the intention to kill, constitutes the act of taking life.

Because one admits [the identity] precisely of that which remains stable by way of a continuum (*santāna*), and because the accomplishment of purposeful action (*atthakiriyā*) is observed in the case of lamps and the like as they proceed by way of a continuum,
there is indeed one who is bound by the kamma of taking life. This analysis should also be clarified, as applicable,
in the cases of taking what is not given and so forth.
“It is not possible to deprive [him] of life” means it is not possible to deprive him of life by means of an effort.

“Merely seven or eight thought-moments” is stated according to the opinion of the Khuddakabhāṇakas. However, the Saṃyuttabhāṇakas, having mentioned two continuities—namely, the continuity of form and the continuity of the formless—state:
“For one who has stepped into water, as long as the line of water stepped upon at the bank has not settled; for one who has come from a journey...”
As long as the state of warmth in the body has not subsided; as long as the state of darkness has not vanished for one who has entered the womb after coming from the light;

or as long as the flickering of the eyes has not subsided for one who, having attended to the meditation subject within the womb, looks out by opening a window during the day—this is called the continuity of form (*rūpa-santati*). It lasts for two or three thought-moments of impulsion (*javana*).
Having stated, "It is called the immaterial continuity," they say, "Both of these are called present by way of continuity.
However, the Majjhimabhāṇakas say: "That which is included within one or two moments of continuity is 'present by way of continuity.
In that regard, for one who has been sitting in darkness and then goes to a place of light, the object does not yet become manifest. But until it becomes manifest—"
It should be understood that within this interval, one or two cycles of material or immaterial continuity are occurring.
Just as for one who has walked in the open air and entered a small inner room, the forms do not immediately become manifest;
rather, until they do become manifest, one or two cycles of material or immaterial continuity occur within that interval.
It should be understood as follows: even after standing at a distance and seeing the hand-movements of the washermen and the striking of their bells and drums, one does not yet hear the sound.
Within that interval, until one hears it, one hundred and twenty moments (khaṇas) should be understood to pass.
Furthermore, in this context, for one who has entered a room from a place of light, let alone for one already sitting there, [the process continues] until the visible form...
It becomes manifest; therein, for half the duration it is not clearly apparent, and for half the duration it is clearly apparent.
Taking both of these together, it is said, "two rounds of the life-continuum. This, however, is not common to all;
for some, it becomes manifest even quickly, which is why the inclusion of the word "one" was made, as in "one or two rounds of the life-continuum."
"By way of a homogeneous continuity (*sabhāga-santati*)" means by way of a homogeneous continuity consisting of the wholesome, unwholesome, joy, equanimity, and so forth.
By this, the immaterial continuity is shown. And "merely seven or eight impulsion moments" should be understood as referring specifically to sense-sphere impulsions, not to other types of impulsions;
for those [other impulsions] do not have a limited duration, and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and other states that arise in the interval are also included within them.
[They] should be seen. By the phrase "or as far as it comes from heat," etc., he shows the continuity of material form (*rūpa-santati*).

"Darkness occurs" means that the darkness does not disappear. Here, the "present by way of continuity" (*santati-paccuppanna*) is what is found in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), while the "present by way of duration" (*addhā-paccuppanna*) is [what is found] in the Sutta.
For instance, in the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta*, referring to the present by way of duration, [it says]: "And whatever, friend, is the mind... and so forth.
"Both these types of phenomena are present; if consciousness is bound to that which is present by desire and lust, then because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in it.
Delighting in it, one is swept away by present phenomena. Thus it was said. For here, "mind" refers to consciousness together with its associated mental factors.
“Dhammas” means objects as mental phenomena (*ārammaṇadhamma*). “Mind” means the mind-base (*manāyatana*). “Dhammas” means the immaterial aggregates, such as feeling and so forth.
“Both of these are present” means that both of these constitute the temporal present (*addhāpaccuppanna*). “Consciousness” means attachment-consciousness;
for that consciousness is bound to that present object by way of desire and lust. “He delights in” means...
One rejoices through delight in craving and views. Being thus disposed, because of the absence of full understanding of the objective basis (*vatthu*), one is swept away by those present phenomena;

the meaning is that one is dragged along by craving and views. And here, since it is stated that "the twelve bases are one present [time]," the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) operating therein has the immediate present as its object.
It is not known as having a momentary present object.
"A being" refers to the continuity of the aggregates (khandhasantāna), for it is there that the designation "being" applies. "Life-faculty" refers to both the material and immaterial life-faculties;
for when the material life-faculty is impaired, the other also perishes due to its connection with it. That [life-faculty] is of the very kind already described.
That method of causing the destruction of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is exactly as described below.
"Excessive destruction" (*atipāta*) means falling prematurely while still in the process of falling by its own nature; the meaning is a swift destruction that does not allow for a slow fall.

Alternatively, "excessive destruction" (*atipāta*) is the destruction [of the life-force] by surpassing it—that is, overcoming it with a weapon or the like. The "destruction of the life-force" (*pāṇātipāta*) is the destruction of a living being (*pāṇa*). By whatever volition (*cetanā*)...

When the great elements that serve as the support for the life-faculty currently functioning are subjected to an act of violence, the great elements arising conditioned by those [supporting] great elements will not arise;
the volition of killing that instigates such an application is *pāṇātipāta*.
Therefore, he said: "By which volition," and so forth.
"Striking" (paharaṇa) is the accomplishment of the intended purpose by means of a murderous volition accompanied by bodily intimation.
"Commanding" (āṇāpana) is the accomplishment of the intended purpose by means of a murderous volition accompanied by verbal intimation. For this very reason it is said:
"One who wishes to make [someone] hear does not make them hear," and so forth. "Placing near" (upanikkhipana) is the placing of swords and other such weapons near that person.
Summarizing the matter stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), he said, "In brief," and so forth. Therein, "reciting spells" (*vijjāparijappana*) means reciting mantras (*mantaparijappana*).
Now, showing the matter explained at length in the commentaries, he said, "But in the commentaries," and so forth.
Therein, "sorcerers" (*āthabbaṇikā*) are those who know the *Atharva-veda*. They employ sorcery (*āthabbaṇa*); that is, [they perform] what is prescribed by the *Atharva-veda*.
They employ the mantra according to the procedure prescribed therein.

For the practitioners of *āthabbaṇa* (sorcery), having eaten food without salt for seven days, having spread out grass, and having practiced asceticism while lying on the ground, they prepare a cemetery site on the seventh day;
standing on the seventh footprint and repeatedly turning their hands, they recite the spell (*vijjā*) with their mouths. Then, for them—
Kamma succeeds. Regarding the term *paṭisenā* (counter-army), this connects with either of the two preceding or following phrases.
"Causing calamity" (*ītiṃ uppādentī*) means they produce affliction by releasing scorpions and other such creatures for the purpose of stinging and killing.
*Īti* means that which comes (*eti*). "Calamities" (*upaddava*) refers to afflictions even greater than those. "Disease" (*pajjaraka*) means irregular fever. "Pain" (*sūcika*)...
*Pavatta-sūla* is a piercing pain that occurs as if one’s limbs and members were being pierced by needles. *Visūcikā* is acute dysentery accompanied by such piercing pain.

*Pakkhandikā* is nocturnal dysentery. *Vijjaṃ parivattetvā* means having recited one’s own lore—such as the Gandhāra-lore (*Gandhāra-vijjā*)—which has been made ready for use, by reciting it according to the sequence of mantra-chanting. *Tehi* means by those [specific] factors.
"Purpose" (*payojana*) means that which is currently occurring. "Having seen," and so forth, is stated in sequence for those [beings] afflicted by the poison of views and the like.
"In the uprooting of nāgas measuring two hundred fathoms" means in the uprooting of nāgas who stand having manifested great bodies measuring two hundred fathoms.
"Of the kumbhaṇḍas" refers to the kumbhaṇḍa deities. It is said that those deities have large bellies, and their private parts are like a jar (*kumbha*).

It is large; therefore, they are called "kumbhaṇḍas. Although Vessavaṇa is the lord of the yakkhas, his authority over the kumbhaṇḍas should be understood here as well, since it is stated that the kumbhaṇḍas die by the weapon of his eye.
"Some" refers to the Mahāsaṅghikas. "Alas, may that fetus which has entered the womb not emerge safely!"
The reading *pāṭho* is more excellent. There is also the reading: “Aho vatāyaṃ taṃ. It should be said: “This woman might not safely bring forth that fetus residing in her womb.
Regarding *kulumbassa*: it means either of the family of the womb, or of the household; thus it is said to mean *kuṭumbassa*.

They say that by “the supernormal power consisting in development” (*bhāvanāmayiddhiyā*), they refer to the supernormal power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*). [Then follows: “The breaking of the jar.”

The correlation of the similes is as follows: the loss of psychic power (*iddhi*) is like the extinguishing of a fire, and the harming of others is like the quenching of that flame. Regarding the statement, "That [harming] is merely their wish," this is the analysis:

you speak of harming others by means of psychic power; yet this so-called psychic power consists of the psychic power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*), the psychic power of transformation (*vikubbaṇa-iddhi*), the psychic power of mind-made form (*manomaya-iddhi*), the psychic power of the expansion of knowledge (*ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi*), the psychic power of the expansion of concentration (*samādhivipphāra-iddhi*), noble psychic power (*ariya-iddhi*), and the psychic power born of the ripening of kamma (*kammavipākaja-iddhi*).

There are ten kinds of success (*iddhi*): success through merit, success consisting of knowledge (*vijjāmayiddhi*), and so forth; it is called "success" in the sense of succeeding due to the condition of right application in various instances.
Among these, which kind of success do you speak of? "Success consisting of meditation. But can there be an act of harming others through success consisting of meditation?
"Yes, it occurs once. For example, as when water-filled [buckets] are placed upon a burning house..."
Just as when a pot is struck, the pot itself breaks, and when fire is struck, it goes out, even so,

if an act of harming another occurs even once through psychic power consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya-iddhi*), that power is destroyed from that point onward. Therefore, having told them, "By means of psychic power consisting of meditation,
an act of harming another does not occur even once, nor twice," one should question those who come seeking to be instructed.
“Is the supernormal power consisting in development wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate? Is it associated with pleasant feeling, painful feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
Is it accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought and with sustained thought only, or without applied thought and without sustained thought?
Does it belong to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere?”
However, those who know this question will say: “The supernormal power consisting of development (bhāvanāmayiddhi) is either wholesome or indeterminate;
it is experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling only; it is without applied thought and sustained thought only; and it belongs exclusively to the fine-material sphere. They should be asked:
“To which category among the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, does the volition of taking life belong? Those who know will say:

“Volition regarding the destruction of life is exclusively unwholesome, exclusively to be experienced as painful, exclusively accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and belongs exclusively to the sense-sphere.

This being so, [you argue that] “your statement does not accord with the triad of the wholesome, nor with the triad of feeling, nor with the triad of applied thought, nor with the triad of the limited. But is such a great Sutta then useless? It is not useless.

You, however, do not know its meaning. Regarding the phrase "one possessed of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind," it is not psychic power consisting of meditation (*bhāvanāmaya-iddhi*) that is intended here;
rather, it is the psychic power of sorcery (*āthabbaṇa-iddhi*) that is intended. For that [latter] is what is obtainable here, as it is said, "it is obtained.
It is called *hāra* because it is to be taken away or deposited; thus he says "or else" (*atha vā*), etc., explaining it as *hāraka* because it is itself a taking away—that is, it takes away life.
He states two alternatives: "either the weapon should be placed down, or one who carries the weapon [should be found].

Although it should have been said "hāraka-satthaṃ" (weapon-carrier), it is stated as "satthahārakaṃ" by placing the qualifier after the headword. He states the intended meaning as "one should act in such a way that [the weapon] is obtained.
"Upanikkhipeyya" means "he should seek out"—this is the ultimate sense of that term.
...it shows. "Otherwise" means: if, instead of taking the sense of "he should search for" (*pariyeseyya*) to be "he should set it down," the intended meaning were merely the act of searching itself.
"By the mere act of searching" (*pariyiṭṭhamattena*) means by the mere fact of having searched.
This is because the meaning expressed by the phrase "or he should search for someone to bring him a knife" conforms to the literal expression (*byañjana*).
Because it was not stated [explicitly] that [the weapon] must be complete, he said, "without taking into account the specific form (byañjana).

It is called *sattha* because it pierces (*sasati*) or harms (*hiṃsati*), or because one pierces or harms by means of it; thus, since even clubs, stones, and so forth are included under the category of *sattha*, he said:
"In order to show specifically what kind of *sattha* is included here as being employed by a stationary agent."

*Vuttāvasesaṃ* means what remains after what has been stated by means of the "asī" (sword) and so forth. *Laguḷaṃ* is a designation for a club. *Satthasaṅgaha* refers to the inclusion of the "weapon" mentioned in the matrix (*mātikā*) under the term "one who carries a weapon.
Because... [omission] ...therefore, it should be understood that the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) was stated by dividing [the subject] into two parts;
this is a demonstration of the distinctions in the method of analysis (*vibhaṅga*) stated previously.

Regarding the phrase "or falls into hell," etc.: here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), all means of death are included—both those explicitly stated later, such as "or falls from a precipice," and those not yet mentioned, such as "or falls from a tree.
For this very reason it was said: "It is not possible to state everything in its specific form.
"By the method stated later" refers to the second clause, which is stated later by way of a conclusion.

Because it follows the method already stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). "It has already been stated according to its meaning" means that for the purpose of demonstrating the manifold nature of the means of death, once a portion of them has been shown, it is intended that everything has indeed been stated;
for it is not possible... [to speak]—the meaning is that it is not possible to state every single means of death in its specific form by concluding with "or falling from a tree," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "Death is better than life," since the word *iti* indicates the death mentioned there, he spoke thus—taking that death as well—to show the meaning: "The meaning is 'one whose mind is on death, one whose thought is on death.
He said it was spoken for the purpose of illustrating the meaning of the mind (*citta*), because the word *citta* has various meanings such as "variegated" and so forth.
This word "citta" should not be understood here as being used in any other sense; rather, it should be known as being used specifically for consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
It is stated for the purpose of restricting its meaning. By this, he shows that there is no room here for the fault of tautology.
Although the meaning has not yet been fully explained, even after citing the phrase "thus mind and intellect" (*iti cittamanaso*), [it refers to] that which is indicated by the word "iti."

This is stated because death is not something to be clung to. However, by means of the word *tāva*, he clarifies that the meaning of the particle *iti* will be explained later in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) on the phrase "mental intention" (*cittasaṅkappo*) as "perceiving death," and so forth.
For there, having taken the meaning designated by the particle *iti*—namely, that which is reckoned as death—it says: "perceiving death, intending death, aiming at death."
It has been stated. For this very reason, he said: “In this phrase ‘cittasaṅkappo,’ the word *iti* must be supplied by virtue of the context. He asked, “Why must it be supplied?
and replied with the words beginning “For this [is]...”. But how is this to be understood?

He replied with the words beginning “For thus of it...”. “Of it” means of the word *iti*. “That very meaning” refers to the meaning designated as death. [This is seen] in such passages as “one who perceives death,” and so forth.
For the word *hi* has the meaning of "death"; "perception" (*saññī*) and so forth are the meanings of the word *saṅkappa*.

However, it should be understood that here the word *citta* signifies "variety," while the word *saṅkappa* is shown to have three meanings by way of perception (*saññā*), volition (*cetana*), and intention (*adhippāya*).
Therefore he said: "Citta is a saṅkappa of various kinds," and so on. By the word *adhippāya*...
To the question, "What is meant here? he says: "Intention (adhippāya) should be understood as applied thought (vitakka).
This is stated not merely to show that this is the name for applied thought alone; rather, it is said to demonstrate that it is the name for [the entire process].
It should be understood as having a high pitch because it is manifest and gross, and as having a low pitch because it is unmanifest and subtle.
174. Since the word *kāya* (body) can also apply to a part of the body, he says “or with the hand,” and so forth. “With a weapon” (*paharaṇena*) means with a knife (*satthena*).
For it is called a “weapon” (*paharaṇa*) because they strike (*paharanti*) with it.

“One is bound by action” means one is bound by the action of taking life; what is meant is that [the action] is accomplished through the act of taking life. Regarding the phrase “let anyone die,” here, for whom—
It should be understood that the murderous volition (*vadhaka-cetanā*) arises with reference to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of only a single individual;

it does not arise with reference to the life-faculty of one who dies from a blow, nor with reference to a group. "In both ways" means by way of whether there is a formal declaration (*uddesa*) or no declaration.
Even though the murderous mind has a present object, the life-faculty is its object in the sense of cutting off its continuity.
He said, "It proceeds after having been done," and so forth, with the words "or later by that very same disease.
For when the continuity [of life] is severed by producing such an application, the murderous mind proceeding at that time becomes bound by the kamma at the mere moment of striking.
And even in the case of a human Arahant, if a blow with a weapon or poison is administered while he is still an ordinary person (puthujjana), [the kamma is likewise bound].
If he dies while still an Arahant after having attained that state, he is indeed a murderer of an Arahant.
However, the gift given during his time as a worldling (*puthujjana*) which he consumes after attaining Arahantship is considered a gift given to a worldling alone.
But is it not the case that even what is consumed after attaining Arahantship remains a gift to a worldling, because it was given during the period when he was a worldling?

If this is so, why is one who strikes with the intent to kill while still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) considered a murderer of an *arahant*—and not a murderer of an ordinary person—once he has attained *arahantship* and dies from that very blow? It is because of the presence of a distinction.
For a gift consists merely in the relinquishment of the object to be given; likewise, the volition of giving takes the object to be abandoned as its focal point (*ārammaṇa*).

The act of giving becomes merely a relinquishing; that relinquishing is like making something the property of another. Therefore, it is given to the very person for whom that thing was made the property, and thus it is not a killing.

For that indeed constitutes killing only when there is the fulfillment of these five factors: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the volition to kill, the means employed, and death by that means—not when they are incomplete.
Therefore, only the killing of one who has attained *arahatta* constitutes the crime of being an "Arahant-killer," not the killing of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).

For when one intends, "I shall kill this person," and directs the desire for death toward a particular continuum, there is no difference in that continuum—even though a distinction exists between the states of an ordinary person and one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*)—due to the nature of the preliminary effort and the moment of death. And when the purpose is accomplished...
At that time, his state of having exhausted the taints (āsava) has ceased; therefore, one must conclude that he is indeed a murderer of an Arhat.
"With another mind" means with a mind that lacks the intention to kill, a mind desiring not to take life. "There is no taking of life" because it was struck with a mind desiring not to kill.
Although the first blow cannot by itself cause death, if it receives a second [blow],...

If one is capable [of killing], it becomes the cause for the destruction of life; therefore, because of the connection with the phrase "the effort and by that, death," it is logical that the bond of kamma occurs through the very first blow, not the second, since that was administered by another's mind.
Thus it is said: "Even if [the victim] dies from both, he is bound by the kamma of the first blow alone."

"For the purpose of clarifying the distinction between actions and offenses" means for the purpose of elucidating the classification of actions such as those of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) and the like,
and the classification of offenses such as the *pārājika* and the like. He said this because one is indeed bound by the action according to its basis,
since the volition that precedes the thought "I am killing a sheep" is present at that time within the determinative volition that thinks "I shall kill this [being]."

“Because of the existence of the volition [thinking], ‘I shall kill this being,’ and so forth. For in all cases, the preceding intentional thought (*abhisandhicitta*) is not the decisive factor, because the intended result is not accomplished by it alone;

rather, it should be understood that the murderous intent (*vadhakacitta*), its object, and the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) are the decisive factors in establishing the state of an immediate offense (*ānantariya*) and the like.
And he is a slayer means he is a killer of living beings, precisely through the kamma of taking life.
The meaning is that he becomes bound. It should be understood according to the method already stated;
that is, the *pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, and *pācittiya* offenses should be understood in their respective order.

Because the volition directed toward those of great worth—such as one’s mother, father, or an arahant—is inherently cruel, the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*) accompanied by such preliminary volition is likewise indeed cruel.

He said: "But here, the volition (cetanā) is cruel. By this, it should be understood that even when one kills one's mother, father, or others with the thought, "I will kill a sheep," because the preliminary volition is not cruel, the immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma) arising in such a manner is stated to be no more severe than the immediate retribution arising in other ways.
*Lothitakanti lohitamakkhitan*: smeared with blood. *Kammaṃ karonteti yuddhakammaṃ karonte*: while performing his duty, that is, while engaged in the act of battle.
*Yathādhippāyaṃ gateti yodhaṃ vijjhitvā pitari viddhe*: "gone according to his intention" means that after he had pierced the warrior, his father was struck.

This is stated for the purpose of showing that he went in such a manner as intended by him. However, even if his father were struck by going straight ahead in a manner not intended [by the son], yet through the intention to kill, it would be by himself...

They say that because the preliminary effort has been completed, there is no longer a breach of convention (*visaṅketa*). However, there is no immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) because there was no preliminary effort directed toward the father.
"Having resolved" refers to the explanation of the preliminary effort involving a command by way of a formal agreement (*mātikā*):
"Pierce thus" means pierce after drawing the bow thus; "strike thus" means strike after grasping the sword firmly thus.
"Strike. "Kill in this way" means: having prescribed such a method of execution, put him to death. "In the middle" means on the back of the elephant.
"By this" refers to the passage beginning with "having resolved, he commands," and so forth.

Regarding that, although the specific details of the action have not been recorded in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), they are found in the Canon (*pāḷi*) as: "Pierce in this way; strike in this way..."

Having thus stated, "Kill in this way," because a specific action is being referred to, [the author] says "Another method" and so forth, showing that he has taken and presented a specific action transmitted through the lineage of teachers by correlating it with the Canon (pāḷi). "Cutting" means the cutting off of hands and so forth.
"Breaking" means splitting open the belly and so forth; or alternatively, piercing with an arrow, cutting with a sword, [striking] with clubs and the like.
"Breaking the head, etc."—this is how the meaning should be understood here. "The conch-shell shaving" refers to the punishment of being shaved like a conch-shell.
Those who carry it out cut the skin along the boundaries of the upper lip, both ears, the crown of the head, and the nape of the neck;
they gather all the hair together into a single knot, wrap it with a stick, and pull it out. Along with the hair, the skin comes away.
Then, having rubbed a lead skull with coarse gravel, they wash it until it takes on the color of a conch shell.

By the word "and so forth" (*evamādī*), the following are included: the *bilangathālika*, the *rāhumukha*, the *jotimālika*, the *hatthapajjotika*, the *erakavattika*, the *cīrakavāsika*, the *eṇeyyaka*, the *baḷisamaṃsika*, the *kahāpaṇika*, the *khārāpatacchika*, and the *palighaparivattika*.
The phrase "a bed of straw" and so forth includes all forms of penal servitude.
Among these, "the cauldron of sour gruel" refers to the punishment involving fermented rice-water.
While undergoing that punishment, they force open the skull, take a red-hot iron ball with tongs, and cast it therein; by this, the brain—
Having boiled, it rises to the surface. "Rāhu’s mouth" refers to the torture known as Rāhu’s mouth.
While undergoing this, they force open the mouth with a wedge and set a lamp alight inside;

or, starting from the ears and the crown of the head, they gouge out the mouth with chisels until blood flows and fills the mouth. "A garland of flames" refers to [covering] the entire body with a cloth soaked in oil.
Having wrapped [the hands], they smear them [with oil]. "Hand-torches" means that having wrapped the hands with an oil-soaked cloth, they set them ablaze like lamps.
"Eraka-vattika" refers to the punishment of the *eraka*-coil. Those inflicting it begin by cutting strips of hide from below the neck and let them fall down to the ankles;
then, having bound the victim with ropes, they drag him along, and he, by his own...
Having stepped upon a hide-wheel, one falls. "Wearing bark" (*cīrakavāsika*) refers to the punishment of wearing bark.
While undergoing that, they carve it in the same manner onto a hide-wheel and place it around the waist;
starting from the waist, they carve it down and place it upon the ankles, so that the lower body appears as if clothed in a garment of bark. "A deer-skin" (*eṇeyyaka*).
The "Eneya-antelope torture": while performing this, they place iron rings on both the elbows and the knees and drive iron spikes through them;
he stands upon the ground supported by four iron spikes, and then, having surrounded him, they apply fire.
From time to time, they remove the spikes from the joints and leave him standing solely upon the four ends of his bones.
*Baḷisamaṃsika*: Having struck them with fish-hooks from both sides, they tear away the skin, flesh, and sinews. *Kahāpaṇika*:
Starting from the head, they cut the entire body with sharp axes, striking it down piece by piece the size of a kahāpaṇa coin.
*Khārāpatacchika*: Having struck the body here and there with weapons, they scrape it with leather bags filled with caustic lye.
They crush them; the skin, flesh, and sinews having fallen away, only a skeleton remains. "Turning on a bar":
having made him lie down on one side, they drive an iron spike through the ear-hole until it is fixed into the earth as one solid piece, and then, seizing him by the feet, they drag him along.
"The straw mat": a skilled executioner strips off the outer skin and flesh...
Having broken the bones with iron pincers, he seizes them by the hair and lifts them up;
it becomes a mere heap of flesh. Then, wrapping him in his hair and seizing him, they coil him around like a bundle of straw.
The connection is that after deceiving him regarding the location, he kills another. This is because the previous locations and so forth are similar in nature.
He said, "By the very mention of the object, it is included," thus: "having struck in front," and so forth.

Whether the mind has established the restriction "in front" or not, if one says, "Having struck in front, kill," and yet kills by striking elsewhere, because it was spoken with a deceptive intent (*lesa*), it constitutes a breach of the agreement (*visaṅketa*).
However, if [the intention] is simply "having struck anywhere," by the mind...

Even if one desires to kill, should the victim say, "Strike me from the front and kill me," and one, having made a pretext for him, sets aside what was thus said and kills by means of that very same intention which originated the intimation (*viññatti*), there is no discrepancy even if the blow is struck elsewhere and the person dies;
for it is not exempted from the *pārājika* offense involving a human being in its indirect application (*pariyāyena*). Thus they say.
However, some do not accept that [distinction]. "By way of a specific basis" means by way of a specific basis such as a mother and so forth.
"A specific kamma" means a specific kamma such as an *ānantariya* (immediate) deed and so forth. "A specific offense" means a specific offense such as a *pārājika* and so forth.
The phrase "this one standing in the village" mentions the village for the purpose of specifying the person, not for the purpose of specifying the location; therefore...
Because the location is not specified and the person alone is specified, there is no discrepancy in the application of the rule.
However, in cases such as "in a village," because the location is specified, a discrepancy is stated regarding one who has been killed elsewhere.
"With the tip" means with the edge of a sword. "With the hilt" means with the handle of a sword.

In the phrase “going this way,” it is the person alone who is specified by the act of going, not the posture itself. Therefore he said, “there is no ambiguity. In the phrase “only one who is going,” etc., the posture is specified. Therefore he said, “there is ambiguity.

Even when it is said, “Kill the long one,” because there are many things of long shape, and because it is not defined by a characteristic unique to others—such as “this name is long and of such a form”—it is said that “he commands without specifying. For this very reason he said:

“Whoever kills such a person as that. Here, they say: “Even though it was stated by mind with reference to one among many long-shaped beings, because it was not specified by speech, there is no discrepancy [of the offense] when another such person is killed.
Because the factor of perceiving a living being in another living being is absent, there is no transgression of taking life; thus he says, “The commander is released.”
If that is so, when there is such a restriction of space, how can it be considered "taking life"?
It should be understood that for one who restricts the space, the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of the person sitting in that space becomes the object (*ārammaṇa*).
For, while specifying the space, he intends to cause the death of whoever is sitting in that space; however, at that time, he himself is not present there. Therefore, by means of the space—
They say that one's own life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) does not become an object (*ārammaṇa*).

"Having resolved" (*adhiṭṭhāya*): thus ends the commentary on the discussion of commands and applications according to the summary outline (*mātikā*). Now begins the commentary on the discussion of messengers.
For the teacher who thus commands, there is first a *dukkaṭa* offense. If that command does not proceed according to the intended purpose, there is a *dukkaṭa* at the moment of the command.

However, if that command does proceed according to the intended purpose, then what was stated later as a *thullaccaya* occurs at the very moment of the command. Then, if he inevitably causes her to be killed...

Regarding what was stated by another [authority] that "for all [cases], there is an offense of pārājika," the meaning here should be understood as follows: for this [person], it becomes a pārājika at that very moment.
However, since this meaning can be understood through the same method explained by the Teacher below in the discussion on taking what is not given (adinnādāna), it has not been stated here.
For it was said there: "There is an offense of dukkaṭa... and so forth.
First, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the teacher who gives the command.
However, if that command proceeds according to its intended purpose, then at the moment of the command, there occurs precisely that which was stated later as a grave offense (thullaccaya).

Furthermore, if that property is inevitably lost, then at that very moment there occurs that which was stated later—"for all there is an offense of defeat (pārājika)"—and thus for this person [the offense] arises at that very instant.
"This principle—that it constitutes a *pārājika* offense—is to be understood everywhere. Regarding "it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for them as well":

this refers to the wrong-doing incurred on account of the announcement. Regarding "merely upon being accepted": here, if he necessarily accepts it, the teacher incurs a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) even prior to that;
however, it should be understood that it is not [an offense] once it has been accepted. Why, then, is it a grave offense for him? He said:
“For the great multitude was indeed led by him into evil.
The statement that “there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the one who is the root cause” is merely an illustration of the method found in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*;
