it is not, however, what the Teacher intended. Therefore he said, “This being so,” and so forth, according to the method stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.

"Atthe sati" means "when there is a purpose. "There would be no offense even in the act of accepting" means that for a murderer who accepts [the offer] saying, "Excellent, very well," there would be no offense of *dukkaṭa* in the acceptance of the killing;
thus, if there is even a *dukkaṭa* in the case of an object that is not gross, how much more so in the case of accepting a killing?
It is for the purpose of showing this that the acceptance of acting as a go-between and so forth are cited as examples.

The intention is that if there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even for one who rejoices in death by thinking, "O, may such-and-such a person be killed," how much more so for one who accepts the act of killing?

By the restriction that this wrong-doing applies only to the one who accepts [the offer], he shows that because of the lack of a prior agreement (*visaṅketa*), there is no offense at all for the instigator on account of the acceptance. However, some say: "The wrong-doing mentioned here applies only to the one who accepts."
They say that only this much is shown by way of restriction, but the *dukkaṭa* mentioned in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* regarding the one who is the root [of the offense] has not been rejected.
"In the former method" refers to the immediately preceding description of the messenger who does not disregard [the order]. "This" refers to the *dukkaṭa*.
If this is so, why was it not stated in the *Pāḷi*? He says: "Because there was no occasion for it. Therein, for the one who is the root...
Because it is stated as a *thullaccaya* (grave offense), there is no occasion to speak of a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) for the one who accepts;
thus, it was not mentioned due to the absence of such an occasion, but not because of its non-existence—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase "an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) at the moment of the command," it should be understood that he becomes a murderer of an *arahant* because his volition functions toward accomplishing the purpose by means of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) that is yet to be destroyed.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Messengers is finished.
175. Because he himself was the senior elder of the Saṅgha, it is said, "at the time of attendance. Regarding the offense of wrong-doing for every single word:
this refers to speaking not with the intention, "Let whoever hears my words memorize this," but solely out of a desire to welcome death.
Because it has been stated [in the texts], even in such words as "even thieves will not kill him," only a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is mentioned.
The connection is: "This meaning was stated by him so that he might know. *Vākyabhedaṃ* means a verbal distinction.
*Dvinnaṃ uddissa* means with reference to two, or with reference to the death of two. It refers to the volition (*cetanā*) of one who praises death for the sake of both.
Even when there is only one [act], because it can be described as "two acts of taking life," it attains a state of strength;

and because it produces suffering through the influence of repeated volition (*aparāpariya-cetanā*) over many successive births during the course of existence immediately following the rebirth-linking result (*paṭisandhi-vipāka*), it is called a "mass of unwholesomeness" (*akusala-rāsi*) due to its great karmic fruition.
This same principle applies even when death is praised for the sake of many [beings].
Thus, by such means as "having had one's head cut off" or "having fallen into an abyss," and so forth.

At the mere moment of reporting—just as at the moment of the Noble Path (ariyamagga), the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and the four right efforts (sammappadhāna) succeed by way of their respective functions—so too, although volition (cetanā) is a single entity, various acts of taking life succeed by way of their functions; thus he said, "as many as..."
“...from the destruction of life. For just as one who wishes to manifest himself as pure,
by means of the preparatory work performed with the thought “I am pure, I am pure,” brings about purity even when taking the color of one among the colors included in the mind of purification—
which has acquired a present limited object through the power of that preparation— just so, upon the death of one [person]...

Even though the murderous volition (*vadhaka-cetanā*) arises throughout the entire body, it is unable to seize the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*)—which is arising and ceasing throughout the whole body—all at once;

rather, by taking as its object the life-faculty that has reached a certain stage and is functioning in one part, it destroys the entire life-faculty that constitutes the object. In the same way, [this is true] for a present limited object.

Even though the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of only one among the beings encompassed by the intention to kill and the desire to murder is made the object, all of them are indeed considered killed by way of the accomplishment of the act. 176.
"From whose hands" means from the hands of those relatives who have offered the invitation. "He is released by giving them the price" means [he is freed from the offense].
This was stated in order to show that the application performed by him reaches its conclusion by restoring [the object] to its original state.
Furthermore, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "However, a manuscript purchased for a price is released only after it has been returned to the owners of the manuscript.
But some say: "If one returns the manuscript to the owners but does not take back the price, one is not released."
Having stated, "Because it has not been released from the state of being 'mine' (*attaniya*)," he elaborated at length; yet that should not be accepted as the essential point.
For when the owners of the books have given the books back, how could [the scribe] not be released after receiving what was made by another and thus losing the result of his own labor?
Furthermore, the state of "being mine" is not seen in that which has been relinquished. (Gaṇṭhipada)

But why was it said: "If it has been purchased for a price, [the offense] is cleared by giving the manuscript to the owners of the manuscript and the price to those from whose hands the price was received"? Because this is unallowable (*akappiya*), since the price was taken for the sake of the manuscript.
For if one were to give the manuscript to the owner of the manuscript and take the price oneself, that too would indeed be unallowable.

Furthermore, it has been said: "Even if one were to burn that book oneself without having received the price from the owner of the book, there would still be another offense for the destruction of what was given in faith; therefore, he spoke thus. This too should not be accepted as authoritative.
Therefore, the method stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries should be regarded here as the authoritative view. [Regarding] "the praise of death..."
"‘We shall write,’ [saying this] with a single intention" refers to those acting in that manner;
however, even if they have not so agreed, for one who, with the intent to kill, performs the procedure described in that manuscript, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
"In the measurement" means in the measurement perceived by oneself. "Having scraped" means having scraped away the raised portions. "A dust-heap" (*paṃsupacchi*).

"The very last dust-pile": the volition that accomplishes the final act with the desire to complete it, thinking "this much is enough," is the volition of completion (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*). "Suttantika Theras" refers to those reciters of the Suttantas who are not proficient in the Vinaya.
It is specifically with reference to the teachers of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that they are called "Suttantika Theras" by way of derision, [thinking] "they do not know the Vinaya."
Some also say it is called *Vuttanta*. And here, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, with reference to one acting with the intention, "May they fall and die once the pit is finished;
may they not die while it is unfinished," the "final volition that brings about the conclusion" (*sabbantimā sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*) is stated.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Saṅkhepaṭṭhakathā*, [the view] starting from the first blow is given: "In this pit..."
It is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that when one acts with the intention,

"May they fall and die," the phrase "even when a single blow of a spade is given" and so forth refers to the *sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā* (the volition of final determination) which accomplishes each respective action in which they fall and die as a result of that action being performed.
Therefore, by those various methods, the arguments of the Aṭṭhakathās—

Mutual non-contradiction is logical. Alternatively, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the "final volition of completion" (*sabbantimā sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*) is stated with reference to one who completes [the work] by digging on the very same day without the undertaking having subsided;
however, in other cases, when one has dug something on one day with the intention, "Let them fall into this and die," and then [continues] on another day...
This was said with reference to one who completes [the work] by digging a little bit each day; thus, it is our view that even in this way, there is no contradiction between the various commentaries.
"By their own nature" means either unknowingly or through negligence. "Even Arahants are included" means by others...
It is stated that death occurs even for Arahants who are being protected and who do not wish to die. "In the manner previously described" refers to the method stated as:
"Those who wish to die shall die here. Regarding the phrase "having carried out what fell therein":

since there was no restriction such as "let them die right here in this pit," it is stated that the offense of *pārājika* applies even if they are killed after being carried outside the pit. In the pit...
Some say that if one falls, delays for a short while, and then seizes and kills someone who is walking away because they were not caught in the very pit [where they fell],
there is no *pārājika* offense; however, this must be examined and accepted, as the reason stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*— namely,
"because it was seized through the effort of causing them to fall"— is applicable here as well, since the intention "even if they do not wish to die" may also be present.
It is stated that even if one is unable to cross over spontaneously (*opapātika*) and dies [while attempting to do so], it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

If it is argued that because it is said "having been reborn" (*nibbattitvā*), the act of falling is not seen [to occur], there is no contradiction; for in the case of a spontaneous being, the very process of rebirth therein is what constitutes "falling.
Since he becomes a matricide when his mother—whose gender has changed after he fell upon her—is dead, he is not merely a killer of a human male.
Therefore, with the intention that the offense occurs by virtue of the person having fallen [from their status], it was stated that "the nature of falling is the criterion.

However, this is not the reason. For in the Aṭṭhakathā, it is stated only thus: "For one who deprives of life a mother or a father who has become human—even if their gender has changed—the kamma constitutes an ānantariya (immediate) deed."

In that regard, even when the gender changes, the very same continuity of the life-constituent (*bhavaṅga*) and the continuity of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), produced by a single kamma, persists and is not something else;

thus it is said, "even when the gender has changed. For the continuity of the life-constituent and the life-faculty that exists in that particular personal existence (*attabhāva*) before the change of gender remains the same even after the gender has changed, and based on that very [existence], there is the common designation of a single birth (*ekajātisamaññā*).
Nor should an objection be raised here on the grounds of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) belonging to the category of existing things (*bhāva*), because that is not what is intended;

for it is that [life-faculty] which receives the designation "continuity" (*pabandha*) due to its uninterrupted occurrence therein, or else the other [the stream of consciousness] may do so by virtue of the commonality of protecting existing things.
Thus, the objection is out of place. Therefore, even when the gender is reversed, it is precisely that same continuum produced by a single kamma—
Whether he be a female killer or a male killer, from the taking of life and the breaking of speech, he is not released from the *ānantariya* (immediate) kamma;

this much alone is to be said in that regard. But here, whatever kind of beings those sentient beings may be, at the time of death they die in their own respective birth-forms and not in another form;
and by way of that very birth-status, [they are affected] by the *pācittiya*, *thullaccaya*, and *pārājika* offenses.

It must be so. Therefore, whether it be a nāga, a supaṇṇa, or one in the form of a yakkha or a peta who falls and dies in his own animal form, in that case only a pācittiya is appropriate, not a thullaccaya, because the death occurred as an animal itself.
For this very reason, in the second Elder’s opinion, the form at the time of death is the criterion; therefore, it is stated that it is a pācittiya.
And this very interpretation is more logical; for that reason, it was stated later.
By this same method, when one falls upon a human-shaped being among animals—such as a nāga or a supaṇṇa—and it dies by one's own form, there must be an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
This being the case, [the text] says in the Pāḷi: "A yakkha or a peta, or a human-shaped being among animals..."
If it falls upon him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If, once fallen, painful feeling arises, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he dies, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*). Why was this said? Regarding this, some say:
first, having shown a *yakkha* or a *peta* standing in their own form, [the rule applies] even when they stand in another form.

In order to show those very same *yakkhas* and *petas*, it is said, “or one having the form of an animal or a human,” but this is not intended to show such an animal as a separate category. Therefore, the construction here should be made thus:
“a *yakkha* or a *peta* having the form of an animal or the form of a human. However, in all three *gaṇṭhipadas*, [it is stated]: “In the Pāḷi...”
It is stated that "having made an exception for animals who remain in human form,

a thullaccaya is mentioned [for others]," and by the phrase "the same method applies even when [the victim] has died in the form of a yakkha or a peta," it appears that a thullaccaya is indicated because the form at the time of death itself is the criterion.
"By means of no root" (*amūlena*) means without grasping any root whatsoever. "He is faultless" (*niddoso*) is said because he lacks any application (*payoga*) toward that [root].
However, showing that if he were to perform even the slightest act there, he would certainly not be released, he says:
"Thus fallen," and so forth. In this context, "thus" (*evaṃ*) means "in this way by me performed. "They shall not perish" (*na nassissanti*) means they shall not become invisible.
The intention is that they will not go [away] and will not flee. "When remorse has arisen" is said with reference to the primary factor (*mūlaṭṭha*).

However, if even the latter person, having received [the robe], does something of the kind described therein and then acts thus when remorse subsequently arises, the same rule applies to him as well. "Falls into dust and dies" refers to [a place] filled with fresh [dust].
Having thrust his foot into the dust, being unable to pull it out, he falls right there and dies.
The phrase "the earth that has been born" is stated to show that the state of firmness has reached its absolute perfection.
However, by filling it with dust and by crushing and striking it with the feet, staffs, and so forth, one brings about a state of even greater firmness than that of natural earth.

When the distinction has been made, one is indeed released even before reaching the characteristic of earth that has arisen. Regarding "he carries away the pit," he is released here because it is similar to a lotus pond.
"As soon as it is released from the hand" means as soon as it has been cast and released from the hand. Regarding "having made a fence," if he [is caught] in the snare there...
It does not produce any particular distinction of the kind already mentioned; rather, it is released once the work has been completed by itself.

Or, "it places a bedpost more firmly," meaning it fixes it together with another bedpost for the sake of stability, or it binds that very same post—which had become loose—more firmly and leaves it there. Or, "more strongly" means more solidly.
The same principle applies here as well. "A stump" refers to the stump used for binding the bedstead. Because an effort was made in every instance for the purpose of killing, he is not released.
"When remorse has arisen" means when remorse has arisen in the very person who was the primary agent (the *mūlaṭṭha*). Regarding the phrase "by that firebrand...
he is not released," it means that after having destroyed the effort previously made, [he acts] subsequently with a wholesome mind (*kusalacitta*).
"In spite of the effort being made, one is not released"—this is what should be understood by this statement, as stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
However, the following interpretation would be more appropriate here:

because the effort was made from the very beginning for the purpose of killing, once the trap-spike has been prepared and completed, then according to whichever beings die on account of it, [the result accrues] to him first of all.
"Even if one performs it otherwise with a wholesome mind after the act of taking life has been accomplished, one is not released from the offense.
"A small cord" (*rajjuka*) means a minor cord. "Twisted by oneself" means having twisted many cords together by oneself.
"Having untwisted" means having separated those cords individually. "Makes it more serious" means makes it excessively heavy. Having sought out...
"Made" means having gone to the forest, cut down a tree, and fashioned it [into a seat].
"Or a leaning-tree" is said with reference to one that grows there [already]. "For that very purpose" means for the purpose of killing.
"An uneven circle" refers to an unevenly smeared circle on beds, chairs, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having spoken, he places a sword [there]": here...
The same method applies even when one places [the medicine] down after having mentally contemplated the aforementioned type [of remedy], rather than taking it with the mouth.

"By the previous method" refers to the passage beginning, "from whose hands the price was taken," and so forth. A disease such as leprosy is called a "dissimilar disease" (*visabhāgaroga*) because it causes deformity of the body;
or, it is any disease—such as a tumor or a carbuncle—that is contrary to the maintenance of life, being either unsuitable or unfavorable for the continuation of life.
178. Regarding the phrase "or another disagreeable form" (*paraṃ vā amanāparūpaṃ*):

here, it should be understood as an external-object compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*), meaning "that which has a disagreeable form" (*amanāpaṃ rūpaṃ etassa*). The same method applies to the agreeable as well;

by this, [it is shown that] "he brings forth an agreeable form" (*manāpikaṃ rūpaṃ upasaṃharati*) means he places another agreeable form near himself, or he stands possessed of an agreeable form himself, and so forth.
This shows that [the rule] must be applied. For this very reason, it is said in a certain *gaṇṭhipada*:
"If a man, with a wicked mind, approaches a woman who has come near him thinking, 'She is my prey, let her die,' and he goes [to her], he is a killer of women."
“If he goes for the sake of begging, even though he knows [of her death], he is not a bringer of death;
for he has no concern for her and remains equanimous toward her passing.
Furthermore, it is said in that very same place:
“If one separates [a woman] while knowing, ‘My wife and my mother do not live apart,’ one who acts for that purpose is a destroyer of Māra.
But if one goes for the sake of going forth and the like, knowing [the truth], one is not a destroyer of Māra.”
"For he has no concern for them; he meets death with equanimity.
"He administers it after having adorned [the victim]" means he administers it with the intention: "Let him die having withered away from lack of food.
For this very reason it is said: "If he dies out of fear, there is a discrepancy in the agreement. "He dies having withered away from lack of food" means...
And here, "an offense entailing defeat" (*pārājika*) is to be understood as the remainder of the text. "And the stench of corpses" refers to the odors of corpses such as snakes and so forth.
"Swan-flowers" is said with reference to the wing-feathers of swans and other birds.
(179) "Without intending" is stated with reference to the lack of observation regarding an undertaking that leads to death.

He said, "By this means," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of one who does not know," this was stated with reference to the ignorance of performing an act that leads to death; thus he said, "By this, this person will die," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of one who does not intend death," this was stated with reference to the absence of an intention for death even in one who knows the means; thus he said, "death..."
“Even against one who does not desire it,” and so forth.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis (*padabhājanīya*) is finished.
Commentary on the miscellaneous discussion (*pakiṇṇakakathā*).
By the phrase "he speaks with a mind of displeasure," it is shown that the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*) is associated exclusively with painful feeling (*dukkha-vedanā*).
For although kings, due to an abundance of pleasure, may say "execute him" even while laughing, their laughter pertains to other matters, such as the pacification of a threat;
thus, the decisive volition is associated with painful feeling.
But when there is mental grief (*domanassa*), how is it that it does not manifest? To this he says: "Because it is interspersed with pleasure," and so forth.

The meaning is that because it is crowded on both sides by pleasures arising in the preceding and succeeding moments, and because there is no continuous occurrence of the arisen mental grief due to its lack of persistence, even the mental grief that has arisen at that time does not manifest.
Commentary on the Basis for Discipline 180.
"Being desirous of death" means that, because of the intention to reach heaven upon the breakup of this body, she was in fact desirous of death in the ultimate sense.
"Not knowing her state of being desirous of death" means not knowing that she was one who had such an intention and was thus desirous of death.
"They think it is so" means those who do not know their own state of seeking death; for they are certainly not unaware of the movement of their own minds.

"By way of conventional usage" means by way of the preliminary conventional usage; the intention is that because compassion is absent at the moment of the decisive volition intended for death, it is not like the releasing of a snared pig out of pity. "According to their lifespan" [is the phrase].
The meaning already stated is stated by way of another method (*pariyāyantarena*) "according to the sequence" (*yathānusandhinā*);

that is to say, it is stated according to the sequence and according to the limit of existence. Alternatively, "according to the sequence" means according to the continuous succession (*yathānuppabandhena*);
that is to say, it remains for as long as there is a continuous succession and uninterrupted occurrence of the continuity (*santāna*) within that existence.
"Without examining" means without investigating. "Moving upward or downward" means that they move up or down along the row of those seated for the sake of making room for those who arrive later.
"There is no duty of review" means there is no duty of investigation by those who have arrived later. If anything exists below, the fold of the garment...
"He does not take it," he said, "because no fold is seen on him. This reflection should be understood as applying only to what belongs to householders.
In the text, "when the pestles are raised" means when two pestles are raised while supporting one another.
"The mortar-utensil" refers to the wooden equipment brought for the purpose of the mortar. "Connected" means connected with food.
"An obstacle to food" is what is meant.

Regarding the term *aggakārika*: although one might explain the meaning as "the foremost act" (*aggakiriya*) because the word *kārikā* here expresses a state of being, since it is impossible to give an "act," it refers specifically to the alms-food itself, which is associated with that foremost act consisting of giving.
Here, because it is understood as "the foremost act" in the context of formal conduct (*upacāravutti*), he said, "the first alms-food received," and so forth.
(182–183) "A staff-mallet" means a mallet for digging. "By the transposition of case endings" means by the alteration of grammatical cases.
"The attainment of distinction" refers to concentration (*samādhi*) and insight (*vipassanā*); because these are exceedingly manifest, they are said to be "seen as if within the reach of one's hand."
It has been said. "He cuts off" means he cuts off food [thinking], "May there be no distraction regarding the attainment of distinction.
"Attainment of distinction" refers to the acquisition of supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). "Having declared" means having announced. "He cuts off;
it is not allowable" means that because the Noble Ones declare their own attained distinction only to fellow monks who possess a sense of shame (*lajjī-bhikkhu*), [in such a case]...
The meaning is that when there is a cause [for the offense], they report it; yet those bhikkhus do not seek requisites through an improper search.
Therefore, having given rise to remorse regarding the requisites sought by them, it is not permissible to cut off their food.
For because they have been declared to be of the same class, one may not cut it off. They are indeed a field of what is allowable (*kappiya-khetta*). For this very reason...

"In the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries on all three [texts], it is stated that the phrase ‘for it is proper to speak to fellow bhikkhus who possess a sense of shame’ was spoken as a reason for the statement ‘he interrupts; it is not proper.
Alternatively, the phrase ‘having explained the specific attainment’ was spoken for the purpose of showing the state of having attained the distinction."
Since it was permitted that the cutting off of food should be done only by one who has not yet attained [the goal], but not by one who has already attained it—in order to show this, it is said:
"If he cuts off his food after announcing a specific attainment, it is not allowable.
Now, as for the objection: "Do the Noble Ones announce to others the specific attainment they have themselves realized?"... [end of fragment]
“It is proper to speak to fellow monks who possess a sense of shame,” it is said. This is our preference as being more reasonable here;
this meaning is indeed shown in the *Gaṇṭhipada* as well. “Washing their belongings” means washing their robes.
“A washing-stick” means a stick for washing belongings.
184. "I am one who has remorse" means one who has become remorseful, thinking, "Might I die as a result of my action, or might I not?

In all such cases here, since a grave offense (thullaccaya) is stated for such matters when there is no death, they say that whether or not painful feeling arises through the effort performed by her, it is only a grave offense according to the word of the Blessed One, because there was no [act] constituting a defeat (pārājika).
185. "Gabbhapātanaṃ" means that by which the fetus falls; it refers to such medicine. Therefore he said, "by whatever has been consumed," and so forth.
Because it was stated, "or one might praise the appearance of death," there is no escape from the offense by way of a pretext; thus he said, "there is no such thing as a pretext.
"Does not conceive a fetus" means she does not carry a fetus. When a fetus is destroyed by wind or by microorganisms (pāṇaka), [it constitutes] an act...
It is stated that "in two ways" with the intention that [the embryo] does not perish otherwise. However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:
"The embryo perishes due to three causes: wind, microbes, and karma. Furthermore, it is stated therein:
"But when [the embryo] perishes due to karma, even Buddhas are unable to prevent it. In that context, regarding wind and microbes...
Or, when the embryo perishes, it is not because space was made by previous karma; rather, it is because karma ripens due to those conditions.
However, when space has been made by karma itself, one need not necessarily depend upon wind or insects.
It is with this intention that the separate causal status of karma is stated. As for "insects devouring and making [the embryo] disappear": [this refers to the following].

It should be applied as follows: for one who gives medicine for the purpose of preventing birth, if it is given with the intention that "they shall arise in the womb and then perish," there is a bond of karma, just as in the case of digging a pit or similar acts;
however, if it is given with the intention that "they shall not arise in the womb at all," there is no bond of karma whatsoever.

“Of those who share the same Dhamma” means those who, within the teaching of a single Teacher, have undertaken the training together. Because all five possess virtue, faith, and wisdom based on turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭa*), it is said:
“of equal virtue, faith, and wisdom. “From a place invited by kinsmen” means from a place invited by one’s own kinsmen or theirs.

Even though it is permitted to request [food] from a place not invited, because it is done for the sake of one who is ill, it is considered as if unasked; thus it is called “unasked for” (*akataviññatti*).
“Speak, venerable sir, with a requisite”—in such a place where the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) has not been made, this is a request, an unmade request (*akataviññatti*). “He prepares” means he procures.

“It is not permissible not to make it” — regarding this, they say there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). “In the same manner as stated concerning those who live in accordance with the Dhamma” means:
“For these five as well, it is permissible to prepare medicine even through an unmade request.”
It is stated because it is so said in the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā*. "As far as her relatives see" means as far as his relatives see.
"Paternal aunt" (*pitucchā*) is the sister of one's father. "Maternal uncle" (*mātula*) is the brother of one's mother. "They are not sufficient" means they are not able to perform [the service].
"Even if they do not ask" means even if they do not ask with the intention that "it is difficult to ask. "Having made an application of mind" (*ābhogaṃ katvā*)—this...
This was stated by way of showing what ought to be done; however, it is recorded in all three *gaṇṭhipadas* that "it is permissible to give even without making an effort [to identify the recipient].
Regarding the phrase "setting aside these ten relatives," their sons, grandsons, and so forth are also included here, as they too are relatives by virtue of being connected to them.
Therefore, by the expression "others than those," it should be understood that non-relatives are being referred to.
For this very reason, he said: “Of their succession of sons,” and so forth. *Kulaparivaṭṭo* means the sequence of families; it is what is meant by “the lineage of families.

They say that even for one who acts out of the expectation that “they will give to me” or “they will do [a service] for me,” there is no offense of medical treatment among relatives or the offense of defiling a family, because it is a place where one may receive [services] even after having requested them. This is the analysis for all these locations.

Regarding the phrase "should be understood": in all instances such as "of the younger mother," the explanation should be understood by applying the construction "the husband of the younger mother," etc., according to the method stated below.
By the expression "having sought in the manner stated," the matter previously mentioned in the passage beginning with "or by the novice monks who are relatives" is indicated.
“Without expecting anything in return” means: one should not expect anything for one’s own benefit, such as thinking, “They will give to me” or “They will do it for me.
However, it is permissible to act while expecting that one is providing assistance to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Just as when it is said, “Speak of medicine,” this [speaking] is permissible because it is a figurative expression—according to the principle that “one may converse with one another”—so too, as stated below...
The teachers say that even for one who speaks by way of this method—“Having taken this and that, she makes it”—there is no fault whatsoever.
Since it is impossible for one who does not know the characteristics of the Vinaya and is not a teacher to employ the corresponding terminology, such a gain cannot arise;
thus it is said, “This is called the teacher’s portion,” referring to a teacher who is proficient in the Vinaya.

The meaning is that they come to receive their share. Although [the flowers] were given for the purpose of making an offering, it was stated "by way of what is allowable" (*kappiya*) because the procedure would be improper through the use of unallowable terminology (*akappiya-vohāra*). The sense is: by way of allowable terminology such as "bring the flowers.
If they perform [the rite] when told, "Recite the protective chant" (*parittaṃ karotha*), then it stands in the place of performing services for a householder; thus, "protective chant" (*parittaṃ*).
When it was said, "Do so, venerable sir," it was stated that [the recitation] should not be performed;
however, when it was said, "Speak," it was stated that it *should* be performed because one stands in the position of being requested for a Dhamma discourse.

For it is proper to speak the Dhamma even when unrequested, let alone when requested. "Having moved the thread and smoothed it" refers to the procedure to be performed by one who is performing a protective chant (*paritta*).

[The text] shows this. "From the monastery... down to 'an offense of wrong-doing' (dukkaṭa)" means that an offense of wrong-doing is incurred only by one who gives [the gift] to those who are unrelated.
"If they do not know" means if they do not know how to speak in such a way. "Water" refers to the water of hospitality (*dakṣiṇodaka*).

He said, "The feet must not be removed," because people would perceive it as inauspicious when the feet were removed. "It is permissible to go" means [saying], "Let them come for the sake of an entourage."
Even when this has been said, it is proper to go after having observed in this manner.
"Almsfood that has not been touched" means almsfood received from the hand of one who is not ordained, where the first portion has not been taken by oneself or by another ordained person.
By the word "bowl," it should be understood that the alms-basin is also included. "Of a murderous thief" refers to [one who seizes] the kingdom...
For one who longs for it, like a thief in broad daylight. Regarding the story of the thief-nāga:

here, thinking, "He will be angry if I give him what has been touched by the thief-nāga, but it is not proper to give what has not been touched," the Elder took the very tip with his hand that was holding the bowl and gave all the alms-food into the bowl;
he (the nāga) was satisfied by that. [Thinking], "This much is mine," [he took] from just one side of the food...
"Even if one sets aside a small portion, it is proper to give everything back to him again," so it is said in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*.

"Patisanthāra" (hospitality) is the smoothing over, the closing up, the mending, and the taking hold of the gap, the opening, or the breach that arises between oneself and another due to the lack of material goods or the Dhamma. For this is how people dwell in the world...
"By means of both material things and the Dhamma" refers to two kinds of openings.

Just as those openings are not visible, so too the "spreading out" (paṭisanthāra) by means of material things and the Dhamma—like a rug over a bench—is called "welcoming with material things" (āmisa-paṭisanthāra) and "welcoming with the Dhamma" (dhamma-paṭisanthāra).
Among these, there is no one for whom welcoming with the Dhamma should not be performed.
For anyone at all, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, support should indeed be rendered according to the Dhamma.
However, the question of "to whom hospitality should be extended and to whom it should not" was stated with reference to material hospitality (*āmisa-paṭisanthāra*).
"Having cleared out" means having plundered for three *yojanas* all around, having caused the people to flee, and having made it a place where others cannot dwell.
"Bringing for the sake of the Saṅgha" means brought on that very day for the purpose of a meal-offering (*pākavaṭṭa*).
"A variegated cloth-covering" refers to a covering of many kinds, adorned with excellent and diverse patterns. 187.
Among the group of seventeen, because one had previously been killed by the poking of a finger, the belly of the remaining sixteen...
Having climbed up, it is said that one person was seated while the others—“the remaining fifteen people”—were set aside. “Like millstones” means like stones placed upon a millstone.
“With the intention of performing formal acts” means with the intention of carrying out formal acts such as the act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*).
“Having caused to enter” means having caused them to go inside. “A dwelling infested by wild beasts” means a monastery inhabited by fierce creatures.

189. Regarding what should be said concerning such passages as "one who, even when crushed by a tree, does not die," etc., he himself will explain it in the commentary on the Bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada (the training rule regarding plants). For it is stated there:
"In the commentary on the Pārājika offense involving human beings, however, all the commentaries state:
'If a bhikkhu is crushed by a tree or has fallen into a pit, and it is possible for him to escape by cutting the tree from one side [to reach] the ground...'"
"Or, even for the sake of one's life, one must not dig the earth oneself to escape;

however, it is permissible for another bhikkhu to dig the earth, cut down a tree, or cut a branch from a living tree and roll that tree [over the person] so as to cause them to escape—it is no offense.
No reason for this is seen there, [as the Buddha said]: "I authorize..."
Monks, when a forest fire is burning, one may give a counter-fire and perform a protective rite (*paritta*)—this is the only single discourse found.
If this is consistent [with the Dhamma], then it is impossible to find a distinction such that "it is not permissible for oneself, but permissible for another.
One who performs it for his own sake does so with an unwholesome mind due to self-attachment; whereas another...
"But [he did it] out of compassion. Therefore, if you say there is no offense, even this is not a valid reason.
For one may incur this offense even with a wholesome mind; however, because it is stated in all the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), it cannot be refuted.
One must seek the underlying logic here, or else proceed by faith in the teachers of the Commentaries."

Therefore, whatever has been elaborated here by others in a manner different from this, and whatever reason has been stated in the *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, should not be accepted as being essential.

190. Regarding the offense of *pācittiya* for [extinguishing] what is wet... even in the case of dry matter, if one sets fire to it and ignites it with this same intention, it is indeed a *pācittiya*.
It is a *dukkaṭa* if [one acts] toward dry matter, or if one fails to determine that dry matter is "dry."
For one who throws fire [into water], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). The same principle applies even when the intention is for sport.

And the intention for sport is to be understood solely by way of the relish for the crackling sound. "Counter-fire" (*paṭaggi*) is fire that serves as an opponent. "Performing a protective rite" (*parittakaraṇa*) means performing a protection.
"Arising spontaneously" refers to fire produced by the mutual friction of bamboo and other materials stirred by the wind. "Without fuel" (*nirupādāna*) means devoid of combustible material.

191–192. Regarding the offense of *pārājika* due to entering a field: when it is said "by two," it is a *pārājika* because death is expected from both blows, and because one blow without the other is insufficient for that purpose.

However, they say that if it is restricted to "only by two," there is no *pārājika* in the case of someone being killed by a single blow. This is because the force and momentum were previously established by the first blow.
Setting aside the mere movement [of phenomena] through their arising in another location, because the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) does not exist there, it is said, "for one who cuts off the head.

"Of this matter" refers to the matter of the execution ground (*āghātana*). Because it is stated, "by the consumption of living beings," they say that salted sour gruel (*loṇasovīraka*) is "to be used within the watch of the night" (*yāmakālika*).
The commentary on the *Vinītavatthu* is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the third *Pārājika* in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a sub-commentary to the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
4. The Fourth Pārājika:
"One who knows the Four Truths" (*catusaccavidū*): the four truths combined are called the "four truths"; one who has known—that is, penetrated—them is "one who knows the four truths.

Although disciples and paccekabuddhas also possess the quality of knowing the four truths, because the Blessed One was not preceded by anyone else [in this realization], he is uniquely designated as such.
Because he has attained the vision of the Four Noble Truths therein, as well as omniscience and mastery over the powers (bala),

and because this is made manifest by his extending [his compassion] toward the mental continuums of others, the Blessed One alone especially deserves the praise of being "one who knows the Four Noble Truths.
Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Bhikkhus from the Banks of the Vaggumudā River.
193. "Adhiṭṭhema" means we agree. "Messenger service" (dūtakamma) refers to traveling here and there after taking a letter or a message from householders.
"Having composed their deportment" means having made it conform to their exertion.
"To those who ask" means to those asking, "The noble ones have such a peaceful deportment and are exceedingly tranquil; what specific distinction have they attained?"

Regarding the phrase "but when there is no connection with the future," one should supply the words "will be spoken" (*bhāsito bhavissati*) to complete the sense; thus, it means "when there is no connection with the future.
To the question, "How can the past tense 'was spoken' (*bhāsito*) enter into a connection with a future tense? he says:

"The grammatical rule (*lakkhaṇa*), however, must be sought from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). For in such a case, [the rule] "suffixes [are used] when there is a connection with a verbal root" (*dhātusambandhe paccayā*) applies.

Grammarians state that when there is a connection between the meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātu*), suffixes (*paccaya*) are valid even if they are applied at an incorrect time, provided this characteristic is present. 194.
By the term *vaṇṇavā* (possessing beauty), the loveliness of the complexion pervading the entire body is expressed. *Pasannamukhavaṇṇā* (with a clear facial complexion) [is likewise stated].
By this, the pleasantness of the complexion of the face is stated to be even greater than that of the entire body’s complexion.

By the phrase "with a perfectly clear skin-complexion," however, the extreme clarity of the existing bodily complexion itself is expressed. Because there is neither deficiency nor excess in the sense faculties, it is said: "because the space occupied [by each faculty] is complete."

The heart-base is the location where the sixth [consciousness] is established; by the very statement that the locations where the five sensitive organs (pasāda) are established are complete, the completeness of the entire body, including the heart-base and so forth, is already shown.
Thus he said: "of the faculties with the mind as the sixth. Regarding the phrase *yathā tanti*:
here, *tanti* is a mere particle (*nipātamatta*). "Resembling a wandering deer" refers to what should and should not be done.
They are like bewildered deer because they do not know [the way]. "Four wheels" (*catucakka*) refers to the four postures (*iriyāpatha*).

For here, "wheel" is intended in the sense of proceeding. "Nine doors" (*navadvāra*) means having nine openings for wounds. "Suffering" (*dukkha*) refers to suffering such as diseases of the head and so forth.

"In all duties" (*sabbakiccesu*) refers to duties such as cooking rice-porridge, dyeing robes, and the practice of yoga. "To maintain" (*yāpetuṃ*) means to carry on, to cause to proceed. Therefore he said, "to go."
195. By the word *santi* (“they exist”), he shows their actual presence; by the word *saṃvijjamānā* (“being found”), however, he shows their being apprehended.
Therefore he said: “They both exist and are apprehended. *Upalabbhanti* means they are seen; the sense is that they are known.
*Panthadūhanakammaṃ* is the act of highway robbery. *Hananto* means killing; *ghāyanto* means causing to be killed.
Alternatively, "striking" (*hananto*) means harming by means of binding, beating, and so forth; "killing" (*ghātanto*) means causing death;
"cutting" (*chindanto*) means cutting off the hands and other limbs of others; "roasting" (*pacanto*) means oppressing with a staff.
Here, "roasting" is intended to mean burning or afflicting. Or, "roasting" means threatening and terrifying. Alternatively, "roasting" refers to the act of setting fire to villages.
Having set fire to houses and the like, he cooks goats, sheep, and so forth therein.
Those who do not have great reverence for the training rules and are prone to transgressing them should instead have excessive reverence for those training rules. "Agitated" means:
perceiving what is improper as proper, perceiving what is proper as improper, and perceiving what is blameless as blameworthy.
And [avoid] those who perceive what is blameless as blameworthy and those whose nature is agitation. "Haughty" (*unnaḷa*) means with a raised stalk;
it is said to mean one who has risen up in empty pride. "Fickle" (*capala*) means joined with fickleness through the decoration of bowl and robes and so forth.

"Garrulous" (*mukhara*) means harsh-mouthed; it is said to mean one of harsh speech. "Loose-tongued" (*vikiṇṇavāca*) means one of unrestrained speech, who prattles meaningless words even throughout the day.
"Those whose mindfulness is muddled and lost" (*muṭṭhassatī*) means they are devoid of mindfulness; this is what is meant.

"Lacking clear comprehension" (*asampajāna*) means lacking wisdom (*paññā*). "With unrestrained faculties" (*pākatindriya*) means having their faculties left open due to a lack of restraint, just as in the time of being a householder.

"Abandoned by teachers and preceptors" (*ācariyupajjhāyehi pariccatta*) refers to those who have been forsaken by teachers and preceptors—left without a protector—having not been sustained by them either through the Dhamma or through material goods.
"Without a foundation. "One who values gain" means one who values the requisites (*paccaya*).
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "establishing the postures, etc.," it should be understood that the use of requisites and indirect speech are included.
For in the *Mahāniddesa*, it is stated to be threefold by way of establishing the postures, using the requisites, and indirect speech.

The subject of hypocrisy (*kuhakavatthu*) has been introduced. Therein, the act of deceiving by means of a deportment performed with the intention of gaining esteem while being one who possesses evil desires—this is what is termed the "subject of hypocrisy" as the maintenance of a specific posture.

Likewise, when invited with robes and other requisites, although one actually requires them, one refuses them out of evil desire; thereby, those householders place their faith firmly established in oneself.
Having understood this, [the people] thought, "Oh, this noble one is of few desires; he does not wish to accept anything at all.

It would be a great gain for us if he were to accept even a small thing. Thus, while they presented various excellent robes and other requisites through diverse means, [the Blessed One], manifesting only his desire to favor them, accepted them from that time forward.

The act of deceiving by means of offering eighty cartloads [of goods] as a cause for [receiving requisites], which is termed the "acceptance of requisites," should be understood as a ground for hypocrisy (*kuhakavatthu*).

Furthermore, the act of deceiving by speaking in various ways to indicate the attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) while still being one of evil desire, which is termed "bordering chatter" (*sāmantajappana*), should be understood as a ground for hypocrisy. [This occurs at] monasteries such as Cittalapabbata.
This refers to "lodgings approved by the world. The connection is: "the qualities being praised through various means, approved by the world...
"To bring to maturity" (*paripācetuṃ*) means "to transform. The passage beginning with "But those who...

was stated to show that there is no fault in the use of requisites derived from [their work] for those who wander about performing their own duties, such as the burden of composing texts, with a pure mind. Regarding the practice of alms-gathering (*bhikkhācāra*):
"In not succeeding" means that when they go for alms in the village of their resort and the alms-food to be obtained does not succeed.
They perform all of this under the heading of duty (*vatta*), not for the sake of gain. Therefore it is said: "Those who maintain the continuity of the lineage and illuminate the Dispensation.
"With difficulty" does not mean by way of a painful practice; for to the Buddhas, even all four paths are indeed practices that are easy.

Furthermore, at the time of fulfilling the perfections (pāramī), while still possessing lust, hatred, and delusion, he would cut off his head—though it was adorned and prepared for the occasion—and offer it to beggars who had arrived;
he would draw out blood from his neck and give it; he would pluck out his well-anointed eyes and give them;
and he would give away a son who was the perpetuator of his family line, or a wife of pleasing conduct, and so forth—even while in such bodily forms as those of the likes of Khantivādi.
This was said with reference to the path of progress for one who incurs [offenses] such as those involving cutting or breaking. "With difficulty" is a synonym for that same term.
They are called "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍāni*) because of their weightiness due to the impossibility of giving them to even a single person;
they are called "heavy requisites" (*garuparikkhārāni*) because of the impossibility of taking them away even by distributing them among all. By way of being common property of the requisites...
"Because it belongs to the Saṅgha" means by virtue of being a requisite held in common by all bhikkhus.
"He gathers [them] together" and "he flatters" is said with reference to a mind free from theft. For this very reason he says: "having stolen because of such a state";

the meaning is "having stolen because of its being something that cannot be given away or divided. For one who, for the sake of gathering families, gives away or divides heavy goods (garubhaṇḍa) belonging to the Saṅgha...
“He misappropriates something that is not to be given away and is not subject to forfeiture”: he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for corrupting a family.
In this context, because it is stated, “Whoever should give it away, there is a grave offense (thullaccaya),” one is not exempt from the grave offense even on account of giving it away.
“Non-existent” (asantaṃ) means not present; “unreal” (abhūtaṃ) means not arisen. For because it has not arisen, it is non-existent.
The latter [phrase] is the statement of the reason for the former. "He boasts" (*ullapati*) means he speaks with an inflated life-span. For virtue (*sīla*) is indeed the life-span of a bhikkhu;

that very virtue vanishes at the same moment he speaks in such a manner. "For the sake of gaining esteem for oneself" (*asantasambhāvanāya*) means for the sake of gaining esteem through qualities that do not actually exist in oneself.
Thus, for one who accepts [gifts]... [etc. ...they are taken after having been enticed; herein, it refers to "for the sake of gaining esteem for oneself."
Because one has stolen and taken the alms of the land, even the supramundane Dhamma becomes stolen. "Like a gambler" means like a gambler’s catching of birds.
"Of a kerāṭika" means of a deceitful person. "Gotta" refers to a common name; the word *matta* is indicated by elision.
Therefore, those who experience and maintain the mere state of being a recluse (*samaṇa*) are "those who belong to the lineage" (*gotrabhū*).
It is said that they are "merely sham ascetics.
The commentary on the account of the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the account of overweening pride.
196. Because it knows the Noble Truth (ariyadā) through the lower paths as already known, the wisdom of the highest path is called "higher knowledge" (aññā).

Since it is the fruit of that [wisdom], the wisdom of the highest fruit (aggaphala-paññā) and the right intention and so forth associated with it are also called "higher knowledge. Thus it was said: "They declared higher knowledge" means they declared Arahantship.
First of all, it does not arise for a noble disciple because the condition of overweening pride (adhimāna) has been abandoned.
It does not arise. Even for one possessed of virtue... [and so on] ...it does not arise because of the state of being a non-doer.

"Having applied the three characteristics" means having applied the three characteristics by way of the comprehension of aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*). "For one who has commenced insight" means for one who has commenced insight through the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*).
One who has attained pure serenity (*suddhasamatha*), even without performing the work of insight, seeing no manifestation of defilements, [remains] solely...
Because one conceives "I am an Ariyan" through the power of ignorance, it is said: "or one who has attained pure serenity (samatha).
One conceives "I am an Arahant," just like the Elder Mahānāga, the resident of Uccavālaṅka.
It is said that there was a certain Elder Dhammadinna, a resident of Talaṅgara, who had broken through to the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and whose taints (āsava) were utterly exhausted.
He was one who gave exhortations to a great community of bhikkhus. One day, while sitting in his own daytime resting place, he reflected:
"Has our teacher, the Venerable Mahānāga of Uccavālika, reached the culmination of the duties of a recluse, or not?
Perceiving that he was still at the stage of an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*), he thought: "If I do not go to him, he will surely pass away as an ordinary worldling."

Knowing that he would do so, he rose into the air by means of his psychic power (*iddhi*), descended beside the Elder who was sitting in his daytime resting place, paid homage, performed the proper duties, and sat down to one side.
When asked, "Friend Dhammadinna, why have you come at an improper time? he replied, "Venerable sir, I have come to ask a question. Thereupon [the Elder said], "Ask, friend."
When he was told, "We shall speak knowing [the answer]," he asked a thousand questions. The Elder answered each question as it was asked without hesitation.
Then, being asked, "Venerable sir, your knowledge is exceedingly sharp; when did you attain this Dhamma?
he replied, "Friend, sixty years ago. [The other said,] "Venerable sir, please employ your concentration."
"Friends, this is not heavy. "In that case, venerable sir, conjure up an elephant. The elder conjured up an all-white elephant.

"Now, venerable sir, let it come toward you just as this elephant approaches with its ears lopped, its trunk extended, its tail tucked in, throwing back its head, and uttering a terrifying trumpeting cry."
"Do not do so. Having done as instructed, the elder saw the terrifying appearance of the elephant rushing toward him at great speed;

he stood up and began to flee. Then the elder who had destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) reached out his hand, caught him by the corner of his robe, and said, "Venerable sir, does one who has destroyed the taints feel timidity? At that moment, he realized his own state as an ordinary worldling (puthujjana).
Recognizing this, he said, "Friend Dhammadinna, you must be my refuge," and sat down in a squatting position at his feet.
"Venerable sir, I have come for no other purpose than to be your refuge; do not worry," he said, and then gave him a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having taken up the meditation subject, the Elder descended to the walking path (*caṅkama*) and, on the third step, attained the supreme fruit of Arhatship.
It is said that the Elder was of a temperament prone to hatred.
The commentary on the basis for overweening pride is finished.
The commentary on the training rule with its analysis.
197–198. The phrase beginning with "Yasmā pana" (But because... is the statement of the reason for [the terms] "non-existent," "unreal," and "not found.
In that context, "yaṃ" refers to that superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*). "Anabhijānanto" means not knowing its existence within oneself.
"Samudācarati" means he speaks or makes known [others] that "this state exists in me. "Asantaṃ abhūtaṃ" means...

The statement of the reason for this is: "it has not arisen in the mental continuum. Furthermore, the phrase "and not realized through knowledge" is the statement of the reason for the term "non-existent.

Regarding the phrase "of superhuman beings" and so forth: the Dhamma attained by those superior to ordinary persons—namely, the supreme persons such as the Buddhas—is the "superhuman Dhamma" (*uttarimanussadhamma*);
thus he said "of superhuman beings," etc. "That" refers to the superhuman Dhamma. Now...
Regarding the question of why the plural designation is used in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), he says:

“But in the word-commentary,” and so forth. Although the superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*) is also indeterminate (*abyākata*), it is nevertheless described as “wholesome states” (*kusale dhamme*) in the sense of health, as in the *Bāhitika Sutta*.
The term “his” (*assa*) refers to the superhuman state. While the words *khaṇa*, *laya*, and *muhutta* have different meanings elsewhere, here—
However, it is stated in the Pāḷi—“that moment, that instant, that brief duration”—solely by way of the sequence of moments.

It is called *adhigama* (attainment) because it is to be attained; it refers to the jhānas and so forth. An inquiry regarding attainment is an *adhigama-pucchā*. Therefore, he said: “In regard to the jhānas, liberations, and so forth,” and so on.
An *upāya-pucchā* is an inquiry regarding the means for attainment. “Kinti” means “in what manner? or “by what method? [The question] “Of which ones?”...

Regarding the statement "You are an attainer of the Dhammas," this now demonstrates the manner of questioning after having specified those particular distinctions—such as the jhānas and so forth—which were previously asked about in the question, "What have you attained? without their specific divisions being determined.
"Therefore" means because the declaration of attainment must be verified by the six modes already described; therefore. "By this much" means...
One should not be satisfied with the mere declaration alone; for a declaration may even be made by someone who does not possess the truth.
Therefore, he must be examined regarding these six points for the sake of purification.
Just as counterfeit gold, which appears like real gold, must be purified by rubbing, heating, and cutting, so too [must he be examined].
Having included these within the six points just mentioned, it should be stated for the purpose of purification.
Regarding the phrase "in the liberations, etc.," the word "etc. includes concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, the development of the path, the realization of the fruit, and so forth.

"It becomes manifest" means that there is no lapse of mindfulness regarding the specific distinction attained. The same principle applies to the phrase "it becomes manifest" in the remaining questions as well.
The statement that "for all [beings], the defilements abandoned by the path attained by themselves become manifest" is said with reference to the majority.
For in some cases, doubt indeed arises regarding those defilements to be abandoned by the path attained by oneself, as in the case of the Sakyan Mahānāma.
Although he was a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), it occurred to him: "Venerable sir, this thought occurs to me: 'Who..."
“There is a certain state within me that has not yet been abandoned, because of which at times states of greed still take possession of my mind and remain there;
states of hatred still take possession of my mind and remain there; and states of delusion still take possession of my mind and remain there.
Thus he questioned the Blessed One. It is said that this king, by means of the path of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmimagga*), [had attenuated] greed, hatred, and delusion...
He perceived that [the defilements] were abandoned without remainder. One might ask: "Does such a doubt arise even for a noble disciple?

Yes, it does. Why? Because of his lack of proficiency in the designations (paṇṇatti). For a noble disciple who is unskilled in this designation—namely, that "this defilement is to be abandoned by such-and-such a path"—such a thought occurs to him. One might ask: "Does he not have reflective contemplation (paccavekkhaṇā)?"
It exists, yet it is not complete for everyone. For one person reviews only the defilements already abandoned;
another, only the remaining defilements; another, only the Path; another, only the Fruit; and another, only Nibbāna.
Among these five kinds of reviewing, it is not permissible not to obtain at least one or two. Thus, for whomever there is reviewing—
It is not fulfilled because, due to a lack of skill in the designation of those defilements that are to be destroyed by the path, this occurs.
"Skilled in learning and inquiry" means they are proficient in recitation and the commentaries on the path.
That preliminary practice by which the noble path arrives for a particular individual is the "practice of arrival."

“Should be cleared” means they should be cleared by way of investigation as to whether they are pure or not pure. “Is not purified” because of the presence of negligent conduct in various instances here and there.
“Should be removed” means he should be removed according to his own admission.
Having said “is purified,” the phrase beginning with “for a long time” was stated to show the manner of purification. Regarding “is evident,” here too [the word] “if” [should be understood].
The connection is: "If, having brought [the matter] to this point, that bhikkhu is recognized by that practice. Because of being unattached to the four requisites, it is said:
"with a mind like a hand in the air. "Similar to what was said" means that the bhikkhu’s explanation is similar to what was stated in this sutta; the meaning is "equal."
The practice is said to be similar to that of one whose taints are destroyed because the defilements have been well-subsided for a long time. As for the one whose taints are destroyed...
[it] does not occur because he has abandoned the perversions and lacks attachment to life.
However, for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), it occurs even with regard to a trivial matter because the perversions have not been abandoned and attachment to life still exists.
In this regard, there are these instances: it is said that the Elder Abhaya, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, being unable to win over a certain alms-collector, gave him a signal.
When the latter was bathing at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River, he submerged himself and seized his feet.
The alms-collector, perceiving him to be a "crocodile," let out a great cry; at that moment, [the elder] addressed him as a "worldling."

They came to know this. However, during the time of King Candamukhatissa, there was a senior monk (*saṅghatthera*) in the Mahāvihāra who, being an *arahant* with failing eyesight, remained within the monastery itself.

The king, thinking, "I shall take hold of the elder," approached him quietly while the monks were out on their almsround and seized his feet like a snake. The elder remained as motionless as a stone pillar.
Having offered it, he asked, "Who is here? "I am Tissa, Bhante," he replied. "Do you smell the fragrance, Tissa?
Thus, for one whose taints are exhausted, there is no such thing as fear. However, even a certain worldling may be exceedingly brave and fearless;
he must be tested by means of an alluring object. For King Vasabha, while testing an elder monk, also said:
Having seated him in the house, he sat down near him crushing jujube leaves.
The elder’s saliva began to flow, and his state as an ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) became manifest. For one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), craving for flavors is thoroughly abandoned;
there is no attachment even toward divine tastes. Therefore, having examined him through these means, if there is fear in him—
If trembling or craving for flavors arises, he should be removed [from the assembly] with the words, "You are not an Arahant.
Regarding the characteristic of praising non-existent qualities, it is said that they have "evil desires," as stated in the passage beginning, "Herein, a certain person... and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is meant: "Being faithless, one desires, 'May people know me as faithful'; being of little learning..."
Though he is fond of company, he desires: “May people know me as one who is learned”; though he is lazy, he desires:
“May people know me as one who has aroused energy”; though he is muddled in mindfulness, he desires:
“May people know me as one whose mindfulness is established”; though he is unconcentrated—
“One who, while being of poor wisdom, desires: ‘May people know me as one who is concentrated’;
who, while being of poor wisdom, desires: ‘May people know me as wise’; who, while having taints that have not been destroyed, desires:
‘May people know me as one whose taints are destroyed’—such a desire, a state of desire, evil desire, lust, infatuation, the infatuation of the mind: this is called evil desire.”
This summarizes the passage from the Pāḷi as it has been stated. "By an evil desire" means by a base desire.
"Overcome" (apakato) means one who has been made to depart from right livelihood due to an evil desire; thus he is "overcome by desire.
Being in such a state, one is called "overpowered and defeated" by wrong livelihood; hence it says, "overpowered and defeated."

"The ascetic life, when wrongly grasped, drags one toward hell": just as a blade of kusa grass, if wrongly seized, cuts and gashes the hand that holds it, even so the ascetic life—known as the *samaṇadhamma*—when wrongly grasped through such things as broken virtue, drags one toward hell;
the meaning is that it causes one to be reborn in hell. "Lax" means by acting with slackness and a loose grip.
"Done. "A wanderer" (*paribbājaka*) refers to one who has reached a state of brokenness and so forth regarding the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
"He scatters even more dust" means that such a state of the duty of a recluse is unable to remove the dust of passion and so forth existing within;

rather, it scatters yet further dust of passion and so forth upon him—this is the meaning. "The state of a bhikkhu" refers to one who, having committed a *pārājika* offense, [is no longer] a recluse...

Because he admits "I am [a monk]," his status as a monk is established merely by conventional usage (*vohāramatta*). In the reading *ajānameva*, the word *eva* is a particle used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇatthe nipāto*).
However, in the reading *ajānameva*, it should be construed with the phrase: "They say, 'I know thus; I see thus.
Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis (*Padabhājanīya*)
199. Regarding the phrase "the jhānas of the foul (asubha), etc.," the word "etc. includes both the jhāna of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) and the jhānas of the kasiṇas.
Therefore, it should be understood that even one who says, "I attained the jhāna of mindfulness directed to the body, the jhāna of the earth-kasiṇa," and so forth, incurs a pārājika offense.
Here, in the term "liberation" (vimokkho), the prefix *vi-* is shown to have the sense of distinction (*visesa*) or variety (*vividha*).
He said, “Well liberated,” and so forth. “Liberation” (*vimokkha*) refers to the four noble paths.
Showing how it receives the names of emptiness (*suññatā*) and so on by virtue of its own qualities, he said, “But that [path],” and so forth. For a path receives its name for five reasons:
by its own essence, by its opposite, by its quality, by its object, or by its lineage. If it is equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*)...
Having comprehended formations as impermanent, he emerges; he is liberated by the signless liberation.
If he emerges having comprehended them as suffering, he is liberated by the desireless liberation. If he emerges having comprehended them as non-self, he is liberated by the void liberation.
This is what is called "emerging by way of its own essence" (*sarasato*). Furthermore, because of this [practice] of the contemplation of impermanence...
Having performed the resolution of the compactness of formations (*saṅkhārā*) and abandoning the signs of permanence, stability, and eternity, he has arrived;

therefore, it is "signless" (*animitta*). Furthermore, because one has abandoned the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*), and has dried up longing and aspiration, it is "desireless" (*appaṇihita*).
Through the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*), having abandoned the perception of a self, a being, or a person...
Because it is seen as empty of formations (*saṅkhārā*), it is called "emptiness" (*suññatā*); this is its name from the perspective of its opposite.

Furthermore, it is "empty" because it is empty of lust and the other [defilements]. It is "signless" (*animitta*) due to the absence of the sign of form and so forth, or specifically the sign of lust and so forth.
It is "wishless" (*appaṇihita*) due to the absence of longing for lust and the rest; this is its name from the perspective of its own qualities. This, moreover—
Because it takes as its object Nibbāna—which is void, signless, and desireless—it is called "void," "signless," and "desireless";
this is its name according to its object. As for its arrival, however, it is twofold: arrival by way of insight and arrival by way of the path.
Among these, arrival by way of insight is found in the path, while arrival by way of the path is found in the fruit. For the contemplation of non-self is the state of voidness.
The path of insight into emptiness is called "empty. Insight into the signless is called "signless," and the path of insight into the signless is "signless.

However, this designation is not obtained according to the Abhidhamma method; for that [path], because it does not abandon the signs of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*), is not signless in the primary sense. Nevertheless, it is obtained according to the Sutta method. For therein:

They say that the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), having made the signless Nibbāna its object and thus itself becoming "signless," stands in the position of what is to be reached and gives the name to the path; therefore, the path is called "signless.
Furthermore, it is indeed logical that the fruit is signless by virtue of the arrival at the path. Contemplation of suffering dries up aspiration toward conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
Because it has come [from that], it is called "wishless" (*appaṇihita*); the path of wishless insight is wishless, and the fruit of the wishless path is wishless.
Thus, insight gives its own name to the path, and the path [gives its name] to the fruit; this is the name "according to arrival.
"By emptiness" means by way of being secluded. For lust and the other defilements do not exist in the path, nor do the lusts and so forth that arise successively [in the future].

Because they are the causes, lust and the others are the "signs" (*nimitta*); thus he said, "by the signs of lust, hatred, and delusion. They say that here the "sign" refers to their appearance as if they were graspable objects.
Lust and the others themselves are the "aspirations" (*paṇidhi*) in the sense of being the basis for occurrence; thus he said, "of the aspirations of lust, hatred, and delusion.

Since [the word] was not mentioned with reference to the sciences such as *vatthu-vijjā* (science of sites), even when it is said, "I am a possessor of the sciences," it is understood [to include them]. "By way of each individual category" (*eka-eka-koṭṭhāsa-vasena*).
This is by way of each individual section, beginning with the tetrad of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

Although even in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* it is shown by way of each individual section, there the statement "of the supramundane foundations of mindfulness" and so forth applies the term "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) to each one individually before describing them by way of their respective sections; here, however, it is stated without the term "supramundane"—this is the distinction between the two.
"In those" means among those sections.

Now, why was it said, "only the abandoning of the defilements"? This was said with reference to one who might argue that the mere abandoning of the defilements does not constitute a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma).
[The answer is: because the function of the path is the abandoning of the defilements, the path is so designated by way of its function.

In order to show that it has been "explained," the passage beginning with "But that" was stated. With reference to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), it is said: "For by the third path there is the abandoning of lust and hatred";

however, this does not refer to lust for the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*) or lust for the immaterial realm (*arūparāga*). For these are not abandoned by that [third path], since they are to be abandoned by the fourth path.
"From lust the mind is unobstructed" means "from lust there is the non-obstruction of the mind. For one who is liberated from lust...
The meaning of "unobstructed" (*vinīvaraṇa*) should be understood as the state of being free from hindrances due to the absence of that very hindrance of lust (*rāga-nīvaraṇa*) within the mind.
This same method applies to the remaining [hindrances] as well.

And the phrase "the five true knowledges" (*pañca vijjā*) should be connected [to this]. Because they have been produced as supramundane (*lokuttara*), they are distinct from the world precisely because they have departed from the world.
Just as it would constitute a *pārājika* offense even if one were to say, "I am an attainer of the *satipaṭṭhānas*," without using the term "supramundane" (*lokuttara*),
so too here it is logical to say that it would likewise be [an offense] even if one were to say, "I am an attainer of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
Although this is indeed logical, nevertheless, because it was stated with specific distinctions in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is not possible to state it in this manner.
To demonstrate this, it was stated: "But in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*... [it continues] ...it is not possible to make another authority.
The connection is that even that [position] has been rejected right there.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the pure section (*suddhikavārakathā*).
200. "The mode of exaggeration" refers to the mode of exaggeration beginning with "they enter into meditative attainment.
"The classification of offenses" refers to the classification of offenses beginning with "for one who does not understand, there is an offense of thullaccaya.

Regarding the statement "it was not again brought back and joined with the first jhāna, etc.," the *Gaṇṭhipada* states that the reading here is "by means of the first jhāna" (*paṭhamajjhānena*), and that alone is correct.
He says "Alternatively," and so forth, because the word "speaks" (*bhaṇati*) can also refer to the means of accomplishment (*kattu-sādhana*).
It is not possible with that very same mind by which one speaks a falsehood to know "I am speaking a falsehood"; however, from time to time, with another mind, one knows "I am speaking a falsehood.
Thus it is said: "For one who is speaking, there is the thought: 'I am speaking a falsehood. This is the meaning here.
"Shown" means that the meaning here is shown as "false speech endowed with three factors.
"It cannot be said not to have occurred" means that because it was spoken after applying attention starting from the preliminary stage, it cannot be said not to have occurred.
"He is not to be dealt with for an offense" refers to one who speaks impulsively at the preliminary moment without the intention, "I shall speak falsely."
Even if, at the moment of speaking, the thought "this is a lie" arises, because it cannot be turned back and thus falls outside the scope [of the offense], one is not to be charged with an offense.
*Dava* means impulsively. *Rava* means the uttering of something else by one who intended to say something different due to a lapse.

*Taṃñāṇaṃ* (knowledge of that) means the knowledge of that; its state is *taṃñāṇatā* (the state of knowing that); the meaning is the perception of the object by knowledge. *Ñāṇasamodhānaṃ* (convergence of knowledge) means...
