The "multiplicity of knowledge" means that there would be many knowledges within a single moment of consciousness. The statement "it is not possible...
to know" is said because of the absence of the act of making [the object] an objective support (ārammaṇa). Furthermore, there is no unconfused comprehension of such knowledge;

for the thought-process occurring with the intention "I shall speak" ceases after having acted as a condition for the thought-process occurring with the intention "I am speaking," and that [latter] [ceases] for the thought-process occurring with the intention "It has been spoken."
Having stated that it acts as a condition, he says: “But the preceding, preceding... ceases.
When that prior stage exists, the statement “the remaining two will not exist” does not apply; rather, it is meant that they necessarily do exist.
Similarly, when the prior stage exists, the pair of statements “I shall speak” and “I have spoken” is not non-existent; the intention is that they certainly do exist.
"It manifests as if it were one" means that even though consciousness arises over many moments, it manifests as if it had arisen in a single moment.
Regarding the phrase "entering [attainment], etc.," the word "etc. includes these two: "I enter" and "I have entered.
Therein, although there is no difference in time between "I entered" and "I have entered," they are mentioned separately with reference to the distinction in verbal expression.
207. "By way of relinquishing one's own being" means by way of relinquishing the state of what belongs to oneself.
Because, unlike before the arising of the Path, there is no longer the possibility of saying "he has lust" or "he has hatred," some take it as four [factors];
however, in order to show that this is not the case, it is said "one who has vomited. For indeed, that by which something has been vomited does not take it up again. Therefore he said:
“By way of seeing the state of non-grasping. Even that which has been vomited out might still cling to a continuity (*santati*);
it is said “freed” (*mutta*) in order to show that this is not so. Therefore he said: “by way of liberation from continuity.
Even that which is freed might remain somewhere like a fruit whose bond has been released; it is said “abandoned” (*pahīna*) in order to show that this is not so.
Thus it was said. Therefore he said: "In some cases, by way of showing non-abiding.

Just as something that was poorly relinquished is called "re-relinquished" (paṭinissaṭṭha) when it is taken up again and then properly relinquished, so too, what was relinquished by insight—which is like taking it up again—is called "re-relinquished" when it is abandoned by the Path. It is for the purpose of showing this that he says "re-relinquished."
It has been said. Therefore he says: "By way of showing the relinquishing of what was previously taken up. "Ukkheṭita" means terrified;
it is said that having been terrified, one is made to flee. And since one who has been terrified and made to flee does not return to that place again, he says:
"By way of showing the state of not returning," which means by way of showing the state of not arising again within the mental continuum after having returned.

The meaning [is as follows]. Since those learned in the science of grammar (saddasattha) recite the word *khiṭa* in the sense of "frightened," he says: "This meaning is to be sought from the science of grammar.
*Aṇu* itself is *aṇusahagata*; what is meant is that it is extremely small.
The commentary on the discussion of the pure section (*suddhikavārakathā*) is finished.
Commentary on the Section on the Desire to Speak (Vattukāmavārakathāvaṇṇanā) 215.
Regarding the phrase *kevalañhiyaṃ*: this [phrase] is indeed *kevalañhi*. The word “turn” (*vāro*) must be supplied.
“He knows at that very moment” means that when it is stated, “He attained the first jhāna,” and so forth, there is the characteristic of naturally knowing that meaning.

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). However, in cases such as departing without having made a verbal announcement, if a certain bhikkhu departs first from that residence thinking, "Let them know me to be an arahant," then—as in the case of the narrative regarding the one who arrived [late]—the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) occurs at the very moment of departure, even if it is not known at that instant.
Regarding the characteristic of knowing: "What is called 'knowing at that moment' is of this nature."
This refers to the characteristics already stated. "Within the range of intimation" (*viññattipathe*) means a place suitable for the perception of bodily and vocal intimations;
it is said to be a location that can be seen with the natural eye and heard with the natural ear.
Therefore, if someone standing beyond the range of intimation perceives and hears by means of the divine eye and the divine ear-element, and knows [the offense], there is no *pārājika*.
It illuminates. Because doubt may arise in one who has not heard it before, asking "What was this said?", it is stated: "It has been heard.
Even for one who has not heard the mere words before, when it is said, "He attained the first jhāna," if he does not entertain the doubt "What was this?
but simply understands as much as that "he indeed attained what is called jhāna," there is still a *pārājika* offense.
Commentary on the Discussion of Non-offenses (Anāpattibhedakathāvaṇṇanā) 222.

“For one who does not intend to report”: the intention is for one who, having transgressed, does not wish to speak, and who does not perceive [the act] as “this is a superhuman state” (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
As for the literal form, however: “There is no offense for a monk who does not intend to report.”
This should be understood according to the various cases found throughout the Vinītavatthu.
Even one who speaks without having discerned that "this is a superhuman state" is said to be "answering otherwise than the fact" in conventional usage; thus it is said, "of one answering otherwise.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis (*padabhājanīya*) is concluded.
“Even though he is afraid”: even though he is afraid, thinking, “Do others who know of my lack [of faults] in this regard also [fear me]?
Commentary on the *Vinītavatthu* 223.

By the phrase “on the plane of the trainee” (*sekkhabhūmiyaṃ*), he includes the planes of meditative absorption (*jhānabhūmi*) as well. “Of the three kinds of seclusion” refers to the seclusion of body, mind, and requisites (*upadhi*).

Because walking for alms ends with the meal, it is said: "until the end of the meal. Even for one who has eaten and is returning, if they perform acts such as adjusting their robes out of a desire for esteem, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), according to the same method already stated.

225. Regarding the two cases—"The Dhamma, friend, is to be realized by one who has aroused energy"—although the subject matter is identical, the Blessed One adjudicated them separately because they were reported by two different monks; thus, they are both included among the *vinītavatthu* (cases of adjudication).
"Should be included" means it has been included in the Canon. 226.
"Speaking out of mere confidence" refers to speaking solely on the basis of faith alone, and not by reflecting that "these individuals are indeed Arahants by their very nature.
For this reason, no offense is mentioned here. However, if one were to think, "These individuals are indeed Arahants by their very nature," [an offense would arise].
If he says things such as, “Come, worthy ones, you arahants,” it should not be accepted.
Regarding the phrase “by means of a vehicle,” etc., this was said because an agreement had been made concerning travel on foot.

In that context, “by means of psychic power” (iddhiyā) is said with reference to the psychic power consisting of knowledge (vijjāmayiddhi). “Protecting one another” means: “Whoever shall depart first from this residence...”

Thinking, "We shall know him as an arahant," because they have made such an agreement, even though they walk one after another with impure minds, they protect one another by virtue of having set out together.
Some, however, say that even those who walk while not letting go of each other's reach, as if grasping one another's hands, saying, "Stand up, let us go; come, let us go," [are protected].
They say that having made such an agreement, even one who goes before or after [the others] does not incur an offense.

However, this is an illegal formal agreement (*adhammika-katikavatta*), for it is stated in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*: "If monks make an agreement saying, 'Only an Arahant should dwell here,' this is an illegal formal agreement. This refers to all formal agreements mentioned previously.
"This has been said" is our conviction; it should be accepted after investigation. "Inhabitants of various kingdoms" means those dwelling in various provinces.
"The Saṅgha’s share" refers to the portion that comes to one according to seniority.
And this prohibition was made with reference to establishing ownership of the Saṅgha’s share without distinction for those situated outside the boundary (*sīmā*) by this very method. Specifically...

However, it is permissible to give [the robe] even to one standing outside the boundary, provided that the area has been demarcated and a formal act of consultation (*apalokanakamma*) is performed for each individual portion, stating: "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha to give this much, or to give such a thing, or to give to this many people, or to give to such a person.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Venerable Lakkhaṇa," who was the Venerable Lakkhaṇa, and why was his name Lakkhaṇa?
In order to explain all of this—namely, who the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was, and for what reason he manifested a smile—the passage beginning with “yvāyaṃ” was commenced.
“Endowed with the marks” means endowed with the marks of a Great Man (*purisalakkhaṇa*). “Equal to Brahmā” means equal to the personal existence (*attabhāva*) of Brahmā.
Since even a slight smile is called a “smile,” he said “gentle smile. “A skeleton of bones” means...
"This is not a mere chain of bones devoid of consciousness; rather, it is a single *peta*," he said, meaning "a being reborn in the *peta*-world.

These "personalities" (*attabhāva*) refer to the personalities of *peta*s. "They do not come into range" means that, unlike the personalities of devas, they do not naturally come into range; however, they may come into range through their own desire. [This applies] to humans.
"Compassion has as its proximate cause the perception of the state of helplessness in those overcome by suffering," thus he said, "when compassion is to be exercised.
The word *sampatti* (success/attainment) should be applied to each [term]: one's own success and the success of the Buddha-knowledge.
To clarify both of these, the passage beginning with "For therein... was stated. In that context, "having recollected one's own success..."
The phrase "Sitaṃ pātvākāsī" should be brought forward and connected [to the context]. By "dhammadhātu," he refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*);
alternatively, "dhammadhātu" means the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena. "Upapatti" means birth.
For by the term "upapatti," he speaks of such a personal existence (*attabhāva*). They are difficult to convince; that will lead to their harm and suffering for a long time.
"Difficult to convince" refers not to the Elder Lakkhaṇa, but rather to those who hear that "this was indeed said.
Why did the Elder Lakkhaṇa not see it? Was it because he lacked the divine eye?
No, he did not lack it; however, while Mahāmoggallāna saw it by means of mental advertence (*āvajjana*), the other did not see it because he did not advert his mind.

“Vitudentī” means they pierce and strike; the sense is that having pierced them again and again with sharp iron beaks resembling the edge of a sword, they move here and there. Therefore he said, “piercing and moving.
Alternatively, the reading is “vitudantī. “Phāsuḷantarikāhi” is an ablative used in the sense of a locative. “Lohatuṇḍakehi” means with those resembling iron needles.
"Or with beaks made of black iron. By the phrase "excessively tender," he shows that even when appearing as a mere collection of bones, the physical sensitivity (*kāyappasāda*) is still powerful.
By the phrase "resembling a boil on a scalded area," however, he shows that it is of an extremely soft nature.
"It is indeed a marvel" refers to a marvel of censure.

“Becoming the eye” means having attained the divine eye; or rather, the meaning here should be understood as “becoming the eye for the world. Regarding the phrase “wherein,” he says, “‘Wherein’ is a particle used in the sense of a cause,” meaning it is a statement regarding the reason.
[This refers to] the immeasurable mass of beings, and specifically, in their various divisions:

existence (bhava) divided into the realms of sense-desire and so forth; destinations (gati) divided into hell and so forth; and stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) such as those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, and so on.
And while making manifest and bringing before my very eyes all-knowing wisdom regarding such an abode of beings;
"ox-slaughterer" means one who habitually kills oxen. Therefore he said, "having killed again and again. "Of that" refers to the act of killing oxen.
"Of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives" refers to karma to be experienced in successive births (*aparāpariya-vedanīya-kamma*). By the powerful karma of an ox-slaughterer...
When the ripening [of karma] is being given, that which is to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparāpariya-vedanīya*) has not yet found its opportunity;

once that ripening has matured, that which now finds its opportunity is called "remaining karma" (*avasesa-kamma*). "By way of similarity of karma" means by way of the state of being similar or alike in terms of the karma itself.
"By way of similarity of object" means by way of the state of being similar or alike in terms of the object. For in whatever kind of object...
Previously, that kamma and its result occurred; considering that this kamma and its result occur upon a similar object, it is said, "by the remainder of the result of that very same kamma.

For indeed, the designation of one thing is applied even to something similar to it, as in the expressions, "that is the very same partridge," or "those are the very same medicines. This is because, in the case of an object similar to the kamma—
Only two things are mentioned: "either the kamma or the sign of the kamma.

And because, unlike the sign of the destination (gatinimitta), the kamma and the sign of the kamma do not exist separately or apart from the kamma itself, they are therefore the causal basis for the yielding of a similar result;
thus, wherever there must be a result similar to the kamma, there it is either the kamma or the sign of the kamma.
Or they say that rebirth-linking occurs by grasping [that object]. For this very reason it was said: “It is said that for him...

there appeared a sign. In that context, “there appeared a sign” means that the sign of his past karma—which had been performed and accumulated previously, which had made room for the production of birth as a peta, and which now stands manifest in such a way—becomes the sign, the objective support (ārammaṇa), for its result.
He was that cow-killer. He was reborn as a skeleton-peta by way of a result corresponding to his action.
"Having made balls" means having slaughtered cow after cow, cut the beef into pieces, and formed them into balls.
"Having dried them" means having dried them for the purpose of storing them for a period of time; for dried meat-balls are known by the name *vallūra*. "With skin stripped off" means...
"Devoid of feathers and skin. One who kills sheep is a "sheep-slayer" (*orabbhika*). "Goats" refers to *eḷaka* (sheep/goats). "Fed on fodder" means those reared on fodder provided by oneself;
he slaughters them repeatedly with a sword and sells them. "A certain wild animal" refers to the *dīpaka* deer. "By means of torments" means by means of agonies.
"Having known" means having known the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "On account of the instigation of slander" means what was heard from here [is spread elsewhere].
A "sūcaka" (informant) is one who reports what was heard here about such-and-such or that-and-that. The connection is: "He brings ruin and disaster upon the person.
A "vinicchayāmacca" (judge) is a chief minister of justice appointed by the king for the administration of legal cases.
For he deceives the village populace by means of fraud; thus he is called a "gāmakūṭa" (village cheat). Some say: "A village headman of that same sort is a gāmakūṭa."
They say: "One must be impartial, for one is called a 'stander in the Dhamma'.
Sitting in a secluded place constitutes an uneven sitting. "Touching" means touching with intent to steal.
"Without authority" means that a woman who has a husband is not her own master regarding her own touch. "Having brushed against" means having spoken and then moved away.
It is called *maṅguli* because it moves (*ulati*) by way of its body parts; the meaning is that it exists in a state that is deformed and loathsome. Therefore, he said:
"deformed, unsightly, and loathsome.
It is *uppakka* because the body has been cooked upwardly by fire, and [it is so called] because the body is drenched from below by the process of trickling.
*Okilinī*: she who is strewn [with coals] because of being surrounded by embers here and there.
Therefore he said, “She, it is said,” and so forth. *Aṅgāracitake*: in a heap of embers. The sweat-born impurities, foul-smelling and loathsome, exude from his body.
“Of that king” means of King Kāliṅga. *Nāṭakinī*: a woman engaged in the duty of dancing. *Sedam*: sweating; the meaning is “heating.”
He was reborn as a headless trunk because, at the time of accumulating kamma, he was habituated to grasping such signs.
He is called a "wretched bhikkhu" because he is wretched due to his base conduct, yet he is a "bhikkhu" because he wears the appearance of a bhikkhu and lives on alms-food.
"Playing with a picture" means playing with various things according to one's fancy. "This very same [method]" refers to the method explained in the section on the bhikkhu.

231. "Free from *nisevāla*, *paṇaka*, and mud" means it is devoid of *sevāla* (aquatic moss) such as *tilabījaka* and the like—which covers the surface of the water with its blue, frog-back color—and of the *paṇaka* and mud that arise therefrom.
"With beautiful landing places" (*sundarehi titthehi*) means with landing places that are beautiful because they are easy to enter and free from defects such as mud. From that body of water...
“By that cause, depending on that” is the meaning. For even though that lake is located in the abode of the nāgas, it is connected to a body of water in the human world above;
therefore it is said, “From there this Tapodā flows.
Alternatively, “from there” means from the pool of water in the nāga-abode this Tapodā flows; for it ascends to the surface of the ground above by virtue of its heat.
Because she performs *tapa* (asceticism) through her heat (*tapanato*), she is called *Tapodā* by way of a name corresponding to her function; *petaloka* is the dwelling place of the *petas*.

Some, however, say that "the world of *petas*" here refers specifically to the Lohakumbhī hell, yet there are many *peta* dwellings even in the mountain foothills and forest thickets surrounding the city. This matter is [confirmed] by the *Petavatthu-pāḷi*.
This is to be illustrated by this collection of disciplinary cases (*vinītavatthu*) endowed with characteristics.
"Skilled" (*katahattha*) means having firm mastery over the targets, such that one’s shots do not miss.
Those who have attained such proficiency therein are called "skilled. Therefore, one who merely learns the craft does not become "skilled."
"However, these have 'finished their task' (katahatthā); what is meant is that they have attained mastery (ciṇṇavasībhāva).

Because they approach royal families and perform their craft, there is the 'offering of food and the throwing of the ball' (asana-sarakkhepa) by them; what is meant is that they have displayed their craft in royal families and the like.
'Pabhagga' means defeated."

232. Because of the thorough abandonment of perceptions of resistance (*paṭighasaññā*) by means of the development of the antidote—namely, the development of dispassion toward form preceded by the vision of its defects—one does not emerge from the formless attainments even with a loud sound.
However, because they have not been thoroughly abandoned, there may be emergence from all the fine-material-sphere attainments;
thus, here "unshakable concentration" (*āneñjasamādhi*) refers to the attainment of the fourth jhāna.
He says, "The intended [meaning] is the fourth jhāna concentration, which is undisturbed, immovable, and devoid of the agitation of body and speech.
In other contexts, however, the formless-sphere concentration is called "unshakable" (āneñja) because it does not waver due to the extreme distance from the opposites of concentration.
He speaks with reference to factors that obstruct concentration, such as applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), and so forth. Regarding applied thought and the others...
He said, "without having thoroughly purified it," with reference to the fact that the discernment of the danger [of sensual pleasures] had not been well performed.

But surely this venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained the state of an arahant only in the first year after becoming a follower of the Blessed One, and yet this offense involving defeat regarding superhuman states was prescribed only after the twentieth year; how then can this [be explained]?
Is it stated that the subject matter of this *pārājika* rule was already determined by the Blessed One? This is not a fault.

For this is the method of exposition used by the teachers here: even though the training rule had not yet been laid down, upon hearing the elder’s words, the monks—thinking, "He speaks of a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) which is unbecoming for himself"—raised a charge against the elder and complained.
The Blessed One, having shown the reason for the Elder’s statement and establishing its faultless nature, said:
"There is no offense, monks, for Moggallāna. However, the compilers of the Canon, because it concerns a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), brought that matter forward and included it here.
He said "not out of sequence" in order to show that there is no recollection by disciples out of sequence.
He speaks of the "attainment of non-perception" as the attainment of the fourth jhāna produced from the air-kasiṇa through the cultivation of the fading away of perception.
Even when the knowledge of past lives takes up death and rebirth-linking, it does so solely by way of immaterial phenomena which possess a sequence of immediate conditionality.
He said, "He grasps," meaning: "In his third existence, he saw only the passing away. "He discerned by way of method" means:

for beings wandering in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), there is no time when the aggregates (khandhā) do not exist; however, in the non-percipient realm (asaññabhava), they proceed for five hundred eons while being without consciousness—it was by this method that he discerned. "A difficult task was performed" refers to one who is devoid of the aggregates.

The intention is that even for one who observes the underlying principle—that it is impossible for anyone other than the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) to perform the recollection of past lives—it is difficult to accomplish. "Penetrated" (paṭividdhā) means similar to being penetrated;
just as someone skilled in the art of archery, having split a single hair known as a "hair-tuft" a hundred times, [proceeds] from there...
Having taken one end and tied it at the center of a vāṭiṅgaṇa fruit,
and having tied the other end at the tip of an arrow such that it stands out from the arrow-tip by no more than the measure of a louse or a nit,
he stands at a distance of a bull’s length [from the target] with the hair-tip bound to the arrow.
It is said that this too was a difficult feat to accomplish, just as one might pierce the tip of a hair tied to a vātiṅgaṇa fruit.
"Etadaggaṃ" means this is the foremost. "Yadidaṃ" refers to that which is this; it is stated thus by way of a change in grammatical gender.
The commentary on the narrative of the training (vinītavatthu) is concluded.
Commentary on the Conclusion (Nigamanavaṇṇanā) 233. *Idha* means in this Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga.

*Uddiṭṭhā* (recited) should be understood here as meaning that the four Pārājikas alone have been recited or spoken because they have not been abrogated by means of the Pātimokkha. If that is so, then [one might ask] regarding the Thullaccayas and Dukkaṭas mentioned below...

Because they are stated [in the section on offenses], they are indeed recited as *pārājikas*. Why are they so stated? Because this is the section concerning *pārājikas*, only the *pārājikas* are mentioned here, even though there are also *thullaccayas* and *dukkaṭas*.
Or, wishing to illustrate the meaning of the phrase "there is no communal living (*asaṃvāsa*) for those who...," he said, "The four *pārājikas* have been recited," in connection with that.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Therein, venerable sirs... also indicates the sequence for the authorized recitation of the *Pātimokkha*.
This was stated for the purpose of showing that "this alone, and no other. Regarding the four offenses not shared by bhikkhunīs:
the four—namely, *ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā*, *vajjapaṭicchādikā*, *ukkhitānuvattikā*, and *aṭṭhavatthukā*—are called those not shared by bhikkhunīs with bhikkhus.
Among these, *ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā* refers to one who, being lustful through passion for physical contact, [acts] by that very [lust].

It is a designation for a woman who, being lustful, consents to the touching or similar acts by any part of the body of a lustful man— below the collarbones, above the knees, and including the elbows. Furthermore,
a nun who knowingly conceals a fault (vajja) that constitutes a *pārājika* offense for another nun is called a concealer of faults (*vajjapaṭicchādikā*).
Next, a nun who follows a monk suspended by a unanimous Saṅgha by adhering to whatever view he holds is called one who "follows the suspended" (*ukkhitānuvattikā*).
Furthermore, one who— being moistened by the lust for physical contact—
consents to being taken by the hand or by the corner of the outer robe by such a man [who has been suspended].
If she stands within arm’s reach of a man for the purpose of engaging in unrighteous conduct known as physical contact;
or, standing there, converses with him; or, goes to a rendezvous; or, consents to a man’s arrival;
or, enters a concealed place with anyone; or, standing within arm’s reach, moves her body toward him—this is [an offense].
It should be understood that they are called "those of eight bases.
They are "deficient in the basis" because ordination and full admission lack a proper basis. For regarding them, [the Buddha said]:
"Monks, a paṇḍaka must not be given the going-forth; whoever should give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing," and so forth; thus their going-forth and full admission [are invalid].

And they are excluded [from the Saṅgha]. Therefore, because they are incapable of the state of a bhikkhu and resemble those who have committed a *pārājika* offense, they are called "those who have committed a *pārājika*.
The "basis" (*vatthu*) is that wherein the state of a bhikkhu resides due to the presence of that [incapacity]; it is the fitness of individuals for the state of a bhikkhu.

That, however, consists in being endowed with the perfection free from all defects mentioned in the *Pabbajjā-kkhandhaka*. When that is impaired through association with the state of a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) and so forth—

"Those whose basis (vatthu) has failed. By the phrase "those with rootless rebirth-linking" (ahetuka-paṭisandhika), he shows their possession of the obstruction to fruition (vipākāvaraṇa) and thereby states the reason for the obstruction to the Path (maggāvaraṇa).
Because they resemble those who have committed a defeat (pārājika), they are called "defeated" (pārājika).

Since the acts of living in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka) and so forth are not immediate (ānantariya) in the same way as matricide and the like, he said: "For these three, heaven is not barred."
"Lambi" means one whose genitals hang down due to their length. To that extent, he is not defeated;
however, when, oppressed by lack of lust, he inserts his own genitals into his own mouth or anus, then he becomes defeated.
"Mudupiṭṭhika" means one who has a soft back; that is, one endowed with a back that has been made supple through preparatory treatment.
When he, oppressed by lust, inserts his own organ into either his own mouth or anus, he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.

"He takes another's organ with his own mouth" means that one, oppressed by lust, takes the organ of another person—whether they are asleep or heedless—with his own mouth. [The same applies to] another's...

"He sits upon the generative organ" means that one who, oppressed by lack of lust, seeing another's generative organ to be functional, sits upon it with his own anus; the meaning is that he inserts his own anus into it.
Here it is asked: "Do those who kill their mother, kill their father, or kill an arahant fall into the third pārājika? Does the violator of a bhikkhunī [fall into it]?"
Since Lambī and the other three have all committed the first *pārājika* offense, how can there be twenty-four? It is said:
the four beginning with the matricide are intended here as those who are not yet ordained (*anupasampanna*).
Although Lambī and the others are included under the first *pārājika*, they are nevertheless not practitioners of sexual intercourse in this specific sense; therefore [they are excluded].
"Stated separately. By this "method" (*pariyāya*) means by the method consisting of the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of lust for both.
In the second alternative, the word-division for *kaccittha* should be understood as *kacci attha*.
The commentary on the conclusion is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth *pārājika* in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, the commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā*. 2.
The Section on the *Saṅghādisesa* Offenses.

1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Emitting Semen (Sukkavissaṭṭhi-sikkhāpada) Now, immediately following the commentary on the Pārājika rules, the commentary on the thirteenfold rules and so forth has been commenced. Of that [commentary] as well:
It is unconfused, free from doubt, and possesses a complete analysis;
"Endowed with both meaning and phrasing, it illuminates the essential meaning. Regarding "the thirteenfold":
that section whose measure consists of thirteen training rules (*sikkhāpada*) is called "the thirteenfold" (*terasaka*); the meaning is "of that thirteenfold section.

(234) "Discontented" (*anabhirata*) refers elsewhere to one who aspires to the state of a householder; however, here it is intended for one possessed of a distracted mind due to being weary through the power of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). Thus he said, "one of distracted mind," and so forth.
236–237. Regarding the term *sañcetanikā*: here, showing that the prefix *sam-* has the sense of "existing" (*saṃvijjamāna*), he says, "it is one in which volition (*cetanā*) exists.
In this context, "volition" refers to the preliminary volition proceeding toward transgression.
"Of it" (*assā*) means "of the emission of semen. He says "it is simply volition" (*sañcetanāva*) because, in this grammatical analysis, the suffix *-ika* has no separate meaning.

Regarding the term *sañcetanikā*: now, showing that the suffix *-ika* alone expresses the sense of "having" (*assatthi*) without regard for the meaning of the prefix *sam-*, he states the second alternative:
"those which have volition (*sañcetanā*) as their [constituent] are *sañcetanikā*.

Although it should have been stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "those in whom volition is found" (*saṃvijjati cetanā assa*), the phrase beginning with "one who knows" (*jānanto*) was spoken instead, without paying attention to the phonetic form. "I am making an effort" (*upakkamāmi*).
"Knowing" means knowing, "I am making an effort for the sake of release.
"Due to the difference in receptacles" means due to the difference in the receptacles of bile and so forth.

For even in the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, as well as in a universal monarch (cakkavatti), there is indeed one of the four receptacles—bile, phlegm, pus, or blood; however, in those of dull wisdom, all four [are present].

They exist by way of underlying tendency (*āsaya*). "By way of the diversity of elements (*dhātunānattata*)" means by way of the diversity of the four elements beginning with the earth element, or of the eighteen elements beginning with the eye, or of the elements such as lymph and blood.
"The opening of the bladder" refers to the upper side within the bladder sac. "Lust... unable [to restrain]" refers to the obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of lust.

This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). However, they say that the king acted in this way for the sake of investigation, because he had previously heard that "the entire body of Sambhava is the locus.
"The stream of water" (*dakasota*) refers to the urinary passage; what is meant is the region of the genitals.
But from the moment of entering the stream of water, because it is released from being clung-to (*upādinnaka*), only temperature-originated matter (*utusamutthāna-rūpa*) remains in Sambhava.
It should be understood that the remainder has no threefold origination (*tisamuṭṭhāna*). "Arising" (*sambhava*) refers to a specific state occurring through the continuity of the water element;
it has a fourfold origination, because arising is stated among those things with a fourfold origination in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Furthermore, it arises at the age of sixteen; they say that by means of passion (*rāga*), there occurs a displacement from one's position (*ṭhānācāvana*).

Therefore, it should be understood that when it is stated in the *Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā*—“What is called emission of semen is originated by lust”—this was said with reference to the displacement of the semen from its place, and not to indicate that the semen itself is mind-originated;
for this very reason, the term “emission” (*vissaṭṭhi*) was included there. However, the semen of those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) and of Brahmās...
"There is none," as stated by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla;

therefore, when it is said in the *Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā* that "for those deities there is no such thing as the emission of semen," this too should be understood as being said with reference to the displacement from their station (*ṭhānācāvana*), and not with reference to the absolute non-existence of its occurrence among deities. Furthermore, of all six...
For the deities of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), sensual pleasures are indeed natural.
For like humans, they engage in sexual intercourse by means of the union of pairs; however, it should be stated that for them there is an absence of emission.

Indeed, their fulfillment of the function of desire consists solely in the pleasure of contact which brings about the immediate subsiding of passion. Some, however, [assert this] only of the Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa [deities].
They say that "the fulfillment of sensual desires occurs through the union of pairs; for the Yāma devas it occurs by mere mutual embracing,
for the Tusita devas by mere holding of hands, for the Nimmānarati devas by mere laughing,
and for the Paranimmitavasavatti devas by mere looking," but this is rejected in the Commentary because such [beings] are dispassionate toward sensual pleasures.
Because of the absence of sensual desires therein, and because of their being progressively more refined and most refined.
"In the same way" refers back to the passage beginning with "one who makes an effort toward the sign through the relish of liberation.

Since it has been stated that "emission is said to be the displacement from the position," why was it said [in the commentary] "merely upon entering the stream of water"? To this he says: "And here, the act of descending into the stream of water," and so forth.
"In these" refers to all three views. "Having endured" means having made an effort toward the sign, and then, when remorse has arisen, having endured it.
"To restrain in the interval" means to restrain [the mind] in the interval, not allowing it—once fallen from its place—to descend into the stream of water.
Therefore he said: "For that which has fallen from its place necessarily descends into the stream of water. "Merely by falling from its place" refers to the stream of water.

The intended meaning is "even without having crossed over. And here, regarding the statement that "the entire body is the location," it was said by one who asserts the "falling from the location" because even for one who has passed away from the whole body, a slight interval occurs prior to descending into the water.
Or else, it refers to falling from the specific locations within the entire body, with the phrase "merely by falling from the location" being used in reference to that.
It has been stated: "For one who makes an effort toward the sign" means for one who makes an effort with the desire for emission.
Since there is no offense when there is no effort toward the sign—even though there may be a desire for emission during hand-massage and so forth—it says:
"In hand-massage... [etc.]... there is no offense. This is the decision common to all teachers, as shown by the passage beginning: "And here, descending into a stream of water... and so on.
This is the common exposition shared by all three teachers.
A "disturbing condition" refers to conditions such as unsuitable medicine, lodging, or food.

"Whether out of a desire for welfare or a desire for harm" means that those who are pleased act out of a desire for welfare, while those who are angry act out of a desire for harm; or [it means] for the sake of benefit or for the sake of non-benefit.
It blows by its own nature for the sake of either benefit or harm that is destined to occur. "They bring forth" means they cause [the child] to arrive through their own divine power.

Regarding the phrase "like the mother of the Bodhisattva, as a sign of obtaining a son": it is said that at that time, starting from the seventh day before the full moon, the people were enjoying festivities under the stars, abstaining from the drinking of intoxicants and adorned with the splendor of garlands, perfumes, and other luxuries.

On the seventh day, the Bodhisatta’s mother, having risen early at dawn, bathed in scented water, adorned herself with all her ornaments, partook of excellent food, and undertaken the observance of the Uposatha precepts, entered the inner chamber and lay down upon her splendid bed;
as she fell asleep, she saw this dream: "Indeed, the four Great Kings are carrying me on their shoulders."

Having lifted him up together with [the elephant], they led him to Lake Anotatta, bathed him, dressed him in celestial garments, anointed him with celestial perfumes, and adorned him with celestial flowers. Not far from there was a silver mountain;
inside it was a golden palace, and there they laid him down with his head toward the east. Then the Bodhisatta became a magnificent white elephant.

Not far from there was a golden mountain; having wandered there, he descended from it, ascended a silver mountain, entered a golden palace, circumambulated his mother, and splitting her right side, he became as if he had entered her womb.
It is with reference to this dream that it is said: "Like the mother of a Bodhisatta, for the sake of obtaining a son."
"The five great dreams" (pañca mahāsupinā) are so called because they are to be seen by great men and because they serve as signs for great matters.

Furthermore, these five great dreams are seen neither by the common people of the world, nor by great kings, nor by universal monarchs (cakkavatti-rājāno), nor by chief disciples, nor by paccekabuddhas, nor by perfectly enlightened Buddhas; rather, they are seen by only one: the omniscient Bodhisatta.
He saw them. Therefore it was said: “Like a Bodhisatta, he saw the five great dreams. But when did our Bodhisatta see those dreams?
He saw them on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, at the time of nightfall, thinking, “Tomorrow I shall become a Buddha.
For a dream seen by day does not accord with reality due to the influence of time; likewise [a dream seen] during the first watch or the middle watch [does not accord].

Furthermore, during the last watch of the night, at the powerful dawn, when what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted has been properly digested and the vital essence (*ojā*) is established within the body, a dream seen at the rising of the sun comes to fruition.
One who sees a dream with a desirable sign obtains what is desirable; one who sees a dream with an undesirable sign obtains what is undesirable. Therefore, the Bodhisatta also [saw] a dream...
While walking about at the time of dawn, he saw them.

What were those five great dreams? To the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—while he was still a Bodhisatta, prior to his enlightenment and before he had awakened—five great dreams appeared: this great earth...
There was a great couch; Himavā, the king of mountains, was the pillow;
his left hand was placed in the eastern ocean, his right hand was placed in the western ocean, and both his feet were placed in the southern ocean—this was the first great dream that appeared.
Furthermore, there is a species of grass called *tiriyā*, known as *dabbatiṇa*, which rises from the navel [of the earth] with a stalk as thick as a plough-handle;
while one is looking on, it grows to the measure of a span, a cubit, a fathom, a staff-length, a league (*gāvuta*),
half a *yojana*, or a full *yojana*, and thus continues to rise into the sky for many thousands of *yojanas*.
She remained standing there; this was the second great dream that appeared.
Furthermore, white worms with black heads crawled up from her feet as far as her knees and covered them; this was the third great dream that appeared.
Furthermore, four birds of different colors came from the four directions, fell at her feet, and became entirely white; this was the fourth great dream that appeared.
Furthermore, the Bodhisatta walked back and forth upon a great mountain of filth, unsullied by that filth; this was the fifth great dream that appeared. These were the five great dreams.
Among them, the first was a precursor to his unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā sammāsambodhi*);
the second was a precursor to the noble eightfold path being well-proclaimed among gods and humans; the third [was a precursor] to many [beings] dressed in white garments...
The first is for householders who, having approached the Blessed One, [attain] the preliminary sign of going for refuge;

the fourth is for the four castes, beginning with the khattiyas, who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, [attain] the preliminary sign for the realization of unsurpassed liberation; and the fifth is for the attainment of the four requisites.
And among these, it was a preliminary sign of his state of being unstained.
Furthermore, that he saw the great earth of the world-system as his glorious couch was a preliminary sign of his Buddhahood;
that he saw Himavat, the king of mountains, as his pillow was a preliminary sign of the pillow for his omniscient knowledge.

The foretoken: that he saw the four hands and feet traveling along the upper surface of the ocean and standing upon the rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) was a foretoken of the irreversible nature of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*).
That he saw himself lying on his back was a foretoken of the state of having faces turned upward for beings who are otherwise head-downward within the three realms of existence (*bhava*).
That which was as if he were seeing with his eyes wide open was the omen for the acquisition of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
That which became a single light reaching as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) was the omen for unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Thus, he saw five great dreams that served as signs for the attainment of various specific distinctions. Therefore it is said: "The Bodhisatta..."
“...like the five great dreams.
Regarding the sixteen dreams like those of the King of Kosala:
“The bull, the trees, the cows, and the ox;”
A horse, a bronze vessel, and a female jackal;
a water-jar, a lotus pond, and unripe sandalwood;
gourds sink and stones float.
“Frog-mothers swallow black snakes;
golden birds surround crows;
and weasels flee out of fear of rams.”
The King of Kosala saw these sixteen dreams, just like [the Buddha].
1. It is said that one day, while the King of Kosala was asleep at night, he saw sixteen dreams during the last watch.
Among them, four black bulls, the color of collyrium, came from the four directions into the royal courtyard, saying, "We shall fight."
When the great multitude had gathered together, thinking, "We shall witness a bull-fight," they displayed the manner of fighting, bellowed, and roared;
yet, without fighting at all, they departed. This was the first dream he saw.
2. Small trees and shrubs, having burst forth from the earth, flowered and bore fruit without rising even a span or a cubit above it. This was the second [dream] he saw.
3. He saw cows suckling the milk of their calves born that very day. This was the third dream.
4. He saw strong, well-proportioned, great oxen fit for the yoke being unyoked from the succession of yokes, while young, untrained bullocks were being yoked to the burden;
unable to bear the burden, they stood there having cast it off, and the carts did not move forward.
This was the fourth dream. 5.
He saw a horse with two heads; fodder was being given to it from both sides, and it was eating with both mouths. This was the fifth dream. 6.

A great crowd of people, having swept a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], presented it to an old jackal, saying, "Empty your bowels here," and he saw it emptying its bowels there. This was the sixth dream.
7. A man wound a rope and placed it at his feet; while he was unaware, a famished female jackal lying beneath the seat where he sat devoured it. This was the seventh dream he saw. 8.
At the king’s gate, he saw a single large jar filled with water, surrounded by many empty jars;
furthermore, people of all four castes were bringing water in jars from the four cardinal and four intermediate directions.

They filled [the jars] that were already full; having crossed over the water that was already full to the brim, it flowed away, yet they kept pouring water back into those very same places again and again.
Even though they looked for empty jars, there were none. This was the eighth dream. 9.
He saw a deep lotus pond covered with five kinds of lotuses, with a ford on every side. On all sides...
Bipeds and quadrupeds descend there and drink the water;
in its deep central part the water is turbid, but in the areas near the banks where bipeds and quadrupeds tread, it is clear, serene, and undisturbed. This was the ninth dream. 10.
Furthermore, he saw rice being cooked in a single pot, yet it remained uncooked; having reflected on this, [he thought], "It is uncooked."
It was as if it had been set aside after being divided, cooking in three ways:
on one side it was overcooked, on another it was undercooked, and on another it was perfectly cooked. This was the tenth dream.
11. He saw someone selling the finest sandalwood, worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold], for rotten gruel. This was the eleventh dream.
12. He saw empty gourds sinking in the water. This was the twelfth dream. 13.
He saw massive boulders, as large as gabled houses, floating upon the water like boats. This was the thirteenth dream. 14.
He saw small female frogs, about the size of madhuka flowers, swiftly pursuing large black snakes, cutting them like lotus stalks, and devouring their flesh. This was the fourteenth dream.

15. He saw a village-roaming crow, possessed of ten unrighteous qualities, surrounded by golden-colored royal swans who, because of their golden hue, were named "Suvaṇṇa" (Golden). This was the fifteenth dream. 16.
Previously, leopards used to eat the goats; however, he saw those leopards pursuing the goats and devouring them with a "murā-murā" sound.
Then, other trembling cranes, seeing the goats from afar, became terrified and seized with fear out of dread of the goats.
Having fled, they entered thickets and dense groves and hid there. This was the sixteenth dream.

1. In that regard, when unrighteous kings and unrighteous people prevail, when the world is in a state of upheaval, when wholesome qualities have declined and unwholesome qualities have increased, and when the world is in a time of decay, the rain-god does not rain properly; the bases of the clouds—
The crops will be destroyed, the grain will wither, and there will be famine; when clouds rise from the four quarters as if wishing to rain,
and at the moment when the women, fearing that the rice and other grains spread out in the sun will become moldy,
bring them inside, and the men take spades and baskets and set out to build embankments, the manner of raining [will occur].
Having shown themselves, having thundered, and having flashed forth lightning, they will flee away like bulls without even engaging in combat or shedding their seed.
This is the first ripening.
2. In an age when the world has declined and when the lifespan of human beings is short, sentient beings will possess intense passion; even before reaching maturity—
The young maidens, having gone to other men, will become subject to their seasons and pregnant, and they will increase through sons and daughters.
For their state of being subject to the seasons will be like the flower of small trees, and their sons and daughters will be like the fruit.
This is the second ripening of the result.

3. When the duty of honoring one’s elders among human beings had perished, sentient beings, failing to establish a sense of shame toward their mothers and fathers or their mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law, managed the household themselves.

Those wishing to give even mere food and clothing to their elders would give it; those not wishing to give would not give it. Thus the elders became destitute and lacked self-control over their own children.
Having propitiated [the king], they will live like great cows drinking the milk of calves born on that very day. This is the third result.

4. In the time of unrighteous kings, those unrighteous kings do not grant honor to wise ministers who are skilled in traditional lore, capable of accomplishing their tasks, nor to the wise who are proficient in legal procedure even in the Dharma-hall or at the place of adjudication.
They will not appoint elderly ministers; rather, they will grant prestige to those who are their opposites—those who are very young—and appoint such individuals to positions of judicial authority.
Being ignorant of both royal duties and what is appropriate or inappropriate, they will be unable to maintain that prestige nor carry out the royal affairs. Being unable to do so, they...

They will abandon the burden of administrative duties; even the elderly and wise ministers, though capable of accomplishing their tasks, will not undertake the work that arises, thinking, "What use have we for these? We are outsiders;
the young courtiers who are insiders will know. In this way, there will be decline for those kings in every respect.

It will be like the time when young oxen unfit to bear the yoke are yoked to it, and like the time when great oxen capable of bearing the yoke are yoked in succession to the pole. This is the fourth result. 5.
Only during the time of unrighteous kings will foolish, unrighteous kings appoint unrighteous and greedy men to the position of judges.
Those fools, indifferent to both demerit and merit, sit in the assembly hall and deliver judgments;
having accepted bribes from the hands of both the plaintiff and the defendant, they will consume them like a horse eating fodder from two mouths. This is the fifth ripening.
6. Furthermore, unrighteous kings of low birth, out of suspicion toward noble sons of pure lineage, will not grant them honor.
They will increase the numbers of those of low birth; thus, great families will become impoverished, while base families will become powerful.
Those men of noble birth, being unable to make a living, will give their daughters to those of low birth, thinking, "We shall live by depending on them.
Thus, the union of these daughters of good family with those of low birth is like the golden bowl for the old jackal.
It will be like a drainage ditch. This is the sixth ripening.
7. As time goes on, women will become lustful for men, lustful for liquor, lustful for ornaments, lustful for the streets, and lustful for material gain;
they will be immoral and of evil conduct. Having performed such tasks as plowing and cattle-tending for their husbands, they...
Having acquired wealth with great difficulty and toil, they drink liquor with their paramours;
wearing garlands, perfumes, and ointments, they disregard even urgent duties within the house, watching for their paramours through the upper parts of the house walls and even through holes;
and having pounded seeds fit for sowing the next day, they prepare rice gruel, cooked rice, and snacks.
Having prepared it, they will devour and plunder it, just like a starving female jackal lying beneath a seat, repeatedly rolling about over a rope placed at her feet. This is the seventh ripening. 8.
As time passes on, the world will decline; the kingdom will become devoid of essence; and kings...
They will become miserable and wretched. He who becomes the lord will have about one hundred thousand kahāpaṇas in his treasury;

thus all those miserable ones will make their people perform labor for him throughout the countryside, and the oppressed people, abandoning their own work, will plant both early and late crops solely for the sake of the kings.
Guarding, plowing, treading, and sowing; making sugar-cane fields, operating machines,
cooking molasses and the like, and establishing flower and fruit orchards— they will bring back the flowers, fruits,
and other produce grown here and there to fill the king’s storehouse alone, even while looking at their own empty storehouses in their own homes.
It will be just like filling a full jar without even looking at an empty, hollow jar.
This is the eighth result. 9.
As time passes, kings will become unrighteous, following improper courses under the influence of desire and other such passions.
They will exercise sovereignty, yet they will not administer justice according to the Dhamma;
they will be greedy for bribes and covetous of wealth. They will have no patience, loving-kindness, or compassion toward the inhabitants of the realm;
being harsh and cruel, they will oppress the people like sugarcane stalks in a sugar-mill, and having raised various kinds of taxes—
They will seize wealth; men, oppressed by taxes and unable to give anything, will abandon their villages, towns, and so forth, and go to live in the border regions.

The central provinces will become empty, while the border regions will become densely populated—just as in a lotus pond, the water is turbid in the center and clear at the edges. This is the ninth ripening result.
10. As time passes on, kings will become unrighteous;

when they are unrighteous, those associated with the king—whether brahmins, householders, or people of the towns and countryside—as well as all people including ascetics and brahmins, will become unrighteous.
Consequently, their guardian deities, the deities who receive offerings, the tree deities, and the deities dwelling in the sky [will depart].

In this way, even the deities will become unrighteous; under the reign of unrighteous kings, winds that are irregular and harsh will blow, causing the celestial palaces situated in the sky to tremble.
When those palaces tremble, the deities, becoming incensed, will not grant rain.
Even if it does rain, it will not fall simultaneously throughout the entire kingdom; and even where it does rain, it will do so everywhere [only sporadically].
It will not rain to assist with the work of plowing or sowing. And just as it does not rain in the kingdom, so too in the provinces and in the villages;
it will not rain simultaneously even over a single reservoir. Raining on the upper part of the reservoir, it will not rain on the lower part;
raining below, it will not rain above; in one [place]...
In one portion the crop will be destroyed by excessive rain; in another, not receiving rain, it will wither;
in another, receiving rain properly, it will reach maturity. Thus, in the kingdom of a single king, the crops will be of three kinds, like rice from a single pot. This is the tenth ripening.
11. As time passes and the Dispensation declines, there will be many shameless monks who are greedy for requisites.
Having crushed out the Blessed One’s teaching on the destruction of greed for requisites, they will preach the Dhamma to others for the sake of the four requisites, such as robes and so forth.
Being infatuated with requisites and standing on the side of the useless, they will turn [the teaching] toward Nirvana [only in name].
They will not be able to teach [the Dhamma]; they will teach only in this way: "Having heard the excellence of the words and phrases and the sweet sound, people will give costly robes.

Others, sitting in the middle of streets, at crossroads, at royal gates, and so forth, will teach even for the sake of coins, half-coins, quarters, māsakas, rūpakas, and the like. Thus, by the Blessed One—
By selling the Dhamma— which was taught at a price equal to Nibbāna— for the sake of the four requisites or for coins such as kahāpaṇas and half-kahāpaṇas,
they will be like those who sell the finest sandalwood, worth hundreds of thousands, for rotten liquid.
This is the eleventh result.
12. While the world is thus revolving during a time of unrighteous kings, kings will not grant honor to sons of noble family who are endowed with good birth;
they will grant it only to those of low birth. Those [of low birth] will become masters, while others will be poor.
Even in the presence of the king, at the royal gate, in the presence of ministers, or in the place of legal judgment, [the noble ones] will be like empty gourds.
The talk of those of low birth alone will remain stagnant as if it were fixed, yet it will become well-established; even in the assemblies of the Saṅgha,
in matters of formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) and the Gaṇa (saṅghakammagaṇakamma), and in places for deciding on alms-bowls, robes, monastic cells, and so forth,
the talk of only immoral and wicked persons will be decisive, not that of modest bhikkhus— in this way, in every respect...
It will be like the time when a hollow gourd sinks; this is the twelfth result. 13.
At such a time, unrighteous kings will grant honor to those of low birth, and they will become masters while those of noble birth fall into misfortune.
No one will show respect toward the latter, but will show it only toward the former, even in the presence of the king.

Or, in the presence of ministers or in a court of justice, their discourse will not penetrate deep and find firm footing among those sons of noble family who are skilled in legal judgment and resemble solid rock.
While they are speaking, others will merely mock them, wondering, "What are these people saying?
Even in an assembly of monks, at the aforementioned places, they will not hold the virtuous monks in high esteem.
They will conceive such notions, and their discourse, though thoroughly investigated, will find no firm footing; it will be like the time when stones float.
This is the thirteenth fruition. 14.

While the world is indeed declining, humans—being of a nature characterized by intense lust and other passions, and following after the defilements—[will act] toward those who are ever more youthful...

They will act under the control of their own wives; even the slaves, laborers, and others in the house, as well as the cattle, buffalo, and so forth, and all the gold and bullion—everything will come under their authority. When asked, "Where is such-and-such gold or bullion, or this particular item?
they will reply, "Let it be wherever it is; what business do you have with that? You are in my house..."

Having said, "I am born desiring to know whether he is virtuous or not," they will revile him in various ways, strike him with the weapons of their mouths, and, having brought him under their control like a slave or a servant, they will exercise their sovereignty over him;
thus it will be like the time when one swallows a black cobra—the venomous serpent—for a young frog the size of a *madhuka* flower. This is the fourteenth ripening of karma.
15. In times of weak kingship, kings will be unskilled in the arts of elephants and the like, and lacking confidence in battle.
Fearing for their royal sovereignty, they will not grant authority to noble sons of similar birth, but will instead bestow it upon those who serve at their feet—such as bath-attendants and barbers.
Consequently, noble sons endowed with high birth and lineage [will find themselves excluded] from the royal family.
Failing to find a firm footing and becoming unable to maintain a livelihood, they will wander about attending upon those who are low-born, of inferior lineage and family, yet hold positions of power;
it will be like the time when a crow was surrounded by golden royal swans.
This is the fifteenth result.

16. And precisely during the time of an unrighteous king, those of low birth who are royal favorites will become powerful lords, while those of noble birth will remain unknown, impoverished, and destitute.

Those royal favorites, having caused the king to adopt their own views and having become influential in the courts of justice and other such places, will seize ancestral fields, lands, and so forth from the weak, asserting, "These belong to us."

When they come and dispute in the courts of justice and other such places, saying, "This is not yours, it is ours," [the guards] will strike them with cane-whips and the like, seize them by the neck, and drag them away, intimidating them by saying, "You do not know your own measure;
you dispute with us! Now, having informed the King, we shall have your hands and feet cut off and so forth."
Out of fear of them, they will hand over their own fields and lands, saying, "These are yours;
take them," and having entered their own homes, they will lie down in terror. Even wicked bhikkhus will harass the virtuous bhikkhus according to their pleasure;
and the virtuous bhikkhus, finding no refuge, will enter the forest.

They will hide in dense thickets; thus, for those high-born sons of noble family and for the virtuous monks who are oppressed by those of low birth and wicked monks, it will be like the time of flight for sheep terrified by the fear of wolves.
This is the sixteenth fruition. In this way, he saw sixteen dreams that were omens of various future events.

Therefore it was said: "Like the King of Kosala [seeing] sixteen dreams. Herein, it should be understood that one who sees a dream as a precursor indicating one's own welfare or misfortune sees it through the power of one's own karma;
whereas one who sees a dream indicating the welfare or misfortune of the world, like the King of Kosala, sees it through the power of karma common to all beings.
"Angry deities" refers to the case of the Great Elder at the Nāgamahāvihāra, like the deities who were angry with him.
It is said that at the Nāgamahāvihāra in Rohaṇa, the Great Elder had a certain *nāga*-tree felled without even taking leave of the Saṅgha of monks.
The deity dwelling in that tree was angry with the Elder; first, she tempted him with a dream of truth, and afterwards [she said], "Seven days from now..."
“The king who attends upon you will die,” he announced in a dream. The Elder brought this report and informed the king’s women.
They all broke out in a great cry at once. The king asked, “What is this? They reported, “The Elder spoke thus.
The king had the days counted, and when seven days had passed, [he cut off] the Elder’s hands and feet.
He had it cut down. "It is exclusively true" is said because of the truthfulness of the result; however, the vision itself is indeed perverted.
For this very reason, those who have abandoned the perversions do not see even a dream that serves as a precursor [to death];
yet, due to two or three causes, they may occasionally see a dream—thus he said, "due to the breaking of association. "The Asekhas do not see them because they have abandoned the perversions."
According to the statement, it should be understood that the perversion of all four causes is itself the root cause.

"That" refers to the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) occurring at the time of dreaming. "An object such as a visible sign" means there is no object such as a visible sign other than the sign of karma (*kamma-nimitta*) or the sign of destiny (*gati-nimitta*).
"Such as these" refers to objects consisting of visible forms and so forth that were previously experienced through direct perception or are merely imagined.
And those associated with lust and so forth. "By the ordinary mind" means by the natural (pakati) consciousness.
"Released from two extremes" means released from the two extremes known as the wholesome and the unwholesome.

"At the moment of adverting and that object" is said with reference to the series of moments of consciousness that proceed until the arising of the registration (tadārammaṇa). "Seen even in a dream..."
"But at the time of saying 'it is as if seen by me' or 'it is as if heard by me,' it remains indeterminate (abyākata), because it arises merely as a preliminary adverting (āvajjana)," they say.

For those who speak thus, it should be understood that—just as in the second section on the "floods" (moghavāra) regarding the five sense-doors—it is intended that even in the mind-door (manodvāra), the adverting consciousness arises two or three times, stays in the position of impulsion (javana), and then sinks back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); for [the object] lasts for only a single moment of consciousness.
Because, at the moment of the arising of adverting consciousness, there is no possibility of the mental construction [thinking] "it is as if seen by me" or "it is as if heard by me.

And here they say: "Since it is stated that even in a dream there is an object for that [consciousness], then even phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) become objects in a dream, whether by way of the present or the past. "Even though [the object] appears clearly and stands manifest in a dream..."
"In the case of the visible form and other bases, it is said that they are their respective objects;

nevertheless, because the sign appearing in a dream must be apprehended through mental construction (*parikappa*), it is weak, and thus it is said to have a 'weak basis' (*dubbalavatthuka*). This is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
However, some say: "Because the body born of kamma has reached a state of being effortless and tranquil, the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*) dependent upon it [does not function]."
It is not well-purified; consequently, even the arising of consciousness dependent upon it is not well-purified, like the light of a lamp dependent on a poorly purified wick.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "because its basis is weak," they explain the meaning as "because its heart-basis is weak";
however, one should investigate and accept what is more appropriate.
"Volition at the end of a dream" refers to the volition occurring by way of mind-door impulsion at the conclusion of a dream.

For one seeing a dream sees it only through a mind-door impulsion, not through a five-door [consciousness]. And when waking up, one wakes up only through a mind-door [impulsion], not through a five-door one.
Indeed, for one who is sleeping, even if a great fire is lit and a lamp is brought near the eyes...
When [the object] has been presented, the first adverting consciousness pertaining to the eye-door does not turn back the life-continuum; it turns back only the mind-door.
Then, after the impulsion has impelled, it sinks back into the life-continuum. On the second occasion, the adverting consciousness pertaining to the eye-door does turn back the life-continuum;
thereafter, the visual consciousness and the others proceed until the end of the impulsion, after which—
The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) proceeds. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum is turned back by mind-door adverting consciousness, a mind-door impulsion (javana) impels;
by that consciousness, one knows: "What is this light in this place?
Likewise, for one who is sleeping, when musical instruments are played near the ear, or when fragrant or foul-smelling flowers are brought near the nose—

When clarified butter or molasses is placed in the mouth, and a blow is struck on the back with the palm, the advertings (*āvajjana*) associated with the ear-door and so forth do not turn back toward the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*); rather, only the mind-door adverting turns back.
Then, after the impulsion (*javana*) has impelled, it sinks back into the life-continuum. On the second occasion, the advertings associated with the ear-door and so forth [do not turn back].

They turn back [the mind from the life-continuum]; then ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and so forth, proceed until the end of the impulsion (javana) stage;
immediately after that, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) proceeds. On the third occasion, when the life-continuum has been turned back by mind-door adverting consciousness, mind-door impulsion impels;
having known by means of that consciousness, one thinks: "What kind of sound is this in this place? Is it the sound of a conch, or the sound of a drum?"
Or one might speak thus: "What is this fragrance in this place? Is it the scent of roots or the scent of heartwood? or "What is this that has been placed in my mouth?
Ghee or molasses? or "By whom have I been struck on the back? My blow was very hard.
One awakens by means of the mind-door javana alone, not by the five doors. This applies even in dreams.
He sees by means of that very [method], not by means of the five doors.
"Assa" means "of this class of offenses. But is this not an improper formulation: "The Saṅgha should be desired at both the beginning and the end"?
For it is not the case that the Saṅgha is desired at the beginning and the end of a class of offenses; rather, what then?
Regarding the phrase "of the emergence" (*vuṭṭhānassa*): keeping this censure in mind so that there is no contradiction, he explains the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) by saying, "What is meant?

and so forth. The intended meaning here is this: since the Saṅgha is required both at the beginning and at the remainder of the emergence from an offense, it is said to be "required because of the offense. "Emergence from an offense" (*āpattivuṭṭhāna*) means [emergence] from an offense.
"Emergence" means the attainment of the state of being without offense.

"The reason for the designation" refers to the reason for designating it as a *saṅghādisesa*. He says "by way of conventional usage" because the word *nikāya*, though established in its collective sense, is applied to a part of that whole by virtue of that very same convention.
Alternatively, having grasped some characteristic—even when another [characteristic] exists—that which is associated with that characteristic...

*Ruḷhi* (conventional usage) is the established application of a term even in the absence of its literal etymological basis (*nimitta*), due to long-standing common convention regarding a particular object.

For example, just as one who "lies on the earth" is called a *mahisa* (buffalo), and that which "goes" is called a *go* (cow), so too should the conventional nature of the word *nikāya* be understood.
Furthermore, just as a general term may apply to a whole as if it were a universal (*sāmañña*), so too does the linguistic usage that applies to a collection also extend to its individual parts.
"It occurs" means it is expressed by applying the term for the whole to its parts. "Of the ninth intention" means of the intention consisting of inquiry (*vīmaṃsādhippāya*).

238–239. "Lomasā" means those who have body hair (*loma*); thus, "those with abundant hair" is what is meant. "I shall be healthy" means that through the subsiding of the fever of passion (*rāgapariḷāha*), I shall be free from disease.
"By means of release" means by performing the necessary measures for the sake of release. For here, the performance of such measures is intended.
"Releasing" is intended in the sense that "one releases by means of this. The phrase "there will be seed" is said with reference to actions such as taking hold of a cloth.
240. "Two thousand offenses" is stated without taking into account the distinctions such as the *khaṇḍacakkā* (broken wheel) and so forth;
however, one who desires precision should calculate the number of offenses according to those distinctions of the *khaṇḍacakkā* and so on. "Mixed wheel" refers to that which increases on both sides.

This has been stated. Furthermore, the statement beginning with "blue and yellow" and so forth—intending the release of multiple colors at a single moment—is for the purpose of showing that an offense occurs for one who makes an effort with this intention, whether or not the release actually occurs according to that intention.
For it is not possible for the release of all [colors], such as blue and the rest, to occur in a single moment.
“He says something else” means that, being unable to speak directly about his own fault, he speaks of another thing when questioned again.

“The gratification of release” (mocanassāda) is the gratification occurring in the preliminary stage of releasing; for this very reason it is said: “the gratification for the sake of releasing is the gratification of release.
“Affection based on the household” (gehassita-pema): here, by the word *geha*, those who reside in the home—such as one’s mother, sisters, and other internal relatives—are meant.
They have been taken up. Among them, "affection based on the household" (*gehassita-pema*) is the endearment that arises by way of maternal love and so forth;

elsewhere, however, "affection based on the household" refers to lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. "By way of the relish associated with it" means by way of the feeling of pleasure associated with lust.
"By one term" means by the term "affection based on the household."

“Just so” means precisely by way of the volition that relishes the act of emission. Because he lay down without having abandoned the effort previously made by way of relishing the emission, it is said:
“But if... [etc.]... there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense. When, however, a pure mind arises again, because that effort has subsided, it is said:
“If he is of a pure mind... [etc.]... there is no offense. “For the sake of nursing” means for the sake of washing.
*Anokāsaṃ*: the region of the private parts.
263–264. *Gehasita-kāmavitakkaṃ*: sensual thought based on the five strands of sensual pleasure. *Vatthiṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā*:
having firmly grasped the skin at the tip of the private part, the place where urine issues forth. *Nimitte*.
Because there is no physical effort involved, it is stated: "Even for one whose intention is the enjoyment of release, there is no offense if emission occurs.

(265) Regarding the instruction, "Come, friend, you [act as] a novice for me," since even an action performed by another through such a command is considered as if performed by oneself, an offense is stated.
However, if one acts on one's own initiative without being commanded, [the offense is established] due to the completion of all factors.

They say, "There is no offense because of its non-existence. In the case of the *Suttasāmaṇera* story, although there was impure emission, a *dukkaṭa* was stated on account of the grasping of the sexual organ, not on account of the emission itself.
In the case of the *Kāyatthambhana* story, just as an effort can occur in the sexual organ by way of movement, so too [is it here].
Nevertheless, an offense is stated because of the act of stretching out. From the statement "or behind," it should be understood that the region of the thighs at the waist is included on both sides;
therefore, even for one who stands on both sides and contemplates, "The sign is in this place," there is indeed an offense.
Because of the term "the organ" (*aṅgajāta*), the "sign" refers specifically to the urinary passage.

It has been stated. However, "he should not be made to undergo [the penalty] by way of opening and closing [the eyes]" means that no classification of offenses should be applied based on the act of opening and closing the eyes.

This implies that even if one stares repeatedly, opening and closing the eyes many times, there is only a single *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). [This applies when staring] at a woman who has approached facing him, without rolling the eyes.

It should be understood that even in the mere looking at the sign, it is indeed an offense. They say: "There is an *dukkaṭa* even for the gazing at the genitals of wooden statues, plaster figures, or paintings.
(267) "Flower-garland" (*pupphāvalī*) is a designation for a particular kind of game. While playing that game, [if] a broken bank of a river or similar body of water [is swept away] by the water...
Having made a mud-puddle, they sit there with both feet extended and fall [into it].

There is also a reading, "pupphāvaliyaṃ" (in a flower-garland). Regarding the word "pavesentassa" (of one who causes to enter): because it has two objects, the accusative case is used for both "vālikaṃ" (sand) and "aṅgajātaṃ" (the sexual organ).
"Vālikaṃ" means "vālikāya" (in the sand). Here, three factors should be understood: volition, the preparatory effort, and the emission.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the emission of semen is finished.
2. Commentary on the second training rule concerning physical contact. 269.
Regarding the second [rule]: "in those [parts] which are open and where there is darkness, he opens them"—this refers to physical contact with a brahmin woman.
He did this because he desired to attain [the meditative absorption]. Although it was performed by him, because it was performed within himself, it is called "his own failure.
