"Exaltedness" (*uḷāratta*) means exaltedness of mind; what is meant is that it is a superior inclination.

270. Regarding the word *otiṇṇo* (plunged/entered), since it can function as either an object (*kamma-sādhana*) or an agent (*kattu-sādhana*), he demonstrates the meaning according to both possibilities:
He said, “Beings [are like those] by yakkhas and so forth. Regarding the phrase “without having scrutinized”:

it means without having investigated according to their true nature; that is to say, without seeing how those objects such as forms—which produce delight—are established in the mode of being impermanent, suffering, foul, and non-self.

271. *Saññamavelan* means the boundary of virtue (*sīla*). *Ācāra* means conduct, such as the act of taking the hand and so forth. *Assa* refers to the phrase “he should engage in physical contact. 273.
*Etesaṃ padānaṃ vasena* means by way of the terms beginning with “touching” (*āmasana*).
*Ito cito ca... pe... sañcopeti* means he moves his own hand or body horizontally here and there. This is because of the statement: “without releasing [the body] from the body.”

They say that for one who lowers the hand starting from the head and touches the body after releasing it from the cloth, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; but for one who, having removed the hand from the cloth, touches the body starting from the shanks, there is again a *saṅghādisesa*.

Thus, they maintain that among all twelve modes of contact such as touching and so forth, as long as the body has not been released from the cloth, there is only a single offense for each individual act.
He said, "The grasping of the root itself is the measure. This was stated with reference to taking hold of the body with one hand and stroking the body with the other.

However, for one who takes hold of something attached to the body with one hand and strokes the body here and there with the other, the offense is according to the number of applications. Moreover, this *saṅghādisesa* is not only...
It is by way of the object itself; however, it is also by way of perception that he said, "If there is a woman and one perceives her as a woman, it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
In the canonical text, regarding the phrase "and it is an animal," it should be understood that this includes both an animal female and an animal male.

"Equal passion" (*samasārāga*) means a passion identical to that of physical contact. "In the same manner as before" refers to the method previously stated regarding grasping after encircling with ropes, cloth, and so forth.
Again, "in the same manner as before" refers to what was called "equal passion. "In the manner immediately preceding" refers to the method of touching what is attached to the body.
Since body hair is included by the mention of the "veins," a *saṅghādisesa* offense is stated even for the touching of body hair. Now...
Desiring to clarify this very point, he said, "By what is clung to," and so forth.
"In the exposition as it was pointed out" means in the exposition of bodily contact as previously described. "By that" means by that aforementioned cause.
"When perception has been missed" means when perception has failed; it is expressed as "virāgitamhi" (missed) through a change of gender.
“This particular matter” refers to what is stated in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

Some say it may also refer to any other matter whatsoever. “Lusting” means lusting with passion for physical contact. “Not lusting” refers to one who is free from passion for physical contact, such as a mother or a sister; thinking, “I will take one who is not lusting.”
"Taking what is detached [from the body] is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This means that taking [an object] out of affection for one's mother or similar motives is stated to be a dukkaṭa.
The connection is: "This accords with the canonical text (pāḷi).

If one asks, "How does it accord?"—if, when the thought "I shall take what is attached to the woman's body" has arisen, the perception of her as a woman were to become detached, then there would be a grave offense (thullaccaya) in the act of taking what is attached to the body.
If the Blessed One were speaking [in that way], he would not have said, "She is a woman and she perceives her as a woman. Yet it was so stated;
therefore, for one who takes hold of the body with the thought, "I will take what is connected to the body of a woman," the perception of her as a woman is not said to be "lost.
Thus, "one who takes hold of the body with the thought, 'I will take what is connected to the body,' incurs an offense according to the actual basis (the object) itself."
The teaching spoken by the Elder Mahāsumma accords with this canonical text. However, one might here object:

"Even though there is the perception of a woman, for one who takes hold of something connected to the body, at the moment of grasping, because the perception 'I shall take hold of something connected to the body' has been established and the perception 'I am taking hold of a woman' is absent, it is incorrect because the perceptions of the objects are distinct."
He should be asked: "When taking clothing or other items connected to the woman's body, does one take them out of lust for the woman, or out of lust for the clothing and other items?

If he should say, "One takes them out of lust for the clothing and other items," then even one who takes clothing or other items situated elsewhere—rather than being directly connected to the woman's body—would incur a *thullaccaya* offense; therefore, [the factor is] a woman, with the perception of her as a woman.
Because the factors of "being impassioned" and "grasping" are fully present, the opinion of the Elder Mahāsiva alone is the logical view;
furthermore, it accords with the determinations of the commentaries. Here too, this is the intended meaning:

if something were called "dispassioned" merely by being dispassionate toward perception, then for one who perceives, "I am grasping many women by encircling them with my arms," [the act] would apply even to the women standing between [his arms] who are connected to his body.
Because such a perception as "I am taking [it]" is absent for those who have reached the middle [of the act], there would otherwise be no *thullaccaya* (grave offense) by way of that middle state;
nevertheless, since a *thullaccaya* is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is established that this meaning holds:
what has been relinquished through the fading away of perception is not truly called "relinquished. A dark woman is mentioned because her nature is difficult to discern from a distance.

279. "With the intention of enjoying" means with the intention of enjoying the pleasure of contact. Regarding the phrase "even when a woman touches a monk’s body with her own body," this is stated because there is a natural connection of the body even when she touches what is connected to his own body.
"In this case" refers to the section on the forfeiture of what is forfeitable. "With the intention of liberation" refers here first to passion for bodily contact.
Even so, there is no offense for one whose intention is liberation later on. 281.

"Obstructive" means a robber; "an obstacle" is what is meant. The phrase "a mother being carried away by the current of a river" is stated for the purpose of showing the upper limit [of the severity of the offense];
however, with regard to other women as well, if one acts with an intention of compassion...

They say that for one who proceeds according to the method stated regarding a mother, there is no fault at all. However, there are also those who say that because it is specified as "a mother," it is not permitted for others.
A *tiṇaṇḍupaka* is a foot-washer made from the roots of *hirivera* and other such plants.
A *tālapaṇṇamuddikā* is a finger-ring made from palm leaves. "Having turned it over" means [having turned it] from its state of being one's lower garment (*nivāsana*) or upper robe (*pārupana*).

"Having removed it" means having diverted it for the purpose of a robe; this is what is expressed. "It is permissible to place it at the feet for the purpose of a robe"—this is merely an illustration;
it is likewise permissible for the purpose of a rug, a canopy, and so forth. It is also permissible to take it temporarily for the purpose of worship and the like.
Regarding "made in the shape of a woman," here, from the lower limit, even female animals that constitute an offense involving defeat (pārājika) are included.
Because it lacks the nature of a woman, even a form belonging to the animal realm made in the shape of such a woman should be regarded as "untouchable" (*anāmāsa*).
The teachers say: "It is permissible for bhikkhunīs to touch an image of a woman.
Furthermore, it is permissible to take up a cloth, a bedspread, or a wall that has been decorated with images of women, provided one does not touch the female forms themselves.
"Having broken" means that here it should be broken by some object such as a staff or the like, without having grasped it with the hand.

And in this context, because it is stated here that "it is permissible to break even something not belonging to oneself with a staff or the like without touching it with the hand," and because it is stated elsewhere that "one who takes rag-robes (paṃsukūla) may take them even from the body of a woman after making a wound with a knife or similar instrument," [the two cases are distinct].
It is permissible to squeeze a snake that has seized a frog with a stick or other means in order to release the frog.
"Having resolved upon the path" means having the perception of the path, thinking, "I am going on the path.
The phrase "while playing" is said with reference to what belongs to a householder; however, that which belongs to a bhikkhu must not be touched by anyone for any purpose whatsoever.

Because of their state of being difficult to handle. Regarding the phrase "palmyra, jackfruit, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) should be understood as including coconut, watermelon, cucumber, bottle-gourd, pumpkin, eggplant, and plantain fruits.

Since it is stated that "in this context, touching even the aforementioned fruits with the intention of playing is not permitted," it is permissible to touch stones, gravel, and the like even with the intention of playing.
"Mother-of-pearl" (*muttā*) refers to the eight kinds of mother-of-pearl, such as that produced from an elephant’s frontal globe and so forth.

For indeed, there are eight sources of mother-of-pearl: the elephant’s frontal globe, the boar’s tusk, the serpent’s head, the cloud (valāhaka), the bamboo, the fish’s head, the conch, and the *sippī* shell.

Among these, that produced from the elephant’s frontal globe is yellow in color and lacking in luster. That produced from the boar’s tusk has the very same color as the boar’s tusk. That produced from the serpent’s head...

The *nīlāja* pearls are of a very pure blue color and are round; born from clouds, they are radiant and difficult to distinguish [from other gems], and they remain throughout the night dispelling the darkness, serving as the exclusive enjoyments of the gods.
The *veḷuja* pearls are the color of the fruit of the *karakā* creeper and are not radiant;
these *veḷu* plants grow only in places that are the domain of non-human beings (*amanussa*). The *macchasiraja* pearls are the color of the back of a *pāṭhīna* fish.
The round pearls are small and lack luster; these fish are born only in the middle of the ocean.

Those born from shells have the color of the interior of a conch shell and are the size of a *kola* fruit, yet they likewise lack luster. Those born from oyster shells possess an excellence of luster and come in various shapes.
Thus, among the eight kinds of pearls according to their species, those born from fish, shells, and oysters are oceanic.
Some pearls are produced from serpents and are marine, while others are non-marine.

Since marine pearls are predominantly what are seen in the world—and even among those, only those produced from serpents [are common], whereas other types appear only occasionally—therefore, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated:
"Pearl means a marine pearl."
"Jewel" (*maṇi*) refers to all gems other than beryl and so forth, including various types such as *jotirasa*. "Beryl" (*veḷuriya*) is a gem the color of bamboo.
"Conch shell" (*saṅkha*) is a marine conch. "Stone" (*sila*) includes all stones, such as black stone, yellow stone, white stone, and so on.
"Silver" (*rajata*) refers to the remaining items considered precious, such as the *kahāpaṇa* coin. "Gold" (*jātarūpa*) is gold. "Ruby" (*lohitanka*) is a red gem.
“Masāragalla” means a *kabara* gem. “For the sake of the cost of requisites” means for the sake of the cost of requisites such as bowls, robes, and so forth.
“Of the disease of leprosy” is merely an illustration; it is likewise permissible for the sake of any disease whatsoever that is to be cured by it.
“And having determined it for the purpose of medicine, the pearl is permissible”—this is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. “A pearl from a mine” means...
“Merely released from the mine. By the phrase “it is permissible to accept it for the purpose of its commodity value,” he shows that it is also permissible to touch it.
“Made by melting” means made by glass-makers after melting.
“Washed, pierced, and mixed with gems” means made for the purpose of ornamentation by displaying gold vines and the like, and then inlaid with gems.
"Cleaned and pierced, not yet a month old. The phrase "cleaned and pierced" and "mixed with jewels" may be connected as separate items.
By the term "water-conch," it is established that it is also permissible to touch monastic requisites such as the lid of a water-vessel made from a conch.
"The rest" means everything remaining after setting aside the item mixed with jewels. It is specifically the color of mung beans that is mixed with jewels.
He said, "They are like the color of mung beans," meaning that even those mixed with gems must not be like the color of mung beans.
"The rest" refers to the remaining blue stones, excluding those mixed with gems.
"Starting from the seed" means starting from the mineral ore. "A golden cetiya" refers to the relic casket. "He rejected it."
He refused because [the donor] had sent it saying, "Take this for yourselves," rather than saying, "Take this for the purpose of enshrining the relics.
"A golden bubble" means a golden star-shaped ornament. "It is permissible to play with it" means it is allowed to be touched and moved here and there;
thus it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. "It is permissible to remove only the refuse" refers to the guardians of the cetiya.
Whether they be monks or others, it is permissible to remove rubbish by wiping with the hand; it is likewise permissible to wipe away dirt.
"Ārakūṭa metal" refers to base metal.
For there are three kinds of base metals: bell-metal (*kaṃsaloha*), brass (*vaṭṭaloha*), and ārakūṭa.
In this context, *kaṃsaloha* (bronze) is made by mixing three parts of tin; *vaṭṭaloha* (round metal) is made by mixing lead and tin;
and *ārakūṭa* (brass) is made by mixing natural copper and tin. Because it is produced by that very process, it is called "dross-metal.
Since it is stated that [it] "shares the same category as gold," it is not permitted to touch *ārakūṭa*, even though it resembles gold.
"However, another [type] is permissible," so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. Some, however, say:
"Because it is not to be touched, *ārakūṭa* (brass) is included in the category of gold (*jātarūpa*); therefore, both are not permitted to be touched, just like gold.
And the meaning stated first is precisely what the authors of the *gaṇṭhipadas* intended. It is permissible to tend to [it].
It is said because of being connected with lodgings (*senāsana*).
"A message should be sent to the owners" means a message from the owners should be sent. "Having broken it" means having broken it by some means other than grasping it with the hand.
"A drum made of joined hides" (*bherisaṅghāṭa*) is a drum whose hide is joined together. "A lute made of joined parts" (*vīṇāsaṅghāṭa*)...

A *saṅghaṭita-cammavīṇā* is a designation for drums and lutes covered with hide. A "hollow bowl" (*tuccha-pokkhara*) refers to the bowl of a drum or the bowl of a lute that has not been covered with hide.

"Hide fastened on" (*āropita-camma*) refers both to the hide fastened onto the rim of drums and the like for the purpose of covering them, as well as to the hide that has been removed from there and set aside separately. "Or to cover" (*onahituṃ vā*).
To string [the leather] upon drums, lutes, and so forth, after having stretched it over the hide. "To have it covered" means to have it strung by others in that same manner.
"At the time when it becomes an offense of defeat (pārājika)" means at the time before it has rotted.

Regarding the bridge and so forth: because they belong to the category of the ground, they do not stand in the place of what is attached to the body; therefore, a dukkaṭa offense is stated. "A footpath bridge" means...
A small bridge (*khuddakasetu*). A "crossing over a cart-track" (*sakaṭamaggasaṅkamo*) refers to a large bridge that serves as a cart-track.
"To move from its place" means to move the rope from its position. "Should be concealed" means it should be removed.

Here, the five factors are: a human female, the perception of her as a female, lust for bodily contact, the exertion arising from that lust, and the actual engagement in grasping the hand and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning physical contact is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Lewd Speech (Duṭṭhullavācāsikkhāpada): 283.

Regarding the third [rule], it is said that one who has severed their sense of shame (*ottappa*) is called “one who is cut off” (*chinnikā*); thus he says, “‘One who is cut off’ means one whose sense of shame is severed.”
285. By the phrase "as a youth [approaches] a young woman," he shows the state of being free from apprehension regarding the illumination.
"Connected with sexual intercourse" is a demonstration of the characteristic of speech that has reached the pinnacle of impropriety (*duṭṭhulla*).

The expression "by the characteristic of a woman" is stated in order to clarify the meaning already mentioned as "by the characteristic of beauty. "It does not yet reach the head" refers to the passage beginning with "you were endowed with the characteristic of a woman," and so forth.
Speaking in praise, while giving rise to an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*), does not reach its ultimate conclusion.
For in whatever manner speaking in praise results in an offense entailing suspension for one who speaks, in that same manner it reaches its peak for one who speaks.

However, [speaking] such things as "you were endowed with the characteristics of a woman" and so forth, when spoken by one out of lust for the sound of improper speech, [does not result in an offense entailing suspension].
"In the *Gaṇṭhipada* it is stated: 'It is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Regarding the phrase 'if not joined with the eleven words,' it means that if [the speech] is not joined with the eleven words beginning with 'animittāsī,' the speaking of dispraise does not reach its head;
in other words, it is said that it does not constitute the speaking of dispraise. 'Even when joined'..."
Even though the expression of dispraise may be composed of eleven words, it is only when composed of these three [specific] that it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa*.

It is only when the expression of dispraise is composed of exactly these three words—“*sikharaṇī*,” etc.—that it is a *saṅghādisesa*, because the term for the urinary passage is fixed and because of its extreme coarseness.
However, when composed of the eight words beginning with “*animittāsī*,” there is merely the expression of dispraise.

Some say that since it is accomplished [as an offense], but not as a *saṅghādisesa*, those cases are therefore grounds for a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). Others say they are grounds for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because they consist merely of verbal abuse.
However, as in the case of the female wanderer (*paribbājikā*), a grave offense appears more appropriate here.
"The mere size of a keyhole" means the mere size of a hole for a key.
286–287. "A grave offense" refers to the *pārājika* offense for a nun regarding physical contact.

The phrase "laughing, laughing" is stated for the purpose of indicating the actual nature [of the act]. Even if one is not laughing, if one speaks repeatedly out of a lustful attachment to the sound of her voice, it is likewise an offense.
"From body and mind" means that for one who makes a sign with the hand, it originates from both body and mind.

288. Therefore, regarding "it is an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*): it is an offense of wrong-doing because she does not understand [the meaning]; however, for one who does understand, since it is not a non-field of action, it ought to be a serious offense (*thullaccaya*).
For this very reason, in the case of the female wanderer (*paribbājikā*), he will state that there is a serious offense for one who understands.

289. He said this with reference to "that which is not the true Dhamma" (*asaddhamma*); this was stated because the word "sown" (*vāpita*) is a term for the depositing of seed. "It sinks down" (*saṃsīdati*)...

It carries; it proceeds. Alternatively, "it sinks" means it will sink. A human woman, the perception of her as a woman, lust for the sound of her indecent speech, the illumination by that lust, and the awareness at that moment—these are the five factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning indecent speech is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Service according to One’s Desire (Attakāmapāricariyā-sikkhāpada) 290.
In the fourth [rule], "a robe" (*cīvara*) refers to any kind of robe, such as the lower garment (*nivāsana*) and so forth. "Almsfood" (*piṇḍapāta*) refers to any kind of food.
For it is called "almsfood" (*piṇḍapāta*) because it falls into the bowl of a bhikkhu through his wandering for alms (*piṇḍolya*), being obtained here and there from various portions of food.
"Morning meal" (*pāta*) or "congregation" (*sannipāta*) is what is called "almsfood" (*piṇḍapāta*). "Recluse’s lodging" (*senāsana*) means both a bed (*sayana*) and a seat (*āsana*).

For that place, such as a monastery (*vihāra*), where one lies down, reclines, sits, or remains, is a "recluse’s lodging. It is called a "condition" (*paccaya*) because one goes toward it (*pati eti*);

thus he said, "it is a condition in the sense of being a support (*patikaraṇa*). Alternatively, it is a condition in the sense of being the basis for the approach of disease (*rogassa patiayana*), or in the sense of going against [it] (*paccanīka-gamana*).

The meaning is "in the sense of subsiding"; this is what is meant. For the sense of "relying upon" (*pati-aya*) is the state of being an antidote to a disease characterized by the disturbance of the elements (*dhātu-kkhobha*) or characterized by the painful feeling caused by that [disturbance].
"Of whatever" refers to any one among the [remedies] such as ghee and so forth.
"Suitable" (*sappāya*) means beneficial; the intention is [that it leads] to the subsiding of the morbid change. It is the "work of a physician" because it is to be performed by him.
Therefore he says, "because it has been authorized. "By the city's requisites" means by those who protect by surrounding the city. They say there are seven city requisites:
the trench-ditch, the moat, the rampart, the watchtower, the pillar, the crossbar, and the circular coping on top of the rampart.
"The white requisite" refers to the ornament of perfectly pure virtue (*sīla*). For here, the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is intended by the term "chariot."
And right speech and the others are called "requisites" (*parikkhāra*) in the sense of being ornaments. "Wheel of energy" (*vīriyacakkā*) means the wheel of energy.

"Requisites for life" (*jīvitaparikkhārā*) are the causes for the continuation of life. "To be acquired" (*samudānetabbā*) means they must be properly brought forth from below upwards, or sought after.
It is also a "retinue" (*parivāra*) because it wards off obstacles on all sides; hence he said: "For life... [etc.]"
"From guarding. In this context, "between" (*antara*) means an opening or an interval;
"from guarding" means from protecting by surrounding one's own master without giving an opportunity to enemies, like attendants standing guard. "Of it" refers to life.
"By way of being the cause" means by way of being the cause for its long-term continuation; for even a medicine that has become an elixir (*rasāyana*) [lasts] for a very long time...
It simply means that one carries on with life for a certain time. 291.

*Upacāre* means in such a place where, while standing, one is able to communicate. *Kāmo ceva hetu ca pāricariyā ca attho*—in these phrases from the Pāḷi, having extracted the word *attakāma*, it means "one's own desire," and so forth.

The rest is the phrasing (*byañjana*). The remainder is as follows. *Sesam* means the rest. *Byañjanam* means the phrasing. *Ādi* means and so forth. Having extracted the word *attakāma* from the Pāḷi, [it refers to] one's own desire.
In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), four meanings are stated: "for one's own sake" (*attano hetu*), "one's own intention" (*attano adhippāyaṃ*), and "one's own service" (*attano pāricariyaṃ*).
Among these, in the first interpretation of meaning, desire (*kāma*), cause (*hetu*), and service (*pāricariyā*) constitute the meaning;

the remaining single term, "intention" (*adhippāya*), is merely the phrasing (*byañjana*). This is because, in the first compound, that [intention] cannot possibly be the actual meaning, and thus it would be purposeless. However, in the second...

In the *Atthavikappa*, some say that the two remaining phrases—"purpose and service" (*attho ca pāricariyā ca*) and "desire and cause" (*kāmo ca hetu ca*)—are the phrasing (*byañjana*), because their meaning (*attha*) is not present there;
thus, they maintain that the four phrases have been joined according to two types of grammatical analysis (*viggaha*).
This same meaning is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, and likewise in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada*, *Majjhimag-aṇṭhipada*, and *Mahāgaṇṭhipada*.
However, in the first interpretation of the meaning, "desire," "cause," and "service" constitute the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*);

the remainder—beginning with "by desire reckoned as the act of sexual intercourse"—is merely the analytical statement (*viggahavākya*) and the mere phrasing (*byañjanamatta*) consisting of a literal word-for-word explanation.
In the second interpretation of the meaning, "intention" and "service" constitute the intended meaning; the remainder refers to that which has been desired by oneself.
The analysis of the compound *icchitādi* is merely a verbal expression consisting of a simple phonetic arrangement; such is the meaning stated.
From the statement, "without regard for the verbal expression (*byañjana*)," it is understood that this very meaning is more appropriate here.

For by the phrase "without regard for the verbal expression," the meaning indicated in the commentary—that one should not be concerned with the verbal expression according to the analyzed form stated therein—is illuminated.
Now, in order to demonstrate that very same meaning already stated by correlating it with the word-analysis (*padabhājana*), the following was begun:
“When it is said, ‘for one’s own desire, for one’s own sake, for one’s own service,’ the wise will understand. This is what is meant:
when “for one’s own sake” is said, the meaning “for one’s own benefit” is understood; [and when] “for one’s own desire”...
When it is said, “one’s own service,” the meaning understood is that the service is for the sake of desire.

Therefore, the wise will understand that by these three terms—“one’s own desire,” “for one’s own sake,” and “one’s own service”—the alternative interpretation of the meaning is stated as *attakāmapāricariyā*, which means service performed through desire for one’s own benefit. [Regarding] “one’s own intention”:
Furthermore, since the word *adhippāya* has the same meaning as the word *kāmita*, and because both compounds share the common form of "one's own service" (*attano pāricariyā*),

the wise will understand that this alternative interpretation of the meaning— namely, "service to one's own desires" (*attakāmapāricariyā*) in the sense of what is desired and wished for by oneself— is shown by these two phrases.

"Etadagga" means "this is the foremost. Although in the training rule concerning indecent speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*) the request for sexual intercourse is mentioned, that was stated by way of a craving for the indecent speech of another;
here, however, it is by way of a craving for one's own sexual intercourse—this is the distinction.
Among the cases of disciplinary offenses (*vinītavatthu*), the phrase "Therefore, sister, give the best gift" refers to [the gift] for one's own sake.

It should be understood that this has been stated. A human woman, the perception of her as a woman, lust for the service of one’s own desires, the speaking of praise because of that lust, and the awareness at that moment—these are the five factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the service of one’s own desires is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Meddling (Sañcaritta-sikkhāpada) 296.
In the fifth [training rule], "wisdom" (*paṇḍicca*) is the state of being wise; this is a designation for knowledge.

"Possessing intelligence" (*gatimanta*) means endowed with the course of knowledge. By the term "wise," the possession of natural knowledge is expressed; by the term "skilled" (*byatta*), [the possession of knowledge] regarding what is to be done by women is expressed.
"With confident wisdom. Therefore he said: "Skilled in means and confident.

"Wise" means endowed with the wisdom that arises instantly and at that very moment when any duty regarding a particular matter presents itself—this being what is termed "wisdom arising from the occasion" (*ṭhānuppattipaṇṇā*).
Therefore he said: "She does what she sees. "Clever" means dexterous in preparing rice gruel, meals, and so forth. "Endowed with initiative and energy" means...

It means that she is endowed with physical energy such that, unlike other indolent people who remain exactly where they were when sitting and remain exactly where they were when standing, she does not do so, but rather accomplishes all her tasks with an expansive mind.

"By a young girl" (*kumārikāya*) is the locative case used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*), or the instrumental case used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Therefore he said, "for the sake of the young girl. *Āvahanaṃ*.

*Āvāha* is the taking of a girl through the act of formal acceptance (*pariggaha*); likewise, *vivāha* is the giving [of her] in that same manner. Therefore, he said, "of the son-in-law," and so forth. 297–298.
"Causing to cook" (*randhāpana*) is stated with reference to cooking one's own food; "causing to cook" (*pacāpana*) is stated with reference to having anyone else cook [food].
He said, "wherever she has gone," and so forth, in order to show the meaning of "she who has gone to a bad family is 'ill-fated' (*duggatā*)."
*Āharaṇaṃ* (bringing) is *āhāra* (food). *Na upāhaṭanti* means not brought; *na dinnaṃ* means not given. *Kaya* is taking, and *vikkaya* is giving.
Having included both of these, it is called "trade" (*vohāra*). Regarding the phrase "adorned and embellished":
here, *maṇḍana* is the decoration with external requisites, while *pasādhana* is the grooming of internal things such as the hair and so forth.
300. By the phrase “it is not proper to perform a marvel,” it is indicated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Because it is stated, “It must be given by one who has been defeated,” he who does not give it is to be dealt with for relinquishing his responsibility. It is called *acirakālādhikārika* because its jurisdiction (*adhikāra*) exists over a short period of time;

it refers to matchmaking (*sañcaritta*). Alternatively, the reading is *acirakālācārika*; it is called *acirakālācārika* because its conduct (*ācāra*), or transgression (*ajjhācāra*), occurs within a short period of time.
Although those ordained by the "Come, monk" formula and those ordained by going for refuge may incur offenses such as acting as a go-between—
which are offenses prohibited by rule (paññattivajja)— the Blessed One, excluding them because such ordinations are not valid at all times,

established the tradition here as well by showing that one who is ordained through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*) is a monk in accordance with the requirements for all times.

In this context, he stated the word-commentary: “The monk who... [as before] ...this is the monk intended in this sense,” not because those [arahants] are incapable of committing offenses such as matchmaking (*sañcaritta*).

For even arahants who have little learning, though they do not commit what is blameworthy by worldly convention, may—due to their lack of familiarity with the formal rules (*paṇṇatti*)—build a large dwelling, a small hut, or a shared residence.

"Sleeping together" refers to the kinds of offenses one incurs through the door of the body; "acting as a go-between," "reciting the Dhamma word-for-word," "speaking more than five or six words," and "reporting what has actually occurred" refer to the kinds of offenses one incurs through the door of speech;
and by way of consenting to what has been set aside, one incurs the offense of accepting money through the door of the mind.

301. *Sañcaraṇa* means wandering; one who possesses that is a *sañcarī*. The state of being such is *sañcaritta*. Therefore he said, "the state of wandering," meaning the state of wandering between women and men.
In the phrases "in the state of a husband" (*jāyattane*) and "in the state of a paramour" (*jārattane*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimittatthe*);
thus, it is meant "for the sake of the state of a husband" and "for the sake of the state of a paramour. [The phrase] "in the state of a husband" (*jāyabhāve*)...

“To the state of a wife. “To the state of a lover” means to the state of a husband. Although in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for this, the commentary is stated using the feminine gender as in “you will become a female lover,” nevertheless, because the explanation “in the state of being a lover” is common to both genders, he shows the meaning by applying it also to the masculine gender:
“In the state of being a lover, while communicating the intention of a woman to a man...”

He said, beginning with the words, “He announces,” and so forth. For here, one who announces to a man the intention of a woman, saying, “You will become her lover,” is said to announce [her] in the state of being a lover (*jāra*).
However, in the Pāli text, the construction is made using the feminine gender;
nevertheless, following that, it is also possible to construe it according to the masculine gender.

Now, demonstrating the meaning according to the method stated in the Pāḷi, he says, “Moreover,” and so forth. He shows the very same meaning already stated—“you will be a husband”—by specifying it with a synonymous term:
“you will be a master. And this was said because the explanatory description “in the state of a paramour” (jārattaṇe) is common to both genders.
“You will be a momentary wife” (muhuttikā) is said with reference to one who has no husband.
“You shall become a paramour” refers to one who already has a husband. “At the very least, for even a momentary [act]”—this is merely an illustration;
thus he said, “by this very means,” and so forth.
(303) “Living according to one’s own will” means wandering according to one’s own desire. “One’s own authority” means one’s own command. “Lineage” refers to the Gotama lineage and so forth.
*Gotta* means lineage. *Dhamma* refers to the religious tradition of the Paṇḍaraṅga ascetics and others, or the specific custom of various clans.
Since the word *gotta* applies to those possessing a clan, and the word *dhamma* applies to those who practice the doctrine, he said, "by those of the same clan," and so forth.

In this context, *sagottehi* means by those of the same clan; the meaning is "born of the same lineage. *Sahadhammikehi* means by those who should practice together with one another within the teaching of a single Teacher.
Or by those with similar family duties. Therefore he said, "By those who have gone forth under one teacher," and so forth.

Therein, by the phrase "by those who have gone forth under one teacher," the white-robed wanderers and others are meant; "by those included in the same group" means by those such as florists who are included in the same group.
"With a master" means with protection. "With legal penalty" refers to her for whose going out a punishment has been established by the king. Of the latter...
"Of two" means that sexual misconduct exists for those who are protected by a guardian or subject to punishment, because they have an owner.
"Not for others" means that for the other eight types—those protected by their mother and so forth—there is no sexual misconduct when they go to another man, because they lack an owner.
For those who, having stolen the touch belonging to an owner, produce pleasure in others, there is sexual misconduct.
Nor are the mother and others masters over their touch. For the mother and others do not guard them for the sake of their own experience of that touch;
rather, they prevent improper conduct by forbidding them from going to other men.
However, in all eight of these cases, sexual misconduct on the part of the man still occurs, just as it does when he has cohabitation with his mother and the others.
She does not permit [it], because she has protected herself; thus, by having stolen contact that was protected and guarded by others, it becomes something touched [by her].
"Bought with wealth" means bought with wealth for the purpose of becoming a wife. Therefore he said, "But because... and so forth. "By means of enjoyment" means for the sake of enjoyment.
For she who lives for the sake of enjoyment is called a "lifestyle-wife" (*bhogavāsinī*). "Having obtained" refers to him who makes her live there.
"Having received it from his hand. "The one with the water-bowl" refers to her having been taken after touching the water-bowl.

Therefore he said, "Of both," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "brought by a banner": here, because of its association with a banner, the army itself is expressed by the word "banner"; thus it means "brought by an army with raised banners.
Therefore he said, "By [an army] with raised banners," and so forth.

305. "Announced externally" means it has been announced elsewhere. "She will perform that action" is said with reference to her fitness for performing that action, whether she actually performs the task after being informed or not.
Without informing the boy or girl, [the transaction is made] by their parents and so forth directly to the parents and so forth themselves.

It should be understood that even when a message has been sent, it remains a *saṅghādisesa* offense due to the fulfillment of the three factors consisting of the sending, the testing of whether it was received, and the bringing back of the report.

With reference to the very person for whose sake the message was sent, when it is reported to that mother or others, because the object is one and the same, the mother and so forth are also indeed the "field";
thus, it is shown that the state of having entered the field remains.
“‘I renounce the Buddha,’ and so forth, was uttered. It corresponds to this; here the intention is as follows:

just as there is no discrepancy for one who causes another—such as a pupil or attendant—to announce [the renunciation] without announcing it oneself, so too there is no discrepancy for one who speaks to her mother or others for the purpose of making her announce it, without announcing it herself. ‘He leads her home’ means...”

Regarding the term *gharaṇī* (wife) and the phrase "by way of the fundamental position" (*mūlaṭṭhāna*): here, for a man, his mother and others are called "fundamental positions" (*mūlaṭṭhā*) because they are the primary basis for sending him on a mission.

In the case of the phrase "the mother of a woman protected by her mother sends a bhikkhu," it means either that she sends the bhikkhu to her own daughter, saying, "Let him be the wife of such-and-such a person," or she sends him to another man.
"It should be understood that [the messenger] sends [the message], saying: 'Let my daughter become the wife of such-and-such a person. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
'Because of the method stated previously' means because of the method stated regarding the first *saṅghādisesa* offense.
'He departs from right there' means he departs from that very spot without returning again and without informing the one who sent the command. By another..."
The phrase "by means of what ought to be done" is stated for the purpose of showing the purity of the motive for going.

However, even after having gone for that very purpose, if one does not report anything, one is said to "not investigate. The term "without rejoicing" is stated with reference to one who proceeds in such a manner;
yet, even if there is rejoicing, one who does not report the matter to the Teacher is still said to "not investigate. Regarding the third clause:
"By the method stated" means by the method stated in the passage beginning, "He, not rejoicing in her words...
"By the counting of the bases" means by the counting of pairs of female and male bases when there is an equal number of many women and men;
however, if one side is in excess, the classification of the offense should be understood according to the count of those in excess.
339–340. Regarding the fourth section in the Pāḷi: although the words "one who goes does not fulfill [the agreement], one who comes breaks it;
there is no offense" are not explicitly stated, they are nonetheless implied by the sense; thus it is said, "there is no offense in the fourth case.
"Artisans" (kārukānaṃ) refers to carpenters and the like. The five types of artisans—namely, the woodworker, the metalworker, the weaver, the dyer, and the barber—are called "artisans" (kārukā).
"By such [a person]... pe ... there is no offense": this is said with the understanding that even such service for a layperson does not exist [in this case].
"It originates from the body": for one who does not know the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*) or the state of being fit to be addressed, it originates from the body.
"It originates from speech": here too, the same method applies. "It originates from both body and speech": having known the formal rule...
It should be understood that even for one who does not know the status of being "one with whom one need not speak" (*alaṃvacanīya*), [the offense] arises from body and speech.
"They become ones with whom one need not speak" means they have been relinquished by the giving of a leaf-token (*paṇṇadāna*) and so forth, according to local custom.

However, regarding the phrase "but having known the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*)," it should be understood as "or the status of being one with whom one need not speak. For this very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "Both of these..."

However, it is stated: "But for one who enters [the attainment] having understood by means of these very three methods, those same three become 'with mind' (sacittaka) through the consciousness that understands both.
Therefore, even in the phrase "by the consciousness that understands the designation" (*paṇṇatti-jānana-citta*), "understanding both" (*tadubhaya-jānana*) must be mentioned.
This applies even to one who takes away what has been given after writing down his own intention on a leaf without having informed the bhikkhu.
One should not conclude that there is an offense simply because this training rule is "without intention" (*acittaka*). However,

since the text says "he informs" (*āroceti*) and the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) likewise demonstrates that it is specifically the act of informing that is shown in various places, one must understand that an offense occurs only for one who informs by means of either body or speech.
341. Regarding the phrase "in cases such as *duṭṭhulla* (grave offenses) and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes *sañcaritta* (mediating between men and women).

Here, although it is not explicitly stated that a "woman" refers to a human woman and not a *yakkhinī*, a *petī*, or an animal, nor that a "man" refers to a human man and not a *yakkha* and so on, nevertheless, it is precisely human women and men who are intended here. Therefore...
In those with whom one enters into matchmaking, there must be their human status, not being of an age unfit for marriage, and the acts of accepting, investigating, and returning [the proposal];
these are the five factors here.
The commentary on the training rule regarding matchmaking is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Building of a Hut (Kuṭikārasikkhāpada) 342.
Regarding the sixth [rule]: "By so much" means by so much wood and so forth. "Of unlimited measure" means those whose measure of wood and so forth is not delimited.
It is not permissible to ask for a person [to provide materials] so as to cut off the root [of their ownership], because it would deprive another of what belongs to them and make it one's own.

It is not permissible to ask for something after having made it one's own. Thus, for one who asks from a place where they are neither related nor invited, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to requesting from a non-relative.
Even for one who consents to accepting a slave for their own sake, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing, because of the statement:
"He abstains from accepting male and female slaves. However, [requesting] a slave from a place where one is related or invited...
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who consents while requesting [the act] for the purpose of cutting off the roots [of life].

"One should not request one's own action" is stated for the sake of protecting the training rule against taking life. "Even without specifying [the victim], one should not request it" is stated because there is the possibility that people might otherwise misunderstand [the intent].
However, for one who requests manual labor with a pure mind, there is no offense whatsoever.
"For the purpose of illustrating the state of being entirely allowable" means for the purpose of illustrating the state of being allowable in every respect.
"It is permissible to say, 'Give the root'" is said because, since they first said, "We shall give the root," there is no *viññatti* (requesting);
and because, since "the root" was spoken, it is not an unallowable statement due to its being a general term; therefore, it is permissible to say, "Give the root."
It is permissible. "Uninhabited" means unclaimed. Regarding "unfit coins and so forth should not be given":
although it is permissible for one who does not accept unfit coins and the like to give them by using a term for what is allowable (*kappiya-vohāra*), nevertheless, it is not appropriate.
Furthermore, people might think that he possesses something belonging to him and thus feel inclined to harass him; therefore, the giving of unfit coins and such is [forbidden].
It is prohibited. "Having cooked it in that same way" means having cooked it by means of manual labor alone.
When asked even this much—"Venerable sir, what is it?"—it is permissible to state the purpose for which one entered, because it is a question that has been asked.
"Are they allowable" refers to conduct; the intention is that there is no offense. "They should be accepted after having had them made allowable."
Even when dust clings to a branch and falls, if there is a desire to cut and eat the branch, it is stated [that this is permissible] for the sake of comfortable enjoyment.
Regarding the statement, “It is allowable to fetch a river...,” it is said because [the water] is unappropriated. Regarding the statement, “From a house...
it should be used,” the intention is that since the water is appropriated, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to making a formal request (*viññatti*). ...by those who are shameless...
"Should not be made to do" refers here to food intended for consumption, as this discussion concerns solid food (*uttaribhaṅga*).
However, regarding external articles of use, it is permissible even for those who are shameless to have manual labor performed [for them].
But as for a bull... "it is not permissible to have it brought" means that one may not have it brought by cutting off its source for one's own sake.

It is not permissible. "For one who causes [something] to be brought, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that for requesting from one who is not a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

Even if one consents for one's own sake, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing, because it is stated: "He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. For this very reason, he said:
"It is not permissible to ask for something even from a place where one is invited by a relative, if it would result in the cutting off of the root [of their livelihood]. "Having protected" means...
"Having guarded it so that thieves do not carry it off. "Having tended it" means having tended it with the provision of grass, fodder, and so forth.
"It should not be accepted" is stated because accepting oxen for one's own use has been prohibited.
"Give us a cart... "...it is permissible": it is not permissible to say, "Give us a cart," by way of cutting off the source [of the oxen].
"It is permissible as a temporary loan" means that it is permissible to ask for anything after making it a temporary loan.
This same principle should be applied to creepers and other items belonging to others.

Regarding the phrase "only in the case of creepers and so forth sufficient to constitute 'heavy goods' (*garubhaṇḍa*)," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here should be understood as including bamboo, muñja grass, pabbaja grass, ordinary grass, and clay. As for the basis [of the offense], by way of the object...
They say that it is not permissible to ask for heavy goods—even if one does not possess them—such as yellow orpiment, vermilion, and so forth, which, though small in quantity, are of great value.
The word "sā" (she/that) refers to the solicitation (*viññatti*).
And here, that [solicitation] consists of making one's intention known by any means whatsoever, such as indirect talk (*parikathā*) and the like.
“Intimation” (viññatti) is to be understood as that which is to be accepted. Therefore he said, “in every way,” meaning in all its modes.
By this, he demonstrates that even making known [one’s needs] by means of indirect talk (*parikathā*) and so forth is not permitted.

For indirect talk, hinting (*obhāsa*), and giving signs (*nimittakamma*) are not permitted regarding the two requisites of robes and almsfood. Now, regarding the requisite of lodgings, the intended intimation—by means of indirect talk and so forth—[is explained].
Showing this by way of distinction, he said: "The mere act of requesting, such as saying 'Bring it' or 'Give it,' is not permissible.

Regarding the statement that indirect talk (*parikathā*), hinting (*obhāsa*), and giving signs (*nimitta-kamma*) are permissible: here, "indirect talk" means speaking by way of a circuitous route, such as saying, "The lodgings for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus are crowded," and so forth.
"Hinting" means making an indirect suggestion so that one's intention becomes clear without speaking directly, [for example]: "Lay followers..."
“Where do you live? “In a palace, venerable sir. “But, lay follower, a palace is not permitted for bhikkhus,” and so forth.
What is called “making a sign” (nimittakamma) is making a sign regarding requisites such that one’s intention is made known;
for example, when one is preparing the ground and so forth for the purpose of a dwelling, [others ask]: “Venerable sir, what are you doing? Who is having it built?”
When this was said, the words beginning with “no one at all” [were spoken].
Now, showing that everything including the formal request for requisites for the sick is permissible, he says: “But regarding requisites for the sick,” and so forth.
Furthermore, medicine that has arisen in such a way may be used once the illness has subsided; it is not [otherwise].
"Is it allowable? Regarding this, those who uphold the Vinaya say: "The Blessed One has provided an opening for its use under the pretext of illness;
therefore, it is allowable to use it even when one is not ill, and there is no offense. However, those who uphold the Suttas say:
"Even though there is no offense, it nevertheless disturbs one's livelihood; therefore, it is not allowable for one established in the practice of effacement (*sallekha*)."
“They say he practices self-effacement (*sallekha*). “They depart” means they go away. 344.

“Maṇikaṇṭho” means one who has a jewel on the neck; or, it should be understood as a *madhyapadalopa-samāsa* (compound with the middle term omitted), meaning one whose neck is distinguished by a jewel.
“Devavaṇṇaṃ” means the state of a deity (*devattabhāva*). “Pasannākāraṃ” means [the manner] of those who are confident (*pasanna*).
What is to be done is service, which is to say attendance; this is what is meant.

It should be understood that he said, "I have need of the gem," because his own prosperity would come about through the non-returning of that gem due to his requesting it, or else it was spoken thus by way of a cryptic utterance (*mantapada*).
345. “In the vicinity of the present” means in the past that is near the present. It is thus permissible to speak in this way:
when one ought to say “you have come,” because it is in the vicinity of the present, it is permissible to speak using the designation of the present tense, namely, “you are coming.
However, the grammatical characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) here should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). This is the same method [when one ought to say] “we have come.”
The phrase “I am coming” (*āgacchāmi*) is shown to be a conventional expression for that which is near to the present.
Since nothing can be accomplished by mere begging alone, the intended meaning is stated as “with requisites begged for by oneself.
*Ullittā* means plastered facing upwards; *ullittā* [in this context] means plastered facing downwards.

“Lined inside” (ullittā). Since those who plaster with the face upwards mostly plaster the interior, and those who plaster with the face downwards plaster the exterior, it is therefore said: “Lined inside means plastered on the inside;

lined outside means plastered on the outside. In that context, “lined inside” refers to the remaining areas to be plastered, excluding the un-plasterable spaces such as the surfaces of the rafters, the framework of the joints, the openings for windows, and the vents for smoke.
Having joined it with the rafters, it is "plastered inside" when smeared with lime or clay on the interior of the roof.

It is called "plastered outside" when smeared on the exterior of the roof in the same manner as described. It is called "plastered both inside and outside" when smeared in that same way on both the interior and the exterior of the roof.

The phrasing is consistent because the explanatory statement (*niddesa*), "by one who has it made," is formulated with the causal agent (*hetukattā*)—just as the introductory term (*uddiṭṭhapada*), "by one who is having it made," was formulated with the causal agent.

If this is so, why was its word-commentary (*padabhājana*) stated as "either doing it oneself or having it done"? To this he says: "But because... [and continues with] "what was poorly done by oneself."
Because of such statements as, “he causes others to complete it,” it is said: “Even when performing [the act] oneself, one should proceed according to the method stated here.
In this context, “according to the method stated here” means according to the method stated in this training rule (sikkhāpada).
Regarding the phrase “both of them,” namely the one who performs and the one who causes to perform—how are they included by the single expression “by the one causing to perform”? For it is not so.
"One who causes [it] to be made" is indeed one who "makes" it; however, the intended meaning here should be understood as follows:

since one must proceed according to the method stated here by both the one who makes it himself and the one who causes it to be made, therefore, when it is said that "the one causing it to be made should proceed in this way," the fact that "the one making it himself" should do so even more so is already implied by the sense of the matter; thus the Blessed One said, "by the one causing it to be made."
Therefore, when it is said "by one having [it] made," even a meaning obtained through implication is indeed included by that very term.

As for the phrase "the phrasing would be reversed": since "by one having [it] made" is not a synonymous expression for "by one doing [it]," therefore, by way of the word-meaning, it is either "by one doing [it]" or "by one having [it] made."
The intention is that if the detailed exposition (*niddesa*) were made, the phrasing (*byañjana*) would become contradictory.
"Only the mere meaning" (*atthamattameva*) means only that meaning which is obtainable from the word-meaning (*padattha*) and from the functional capacity (*sāmatthiya*).
"Enumeration" (*uddesa*) means that which is to be enumerated. "Indeterminate" (*abbohārika*) means not authoritative (*appamāṇa*). This is said without specifying "in length and in breadth."
Because the word *vā* is used in the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*), he says “But whoever...
and so forth to show that even when increased by one side, it is still an offense. “Three cubits” means three cubits by the carpenter’s cubit.
“A bed of standard measure” refers to a bed measuring nine standard *vidatthi*s. It should be made according to the measure; this is said with reference to the maximum measure.
A hut that is exactly the maximum size and whose site has not been formally authorized (*adesitavatthuka*) is not permitted;

however, one that is smaller than the prescribed measure, even if its site is not formally authorized, is permitted. To prevent anyone from having doubt on this point, it is said: "even smaller than the measure," and so forth.
In this context, "smaller than the measure" means smaller than the measure stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*). By the latter measure, [it refers to] four cubits.

Regarding the phrase "there is no hut that is smaller": in order to show what constitutes a hut that possesses the defining characteristics of a hut starting from four cubits, it is said, "four cubits or five cubits.
"Mud-plaster" refers to plaster made with some kind of cement, or plaster made of red clay and so forth.
"Even without plaster" means that it is indeed not subject to the designation [of a hut]. "A door-frame of planks" refers to the door-posts. "Even after looking" means...
The intention is that it is permissible to do so either by obtaining permission or by means of a formal act of seeking permission (*apalokana-kamma*).
353. Just as a fixed route for travel is not permitted for lions and other such animals when they set out on their range, likewise a fixed route for travel is not permitted for elephants.
"Of these" refers to lions and the rest. "Grounds for wandering" (*cāribhūmi*) means the range of their hunting grounds (*gocara-bhūmi*).

"Not taken" means not prohibited; this is the intended meaning. "For the sake of health" means for the sake of being free from affliction. "The rest" refers to those things dependent on grain-crops and so forth.
Regarding "dependent on grain-crops," here the word "grain-crop" (*pubbaṇṇa*) refers to the place where the grain-crop grows.
Therefore he said: "standing upon the seven kinds of grain... and so on. "Abbhāghāta" means that which is struck down (*abhihananti*) there. It is also called a "house of enemies" (*verighara*).
To clarify this very point, it is said: "It was made for the purpose of killing thieves.
"Dhammagandhikā" means those who have the scent of having their hands, feet, and so forth cut off.
"It cannot be moved about" means that because of the presence of the places where the cutting occurred and so on, it is not possible to move it about. "Pācinaṃ" means...

The determination to be built must be made in the vicinity of the site for the hut. Although there is no distinction here between prior effort and simultaneous effort as there is in the case of taking what is not given, nevertheless, their distinction is shown by the statement, "having cut [the trees], they must be made again";
this is done here to demonstrate the limits of the breaking down of the hut. "For that purpose" means for the purpose of scraping it. "Thus made" means...
It was built on a site not formally authorized, or it exceeded the prescribed dimensions. A *dārukuṭṭikā* is a hut (*kuṭi*) where the walls are made of wood;

the same principle applies to terms such as *silākuṭṭikā* (stone-walled) and so forth. By *paṇṇasāla* (leaf-hut), he refers specifically to a hut that is to be covered with leaves on the outside and plastered both inside and out.
For this very reason, he said: "I shall plaster it, including the walls and the roof."
The phrase "or on the inner plaster" (*antolepe vā*) and so forth is stated with reference to one who wishes to finish [the work] by means of the inner plaster.
The same principle applies here as well regarding "or on the outer plaster" (*bahilepe vā*). It should be construed as: "placed either in that door-panel or in the window.
"Its space" (*tassokāsaṃ*) means the space of that door-panel or window. "Having increased it again" (*puna vaḍḍhetvā vā*) refers to the space previously set aside.
"If it is small, having increased it again by breaking [the wall]. "The plaster does not join" means that the plaster previously applied does not join with the door-frame or the window;
what is meant is that it does not remain as a single continuous whole.
"That" refers to the door-frame or the window. "An offense of Saṅghādisesa from the very first" is because the function of the plastering has been completed.

If one places it against a closed door or a window, it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense even beforehand. Regarding the phrase "having made it so that it does not reach the covering by at least eight finger-breadths":

they say it is permissible if one places it such that there is not even a space the size of a single finger-breadth on the wall or the roof that has not been joined with plaster, thinking, "In this way, may no offense accrue to me. Only a mud wall is reckoned as a "plastered [wall]."
Regarding the statement "he goes," it is said: "If he builds a wall of clay, there is an offense when it is joined together with the roofing and plastering.
There is no offense for both because the first [layer] has not been joined and the second can be considered as being for one's own sake;
therefore, even without the pretext of a formal duty (*vattasīsa*), if one acts thinking, "I shall do this for him" without being commanded by him, there is no offense.
There is no offense for both. If he acts having been commanded by him, the offense belongs to the one who gave the command alone.
354. The thirty-six tetrads refer to the first section beginning with "A bhikkhu builds a hut," which consists of:

the tetrad on the ground not being designated, the tetrad on the ground being designated, the tetrad on exceeding the measurement, the tetrad on the measurement being observed, and the tetrad on the ground not being designated and exceeding the measurement.

The "fourfold group of the measure of the site as taught" consists of six fourfold groups; likewise, there are five such groups for each of the [five] modes beginning with "if he so commands," making thirty-six in total.

These are stated for the purpose of showing the classification of offenses. Because it is stated without distinction in the *mātikā*—namely, "If a bhikkhu, on a site that has living beings and lacks space for movement"—there might be a misconception that even in cases where there are living beings and no space for movement, it would still be a *saṅghādisesa* offense; therefore, [these details are given] to prevent such a wrong understanding.

“An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs in the case of [building] with encroachment and without a cleared space; and it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) due to the fact that the site has not been formally dedicated and because it exceeds the prescribed measurement.
These [rules] are stated for the purpose of showing the classification of offenses.

Regarding the phrase “with two offenses entailing suspension,” although one should have said “by two,” it is expressed as such through the alteration of grammatical number and the alteration of verbal inflection.
And because it is stated, "and for two [offenses] there is a *saṅghādisesa*," he says: "The meaning should be understood by means of two *saṅghādisesas*...

Since it is stated, "or it may be given to another," they say that even for one who, having obtained an unfinished hut, builds it for his own sake, there is no offense at all, because from the beginning it was not yet completed.
"To be cleared away" (*apacinitabbā*) means to be demolished. "Level with the ground" (*bhūmisamaṃ*).
"Having made" means having made it level with the site of the hut.
"For here no plaster is required" is said because of the absence of plaster for the roof;
however, since it has been separately permitted, if they apply plaster inside the cave on the upper part for the sake of painting and so forth, it is indeed allowable.
In the *Gaṇṭhipada* it is stated that a cave made of bricks and so forth, but not constructed by means of clay (*lepadānava*), is what is called a "cave" (*guhā*).

Furthermore, since it was said that "a hut covered with grass or leaves is permitted," and then [the text] again shows this by saying "the roof [is made] with sticks" and so on, it is clear that what is intended is a small hut covered with grass and leaves. The roof is a lattice-work bound together with sticks.
"Having made" means having bound it like a net with poles placed lengthwise and crosswise. "Having plastered over" means having destroyed the grass and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the plaster was joined with the wall-plaster," since this is said with reference to the state of being plastered on both sides (ullittāvalitta) of the roof, even if one has no need for wall-plaster, [one should apply it] all around the roof-plaster.
They say that even if a wall is joined together by a small amount [of plaster], it is indeed an offense even without the application of wall-plaster.

However, this does not accord with the statement in the Aṭṭhakathā: "If one makes a stone foundation below solely for the purpose of releasing termites, and then plasters over it without plastering that [foundation], the plaster is said not to be 'joined';

As for the statement, “Because there was no intention to plaster or coat, even though it was joined with a stone slab, no offense is said to have occurred therein,” that too is not correct.
For since it was stated, “solely for the purpose of releasing the termites,” it is understood that there was simply an absence of any desire to plaster the stone slab again;
it is for this very reason that it says, “without plastering it. Therefore, [the condition of] being plastered on both sides... etc.

Regarding the statement, "This was said with reference specifically to the roof-covering," they say that this was spoken for the purpose of showing the preeminence of the roof-covering plaster— since even when wall-plaster exists, there is no offense without the roof-covering plaster—

"Herein" means in the grass hut.
