7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Building of a Monastery (Vihārakāra).
365. "In the city named Sattama" means in the city named Kosambī.
It is said that because *kosamba* trees were abundant in various places such as the parks and lotus ponds of that city, it came to be known as Kosambī.
Some say it was built not far from the hermitage of the seer named Kusumba. This is what is meant: [of] Kusumba...
The dwelling place of the Buddha was Kosambī; because it was situated not far from that [monastery], the city came to be known as Kosambī.
Regarding the statement, "It was built by a merchant named Ghosita," who was this merchant Ghosita, and how did he cause that monastery to be built?
It is said that in former times there was a kingdom called Addilaraṭṭha. There lived a poor man named Kotūhalaka.
Out of fear of starvation, a man traveling with his wife and son toward a land of plenty was unable to carry his son;
he left him behind and went on. The mother turned back, took him, and they departed. They entered a village of cowherds.
At that time, the cowherds had prepared much milk-rice (*pāyāsa*); having obtained some from them, they ate it. Then...
That man, having eaten a great deal of milk-rice, was unable to digest it;
he passed away during the night and took rebirth right there in the womb of a female dog, being born as a dog. He became dear to the cowherd.
And the cowherd attended upon a paccekabuddha. At the time for the meal, the paccekabuddha [would go] to the dog...
He gave him a single morsel of food. Having conceived affection for the Paccekabuddha, he went to the leaf-hut together with the cowherd;
when the cowherd was not present, he would go there himself at mealtime and bark at the door of the leaf-hut to announce the time.
And on the way, upon seeing fierce wild beasts, he would bark to drive them away. He [served] the Paccekabuddha with gentleness...
Having passed away with a virtuous mind, he was reborn in the world of the devas. There, his name became "Ghosaka-devaputta.
Falling from that heavenly realm, he was reborn in a certain family home in Kosambī.
It is said that a merchant who had no sons gave wealth to Ghosaka’s parents and took him as a son. Then, after his own sons were born, [the merchant] seven times...
He set about having him killed. Because of his merit, however, he did not meet death in any of those seven places;

finally, having obtained his livelihood through the ingenuity of a merchant’s daughter, he later succeeded to the position of treasurer upon his father’s passing and became known as Ghosita the Treasurer.
There were others as well in Kosambī, such as Kukkuṭa the Treasurer and Pāvāriya the Treasurer.
There were two merchants; with him, there were three.
At that time, five hundred seers who were spiritual counselors to those merchant friends lived at the foot of a mountain.
From time to time, they would come to the path of men for the sake of partaking of salt and sour food. Then, on one occasion—
In the summer season, while traveling along a human path, they passed through a great waterless wilderness;
having reached the end of the wilderness and seeing a large banyan tree, they thought: "Such as this tree is, there must surely be a powerful deity dwelling here;
it would be well indeed if she were to give us drinking water or water for washing."

The deity, having understood the intention of the seers, thought, "I shall provide for them," and by her own supernatural power, she caused a stream of water as thick as a plowshare to flow from between the branches.
When the company of seers saw that column of water resembling a mass of silver, they took water in their own vessels, used it for their needs, and then reflected: "By the deity..."
“Water for our use has been given to us, but this is a great wilderness without a village; it would be well indeed if she were also to give us food.
The deity, providing divine rice gruel, solid food, and other requisites for the sustenance of the seers, satisfied them.
The seers thought: “The deity has given us everything—both the water for our use and the food. It is well...”
“Vata, if you would show yourself to us. The deity, understanding their intention, revealed half her body.
“Deity, great is your prosperity; what deed did you perform to attain this prosperity? “It was not a very great or extensive deed that I performed,” she replied.
For it was by relying on the practice of the half-Uposatha that the deity [attained this state].
"Having attained prosperity. It is said that this son of a deity was formerly a laborer in the house of Anāthapiṇḍika.
For on the Uposatha days, everyone in the merchant's household—even down to the slaves and laborers—would observe the Uposatha.
One day, this laborer rose alone early in the morning and went to his work. The great merchant [prepared] the fodder...
Observing the people who were receiving [alms], and realizing that he alone had gone to the forest, she gave him fodder for his evening meal.
The female cook, having cooked rice for only one person, increased the portion for him when he returned from the forest and gave it to him.
The laborer thought: "On other days at this time, there was but a single sound in the house..."
“Today [the house] was exceedingly quiet; what could this mean? She explained to him:
“Today all the people in this house are observing the Uposatha; the Great Merchant gave provisions for you alone. “Is that so, mother? “Yes, master.
“In such a time as this, does one who has undertaken the Uposatha have the merit of the Uposatha observance, or not?”
“Mother, ask the great merchant. Having gone there, she asked him, and the great merchant replied:
“The entire Uposatha observance is not fulfilled; however, half the observance is fulfilled, and he is indeed an Uposatha-observer.
Without eating his meal, the laborer rinsed his mouth, observed the Uposatha, took his place in the dwelling, and lay down. As his body was deprived of food...
At night, the wind grew turbulent. Having passed away at dawn, by the result of his half-observed Uposatha ceremony, he was reborn as the deva-son of the Nigrodha tree at the gate of Mahāvattaniya.
He reported this occurrence to the seers. The seers asked, "By you, we were told: 'The Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha'..."
“Has it ever been heard before by you, O seer, that a Buddha has arisen in the world? “Yes, venerable sir, it has been heard. “Where does he dwell now?
“In Sāvatthī, venerable sir, at the Jeta Grove. Delighted and joyful, the seers said, “Stay here;
we shall see the Teacher,” and having departed, they eventually reached the city of Kosambī.
The great merchant, hearing that "the seers have arrived," went out to meet them and invited them, saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept our alms tomorrow.
On the following day, they gave a great offering to the company of seers. The seers asked for leave, saying, "We shall depart after we have eaten. [The merchant replied:
"Venerable sirs, at other times you would stay for one month, two months, three months, or even four months."
“Stay and then go; however, on this occasion, come back yesterday and say, ‘We shall go today.
Why is that? “Yes, householders, a Buddha has appeared in the world. It is not possible to know if there will be an obstacle to life;
therefore, we are going in haste. “In that case, Venerable Sirs, we too shall come; let us go together with you.”
“Go! they said. “You are householders with great tangles of hair; you stay behind, we shall go on ahead.
Having departed, they stayed for two days in one place, and traveling with haste, they reached Sāvatthī and went straight into the presence of the Teacher at the Jetavana Monastery.
There, having heard the sweet discourse on the Dhamma, they all went forth into homelessness.
They attained arahantship.
Those three merchants also, taking five hundred carts each filled with ghee, honey, molasses, and other provisions, as well as fine woolen cloth, linen, and other goods, departed from Kosambī.
Traveling by stages, they reached Sāvatthī and established their camp on the outskirts of Jetavana.
Having bound [the goods], they went into the presence of the Teacher; having paid homage and exchanged greetings, they sat down to one side.
The Teacher delivered a sweet discourse on the Dhamma to all three companions.
Filled with intense joy, they invited the Teacher and gave a great almsgiving on the following day; inviting him again, they did so on the next day as well—thus for half a month.
Having given the gift, they prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, saying, “Venerable Sir, please give us your promise to come to our country.
The Blessed One said, “Householders, Tathāgatas indeed delight in empty dwellings.
The householders, perceiving that by this much a promise had been given, thought, “A promise has been granted to us by the Blessed One,” and [remained] at his feet.

Having lain down and paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, they departed; along the way, they had monasteries built at every *yojana*, and having reached Kosambī in due course, they announced, "A Buddha has arisen in the world!
The three men each made a great sacrifice of wealth in their own parks and had monasteries built for the Blessed One. Therein, by the merchant Kukkuṭa...
The one built by [the householder] Kukkuta was called Kukkuṭārāma. The one built by the merchant-seṭṭhi Pāvārika in his mango grove was called Pāvārikambavana.
The one built by Ghosita was called Ghositārāma; it was with reference to this that it was said, "It was indeed built by a merchant named Ghosita."
He who departed together at the time of the Great Renunciation, and for whom the Teacher issued the "Brahma-punishment" (brahmadaṇḍa) at the time of his Parinibbāna—
it is with reference to him that he says, "of the one disguised as an attendant during the Bodhisatta period.
And by this [it is meant] that even when being exhorted by the General of the Dhamma while ill in the *Channovāda Sutta* of the Majjhima Nikāya, he was unable to endure the terminal agony.

Being unable [to stop it], he cut his windpipe with a sharp blade. When the fear of death arose and the signs of his future destination appeared, he realized his own status as a worldling (*puthujjana*).
Trembling with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he established insight (*vipassanā*) and, while comprehending conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), attained *arahantship*.
Having become one who has reached the summit (*samasīsin*), he attained final Nibbāna; this shows that "he was not such a person."
Because the genitive case is also desired for the agent when used with the word *pūjā* (worship), he says: "or worshipped by a village.
Furthermore, the grammatical characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) here should be understood according to the rules of the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). "Each part" means each portion.
366. "The state of originating from action alone" rejects the state of originating merely from action itself.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this offense originates from both action and non-action, arising from the act of building a hut and from the failure to point out the site.
In this training rule, in the phrase "or not having had [the site] pointed out by monks," the word *vā* (or) should be regarded as having the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*),
as in such expressions as "this, indeed, is that great nāga."
The commentary on the training rule concerning the construction of a monastery is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Malice: 380.
In the eighth [rule], the connection is with the phrase "enclosed by a wall. "Furnished with gate-towers and watchtowers" refers to the gate-palace.

And it was provided with watchtowers erected here and there upon the top of the rampart. Because it was surrounded by bamboo and because its interior was covered with trees bearing flowers and fruits, it had a green appearance.
It was delightful due to the excellence of its shade and water, as well as the excellence of its ground. "In the guise of a crow" means in the form of a *kalandaka* (woodpecker). "Nivāpa" means food.
*Tanti* means "that. *Dabbo* is the name of that elder; because he fell upon a *dabba*-pillar (a kind of reed or bamboo), that elder received the name Dabba.
It is said that at the time when the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa was being undermined, seven monks became of one mind and [encouraged] others in the teaching...
Seeing them acting with disrespect, [he thought]: "What shall we do here? Having practiced the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) in solitude, we shall bring an end to suffering.
So saying, he fastened a ladder and climbed to the high peak of a mountain. Knowing the strength of his own mind, he said:
"Let those who wish to descend the ladder take it; let those who still cling to life come down; do not be full of regret later!"

Having spoken thus, they all became single-minded; they lowered the ladder and, exhorting one another, saying, "Be diligent, friends," sat down in places according to their own preference and began to practice the duty of a recluse.
There, one elder attained Arahantship on the fifth day and thought, "My task is accomplished; I am in this..."
"What shall I do in this situation? he thought. Then, by means of his psychic power (*iddhi*), he brought almsfood from Uttarakuru and said:
"Friends, eat this almsfood; let the duty of going for alms be my responsibility, while you attend to your own work.
"Friend, did we say such a thing as we were setting up the ladder: 'Whoever first [attains] the Dhamma...'"?
“Let that monk bring almsfood; having eaten what he brings, the rest of us will practice the duty of a recluse.
“There is none, friends,” they replied. “You have received this through your own past causes alone; we too, being able, shall bring an end to the round of existence. Go, then!
Unable to convince them, the Elder [set out] for a comfortable place for almsfood.
Having partaken [of the meal], he departed. Another elder, having attained the fruit of non-returning on the seventh day, passed away from there and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahmā-world.
The other elders, after wandering through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one *buddhantara*, were reborn in various families.
One was reborn in the royal palace in the city of Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra; another was reborn in a border region.
One was reborn in the womb of a female wanderer; one was reborn in the house of a householder in the kingdom of Bāhiya; and one was reborn in the house of a householder in Rājagaha.
This Elder Dabba, however, took conception in the house of a Mallan king in the city of Anupiya in the kingdom of the Mallas.
He took it. His mother, while in the throes of childbirth, passed away.
Having carried her corpse to the cemetery, they placed it upon a wooden pyre and set fire to it. By the force of the flames, the lining of the womb was split apart.
By the power of his own merit, the boy leaped up and landed upon a wooden pillar. They took the boy and gave him to his grandmother. She [raised] him...
Because he fell against a wooden pillar while being given his name and thereby sustained his life, they gave him the name "Dabba.
Thus it is said: "Dabba is the name of that Thera.
When he was seven years old, the Teacher, wandering on tour through the Mallan country accompanied by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, [arrived there].
Having reached the town of Anupiya, he was dwelling in the Mango Grove of Anupiya. When Prince Dabba saw the Teacher, he gained faith at the very sight of him;
desiring to go forth, he asked his grandmother, "I shall go forth in the presence of the One of Ten Powers.
She replied, "Very well, dear child," and taking Prince Dabba with her, she went into the presence of the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, this prince..."
“Please let him go forth,” he said. The Teacher gave instructions to a certain bhikkhu, saying, “Bhikkhu, let this boy go forth.
Having heard the Teacher’s words, that elder, while ordaining Dabbakumāra, explained the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna*).
Being endowed with past roots of merit and having made his resolve, at the very moment the first tuft of hair was shorn, [Dabba] attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
When the second tuft of hair was being shaved off, he was established in the fruit of a once-returner; with the third, in the fruit of a non-returner;
and the shaving of all the hair and the realization of the fruit of Arahatship occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after.
With reference to this, it is said: "The Elder, it is said, attained a sense of spiritual urgency at the age of seven and went forth; even at the very moment his hair was cut..."
"One should understand that he attained arahantship.

Regarding "to be attained by a disciple": this refers to whatever may be attained by a particular disciple according to their specific capacity (upanissaya). The passage beginning with "the three knowledges" is stated according to what is possible for each case.
The term "set of qualities" (*guṇajāta*) is used to indicate its connection with the neuter gender in the phrase "whatever may be attained by a disciple."
It has been stated: "Because the sixteenfold function has been performed by means of the four paths regarding the four truths.

This refers to the performance of the sixteenfold function by way of the four functions—namely, the full understanding of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path—applied respectively to each of the four truths known as suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
"Having stepped back from this and that" means having turned away from various duties and objects.
"On a stone slab" means on a stone bench.

"Even the thirteen" refers to the formal appointments (*sammuti*) for the meal-designator, the assigner of lodgings, the storekeeper, the receiver of robes, the distributor of robes, the distributor of rice-gruel, the distributor of fruit, the distributor of solid food, the distributor of minor items, the assigner of *sāṭiyā* cloths, the assigner of bowls, the supervisor of monastery attendants (*ārāmika*), the supervisor of novice monks (*sāmaṇera*), and the supervisor of novices.
By this means, even the thirteen formal permissions (sammuti) may be granted.
382. Regarding the word *apisu*: here *su* is a mere particle (*nipātamatta*);

the word *api*, used in the sense of "even," should be understood as following immediately after the word "at an improper time" (*vikāle*), meaning "even if they come at an improper time. "Knowing" (*jānantā*) means knowing their distant location. Thus...

Regarding the phrase "in all locations": it should be understood that because there are various types of agreements (katika), such as those concerning shape and so forth, one should have the specific rules of agreement (katikāvatta) and so on explained separately for each respective monastery.
Furthermore, they say that one resolves (adhiṭṭhāti) after making the walking paths in all monasteries equal in measure.
For this is the nature of things created by resolve (nimmita): when things are created without being specifically determined, this—[in] one...

"It appears as such," and so forth, is the natural law (*dhammatā*). For indeed, those who are created without being restricted by specific qualities of complexion, age, bodily parts, requisites, actions, and so on, become identical to the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*) because they were created without such restrictions.
Whether in standing or sitting, or in speaking or remaining silent, whatever the possessor of psychic power does, they do that very same thing.
But if he wishes to create them in various ways—some in the first stage of life, some in the middle stage, and some in the final stage; likewise with long hair, half-shaven heads, or mixed hair;

wearing half-red robes, or yellow robes; performing word-by-word recitation, preaching the Dhamma, expositions, asking questions, answering questions, sewing robes, washing them, and so forth—or if he wishes to create others in various ways, then, having emerged from the foundational jhāna, [he resolves]: "Let there be this many..."

Having performed the preliminary work in the manner of "Let the monks be of the first stage of life," and then having re-entered meditative absorption and emerged, when [the objects] are resolved upon, they appear exactly in whatever form is desired, together with the resolving consciousness.
Regarding the statement that "there is no lack of basis": the speech of the created beings, such as "This is a bed," is not without a basis, because beds and chairs exist everywhere.
383. *Ekacārikabhattaṃ* means alms-food that should be brought separately because it is very pleasing.
*Taddhitavohārena* means by way of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) expression, such as "that which has four as its measure is a *catukka*.

He said, "The instrumental case is used in the sense of the instrument itself," because the rice is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the inquiry; thus it is stated that "she asks by means of the rice acting as the instrument."
[It] exists. And as for those who ask by means of boiled rice acting as the instrument, in order to show the manner of their questioning, it is said:
“Venerable sir, do they ask, ‘Shall we give you boiled rice?
*Bhava* means that which is to become. *Asamannāharitvā* means without applying attention (*ābhoga*). *Rattiṃ sammantayamānā* [means] regarding someone at night...
Having slept through the time and then waking up while reflecting:

for those who have slept during the first and middle watches of the night and have awakened, even at the present time there arises the conceit that it is not the present; therefore, they said, "Yesterday.
But for those who are diligent in their duties and devoted to wakefulness throughout the night, there is only the conceit that it is the present; therefore—
They speak thus, “Today,” not “Yesterday. “Fuming” means fuming by way of repeatedly arising anger.

Regarding “Dabba, Dabba,” he says “the wise ones (dabbā) are the second word *dabba*,” because the word *dabba* is a designation for the wise (*paṇḍita*). The connection is: “they do not explain it in this way.
“They explain” (*nibbeṭhenti*) means they free themselves from fault. [This is] the characteristic of emergence (*vuṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ*).
"Thinking" means thinking that it is the characteristic of emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-lakkhaṇa*).

"It does not fit" means the intention is that the Elder’s claim of being virtuous (*susīla*) does not accord with her statement claiming to be immoral (*dussīla*). Whatever needs to be said regarding this matter will be made clear further on.
"Destroy" means to cause her to return to the state of a householder by giving her the white cloth; for here, "destruction" refers to the destruction of the [monastic] marks (*liṅga-nāsanā*).
[These are] intended. And in order to demonstrate this very point, it was said: “Three kinds of banishment,” and so forth.

Non-participation in communal life (*saṃvāsa*) due to a single formal act (*ekakamma*) and the like is “banishment from communal life” (*saṃvāsanāsanā*). What is called “banishment by means of a disciplinary act” (*daṇḍakammanāsanā*) is the expulsion by way of a penalty, such as by scattering sand and the like, for as long as one does not ask for forgiveness.
“Go away! Perish! Be destroyed! is a demonstration of the manner of expulsion. In that context, *cara* means “go.”
"Go away" is what is meant. "Pire" means "one who is not of our own kin," that is, one who has not become internal to us;
for "pire" is a vocative term synonymous with the word "para" (other). Alternatively, "pire" is a particle synonymous with "parato" (from elsewhere);
therefore, the meaning of "cara pire" is "go elsewhere, do not stay here. "Vinassa" means "go out of sight."
Because those bhikkhus remained without revealing themselves, the phrase "therefore, investigate" means "search for this;
find out. "He is the perpetrator" means that because she confessed, "I have been defiled by the Venerable One," if she was expelled on account of that confession, the Elder is the perpetrator;
the meaning is that he is guilty of an offense. "He is not the perpetrator" refers to that confession made by her...
If she was expelled by the Blessed One without regard for anything else, but solely with reference to his own state of natural immorality, then the intention is that the Elder is not the perpetrator.

When it was said, "Expel her on her own admission," he replied, "Venerable sir, according to the truth of her admission—'I have been defiled by the Master'—it follows that the Elder is indeed the perpetrator and is possessed of fault. [He addressed] the bhikkhunī...
"Anuddhaṃseti, dukkaṭaṃ" (if one reviles [her], it is an offense of wrong-doing)—by this, the opinion of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is shown.
"In the case of lying, it is a pācittiya"—this was said because for one who reviles a bhikkhunī by means of lying, it is stated that it is a pācittiya.
"Therein" (tatra) refers to those two cases of wrong-doing and pācittiya. From here onwards, the passage concludes with the words: "Therefore, only a pācittiya is appropriate."
The clarification of the intended meaning in both commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). Regarding that, as for the phrase "in the former method":
it refers to the method of the commentary where it is stated, "If one slanders a nun, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

If one asks why it is said that "only an offense of wrong-doing is appropriate" there, he says "just as," etc., showing the reason for that. [The text continues: "For a monk, in regard to a monk, it is a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*). [Regarding] a monk...
The meaning is that for a monk who accuses another of an unfounded matter involving an ultimate offense (antimavatthu), it is a *saṅghādisesa*.

In the latter method as well, it is stated: "For one who accuses a nun [of such a thing] through false speech, it is a *pācittiya*. In the *Kurundi*-method also, because it is false speech, only a *pācittiya* is appropriate;
the intention is that only a *pācittiya* is appropriate because of the priority given to the intent to deceive.

If it is argued that for one who groundlessly charges a bhikkhu with an offense involving the ultimate (antimavatthu) and who also reviles him, there must be an offense of expiation (pācittiya) solely on account of the lying, [the author replies:

although there is indeed lying in this case, because the measure is determined by the specific statement made, there must be an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa) for the false accusation and an offense of expiation for the reviling;
it is not an offense of expiation for conscious lying (sampajānamusāvāda). To demonstrate this, he says: "Because the measure is determined by the specific statement," and so forth.
In this context, "by the authority of the word" means by the authority of the canonical word spoken by the Blessed One. Now, in order to show that word, it is said:

"with the intention of reviling," and so forth. Regarding the statement, "for a monk [it is] an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for a nun," there is no such statement as "for a nun [it is] an offense of wrong-doing for a monk" when she reviles him; thus it is in the Canon.
"Because it has not yet occurred. Since there is a statement that "in the case of a deliberate lie, it is an *pācittiya*," he shows the training rule on deliberate lying as stated in general terms.

Now, having clarified the intended meaning in both commentarial positions and having pointed out the fault in the latter position, the Master, wishing to establish the former position, said: "In that regard... and so forth. Therein: "It is indeed an *pācittiya*..."

Regarding the statement, “It is appropriate,” the phrase “when there is no intention to disparage, it is a *pācittiya*” indicates that this provides an occasion for a *pācittiya* offense in the case of a deliberate lie (*sampajaññamusāvāda*).
The statement that “a separate *pācittiya* is mentioned” means that a *pācittiya* distinct from—and other than—the *pācittiya* for a deliberate lie has been stated.
The statement “there is no destruction by these” was made in a general sense; however, regarding this [specific case]...
The intention is that there is no forfeiture by means of a *dukkaṭa* offense. If this is so, why does the Blessed One cause it to be forfeited? He says, “Because,” and so forth. 385–386.
By the word “defiled” (*dūsito*), he shows that the term *duṭṭha* functions as a passive construction (*kamma-sādhana*). One who defiles another, destroys them, is a “defiler” (*dūsaka*).
By this, he states that the term *dosa* functions as an active construction (*kartṛ-sādhana*) in the sense of “he defiles, therefore he is a fault. [He also mentions] the state of being natural...
It is said that *jahāpito* is used because it is recited as a derivative (*vikati*) of the word *duṭṭha*. The meaning is "having abandoned his natural state of gentleness" (*sommabhāva*);

what is meant is that he has been brought to a state of transformation (*vikāra*). "By way of difference in appearance" (*ākāranānattena*) means by way of the difference between the appearance of the corrupted and the appearance of the corrupter.
"Discontented" (*anabhiraddho*) means not satisfied. For one who is not satisfied is not called "happy."

He said, "Not happy. Regarding phrases such as "the king was won over," since the sense of "inspired with confidence" (*pasādita*) is possible there, he said "or not inspired with confidence" (*na vā pasādita*).

Since the word *khīla* denotes both a state of rigidity and a synonym for refuse, he said: "the resentment-thorn (*paṭigha-khīla*), which consists of the mind's state of rigidity and the mind's refuse.
It is called a *khīla* because by means of it the mind enters into a state of rigidity; thus it is a thorn of the mind.
It is the state of rigidity. And in its actual meaning, it is simply aversion (*paṭigha*). For aversion has the characteristic of rigidity in the mind;
when it arises, the mind becomes unpleasant, like a place that has become fouled. Therefore, because it is similar to refuse, aversion itself is called a "stake" (*khīla*).
Hence he said, "the stake of aversion. Because of the mind's state of rigidity and because it is similar to refuse—
And resentment itself is a stake; thus it is "the stake of resentment. "Not arrived" means not approached, not followed, or not attained by joy, bliss, and so forth—this is the meaning.
And since one who has not approached joy, bliss, and so forth is said to be "devoid" of them, he says, "devoid of joy, bliss, and so forth.
And since one who is devoid of them is not said to have been "assailed" by them, he says...
“*Na abhisato*” means not overwhelmed by joy, bliss, and so forth. “*Yena*” means by which anger.
He shows that *duṭṭho* is the word as it appears in the *mātikā*, while *kupito* is the word as it appears in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
Although the two words are identical in meaning, the phrase “both of them” is stated by way of both terms. Thus, “by that anger... [and so on].
The phrase "by those two" is stated on account of these words, "and by that fault"; however, in terms of meaning, it is simply the fault (dosa).
And since that [fault] is included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), he said: "By these two, he shows precisely the aggregate of mental formations.
By the expressions "displeasure" (anattamanatā) and "lack of joy" (anabhiraddhi), only the feeling of mental grief (domanassavedanā) is stated; thus he said: "By these two..."
"...he shows the aggregate of feeling.
But when it is something not seen, not heard, or not suspected by the accuser, then it is called "groundless"; thus he said, "That, however, for him...
is intended according to the accuser. If it were intended according to the accused, [it would be otherwise].

The intention is that one might say, "What is called 'groundless' (amūlaka) means 'not having committed [an offense]'"; this refers to any one of the nineteen *pārājika* offenses appropriate for a monk.
However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), having taken only those actually occurring in the Canon (*pāḷi*), it is stated:
"by any one of the four. "This" (*etaṃ*) refers to whether the one being accused has committed or not committed [the offense]. "Here" (*idha*) means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
“‘In the same way’ refers by extension to this meaning: ‘by the ear of confidence (pasāda-sota) or by the divine ear (dibba-sota).
It is said that ‘it remains in the very place it was heard’ because it must be known precisely through what has been heard. ‘Suspicion’ (parisaṅkita) means that which is suspected;

‘following after what has been seen’ (diṭṭhānugata) is ‘suspicion based on what has been seen. The same applies to the remaining cases. ‘Of these’ is the genitive case used in the sense of the agent; the meaning is ‘by these.’”
Regarding the phrase "they will do so," one should apply the word "these" (*ime*) by changing the grammatical case. The statement "there is what is seen with its root;
there is what is without root" is said with reference to the presence or absence of the actual transgression. The statement "there is what is rooted in perception;
there is what is without root in perception," however, is said with reference to the presence or absence of the perception of having seen it.
Regarding the phrase "standing nearby," it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that this means "standing within twelve cubits.
However, since it is later stated that "for one who reproaches by sending a messenger, a letter, or a message,

the offense does not reach its head," and thus an offense is absent only for reproaching in the absence of the person, the expression "standing nearby" is intended merely to indicate the state of being face-to-face.
“Vuttaṃ” means our own opinion. For that very reason, when showing the factor (*aṅga*) in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:

“Accusation in the presence [of the accused] with the intention of causing them to fall away”; nor can it be maintained as a fixed rule that the state of being "in the presence" occurs only within a distance of twelve cubits.
Furthermore, it is stated that upon reaching a decision regarding the Vinaya, one must stand firm in what is weighty; therefore, having investigated [the matter],...

The more appropriate [interpretation] should be accepted. "For every word of the accuser, it is a *saṅghādisesa*" means that for every word of the accuser who has been commanded, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
The statement "I have also seen and heard it" is said for the purpose of showing that even one who has been commanded possesses the status of an accuser;
however, even without saying this, the very words "You have committed an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*)" [constitute the accusation]. Regarding the other person...
If one speaks with the intention of not exposing [the offense], even though it is like repeating the words [of another], there is indeed a *saṅghādisesa*.
However, they say that for one who speaks while showing [the source] by saying, "So-and-so said this," even though the intention is to expose [the offense], there is no *saṅghādisesa*.
Regarding the phrase "many [monks] accuse many [monks] on many grounds": here, "many" (*sambahula*) is a designation for plurality.

No reason [for this] is seen. For this tetrad has come about solely according to the single or multiple nature of the *vatthu* (the basis of the charge) and the *codaka* (the accuser), and not according to the single or multiple nature of the *cuditaka* (the accused). Indeed, it is by way of a single accused person that this tetrad has come about, being divided into: one *vatthu* with one accuser; one *vatthu* with various accusers;

various *vatthus* with one accuser; and various *vatthus* with various accusers. It is for this very reason that when showing the fourth accusation, he says: "In this accusation there are various *vatthus*..."
It is stated as "accused by various [persons]," but not as "accused by various [charges]";
therefore, no reason is seen for the designation of plurality in the term "sambahule" (many).

Alternatively, although the accused was previously designated as a singular entity across all three types of accusations, the designation here as a plurality implies that "the accusation does not occur against only one accused person, but rather..."
This was composed to demonstrate the meaning of the phrase “even among many.
However, the statement beginning with “Who is entitled to reprove, and who is not? is said to show the characteristic of reproving even without the intention of exposing [faults].
The expression “one endowed with virtue” is stated with the underlying intent that the word of one who is immoral is not authoritative.
However, because a bhikkhu lacks the authority to reprove a bhikkhunī, it is stated, "only a bhikkhunī.
Even though bhikkhunīs lack authority over bhikkhus, the reproval made by them is still considered a valid "reproval" (codanā) because it possesses the essential quality of being a reproval;

this is the intended meaning behind the statement, "all five who are in accordance with the Dhamma may [reprove]. By the phrase "having heard from a bhikkhu, he reproves," etc., it is shown for whom the reprover [acts].

The Elder cited the Sutta to show that even their censure is valid, because they accepted it by saying, "Having heard it, we shall urge [the offender]," and thus the word of those [messengers] is indeed authoritative.
"By sending a messenger, a letter, or a message" means either by sending a messenger with the instruction, "Go yourself and urge [him]," or...
If one is able to urge him [to confess], one may send either a verbal message or a letter to him. "It does not reach its head" means that it does not constitute a *saṅghādisesa* offense;

this is the intended meaning. Although it appears from the fact that the text states the general rule "whether one urges oneself or causes another to urge" that an offense occurs even for one who causes another to urge by means of a messenger’s message and so forth, nevertheless, regarding the phrase "it does not reach its head":
It should be understood according to the authority of the commentators of the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "At the proper time" means at the time of understanding the meaning after having heard the sound by nature.
"Of the two heavy [offenses]" refers to the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* offenses. "By way of the remainder" refers to the five light offenses.
The ten bases of wrong view begin with "There is no giving," and so forth; it proceeds in the manner of "The world is finite, the world is infinite," and so on.
"Grasping at extremes" (*antaggāhikā*) means that the view grasps at an extreme, namely, what is reckoned as eternalism or annihilationism.

"On account of livelihood" refers to the six training rules (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed for the sake of livelihood. On account of livelihood, for the sake of livelihood, one who has evil desires and is overcome by craving falsely proclaims a non-existent, unreal superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*);
there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*). On account of livelihood, for the sake of livelihood...
If he engages in matchmaking, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).

If, for the sake of livelihood and as a means of livelihood, he says of someone living in a monastery, "That monk is an arahant," there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for one who understands [the meaning].
If, for the sake of livelihood and as a means of livelihood, a monk who is not ill, having requested fine foods for his own benefit, eats them, there is an offense.
If a nun, for the sake of livelihood and as a means of livelihood, being not ill, requests and eats fine foods for her own benefit,
there is an offense of *pāṭidesanīya*. If a monk, for the sake of livelihood and as a means of livelihood, being not ill,
requests and eats either soup or boiled rice for his own benefit, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*, on account of failure in livelihood.
"‘One incurs these six offenses’ refers to the six training rules (sikkhāpada) shown in the Parivāra-pāḷi.
Even when one reproaches someone for failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti) or failure in livelihood (ājīvavipatti), one is reproaching them specifically for the offense rooted therein.
When asked, ‘Why do you not pay homage to me?’, [the reason for not paying homage] is: ‘You are not an ascetic; you are not a son of the Sakyan.’"
Because it is so stated, they say that one who has committed an offense involving the ultimate defeat (antimavatthu) is not to be saluted.

However, in the *Cūḷagaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated that simply because one wishes to reprove [the offender], not saluting them does not constitute a reason for their being unsalutatory, provided that the matter one intends to state oneself has already been addressed.
This is because one who has committed an offense involving the ultimate defeat is not mentioned among those who are unsalutatory.

Because there is no offense of sharing a bed with him when one sleeps together with him, and because that [act of] receiving [him] takes root, it is understood that this very [method] is more appropriate.

Furthermore, although he is to be saluted as long as he professes his status as a monk, once he professes, "I am no longer a recluse," then he is not to be saluted; this distinction should be understood here.
For one who has committed an *antimavatthu* (an offense involving defeat), the status of a monk exists only so long as he still claims to be a monk;
beyond that, it no longer exists. Indeed, one who does not claim the status of a monk falls into the category of those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
Since one giving material gifts gives them only to those in the place where they are desired, therefore, when giving rice-gruel, meals, and so forth to those seated in order of seniority—
He said, "To such an extent there is no accusation," because even when one desires to accuse another, it is not yet called an accusation if [the fault] has not been given [to him].
"Thirtyfold" (*tiṃsāni*) means those which possess thirty; the sense is that they are "possessors of thirty," meaning they exceed thirty.
Because it is a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*), the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is elided, and thus it is stated as "thirtyfold. Alternatively, it refers to thirty accusations.
"Thirty" means "there are more than these"; this form is to be understood as occurring when the suffix *ḍa* is added to the word *adhika*.
The same principle applies here to the term "ninety.
Regarding the phrase "that legal issue (adhikaraṇa) is to be decided by a committee," it means that the legal issue is to be adjudicated by those appointed to the committee.
It must be adjudicated. For in an assembly crowded with shameless persons, a bhikkhu endowed with ten factors should be appointed to the committee (*ubbāhikā*).

Having selected two or three bhikkhus who possess the perfection of the ten factors as described in the *Samathakkhandhaka*—beginning with, "He is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, he is perfect in conduct and resort"—one should proceed right there.
After the formal proclamation consisting of one motion and two announcements (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*) has been recited, they should be appointed.
Once thus appointed, those monks—either sitting separately or within that very assembly—should announce, "Nothing should be said by anyone else," and then adjudicate that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
The phrase "to you" is said with reference to both the accused and the accuser.
“Kimhi” means “in what matter. “You do not even know ‘kimhi nan’”—this means you do not even know the expression “kimhi nan.
“No further questioning should be given to him” means no questions or counter-questions should be directed toward him.

It is stated that [the rule] was “laid down for the restraint of shameless persons,” and so forth; thus it is said: “for the purpose of restraining those who are shameless... [etc. … it was laid down. “Ehiti” means “he will come.”
"By way of the seen continuity" means by way of a connection with what has been seen; it is said to mean by way of a fixed rule of what has been seen.
"Adversaries regarding the matter" refers to those who are opponents concerning the point designated as the subject of dispute.

"Having given a sign" means having made a signal in order to cut off their speech and establish his own position. He said "it is unbecoming" because it arose from an impure perception. "Sharing and enjoying together."
This was spoken for the purpose of releasing them from his own presence, and not for the purpose of joining them in mutual sexual intercourse.
Regarding the phrase "no judgment should be made": one who knows, "These shameless ones are of a nature that must abide by our word" should not pass judgment.
"It has been transgressed" means that it becomes a transgression because one has uttered some falsehood for the purpose of concealing the fault committed by oneself.
"He does not give his confession" means that thinking, "If I speak of the fault I have committed, those who follow me will break away," he does not give his confession, saying, "It was done by me.
"Let him be pure" means: let him be called pure according to their word; [let him be pure] for them.

The intention is that a decision should be given to him by means of speech once or twice. "He does not stand in the proper place" means he does not stand in the place of one who possesses shame (*lajjī*).
"A decision should not be given" means it should not be given because he has fallen into a state of shamelessness (*alajjī*).

He says "two grounds" because they speak while taking up a ground, whether it be baseless (*amūlaka*) or with a basis (*samūlaka*). Regarding the phrases "I shall speak at the proper time," and so forth:

When one person, having obtained leave from another, reproves them, it is called speaking at the proper time. When reproving in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, at the place for voting sticks, at the top of a row of alms-bowls, in a hut for reflection, on the path to alms-gathering, in the refectory, or at a moment when one is surrounded by attendants, it is called speaking at the improper time. Speaking truthfully is called speaking what is factual.
"O you who are an elder, a frequenter of assemblies, a wearer of rag-robes, and a semblance of a preacher of the Dhamma! [Thus he speaks.]
One who speaks thus, "This [is improper]," is said to speak harshly. However, speaking with dependence on a reason—saying, "Venerable sir, you are elderly;
you are a wanderer among assemblies, a wearer of rag-robes, and a preacher of the Dhamma; this is fitting for you"—is said to speak gently.
Speaking with dependence on a reason is said to speak in a way that is beneficial. [This is done] with a mind of loving-kindness.
"I shall speak with a mind free from ill will"—having established a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), I shall speak, not with a corrupted mind.

Regarding the "fifteen qualities": purity of bodily conduct, purity of verbal conduct, a mind of loving-kindness toward fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārī*), great learning, and the detailed mastery, thorough analysis, correct exposition, and precise determination of both *pātimokkhas*.

Regarding these fifteen qualities—namely, the five qualities stated by the phrase “I shall speak at the proper time,” etc., together with compassion, the desire for welfare, sympathy, restoration from offenses, and having the Vinaya as one’s primary concern: therein, “compassion” (kāruññatā) is the state of being compassionate.
By this, both compassion (*karuṇā*) and the preliminary stage to compassion are shown. “The desire for welfare” (*hitesitā*) is the seeking of what is beneficial. “Sympathy” (*anukampatā*)...
"Connection with that benefit" means being joined with that welfare. By these two, both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the preliminary stage of loving-kindness are shown.
"Emergence from an offense" means establishing one in the state of purity after having emerged from the offense.

"Having regard for the Vinaya" means performing the formal act (*kamma*) according to what was admitted—after having charged the person with the basis of the offense, reminded them of it, and made them admit it. "In truth and without wavering" refers to verbal truth (*vacīsacca*).
And for the sake of being unshakable. For by the one who has been reproved, both the truth must be spoken and anger must not be felt;
the meaning is that one should neither be angry oneself nor provoke another.
"Upon reaching the ground" means when the expression for the ground is reached; it is stated that this is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative.
They are called *adhikaraṇāni* because they are "administered" (*adhikarīyanti*) therein. What is administered? The methods of settlement (*samatha*). How are they administered? By way of settling.
For the methods of settlement (*samatha*) are so called because they settle (*samenti*) and pacify disputes.

Alternatively, they are called *adhikaraṇāni* because they are to be administered by means of the methods of settlement that proceed for the sake of settling. Just as, by way of settling, there is the administration of the methods of settlement...
The state of being the subject in disputes and so forth; likewise, the fact that disputes and so forth must be dealt with by those [means].
Therefore he said, "the state of being a legal issue (adhikaraṇīyatā) through the means of settlement (samatha). By this, the accusative derivation of the word *adhikaraṇa* is stated.

"Grasping" (*gāha*) refers to the mental grasping of an accusation, thinking, "I will accuse such-and-such. "Intention" (*cetanā*) refers to the intention arisen [in the mind] thinking, "I will accuse. "Impatience" (*akkhanti*)...

"Impatience arisen toward one who has been reproved. "Discourse" (*vohāra*) means speech that has reached the stage of reproval. "Designation" (*paṇṇatti*) means the designation consisting of the name applied to the process of reproval.
"Having taken it to heart" means having grasped the reproval mentally. "That legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*) refers to the legal issue characterized by that grasping.
Therefore, after demonstrating the conclusion established in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "the designation is the legal issue," [it is now stated] that even this...
In order to show that this is appropriate, he said, "But as for this," and so forth. "They" refers to the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*).

"An offense entailing defeat" (*pārājikadhamma*) means an offense of defeat (*pārājikāpatti*). "Because of its absolute unwholesomeness" means because the offense of defeat is exclusively unwholesome due to its nature as a worldly transgression (*lokavajja*).
"By which designation" refers to the designation of names (*nāmapaññatti*). "By expression" is a synonym for that same term.

"Designation" (paññatti) means spoken of by way of conventional usage (vohāra). And because it occurs in the sense of a locus (adhikaraṇa), it is called a "legal issue" (adhikaraṇa), just as the term "bed" is applied to beds and couches.
Since one who accuses with groundless [charges] perceives that the legal issue does not exist in the person being accused, his statement is empty of the thing signified;
therefore, he says, "it does not exist by way of intrinsic nature" (sabhāvato natthi). And that...

"Right here" (*kho idhevā*) means that, according to the manner already explained, the status of being a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa-bhāva*) belongs "right here," in this very training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

He said, "Here, a certain dispute," because a dispute occurring in the manner of "even a mother disputes with her son" and so forth cannot possibly have the status of a legal issue, as it is not to be settled by the methods of reconciliation (*samatha*).
“The eighteen grounds for schism” is a term denoting characteristics, just as one might say, “If those who are ill should consume it, this medicine must be given.
Therefore, a dispute that arises based on any one of those [grounds] is said to have “arisen on account of the eighteen grounds for schism.
“Reproach” (anuvāda) means both censuring and accusing. Therein, censuring...
"Name" refers to verbal abuse. "The five classes of offenses" refers to the five classes of offenses as they appear in the *Mātikā*.
"Seven" refers to those same five, plus the two offenses of *thullaccaya* and *dubbhāsita* as they appear in the *Vibhaṅga*, making seven. "Duty" (*kiccayatā*) means that which is to be done;

"that which is to be performed" (*karaṇīyatā*) is a synonym for the same. By both terms, it is specifically the formal acts of the Saṅgha, such as the act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*), and so forth.
He shows this, which is why he says, “the act of seeking permission,” and so forth.

Since there is no formal accusation by means of the remaining legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) once the legal issue of an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) has been set aside, he says, “But in this context... [etc. ...only the legal issue of an offense is intended.
Regarding the exposition according to the sequential order of the words (*sapadānukkamaniddesa*): it is an exposition following the sequence of the words.
“Exposition according to the sequence of words” (*padānukkamaniddesa*) is a designation for the word-analysis (*padabhājana*).

That which occurs together with that is the “exposition according to the sequence of words,” namely the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The meaning is: “of that training rule accompanied by the exposition according to the sequence of words”;

what is meant is “accompanied by the word-analysis. The genitive case in *assa* is used in the sense of the agent; the meaning is “by this. Therefore he said, “by this accuser,” and so forth. “In those cases that have come here” means:
"In these training rules" means those included herein. "In others" means in the textual tradition of the training rules other than this one, such as those concerning slanderous speech and so forth.

"One of bad character" (*dussīla*) means devoid of virtue, lacking in moral conduct. "Of evil nature" (*pāpadhamma*) means, precisely because of that lack of virtue, having a base disposition and a reprehensible character.
"Of impure and suspicious conduct" (*asucisaṅkassarasamācāra*) means being impure due to the impurity of one's bodily actions and so forth, and thus being a source of suspicion.

One must maintain conduct that inspires confidence. For an immoral person, upon seeing anything improper, becomes an object of suspicion for others, thinking, "This must have been done by such-and-such a person.

Or, seeing monks consulting together on some business, he becomes suspicious even of himself, thinking, "Could it be that they are consulting because they know of something I have done? Thus, one must maintain conduct that inspires confidence.
"One whose actions are concealed" means one whose actions ought to be hidden because they are shameful. "Not an ascetic" (assamaṇo) means he is not a true ascetic (samaṇo).
One who claims to be an ascetic through the false pretension, "I too am an ascetic," during the taking of voting sticks and other such occasions.

Because his conduct is not noble, he is a non-celibate (abrahmacārī). One who claims to be a celibate through the false pretension, "I too am a celibate," during the observance days (uposatha) and other such occasions.
"Internally corrupt" (*antopūti*) because of having entered within through an impure action and a failure in virtue.

"Leaking" (*avassuta*) because of being drenched by the flow of defilements such as lust through the six sense-doors. "Putrid" (*kasambujāta*) because of having produced the refuse of lust and so forth, and because of being something to be discarded by those possessing virtue.
"In this text" (*idha pāḷiyaṃ*) means in the text of this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "The eldest brother" (*jeṭṭhabbatika*) refers to one connected with Kalidevī. Kalidevī...
It is said that Sirīdevī was his elder [sister]; therefore, one who observes her vow is called a "Jeṭṭhabbatika.

Having undertaken and fulfilling that vow, he smears his entire body with soot, holds crow feathers in his fist, has Kalidevī painted on a wooden board, and wanders about praising her while tying it to the tip of a carrying-pole. By which extent...?
The intention of the Elder Mahāpaduma is that the phrases "by so much," "to that extent," and "it is not allowable" are stated solely for the purpose of illustrating a state of doubt.
However, the second elder [holds] that because a state of doubt is not illustrated by these terms— "it is not allowable," "he does not remember," and "he has forgotten"—
there is a different kind of doubt and there are other instances of "not being allowable" and so forth.
He shows the meaning by way of the fourfold division; therefore, his doctrine is more logical and is stated last.

"One is doubtful regarding seeing" means that even though the person is known, because one has not correctly seen their action or because a long period of time has passed, while performing that action one is doubtful regarding the seeing, thinking, "Has this person been seen by me, or not? Regarding the person...

“He is doubtful” means that even though it is known that the act was performed by him, because he has not clearly seen that he is performing that act, or because of the passage of time, he is doubtful regarding the person, thinking: “Is this one the performer of that act, or is he not?
(389) The intention of one who accuses another of an offense with the thought, “We shall perform the sevenfold formal acts, such as the act of censure,” is as follows:
The intention regarding the action (*kammādhippāyo*). The intention regarding restoration (*vuṭṭhānādhippāyo*) is the intention: "I shall restore him from his offense.

By the phrase "of one who reviles," he shows the intention regarding causing to fall away (*cāvanādhippāya*). For one who speaks with the intention of abuse, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);

that is, for one who speaks in the presence [of the other] using any of the seven classes of offenses with the intention of abuse, there is an offense of expiation. "An offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*) refers to [speaking] with the intention of abuse.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who speaks thus. Since it is said, “For the assembly of that Blessed One was thus brought up:

namely, by means of mutual speech and mutual exhortation,” he spoke the passage beginning with “But in the Kurundi” while establishing the method of the Kurundi Commentary. “In all cases indeed” means...

In all the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā), it is said that when the *yya*-sound is reached, the *re*-sound is said to have been transcended; thus [the author] says, "when the *re*-sound has not been transcended.
Because the formal act (*ñattikamma*) of the Uposatha consists of a motion (*ñatti*), it is said that the Uposatha is considered performed only when the motion is completed;
therefore, [the author] says, "it is not permitted when the *yya*-sound is reached."

"This and that" refers to "killing living beings, taking what is not given," and so forth. For one who speaks in the absence of another with the intent to insult, saying, "So-and-so and so-and-so are neither ascetics nor lay followers," there is an *dukkaṭa* offense; however, for one who speaks in their presence, it is a *pācittiya* offense.
Just as in the expression "the maiden sees no sun," the meaning "the maiden does not see the sun" is obtained here.

Thus, regarding the phrase "having caused [the person] to give no opportunity," the meaning "without having caused [the person] to give an opportunity" is also obtained; this is why he said "But as for that which... and so forth. That is:
the fact that the one who accuses has attained the status of being counted as "fully ordained" (upasampanna); the perception of purity regarding that [accusation];

the groundlessness of the offense of defeat (pārājika) with which he accuses, by way of [seeing it] and so forth; and [accusing] in the presence of the accused with the intention of causing him to fall away.
The prompting and the understanding of it at that very moment—these are the five factors here.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning corrupting faults is finished.
9. Commentary on the second training rule concerning corrupting faults.
391. "Having seen in the ninth watch" means having seen a goat that was misbehaving toward a she-goat.

They address the nun Mettiyā by her former name, referring to her time as a nun. "In Veḷuvana itself" is said with reference to the very time those [laypeople] were assigning the meal, rather than the Elder’s own time for wandering for alms. "Kacci... (Is it not?)...

"Is it not so?"—they reported this matter, meaning they reported that he had been charged with an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) by taking up some slight pretext or mere semblance of a legal issue belonging to a different category.

"Belonging to a different category" means belonging to another class; that is, other than the Elder’s status as a human being and a monk, [the charge concerned] his status as an animal, specifically a goat.
"Of the category" (*koṭṭhāsa*) is what is meant. "This" (*idaṃ*) refers to the goat by means of a neuter general designation;
the meaning is "this belongs to the class of goats," which is to say, "this is a goat.
Alternatively, the neuter designation is dependent on the word for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); it is meant that "this is the locus designated as a goat. "Another class" (*aññabhāga*)...
The meaning of *aññabhāga* is the state of being a different part, namely the condition of being a beast of prey or a goat as previously described;

it means another portion. Regarding the word *assa*, it refers to the goat. The meaning of the first compound (*aññabhāgiya*) is "that which is connected with another part," while the meaning of the second compound is "that which possesses another part.
By both compounds, the term *aññabhāgiya* refers to the goat itself.
Setting aside the state of being a goat born among animals, although in the ultimate sense there is no separate goat apart from that state,
it is nevertheless said— “this is another part,” or “another part belongs to it”— by way of worldly convention which proceeds by conceiving a distinction where there is none,
just as in expressions such as “the body of a statue.”
Now, explaining in detail the meaning already stated by means of both arguments, he says, "For he who... and so forth. "He" refers to that goat.
It is connected with the word "there is. "From that" means from that human birth and from the state of being a monk.
"Or another portion" means another portion consisting of the aforementioned animal birth as a goat. "Of him" (assāti) [refers to the goat].
“Of the goat. It should be construed thus: “That goat receives what is termed ‘belonging to another case’ (aññabhāgiya).

To show the meaning of the passage previously stated—namely, that “a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is the support (*ādhāra*), the basis (*vatthu*), the foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*)”—he says “And because,” and so forth.
“Of them” refers to Mettiya and Bhūmajaka. “This” refers to the goat. “By way of the designation for naming” means by way of that which is reckoned as the designation for naming.

(393) ... [omitted] ... “a legal issue. Herein, the word *adhikaraṇa* means “that which is brought forward” (*adhi-karīyati*); it is a *kamma*-derivative formed from the root *kṛ* with the prefix *adhi*. It refers to a case, a dispute, or a litigation that has arisen. Alternatively, it is a *bhāva*-derivative formed from the same root with the suffix *-ana*; it refers to the state of being brought forward, the state of being litigated, or the state of being disputed. Or again, it is a *kamma*-derivative formed from the root *kṛ* with the prefixes *adhi* and *ava*; it refers to a case, a dispute, or a litigation that has been decided or settled. Thus, it is called a “legal issue” (*adhikaraṇa*) because it is a case, a dispute, or a litigation that has been brought forward, litigated, or decided. Furthermore, it is called a “legal issue” because it is a case, a dispute, or a litigation that is to be brought forward, litigated, or decided. This is the meaning of the word *adhikaraṇa*. Now, regarding the word *aññabhāgiya*: here, the word *añña* means “other,” “different,” or “distinct”; it refers to a different category or a different class. The word *bhāga* means “part,” “portion,” “side,” or “category”; it refers to a division or a classification. The word *aññabhāga* means “another part,” “another portion,” “another side,” or “another category”; it refers to a distinct division or classification. That which belongs to this other part, portion, side, or category is called *aññabhāgiya*. Thus, it is called *aññabhāgiya* because it pertains to a different category or class. This is the meaning of the word *aññabhāgiya*. It is said: “There are four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). For one who intends to show the meaning by way of extracting the sense (*atthuddhāra*), another word that serves as a synonym for the words occurring in the text must be extracted to express the meaning of both terms;

nor should the meaning of one thing be stated after having extracted another. Therefore, a different word altogether—one that serves as a synonym for the term *adhikaraṇa* found in the text and is common to both terms—[must be used].
It should be understood that the word *adhikaraṇa* has been extracted [from the compound]. For this very reason, he said:

"Regarding 'legal issue' (*adhikaraṇa*), by way of a common grammatical designation and through the extraction of its meaning, there are four legal issues. And as for that which was stated at the end... [the] accusation:
a monk is seen committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense; he holds the view that it is a *saṅghādisesa*; and if [he is accused] of a *pārājika* offense...
He speaks with reference to "exhortation" (codanā) and so forth.

Sexual offenses (*methuna-vītikkama-āpatti*) are similar by way of their objective basis (*vatthu*); however, as for other offenses such as taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), although they share the status of being offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*), they are dissimilar by way of their objective basis.
Thus he says: "by way of similar and dissimilar objective bases. [The phrase] "by way of similarity to their own nature" (*sabhāva-sarikkha-sarikkhatō*)...

Because of the state of being similar or dissimilar by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). For the first *pārājika* is similar to the offense of the first *pārājika* by way of intrinsic nature through the lust for sexual intercourse (*methunarāga*), but it is dissimilar to it by way of its association with hatred (*dosa*) and its object being a human being.

But is it not said that "a legal issue arising from an offense may be of the same category as another legal issue arising from an offense, or it may be of a different category"? Therefore, [should it not follow] according to the sequence of the enumeration?

He says, "Starting from the beginning," etc., because he has not yet specified its belonging to that category (*tabbhāgiyataṃ*), but has first specified its belonging to another category (*aññabhāgiyatā*).
"In the manner already stated" means by the method stated in the passage beginning with "from similar and dissimilar bases.

Because it was stated that "it arises depending on formal acts of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*)," the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) is, as it were, separate from the formal act of the Saṅgha itself.

He said, "What then? and so forth, because it is seen [in the texts]. Since it is stated that "the duty itself is the legal issue concerning duties" (*kiccādhikaraṇa*), it is said that "this is a designation for the formal acts of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghakamma*).
If this is so, why was it said that "it arises depending on the formal acts of the Saṅgha"?

To this he replied, "Even though this is so," and so forth. It is precisely the characteristic of the "way of acting" (*itikattabbatā*) taught by the Blessed One for each respective formal act of the Saṅgha.
Therefore, because it results from a formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma), it deserves to be called a "formal act of the Saṅgha" by way of metaphorical designation for its fruit; thus he said:
"Because it arises depending on that which one attends to as the characteristic of a formal act.

This is because probation (parivāsa) and other such formal acts of the Saṅgha arise depending [on them], and because acts such as the suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma), the authorization of a boundary (sīmāsammuti), and so forth, arise depending on acts such as reconciliation (osāraṇa) and the removal of a boundary (sīmāsamūhanana).
And because they arise [in sequence], it is said: "The preceding formal act of the Saṅgha," and so forth.
(395–400) "Making it have a basis" means making it refer to a specific person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*). "Long and so forth" refers to long, short, black, white, and so on.
"Seen and so forth" refers to what is seen, heard, and so on. "Like a copper bowl" means like an iron bowl. The factors [of the offense] are the first two corrupt faults.
These are similar to what was stated previously; however, here there is an addition consisting of taking up some slight pretext (*lesamatta*).
The commentary on the second training rule concerning corrupt faults is finished.
10. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Schism in the Saṅgha.

410. Regarding those who are weak and lacking in strength in their tenth year, and who are unable to bring an end to suffering while resorting to forest-dwelling and other such practices—it is with reference to them that he said, "they lead to obstacles on the path for many sons of good family.

"Endowed with patience through endurance" means being possessed of that patience characterized by the ability to endure cold, heat, and so forth, as described in the passage beginning, "He is patient with cold."
One for whom the mere phrasing and words are supreme is "one for whom the word is supreme" (*padaparamo*).

For that person who, despite hearing much, speaking much, retaining much, and reciting much, does not achieve the realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*) in that very lifetime, this one is called "one for whom the word is supreme.
"Having accomplished" (*abhisambhuṇitvā*) means having brought to completion. "Does not accomplish" (*nābhisambhuṇāti*) means does not bring to fulfillment.
It is said that he is unable to accomplish dwelling in the forest (*araññavāsa*). It is contrary to the Dhamma (*uddhamma*) because it deviates from the Dhamma.
He would be "not omniscient" (*asabbaññū*) because he would not know what is appropriate for them.
Because of the statement, “Monks, one should not enter the rains residence without a lodging,” it is said: “But four... [etc. ...is indeed prohibited. This very [point].
Referring to this statement, it is also said in the Pāḷi: “Devadatta, for eight months I have authorized the lodging at the foot of a tree.
“By three points” means by three modes, that is, by three reasons.

“Suspected as being free from both” means not relying on either of these two—what has been seen or what has been heard—but [thinking], “What indeed is this, having killed [it] for the sake of the monk?”...
“Prepared” means merely suspected [of being so]. A “fish-trap” is a net; a “snare” is a deer-trap.
“Is allowable” means that if, by their word, the suspicion is removed, it is permissible. “Meat from what is already on hand” refers to meat for sale. By the word “etc.
in the phrase “for auspicious occasions, etc.,” one includes offerings to guests (*āhunapāhuna*) and so forth. “Only for the sake of the bhikkhus” — here:
The word *eva* is used here in the sense of "impossible" (or "not the case"). It should be connected as: "it was not made for the sake of the monks alone.

Therefore, it should be understood that even if one makes [an offering] by mixing [the purposes], thinking, "We shall give this to the monks, and it will also serve the purpose of auspicious ceremonies (*maṅgala*) and so forth," it is not permissible.
However, some [commentators] interpret the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "for the monks alone" as meaning "for the sake of the monks and others as well."
When they say, "It is permissible," that is not correct. Regarding the phrase "where one is free from doubt":
this refers to the total absence of suspicion even when [the robe] was made for the sake of the monks. To clarify that same point, the passage beginning with "But if... was stated.
"It is permissible for others" means it is permissible for those who do not know; for one who knows, there is an offense in this case. "Those very ones" refers to...

It is only those [meats] intended specifically for him. To show the distinction between the consumption of meat intended for oneself (*uddissakata-maṃsa*) and the consumption of unallowable meat (*akappiya-maṃsa*), the passage beginning with “But as for unallowable meat” was stated.
In the former case, there is an offense involving volition (*sacittaka*);

in the other, there is an offense without volition (*acittaka*). Therefore he said: “Even for one who eats unallowable meat without knowing it, there is indeed an offense. At the time of consumption...
Because of the statement, "Having asked, one shall eat," or "Having taken it, one shall eat after asking," there may be no offense for one who takes unallowable meat without knowing it to be so.
For it is said that the offense applies only to one who eats it without knowing.
By the phrase "they say it is proper," he shows that there is no offense.
“Those whose mode of life is *sallekha* are *sallekhavuttino*. ‘*Bāhuliko*’ is stated by eliding one *l*-sound [from *bāhullavuttiko*].

‘For an *āyukappa*’ means for the duration of a lifespan. For it is said, ‘He who causes a schism in the Saṅgha shall boil in hell for a *kappa*,’ with reference to a lifespan; for if one divides a *kappa* into eighty parts, he would remain in hell for only a single such part.”
In the *Kappaṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said: "When an eon is forming or during the middle of an eon, one who has caused a schism in the Saṅgha is liberated only at the destruction of the eon.
For even if one causes a schism in the Saṅgha today with the thought, 'The eon will be destroyed tomorrow,' one is liberated on that very day;
one suffers in hell for only a single day. In this context as well, the phrase "only at the destruction of the eon" means:
If the meaning is "only at the destruction of the world-age," there is no contradiction.
The phrase "while it is still standing" is also stated by way of an unreal hypothetical assumption, as if saying, "it will perish tomorrow.

Regarding the statement, "he is roasted in hell for only a single day," the application of the meaning should be understood as being without contradiction, because if there is no subsequent world-age, there is likewise an absence of a full life-span. Brahmā...
"Merit" (*puñña*) means the most excellent merit. "He rejoices in heaven for an *kappa*"—here too, it refers specifically to a lifespan of one *kappa*.
(411) Regarding the phrase "by one who is of a different communion due to difference of tenet" (*laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka*), this is an expression emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāva*);

the meaning is "by way of the state of being of a different communion due to difference of tenet. The same method applies here to the phrase "by one who is of a different communion due to difference of action" (*kammanānāsaṃvāsaka*). Otherwise, [it would refer to] one who is together with one of a different communion...
One who is a member of the same community (samānasaṃvāsaka) may nevertheless fall into the state of being one who does not belong to the same community (asamānasaṃvāsaka).

In this context, "one who is separate by way of tenet" (laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka) refers to one who follows a suspended person (ukkhitānuvattaka). For he has become separate from the community by virtue of his own tenets; thus, he is called "separate by way of tenet.

"One who is separate by way of formal act" (kammanānāsaṃvāsaka) refers to one who has been subjected to a formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma). For he [is separate] by means of that formal act of suspension.
"One who is of a different communion" (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*) means one who is "of a different communion by way of formal act" (*kammanānāsaṃvāsaka*). "Separated" (*virahita*) means liberated (*vimutta*).
The granting of physical concord (*kāyasāmaggī*) should be understood as approaching within arm's reach for various formal acts of the Saṅgha.
Because it is stated separately as "should strive for schism," it refers to undertaking a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that leads to a split.

It should be understood that for one who, even before taking up a side, strives toward a schism in the Saṅgha by means of seeking partisans and so forth, a formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*) must be performed.
"These matters" refers to the eighteen grounds for causing a schism.
"By a formal act" means by any one of the four formal acts, such as the motion (*apalokana*) and others. "By a recitation" means by any one of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha.

By the recitation. By the conventional expression (*vohārena*): by the conventional expression that illustrates the eighteen grounds for schism, such as "what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma," according to various respective rebirths.
By the proclamation (*anussāvanāya*): [the thought], "Do you not know my noble birth, my having gone forth, and my great learning?

Would anyone like me ever conceive even the thought of causing one such as you to adopt what is contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, and opposed to the Teacher’s instruction? [is what is meant].
By means of a proclamation made by whispering into their ears in such a manner as: "Is it fitting? Is Avīci like a grove of blue lotuses cool to me? Do I not fear the states of misery? and so forth;
and by the taking of voting sticks (*salākaggāha*), that is, having thus proclaimed, steadied their minds, and rendered them incapable of turning back, [saying] "Take this voting stick."

Regarding the statement, "The schism of the Saṅgha occurs through five causes," it should be understood that in this context, the formal act (*kamma*) itself—whether it be the proclamation (*uddesa*) or the act—is the primary cause for the schism.
The consultation, the announcement, and the taking of voting tickets (*salākā*), however, are preliminary stages.
For even if one consults by way of illustrating the eighteen grounds, makes an announcement there to generate consent, and the voting tickets have been taken, the Saṅgha remains undivided.
