The Saṅgha. But when four or more [monks] take voting tickets (*salāka*) and perform a separate formal act (*kamma*) or recitation (*uddesa*), then the Saṅgha is said to be "divided.
"Risen up" (*abbhussita*) means "arisen" (*abbhuggata*). "Should maintain" (*accheyya*) means "should dwell," that is, "should continue"; this is the meaning.

Because of the statement, "One who is conscientious (*lajjī*) will protect [the Saṅgha]," the burden of reporting [the offense] out of fear of transgression falls upon those who are conscientious; thus he says, "by the conscientious ones..."

“...by the monks. Even for one who is shameless, there is indeed an offense for not reporting [it], because of the statement: “those who see, those who hear. “Let him come together” means let him become one.
And this state of being one occurs by way of having the same view; thus he said, “let him be of one view. “By way of attainment” means by way of the attainment of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
Because there is no offense for one who relinquishes [the wrong view], it is called “a state of safety.”

Regarding the phrase "of that bhikkhu": for one who does not relinquish [the offense], there is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) for each individual instance, according to the count of those speaking. "By one who is able" means by one who is capable of going and is not ill.

Because schism in the Saṅgha is a grave matter, it is stated—"even at a distance, it is indeed a burden"—to show that it must necessarily be carried out; however, the offense [of the carrier] occurs within half a *yojana*.
It should be understood as applying only to one who is capable of going and is not ill.
Regarding the phrase "without having admonished": since this is an instruction regarding the agent of the formal act (*kamma*), he says "to one who is being admonished.

One who relinquishes [the course of action] at the third proclamation incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the motion (*ñatti*), and two offenses of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*) for the two preceding proclamations.
And he indeed incurs [the offense]; thus it is said: "For one who relinquishes, there is no offense of *saṅghādisesa*. "Of him" means of Devadatta.
"It must have been performed" means it must have been performed by the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*).

One might say, "Because he is a first-offender, there is no offense even for one who does not relinquish," with the underlying intention that one may speak merely according to one's own preference. This was said before the rule had been laid down.
Because there is no formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*) regarding the training rule itself, it is said: "For one who transgresses a promulgated training rule.
Indeed, the formal act of admonition was authorized precisely by the one who promulgated the training rule.
Regarding the phrase "authorized specifically for the purpose," this refers to what was authorized specifically for a certain case, such as: "Monks, I authorize the rumination of one who ruminates."

They say. "In the section on non-offenses" means in the portion concerning non-offenses. "The offense is to be laid upon him" means that the *pācittiya* offense incurred due to the failure to relinquish [the robe] is to be formally charged (*āropetabba*) for the purpose of carrying out a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*); this is the meaning.
"An offense was not even born" means that the *saṅghādisesa* offense was indeed not born; this is the meaning. "But that very one" means but that very one.
There is no offense. "Threefold factor" means threefold by way of body, speech, and mind; it is said that it originates from body, speech, and mind.
It is "liberation through perception" because one is released due to the absence of the perception, "I do not relinquish.
It is "with mind" because of the conscious mind that knows, "I do not relinquish. Striving for schism [is] by means of a formal act of the Dhamma (*dhammakamma*).
Exhortation, the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), and non-renunciation—these are the four factors here.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning schism in the Saṅgha is finished.
11. Commentary on the second training rule concerning schism in the Saṅgha.

417–418. Regarding the eleventh [offense]: that speech which one utters even within a complete assembly, thereby acting as a constituent part [of a schism] and causing it to split—that speech which causes strife is here called "factional" (*vagga*).
Thus it is said: "They speak factional speech, speech belonging to the side of non-harmony.

That which exists on the side of non-harmony is "belonging to the side of non-harmony" (*asāmaggipakkhiya*); these are those who cause strife. Their speech is "speech belonging to the side of non-harmony."
Or, speech belonging to the side of discord is "speech siding with discord.

Since it is permissible for even many people to perform formal acts such as those of a committee (*ubbāhika-kamma*), it should be understood that the statement, "The Saṅgha does not perform a formal act upon itself," was spoken with reference to a formal act that must be performed by way of censure.
Furthermore, the factors (*aṅga*) here consist in striving for schism.
Having omitted the section on compliance, it is exactly as described below.
The commentary on the second Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada is finished.
12. Commentary on the Dubbacasikkhāpada.
424. In the twelfth [case], *vambhanavacanaṃ* means words of reproach. *Apasādetukāmo* means wishing to cast out, or wishing to threaten;
it is said to mean wishing to strike. The word *saṭa* has the same meaning as the word *patita*.
Having placed the qualifier in the subsequent position, it is stated as *tiṇakaṭṭhapaṇṇasaṭa*; thus he says: "grass, wood, and leaves fallen here and there."
"By someone whatsoever" means by someone who is like the wind or like a river.
(425–426) "Incapable of being spoken to" means one who cannot be instructed because they do not tolerate anything that is said to them.
A person in whom speech is difficult—due to their contrary grasping, their opposition, and their disrespect—is called "difficult to speak to."
Therefore he said, "It must be spoken with difficulty and hardship," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by those things that produce a state of being difficult to speak to": this refers to those factors that cause one to be difficult to speak to. The suffix *-anīya* should be understood here in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

For this very reason he said, "those qualities which make a person difficult to speak to," and so forth. One who has evil desires is *pāpiccha*; the state of being such is *pāpicchatā*, which is the estimation of non-existent virtues in what one receives.
And lack of moderation and evil desire are to be understood [as these]. "Those who exalt themselves and disparage others" means those who exalt themselves and disparage others.

This is a designation for those who exalt themselves—lifting themselves up and placing themselves in a high position—and who disparage others—reproaching them and placing them in a low position. The state of being such is "the quality of exalting oneself and disparaging others."
One whose nature is to be angry is *kodhana*; the state of being such is *kodhanatā*. This is a designation for anger (*kodha*), which has the characteristic of being prone to wrath.
Anger occurs at an earlier time, while resentment (*upanāha*) occurs at a later time; thus it is said, "due to anger, there is resentment.

In this context, one whose nature is to harbor resentment, or one who possesses resentment, is *upanāhī*; the state of being such is *upanāhitā*. It has the characteristic of repeatedly binding the mind.
This is a designation for anger itself. For when anger has arisen, it is simply anger; beyond that, there is resentment (*upanāha*).
"Clinging" (*abhisaṅga*) refers to a powerful resentment that is difficult to release. One who possesses this is "clinging" (*abhisaṅgī*); the state of being so is "clingingness" (*abhisaṅgitā*).
This is a designation for a powerful resentment that is difficult to release. "Opposing the accuser" means [acting] with hostility toward the accuser.
Standing in opposition; "dismissing the accuser" means provoking the accuser by saying, "What is the use of what you, a fool and incompetent person, have said?
Do you really think you yourself should be the one to speak?
"Reversing the charge against the accuser" means saying, "You too have fallen into such-and-such an offense; first, deal with that."
Thus is the state of shifting the burden onto the accuser.
"Dealing with one thing by means of another" means acting by concealing one reason or statement through another reason or statement.
Alternatively, the word *carati* (to act/deal) has the sense of "concealing," because verbal roots have multiple meanings.

"Concealment" means hiding. For a person endowed with that [concealment] hides whatever reason for revealing a fault has been stated by the accuser, or whatever word has been spoken, by means of some other reason that demonstrates the groundlessness of the accusation, or by means of a statement intended to obscure its meaning.
When it is said, "You have fallen into an offense," he asks: "Who has fallen? What has been fallen into? In what?"

Having said, "You have fallen [into an offense]; whom do you speak of? What are you saying? and when it is replied, "Have you seen anything of this sort?", he either says, "I did not hear it," or he diverts the conversation by pretending to listen;
thus, even while creating a distraction, he conceals one thing with another.
When asked, "Have you fallen into such-and-such an offense?", he says, "I went to Pāṭaliputta," and then again, "Your going to Pāṭaliputta..."
When it was said, "We ask you; we ask about an offense," he replied, "I have gone to Rājagaha.
When it was then said, "Whether you go to Rājagaha or to the brahmin village, you have committed an offense," he replied, "I got pork there," and so forth.
Even this evading the question by diverting the conversation externally is, in substance, merely evading with one thing after another; therefore, it is not treated as a separate category.

"By means of an *apadāna*" means by means of one's own conduct (*cariyā*). For it is called an *apadāna* because by it faults (*dosā*) are pointed out (*apadiyanti*), or because they are examined (*dakkhīyanti*), or because they are worn away (*luyanti*) or cut off (*chijjanti*);

it is the application of behavior toward beings, whether correct or incorrect. "Not by way of conciliation" refers to such questions as: "Friend, where do you live? On whose authority do you live? or "Regarding what you say, 'This person committed an offense by me... [and so forth].
When asked about his conduct in such a manner as, "At that time you saw him; what were you doing then? What was he doing? Where were you, and where was he?
and so forth, it is the failure to provide an answer after having been questioned. Regarding the term *makkhipaḷāsitā*:
here, *makkha* is characterized by the smearing over of another's virtues; one who possesses this is a *makkhī*.
Such a person, whether as a householder or one gone forth from the household life, destroys the good work of others.
For even a householder, though poor, might be placed in a high position by someone compassionate; yet at a later time, thinking, "What have you done for me?", he destroys that person's good work.
Likewise, one who has gone forth, from the time he was a novice monk onwards...
Having been assisted by his teacher or preceptor with the four requisites and through instruction in recitation, interrogation, and so forth,
and having been trained in proficiency in the methods of Dhamma-exposition and the technical manuals, he later— honored and revered by kings, royal ministers, and others,
yet disregarded by his own teacher and preceptor while wandering about— [thinks]: "This man, when we were still young..."
When told, "He was supported and brought up by you, yet now he has become devoid of affection," one says, "What have you done for me?
and thus destroys the merit they performed for him.
Even toward a person of great learning, one overreaches them, thinking, "The destiny of even such a learned man as this is uncertain; what of yours?"
The term *paḷāsa* refers to the characteristic of seizing upon equality, arising in the manner described by the passage beginning, "What difference is there between him and me?
Its function is to equalize one's own qualities with those of others. For it is called *paḷāsa* because, as if biting at the virtues of others, it makes them equal to one's own;
one who possesses this is a *paḷāsī*. One who is both *makkhī* (slanderous) and *paḷāsī* (envious) is a *makkhipaḷāsī*.
Their state is *makkha-palāsitā*. In terms of meaning, however, it is both flattery (*makkha*) and disparagement (*palāsa*).
One who envies (*issati*) the prosperity of others and cannot endure it is *issukī*.

One who is stingy (*maccharāyati*), conceals one's own prosperity, and cannot endure the common sharing with others—or who possesses stinginess (*macchara*)—is *maccharī*. One who deceives (*saṭhayati*)...

One who does not speak rightly is a *saṭha*—a person who is deceitful (*kerāṭika*), possessed of the craftiness (*sāṭheyya*) characterized by the manifestation of qualities that do not exist in oneself.

And such a deceitful person is like the *ānandamaccha* fish. It is said that the *ānandamaccha* shows its tail to other fish and its head to snakes, thinking, "I am like you," in order to make them know this; even so is the deceitful person.
Whatever person among those who specialize in the Suttas or the Abhidhamma he approaches, he says to them:
"I am your pupil; you have compassion for me; I will not let you go. [He does this thinking:
"In this way, they will think, 'This man has respect for us; he has deference toward us. For one who is possessed of deceit...

Because one who dwells performing actions that conform to their own mind while falsely imagining qualities they do not possess is difficult to discern—such that it cannot be known whether they are "of such a mind" or "of such conduct"—it is impossible to know their belly or their back. Thus it is said:
"With the left he is a pig, with the right a goat; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
"He has a trunk but no tusks; he is like an old ox with its horns gone.
Thus, he is like the ogre-hog described there. Deceit (*māyā*) is characterized by the concealment of committed evil; one who possesses this is a deceiver (*māyāvī*).
He is "stiff" (*thaddho*) due to being possessed of stubbornness. He is one who acts without restraint, holding his head high with a stiffness like that of a leather bag filled with wind.
Stiffness (thambha). A person endowed with this is like a python that has swallowed a plough, or like a bellows filled with air;
being rigid, he does not wish to bow even upon seeing those worthy of reverence, but moves only within his own limits.
Excessive conceit (atimāna) has the characteristic of haughty elevation; one who possesses this is called "conceited" (atimānī).
One who clings to one's own view (*saṃ*) by grasping it beyond its true nature (*sabhāva*) and reaching out toward something else is called *sanditṭhiparāmāsī*.
One who takes up a fixed position is called *ādhānaggāhī*; "fixed position" (*ādhāna*) means firmness, so the meaning is "one who holds firmly.
One who relinquishes a tenet only after seeing a logical reason is called *paṭinissaggī*; [this refers to one who does so] with difficulty, hardship, and labor.
"Difficult to relinquish" (*duppaṭinissaggī*) means that even after many reasons have been shown, it is not possible to cause one to relinquish [the view].

This is a designation for one who firmly grasps their own view, thinking, "This alone is the truth," and does not relinquish it even when being addressed by the Buddha and others who show the reasons. For such a person, whatever [teaching]—whether Dhamma or...
Or when he hears what is contrary to the Dhamma, he withdraws all of it within himself, thinking, "Thus it was spoken by our teachers;
thus have we heard it," just as a tortoise, when its limbs such as its feet are touched by anyone, withdraws all its limbs into its own shell and does not extend them outward.
Just so, when a tortoise's limbs are touched by anyone, it withdraws all its limbs into its own shell and does not bring them out.

Thus, even when told, "Your grasp is not good; let it go," he does not relinquish it; keeping it right there within his own heart, he continues on. Just as crocodiles do not let go of what they have seized, so he grasps with a "crocodile-grasp" and does not release it.
Now, regarding the triad of pairs presented by way of hypocrisy (*makkha*), spite (*paḷāsa*), and so forth: hypocrisy, spite, and the rest.
Having taken six factors individually, it is stated that there are "nineteen factors.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Anumānasutta*, even such pairs as hypocrisy (*makkha*) and disparagement (*paḷāsa*) are treated as one, and it is stated that there are "sixteen factors.

Bringing [the result] by means of various modes is "favorable" (*padakkhiṇa*); one who has the habit of grasping from that which is favorable is "one who grasps favorably" (*padakkhiṇaggāhī*), and one who is not so is "one who does not grasp favorably" (*na padakkhiṇaggāhī*).
"One who does not accept instruction respectfully" (*appadakkhiṇaggāhī*): when being spoken to, he says, "Why do you speak to me?

I myself know what is appropriate and inappropriate for me, what is blameworthy and blameless, and what is beneficial and harmful. Such a person does not accept instruction from the right side; rather, he accepts it from the left.
Therefore, he is called "one who does not accept instruction respectfully. For this reason, it is said: "As instructed," and so forth.

"In the recitation of the Pātimokkha" means in the formal recitation of the Pātimokkha. Now, one might ask: "How are all the training rules (sikkhāpada) included within the recitation of the Pātimokkha?
To this he says: "Because they are comprised by the words, 'Whosoever has committed an offense, let him reveal it.

For by the phrase "whosoever has committed an offense," all offenses whatsoever are indeed included within the recitation of the Introduction (nidāna). [Together] with the five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma...
“Because it must be trained in” is stated by way of what is currently obtainable; the meaning should also be understood as “by means of a legitimate cause together with a legitimate companion.
Regarding the phrase “for the sake of speech,” he says “from my speech” because the term for the recipient (sampadāna) is used in the sense of the ablative (nissakka).

Furthermore, the constituent factors here are similar to those in the first instance of schism in the Saṅgha; however, this is the distinction: whereas in that case there was an effort toward schism, [here it is different].
In this way, the state of being subject to the "act of not speaking" (*avacanīyakaraṇa*) here is to be understood.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the abusive person (*dubbacasikkhāpada*) is finished.
13. Commentary on the training rule concerning the corrupter of families (*kuladūsakasikkhāpada*).
431. In the thirteenth [case], "Kīṭāgiri" is the name of that town (*nigama*). Indeed, with reference to it, it will be stated later:
"The monks Assaji and Punabbasu must not dwell in Kīṭāgiri. Because of its association with that [town], the district (*janapada*) itself came to be designated as "Kīṭāgiri";
thus he says, "in the district of such a name. Those who are attached to a residence are *āvāsika*, meaning those who reside there permanently.
They build dwellings that have not been built, they repair those that are dilapidated, and they exercise authority over those already constructed.

Therefore he said: “Those to whom it belongs... they are the residents (āvāsikā). Because they possess a dwelling, or even merely the state of having a dwelling, they are called “resident monks” (nevāsikā); thus he said: “But those who are merely...
and so forth. “They” refers to Assaji and Punabbasuka. “Six persons” refers to Paṇḍuka, Lohitaka, and Mettiya.
These six persons were Bhūmajaka, Assaji, and Punabbasuka. "Samma" is a term of address. "Becoming the mouth of income" means they became the source of income.
"In the place of the burden" refers to a location not far from Sāvatthī. Because it rains during two seasons—the rainy season and the winter—it is said, "by two clouds.
[This refers to] the teachers of the groups from among the one thousand five hundred bhikkhus.
Because it exceeds [the measure] for ordinary people, it is called "exceedingly" (*samadhika*); the meaning is "with an excess.
The letter *m* has come about through euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). "A site not yet prepared" means a new site that has never been prepared before.
"Flower trees" refers to trees such as the *kaṇikāra*; "flower shrubs" refers to shrubs such as the *jātisumana*. "Cutting" means cutting it oneself.
“Causing to be dug” means having others dig it by saying, “Cut this! Break this!
“Binding with a rim” means binding it all around so that water remains at the base of a tree. “Of water” refers to improper (akappiya) water.
By the phrase “pouring proper (kappiya) water,” it should be understood that causing [others] to pour is also included. Is it not said, “the pouring of water and causing [others] to pour”?
By this very [rule], it would have been possible to include, in a general sense, the sprinkling of water that is either allowable or unallowable;

therefore, why is the sprinkling of allowable water and so forth stated separately? Because it will be stated later that "even when trees are planted for the sake of a monastery and the like, the sprinkling of allowable water and so forth is permitted," a distinction has been made here as well, and the sprinkling of allowable water and so forth is shown separately.
“Sprinkling water for washing the hands, face, feet, and bathing”—by this alternative method as well, he shows that it is specifically the sprinkling of allowable (kappiya) water.
As for the phrase “unallowable transaction” (*akappiyavohāra*): how is even one’s own performance of actions such as pounding or digging included here?
It is called an “unallowable transaction” because it is spoken of as unallowable; thus, it includes everything such as performing unallowable acts oneself or causing others to perform them.
It should be understood that this includes [the act itself], and not merely the use of improper speech. The same principle applies to the use of proper speech as well.
By the phrase "straightening a dry furrow," it should be understood that the removal of old leaves and such is also included.

Having placed spades and other tools on the ground, when one grasps them by the handle from their place, the location [of the tool] becomes more manifest; thus it is called "manifestation" (*obhāsa*).

In the *Mahāpaccarivāda*, one who wishes to establish [the rule] speaks later. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of a fence" (*vanatthāya*), some read it as "for the sake of a boundary" (*vatatthāya*);
for them, the meaning is "for the sake of an enclosure" (*vatiatthāya*). To show that even in the case of an improper expression (*akappiyavohāra*), certain things are permissible, he says:
"And not only the remainder," and so forth. "Any kind of outline" (*mātikā*) refers to either a dry outline or a non-dry outline.
Or: by the phrase “to sprinkle allowable water,” it is shown that it is also permissible to say, “Sprinkle allowable water.

By the phrase “it is also permissible for one to plant it oneself,” it is established that it is likewise permissible to say, “Plant it. Regarding the phrase “for one who does it for another purpose”:
this refers to one doing it for the purpose of venerating the site (vatthupūjā) and so forth. Why is there no offense? Because it is for the purpose of venerating the site.

Why is there no offense in the case of tying [a tree] and so forth? Having given the reply, "There is indeed no offense," he now states "For as it has been said," etc., in order to demonstrate that very state of non-offense.
"Therein" refers to the planting of trees for the sake of a monastery and so forth. Likewise, there is no offense even for the purpose of honoring the site;
thus, there is no offense even when having [trees] tied [together] by means of appropriate terminology (*kappiya-vohāra*) and indirect methods (*pariyāya*) for the purpose of honoring the Triple Gem.

The meaning is: "there is indeed no offense. For although it was stated in general terms as "likewise for the purpose of honoring the physical object," because it was further specified that "just as there, by means of allowable terminology and figurative expressions," it is understood that there is no offense only when having [the text] written down by means of allowable terminology and so forth.
Challenging the point that while one may not tie [a garland] oneself, why should it not be permissible for another to tie it oneself, he said, beginning with "But surely...

The challenger's intention is this: just as it is permissible to plant [trees] oneself on allowable ground for the sake of a monastery and so forth, why should it not likewise be permissible to tie [a garland] oneself for the purpose of honoring the site? "It has been stated," etc.
This is the privilege of the teacher. Now, as for why he says, "But not in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*":
this is not a contradiction, because even what is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries is indeed authoritative.

He spoke thus in order to establish that even if it is not stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is nonetheless authoritative when harmonized with what is stated in those very [other] works. The connection is: "How would you think that [is stated]?"
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the sprinkling of "allowable water" (*kappiya-udaka*) is mentioned; as for how that is so, this is the intended meaning here.
Although in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* the personal planting of allowable soil for the sake of a monastery and so forth is not mentioned, the personal sprinkling of allowable water is indeed mentioned.
Therefore, just as one may personally sprinkle allowable water for the sake of a monastery and so forth...
"It is permissible; likewise, why is it not permissible to tie it up oneself for the purpose of worshipping the object? [The answer is: "That too is not contradictory.
Regarding what was stated—that one may plant trees oneself for the sake of a monastery and so forth, as well as sprinkle water that is allowable (kappiya)—that too is not contradictory.
To explain how that is not contradictory, he says: "For in that case," and so forth. This has been stated.
This is what was said: "They plant flowering shrubs themselves or have them planted, they water them themselves or have them watered.

However, there is another way of explaining this: because the planting and watering for the purpose of maintaining families is intended by the phrase "they plant flowering shrubs themselves or have them planted, they water them themselves or have them watered," it excludes the planting of flowering shrubs for other purposes, such as for monasteries (*ārāma*) and so forth.
There is a figurative sense (pariyāya). In this context, "having understood both the figurative sense there and the absence of a figurative sense here" means:
having understood that in passages such as "they plant flower bushes" (*mālāvacchaṃ ropenti*), there is a figurative sense because of the presence of the specific term "flower bush" (*mālāvaccha*);
and having understood that in passages such as "they tie [garlands]" (*ganthenti*), there is an absence of a figurative sense due to the lack of such a specific term.

But surely, just as because it is stated generally as "they sew," no figurative sense is obtained such that sewing for any purpose whatsoever is not permitted, so too, because it is stated generally as "they have [it] sewn," it follows that having it sewn even figuratively is not permitted.
And this being the case, [the following objection arises]: "Know this: if it were done thus, it would look beautiful..."

"If it is argued that this contradicts the statement, 'It is permissible to have [the flowers] done by means of a permissible instruction such as, "Act in such a way that these flowers are not scattered,"' it does not contradict it.
For having something done by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*) is not the same as having it woven (*ganthāpana*);
therefore, having it done figuratively according to the manner described above is permissible. All of this is in accordance with the stated method."
"Should be understood" concludes, in brief, the very analysis already stated above. Regarding "why there is no offense in carrying [the requisites] and so forth":
why is there no offense in carrying them for the purpose of honoring the object? Regarding "carrying for the sake of prostitutes and so forth":
the intention is that carrying for the sake of prostitutes and so forth has already been discussed therein. For this very reason, he says: "In the section on carrying," and so forth. "A garland."
"A garland of flowers. "Like a cluster" means like a cluster of blossoms (*kusumamañjarī*). "Resembling a necklace" means resembling a pearl necklace.

"An offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) as well as an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)" means: there is an offense of expiation on account of digging the earth, and an offense of wrong-doing on account of supporting a family.
"By means of improper speech" means by such improper speech as "Dig this," "Plant this," and so forth. "Only an offense of wrong-doing" [means...]

There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the purpose of winning over a family. "In both cases" means on ground that is either allowable or unallowable. "In all cases" means regarding those trees planted for the sake of winning over a family, for personal enjoyment, or for the monastery and so forth. "Also an offense of wrong-doing" means that it is not only a formal offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"With what is allowable" means with allowable water. "Of those two alone" refers to the corruption of a family and personal enjoyment.
"An offense of wrong-doing" refers to when one sprinkles oneself for the purpose of winning over a family, even using allowable terminology.

There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for causing [water] to be sprinkled using improper speech; furthermore, there is an offense of wrong-doing for sprinkling it oneself for the purpose of consumption, as well as for causing it to be sprinkled using improper speech.

It should be understood that there is a multiplicity of offenses here: in the case of sprinkling it oneself, the number of offenses should be understood according to the number of times the stream is interrupted.
However, in the case of causing it to be sprinkled, for one who repeatedly gives the command, there is an offense for every single utterance.
Even if many [plants] are sprinkled when commanded only once, there is still only one offense:
a *dukkaṭa* for the sake of gathering a family, and a *pācittiya* for the destruction of living beings.

"For another purpose" means in the case of plucking for the purpose of honoring a site (*vatthupūjā*) and so forth. "Commanded only once" means commanded by means of an improper expression. It is indeed a *pācittiya*.

Because of being commanded by means of an improper word, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). However, for one who has flowers gathered by means of a proper word for the purpose of honoring the site (vatthupūjā) and so forth, there is no offense at all.
That which is produced by weaving is "woven" (gantima). This same method applies to the others as well.

"It is not allowed" means that for one who acts or causes another to act according to the stated method—either for the sake of maintaining family ties or for the purpose of honoring the site—it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“By the same method as before” means by the method stated in the passage beginning with “for a bhikkhu.
The connection is: “having pierced flowers into the thorns fixed upon the canopy of the Dhamma-seat, they place them there.

Because they are strung together by piercing them one above another and making it resemble an umbrella, it is said, “like an umbrella over an umbrella (chatțāticchatta). All that has been stated in the passage beginning with “in a plantain trunk,” etc., [is to be understood].
With this in mind, it is said: "That is indeed too coarse. The meaning is that for one who acts oneself or causes another to act by means of an improper word, there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Because it is stated "for the purpose of piercing flowers," it is not permitted to tie on a thorn solely for the purpose of piercing flowers;
however, it is permitted for the purpose of tying flower garlands and the like. [It is also permitted] to tie on a thorn...
And "it is not allowable" (na vaṭṭati) is to be understood according to the authority of the Aṭṭhakathā masters.

Since it is stated that "it is not allowable to insert [the flowers]," it is allowable to place them one on top of the other without inserting them through the flower-holes. A canopy made of netting is a "net-canopy.
Even a "tooth-ornament" (nāgadantaka) must be taken as having holes. A "flower-receptacle" is a support for flowers made from sticks and so forth.
That too is described here as having holes. "With an *asoka*-cluster" means with a cluster of *asoka* flowers. In the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated:
"A 'Dhammarajju' is a rope tied by being threaded through a *cetiya* or a Bodhi tree for the purpose of inserting flowers.
Therefore, flowers [were inserted] between the *cetiya* and the rope tied in that manner.
It is understood that it is appropriate to insert [flowers]. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated:
"Having made a loose, circular cord called a 'Dhamma-royal-cord,' one encircles either the Bodhi tree or the Cetiya, or hangs it from the Dhamma-throne, and there inserts flowers.
Therefore, it is also appropriate to insert flowers even through the intervals of a loose, circular cord.
It is understood; having investigated, one should adopt what is more appropriate. However, our own view is that there is no contradiction whatsoever between these two positions.
"A crest-wreath" (*matthakadāma*) refers to a hanging wreath at the top of a Dharma-seat or similar object. "Enveloping with flowers" means they envelop it with a wreath of flowers.
"Of those very [flowers]" means of the blue lotuses (*uppalādi*) themselves. "With linen or with cane" means with [material] cut separately.
"Either with a stalk together with a flower, or with a blade of grass. "With the saṅghāṭī robe placed on the shoulder" refers to the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) placed upon the shoulder;

for it would be possible to tie it up in that manner. By this very statement, it is established that it is also permissible to tie up another similar yellow robe or cloth in the same manner and place flowers therein.
Because it resembles something placed in a bag or a shoulder-bag (*pasibbaka*), it is not considered a "wrapped" (*veṭhima*) cloth;
therefore, they say it is permissible to insert [small items] here and there within a loosely tied one.
And it should be understood as being like a flower-cloth (*pupphapaṭa*); for one making a flower-cloth, by way of taking up and bringing back long rows of flowers—
This was said with reference to filling [the robe]. However, drawing [the robe] across [the body] is called "woven" (*vāyima*), not "filled" (*pūrima*).

Regarding the phrase "he passes beyond the original place," it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that "there is indeed an offense even for one who passes beyond it without having caused it to touch [the ground].
This is appropriate because the expression "he passes beyond the original place" is stated without qualification. Some, however, [say] "mutually..."
It is said that "after having touched it, it is permissible to encircle it many times," yet no reason for this is seen there.
Regarding the statement "it is permissible to bind it," it means it is permissible to bind it with the end of a thread or the end of a fiber that is devoid of flowers.
As for the phrase "having carried it once, or having encircled it," this refers to the previously mentioned encircling of shrines and so forth.

This was said with reference to making a flower-canopy; therefore, when one encircles either a cetiya or a Bodhi tree, having encircled it once, they should hand it over to another upon reaching the starting point, and that person should likewise do the same after encircling it once.
Furthermore, when making a flower-canopy, having carried it once, they should hand it over to another, and that person likewise—
It should be done in that very way. Even if only two monks stand on both sides and carry it in turns, they say it is indeed permissible.
"Filled" means filled by way of stretching out lengthwise. "One does not get to weave it" means [when it has been stretched] lengthwise, across...
Regarding the statement that "it is called 'shifting' or 'moving,'" it is not permitted to shift a flower-garland even once horizontally.
Regarding the phrase "one who places flowers," this refers to one who places loose, unstrung natural flowers.
However, when placing a flower-garland on the ground for the purpose of worship, whether touching it or not, it is not permitted to place it by doubling it over.
They say: "A hanging double-stringed garland with a water-pot shape at the end" means a pair of hanging strings joined at the end by a water-pot-shaped ornament.
Furthermore, each individual string must be hung after being tied precisely at its protruding end;

likewise, for one wishing to join two flower-garlands together, it is proper to join the ends of the threads precisely at their protruding ends. "An enclosure of garland-strings in the shape of a half-moon."
It is the surrounding [of the base] by filling it out through the repeated taking away and bringing back of the garland-string in the shape of a half-moon.

Because of that very [filling], it has entered into the "filled" category; therefore, this too—being filled out by repeatedly taking away and bringing back in the shape of a half-moon—is not permitted.
However, they say that it is permissible to take the garland-string once in the shape of a half-moon.
Regarding "making flower garlands": here they say that even if one takes them from the ends of the threads, it is not permitted to make them into a single [garland].
Because balls (*geṇḍuka*) and rough leaf-garlands are prohibited, they say that a garland made of cloth and so forth is also not permitted, as it conforms to what is unallowable (*akappiya*).
Having said, "they perform the dance of the *lāsiya* dancers," he says, "they give the *recaka*" in order to show that very same thing by way of a synonym.

It is said that she "demonstrates the performance"; the meaning is that, having made her own intention clear, she first stands up and demonstrates the manner of dancing, as it is said: "In this way it should be danced. However, some say:
"By inserting their fingers into their mouths and making a sound, they give what is called a *recaka*, whirling themselves around like a wheel."
It is called *aṭṭhapada* because there are eight squares in each row; they also read it as *aṭṭhāpada*.
The same method applies to the *dasapada* (ten-squared board). "Squares" (*padāni*) refers to the places where the pieces, such as the *sārī*, are established.
A *dasapada* is a game played with twenty squares arranged in two rows. They play in mid-air, saying, "This *sārī* [occupies] such-and-such a square..."
Saying only with their mouths, “I have won; this one [is at] such-and-such a place,” they play dice in mid-air.
“On the gaming board” means on the gambling circle. “Playing the game of pāsaka” refers to the game played by displaying one up to six on each of the six sides;
having increased that, the pieces (sāriyo) are moved according to the number of ones and so forth obtained.
They play by taking away [the pieces] and bringing them back. Some say that "ghaṭikā" refers to playing with a water-pot.
"With a *mañjaṭṭhi*" means having taken the heartwood of the *mañjaṭṭhi* tree; he speaks this with reference to unripe sap.
"A handful of sticks" (*salākahattha*) is a designation for a bundle of palm-leaf pieces and so forth. Among many sticks, one stick that is devoid of distinction—
Some say that they play with sticks in their hands, taking [the sticks] from those [boxes], putting them back in, and then drawing them out again.
A *paṇṇanāḷikā* is a tube made of bamboo in the shape of a leaf; for this very reason, it says, "blowing into it.
Others also say that *akkharikā* is a game of knowing loss, gain, and so forth, by taking the letters that come from the mouth of one who asks questions. Regarding the phrase "in the elephant":

The locative case is used in the sense of the object (*nimitta*); thus, the meaning is "in the art of elephant-signals. The same principle applies to the phrases beginning with "in horses" (*assasmiṃ*).
The meaning of the two words "they shout" (*usseḷenti*) and "they clap" (*apphoṭenti*) is self-evident, so it has not been stated.
In that context, "they shout" means they emit a shouting sound from their mouths; the meaning is that they produce an indistinct sound by making it loud. "Not knowing" (*ajānaṃ*)...
They say that those giving signals are like cowherds, emitting breath from their mouths and producing a subtle, unrefined sound.

"Clapping" means they produce a sound by striking their arms and hands together; the meaning is that they place the left hand on the chest and make a sound by striking it there with the right hand. "Mukhaḍiṇḍima" is a designation for a mouth-drum (mukhabherī).
432. *Pasādāvahena* means by that which produces confidence. He says "by going" (*gamanena*) because going forward (*abhikkamana*) is what is meant by "excellent" (*abhikkanta*).

Going back (*paṭikkamana*) is what is meant by "withdrawn" (*paṭikkanta*). By "by turning back" (*nivattanena*), he indicates the mere act of turning. However, going after having turned back is simply "going.
He says "by looking forward" (*purato dassanena*) because looking directly ahead (*ālokita*) is what is meant by "looked at" (*ālokita*). And "by looking here and there" (*ito cito ca dassanena*)...
This shows the looking around in all directions. Looking toward whichever direction one goes, stands, or sits is "looking ahead" (*ālokita*);
looking back toward that same direction is called "looking behind" (*vilokita*).

There are also other types of looking by way of looking downward, upward, and backward, known as "looking down" (*olokita*), "looking up" (*ullokita*), and "looking behind" (*apalokita*). However, these...
These [actions] are unsuitable for a recluse and inspire lack of confidence; therefore, it is specifically looking ahead (*ālokita*) and looking aside (*vilokita*) that are included here.
By the word "their" (*tesaṃ*), he refers back to the "peaks" (*pabbāni*), even though they have become subordinate members within the compound.

For since it was stated, "by the contraction of the peaks," the peaks are subordinate there because the contraction is the primary factor. "By mindfulness and clear comprehension" means by that which grasps the purposefulness (*sātthakatā*) and so forth.
One is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*) because one knows thoroughly and in all ways through mindfulness and clear comprehension as they proceed accordingly;

or, it is "clearly comprehending" because one knows in an eminent or distinguished manner. The state of that is "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*). This is a designation for knowledge proceeding in such a way.
"Because of being well-composed" means because of proceeding rightly. "With eyes cast down" means with eyes cast downwards, without stretching the neck. The neck—
Indeed, looking downward after having adjusted one’s robes is not befitting a recluse (*samaṇa*). By the term “with downcast eyes,” seeing only the distance of a yoke’s length is expressed.
“Bond” means one who is fickle and of dull temperament. “Making a frown” means making a contraction of the eyebrows.
“Endowed with gentleness” refers to the gentleness described in such passages as: “In this regard, what is gentleness? It is that speech which is blameless and pleasant to the ear,” and so forth.
"Endowed with" means "possessing gentle speech. "Gentle" (*nelā*): *ela* is said to mean "fault"; that which has no *ela* is *nelā*, meaning "faultless. "Pleasant to the ear":
because of the sweetness of its phonemes, it is pleasant to the ears; it does not produce ear-ache, like being pierced by a needle.
"Connected with giving" means "regularly established acts of giving."

Having said, “He addressed Sāriputta and Moggallāna,” and then [said], “Go, you two, Sāriputtas,” it is evident that the term “Sāriputtas” is stated here according to the method of single remainder (*ekasesanaya*);

thus, this meaning has not been explicitly stated. For this term “Sāriputtas” is stated by way of single remainder because even a single remainder of dissimilar items (*virūpekasesa*) is accepted; for that very reason, the plural designation is employed here.
"Of one who has faith and is confident" means: of one endowed with faith in the Triple Gem and, for that very reason, confident;
or, because he is endowed with faith in the results of kamma, he is "faithful," and because of his abundance of serene confidence in the Triple Gem, he is "confident.
433. "The offense should be laid upon him" means: the offense incurred through the act of corrupting families should be laid upon him. "In that monastery" means...

This was stated with reference to a monastery outside the village. However, a monastery within the village is already included by the very mention of "the village," as it is subsumed under the rule: "One must not dwell in that village.

Because of the expression "in that monastery," it is permissible to dwell in another monastery in the vicinity of that village. Regarding the rule "one must not wander for alms in the neighboring village," in that...
Since dwelling in a monastery has been prohibited, the intention is that if one stays there, one must not wander for alms even in the neighboring village.

"One must not wander for alms in that village" means that one must not wander in whichever village the act of defiling families was committed; for in whichever village or town such an act was done, and in which...
He dwells in a monastery; he is not permitted to wander either in that village or town, nor is he permitted to dwell in the monastery.
However, it is allowable for one dwelling in a neighboring monastery to wander in a neighboring village, because dwelling there is not prohibited. 435. Regarding the "eighteen duties":
"One should not confer full ordination, one should not give formal support (*nissaya*), and one should not have a novice attend upon oneself."
One should not consent to being appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; once appointed, one should not instruct the bhikkhunīs.
One should not commit the same offense for which the Saṅgha has carried out a formal act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma), nor another offense similar to it, nor one more serious than it.
One should not criticize the formal act, nor the members who performed the act, nor a regular member of the Saṅgha.
"The Uposatha of a monk may be suspended; the invitation (pavāraṇā) may not be suspended; he may not be made subject to being spoken to;
a formal charge may not be laid against him; leave to speak may not be granted to him; he may not be reproved; he may not be reminded of an offense; he may not be associated with by other monks.
Thus are the eighteen rules of conduct that have come down.
They are called "the exertion of Assaji and Punabbasu" by way of association with Assaji and Punabbasu.

"By not practicing the practice in accordance [with the Dhamma]" means by not practicing the practice in accordance with the Dhamma known as the "proper conduct" (sammāvatta) as it has been prescribed;
that is to say, by not conducting oneself according to that conduct through which the Saṅgha becomes compliant. They are not "downward-hair" (pannaloma).
"They do not have their hair fallen out" means they do not behave in accordance with [the rules].
"They do not enter upon the path of deliverance" means they do not enter upon the means for deliverance known as the *anuloma-vatta* (conformable conduct);

that is, they do not practice that conduct by the performance of which one is delivered from the state of being guilty of an offense, and thus they do not abide in that conduct which leads to deliverance.
It is meant that they do not act with such haste as to be driven by a desire for the sake of emerging from an offense.

"By means of the ten grounds of abuse" refers to the ten causes of verbal abuse, namely: birth, name, clan, occupation, craft, illness, gender, defilement, and offense—these being considered inferior.
In phrases such as "causing them to fall into favoritism," the letter *ya* is indicated as elided, just as in the expression "by one's own direct knowledge" (*sayam-abhiññā*).
He said: "They cause [others] to fall into being led by desire," and so forth. "Of them" refers to Assaji and Punabbasuka, the leaders of the group.
To show that [the village] was not well-known, he said "therein," and so forth. "He gives what belongs to another" means that it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
this is stated with reference to one who takes what belongs to another through trust and then gives it away. And furthermore—
“For the purpose of honoring the recipient” means that even when giving to one’s mother or father, it should be given solely for the purpose of honoring the recipient; this is what he shows.

However, they say: “Since it is stated only as ‘for the purpose of adornment’ or ‘for the purpose of worshipping a *śivaliṅga* and so forth,’ it is permissible to give to one’s mother and others [the proceeds] with the thought: ‘Having sold this, they will maintain their livelihood. “To anyone at all” refers to a relative.
"Or to anyone who is unrelated. It is stated as "only by relatives or novices" because they are suitable [to receive it].
Regarding the statement "it is permissible to give half a share to the novices who have arrived":

this is said on the grounds that since the novices present within the precincts of the boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*) also have a claim to property belonging to the Saṅgha, they likewise receive a half-share. "A small portion" means even less than a half-share.
“Half. This is a designation for one-fourth. “The novices...
set aside,” this was said with reference to what cannot be divided according to the seniority of the rains.
“There and there,” meaning either on the path or at the shrine courtyard (cetiyaṅgaṇa). “They do not obtain to have it given” means that it is inappropriate to have it given by the novices.
It has been stated. For that would not truly be called a "gift of flowers.

If giving to those who have arrived in such a manner were considered a gift of flowers, then even novices (sāmaṇera) would not be permitted to give them. "By themselves" means by the novices themselves.

Regarding the phrase "taking rice gruel, food, and so forth," because this was said with reference to the preparation of rice gruel, food, and the like for the sake of the monks, it is stated without qualification that "it is not allowable."

"By the same method as stated" means that in the case of one's mother and father, it is permissible to give [the flowers] after having carried them oneself, or having had them carried, or having summoned them oneself, or having had them summoned;
however, for other relatives, they must be summoned. Furthermore, when having [the flowers] carried for one's mother and father, they must be carried by kinsmen or novices;
but for others, if they themselves desire it, it is permissible—this is the method stated regarding flowers.
This is extended to fruits as well; therefore, it is permissible to give fruit to one’s mother and father by taking it or having it taken, but for other relatives only after having summoned them.
Now, summarizing the method already stated regarding flowers and applying it to fruits as well—namely, that "for one who, having taken or caused to be taken...
[omission] ...gives out of a sense of lordship, there is a thullaccaya offense"—he says, "But for the sake of maintaining the family," and so forth.
"Of those whose provisions are exhausted" is said with reference to newcomers. "Or by a limit of fruit" means: "so many fruits are to be given," thus by a limit of fruit.
"Or by a limit of trees" means: "these trees are to be given from," thus by a limit of trees.
Even when the trees have been limited, [if one thinks]: "The fruits here are beautiful; from there..."
By saying, "Take it," one is said to have performed an act of socializing with families; therefore, he said, "But it should not be spoken thus.
"Tree-bark" means the skin of a tree. "Messenger-work on foot" refers to carrying messages or replies between various householders located in different villages or distant regions.
Thus he said: "The messenger-work of householders is the task of conveying messages. Messenger-work (*dūteyya*) is the work of a messenger (*dūta*).
"Even without first having received a message... [omission] ...a *dukkaṭa* offense for every step"—this was said with reference to going with the intention, "I shall deliver a message to him.
However, if, after declining that message, one goes out of one's own accord out of compassion and delivers a suitable message oneself, there is no offense. "Of the kind previously mentioned" means:
The first instruction was stated in the manner described by the words, “Worship the feet of the Blessed One in my name,” and so forth.
“Depart, Venerable Sir!”—this was stated by way of an act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*).

“Depart again, Venerable Sir!”—this, however, was stated by way of the proper conduct for one who has been subjected to the act of banishment. These are exactly like the first instance of causing a schism in the Saṅgha.

In this case, regarding the factors as well, just as there was exertion in that [previous] instance, so here the instigation by means of zeal and so forth is to be understood. The rest is exactly the same.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the corrupter of families is finished.
Commentary on the Conclusion.
442. "First-offense" (paṭhamāpattika) means those for whom the first commission of an offense occurs.
"For as many days as" means the duration of time that has elapsed from the day it was concealed until the day it was confessed, calculated by way of days, fortnights, months, and years;
such is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "reluctantly and unwillingly," here [it refers to] an offense that has not been remedied.
The intention is that because it acts as an obstruction to heaven and liberation, one must dwell [in the probation] even against one's will.
"Should be summoned" means he should be called forth by means of the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*). Regarding the phrase "and those monks are to be censured":

here, the meaning—that those who rehabilitate knowing [the offender] to be deficient are themselves to be blamed, are transgressors, are at fault, and incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)—is so evident that it was not explicitly stated. "Propriety" (*sāmīcī*) means the customary observance (*vatta*).
Thus ends the commentary on the Thirteen Khandhakas in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a sub-commentary to the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
3. The Section on the Indeterminate Rules (*Aniyatakaṇḍa*).
1. Commentary on the First Aniyata Training Rule 443.

Because the term "sons" (*putta*) is used as a general designation, or by way of the grammatical principle of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*), daughters (*puttī*) are also included; thus he says, "and many daughters.
"In the giving of gifts" (*dānappadānesu*) means in both small and great acts of giving. A "festival" (*chaṇa*) is [a celebration] in one's own home.
Regarding the phrase "auspicious rites to be performed," he says: "at auspicious occasions such as weddings and marriages. Here, the word "etc.

(*ādi*) includes the performance of auspicious ceremonies for people together with their retinues on specially marked days, such as during the month of Phagguṇa or under constellations like Uttaraphagguṇī.

"During intermediate festivals" (*antarussavesu*) means during festivals held at intervals between the great festivals. "At the Āsāḷhī festival, the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the constellations, and so forth."
Here, the word "constellation" (*nakkhatta*) should be applied to each [term] individually.

In that context, "the Āsāḷhī constellation" is said with reference to the day of the festival for entering the rains retreat; "the Pavāraṇā constellation" is said with reference to the day of the Pavāraṇā festival.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes whatever constellation the inhabitants of villages and market towns announce for three or seven days, according to their means.
Adorned and dressed in finery, they enjoy their wealth and engage in festivities under the stars; this too he includes.
"These children" refers to his own children. "Immediately thereafter" means immediately after the meal for the bhikkhus.
444–445. "That deed" refers to that act of transgression. Regarding the phrase "while a bhikkhu is seated," here the word "bhikkhu" is used in the locative sense.
The term "bhikkhumhi" is either a nominative singular form or a statement made by eliding the locative case ending; thus he says, "when a bhikkhu is seated.

In the Pāḷi, the phrase "secrecy of the ear" is stated by way of enumerating the meanings, but because it is said that "it is possible to engage in sexual intercourse" due to the mention of "a concealed seat," it is the secrecy of the eye that is intended here.

The phrase beginning with "even though" (*kiñcāpi*) was spoken in order to demonstrate this. "The delimitation should be understood" means that the delimitation—the precise definition—of the offense for sitting in private must be understood.
Now, having delimited the offense specifically by means of the eye's privacy, he says "even if," and so forth.
By the phrase "of one whose door is closed," he indicates the presence of the eye's privacy due to the state of being concealed.
[The text] shows this. By the phrase "of one whose door-panel is closed," it shows the state of being uncovered.
And since in the case of an uncovered [space], a boundary must be understood by way of the ear's seclusion according to the method set forth in the second training rule (sikkhāpada), he said:
"even within a space of twelve cubits. For this expression "within twelve cubits" was stated with reference to the ear’s lack of seclusion. If...
For if he were speaking with reference to the state of secrecy regarding the eye itself,

he would not have said "within twelve cubits," because secrecy of the eye is possible even when one is sitting at a distance greater than that from someone who is unshielded. Since, while sitting and sleeping,
overcome by the drowsiness of a monkey, one opens the eyes for some time and closes them for some time, yet does not fall into a deep sleep, therefore—
It is said: “Even one who is sleeping commits no offense. However, one who is lying down and sleeping is not like that;
thus he says, “One who is lying down and sleeping does not commit [an offense],” meaning he does not commit an offense.
“Having attained the fruit of stream-entry” indicates the noble female disciple (ariyasāvikā) by way of her final limit. “Having penetrated the Four Truths”...

Those who have penetrated the Four Truths by means of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). Regarding the rule "he should be dealt with according to one of three things," it is stated that for one who admits to sitting [inappropriately], there is indeed a connection with one of those three things.
However, in the case of a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya* offense, he should be dealt with only if he admits to sitting in that manner. Not otherwise.
"Without confessing" means that even one who is shameless, if he does not confess, should not be dealt with for the offense; this is stated without distinction.
For as long as he does not confess, he can be described as neither pure nor impure;
however, he must be dealt with according to the sequence of the proceedings. For this has been said:
“An admission is accepted from those who are conscientious; it does not exist among those who are unconscientious.
Even if an unconscientious person should speak much, one should have him act according to the connection of the rule.
Or rather, by whatever means that laywoman of trustworthy speech might say, by that means should that bhikkhu be made to act. Herein, the phrase “admitting [it]” refers to this.
Even though it was not explicitly stated, because of the context, it is said: "That bhikkhu should be dealt with by that very person who confesses [the offense].

By means of the words of such a female lay follower (*upāsikā*), since there is no possibility of her speaking otherwise, the phrase "it is indeed seen" indicates that while it is seen as one way, it may also be seen otherwise;
thus, through this observation, he demonstrates the possibility of a different state. "Thus, she is called one of great psychic power... speak thus"—this is [the meaning].
“Even though you possess such great psychic power, why did you sit down in such a suspicious place without first investigating?
Those like you, when sitting within a house, ought to investigate and then sit in a suitable place,” he said, thus admonishing the Elder;
it was not out of a lack of faith. Then the Elder [explained] his own failure to investigate before sitting down.
Showing this, he said, "Friend, it is precisely this that is the fault of entering a house. "I performed such a miracle" means:
while revealing even his own qualities that ought to be concealed, he said, "In this manner, I performed a feat of psychic power. "You should guard this" means:
wishing not to let others know of his own quality, he speaks thus, thinking, "Let no others know me in this way."

Regarding the phrase "practicing the sexual act with a woman" (mātugāmassa methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevanto), one should understand that the word "on the path" (magge) is to be supplied as a textual ellipsis;

thus he says, "on the path of a woman. Although there may be no actual lust for sexual intercourse in one who delights in sitting in private, because it is a defilement connected to that [lust], it is said, "the defilement associated with the sexual act is spoken of. For this very reason, the term "associated" (sannissita) was employed.
Referring to that, it is said: "Even if [the act] has not been committed, because one has gone with an impure mind, when enjoyment arises, it is a *pācittiya*.
It is stated that "no offense occurs if enjoyment arises in secret" because one went and sat down with a pure mind; thus, here there is no offense by the mere arising of the thought.
Regarding the statement "this rule is undetermined (*aniyata*)," among the three offenses, whichever offense—

Whether he admits to the act itself or to the site, since he must be dealt with according to that [admission], it is clear that he is "undetermined" (aniyata); thus, this meaning has not been stated explicitly.
One should understand the distinction of factors (aṅga) here according to whichever offense he admits to.
The commentary on the first undetermined training rule (paṭhamāniyatāsikkhāpada) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on the Indeterminate (Dutiya-aniyata-sikkhāpada) 452.

Because it is stated as "alone" (*eko*), the connection with the phrase "it is forbidden to take a seat" does not fit; therefore, he says: "That which is alone... [the] connection is to be understood. This is the nominative case: the word "alone" (*eko*) is in the nominative case. 453.
"Enclosed on the outside" means enclosed on the outside by a wall or similar structure. "The courtyard of the cell" (*pariveṇaṅgaṇaṃ*) means the courtyard of the cell (*pariveṇamāḷakaṃ*).
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). Regarding the phrase "whether it be a woman or a man":
why does one hundred women not constitute an offense in the first [training rule], while here even a single woman constitutes an offense? It is said in reply:
because the first training rule is stated as "it is possible to engage in sexual intercourse," it is presented in terms of sexual intercourse (*methuna-dhamma*); and yet, for sexual intercourse...
A woman is the companion. For women conceal each other's faults;
thus, when a monk was lying down with the gate opened in the Great Wood at Vesālī, many women did as they pleased and departed.
Therefore, it is said therein: "Even a hundred women do not commit an offense. However, this training rule...
This is because it is stated [in the training rule] that comes under the heading of indecent speech: "It is indeed sufficient to address a woman with indecent words.
Furthermore, having heard such indecent speech, even a woman does not conceal it.

For this very reason, in the training rule on indecent speech, those women who were modest came out and complained to the monks; therefore, in this context, it says: "Even for a woman, there is no offense..."
It is said, "she commits [an offense]. Here, because she is not concealed, even a single woman commits no offense;
there, because they are concealed, they say that even a hundred women do not commit an offense.
She is called "not blind" by way of physical contact, and "not deaf" by way of lewd speech. Within twelve cubits...
The seclusion of the ear is stated; by this it is shown that "the seclusion of the ear is to be delimited by twelve cubits.
Therefore, one sitting beyond twelve cubits does not incur an offense, even though there is no seclusion of the eye, because of the presence of seclusion of the ear.
For in this training rule, due to the lack of concealment, it is indeed the seclusion of the ear [that is the criterion].
This is what is intended. However, in the Pāḷi, it is stated as "the seclusion of the eye" (*cakkhussa raho*) by way of extracting the meaning.
Some have said, "Both kinds of seclusion are intended here," but that should not be accepted.
For the seclusion of the eye is not possible in an uncovered place, even for one sitting at a distance beyond twelve cubits, outside the range of vision.

Because it is possible to see [the object]. Regarding the phrase "even while sleeping," the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries state in three places: "By this, even one who is lying down and sleeping is indeed included.

However, the intention of the authors of the *Gaṇṭhipada* is that "even for one who is lying down and sleeping, although there is privacy of the eye, because the ear is not deaf, there is no privacy of the ear. But as for one who is lying down and sleeping...
It can be said that just as one who is blind sees nothing at all, secrecy regarding the eye exists;
likewise, just as one who is deaf hears no sound at all, secrecy regarding the ear also exists. And in the Commentary, only this much is stated:
"whether standing or sitting," just as in the first training rule [it is not stated] "even while lying down and sleeping."
However, it is not stated that "one does not commit an offense"; therefore, one should investigate and accept [the matter] in such a way that there is no contradiction.
Since what is intended here is secrecy regarding the ear, it is said: "But even a blind person who has sight.
It is said, "or a blind person, even if not deaf," because the first training rule (sikkhāpada) pertains to the category of what is concealed, as even for a blind person, [an act] remains concealed.

“He does not commit [an offense]”: for it should be understood that just as a blind man standing even near the interior of a room whose door is closed does not commit an offense, so too is this case to be viewed.

“In both instances” means in both of the two indeterminate cases (*aniyata*). Since there is no offense whatsoever separately prescribed concerning the Elder Udāyin by means of these two training rules (*sikkhāpada*), therefore—
With reference to the first offenders of each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*), it is stated that there is no offense for those who are first offenders.
For indeed, the Elder Upananda and others were the first offenders regarding sitting in private and so forth.

However, taking only those training rules originally laid down by the Blessed One, the sequence of the *aniyata* (undetermined) offenses was demonstrated in the case of Upananda. If these [subsequent] training rules had been laid down separately...
"There is no such thing as an offense; then why was the two-fold undetermined rule (aniyata-dvaya) prescribed by the Blessed One?

[In response: By demonstrating that even when addressed by such a laywoman (upāsikā), one who confesses must be dealt with according to the offense, whereas one who does not confess is not, the Blessed One—firmly establishing that the admission of guilt (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) is the very characteristic for deciding matters of discipline (*vinaya-vinicchaya-lakkhaṇa*) whenever one is accused of any offense whatsoever—[prescribed it].
It has been set aside. Now, why is the *aniyata* (undetermined) offense for bhikkhunīs not mentioned? This very characteristic applies everywhere;
therefore, it was not stated.
The commentary on the second *aniyata* training rule is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Aniyata* rules in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a sub-commentary to the *Samantapāsādikā* Vinaya commentary. 4.
The Chapter on Forfeiture (*Nissaggiyakaṇḍa*).
1. The Chapter on Robes (Cīvaravagga) 1.
Explanation of the First Rule on the Kathina (Paṭhamakathinasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) 459.
“Samitāvinā” means one who has stilled evil. “At the Gotamaka Shrine” refers to the monastery built at the site of the shrine of the yakkha Gotama.

It is said: "It has been permitted for use. This means that when the Blessed One had permitted the householder’s robe (*gahapaticīvara*), he saw monks who, having received many robes, had made them into a bundle and were carrying it on their heads, on their shoulders, or at their waists;
thus, by establishing the boundary (*sīmā*) regarding robes, the three robes (*ticīvara*) were permitted for the purpose of use, but not by way of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
“Bathing occurs here,” thus it is a bathing place, a bathing ford.
It is said that a certain brahmin thought: “Worship of the Jewel of the Buddha and the Jewel of the Sangha is evident;
how indeed might the Jewel of the Dhamma be worshipped? He approached the Blessed One and [inquired] about this matter.
He asked. The Blessed One said, “Brahmin, if you wish to honor the jewel of the Dhamma, honor one who is learned.
“Venerable sir, tell me who is learned,” he said. “Ask the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,” [the Buddha replied]. He approached the bhikkhus and said, “Venerable sirs, tell me who is learned.
“The Elder Ānanda, brahmin,” they said. The brahmin [offered] the elder a thousand pieces of gold...
He honored him with a robe. Therefore it was said: "arisen by way of acquisition.

Since the word *uppanna* (arisen) can also be a synonym for "produced," he spoke [the following] to reject that: "not by way of production. For that [robe] had already been produced by the work of weaving prior to that.

Regarding the statement, "Having caused him to take the *upajjhāya* (preceptor) relationship in the presence of the Elder, he himself performed the formal proclamation (*anussāvana-kamma*)," here [it refers to] the Elder Sāriputta as well.

It should be understood that he acted in exactly that manner. Thus, by giving his own bowl and robe to each individual and granting them the going-forth, five hundred monks were made to take formal admission under each of them. [The King thought: "Venerable Ānanda holds me in such high regard;
let the Elder Ānanda hold me in regard for now, since he has not yet exhausted his taints. But how can it be so with the Elder Sāriputta?"
"This is not my way" is said by way of affection rooted in attachment to the household, but rather by way of appreciation for his virtues;
thus, there is no fault here. "On the ninth or the tenth day": this is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is "on the ninth or the tenth day. "If it should happen":
if it should so occur to anyone. "Just as was stated": here, it may also be read as "on the very day stated."
They recite [thus]. Regarding the phrase "to retain" (*dhāretuṃ*), one should understand that the word "said" (*āha*) is to be supplied as a textual supplement here.
462–463. As for the expression "when the robe is finished" (*niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ*): this is stated by eliding the locative case-ending; thus he says "when the robe is finished.
This means that the impediment consisting in the making of the robe has been severed. It concludes with the border-strips, the binding-straps, the knots, and the binding-cloth.
"Whatever was to be done, that having been done"—this is how it should be construed.
"The mending of a needle" is stated for the purpose of showing the proper completion of the needle-work; here, the mere finishing of the needle-work is the criterion.
"Of these too" refers back to the ruined [robes] and so forth.
"And when the kaṭhina has been removed" means: when that kaṭhina which was spread for the Saṅgha has been removed;
this shows the absence of the second impediment. It shows the absence of the impediment of the residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*).
And here, by these two phrases—"when the robe is finished" and "when the kaṭhina has been removed"—the [absence] of two impediments is shown.

This demonstrates that for one who has performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony, as long as the impediment of robes (*cīvara-palibodha*) and the impediment of the residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*) have not been severed within the five-month period following the perception of their non-existence, it is permissible to keep an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*)— whether unformally resolved (*anadhiṭṭhita*) or unassigned (*avikappita*)—
even beyond ten days. For indeed, for one who has performed the *kaṭhina*, there is the practice of going without having asked permission (*anāmantacāra*) until the dismantling of the *kaṭhina*.
These five benefits are obtained: walking without having formally undertaken [the observance], wearing as much robe-cloth as required, eating in a group, and whatever robe-offering may arise there.
"Ending with departure" means that departure is its limit; the others should be understood in the same way.
The detailed explanation for this will be made clear at the very place where it occurs in the text.
*Khoma*: a robe made of *khoma* cloth woven from *khoma* fibers; the same applies to the remaining types.
*Sāṇa*: a robe made from *sāṇa* (hemp) fibers. *Bhaṅga*: a robe made by mixing all or some of these, such as *khoma* fibers and others.
Some say that *bhaṅga* is made of wool (*vāka*) alone. *Dukūla*, *paṭṭuṇṇa*, *somārapaṭa*, *cīnapaṭa*, *iddhija* (born of supernormal power), and *devadatta* (given by a deity).
However, these six types of robes are not mentioned separately because they are merely variations of those already listed.
For *dukūla* is a variation of *sāṇa* because it is made of flax (*vāka*). *Paṭṭuṇṇa* refers to cloth produced in the country of Paṭṭuṇṇa;

for it is stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: "A specific kind of silk from Paṭṭuṇṇa. *Somāra* and *cīnapaṭa* refer to cloths produced in the countries of Somāra and Cīna respectively. These include *paṭṭuṇṇa* and the others.

There are three types of silk (*koseyya*) that are compatible [with the Vinaya], because they are made from threads produced by insects. That which is "born of psychic power" (*iddhija*) refers to robes produced through the merit-based supernormal power (*puññiddhi*) of "Come, O Bhikkhu" (*ehibhikkhu*) monks;
since these are made of one of the materials such as linen (*khoma*), they are compatible with those very same [allowable fabrics]. A robe given by deities is "given by deities" (*devadinnam*);
that which was produced on the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*) for the Elder Anuruddha by the celestial maiden Jālinī—[is an example of this].
It is similar to the "given cloth" (*dinnavattha*); that too conforms only to linen (*khoma*) and so forth, because it possesses the nature of one of those [materials].
With reference to the span of a medium-sized man, it is said, "two spans," and so on.
By this, it is shown that what is the measure of a carpenter’s cubit in length, and half of that in width, is suitable for distribution (*vikappanupaga*).
For it is stated in the commentary on the *Kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada*: “What is called a ‘Sugata-span’ (sugatavidatthi) is now three spans for a man of medium height;

it is one and a half cubits by the carpenter’s hand. Therefore, it is established that twelve finger-breadths by the Sugata’s measure is one and a half cubits by the carpenter’s hand. And having done so, by the Sugata’s finger-breadth...
"Eight finger-breadths, the measure of a carpenter’s hand"—this has indeed been handed down.
Regarding the phrase "one who exceeds that": here, "that" (*taṃ*) refers either to the robe (*cīvara*) or the time (*kāla*).

"Of that, the dawn" means the dawn that has passed from the day on which the robe was acquired. "Together with the day of the robe's acquisition" means [together] with the day of the robe's acquisition.
The meaning is "together with the dawn that has passed. For by the word *divasa* (day), the dawn belonging to that day is expressed.
"Having bound" means having bound with ropes and so forth. "Having wrapped" means having wrapped with cloth and so forth.
"Should be addressed" is said with reference to the Saṅgha. "It may also be spoken otherwise" refers here to [speaking] in whatever language [is appropriate].
They say that it is permissible even if the words are not spoken in their sequential order, provided only the meaning is stated.
"By him" means by the one receiving the confession. When the receiver says, "Do you see [the offense]? he shows the statement to be made by the confessant: "Yes, I see it.
He then states the words to be spoken again by the receiver: "You should exercise restraint in the future. When this has been said, again by the confessant—
The words to be spoken are: "I shall restrain myself well and thoroughly. By this, he demonstrates his state of being established in restraint for the future.
Regarding the phrases "in two" or "in many," the distinction in wording should be understood according to the same method as before, whether it concerns two or many offenses.
