In the phrase "he remembers and reveals an offense in the motion (*ñatti*)," there are two offenses.
The intention is that one may say, "many offenses. "Even in the giving of a robe" means even in the giving away of a forfeited robe. "By way of the object" means by way of the number of robes.

It is stated that "the text itself mentioned for a group is the text here," because there is no difference between the two statements, "I relinquish these to you, Venerable Sirs. Thus... it is permissible to speak in this manner.
Having said that, he states the reason therein with the words, “Heavier than this,” and so forth. Therein, “than this” means than the giving away of the robe from here [the saṅgha].
He says, “Heavier than this,” because a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma) is heavier than a formal act consisting of a single motion (ñattikamma).
Regarding the phrase “this robe of mine,” some also read it as “this robe.”
468. “In this case, perception does not protect” is said with reference to one who is doubtful and who has not yet transcended [the state].

The phrase “even for one who perceives thus” means not only for one who has transcended and perceives that they have transcended, but also for one who is doubtful and for one who has not transcended and perceives that they have not transcended.
The meaning stated by the passage beginning “In this case, perception does not protect” applies to the remaining triads as well.

He extends [the rule]. "This method applies everywhere" means that this same method applies to cases such as those where [the robe] has not been lost; it shows that one should apply it by way of the thought:
"When others' robes have been eaten by crickets and so forth, I too perceive my own robe as having been eaten," and so on.
He states the distinction between what is not lost and what is not stolen by saying, "by way of taking it away by force. For that which is taken by way of theft—
"Lost" is what is intended; "stolen" means taken by means of open force.
"There is no offense if one obtains and uses what was made by another"—this was said with reference to a sitting-blanket (*nisīdanasanthata*).
For if someone makes another new sitting-blanket without taking a Sugata-span from the vicinity of an old blanket, that [offense applies] to him.
It is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Therefore, the statement, "There is no offense if one obtains and uses what was made by another," establishes this point:
it is permissible for one person to use what has been forfeited by another.

This was said with reference to the act of using; thus, it applies specifically to one who uses [the item] while perceiving it as having been exceeded when it has not been exceeded, or while being in doubt.
It is an *dukkaṭa* offense, but not for one who sets it aside without having used it; this is the intended meaning. 469.
"To determine the three robes" means to determine them after stating their names.

"Not to assign them" means not to assign them after stating their names. This method applies everywhere. Therefore, by one determining the three robes and so forth, [one should say]: "This outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)..."
After stating the name with "I resolve," and so forth, it should be resolved.
However, by one who is assigning (vikappeti), it should be assigned without taking the specific name of each robe, such as "this saṅghāṭī," but rather saying, "I assign this robe to you.
Whether it be the triple-robe or another, if one assigns it by taking its specific name, it is not properly assigned.

“It remains in the very state of being an extra robe (atirekacīvara). Beyond that, it should be assigned (vikappetun)” means, as stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: “It is permitted to assign it and then use it after four months. However, some say:
“Beyond that, it is permitted to set it aside after assigning it for as long as the four months of the rains in the coming year. “Beyond that... [text continues]

The statement "I allow one to assign it" should not be understood to mean that the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloak) and the *kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi* (itch-covering cloth) are permitted to be assigned by mentioning their respective names; for beyond that point, the very names "rain-cloak" and so forth no longer exist.
Therefore, even when assigning it beyond that point, one should not assign it by mentioning the name. This applies to both as well.

"Beyond that, since its use is permitted after having designated it, one should use it after having determined that which was thus designated under another name"—so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
"I relinquish" (*paccuddharāmi*) means "I set aside" or "I renounce. Regarding the phrase "I determine this outer robe" (*imaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmi*): [the rest of the passage follows].
"In the *Gaṇṭhipada* it is stated: 'It is also permissible to say, "I resolve upon this robe as an outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*)";
that too is equivalent to saying, 'I resolve upon this robe as an accessory cloth (*parikkhāracoḷa*). 'By making a bodily movement' means by touching or shifting the robe with the hand.
'Two-fold' refers to the division into those [resolutions] made in the presence [of the robe] and those made in its absence."
It is twofold. Regarding the phrase "within hand's reach," this is said with reference to twelve cubits;
therefore, that which stands within twelve cubits must be determined by saying, "This. Some say that beyond that distance, it must be determined by saying, "That.
However, nothing is stated on this point in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. In both the Canon and the Commentary, everywhere—
“Hand’s reach” (*hatthapāsa*) refers to two and a half cubits; therefore, one must seek the reason for this specific qualification here.
A “neighboring monastery” (*sāmantavihāra*) is one where it is possible to go and return on the very same day.
The term “in a neighboring monastery” is merely a heading for the teaching; therefore, having identified the designated location, one may determine [the boundary] even if it stands at a distance.

They say: "Having observed the place where it was laid down"—this statement is made because observing the place where it was laid down is appropriate; however, in this context, the observation of the robe itself is the criterion.
"With robes laid down after having determined them" means with robes laid down by determining them under the name of requisites-robes (*parikkhāra-coḷa*).

Because the designation "saṅghāṭi" and so forth did not exist prior to the formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), he demonstrates the separate procedure for relinquishing the robe-material by saying, "I relinquish this.

However, since it has been determined under the name "robe-material for requisites," it should be understood that there is no fault even if one says, "I relinquish this robe-material for requisites. Having relinquished them, they must be determined once again.
This was said with reference to one who wishes to use [a robe] after determining it by the specific name of "saṅghāṭī" and so forth.
However, for one who uses it after determining it simply by the general name of "requisite cloth" (parikkhāra-coḷa), the determination is indeed a "prior determination" (pubbekata-adhiṭṭhāna).

By the statement "there is no need for a formal determination," he shows that there is also no need for the act of applying the "permissible dot" (kappabindu-dāna). [This applies to cloth] measuring three robes, such as five handfuls and so on.
Having in mind [this distinction], it was said, "But the three robes," and so forth. "To determine the requisites cloth" means to determine it after having made it into requisites cloth.
Because there exists a formal authorization for the non-separation boundary within a fixed boundary, there is no fault even when separated from the robe;
therefore, it is not difficult to maintain there. Thus he said, "It is difficult to maintain in an unfixed boundary."
"Of a size not exceeding" means that the measurement does not exceed six *vidatthis* in length and two and a half *vidatthis* in width, according to the *sugata-vidatthi*.

But is it not the case that the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloth) loses its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) upon the passing of the rainy season, and the *kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi* (itch-covering cloth) loses it upon the subsiding of the affliction?
For this very reason, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "The *vassikasāṭikā* [loses its determination] even by the passing of one month of the rains..."

It is said: "The determination [regarding] the itch-covering cloth is abandoned even by the subsiding of the affliction. Therefore, why is it said: "After that, having relinquished it, it should be assigned"? For if there is a determination, relinquishment is appropriate.
Regarding this, first, in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, this is stated: "'Having relinquished'—this is the relinquishing..."

"It was not said [in the previous rule] with this intention; rather, the meaning of 'having relinquished' (*paccuddharitvā*) should be understood as 'having removed it from the status of being a rain-cloak.

Therefore, in order to show the point that from the first day of winter onwards, within ten days, one must relinquish its status as a rain-cloak and then perform the formal assignment (*vikappanā*), it was stated: 'After that, having relinquished it, it should be assigned.'"

However, some say: "Just as a robe-material that arises within the Kathina period becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the lapse of the Kathina month, so too this rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) becomes subject to forfeiture upon the lapse of the months of the rainy season.

Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: having relinquished it on the full-moon day of the month of Kattika, it should thereafter be formally assigned (*vikappetabba*) on the first day of the winter."
They say that the construction of the sentence should be understood as: "Having relinquished it, one may thereafter determine [the robe] for another.

But this is not correct. For a robe that arises during the Kathina month, because it stands in the category of an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*), becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the lapse of the Kathina month if it has not been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) on the final day. However, this rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) must be determined.
Because it has been set aside, it is not similar to that [robe]; how then does it become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the passing of the rainy season?

For it is only when something is neither formally resolved (*anadhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned (*avikappita*) that it becomes subject to forfeiture upon the passing of its respective time limit. Therefore, even in the winter, the *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe) still receives the ten-day grace period.
Likewise, the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*) also loses its formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) through the subsiding of the illness; therefore—
Beyond that, one obtains a ten-day grace period; however, without letting those ten days elapse, it must be formally assigned (*vikappetabba*).

Some, however, say: "Because the characteristics of the breach of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) are not stated [in this case], the *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe) does not lose its formal determination even when the months of the rainy season have elapsed, nor does the *kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi* (itch-covering cloth) lose its formal determination even when the illness has subsided. Therefore, beyond that [period], having relinquished it..."
They say that this [passage] "it should be determined" has been stated [in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*], but that does not agree with the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*;

it does, however, agree with the *Samantapāsādikā*. For instance, the statement in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "The rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) loses its determination even after the lapse of the months of the rains, and the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*) loses its determination even when the illness has subsided"—this is not found in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*. Furthermore, in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*, there is an offense... [text continues].
Regarding the statement, "One commits an offense in the winter, not in the summer," this is what is meant:

"If one wears a *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloth) that was designated and set aside on the first day of the month following the full moon of Kattika, one commits an offense in the winter. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated:
"'If one does not formally relinquish [the cloth] on the full-moon day of Kattika, one commits an offense in the winter'; this too is well-said. One may resolve [to keep it] for four months.
"Beyond that, one may designate [it]"—thus it is stated.

In this regard, the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* states that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) on account of the inner robe (*nivāsana*), whereas the *Kuruṇḍi-aṭṭhakathā* states it is on account of not having relinquished it.
Therefore, according to the method explained in the *Kuruṇḍi*, even when the three months of the rainy season have passed, the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) [is subject to the same rule].

It is understood that one does not relinquish the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). For according to the *Kurundi* commentary, it is stated: "One may determine [the robe] for four months of the rains, and after that, one may assign it.

Therefore, if one does not relinquish it on the full moon of the month of Kattika, the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*)—having reached the winter with its determination unrelinquished—gives rise to an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because the determination still exists within the field of assignment.
Therefore, with the intention that "one should formally relinquish [the robe] specifically on the full moon of Kattika and then designate it for use during the winter," it was stated:
"If one does not relinquish it on the day of the Kattika full moon, one incurs an offense during the winter. Consequently, one should investigate and adopt what is most appropriate.
Because it was permitted for the purpose of bathing, it is said: "Even if it is dyed merely by a change in color, this is allowable.
However, it is stated that two [robes] are not allowable because there is no possibility of performing the formal act of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for both.

"If, during the rainy season, another *vassikasāṭikā* robe-cloth is obtained, one should first relinquish the previous *vassikasāṭikā*, and having performed the act of assignment (*vikappa*), it should then be determined."

They say: "Of proper measure" means it is endowed with these dimensions: two *vidatthis* in length according to the Sugata’s span, one and a half in width, and a border of one *vidatthi*. "Measured" means it is endowed with the dimensions thus described:
four *vidatthis* in length and two *vidatthis* across according to the Sugata’s span. "Having relinquished, it should be formally assigned."
Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated above. Some say: "Once determined, it remains determined;
it is not relinquished again because there is no fixed limit of time. Others, however, say:
"'Once determined, it remains determined' is stated for the purpose of showing that it is also permissible with a single [renewal] utterance. In both cases...
No new purpose for this statement here is seen; for that very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, this phrase “what has once been determined remains determined” was not stated at this point.
[The statement] “In the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is said there is no offense with reference to what is set aside after having released it from being one’s own property” [is explained as follows].
They say: "One should make a formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) by setting it aside with the thought, 'With this I will purchase medicine; I will give this to my mother.
However, once it has been relinquished—thinking, 'This is for medicine' and 'This is for my mother'—and thus released from being one's own property, there is no need for a formal determination;
this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "a rug given for the purpose of bedding requisites," here [it means] "without wearing it as an undergarment..."
They say that even a bedspread belonging to oneself, when used by being spread out only upon beds and chairs without being worn on the body, need not be formally determined (adhiṭṭhātuṃ). However,
since it was stated above without qualification that "even a bedspread must indeed be determined," we hold that one's own [bedspread] must certainly be determined.
One should accept this after investigation.

Regarding the phrase "returning to the lower state," it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that this refers to "adopting the status of a householder without having formally renounced the training.
This is appropriate, because—as with the giving of anything else—the robe was relinquished precisely without any sense of attachment. Some...
However, having taken the meaning to be "by returning to the lower state" as "a bhikkhunī’s assuming the status of a householder," some say:
"But even a bhikkhu, though disrobing, does not lose his formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) as a bhikkhu so long as he has not renounced the training.
This should not be accepted, because [the text] specifies "by a bhikkhunī’s returning to the lower state."

Because it has not been stated. For in the case of a bhikkhunī’s return to the state of a householder, there is no need to mention separately the relinquishing of the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna), since her status as one who is no longer a recluse follows from her very departure from the order.

However, the phrase "by renouncing the training" is intended to show that if one renounces the training while still remaining in the physical marks of a bhikkhu, even the robe clinging to his body relinquishes its formal determination.
It has been stated. "By way of the fingernail of the little finger" indicates the lower limit.
"Of a robe of standard measurement" is said with reference to the minimum measurement.

"While putting on two robes" means while putting on both the *saṅghāṭi* and the *uttarāsaṅga* together, in the manner prescribed in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) concerning being well-covered when entering inhabited areas.
"At the place where it is hemmed" means at the hemmed places on both ends. By the phrase "this is the method," this meaning is shown:
that in the case of those robes that meet the [proper] measurements, the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is lost wherever there is a hole;
however, in the case of large robes, the determination is not lost by a hole larger than that. "In all" refers to all robes, distinguished as the three robes (*ticīvara*) and so forth.
The intention of the statement that "there is no other final measure" found in the Sutta is that [no such thing] exists.

Now, in order to clarify that very point, the passage beginning with "For... was stated. Because it is stated that "for one who exceeds that, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting," he said, "Because it is forbidden beyond that.
That does not apply; for the final [measure] of a requisite cloth is that which is fit for assignment.

The intention is that if one takes "the ultimate measure" (*pacchimappamāṇa*) to refer to the ultimate measure consisting of five handfuls (*muṭṭhipañcaka*) and so forth for the other robes such as the triple-robe (*ticīvara*),
then the statement beginning with "this is the method" (*esa nayo*) is inconsistent, because such an ultimate measure does not exist in the Sutta.

By this very rejection— that the statement found in the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā* is inconsistent— it follows that [the robe] must be the ultimate measure that is subject to the formal assignment (*vikappanupaga*).
It should be understood that this principle—that wherever there is a hole inside, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is lost—is indeed rejected.
For, with the exception of the three robes (*ticīvara*), there is no such thing as the loss of determination due to a hole in other robes;
therefore, regarding the remaining robes kept after having been determined, one should treat the last one that does not suffice for the purpose of assignment (*vikappaṇūpaga*) [as follows].
Even when it is cut into pieces, there is no relinquishing of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
However, if it was already like that prior to the determination, then because it is not a robe (*acīvara*), there is no need for the act of determination.

"A small robe" refers to a robe that is not deficient in size from the measurements divided into five handfuls and so forth. Regarding the phrase "or makes a large one small," this refers to the three robes.

The intention is that when one cuts away all around a certain area in the four directions where the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) does not cease, and makes it small, the determination does not cease in that area.

Regarding "assignment in the presence" (*sammukhā-vikappanā*) and "assignment in the absence" (*parammukhā-vikappanā*): here, "assignment in the presence" means assignment by being face-to-face, and "assignment in the absence" means assignment by being out of sight.
The meaning should be understood in this way: "the state of being near or far" refers to proximity and distance.
And proximity and distance are to be understood according to the method explained under the heading of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

Regarding the statement "even usage and so forth are permissible," since formal determination is also included therein, if one wishes to use [a robe] after having determined it by the name of *saṅghāṭi* and so on, that is formal determination.

It should be done. If it is not [the case that it should be done], then it should not be done; in this matter, the act of assigning (vikappana) itself is the authority, and therefore it does not constitute "extra robe-cloth" (atirekacīvara).

"A friend" (mitto) means a close friend. "One seen" (sanditṭho) means a friend who has been seen, but not a very close friend. This so-called "assigning of what has been assigned" (vikappitavikappanā) is permissible;
the intention is that it is like the "re-assignment of what has been determined" (adhiṭṭhitādhiṭṭhāna), as the statement is made without distinction.

The statement that one "assigns" (*vikappeti*) all robes without distinction—rather than saying one "formally determines" (*adhiṭṭheti*) the three robes and so forth, or "assigns" the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) and the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi*)—is made because it refers to the assignment of all robes in general.

"By way of the summary of the three robes" (*ticīvarasaṅkhepena*) means by way of the procedure for the three robes; what is meant is: "by way of the formal determination of the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*) and the rest.
In phrases such as "I give to you," even if at that time one does not wish to accept [the gift], if one does not refuse it, there is a desire to accept it again later.
"It is permissible to take it while [the owner] is present," they say. "Of such-and-such a person" refers to one standing in their absence.
When told, "Take it for yourself," he says, "I am taking it for me. Regarding the phrase "well given and well taken":
here, just as when someone else says, "Make this yours," even if it was poorly given, one might say, "Very well, venerable sir, I am taking it for me."

It is said that by the mere word, "it is well-grasped. Likewise here, when it is said, "Take it for you," because it has been well-bestowed, they say, "Even though it was not said, 'I take it for myself,' it is nonetheless well-bestowed.
Furthermore, since the command "Take it" functions by making the act of taking dependent upon that [bestowal], even if the thought "I take it now" has not arisen, one may take it afterwards.
They say, "He does not obtain it.
That is not appropriate, because it was stated [as such] since it was given by way of performing a formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*).
However, if the other person accepts the trust in truth itself, then even if it was later given by him for some reason, it is not permissible for that person.
There is none. However, this was stated for the purpose of preventing one who is taking a forfeitable robe—whether knowing it to be so or not—from doing so, by saying, "Do not take it.

It is said that "it originates from body and speech" because the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and assignment (*vikappanā*) that ought to be performed through body and speech have not been carried out.
[The factors involved are: the robe being one's own property, its being of a suitable type and size, and the fact that obstacles have been removed.
Excess robe-cloth and the passing of ten days—these are the five factors here.
The commentary on the first Kathina training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Udosita training rule.

471–473. Regarding the second [question], it is said, "It is reported that the Elder... and so forth, to explain how the Elder Ānanda obtained leave and what he was doing as he wandered about. In the phrase *avippavāse*, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*);
the meaning is "for the purpose of non-separation. What is meant is: for the purpose of the absence of any offense that would arise on account of separation.
475–476. *Evaṃ chinnapalibodho* means: in this way, the obstacles are severed by these [acts of] the completion of robes and the suspension of the *kaṭhina*.
*Adhiṭṭhitesu* means: when they have been determined according to the method of determining the three robes. Regarding the phrase *ticīvarena vippavuttho hoti*:
it is stated that, just as in expressions such as “the tree is cut” or “the cloth is burnt,” the designation for the whole may be applied to its parts.
477–478. By the phrase "or surrounded by a moat," it is shown that even if it is surrounded on all sides by water such as from a river or a pond, it is indeed considered "surrounded.
By the expression "to this extent" (ettāvata), he refers to the word "surrounded.
"He causes the dawn to rise in the air" means he causes the dawn to rise after the sun has passed two and a half ratanas above the space over the house.

The "house" (*ghara*) is characterized precisely by its being a dwelling place for those who have fallen into ruin and so forth; there is no such thing as a "house" existing separately [from that]. Thus he says, "And here," and so on.

(479) In the canonical text (*pāḷi*), instead of saying "in the assembly" (*sabhāye*) according to the stated method, the accusative form "the assembly" (*sabhāyam*) is used in order to clarify that the word *sabhāya* is neuter.
For the word *sabhāya*, which is a synonym for the word *sabhā*, is also connected with the neuter gender.
Showing the meaning of the phrase "stated here," he said: "The assembly hall (sabhā) is stated by means of a change in gender.
"There is no need to stay within the handspan of the robe" means that one must not stay even within the handspan of the robe itself. Regarding the passage, "That which of it...
must not be abandoned," here, by the inclusion of the doors of the assembly hall at the spot directly facing that street, all the houses there are also included.
And that inner street is indeed included [within the boundary]. "Having brought it across and deposited it in a house" means she deposits it in another house situated beyond that street.
"In front or behind within arm's reach" refers to the arm's reach of the house.

It should be understood that in the case of dwellings and the like, there is a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*) when they are enclosed by a wall, and separate precincts (*nānūpacāra*) when they are not enclosed.
Showing this, he said, “By this very means,” and so forth. It should be understood that dwellings (*nivesana*) and the like are included as those situated outside the village.
For since those standing within the village are already included by the mention of the “village,” they would otherwise be excluded from the category of the village.

“In all instances” refers to the fifteen locations beginning with the village and ending with the open air (*ajjhokāsa*). Regarding the phrase “by way of the enclosure and so forth,” here the word “and so forth” (*ādi*)—
It should be understood that this refers to the taking [of property] from what is unenclosed, and not even from a single family or the like.

480–487. "Ovaraka" (an inner chamber) is said by some to be another room within a room. "Muṇḍacchadanapāsāda" (a pavilion with a flat roof) is a palace provided with a courtyard for the *candikā* (open-air hall).
489. "Sattha" (a caravan) means either a foot-caravan or a cart-caravan. "Pariyādiyitvā" (having surrounded) means having pierced through. This very meaning has already been stated.
He clarifies this by saying: “...having entered within [the village], he stands... Herein, “having entered within” means having entered within a village or a river.
Regarding the phrase “and the exemption for a river is obtained,” it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that:
“Since no separate exemption for a river has been mentioned here, the ‘exemption for a river’ is simply the reach of the hand (cīvarahatthapāsa) as in other cases, such as with a village.”
This was said with reference to the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*) and the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīma*).

"Having gone to the monastery, one must dwell" means that one may dwell anywhere within the boundary. "Only in the vicinity of the caravan" is stated according to the aforementioned internal demarcation.
In the text, it says: "There is a caravan belonging to various families; having deposited the robe in the caravan, [one must not go] beyond the reach of the hand."
Regarding the phrase "should be abandoned," here "the range of the hand" (hatthapāsa) should be understood as the range of the hand of a weapon.
490. "In the field of a single family": this is said with reference to an unfenced field.
For it is stated: "Having deposited one's robe in a fenced field belonging to various families, one may stay at the entrance of the field or within the range of its hand."
Therefore, even when staying elsewhere within the monastery grounds, one must remain keeping the robe within arm’s reach from the base of the door.
(491–494) They say that "a vihāra" refers to the entire dwelling, whether it has a surrounding wall or not.

However, in the phrase "in which vihāra," only a single house is intended. Furthermore, in this context, the distinction between being owned by a single family or various families depends on the donors who built them.

[This] is to be understood by way of [the following]. "Within the area touched by the shadow" means that when the solar disc, traveling directly along the main road, reaches midday, this is said with reference to the space pervaded by the shadow at that time.
"On the path of no return" means this is said with reference to such a place where, having gone on that very day, it is not possible to return again.
495. "He descends into the river" means he descends after letting go of the hand's reach (the distance of an arm’s span).
"He does not incur [an offense]" means he does not incur a *dukkaṭa* offense on account of using it. Therefore he said, "For he," and so forth.

By the phrase "unfit for use," it is established that the *dukkaṭa* incurred by one who uses a robe that should have been relinquished (*nissaggiya*) without having relinquished it is unintentional (*acittaka*). Having put on one robe, [he places] the other on his shoulder.
"Having set it aside, one may go"—this was said because going without doing so in a place where many people are moving about would be improper.

Since it is stated that "having set it aside outside the village... [etc.]... the formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma) should be performed," it should be understood that even when standing in the absence of another, it is permissible to relinquish a robe that has been forfeited (nissaggiya-cīvara) just as in the case of a formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), and to give away a robe that has already been relinquished (nissaṭṭha-cīvara).
Regarding the journey, because there was an intention [to go], it is said: "But the formal support (nissaya) is not suspended. Having slept for a moment...

[etc. ... "and the support is suspended"—herein, even though the intention has not been relinquished, because the journey has been interrupted, for those who rise again and proceed with the intention, the support is indeed suspended when dawn breaks while they are on the way.
They say: "Having stayed for a moment beyond [the appointed time]"—here too, the same principle applies. Regarding the phrase "they went without taking one another's word":

if those going there had gone without the resolve, "We shall see one another before dawn," then at the rising of the sun, the cessation of the formal support (*nissaya*) cannot be said to have occurred, because it would have ceased even earlier.
Now, if they go with enthusiasm, thinking, “We shall see the dawn,” then indeed there is no cessation of dependence (*nissaya*).
This being so, why was it said: “With the rising of the dawn, the dependence ceases”? It is replied:
Because of their enthusiasm, the earlier cessation was not mentioned. And even though there is enthusiasm, [the rule applies] to going together.
Because it has been cut off, as in the expression "having stood for a moment," only the subsiding [of the offense] simultaneously with the rising of the sun is mentioned.
He says "a village within the boundary" with reference to a village established after the formal authorization of the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*);
this is because there is no formal authorization of a non-separation boundary that includes a village within its limits. Thus, the robes do not become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

It is said [that the formal act] does not cease because there is no boundary of non-separation (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), yet the formal support (*nissaya*) does not become suspended because it remains accompanied by a formal undertaking (*saussāha*).
Furthermore, "the dawn breaks for them right on the road" means that the dawn breaks for those who are returning after having heard the Dhamma.
"He goes away through lack of mindfulness" means that through lack of mindfulness he has neither formally relinquished his own robe nor caused the Elder’s robe to be formally relinquished.
He goes. Having gone, this shows the procedure to be followed by the elder after he has remembered:
"Having relinquished one's own robe, one should take the junior monk's robe in trust and set it aside.

"Having gone, he should speak" shows the procedure to be followed by one who has returned to the monastery after completing his business upon arrival. [This concerns] the state of the robe not being formally determined (*anadhiṭṭhita-cīvaratā*).
The four factors here are: the kaṭhina not having been spread, the formal authorization not having been obtained, and staying apart during the night.
The commentary on the Udosita training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Third Kaṭhina Training Rule.
497–499. Regarding the third [offense], in the Pāḷi it says, "having set aside the expectation of a robe" (*cīvarapaccāsā nikkhipitun*);

here, the meaning should be understood as "having set it aside while still having an expectation for a robe. They also read *bhaṇḍikābaddhāni bhaṇḍikabaddhāni*, which means "tied up in bundles" (*bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā baddhāni*).
Regarding the phrase "when the robe is finished, for a bhikkhunī," here, as in the previous training rule...
The meaning of the instrumental expression should be understood as being like "by means of" or "by way of.

500. It is said, "having set aside one month of Kattika," because when the Kathina has not been spread, it is permissible for a monk to keep for that month a robe that has arisen for him which has neither been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned to another (*avikappita*). However, some [say]:

Regarding the statement, “Even if given at the proper time, because it is said ‘this is out-of-season robe-cloth (akālacīvara),’ even for robe-cloth that has arisen during the robe season—counted as the last month of Kattika—when there is no expectation of further robe-cloth, there is still a ten-day limit;
beyond that, it is not permitted to keep it,” this does not accord with the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). For instance, in the commentary on the training rule concerning urgent robe-cloth (accekacīvara):

It is said: “On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the invitation month (pavāraṇa-māsa), for an urgent robe-material that has arisen when the kaṭhina has not been spread, there is a period of indulgence of one month plus eleven days; when the kaṭhina has been spread, there is a period of indulgence of five months plus eleven days.
And referring to that very same period of indulgence: “But from the sixth day onwards, even robe-material that has arisen which is not urgent...”
It is said: "Even a robe that has been set aside after being formally relinquished receives this very exemption.
Therefore, it is permissible to keep a robe for more than ten days during the robe season, even if it has neither been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned to another (*avikappita*).

If this is so, one might ask: "Why was it stated, 'Even if given specifically at the proper time, this is an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*)'? It is because of the commonality with the category of out-of-season robes.
This was stated by way of extracting the meaning, like the privacy of the ear in the first *niyata* (fixed rule).

For a robe that arises in the eleventh month or the seventh month may be distributed among those who have completed the rains-residence and those remaining, provided they are present; thus it is called "out-of-season robe" (*akālacīvara*).
However, at the proper time, without designating it as "I give this out-of-season robe to the Saṅgha," [one should say] "to the Saṅgha..."
That which is given with the words "I give" must be distributed only by those who have completed their rains-residence (vutthavassa), and not by others;
this is called "out-of-season robe-cloth" (akālacīvara). However, that which is given specifically (ādissa) must be distributed by all who are present; this is "in-season robe-cloth" (kālacīvara).

Therefore, because even in-season cloth given specifically is to be shared by those who have completed their rains-residence as well as by others who arrive later, it shares the common characteristic of being "out-of-season robe-cloth."
“Even if it is given specifically at the right time, this is ‘out-of-season robe-cloth’”—this was said by way of extracting the underlying meaning. If that is so, why was it said:
“It was given specifically to one person, saying, ‘I give this to you’”? For surely something given specifically to an individual cannot be shared by anyone else?
This is not a contradiction; for it was stated in that way to show the meaning that can be obtained through the commonality of the word *ādissa* (specifically).
"But not saying this" means: without stating the word-commentary for "beyond that" as "beyond [the limit of] one month.
The singular form "paccāsācīvaraṃ" (expectation-robe) in the phrase "arisen to that extent" functions as the agent (*kattubhāva*) of the action of making it "one's own possession.
For an expectation-robe arisen in the interim is a basic robe (*mūlacīvara*) limited to one month.
By not setting it aside and instead delimiting it as lasting for at most ten days from its own [date], one makes it "one's own" (*attano gatika*).
Beyond that point, regarding the phrase "the basic robe" (*mūlacīvara*), here "basic robe" is a term used in the singular.
For a robe of expectation (*paccāsācīvara*) that arises after the twentieth day, without being allowed to last for more than ten days, becomes a "basic robe" together with oneself.
By means of the intoxication of connection with the instrument, one delimits [the robe] according to its own time and thus makes it one's own possession.
However, for one who sets aside a "hope-robe" (paccāsācīvara) after having obtained it, there is no offense on that account as long as ten days have not elapsed.
In the Pāḷi, regarding the phrase "it must be made [ready] within ten days," the word "dasāhā" is an ablative used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is "within ten days" (dasāhena).
They also recite "pañcāhuppanne" and so forth with a short vowel. The passage beginning "when twenty-one days have elapsed...
[and] nine days must be made to pass" is stated with reference to the day on which the expected robe (paccāsācīvara) actually arose.
It should be understood that the statement "another expected robe... must be made to pass" is spoken specifically when there is still an expectation.

If, however, the expectation has been cut off by thinking, "From now on, I shall not receive a robe," then even a basic robe (mūlacīvara), if it arrives within ten days, must be determined on that very day.

Regarding the statement that even an expected robe (paccāsācīvara) may be determined as a requisite cloth (parikkhāracoḷa), this is said with reference to an expected robe of a different kind that arose earlier. "Mutually" means another.
"Aññaṃ," or this very reading [is used]. However, the "aṅga" (factor) here is exactly the same as what was stated for the first *kathina*.
For the only difference is that there, it was the passing of ten days, whereas here it is the passing of a month.
The commentary on the third *kathina* training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Old Robes (Purāṇacīvarasikkhāpada) 503.

Regarding the fourth [training rule], the phrase *bhattavissagga* should be understood to mean "the completion of the meal-duty" (*bhattakicca*). Some, however, say it means "the preparation of the meal" (*bhattasaṃvidhāna*).
As for the expression *nāma tvaṃ*, the meaning of this should also be understood as *so nāma tvaṃ* ("you who are such-and-such"); some, however, say it means *tāya nāma tvaṃ* ("you by that name").
505. "Father and mother" means parents; "the fathers of the fathers" means grandfathers;
"their generation" means the grandfather-generation. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "as far back as the seventh grandfather-generation," that is, up to the pair of grandfathers.
For in this way, by the mention of "grandfather" alone, the grandmother is also included. From the expression "as far back as the seventh grandfather-generation," [it follows] that below...
And beyond the eighth generation upward, one is no longer called a "relative. The phrase "starting from the grandfather" (*pitāmahayuga*) is merely a point of entry for the teaching;

the mention of the "grandfather" is intended to include the grandmother, the maternal grandmother, and so forth. The father’s mother is the paternal grandmother (*pitāmahī*); the mother’s father is the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaho*);
the mother’s mother is the maternal grandmother (*mātāmahī*). Here, although [the text] refers to five hundred Sākiyānīs...
A nun who has received full ordination on one side (*ekatoupasampannā*) is possible by way of a nun who, while remaining in the state of a monk, has changed her gender;
nevertheless, it is stated that "a nun is one who is fully ordained in both Sanghas" in order to show [the definition] according to the standard rule.
They say: "Because of the words 'having made an agreement' (*kappaṃ katvā*), only an agreement that has been formally granted produces an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). "An old robe..."
“Even that which has been worn once or put on once”—this is merely an illustration; thus he said, “at least by way of use,” and so forth.
The intention in the *Kurundi* is that “use indeed means using after having touched it with the body.
(506) “Having made a movement of the body”: this should be connected to all the following phrases up to the word “places it within.”
The meaning is: "having made a bodily gesture" in such a way that she knows, "This one wishes to have it washed.
Because of the expression "having made a bodily gesture," there is no offense even for one who gives hand-to-hand without making any alteration by means of body or speech.
The qualification "within a space of twelve finger-breadths" should be applied according to what is possible; for instance, [in the case] of giving with the hand...

Regarding the phrases "giving while holding [the object] in the hand" and "placing it at the feet before giving," there is no need to specify "within a space of twelve cubits," because otherwise it would be impossible [for the action to occur].
Indeed, a qualification is meaningful only when its application is possible and when there is the possibility of deviation.
This qualification was stated with reference to the subsequent terms such as "throws," and therefore, within a space of twelve cubits—
There is an offense for one who, standing in a place, throws [an object] upward or hands it into the hand of another.
However, there is no offense even for one who, having released the range [of the hand], issues a command by means of bodily or verbal gestures.
"Within the range" refers specifically to the space within twelve cubits. "Having released the range" means having released the twelve-cubit range.
"By one instance" is said with reference to that which was first undertaken and then completed.

"There is no offense regarding the dyeing" means that even for one who expects the dyeing, there is no offense because it was done without being instructed, since he had been told, "Bring it back after washing it.
By the phrase "she washes without being told," it is implied that "she dyes without being told" and "she beats [the cloth] without being told" are likewise included; thus he says this.
“By the characteristic ‘she washes it without being told,’ there is no offense. She incurs several offenses;
that is, together with the *pācittiya*, she incurs two *dukkaṭas*. “In accordance with the basis [of the offense]” means “it is indeed a *nissaggiya*.
“Five hundred is their measure” means they are five hundred.
507. “He washes a robe” … “to one who causes [it] to be washed”: here there is no offense even for one who expects her to wash it.
The three factors here are: that it is an old robe, the commanding of an unrelated nun while standing within range, and her performing the washing and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning old robes is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes. 508.

Regarding the fifth [training rule], "when the training rule has not been laid down": this refers to when the training rule concerning leaving the community has not yet been laid down. "The turn for the monastery" means...
The section on the maintenance of the monastery. "Perfection of parts" means the perfection of all the major and minor limbs [of the robe]. "Limit of all" (*sabbapariyanta*):
because there is no sixth robe other than these, each one of the five robes is the limit of all; thus it is called "the limit of all.
For among the five, such as the inner garment (*antaravāsaka*) and so forth, each one is the limit of the others due to the absence of a sixth. Of the five...
It is indeed the end. Or alternatively, because there is no other companion for oneself among the five robes, each one is indeed the end;
thus, it is "all-encompassing" (*sabbapariyanta*) because everything is limited, or it is "all-encompassing" because it is completely limited.
Therefore he said: "There is nothing else... [etc.]... there is none. Just as his wish is not fulfilled, [he speaks of] "the fullness of the body" (*sarīrapāripūriṃ*).
“...I shall see [him],” thus his arisen desire was not fulfilled. “Having shown it upon the palm of the hand” means:
without showing the body at all, having shown the robe to be given upon the palm of the hand, saying, “Here it is.
510. “Because of having a struck hand” means because of having a hand that is struck, because of being without a leader, without support, and without a refuge.

This is what is meant. "Because it has been struck evenly" means because it has been pressed. "To be exchanged" (*parivattabba*) means that which is to be turned over; "exchange" (*pārivattaka*) is simply that which is to be turned over; the meaning is: that which is given after having been turned over. 512.
"In the vicinity" (*upacāre*) refers to the twelve-fathom vicinity. Or, "throwing [it] while releasing the vicinity."
The intention is that they set it down within twelve *hattha*s, rather than strictly within the interior of twelve *hattha*s as in the previous training rule.

"Except for an exchange" means setting aside any case where one takes something in exchange—even if it is merely a piece of myrobalan (*harītakī*)—either by actually giving something or by forming the mental intention, "I will give.
It does not coincide [with the offense] because of the absence of a [specific] mental state.

Just as there is an offense for one who takes [an item] from a non-relative while perceiving her as a relative or being in doubt—due to the absence of intentional consciousness (acittakattā)—so too here, the intention is that there is likewise an offense even for one who takes it without knowing, "This belongs to a bhikkhunī.
"He gives it as a rainy-season gift" means he gives it after making it his own personal property. Even by one who takes a rag-robe (paṃsukūla) knowing that it has been set aside for his own use...
He said, “If it has been taken from a rubbish heap and so forth,” because what belongs to another is not considered [a rag-robes].
Indeed, that which is ownerless is called *paṃsukūla*. “Having determined it as a *paṃsukūla*” means having generated the perception:
“This is ownerless. However, it is not permitted to take it without generating such a perception of it as a *paṃsukūla*.

513. Regarding the phrase "perceiving one who is unrelated as unrelated" in the *tikapācittiya* (triple-offense involving a *pācittiya*): here, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning. That which has three as its measure is a *tika*; and since it is both a *tika* and a *pācittiya*, it is called *tikapācittiya*, meaning "three *pācittiya* offenses.
514. Regarding the phrase "any [article] such as a bowl or a bag": this is said with reference to that which does not admit of formal determination (*anadhiṭṭhānupaga*).

For it is stated: "What is called 'robe' (*cīvara*) is any one of the six types of robes; the last [type] is that which admits of assignment (*vikappanupaga*). Consequently, that which admits of formal determination [is excluded].
Nothing at all is permissible. For this very reason, it says: “the measure of the last robe that does not admit of assignment,” and so forth.

Since even a large piece of lotus bark, because it is included among lodgings, does not fall under the category of a robe, it is therefore neither fit for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) nor fit for assignment (*vikappa*);
thus, it is described by way of its common characteristic of being unfit for determination. Even if it were the size of a bed...
"It becomes a gourd-skin; it is indeed permissible. What then need be said regarding bowl-bags and the like?
The intention is this: since even a large gourd-skin does not require formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), there is no offense;
so what more need be said regarding smaller items such as bowl-bags that do not require formal determination? Receiving is an action; non-exchange is...
Non-action. The three factors here are: the robe being of a type subject to distribution, the absence of an exchange, and receiving it from the hand of one who is not a relative.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the acceptance of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule regarding requesting from one who is not a relative.
515. In the sixth [verse], *patikiṭṭho* means inferior; the meaning is "base. *Lolajātiko* means one whose nature is fickle. *Paṭu* itself is *paṭṭo*.
Therefore he said, "skilled" (*cheko*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase *kismiṃ viya*, he stated *kiṃsu viya* as a synonymous particle used in the sense of *kismiṃ viya*;
the meaning is "like what?"—that is, "like suffering" (*dukkhaṃ viya*).

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Therefore, he said, "like a defilement," and so forth. The meaning of the Pāḷi phrase *dhammanimantanā* should be understood as an invitation by way of the Dhamma, by way of a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
However, if it were truly said, "Venerable sir, please say what you need," then one would indeed be invited.
But because one who, even after being invited, is unwilling to give, [the invitation is considered invalid] only in a place where one has not been invited.
He remained [silent]. Therefore, without investigating whether [the bowl] had been offered or not offered, the Blessed One investigated only the state of being a relative or a non-relative, saying:
"Upananda, is he a relative to you, or is he a non-relative? "They plundered" means they robbed. 517.
"Gradual discourse" means a discourse on legal decisions given in successive order. Regarding the remaining requisites, by the *saddhivihārikas*...
Because [the robes] have already been taken, only the undergarment and upper robe remain; thus he said, "having carried away only the undergarment and upper robe.
Regarding the statement, "The elders must not break [the meal] until...," this was said because they did not know whether the co-residents would come or not.
"They receive [robes] for the sake of others" means their own robe.
Because it says, "giving [the fruit] while covering it with a break-off from the branch," they are permitted to break [the branches] even for their own sake.
Since it says, "one must come after covering it with grass or leaves," the destruction of vegetation (*bhūtagāmapātabyatā*) is likewise permitted in such cases;
thus he said, "there is no offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the destruction of vegetation. Not for them...
“Dukkaṭa for wearing” means that there is no offense of dukkaṭa even for wearing those banners of the heretics (titthiya).
And the connection is: “and those robes which they give. Because the elders gave them themselves, it is said: “because they stood in the place of one whose robe had been stolen.
If he adopts their tenet (laddhi), he is called one who has gone over to the faction of the heretics; therefore it is said: “the tenet...”

Regarding the phrase "having taken [it]," the offense of *dukkaṭa* is stated for one who, having left the monastery entered upon the way, goes elsewhere to a place of his own choosing—by the rule: "If there is no robe belonging to the Saṅgha in the monastery...
[etc.]... there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. And by this [rule], it is stated that for one who first enters whichever residence [he reaches] on the way...
It should be understood that even while staying in a monastery, if one goes about naked, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If this is so, why was it not stated there? Because there was no occasion for it. For in that context, by way of the connection: "I allow you, monks, for one whose robe has been lost... [etc.
...to request a robe," it is permitted to wear and drape even a robe belonging to the Saṅgha.

By permitting, he said, "Having first taken whichever dwelling... [etc. ...one may wear it"; therefore, because there was no opportunity for that [specific case], an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) was not mentioned.
"Monastery robe" means a robe for lodgings. "With rags" means with scraps of cloth. "Upon that" means upon the floor-covering.
"By one who has gone abroad" means by one who has gone abroad and failed to obtain another robe. "In one place... [etc. ...it should be placed."

Regarding this, they say: "Because it was taken [as a robe] by way of a minor offense (*lesa*), and because it was set aside by one who was setting it aside [thinking] only for the use of the Saṅgha, it is permissible to place it elsewhere even if it has been designated for another lodging.
"By way of use" means by using it as a robe when no other robe is available.
519–521. "Worn out through use" means worn out to such an extent that it is no longer possible to cover the body with that robe.
"By means of allowable speech" is stated for the purpose of avoiding the offense of buying and selling.

The phrase "to one who requests" clarifies the meaning of this very term as "one who causes to be bought" or "one who causes to be exchanged. For requesting by means of one's own wealth is what is meant.

The intended meaning is that it is merely a change of name. He shows the proper conduct regarding the solicitation of those who have been invited by the Saṅgha with the words, "only the [stipulated] measure is permissible.
For when one has been invited by the Saṅgha, because it is common to all, it is not permissible to solicit more than that.
"Whatever he invites" means whatever, such as robes and so forth, he invites, thinking, "I shall give this. This refers to the act of soliciting.
"There is not" means that since it is being given without a formal request (*viññatti*), the intention is: "What will he do after having requested it?
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of another," here too the words "of relatives who have invited him" continue to apply; thus he says, "to his own relatives who have invited him," and so forth.

Herein, there are four factors: the robe being of a type suitable for distribution, the absence of a [permissible] occasion, a request made by one who is not a relative, and the acquisition [of the robe] through that [request].
The commentary on the training rule regarding requesting from an unrelated person is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning more than [the permitted amount]. 522.
Regarding the seventh rule, "a shop for those who buy" (*paggāhikasālā*) refers to the shop of cloth merchants. They also read it as "a shop for those who sell" (*paggāhitasālā*).
523–524. *Abhi* is a prefix (*upasagga*); this shows that it lacks any specific meaning [of its own]. Therefore he says, "the meaning is 'to take'.

Because the word *vara* functions in the sense of "desire," he says, "one should desire. In the phrase *daṭṭhu khemato*, the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika-lopa*) should be understood as being for the sake of the metrical structure of the verse.
*Sāntaraṃ* means together with the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*). *Uttaraṃ* means the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).

"Of that robe" means of the robe that is to be accepted. "One whose all robes have been taken away" means one for whom all three robes have been taken away; this is the meaning of "one whose all robes have been taken away.
For when, at the time of the taking away, three robes are present and all of them are taken away, he is called "one whose all robes have been taken away."
It is said thus. For that very reason it is stated: "with only the three robes remaining after all other robes have been taken away.
The phrase "with only the three robes" is spoken with reference to the fact that the three robes were still present at the time they were being taken away;

it does not, however, refer to the Vinaya rule on the "three-robed one" (tecīvarika) nor to the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of the "three-robed one. "One should practice in this way": "having the inner and outer robes as the maximum limit."
That monk should accept the robe-cloth according to the procedure stated as: "He should act in accordance with the rule.
"By another" means by one who does not have all robes stolen; the meaning is: by him for whom one or two of the three robes remain unstolen.
"In another way also" means in a manner other than the rule stated as "at most an inner and an outer robe. For whom...
For among the three [robes], two robes are not cut; one must be accepted. When one is not cut, it is not to be accepted;

thus, the acceptance of "the inner and outer robe as the maximum" (santaruttara-parama-sādiyanā) is not possible for that [robe]. And this very meaning is clarified by the word-commentary (padabhājana).
Therefore, he said: "In order to show that distinction."

However, some say: "Because it is stated as 'the three robes' (*ticīvaraka*), one who has determined [the robe] as the requisites-cloth (*parikkhāracoḷa*) and uses it may take even many [robes] when that one is lost.
This should not be accepted. For, by one who intends to show the meaning of the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it says:
"But because [he is] one whose all robes have been stolen... [etc. ...in order to show that distinction."
This has been stated, yet such a meaning is not found in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*); therefore, that [interpretation] must certainly not be accepted.

As for what is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: “For one whose robe has been determined (*adhiṭṭhita*), three [of the four] are lost,” there too it should be understood that the inclusion of the term “determined” is merely for the sake of stating the literal form, and not that it refers exclusively to a robe already determined by means of the determination of the three robes (*ticīvara*).
The meaning should be understood in this way, because such a meaning is impossible according to both the Canon and the Commentary.
For it cannot be known that this training rule was laid down solely for one who has already formally determined (adhiṭṭhita) his robes by means of the "three-robes determination" (ticīvarādhiṭṭhāna).
Indeed, since the previous training rule permitted a request from an unrelated person for one whose robes had been stolen, there was a case of requesting without knowing the [proper] measure.
This training rule was laid down by the Blessed One permitting [the acceptance] within measure;
therefore, the notion that “it is permissible for one who possesses a set of requisites robes to accept even a great quantity” accords neither with the Pāḷi nor with the intention of the Blessed One.
Regarding the statement, “He whose three are lost may accept two,” this refers to one who has more than the three robes.
It should be understood that there is [a robe] existing elsewhere; because it cannot be obtained for that person's robe, it is permissible to accept it as well.

"He lives with only a single inner and outer robe" means he lives either by virtue of the training rule concerning risky situations, or by virtue of the authorization for non-separation, or due to the failure to obtain a third robe. Because the context concerns "two lost," it is stated, "two may be accepted."
"One who consents to one [robe] will be equal [to him]" means that when two of the three robes are lost,
he will be equal to one who consents to the remaining one, because both abide at the limit of the inner and outer robes (*santaruttara*).
"He who has only one" is said with reference to one whose remaining robe has been destroyed for some other reason.
526. Because it is said, “Giving [it] with the thought, ‘Let the remainder be yours alone,’” one says, “We will take what is appropriate in measure;
we will bring the remainder,” and even at the time of departing after having taken it, they say, “Let the remainder be yours alone.
This is indeed permissible for those who have been invited (*pavāritānaṃ*), meaning for those who have already been invited prior to the time of the interruption. Not by the text...

Because it is stated, "there is no offense for those who are related or for those who have invited [one]," this does not correspond to the purpose of showing that there is no offense when one consents to more than the limit of "inner and outer robes" (*santaruttara-parama*). For indeed, for one who consents to no more than the limit of inner and outer robes, there is no possibility of an offense at all;

rather, the intention is to show that an offense is appropriate only when there is a possibility of an offense under the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), and thus to demonstrate that there is no offense in such a case.
Some, however, say: "The statement 'only the proper measure is allowed' was spoken for the purpose of demonstrating austerity (sallekha).
But as for the passage beginning "since this... was not stated," the intended meaning here is as follows:

if it were said "for the sake of another," it would follow that one may take even beyond the proper measure for the sake of others; and that [consequence] would apply to the case of soliciting for the sake of another.

When compared with the basis [of the rule], it does not coincide because of its being a formal enactment (*paññatti*). For it is not logical that there should be a statement of non-offense regarding that very same basis upon which the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) was enacted.
However, in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, it is stated:
"Because this training rule proceeds by way of being dependent on one's own consent, it is said: 'for the sake of another.'"
It has been stated: "Because there was no occasion [for it], it was not mentioned. Here, since it is not stated "for the sake of another," one might ask:

is there an offense for one who requests more than what is needed from relatives or those invited? No; because in that case, the absence of an offense is established by the preceding training rule itself.

This is because [the conditions] are: being less than that [amount], the reason being that [the robe] was lost and so forth, requesting from someone who is not a relative, and obtaining it through that request.
These are the four factors herein.
The commentary on the training rule that follows this one is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Set Aside.
527. Even in the reading *mayyāpi*, the meaning is the same. However, with the plural form *ayyā*, an address is made. 528–529.
*Apadissa* means having designated [someone] by saying, "I shall give this to such-and-such a monk.
*Paccayaṃ katvā* means making it the cause. Regarding *uddissa*: here, the act of designating (*uddisanakiriyā*) expressed by the word *uddissa* is that which is the agent.
The one who acts is the agent (*kattā*). That by which one causes robes to be purchased or exchanged is "robes-purchase-money" (*cīvaracetāpanna*).

By adding the letter *na*, it is stated as "robes-purchase-money"; however, they also read it as "robes-purchasing" (*cīvaracetāpana*). "By way of common usage" means by way of the most frequent usage.
For it is by way of the most frequent usage that those desiring to see the master of the house go to his house; thus it is commonly said.
The meaning should be understood as "merely a matter of terminology"; the intention is that there is no [offense]. 531.

Furthermore, "there is no offense even in the case of an equal [value]" means that if he wishes to give what has a certain value, there is no offense regarding that which has that same value, because he has not committed an excessive act by increasing the price of the original item. And here, "I am willing to give" refers to [the object] being in his presence.
Even if not explicitly asked, having heard that someone wishes to give, it is permissible to have them bring whatever value they intend to give.

For this training rule is called "one involving an increase in value" (*agghavaḍḍhanaka*); the intended meaning here is that because an increase in value occurs for this [act], it is "one involving an increase in value," and this training rule was formulated with reference to such an increase in value.
"Give me a robe" refers to any robe among the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi) and the others.
In this context, there are three factors: excessive desire for a robe, requesting it from one who is not related, and obtaining it thereby.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning what has been set aside is finished.
532. There is nothing further to be said regarding the second *upakkhaṭa* (prepared) offense.
10. Commentary on the Royal Precept (*rājasikkhāpada*). 537–539.
Regarding the royal precept, however, while the reading is "ajjaṇho," they also read it as "ajjuṇho. "Bhoga" means that which is to be enjoyed.

As it was stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "By saying, 'Having purchased a robe with these robe-funds, clothe the monk named so-and-so with a robe,' this was said to demonstrate purity of transmission (*āgamanasuddhi*).
For if one were to send [the funds] saying, 'Give this to the monk named so-and-so,' because the transmission would be impure, it would concern an improper object (*akappiyavatthu*)."
“Even a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable) should not be pointed out by the bhikkhu.
In this regard, no specific purpose for the purity or impurity of the messenger’s arrival is seen.

For even if the messenger’s arrival is impure, he speaks using allowable terminology (*kappiya-vohāra*) due to his own skill; thus, [the objection] that “a *kappiyakāraka* should not be pointed out” [is refuted].
There is no such deliberation on the part of the donor as to how this was sent when it has been spoken by means of a messenger using allowable terminology;

nor can that be known without such deliberation. Furthermore, if the messenger were not to be designated as a "maker of the allowable" because his arrival was impure, then [the gift] would remain in the hand of the messenger as an unallowable thing for the purpose of robes.
When the sender has sent [the gift] everywhere, the one who makes it allowable (kappiyakāraka) should be pointed out only after asking, "How was it sent?

Therefore, even if there is no purity regarding the arrival [of the gift], if that messenger speaks by way of allowable terminology (*kappiyavohāra*) through his own skill, the word of the messenger itself must be accepted.
For if, in this case, the purity of the arrival alone were the criterion, then by the original owner—

Even if a messenger who has been dispatched by way of allowable terminology (*kappiya-vohāra*) speaks by way of unallowable terminology (*akappiya-vohāra*), the provider of what is allowable (*kappiya-kāraka*) must still be identified;
therefore, in all cases, the word of the messenger alone must be accepted as the authority.
By the phrase "with this robe-fund" (*iminā cīvara-cetāpannena*), etc., however, he shows this point: even that which has come by way of allowable terminology...
The basis for robes becomes unallowable through such a message from a messenger; therefore, it must be refused. For this very reason, it was said:
"That bhikkhu should speak to that messenger thus," and so forth. For these four—gold, silver, the kahāpaṇa coin, and the māsaka—are objects involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*);
as are pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells, stones, coral, [amber, and silver coins].
The ruby, the emerald, the seven kinds of grain, male and female slaves, fields, land, and flower and fruit gardens—
these are improper objects for acceptance, whether for oneself or for the benefit of a shrine, the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual; therefore,
it is shown that it is not permissible to consent to them by saying, "Friends, we do not accept a gift of cloth-money..."
When it was said, “We shall accept [it],” this—namely, “And we shall accept the robe”—is permissible to say because it was brought for one’s own sake;

therefore, it was stated. As for the instruction, “The attendant must be pointed out,” this was authorized because it was spoken by means of an allowable statement (kappiya-vacana), namely, “But does the venerable one have anyone as an attendant? However, if...
The messenger should not say, "Who will take this? or "To whom shall I give it?"; he must not point [the recipient out].

The terms "monastery attendant" (ārāmika) or "lay follower" (upāsaka) are mentioned because they are appropriate; however, anyone who is a maker of what is allowable (kappiyakāraka), with the exception of the five who share the same Dhamma (sahadhammika), is permissible.
The statement, "This, friend, is the attendant for the monks," is intended to show that such a person is an allowable thing for a monk.
It has been stated thus. Indeed, it should be stated in this very way; [phrases] such as "give this to him" and so forth should not be said.
In the phrase "or he will cause it to be bartered," one *vā* (or) is a mere filler for the verse.

However, the statement "he was summoned by me" and so forth is said to show that it is only when the messenger has reported it in this manner that it is permissible to urge him [for payment], and not merely because of the fact that [the object] was delivered into his hand.
For these statements... [pe] ... "it should not be said" (na vattabbo)—regarding this, it is stated in the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* and the *Majjhimagaṇṭhipada*:
"By speaking thus, because one has performed what was prohibited, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense for the breach of a duty (*vatta*), yet the formal accusation (*codanā*) still takes place.
Having shown the section on the formal accusation already recited, [the text says] "he should be told a second time as well," and so forth. "When being questioned" means:
In this context, the meaning should be understood as "by one who is being questioned"; thus he says, "The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
"He destroys the reason for coming" means he ruins the cause for having arrived.
Regarding this, some say: "The 'reason for coming' refers to the taking up of robes; because it is stated that he 'destroys' that..."

"That robe may not be accepted in any manner whatsoever. However, because it is stated that "one breaks the grounds for which one has come," just as by a single exhortation such as "I have need of a robe, friend," one breaks two grounds, so too here:
if one sits on a seat, by that single act of sitting one breaks two grounds;
and if one accepts material goods, by that single act of acceptance one breaks two grounds.
"If one speaks the Dhamma, they say that by a single utterance falling within the limits prescribed for the training rules of teaching the Dhamma, two bases [of offenses] are broken.
However, having rejected the claims of all these [teachers] as "inappropriate," this is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:
"The 'reason for its occurrence' refers specifically to the basis [of the offense]; therefore, regarding that which has been prohibited as 'not to be done'..."
“Because of having performed [the formal act], when the six positions such as sitting have been completed, one breaks [the continuity] at one position.

Regarding the phrase “he stands in this or that place,” this was said by the accuser with reference specifically to a place designated for standing, after he has moved away from his original standing spot.
“Either one should go oneself, or a messenger should be sent”—this is according to its natural meaning.

They say that it must indeed be done even by one who does not wish to be exhorted. One who has opened his mouth and thus voluntarily assumed the role of a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable) is called a "mouth-opening *kappiyakāraka*. Regarding the phrase "because of the desire not to investigate":
in this context, the statement "we have no *kappiyakāraka*" is said with the underlying intention that "there is no *kappiyakāraka* who would do such a thing."

Having said, "One should proceed according to the method stated in the Meṇḍaka training rule (sikkhāpada)," he now spoke the passage beginning with "For this has been said" in order to show that very Meṇḍaka training rule.

Indeed, this statement beginning with "There are, monks, those who have faith and confidence" is called the "Meṇḍaka training rule" because it was spoken in the context of the Meṇḍaka case within the Bhesajjakkhandhaka (the Chapter on Medicines). In that regard:

Indeed, when the merchant named Meṇḍaka requested—saying, "Venerable sir, there are wilderness roads that have little water and little food; it is not easy to travel without provisions. It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to allow provisions for the bhikkhus"—the Blessed One was thus entreated.
“Monks, I allow you to seek provisions for the journey:

rice for one who needs rice, mung beans for one who needs mung beans, black gram for one who needs black gram, salt for one who needs salt, sugar for one who needs sugar, oil for one who needs oil, and ghee for one who needs ghee.
Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“Bhikkhus, there are people who have faith and confidence;
they place gold in the hands of those who prepare what is allowable, saying, ‘With this, give whatever is allowable to the noble one. I allow you, bhikkhus, to accept from them whatever is allowable.
But in no way whatsoever, bhikkhus, do I say that gold and silver should be accepted or sought after.”
Regarding the phrase "depositing gold," it should be understood that the informing of the bhikkhu is indeed required here as well.
Otherwise, since he would fall under the category of one who acts as an unappointed kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable), he should not be reproached.
If one were to reproach him with reference to the root [offense], that [root offense] would already have been admitted; therefore, he said: "by one who does not admit the root."
“The statement ‘one should proceed as if among those who are unrelated and have not invited’ is said for the purpose of showing that one should not act as one’s own accuser.
However, it is permissible to send another person acting as a steward (kappiyakāraka) and, by following worldly custom,
to have them fetch a suitable article, because what has been set aside specifically for oneself belongs to oneself.”
Some say: "Because it is stated emphatically in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—‘One should behave as if toward those who are strangers and have not invited [one];
if they bring the robe themselves and give it, it should be accepted; if not, nothing should be said’—it is our view that it should not be accepted.
For one does not [behave] toward a stranger who has not invited [one] without having first requested [the robe] oneself."
It is permissible to have it conveyed by another, but it cannot be maintained that where it is permissible to have it brought by sending another, one must not go there oneself to have it brought.

For if, in this case, it were permissible to have it brought by another, then statements such as "one should act as if toward those who are unrelated and uninvited" would be rendered meaningless. [The phrase] "by means of a messenger" (dūtena).
He shows an exception to this with the words, “even having brought it oneself. This is connected with the phrase “while they are giving.
However, by the phrase “for the sake of alms-food, etc.,” he shows an exception to the term “monetary gift for robes” (*cīvaracetāpanna*).

Because it is stated that “the same method applies,” even when [a gift] is given for the sake of alms-food and so forth, all matters such as the formal charge regarding the place of residence must be handled according to the method explained below.
