"An offense both in receiving and in using": this means there is a *pācittiya* offense in receiving and a *dukkaṭa* offense in using.
"He himself is one who has committed an offense" is said with reference to the *dukkaṭa* offense. This should be understood solely on the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Some also say: "It was stated that 'he himself is one who has committed an offense' and 'he is one who has fault' in order to show that the other person is without fault."

"In the three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries it is stated: 'Because it is said "he accuses," and because he accuses regarding an offense, the phrase "he is one with an offense" is appropriate only when referring to a *dukkaṭa* [offense].
It is stated that in both the acceptance and the consumption there is indeed an offense; this is said specifically with reference to a *dukkaṭa*.
Since even a pond is included within the category of 'field,' there is an offense in its acceptance as well."
It has been stated: "He gives [the gift] saying, 'May the Saṅgha enjoy the four requisites.

In this context, if one says, "I give the pond so that the Bhikkhu-saṅgha may enjoy the four requisites," or "I give the pond for the purpose of enjoying the four requisites," it is indeed permissible.
However, if one says, "I give the four requisites arising from this pond," [it is not permissible].
There is simply nothing that needs to be said.
When it was stated, "Appoint one of us as a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable)," this was said with reference to exactly such cases.

However, regarding fields, reservoirs, and so forth, which have been accepted through the process of making them allowable, it is indeed permissible to appoint a kappiyakāraka even if one has not been specifically requested.
Because it is not permissible for monks to destroy what belongs to another, it is said: "not during the time of the crops.
Regarding the phrase "the owner of the district," they say that even one who governs that district may give [the land] after having confiscated it, and this is indeed permissible.
"A water-channel" means a watercourse. Regarding the phrase "even in the case of a transaction involving allowable things": here, "arrangement" (vidhānaṃ) [is meant].
The phrase "I shall explain" is the remainder of the text. "By way of water" means for the purpose of using water.

"Of those with pure minds" implies that it is solely for the purpose of using water. He said "by a conscientious bhikkhu" because there is nothing at all to be said regarding something caused to be made by one who is shameless.
"A natural portion" in this kingdom refers to an area measuring four *ambaṇas*. "Unplowed new crop" refers to rice that has not been cultivated before.
“With an undelimited portion” means: when the portion is not delimited such that one might say, “On this much ground, this much portion should be given.
Regarding the phrase “with a rope or with a staff,” they say here that it is not even permissible to measure with one’s feet.
Regarding the phrase “standing on the threshing floor he guards,” here he guards by preventing those who see him taking [the grain] by stealth, saying, “Do not take it!”
[This is] the name. However, if he stands silently without investigating, merely watching for the purpose of protection, it is permissible.
Even if they steal by means of theft while he remains silent, they say that it is permissible to speak thus: "We shall inform the Saṅgha of monks.
Regarding the phrases "he causes to be removed" and "he puts in order," here too, "if he speaks in turn..."
"It is allowable," they say. Because it has not been previously produced [as a formal act], he says, "That is not allowable for him alone," meaning it is allowable for others.
But surely, by the mere fact of having handled it improperly, it becomes unallowable for him alone, and not for everyone—as in the case of the fourth bowl regarding the exchange of money.
For it is said there: "But whoever, without accepting the money, says, 'Buy a bowl for the Elder and give it to him'..."

“Having gone to a smith’s workshop with a designated attendant for what is allowable (kappiyakāraka), and having seen a bowl, he caused [the smith] to give coins by saying, ‘Take these coins and give me this,’ and thus it was accepted. This bowl is not permissible for that very monk because of his improper conduct;
however, it is permissible for others because the price was not accepted. Therefore, whatever they bring, for all [monks]—
It is not allowable. Why? Because it was deliberated upon regarding kahāpaṇas. Why was this said? On this point, some say:
"This was said with reference to what was deliberated upon after having accepted the kahāpaṇas.

Their intention is that because it belongs to the Saṅgha, it cannot be relinquished; therefore, it is not allowable for anyone. However, others [say] that even without having accepted the kahāpaṇas...
They say: "Because it has been deliberated upon, the transaction involving silver has been performed; and because it belongs to the Saṅgha, it cannot be relinquished.
Therefore, it is not allowable for anyone. However, in all three *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, this is stated:
"The fourth bowl [is allowable] for others because it was deliberated upon with coins belonging to householders; but here, [the coins] belong to the Saṅgha."
"Because it has been deliberated upon, it is not permissible for anyone. Thus, the argument of everyone is indeed consistent through their respective methods.

"At the door of the four-sided hall" refers to the dining hall. "Because it was stated by way of a method" means because it was stated by way of a method, saying "the boundary has been reached" instead of saying "take it.
"For the purpose of making the ground level" refers to [the phrase] "the soil taken from below," and so forth.
It has been stated. Regarding the phrase "I give a slave," they say that it is permissible if one says, "I give a human being.
Regarding the passage "chickens and pigs... it is permissible," when chickens and pigs are being given away, it is permissible to say, "We have no need for these;
let them live happily; release them into the forest. This is because of such statements as, "He abstains from accepting fields and lands," and so forth.
This entire analysis regarding the acceptance of fields and so forth has been stated.
Herein, there are four factors: the fact that the monk has designated a steward (*kappiyakāraka*), the act of sending a messenger, the exertion beyond that, and the acquisition through that exertion.
The commentary on the training rule concerning kings is concluded.
The first chapter on robes is finished. 2.
The Chapter on Silk.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Silk.
542. Regarding the phrase "kosiyakārake" in the Pāḷi: those creatures who are commonly called *kosakāraka* (cocoon-makers) because they produce a *kosa* (cocoon) are so named;
that which is produced from their cocoon is *kosiya* (silk), and those who work with it are *kosiyakārakā*, namely, weavers.
*Saṃhananaṃ* means a compact mass or a conglomeration; the meaning is "destruction. *Kosiyamissakaṃ* means mixed with silk thread. Because it is stated as "not woven (*avāyiman*)"— [End of excerpt]

If they do it after it has been blown away, there is no offense. It is stated that there is no offense even when making canopies and so forth for the purpose of canopies and the like, nor when using them in that manner.

Thus, even if something is made by mixing [materials], by this [rule] it is understood that even if it is brought down by the wind and falls, there is indeed an offense because of the absence of intention (*acittakattā*).
It shows [the offense]. Here, the three factors are: the inclusion of silk, making or having made a rug for one's own use, and its acquisition.
The commentary on the training rule regarding silk is finished.
547. The training rule on entirely black [wool] is of plain meaning.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Two Parts:
Regarding the training rule on two parts, "two parts" is the maximum limit for taking an excess of black [wool].

Because the training rule was formulated by way of prohibition. "The third [measure] for white [wool] and the fourth for goat's hair"—this is the lower limit, because there is no prohibition against taking more than that.
Therefore, it is not permitted to have more than two parts of black [wool];
however, for the others, even more than the stated measure is permitted. "Only of the black... [etc.]
And because the taking of more than the limit is prohibited, they say: "It is permissible even if one takes half black [wool] and half white or half *gocariya* [wool];
there is no offense if one makes it by taking a greater amount of white or a greater amount of *gocariya*, or if one makes it by taking pure white or pure *gocariya*."
This corresponds to that [statement]. They say: "Except for the black and the white, the rest are included among those used for ordinary purposes.
Regarding the phrase "two portions of black [wool]," the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* states:

"If there is even a single black hair in excess, it becomes an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). This refers to the instruction: "Having kept [the robe], two *tulā*s [of black wool] must be taken up."
According to the wording, it does not accord with weighing on a scale. For one does not perform a weighing by counting hairs;
if, however, it were necessary to weigh only after counting them, what would be the use of weighing? Therefore, the intended meaning here should be understood as follows:
because the training rule concerns the mind, if even a single hair were to fall onto that [scale] which was previously weighed and set aside, it constitutes an offense of expiation (nissaggiya).
Otherwise, because it would be difficult to discern [the difference], two balances should not be used; rather, only one that is slightly less [in weight] should be taken.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the two parts is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning six years.

Regarding the six training rules concerning grass mats (*chabbassa-sikkhāpada*), the connection between the words of the Pāli text should be understood as follows: "On our mats, children urinate and spit;
on our mats, rats even gnaw. With reference to the meaning of the roots *hṛd* (to void excrement) and *miha* (to sprinkle/secrete), it is said:
"They void both feces and urine. [This applies] on the days of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), the Uposatha, and the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*).

Having made the *santhata* (spread), if one makes it again when the sixth year has been completed on the days of the *pavāraṇā*, the *uposatha*, or the first day of the half-month (*pāṭipada*), one is said to be "making it for six years.
However, if one makes it starting from the second day [of that period], one is said to be making it for more than six years.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the six years is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sitting Mats (565–6).
Regarding the training rule on sitting mats, however, it says "it will be known":
if that agreement is agreeable, the Saṅgha of monks will be reflected in its agreeableness; if it is disagreeable, it will be reflected in its disagreeableness.

The intention is as follows: although the three factors beginning with the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññakaṅga*) are stated in the Canon by way of the factors of exertion (*padhānaṅga*), it should be understood that the remaining factors were indeed undertaken as well.
For this very reason, he said: “On a spread, because it is designated as the fourth robe. *Ujjhitvā* means having relinquished. 567.
Because it serves as a sitting-spread (*nisīdana-santhata*), there is no need for the functions of wearing it as an undergarment or upper robe; thus he said: “If one has sat down once...”
"And for one who lies down. "The measure of a span" refers to the Sugata-span; this is stated to show the lower limit.

It is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries: "Since it is said that there is no offense when making [a canopy] solely for the purpose of a canopy and so forth, if they make it for the purpose of lying down, there is indeed an offense.
However, because it is unallowable (*akappiya*), it is not permitted to use it.
It has been stated. And regarding this, they say that what is called a "seated rug" (*nisīdanasanthata*) is simply a sitting-cloth (*nisīdana-cīvara*), and nothing else.
For it is said in the training rule on the seated rug (*nisīdana-sikkhāpada*): "A 'seated rug' is called that which has fringes," and in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) it says of it:
"Having spread it out like a rug (*santhata*), one should cut two slits in two places at one end, in a region measuring a *vidatthi* of the Sugata’s span, and [provide] three fringes."

Because of the statement, "When ten [lengths] are made, that which has ten [lengths] is called *sadasaṃ*," it appears appropriate here as well to say, "A sitting mat (*nisīdana*) is called *sadasaṃ*," and because of the statement, "[It is used] on a rug (*santhata*), being considered the fourth robe. However, some say:
"They make a sitting-rug (*nisīdana-santhata*) by spreading out woolen fleece and sewing it together like a rug; that..."
"This [robe] is not subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*); however, they make a sitting-cloth (*nisīdana*) out of one of the six kinds of robes so that it becomes subject to determination.
And when making it, they spread out pieces of cloth and make it resemble a patchwork," so they say;
having investigated this, one should adopt what is more reasonable.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting mats is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning sheep’s wool (eḷakaloma). 571.
Regarding the training rule on sheep’s wool (*eḷaloma*), where it says *āsumbhī*, they read it as *asumbhī*. By the word *kilantā* (weary),...
This shows that because of their exhaustion, they are unable to bend down and drop [the goods]. The phrase "one traveling on a long journey" is stated in the Pāḷi merely to illustrate the case;
however, it is indeed permissible to receive and take [goods] by means of a righteous transaction anywhere at all.
Furthermore, the expression "not exceeding three yojanas" refers to a distance of three yojanas measured from the place where the goods were received.
The meaning should be understood in this way.
572. Regarding "with one's own hand" (*sahatthā*), he says "with one's own hand" (*sahatthena*) because it is an ablative expression used in the sense of an instrumental.

The phrase "when there is no one to bring it" is stated in the Pāḷi for the purpose of showing what is appropriate for a bhikkhu; it does not mean that [the offense occurs] when someone to bring it is actually present within three *yojanas*.
This is for the purpose of showing the offense for one who takes it with his own hand. He said, "beyond three yojanas," meaning "he causes it to fall beyond three yojanas.
Therefore, even when it is carried [by another], there is indeed an offense, because it was taken with a prior intention (*saussāha*) and because it was taken without a formal command (*anāṇatti*).

For even though there is a state of having a prior intention, if one carries it by means of a command, there is no offense, according to the statement, "one causes another to carry it. [The thought is: "Another will carry it."
Because there was no underlying intention (*adhippāya*), it is said, "placed with a pure mind. "With exertion" means because of the exertion involved in traveling beyond three *yojanas*.
This [statement] was made with reference to what was placed with an impure mind, thinking, "Another shall carry it";
however, "because of the absence of a mind" refers to what was placed with a pure mind. "There is no offense; this does not accord with the Canon" refers to [the rule regarding] "three *yojanas*..."
This does not accord with the Pāḷi beginning with “harati,” and especially not with the Pāḷi passage “he causes another to take it away.
If one sets it down after informing the owner, it is indeed taking it away by means of an order; therefore, he said, “without the owner even knowing.
“Even though it does not go” means even when the vehicle has stopped after its movement has been interrupted. “Or going downwards” means on the ground.
"Going. Regarding "he causes another to carry it": here, by the inclusion of the word "another," animals are also generally included;

thus he says, "Because of the statement 'he causes another to carry it,' there is no offense. "There is an offense at a customs post": this means there is an offense for one who causes another to carry it. "In that case, there is no offense": because there is an absence of the intention to steal (*theyyacitta*) on the part of one who has been directed [by another], there is no offense.
575. Regarding the phrase “carrying it away,” the *Mahāgaṇṭhipada* states: “Carrying it away again means carrying it for three *yojanas*.
However, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, concerning the factors (*aṅga*) [of an offense], it says: “The first acquisition does not accord with this statement;
for ‘the first acquisition’ indicates that the second acquisition is not a factor for the offense. Therefore, both in the Canon and in the Commentary...

It is our conviction that for one who, having received back what was stolen, carries it away again, there is no offense even if he exceeds three *yojanas*, because of the absence of any specific distinction [in the rule].
Otherwise, one would have to say: "having received back what was stolen, he carries it away again up to three *yojanas*.

One should investigate and adopt the more reasonable interpretation. Regarding the phrase "there is no offense for a finished article," this includes finished articles such as blankets, shawls, and so forth.
They say that even loose fibers attached to a natural robe (pakaticīvara) certainly give rise to an offense.
They insert [the wool] into the interior of a thin alms-bowl bag so that it does not rub against [the bowl]. “Inserted” means inserted into the ear-hole [of the bag].

By the phrase “a receptacle opening,” he shows that it does not count as a manufactured article. This refers to the fact that sheep’s wool is not a manufactured article and its first acquisition [is subject to the rule].
Taking it oneself, or placing it in another’s vehicle without that person’s knowledge, traveling more than three *yojanas*, returning it,
and the absence of the intention to dwell [with it]— these are the five factors here.
The commentary on the rule concerning wool (*eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada*) is concluded.
576. The training rule concerning the washing of sheep’s wool is of plain meaning. 8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Money (Rūpiya-sikkhāpada). 583–584.
Regarding the training rule concerning money, however, "the Teacher’s color" means having a color identical to that of the Teacher. The Teacher’s color...
"Teacher-colored" (*satthavaṇṇa*) should be understood as a compound with the middle term elided (*majjhapadalopī-samāsa*), meaning "that which has a color like the teacher's.
What is called "ordinary" (*pākatika*) is the current standard *kahāpaṇa* coin. "Made from the seeds of tree fruits" means made from the seeds of fruits of trees such as the *tintiṇika*.
"All this" refers to all four types of objects subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya-vatthu*) according to the divisions already mentioned.
The connection is with the word "occurs. A *jātarūpamāsaka* is a gold *kahāpaṇa*.
"Should take" means that he should himself take it, whether it is being given to him for his own sake, or he sees it lying somewhere unclaimed.
Or [he might say], "Let this be for the noble one," either in the presence [of the owner] or [thinking], "In such-and-such a place my gold and silver..."

"Whatever there is, let that be yours"—thus, when something has been relinquished by saying "yours," whether in the absence of the person, or merely by word or by hand gesture, and one does not refuse it with body or speech but consents to it mentally, this is called "consent by what is placed near.
The phrase "he consents" clarifies the same meaning expressed as "he desires to take. "This is a protected place."
"Should be pointed out" refers specifically to the enjoyment of requisites; it should be pointed out [in that context].

When it is said, "Place this here," if one causes it to be taken up according to the characteristic described in the rule "or should cause it to be taken up," it becomes an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya); therefore he says, "One should not say, 'Place this here.
The subsequent statement, "One should not say, 'Take this,'" follows the same principle. And what is allowable...
"And it stands supported by what is unallowable" means that because the enjoyment of requisites arising from that [unallowable thing] is permissible,
it therefore stands supported by what is allowable; however, because even the enjoyment of requisites arising from that [allowable thing] is not permissible due to improper conduct,
it should be understood as standing supported by what is unallowable.
Regarding the phrase "nothing allowable was purchased with that": here, if something has been purchased, there is no means for its use;

therefore it is stated thus. For if one has acquired an unallowable article subject to forfeiture and has not yet forfeited it, then even if an allowable article has been purchased with it and forfeited to the Saṅgha, it is not allowable for anyone. However, some [say]: "Because..."

Having received an article subject to forfeiture and having exchanged it for allowable goods, if one says, "I forfeit [these] to the Saṅgha," it is permissible to use them even without the formal act of forfeiture; therefore, they say, "It is stated that 'nothing was exchanged for allowable goods by him.
Or, regarding the phrase "or a share for the monastery attendants," this refers even to when it has come into the hands of householders.

It is stated [in the *Majjhima-gaṇṭhipada* and the *Cūḷa-gaṇṭhipada*]: "Having considered it as one's own portion, it is said. However, if they give it after having exchanged it for something else with that person, it is permissible to consume it. "Having taken from there" means having taken from the portions received by others.
"The preliminary work for the kasiṇa" refers to the preliminary work for the light-kasiṇa (*ālokakasiṇa*). Regarding the phrase "beds, chairs, and so forth," here: "From there..."
They say: "If, after exchanging the bed, chair, and so forth that were taken, another [set] is taken, it is permissible.
"Even the shade" means even the shade of a dining hall and the like. "Exceeding the boundary" means exceeding the boundary of the house;
the intention is that wherever the shade has gone, that place is no longer called a "house. "Even by way of the path" means here, "if there is another path..."
"There is no [fault]; it is permissible to go after having resolved upon the path," they say. "Purchased with that" means purchased with that property.
Regarding the phrase "the Saṅgha uses the requisites after setting aside a deposit": if a lay follower, saying, "This gold is too much;
this, venerable sirs, should not be lost this very day," himself sets aside a deposit, or [if] by another...

Or if one has it placed [there]—if the Saṅgha, having set aside this as a deposit and consuming the profit from it, consumes the requisite, it is called "unallowable" because that object has been taken hold of. 585.
"It should be thrown down by one who does not attend to the place where it fell"—this is intended to demonstrate the state of being indifferent (nirapekṣabhāva).
It should be understood that, therefore, in this matter, the criterion is simply a state of indifference, like that of a kinsman discarding excrement at the place where it has fallen.
"By claiming what is not true" is said with reference to announcing superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) that do not exist in oneself.
"Enjoyment by theft" means the enjoyment of what one is unworthy of; for in the Blessed One’s own teaching—
The requisites are permitted for one who is virtuous, not for one who is immoral.
Even among donors, their relinquishment is intended only for the virtuous, not for the immoral, because the latter expect in return that their own acts will yield great fruit.
Thus, because it is neither permitted by the Teacher nor relinquished by the donors, the use of requisites by an immoral person is "use by theft" (theyyaparibhoga). It is a use by way of debt.
“Enjoyment of debt” means that it is like enjoying something after having taken on a debt, because there is no purification of the offering (*dakkhiṇā*) on the part of the recipient.
Therefore, with the words “of one who is virtuous,” etc., he refers back to the very meaning already stated by way of its causal nature.
“In each enjoyment of the robe” means in each instance of enjoying it after having released it from the body. “Before the meal... [omission] ...in the last watch of the night.”

The connection is with the word "should be reviewed. If one is unable to do so [daily], then according to the specific time intervals mentioned, it should be reviewed four times, three times, twice, or even once a day.
If dawn rises while he has not yet reviewed it, he stands in the position of one who has consumed what was borrowed; herein, "yesterday... [is used].
"If one does not reflect upon past usage—thinking, 'The robe I have used was only for warding off cold... [etc.
...for the purpose of covering the private parts,' and 'The almsfood I consumed yesterday was neither for sport...
and so forth—then it stands in the place of using something on credit," they say; this should be investigated. Regarding the use of a dwelling as well:
"Consumption" means at every single instance of entering [the mouth]. However, for one who is unable to do so, this should be reflected upon before the meal and so forth.
Since that can be understood through the method already explained below, it is not stated separately here.

"The state of mindfulness being a condition" (satipaccayatā) means the status of mindfulness as a condition; it is appropriate that the act of receiving and the act of consuming have the mindfulness of reflection as their condition.
The meaning is that it should be accepted and consumed only after having reflected. For this very reason, he said, "having established mindfulness," and so forth. "Even though this is so" means:
even though reflection is appropriate in both instances, even so [he says this]. Others, however, say:
"Satipaccayatā" means "the state of being a condition for the use of the medicine of mindfulness"; thus, "even though this is so" [is used].

The claim that "mindfulness [is required] regarding requisites" is merely their own opinion; for it is through reflection that virtue dependent on requisites is purified, not by the mere presence of the requisites.
And does this not mean that the Pātimokkha-restraint virtue was stated by the words, "there is no offense for one who uses them"? Therefore...
What is the distinction between virtue dependent on requisites and the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha? It is said:
first, the distinction among the former three requisites is indeed evident.

Regarding the requisite of medicine, however, just as when a fence is built and the root of a tree is protected, its fruits are likewise protected; even so, through reflection, the virtue dependent on requisites [is protected].
When [the requisites] are protected, the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha, which is bound up with them, is also said to be accomplished.
For one who consumes the requisite for the sick without reflecting, the virtue that is being broken is specifically the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha;
however, the virtue dependent on the requisites [is broken] for one who does not reflect even until the rising of the dawn during the periods after the meal and before the first watch, and so forth.
It is broken. For there is no offense for one who consumes the requisite of medicine even without having reflected upon it before the meal;
this is the distinction between these two.
Having thus shown the purification of virtue dependent on requisites, by that same connection, all purifications—
To demonstrate this, he said, "For purification is fourfold," and so forth. In this context, "purification" (*suddhi*) means that by means of it one is purified;

thus, the teaching according to the Dhamma is itself purification, which is "purification of teaching" (*desanāsuddhi*). Here, the act of emerging from an offense should also be understood as being included within the teaching itself.

Furthermore, for those whose offenses have been severed at the root, the very admission of non-recurrence constitutes the teaching. Restraint distinguished by resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is likewise [a form of purification].
Purity through restraint is purity by way of self-restraint. Seeking the requisites in accordance with the Dhamma and with justice is itself purity;

thus, it is purity of seeking. Reviewing the four requisites according to the method prescribed is itself purity; thus, it is purity of reviewing. This, then, is the brief method regarding the types of purity.
Regarding the precepts possessed of purity: that which has "teaching" as its purity is "purity of teaching. The same applies to the remaining [types of purity].
The same method applies here. In the phrase "I shall not do so again," the word "so" refers to the breach of restraint.

"Having abandoned" means having avoided; the sense is "having not done. It is a "heritage" (dāya) in the sense of being something to be given; they "take up" that heritage, thus they are "heirs" (dāyādā).
This is because monks have no use whatsoever for things not permitted, whereas they have full use of those things that are permitted.
The requisites for use belong to the Blessed One. Here, the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta* (The Discourse on the Heirs of the Dhamma) is the supporting proof:
“Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things. I have compassion for you, thinking: ‘How may my disciples be heirs of the Dhamma, not heirs of material things?
Thus, the *Dhammadāyāda Sutta*, which has proceeded in this manner, is the supporting proof here for this meaning.
For those who have not yet abandoned lust, there is no state of mastery over the enjoyment of requisites because they are subject to the power of craving;
whereas for those who have abandoned lust, there is mastery therein because they enjoy them according to their own preference.

For it is thus that they enjoy requisites: even what is repulsive they enjoy in an aspect of non-repulsiveness, what is non-repulsive they enjoy in an aspect of repulsiveness, and having avoided both, they enjoy them in an aspect of equanimity.
And they fulfill the aspirations of the donors. Therefore it was said: "For, having transcended the state of servitude to craving, they enjoy [the requisites] as masters.
Furthermore, this enjoyment by one who is virtuous, being a reflection upon the requisites, is called "enjoyment free from debt" because it is the opposite of enjoying them as a debtor.
For just as a debtor cannot go to whatever place he desires of his own accord...
Just as one who is bound by debt does not obtain freedom to go, so too one who is engaged in the enjoyment of debt does not obtain escape from the world.
Because it is the opposite of that, the enjoyment of one who possesses virtue, being an enjoyment after due reflection, is called "debt-free enjoyment.

Therefore, this should be understood as a distinct kind of enjoyment, separate from the four [other] kinds of enjoyment; it is not mentioned here separately, but is included within "inherited enjoyment" itself.
Or it is included [in this category]. For even one who possesses virtue is called a "learner" (sekha) precisely because he is endowed with this training.
"Of all" refers to both noble ones (ariya) and worldlings (puthujjana).
How do these enjoyments come to exist for worldlings? By way of figurative usage (upacāra). For even in the case of a worldling...
For one established in the practice of self-effacement (*sallekha*), consumption with a mind unattached—having abandoned craving for requisites—is like the consumption of a master.

For a virtuous person, however, consumption preceded by reflection is like the consumption of an inheritance, because it does not frustrate the wishes of the givers. Therefore it is said: "It is indeed the consumption of an inheritance..."

"Or it falls under the category of the Saṅgha. There is no need to state that a virtuous worldling (kalyāṇaputhujjana) partakes [of the requisites], because he is included among those in training (sekkha).
Indeed, the *Sekkhāsutta* establishes this point.
"Partaking together with one who has a sense of shame" means taking what belongs to one who has a sense of shame and partaking of it. "Together with one who lacks a sense of shame" means...

The same principle applies here as well. By stating that "from the very beginning there is no such thing as one who is shameless," it is shown that one should not entertain suspicion regarding those whom one has already seen [to be shameless].
"One's own burden" refers to the students (*saddhivihārika*) and others.

"He too should be restrained" means that whoever sees [the offense] must restrain him. Since what is called "use by the shameless" is said to belong to the conscientious (*lajjī*), therefore it is an offense.

There is no [such] name for both [types of food], because they are both characterized by shamelessness; what is meant is that the mere name “enjoyment of what is consumed by the shameless” cannot even be applied.
“But there is indeed an offense,” so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.

“Non-dhammic” means obtained through improper search (*an-esanā*) and so forth; “dhammic” means obtained through the practice of alms-round (*bhikkhācariyā*) and so forth. [This applies] only to the Saṅgha.

"He gives" means that he gives only the voting ticket (salāka) he himself has received, without taking the meal. But if one who is conscientious (lajjī) encourages one who is unconscientious (alajjī)...

[etc. ... "He causes it to disappear": here it should be understood that while it is not permissible to do so merely out of a desire to encourage [the other], it is permissible for the purpose of favoring the Dhamma, the Teaching, and those who hear it. According to the previous method, "he [is guilty] of an offense..."

Because it was stated, "he should be made to undergo [the penalty]," they say that this is indeed an offense. The enjoyment of the Dhamma through the recitation and so forth of the teachings is called "enjoyment of the Dhamma.

Although there is no offense for one who accepts [the teaching] out of support for the Dhamma, the Elder spoke the words beginning with "He is surely an evil man" with reference specifically to his shamelessness. "In his presence" means in the presence of the Elder Mahārakkhita.
586. Regarding the passage beginning with “the king’s harem, etc.,” it is stated because the mere volition, “I shall take this,” arises [in such cases].
As for the phrase “given through forgetfulness,” here “given through forgetfulness” means that [the object] has not been relinquished;
therefore, if a kahāpaṇa coin tied to the hem of one’s garment is given through forgetfulness and accepted by a bhikkhu with the perception that it is a cloth, then no money (rūpiya) has been given.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "nor has it been accepted," there is no requirement to confess an offense here;

rather, that [item] must be returned to the donors themselves. If those donors, having purchased ghee and other such items with that unallowable object, give them to the Saṅgha and to that bhikkhu, it is allowable for all, because the property belongs to the donors alone. However, in the Commentary...

This statement—“One who desires merit... [etc. ...is to be understood as one who accepts money while perceiving it as non-money”—refers specifically to that which has been relinquished and given by those desiring merit.
Therefore, even if one accepts what has been relinquished and given with the perception that it is a cloth, it is indeed an offense of expiation (nissaggiya).
Consequently, if those donors do not come and take it themselves, one may [use it] after asking the donors for permission.
If it was relinquished for the sake [of the Saṅgha], one must hand it over to the Saṅgha and confess the offense.

By saying, "Look at your rag," he demonstrates that it is not permissible for a monk to arrange even something belonging to a householder by means of unallowable speech such as, "Take this," and so forth.
"Of a single delimitation" means they are of a single delimitation because of their status as both action and non-action. The nature of gold and silver—
The state of being for one's own benefit, and the state of being any one of the items such as kahāpaṇas—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning money is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Bartering with Money.

587. In the training rule concerning the bartering of silver (*rūpiya-saṃvohāra*), all four types of objects subject to relinquishment—including gold and so forth—are included here by the very term "silver.
Therefore, it says: "the exchange of gold and silver. Regarding "exchange of what has been accepted":

this refers either to the exchange of silver that has been formally consented to, or to the exchange of silver accepted through the acquisition of an allowable object (*kappiya*) without having given formal consent.
589. Having changed the letter *ga* to the letter *ka*, it is written as “*sīsūpakan*” (a head-piece).
In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), “*ghanakatan*” means made into a solid mass. In passages such as “the color of a coin (*satthuvaṇṇo*) and a kahāpaṇa... [and so on]...
and those which enter into commerce,” a conjunction (*samuccaya*) is to be understood in all instances. “Perceiving silver in what is silver” refers to that which belongs to oneself. Silver...

“Exchanges” means he speaks regarding something belonging to another. Why was it said: “The same method applies even when one exchanges an article subject to forfeiture for an article that is merely an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) or for a permissible article”?

For it is not stated in the text of the first triad as: “If, perceiving money as money, one exchanges non-money, there is an offense entailing forfeiture and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya),” and so forth. To this he says: “Because it is in conformity with that,” and so on. This refers to its being in accordance with that [rule].
The intended meaning here is as follows: "Trade in money" does not refer solely to the exchange of money for money;
rather, because it is stated that "one who perceives what is not money as money causes money to be procured," even the procurement of money by means of what is not money is called trade in money.
Thus, according to this view, whenever there is money involved, it is indeed trade in money.
This meaning is understood even though it has not been explicitly stated. "Non-monetary" refers to articles that are either unallowable or allowable.
"Entirely on the side of the monetary" means that it falls on one side of the monetary category; this is how the sense should be grasped.
Alternatively, the reading should be understood as "on one side of the monetary. They also read "in the same monetary category," and there too it means "on one side of the monetary."
This is precisely the meaning that should be understood.
Even in the case of buying and selling allowable goods (kappiya-vatthu) with allowable goods, there is an offense of relinquishment (nissaggiya);
why then would there not be one in the case of buying and selling faulty goods (dukkaṭa-vatthu) with faulty goods? Such is the intention of the Andhaka-ṭīkā. This training rule... [etc.]
The connection is that it was stated with reference to using non-monetary goods to procure monetary goods.
"Here" means in this training rule concerning the bartering of money. "There" means in the training rule concerning buying and selling.
It is called "the great unallowable" because it is impossible to bring it back to a state of allowability again; for it cannot be made allowable by anyone.
They say: "The statement 'it may be made allowable by means of a stratagem' refers specifically to the exchange among the five who share the same Dhamma;
however, that which is received from householders, taken as one's own property, and then given back, is allowable for everyone.
But by the very statement, "It is not possible to make it allowable by any stratagem," [it is shown that] the gold and silver already accepted cannot be made allowable without first relinquishing it.
It is thus established that even allowable goods (kappiyabhaṇḍa) procured by him, if they have been forfeited by the Saṅgha,
are not permitted to be used. As for those who say, "It is permissible to use allowable goods exchanged with money received [by a monk],
even if that money has not been relinquished," for them it is impossible by any means to [make it] allowable...
The statement "to make [it] allowable" is not appropriate here. However, they say this:

"Because one has performed various other acts one after another without having forfeited the article that ought to be forfeited, it is said here—without mentioning the forfeiture—that 'it cannot be made allowable by any means whatsoever' due to the absence of a limit.
Precisely because of the absence of a limit, [the rule states]: 'In the case of the root, it belongs to the original owners...'"
And it is not stated that "once the bowl has been given to the owners of the bowl, it becomes allowable.

If it is permissible for the Saṅgha to use even an allowable article that was purchased with money received [in exchange] without that money having been relinquished, then why—this being the case—is it not also permissible here to take an item from the final source and use it after it has been relinquished to the Saṅgha? "Whoever..."

Furthermore, by the statement, “But having acquired silver... [etc. ...and having given the bowl to its owners, it becomes allowable,” it is established that even an allowable article purchased with silver that was received but not relinquished is not permitted for the Saṅgha to use after it has been relinquished.
If using that which has been relinquished were permissible, then [the rule would have stated]: “The root [money] belongs to the owners of the root.”
One should not say, "Once the bowl has been given to its owners, it becomes allowable. However, others here say:

"If it has been relinquished to the Saṅgha, it is not permissible for the receiver of money; therefore, in order to show how it does become permissible even for him, the words 'to the original owners of the capital' and so forth were spoken."
"Similar to the second bowl" means that by this phrase he shows that it is not allowable for even the five co-religionists. Regarding this, he states the reason:
"Because the root [transaction] was accepted. Now, one might think: "Since the root was accepted, let it be unallowable for the receiver of money for a start;
but why is it not allowable for the others? Thinking thus, he asks: "Why for the others..."

"It is not allowable," he said. He gave the reason: "because the root has not been relinquished. Even though the bowl itself is allowable, because the root accepted by him—which ought to have been relinquished—has not been relinquished, the bowl taken by him is not allowable for the others either.

For if the root accepted by him had been relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha through that formal act of what is allowable (*kappiya-kamma*), then [the bowl] could be provided by the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and so forth.
Having accepted the bowl that was given, it is permissible for the others, with the exception of the one who received the money.
However, others say: "Even if the bowl was accepted after the price was received, if it has been relinquished to the Saṅgha, it is allowable for the others.
This being the case, one should not say, "Because the price was not relinquished," but rather simply, "Because it was not relinquished to the Saṅgha."
By the phrase "because of having been dealt with," it is shown that he has engaged in transactions involving money. However, as for the statement "it is permissible for others":

since he has merely engaged in transactions involving money and has not accepted the principal [value], it is therefore permissible for others from the time the item is relinquished to the Saṅgha by means of a formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma). And this is the authoritative source for this very meaning.
He said, "It is said that [the Buddha] showed [this] to the Elder Mahāsumana," and so forth. Others, however, say:

"By the phrase 'because of misconduct' (dubbicāritattā), only the mere state of misconduct while remaining as the property of a householder is expressed, not the actual engaging in transactions with money (rūpiya-saṃvohāra).
Therefore, because there was no transaction with money, that bowl could not be relinquished; thus it was not allowable for him, even though it had not been relinquished."

It is allowable for others. Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that it remains allowable for others even when not formally relinquished, the cases beginning with "it is said that the Elder Mahāsumma" have been cited.

As for the phrase "he relinquished it to the Saṅgha," this was stated solely with reference to the fact that it was dedicated to the Saṅgha because it is allowable for others, and not to the fact that it was relinquished to the Saṅgha by means of a formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma).
And they say that for this purpose, the statement "having filled it with ghee" is the supporting proof.
591. Regarding the acceptance of money and the bartering of money: by whichever of these two was performed alone, one must relinquish it in the manner prescribed for each respective case.
However, by whomsoever bartering was performed using the very money that had been accepted—by him...
How should it be relinquished? This is not difficult: one should relinquish it simply by saying, "Venerable sir, I have engaged in various kinds of transactions involving money.

Even in this training rule, because non-offense is stated in the final phrase of the threefold formula—namely, "If there is no money, but one perceives it as money, there is an offense of wrong-doing"—it refers only to the case of allowable objects (*kappiya-vatthu*).
"This triplet has been stated" is what is recorded in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. However, some say:

"By the inclusion of the term 'formless' (*arūpiya*), both allowable objects (*kappiya-vatthu*) and faulty objects (*dukkaṭa-vatthu*) are subsumed; thus, the first two phrases are stated by way of allowable and faulty objects, while the final phrase alone is stated by way of allowable objects.
This is not tenable, because the final triplet concerns cases mixed with non-offenses (*anāpatti*).
This is because, setting aside the diversity of perception, there is no diversity of the object [of the offense].
Furthermore, the statement that "exchanging one object of a *dukkaṭa* offense for another object of a *dukkaṭa* offense is neither mentioned here nor in the Pāḷi" serves as proof for this point.
In this case, there are two factors: the fact that the object being exchanged with one's own wealth has the nature of money (*rūpiya*), and the act of exchange itself.
The commentary on the training rule concerning bartering with silver is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Buying and Selling (Kayavikkaya-sikkhāpada) 593.

Regarding the phrase “you should know” (*jānāhi*) in the Pāḷi of the training rule on buying and selling, the meaning here is “you should examine. The intention is: “Having examined it thoroughly, take it; you will not be able to give it back again, saying, ‘This is not pleasing to me.’”
594–595. *Kaya* means the taking of another’s goods; *vikaya* means the giving of one’s own goods. Therefore he said, “‘With this, give me that,’ and so forth.

Since what is called “bought” (*kayita*) is said to be that which has been taken from the hand of another, and what is “sold” (*vikkīta*) is that which has been given into the hand of another, therefore [it is said]:
“And it becomes ‘bought’ by one who makes another’s goods come into his own hand.”
And it is said: "by one who makes his own merchandise go into the hand of another after having sold it.

If this is so, why does the text later state, "it is both bought and sold," and then say, "one's own merchandise has gone into the hand of another, and another's merchandise has come into one's own hand"?
To this he replies: "But because it conforms to the expression 'this for that,' and so forth," and so on.
For by this [phrase], that which belongs to oneself is stated. Accordingly, in the Canon, one's own property is shown first, not in accordance with the sequence of the terms for buying and selling;
for that [latter] stands preceded by the taking of another's property in a perverted manner.
Granted that there is no formal request (*viññatti*) when saying "give this" even to other relatives, yet there is also [the offense of] misappropriating what has been given in faith (*saddhādeyya*).
However, wishing to show the absence [of such a case], he said, "But [if one says] 'to mother or father.
The statement "there is no intimation" (viññatti) is said with reference to a separate act of making known.

He said, "When one speaks thus without saying anything else, one intimates a stranger," meaning that for one who says to a stranger, "Give this," there is intimation. Without saying anything else, "this..."
"Take it"—when given in this way, it is said that "it has been given to one who is not a relative. Regarding the phrase "the squandering of what is given in faith":
there are three offenses, namely, the offenses consisting of requesting from one who is not a relative, the squandering of what is given in faith, and buying and selling.
When he says, "Do this," [the response] "It is permissible" implies: "You have already eaten; why do you not do it now?"—this refers even to the material object (*vatthu*).
It is permissible. Regarding the phrase "an offense entailing relinquishment and confession" (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*):

although it is stated that there is a *pācittiya* offense only when the object to be relinquished exists, the words beginning with "although" (*kiñcāpi*) are used to show that one must accept—on the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary)—that there is a *pācittiya* even when that object does not exist.
The term "consumed" (*paribhutte*) is said with reference to ghee and so forth. That which [is given] by means of one's own wealth...

The three factors here are: the exchange itself, the fact that both the object by which one exchanges and the object for which one exchanges are allowable things (*kappiyavatthu*), and the fact that this is contrary to the Dhamma (*asahadhammatā*) resulting in the commission of buying and selling.
The commentary on the training rule concerning buying and selling is finished.
The second chapter on the Kosiya [cloth] is finished.
3. The Chapter on Alms Bowls (Patta-vagga). 1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Alms Bowl (Patta-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā).

598–602. In the first section of the *Patta-vagga*, "quarrel" refers to merchandise that ought to be sold. This is because the word *vaṇṇa* is seen to be used in the senses of shape, genus, the sense-sphere of form, cause, measure, quality, praise, and so forth.
For instance, in such passages as “having manifested the form of a great king of serpents,” it denotes shape (*saṇṭhāna*).

In such passages as “The brahmin caste alone is the best caste; other castes are inferior,” it denotes genus (*jāti*). In such passages as “endowed with the highest beauty of complexion,” it denotes the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
In such passages as, “I do not take, I do not break, I merely smell the water-born flower from afar;
now by what quality is one called a ‘thief of fragrance’?”—it is the cause (*kāraṇa*).
In such passages as, “Three qualities of a bowl,” it is the measure (*pamāṇa*). [And] in, “But when were they raised up, householder?”...

In such passages as "These are the praises of the ascetic Gotama," *vaṇṇa* means quality (*guṇa*). In such passages as "He speaks praise for one who deserves praise," it means commendation (*pasaṃsā*).
Therefore, it was said: "Three praises of the bowl" means three measurements of the bowl.
Regarding the phrase "it weighs twelve and a half *palas*," they say here: "One takes twelve and a half *palas* of *māsa*-beans. [It is] a Magadhan *nāḷi*.
Some say, "It is called a *nāḷī* of four *paṣa*. Others say, "It is eight *paṣa*.

In that regard, according to the opinion of the former, two *nāḷīs* of three *paṣas* each constitute one Magadha *nāḷī*; according to the latter, two *nāḷīs* of four *paṣas* each constitute one Magadha *nāḷī*.
Furthermore, by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, it is stated: "By nature, four handfuls make a *kuḍuva*..."
It is said: "Four *kuḍuva*s make one *nāḷika*; sixteen *nāḷika*s of that measure make one *doṇa*, and that [Magadhan *doṇa*] is equal to twelve *nāḷika*s of the Magadhan measure.
Therefore, according to that method, it should be understood that what is called a "Magadhan *nāḷika*" consists of five *kuḍuva*s, one fistful (*muṭṭhi*), and a third part of a fistful.
“Prepared from all ingredients” means prepared from all the ingredients such as cumin and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “in proportion to each mouthful of rice,” since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Brahmāyu Sutta* that “the measure of a condiment is one-fourth part of the rice,” it should be understood that a condiment measuring one-fourth the size of a mouthful of rice is what is meant by “in proportion to the mouthful of rice.”

However, here, after showing that the measure of the soup alone is one-fourth of the measure of the rice, and once the characteristic of this has been shown, the characteristic of the other is already shown as well;
therefore, the measure of the curry was not specified in that same way.
He said, "A *pattha* of rice," meaning "half a *nāḷika* of rice by the Magadhan *nāḷi* measure. Thus he spoke.
By this, it is shown that "two *pattha*s make a Magadhan *nāḷī*. And a *pattha* is to be understood according to worldly usage as:
"four *kuḍuva*s make a *kuḍuva*, and four *kuḍuva*s make a *pattha*. "By the use of a vessel" means by the use of a vessel for purposes such as fetching water and so forth.

(607) "Washed" is stated for the purpose of showing the conclusion of the use; however, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is not incurred only when it has been washed, because the offense is incurred at the very time of use prior to that.
608. The phrase "by five or two" is stated for the purpose of showing that "to this extent blackness is accomplished.
However, they say: "If, even by a single cooking, it becomes black in color, it is indeed subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

The words beginning with "if" are stated for the purpose of showing that it may be formally determined even when [the food] has not yet reached the hands. And by this, one may determine it even if it is situated at a distance.
It should be understood that he is permitted to reassign it, and the observation of the place where it was set down is not a sufficient criterion. "Or having heard" means:
having merely heard the words of that person speaking, without being instructed by the messenger sent by the bowl-maker.
It is "not a sufficient criterion" because he was not sent by him. "In a neighboring monastery" (sāmantavihāre) is a mere conventional term; beyond that distance, [it is not so].

It is indeed permissible to resolve [on its status] even while it remains [in that condition]. Regarding the phrase "having observed the place where it was placed," this too is merely a formal convention;

in this case, the actual observation of the bowl itself is the criterion. "Or there is a hole in the bowl" means that there is a hole anywhere from a space of about two finger-breadths down from the rim of the mouth.
The rest here follows the same method as stated for the first *kathina* (robe-making ceremony).
The commentary on the training rule concerning cloths is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning less than five joins. 610.
Regarding the phrase "he wanders for alms with his hands" in the second training rule, the meaning should be understood as: "he wanders for the sake of obtaining alms [to be placed] in his hands."
612–613. “Because of the statement ‘that [bowl] is not a bowl,’ that bowl loses its determined status (*adhiṭṭhāna*) due to being a non-bowl.
Indeed, it is precisely because of its state as a non-bowl that it is not mentioned in the Canon [in the rule]:

‘One may have another bowl made with five bands. Thus it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries. However, some say: ‘The term “not a bowl” is stated for the purpose of showing that it is permissible to ask for another bowl.’”
However, they say that "the bowl does not lose its determined status (adhiṭṭhāna)," which appears reasonable because it will be stated later:
"One whose [bowl] has five, or even one, or ten finger-widths [of cracks], whether bound or unbound, is indeed not a bowl.
For it is not possible to say that the determined status is not lost when there are merely two-finger-width lines at the five places on the rim of the mouth.

However, it is reasonable to say that if a hole of the aforementioned measurement is found in a bowl with a single rim ten finger-breadths wide, the loss of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) would occur precisely through that hole.
Whether or not there is a place for fastening, a bowl devoid of fastening is called "unfastened" (*abandhana*);
yet, it is specifically when the place for fastening is absent that it is called "without a place for fastening" (*abandhanokāsa*).
Regarding the phrase "or having bound it with a cord," here the reading should be taken as "it is to be bound.

For this very reading is seen even in the ancient manuscripts. As for the statement "it is not permitted for pure [substances]...," this was said because [the substance] would melt when placed in a hot meal.
It is permitted to bind molasses after it has been dried with stone powder; thus, together with stone powder—
Having boiled molasses, it is permissible to bind it with stone powder while still uncooked.

Since it is stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who does not accept [the bowl] out of compassion, there is no offense for one to whom that bowl is not pleasing, even if they do not accept it.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "If the elder’s bowl is not pleasing..."
"Or, because of fewness of wishes, he does not take it; that is permissible. "The edge of the bowl" (*pattapariyanto*) means a bowl with an edge;
the meaning is a bowl with a rim. They say: "When having someone take a bowl in the midst of the Saṅgha, it is permissible not to have one who is shameless take it.
Because it was said, "I allow you, monks, a stand (*ādhāraka*)," one may place a stand on any surface such as a bench and [place the bowl] there.
They say, "It is permissible to place [the bowl] because the location for placing the support is not fixed. Regarding "by improper use": by an inappropriate use. In the text:
"With a bowl that has no fastening, one [receives] a bowl with no fastening; a bowl with one fastening... a bowl with two fastenings...
three fastenings... four fastenings... a place for no fastening... one... two... three... four places for fastenings."
"Exchanges it for a bowl"—thus, by means of each individual bowl, ten types of bowls are exchanged in ten ways;

this constitutes one hundred rules of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*). In this training rule, it should be understood that even if the bowl is not yet blackened and is of the proper measure, there is still an offense for one who requests it.
Regarding a bowl that has reached the stage of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*), it must have less than five mends.
The four factors here are: being for one’s own sake, not having made a formal request, and the acquisition [of the medicine] by means of that.
The commentary on the training rule concerning less than five bandages is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Medicines.
622. In the third training rule, the phrase "for whom meat is allowable" is stated for the purpose of showing the objects [of the offense] that entail relinquishment (*nissaggiya-vatthu*);
it is not, however, intended to show that for those for whom meat is not allowable, ghee and other such products are also not allowable.
For even human milk and the like are not allowable; how much less so the ghee of a hare? Thus he said: "For those who have milk, they also have ghee."

"It certainly exists," [he replied]. "And this is said for the most part," they say. "Placed down after being taken up" means placed down by oneself after having taken it up without it being formally offered.
"What is made by oneself must be purely non-material (nirāmisa)" is said with reference specifically to that which is done on the same day before the meal.
Now, why is it that for one who eats what is made by oneself and is non-material, it does not constitute "cooking by oneself" (sāmaṃpāka)?
He said: "For one who heats fresh butter, there is no 'cooking by oneself' (sāmaṃpāka). Because that which is accepted with its base (vatthu) follows the nature of that base, he said:
"Because it was accepted together with its base. "By those accepted after the meal" means by milk and curd accepted after the meal.
And what was prepared even before the meal from items already received should be applied to ointments and the like.
"Connection": "Of both as well" means [the connection] between what was received after the meal—namely, milk and curd—and what was taken before the meal.

"In the same manner" means that it becomes an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*). "In the case of clarified butter from animals whose meat is not allowable" means in the case of the clarified butter of beings whose flesh is forbidden.
"Having stated a semblance of a reason" means having stated a semblance of a reason, namely, that it possesses the quality of being clarified butter due to its belonging to the same genus.
“It should be understood by way of the example of ghee” means that for seven days, only that which is free from meat is permitted. “In this case” refers to butter.
“It is permitted if washed” means that if it is unwashed, it is considered accepted along with its base;
therefore, the intention of the Elders is that once it has been washed and accepted, it is permitted to store it for seven days. “They ate it as soon as it was extracted from the buttermilk.”

In this context, the meaning should be understood as follows: even if they receive and consume what has been extracted from buttermilk while it is still undiluted, they may do so after washing or cooking it.

For the intention is that there is no fault in receiving curd-balls and such items along with their base (the buttermilk), provided one later washes and cooks them before consuming them. This applies to one who receives [the food] together with its base.
Thus, by demonstrating the Elder’s intention, it was said: "Therefore, for one consuming fresh butter...

[etc.]... this is the intention here. However, some, not understanding the intention of the statement, "They ate only what had just been removed from the curd," [claim that] one may consume even at an improper time what has merely been removed from the curd, even if it is unwashed and accompanied by curd-balls and the like.

As for those who say, "It is allowable," that should not be accepted. For it cannot be said that it is allowable to consume butter whose flavor has become mixed with impure food such as curd-balls and the like.
"By one consuming butter" means by one consuming butter that was received [in the bowl] without having washed it.
"Curd itself" is *dadhigata*, just as in the expressions "feces-soiled" (*gūthagata*) or "urine-soiled" (*muttagata*).
From the statement "it will go to destruction," it should be understood that even ghee prepared by adding milk and so forth is permissible at an improper time.
By the phrase "they are scrupulous" (*kukkuccāyantīti kukkuccakā*), he indicates his own state of scrupulousness regarding that matter.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "It is allowable to cook ghee or fresh butter that has already been processed. These...
"Having received" means having received that milk and curd.
"By means of medicines kept after being received" means by means of lifetime-medicines (*yāvajīvika-bhesajja*) kept after being received.

The mention of the modest novice (*lajjī-sāmaṇera*) is because he gives them only after ensuring, in the manner described, that the rice and other items do not cook [by himself], acting out of a sense of shame.
Furthermore, for one who is without shame, it is not permissible to have anything prepared that was intended for consumption; therefore he spoke thus.

"Oil received as sesame oil" refers to oil taken by oneself without having performed the roasting or other such processes. For this very reason, it is said: "Even that which contains meat is permissible.
"Because it has been extracted" means because it has been separated from the category of food to be consumed only during the day. "Both" refers to [the oil] by oneself...
"And by another. "It remains until sunrise": if oil prepared on the seventh day remains until sunrise, it is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya). 623. "Clear substances":
because fat is permitted as an object of an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), [this term refers to] only those similar objects that are likewise offenses of wrong-doing.
The fat of animals whose flesh is not allowable is permitted, but the fat of humans—who are grounds for a grave offense (thullaccaya)—is not; thus he said, "excepting human fat.

"Mixed" means strained. They say: "For one who consumes what was received at the proper time but cooked at an improper time by one who is not fully ordained, as well as what is mixed [with such], there are indeed two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Because...
They cook oil by adding milk, curd, and so forth; therefore, the dregs are not permitted, but the oil itself is permitted.

Thus it was said: "He is scrupulous as if regarding the dregs of cooked oil. When they asked, "Venerable sir, if [oil] is not permitted because it has been cooked together with fat, why is this [other case] permitted?
they spoke the words beginning with "Venerable sir. [The reply was: "This is permitted."
Is it not the case that the meaning is: "This butter cooked with curd-balls and so forth is permissible"?
Regarding the phrase "madhukarī means honey-bees," the *Tīsupi Gaṇṭhipadesu* states: "This is a general designation for both small flies and bumblebees.
However, some [commentators] say: "The males on the stalks are *madhukara*, and the females are *madhukarī*..."
Having said, "They are called flies," they explain: "Honey is that which is made by those three types of flies, beginning with the *madhukarī*.
"By bumblebee flies" means by large bumblebee flies. "Resembling gum" refers to what is described as thick and cooked. "The other" refers to thin honey.
"A layer of honey" (*madhupaṭala*) means a mere layer of honey devoid of honey-juice. "If it contains honey... [and so forth].

They say: "Having received the honeycomb, they set it aside; because the honeycomb serves as a container for the honey, there is an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the lapse of seven days with respect to the honey.
However, this does not accord with the statement: "But that which is smeared with honey is of the same category as honey itself.
Furthermore, since the text states without distinction that "molasses (*phāṇita*) is produced from sugarcane," and the Commentary [states] "the juice of sugarcane... [it follows accordingly].

Because of the statement, “… depending on [the sugar cane]… it should be understood that the product of sugar cane which is without substance is ‘molasses’ (phāṇita),” it should be understood that even pure sugarcane juice is seven-day medicine (sattāhakālika).
However, some have said, “In the case of honey, the four periods of time should be applied as appropriate, and so too in the case of sugar cane,” and then added:
“That which contains insects, grit, or husks is ‘for-as-long-as-the-day’ (yāvakālika); that which is free from husks and mixed with water [is seven-day medicine].”

Having stated: "That which is for a watch of the night (*yāmakālika*), that which is unmixed and for seven days (*sattāhakālika*), pure honey-ferment (*madhusittha*) which is for life-long use (*yāvajīvika*);

likewise, sugarcane or its juice with the pulp is for the time of the day (*yāvakālika*), juice without pulp mixed with water is for a watch of the night, unmixed [juice] is for seven days, and pure pulp is for life-long use," he further elaborated at great length.
In this regard, the statement, "Honey mixed with water, or sugarcane juice mixed with water,

is 'yāmakālika' (suitable for a watch of the night)," is seen neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Aṭṭhakathā. Water— which, while being "yāvakālika" (suitable for as long as the day lasts), brings about the status of "yāmakālika" for the lighter grape-juice it has mixed with,
even though that juice is heavier— and which is itself lighter and "sattāhakālika" (suitable for seven days)...
Regarding the statement, "One brings that which is mixed with oneself to a heavier state of being 'for the watch of the night' (yāmakālika)," the reason for this must be asked of that very source.
Throughout both the Canon (Pāḷi) and the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is shown everywhere that even by mixing with water, something heavy becomes light.
For in the Canon itself it says: "Monks, I allow sugar for the sick, and sugar-water for those who are not sick."
It was permitted that even if it is improper for one who is not ill to consume [raw] sugar while speaking, sugar mixed with water is allowable even for one who is not ill.
Furthermore, having shown the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) passage which states: "If it is sugarcane, it is *yāvakālika*; if it is sugarcane juice, it is *yāmakālika*;
if it is molasses, it is *sattāhakālika*; if it is the bark, it is *yāvajīvika*," [it is concluded that] "sugarcane juice mixed with water is *yāmakālika*."
Whatever has been stated by others should not be accepted as authoritative, because there is no such word from the *Aṭṭhakathā* in this *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
For that very reason, some teachers say in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*: "Even if sugarcane juice is mixed with water or not mixed, it remains valid for seven days only."
And regarding the statement, “Monks, I allow sugarcane juice,” it is stated without distinction in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries that “sugarcane juice is for seven days.
As for the rule that what is prepared by oneself must be entirely free from meat, here [it refers to] even that which was received while unstrained at the time of preparation.
Having strained it and removed the dregs, one should accept it as being made by oneself.
"Molasses from burnt sugarcane" means molasses made from sugarcane grown in a field burnt by fire.
"Molasses from crushed sugarcane" refers to molasses that is mostly with its dregs, having been cooked after the sugarcane has been cut into small pieces, crushed, and pressed. Of such [a kind]...
And because it is not subject to dispute as being "rough" (kasaṭa), it is said to be "proper.

"Made with cold water" means that after placing madhuka flowers in cold water and crushing them, once the flower-juice has entered the water, one takes that water, boils it, and makes it into phāṇita (molasses).
Regarding the statement "madhuka-phāṇita made by adding milk is *yāvakālika* (to be consumed within the same day)": here, the milk—
If it is asked why cooked oil is permitted at an improper time, the reason here is this:
milk that has been added to oil becomes simply oil, whereas milk prepared by adding other [ingredients] retains its nature as milk.
If that is so, why is it permissible to make candied sugar by adding milk? To this he says: "Candied sugar..."
"...and so forth. In this context, "milk-scum" (*khīrajallika*) means the froth of milk.

Regarding the "specified medicine" (*odissa*), when showing what is specified, [the text] says, "For there are seven kinds of 'specified' (*odissa*)," and so on; thus, the others are also mentioned by way of enumerating the categories.

"Vikaṭāni" means they are "vikaṭa" because they are not natural medicines; the meaning is that they are "deformed" (*virūpa*). This also applies to the bases for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭavatthu*).
Because the fat of unallowable meats is permitted, it is stated as "for the sake of fat.
Because ghee and other substances capable of sustaining even coarse food are permitted under the name of "medicine," it is stated as "for the sake of medicine.
Since it is stated that [these are allowed] "starting from after the meal when there is a requisite," the medicines received [are permitted] from the second day onward.

"From the time they are received until before the meal, they may be consumed if there is a requisite need; they are not for the purpose of food, because they were accepted for the purpose of medicine," so they say.
624. "In the door-panels and window-shutters" means on the panels and boards of the main door and the windows. "Placed in the casings."
They relinquish their own inherent nature; therefore it is said, "they must be smeared.

The meaning is that they must be smeared for the purpose of protecting against wood-boring insects and the like. "He resolves" means he arouses the thought: "Now this will no longer be for my internal consumption;
it shall go for external use. For this very reason it was said: "Ghee, oil, and fat upon the head..."
“Oil or an ointment,” and so forth. They say, “And thus the acceptance, having been determined, is relinquished. 625.
Regarding the statement, “If what belongs to two people has been accepted by one and not yet divided, it is not permissible to consume it”—here a portion of the text has been lost;
however, the reading here should be understood as follows: “If [what belongs to] two...”
"If an item belonging to one person has been accepted by another and remains undistributed, there is no offense for either of them after seven days have passed;
however, it is not permitted to consume it. Otherwise, even the application of the words would not be consistent.
This very reading is also shown in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. In that context, "there is no offense for either of them" means that just as an item belonging to another has been accepted by one person...

The intention is this: just as there is no forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) after seven days because it remains the property of another, so too, although this [robe] is common to both [the donor and the recipient], there is no forfeiture because it has not been formally assigned (*avibhatta*) and because its status is inseparable (*avinibbhoga*).
However, it is not permitted to use it; for since it was accepted by a monk, if seven days have elapsed, it may be given to any monk whatsoever.
It is not permissible to consume [these], because the consumption of ghee and so forth once accepted is limited to seven days.
For it is said: “Having accepted them, they may be consumed after storage for a maximum of seven days.
However, in the three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, failing to notice that the text here has been omitted, they state: “To consume...”

However, as for the statement "it is not permissible," this was said with reference to consumption within the seven-day period; because there is no perception that it is "taken in trust," it is not permissible to consume it [after that time].
This is the meaning stated, but it should not be accepted [as a general rule].
For by the words, "Friend, consume this oil for only seven days," it is meant that by the one who received it, [it must be used] within those very seven days.
It shows the state of having been relinquished to another. Regarding the question "Whose offense is it?", first, because it is common to both, it was stated that there is no offense.
Now, however, since one has relinquished it to the other, the state of being common to both no longer exists;
thus, it stands as if divided. Therefore, in this case, when seven days have passed for that which has been received, there is an offense for one.
Thinking, "It must be so," he asks: "Is there an offense for the recipient on account of the acceptance, or rather for the one whose property it has become?

And because it has been relinquished, the reason is stated here not as "because it has not been divided," but as "because it was given away by the one who accepted it. This is also due to its having been relinquished.
Having abandoned the state of being common to both, even though it was the property of one person, it has become the property of another from whom it was received;
therefore, this is stated for the purpose of showing that, as in the case of receiving what belongs to another,
there is no offense for the receiver by reason of his reception, and not because "it was relinquished by the one who received it."
This is for the purpose of showing that when [the robe] has not been relinquished by word, there is an offense even if it has not been distributed after seven days have passed;
for since non-offense is established simply by the fact that it has not been relinquished and not distributed,
if the other person who received it also relinquishes their own share within the seven days, there would be no offense for the one who received it upon the passing of the seven days.
Because it has come under his own possession and because the other has not accepted it.

By this, he demonstrates that even though it is in his possession, there is no offense because it has not been accepted by him, just as in the case of one's own property that has been accepted by another.

However, those who have elaborated on this differently from the above—such as the authors of the *Gaṇṭhipada* and others—have done so without understanding this underlying intention; that should not be accepted as the essential truth.
"It becomes unfit for use" means that because something unpleasant has fallen upon it, it is no longer fit for use. "With whatever mind" refers to the mind desiring to relinquish [the object].
