Because the context concerns "within seven days," the Elder Mahāsumma, referring to the connection in the phrase "having given away without regard within seven days, and having received it back, he uses it," said: "Thus..."
“Having given it within seven days,” and so forth, was said. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma stated:

“If this is so, then since that is already established by the word ‘gives away’ (*vissajjeti*), what is meant here is merely to show the manner of its use—that once the seven days have passed, it is not permitted to use it after having received it back as a relinquished item.
Therefore he said: ‘This should not be asked for,’ and so forth. By another...
Regarding the term "a bhikkhunī": because it was given with a pure mind, it is indeed permissible for her to eat it herself even after having it brought [to her].
In this case, there are three factors: the fact that ghee and so forth have been received, the fact that it has become her own property, and the passing of seven days.
The commentary on the training rule concerning medicine is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule for the Rain-Season Robe (Vassikasāṭika-sikkhāpada) 627.

Regarding the phrase "having finished it by the end of the sewing and dyeing period": this means having finished it through the completion of the needlework, as well as by the mere change of color through dyeing and by the application of the *kappa*-mark (*kappabindu*). "At the proper time" (*samaye*) refers to the rainy season (*vassāna-samaye*).
628. "The period of distress" (*kucchi-samayo*) refers to the internal period. "This one-and-a-half-month period is both the field for seeking [the robe] and the field for making [it]."
In this interval, it is permissible to seek out a rain-cloak that has not yet been obtained, and once obtained, to have it made;

however, it is not permissible to wear it or to formally determine it as one’s own. Such is the reading seen in the manuscripts, but that is an incorrect reading. Rather, the reading here should be as follows:
"This first half-month is the period for seeking. For in this interval, [one may seek] a rain-cloak..."
"It is permissible to seek what has not been obtained; however, once it is obtained, it is not permissible to make it into a robe, wear it, or resolve upon it.
For the first half-month of the last month of summer is not a time for making robes.
However, because of the statement, "It should be worn, considering that 'half a month of summer remains,'" [it refers to] the latter part of the last month of summer.
A half-month constitutes both the period for seeking [robes] and the period for making and wearing them. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
"The last month of the summer is the period for seeking; the last half-month is the period for both making and wearing.
Therefore, one who desires consistency between the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* should adopt the reading according to the method already explained.
By saying, "There is no offense for one who, having made a request, brings it to completion,
under the training rule concerning requests from those not related," it is indicated that there is an offense under this training rule because of the nature of the subsequent period (*piṭṭhisamaya*).

For an offense that could arise merely by the occurrence of a thought during the subsequent period from a place where one has been invited by a relative would not be more serious than the offense arising from a request [made at that time].
It cannot be said that it does not exist. For this very reason, the venerable teacher Buddhadatta said:
"But for a bhikkhu who, having aroused mindfulness, is preparing a rain-cloak (vassikasāṭicīvara) at a time considered [by others] to be the wrong season..."
“There is an offense entailing relinquishment regarding relatives and non-relatives;
likewise, when one makes a request to those very persons and [the robe] is produced.
Regarding the question, “By what does he incur an offense?”—for him who requests a robe from his mother—by which training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is there an offense?
He asks: "Is there an offense for one who makes a request for what has been dedicated, under the training rule concerning dedication?
This shows the absence of a formal charge, as [the gift] was not dedicated to the Saṅgha.

If it is argued that this refers to the training rule concerning requesting from an unrelated person, he says, "And there is no offense when [it is requested] from a relative," because that too does not apply here. The phrase "for one requesting from a relative" is the remainder of the text. This is the meaning.

This refers both to the offense incurred by causing a thought to arise in a place where one has been invited by relatives for the sake of a rain-cloak during the latter part of the rainy season, and to the non-offense under the training rule regarding requesting from those who are not relatives.
The statement "from a place where one is not invited by those who are not relatives... [down to] an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" refers to a rain-cloak that has not been previously given.

It has been stated. For that very reason, a *dukkaṭa* offense is mentioned here in the case of breaking the rules of conduct (*vatta*), but there is no such offense when it concerns things previously given.
Therefore he said: “Those people who... [etc. ...there is no breaking of the rules of conduct. “This” refers to the aforementioned *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
“Having made a request and having brought it about” means: having made a request from a place where one is neither known nor invited, and then having brought it about.
"Those who naturally give rain-season robes" refers to those who, whether on behalf of the Saṅgha or as individuals, do not decline [the offer] and give rain-season robes every year.
Regarding the statement "there is no offense under the training rule concerning requests from strangers," it should be understood that there is likewise no offense under this training rule.
For at the time of pregnancy, one might say, "Give me a rain-season robe," and so forth, from a place where one has been invited by one's own relatives.
There is no offense even when making a request. For this very reason it was said:

“One should not say, ‘Give me this,’ for this was spoken with reference specifically to the time of seeking from those who are neither relatives nor invited. Indeed, it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
“However, from a place where one’s own relatives have invited one, one may seek [robes] even by means of a request such as, ‘Give me a rainy-season robe-cloth (*vassikasāṭikacīvara*).’”
629. "By the statement 'as if by water fallen from the sky,' it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada*s that there is no offense for one bathing with water fallen on the edge of a roof-covering. 630.
"He receives the six-month grace period": by this it is shown that even during the rainy season, he receives the grace period until the final day of the rains retreat.
For, when making a basic robe (*mūlacīvara*), [it must be made] on the very last *uposatha* day of the winter season.
It must be done; therefore, one receives a concession for twenty-nine days from the beginning of the summer heat (gimhāna).
Even so, because a slight deficiency or excess does not affect the calculation, it is stated: "Even beyond that... up to one month. By means of one day, two days, and so forth...
"both obtained and completed"—by this [it is meant] when the entry into the rains retreat (vassūpanāyikā) has arrived after one day.

The meaning shown here is as follows: it has been both obtained and finished; two days before the commencement of the rains retreat... ten days before the commencement of the rains retreat, it has been both obtained and finished; or within the rains retreat itself, it has been both obtained and finished.

In this context, if the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloth) has been both obtained and finished on the full moon of the bright fortnight of the month of Āsāḷha, [it is considered] "one day before" (*ekāhānāgatāya*).
It is said: "On the day of the commencement of the rains (vassūpanāyikā), it was both obtained and finished.
By this same method, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, it is said: "Ten days before the commencement of the rains, it was both obtained and finished.
Until the full moon of the first month of Kattika, it was both obtained and finished within that month.

And it is said: "Obtained and finished within the rains. For what is obtained and finished after the full moon of the first Kattika month may be kept without being formally determined (anadhiṭṭhahitvā) as long as the robe-season has not yet elapsed;
therefore, no such deliberation applies in that case.
Although it is stated without qualification that "it must be determined within that very ten-day period," even when the *vassūpanāyikā* (the day of entering the rains retreat) has not yet arrived—

having been postponed by one or two days prior to the start of the rains— one must determine the boundary for the robe only after reaching the designated area from the day of the *vassūpanāyikā* itself, without exceeding the ten-day limit including those postponed days; there is no determining of the boundary prior to that.

Because it is not a [proper] field. However, having obtained it during the rainy season, it must be determined within that same rainy season, starting from the day it was obtained, without letting the ten-day period expire.
But surely, before the commencement of the rains, it is permissible to let the ten days expire without having determined it; therefore, regarding the determination...

Why is it stated, "Having received [the robe] even on a day that is not a field for determination, it must be determined within ten days"? It is because, just as "even if obtained during the rains-retreat,
it is permissible to let ten days pass without determining it until the work is finished," so too, the days already elapsed—
even though they resemble a non-field for determination because the determination was not made— are counted once the robe is finished after letting ten days pass.

The phrase "they exist" must be determined on the very day it is completed; likewise, here too, it is stated for the purpose of showing that even those days prior to the commencement of the rains—which were not originally fields for determination—become included in the count starting from the day they are obtained.
If this is so, since it is stated without qualification as "within that same ten-day period," then on the sixth day of the rains-retreat when the ten days have not yet elapsed...
Does one incur an offense by resolving on this full moon after having obtained it?
No, one does not, because it has already been prohibited by the very statement, "One may resolve for four months.

If that is so, what is the purpose of the phrase "when ten days have not yet elapsed"? It is so that, even if ten days have passed prior to the beginning of the rains, the robe must be resolved upon on the very day of the *vassūpanāyika* ceremony.
"It is stated for the purpose of seeing" is the reason here. Therefore he said: "When ten days have passed, it being finished, it must be determined on that very day.

Regarding "the robe season must not be exceeded when ten days are not yet complete": the meaning is that within the three-month period, when ten days [of the robe season] are not yet complete, one must not exceed the robe season regarding robes that have been obtained and finished. This is what is meant: "From the full moon of the first Kattika month..."

"Since the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) was obtained and finished before the seventh day, and because the robe-season had already begun less than ten days prior, it is permissible to set it aside there even without formally designating it. By this, he illustrates the following:
if the rainy-season robe has not been made, one receives the exemption precisely because it has not been made during the four months of the rains.
However, once it has been made, the allowance [for use] should be stated as not violating the training rule of "at most ten days.
The intention is that whether now or later, it is permissible to resolve [the robe]; thus, even if ten days have passed within the four-month period, there is no fault.
"When should it be resolved? ... If it is not possible, the allowance lasts until the full moon of Kattika."

By this statement from the *Kurundi* commentary as well—"he obtains"—the meaning is clearly shown that for one who has not made a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*), there is a privilege for four months, whereas for one who has made it, there is a privilege for only ten days; thus he said "Moreover," and so forth.
In the Canon, an exemption from the offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) is stated for one whose robe has been stolen, whose robe has been lost, and so on; or rather—

Is it said that there is no offense for one who bathes naked because of a *dukkaṭa* [offense]? What is there to question here? For in all training rules (*sikkhāpada*), wherever there is a possibility of an offense arising from the root rule, the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*) is commenced in each case for the purpose of showing that there is no offense.
Therefore, it is appropriate to say that here too, it is for the purpose of showing that there is no offense due to the [rule concerning] forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

For the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*) is not commenced for the purpose of showing that there is no offense for an intermediate offense mentioned in between, without first having shown that there is no offense for a root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
For this very reason, it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries:

"Regarding the phrase 'one whose robe has been stolen' and 'one whose robe has been lost,' this refers to one who wears [the robe] at an improper time when he still possesses the remainder of the robe that was stolen or the remainder of the robe that was lost."

"And there is no offense for one who is searching [for a robe]. Regarding 'in times of distress' (āpadāsu): here, there is no offense for one who puts on a robe at an improper time, thinking, 'The thieves are carrying off my unclad self.

It is also stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "There is no offense for one who puts on a robe in times of distress—such as when one's robes have been torn or lost, or when thieves are carrying off one who is unclad—or for those who are insane and so forth."
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, with reference to the non-offense consisting of a *dukkaṭa* for one who bathes naked, it says:
"The phrase 'one whose robes have been stolen' is said specifically with reference to the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloth). For there is no offense in those [monks] bathing naked.
And in this context, for one who bathes having put on a costly *vassikasāṭikā*, a danger from thieves is what is called an 'emergency' (*āpadā*)."
Regarding what was stated there, the reason must be sought.

Alternatively, the intention might be that the passage beginning with “for one whose robe has been stolen” (acchinnacīvarassa) is commenced for the purpose of showing that there is no offense in either case; likewise, [the commentary] says:
“The phrase ‘for one whose robe has been stolen’ is said specifically with reference to the *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe),” and so forth.
It should not be stated without qualification. For it should be stated thus:
"There is no offense by way of *nissaggiya* for one who, having had his robe-cloth either stolen or lost, wears it or searches for it at an improper time;

there is no offense by way of *dukkaṭa* for one who, having had his rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) either stolen or lost, bathes naked; [and] in times of distress, for one who is without clothes."
“There is no offense for one who wears it at an improper time because thieves carry it off;
if thieves carry off a costly rainy-season robe while he is bathing after having worn it, there is no offense for one who bathes naked, as this is a *dukkaṭa* offense. The rest here is self-evident.
As for the factors, however, they are: the robe being intended for oneself, seeking it at an improper time, and obtaining it by means of that [seeking].
These, first of all, are the three factors for the offense of seeking [robes].

Having one’s own set of robes, the absence of an emergency, the robe being one’s own *vassikasāṭika*, and wearing it at an improper time—these are the four factors for the offense of wearing [the *vassikasāṭika*].
The commentary on the training rule concerning the *vassikasāṭika* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Taking Away Robes (Cīvaraacchindanasikkhāpada) 631.
Regarding the fifth [offense], in the phrase "because of which he said to you," the word *yaṃ* is a term expressing a reason. Therefore, the connection here should be understood as follows:
"On account of which reason—namely, 'he will set out on a journey through the countryside together with me'—I..."
"Friends, he was angry and displeased, saying, 'I gave you that robe-cloth, yet you do not make it,' and he took it back. Regarding the word "it" (*yaṃ*):
one should connect it thus: "He touched upon the robe-cloth, thinking, 'He will set out on a journey through the countryside with me;
I shall take back that robe-cloth which I gave to you,' and being angry and displeased, he took it back."
633. "When commanded, he takes many; one [offense] is a *pācittiya*": because the command "take a robe" has as its object a single robe, there is only one *pācittiya*.

"For every utterance, it is a *dukkaṭa*": here, regarding the robes that have been taken away, there are *pācittiya*s according to the number of items. "By a single utterance, there are numerous offenses":
this refers to the *pācittiya* offense that must be incurred according to the number of items taken away.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). However, regarding the offense incurred through an order, there is only a single *dukkaṭa*.

634. By the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), this refers back to the statement: "There are *dukkaṭas* according to the number of instances. "The same method applies" means that when [robes] are placed on loosely or tightly, the multiplicity or singularity of the offenses is clearly seen.
635. In cases such as "Friend, we... and so forth, even though it was spoken with the desire to take [the robe], there is no offense because it was given by that very person. "To us..."
The phrase "he will receive the going forth in the presence [of the teacher]" indicates that this gift applies even to a novice (sāmaṇera).

Therefore, although it is stated in the Canon, "having given a robe to a bhikkhu himself," nevertheless, it should be understood that even if one gives it while the recipient is not yet fully ordained, there is still an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who takes it back after he has been fully ordained.
At the moment of taking it back, the fact of his being fully ordained alone [constitutes the basis for the offense].
This is the measure here. "He gives" means he gives either out of satisfaction or out of anger. "Stop him" means prevent him.

Regarding the statement "but it is not permissible to give in this way," it should be understood that what has been given in such a manner must be used without first designating it as his property (thinking, "this is not yet his").
However, "it is permissible to have it brought back" means that because what was given in this way is like a wage (*bhata*), it is permissible to have it brought back.
"Having given after having desisted" means that, having not given according to the method already described, it was given to him by one who has become indifferent.

"He is to be dealt with according to the value of the goods" means that one who takes [the item] without the perception that it is his own is to be dealt with for an offense after having the value of the goods appraised.

[The factors are: the robe being of the minimum size suitable for dedication, having been given by oneself, the perception that it is one's own, the recipient being fully ordained, and the act of snatching away or causing it to be snatched away out of anger.
These are the five factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the taking away of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning requesting by means of a thread.

636. Regarding the sixth [clause], "at the time for making robes" (*cīvarakārasamaye*): this refers to the month of the robe (*cīvaramāsa*) because it is the period for monks who have completed the rains retreat to perform work on their robes; furthermore, any other time for performing robe-work may also be called the "time for making robes. 638.
"Having mixed with five" means having mixed with the five [kinds of material] beginning with *khoma*.
The term "loom" (*turī*) is a designation for the place where they roll up and store [the cloth]. Having inserted the thread, that by which they beat it to achieve density is the shuttle.
That is called "woven. Whatever application one employs, because the threads are one's own property, the place where they have been woven is already acquired;
therefore it says, "If [the robe] is long... [and so on] ...having woven it, there is an offense of expiation involving relinquishment (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
For in the Pāḷi as well, with this very intention, it is stated that "it is relinquishable by acquisition"; therefore, as long as the robe is being increased, [it remains an offense].
To that extent, offenses increase by this measure.
"The rest is allowable" refers here to [robes] made by means of manual labor or begging. "Forfeiture" (nissaggiya) is according to the method stated previously:
when the cloth is woven to a length of one span and a width of one cubit, it is subject to forfeiture. "By that very same [person]" refers to one who is an unallowable weaver.

"Likewise, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that for every delimitation, there is an offense of wrong-doing. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "by those bound by field-fences, etc.," items such as those bound by eye-sockets are included.
"It should be determined while still remaining on the thread" means that in this case, the place where it was subsequently unwound remains within the scope of what has already been determined;
there is no further need for an act of determination. However, if one shows the delimitation...
They say that if, in between, it becomes unwoven (*avīta*), it must be resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) again.
"The same method applies" means that when the warp has reached the measure of being ready for weaving (*vikappanupagappamāṇa*), one must resolve upon it while it remains exactly as it is.
Here, there are three factors: thread requested for the sake of a robe, its being designated for oneself, and having it woven by an unallowable weaver.

In the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, regarding the phrase "should have [it] woven," they state the meaning as: "‘Friends, please weave my robe’—he should have it woven by means of an improper request.
Furthermore, regarding the constituent factors (*aṅga*), they state: "having it woven by an improper weaver through an improper request.
Yet, such a specific statement is found neither in the Canon (*pāḷi*) nor in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
In the Pāḷi as well, only this much is stated in the section on non-offenses: “when invited by relatives.

And in the Aṭṭhakathā, many methods are shown regarding the permissibility or impermissibility of weaving cloth for the Suttas (monks) and Tantavāyas (weavers), but not by way of requesting what is permissible or impermissible.
By specifically stating, “one should have it woven through an impermissible request,” [the author] implies that this indeed is the permissible request.
It has not been shown separately; therefore, it should be understood after careful investigation.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the weaving of cloth is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning the great weaver.
642. Regarding the phrase "he should give even a little bit" in the seventh [offense], this is merely an indication of the manner in which he ought to act;
however, giving itself is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*) here, because the offense is incurred solely through the act of extending the thread.

For this very reason, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) it says: "By his word, he makes it long, wide, or thick; for the effort (*payoga*), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); with the acquisition..."
The offense is stated as "nissaggiya" (to be forfeited) merely by demonstrating the manner of increasing the thread.
It is also said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "A monk’s act does not become a *nissaggiya* offense merely by giving alms-food.
However, if, at his word, [the weaver] takes thread from the hands of the owners of the robe-cloth and stretches it even slightly longer or wider..."

"Or they cause it to be made ready; then, for their effort, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the monk, and upon acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).

Regarding the seven modes beginning with "stretched" (āyata), he said, "he demonstrates only the mode of extending the thread," because in the first three modes among those seven, it is impossible to perform them without extending the thread.
For in the modes such as "well-woven" (suvīta) and so forth, it is possible even without extending the thread.

It is possible to do so. The rest here is self-evident. Approaching weavers who are neither relatives nor invited, making a formal request, designating the robe for oneself, increasing the thread according to their word, and the obtaining of the robe—these are the four factors here.
The commentary on the Mahāpesakāra-sikkhāpada is finished.
8. Commentary on the Acceka-cīvara-sikkhāpada: 646.
"For the sake of non-confusion" means for the sake of non-confusion regarding the phrase "not ten days away. "Of the first phrase" refers to the phrase "not ten days away."
“On those days” means during those days. “It might arise” means it might arise from the Saṅgha, or from a group, or directly for oneself.

“From the fifth” means that if an urgent robe-cloth arises before the fifth day of the Saṅgha’s residence during the rains, one receives only the benefit of the urgent robe-cloth after having distributed it on the fifth day. Directly...
If it has arisen for oneself, it should be understood that one receives the privilege of an urgent robe (*accekacīvara*) only when it has arisen on the fifth day, and not prior to that.
"Mere faith" (*saddhāmattaka*) refers to the mere faith that arises at that moment through hearing the Dhamma and so forth. "Announced robe" (*ārocitaṃ cīvaraṃ*).

Having announced it, the robe has been given. Regarding the statement, "The eleventh dawn from the sixth [day] arises within the robe-period for a robe that has arisen," he said, "Starting from the sixth," and so forth.

The phrase "even a robe set aside" refers to all extra robes (atirekacīvara) by way of showing the primary robe. Now, as for the statement, "It is permissible to store an extra robe even during the robe-month."
If it is asked, "From where was this obtained?"—even though this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) was not separately authorized—it was stated in the third *kathina* training rule:
"The time for robes (*cīvarakālasamaya*) means, when the *kathina* has not been spread, the last month of the rainy season; when the *kathina* has been spread, the five months.
And: "An out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*) means, when the *kathina* has not been spread, that which arises during the eleventh month."
Some say: "By one who says, 'It arose during the seven months while the Kathina was spread,' it is indeed permitted. Others say:
"It must be accepted according to the authority of the words of the Aṭṭhakathā.
Now, regarding the specific exemptions for each type of robe as obtained through the various training rules beginning with the first Kathina:
Having summarized it right here and demonstrating it, he said: "Thus, there is a ten-day allowance for an extra robe," and so forth. One should accept this very reading:
"When the Kathina has not been spread, it is one month plus eleven days; when the Kathina has been spread, it is five months plus eleven days.
However, some here [interpret] this as: "Granted, this [rule] states, 'An extra robe may be kept for at most ten days.'"

Having stated the reading, "It was established by this very [case]; however, the training rule was laid down by showing a meaning as if it were new, by way of an occasion (aṭṭhuppatti)," some say, "The text should read 'a month plus ten days' and 'five months plus ten days'";
that should not be accepted because it is a careless reading. For [the offense] does not occur when the Kattika full moon of the third month has not yet been reached by ten days.
It would be more than ten days prior to the robe season. This being the case, it should have been stated: "Nine days before the full moon of Kattika, the month of the Invitation.

Furthermore, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, after stating, "The time for storing robes that arise from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of the Invitation is thus shown," it continues: "Granted, this [rule] says: 'An extra robe may be kept for at most ten days.'"

The reading shown as, "It was established by this very [rule], but the training rule was laid down after showing a meaning as if it were new by way of a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti)," is itself merely a careless reading.
Furthermore, because it is stated, "starting from the fifth day of the bright fortnight," there would be an internal contradiction in that very passage;
it should have been said, "starting from the sixth day. For if that were the case, [it would conflict with] the training rule regarding the ten-day maximum.
It can indeed be said that [the rule] is established. And taking this very reading as an instance of negligence, the teacher Bhadanta Buddhadatta stated:
“For that robe-material which is to be made up, when the kaṭhina has not been spread, a month’s delay is permitted;
it is considered to have ten days as the maximum.”
“It has been stated: ‘For one for whom the Kathina has been spread, five months are declared;
the privilege granted by the Lord of Sages, however, is limited to ten days at most.’”
Because it arose during the period for urgent robes (*accekacīvara*), it is said, "similar to an urgent robe. Regarding an urgent robe that arose on the fifth day:
for one who lets ten days pass, the offense occurs even before the robe-season (*cīvarakāla*), not upon the expiration of the robe-season itself.

Therefore, with reference to the absence of any further offense to be incurred upon the expiration of the robe-season, it says: "In the case of a non-urgent robe, perceiving it as a non-urgent robe..."
"There is no offense," it is stated; thus it is said in all three *gaṇṭhipadas*. Herein, there are four factors:

(1) the robe-cloth being one's own property that has reached the maximum permissible size for an immediate need; (2) its having arisen ten days before the full moon of the Kattika month in the month of Kattika;
(3) its not having been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned to another (*vikappita*); and (4) the lapse of the robe-season.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the hurried robe is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning danger. 652.

Regarding the ninth [rule], "in the midst of houses" (*antaraghare*): it is so called because there are houses within it, or because it is situated therein; thus it has acquired the conventional designation "the midst of houses."
In the village that serves as his range of activity. Therefore he said, "within the village. Regarding the phrase in the text, "dwelling apart" (*vippavasanti*):
this is said with reference to those dwelling elsewhere than the monastery where they had deposited their robes in the village.
For since it is permitted to dwell there after depositing the robes in the village, staying in that monastery constitutes "dwelling apart."
There is no [specific] name for it. They are "poorly clothed," "ill-clad," or "ugly-clad"; because they are ill-clad, they wear coarse robes.

Regarding the phrase "having attained and dwelling in the first jhāna," in its analysis (vibhaṅga), when the term "having attained" (upasampajja) is to be extracted, it is extracted as "having attained," and then it is stated:
"the acquisition and attainment of the first jhāna," and so forth.

With reference to this, he says: "as in the case of 'having entered' (upasampajja), etc. By the word "etc.," the inclusion of such passages as "or should depart without asking permission" is to be understood.
He states the meaning of the prefix *upa* by saying "having approached. "Having dwelt" means having dwelt uninterruptedly.
According to the statement, "Whatever is connected with something belongs to that thing, even if it stands far away," [the connection is established] between this... and this.
The connection has been stated. In that context, "of this" refers to the phrase "having entered the rains retreat. "Should set aside" means he should place it [the robe] down.

By this much, it is permitted for one who has entered the earlier period, lived the rains retreat without breaking it, and is dwelling in forest dwellings after having completed the rains, to be separated from his triple robe (ticīvara) for the entire month of Kattika. For one whose Kathina has not been spread...

Indeed, separation from one’s robe during the robe-month is not permitted, because it is only for those who have performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony that wandering without having formally accepted [the robe] is authorized.

However, some, asserting that "wandering without having formally accepted [the robe] is also possible for those who have not performed the *kaṭhina* even during the robe-month," engage in much elaboration;
that should not be accepted. "Analysis of the phrasing" refers to the analysis of such passages as "having rained, having rained."

The phrase “of those who have completed the rains retreat” (*vutthavassāna*) refers to the analytical term (*vibhaṅgapada*). The genitive case in *vutthavassāna* is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe sāmivacana*).
Therefore, he said: “among such monks. Regarding the word “in the lodgings” (*senāsanesu*), the phrase “of such a kind” (*tathārūpesu*) should be connected here.
Regarding the expression “from a place requiring an enclosure” (*parikkhepārahaṭṭhānato*), they say: “a place requiring an enclosure is defined as two *leḍḍupāta*s (the distance of a stone’s throw).”
That should not be accepted. However, for an unenclosed village, the area eligible for enclosure begins from the vicinity of the houses situated at its boundary;
this is the definitive conclusion here. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*:
"For an unenclosed [village], starting from the first stone-throw. "The very first" refers to the direction facing toward the village.
"First of all. "Having made that a boundary" means having made that first lodging and so forth a boundary.
This is stated according to the opinion of the Vinaya-dharas; however, according to the opinion of the Majjhimabhāṇakas, they say:
"It should be measured by throwing a single clod of earth from where one stands within the vicinity of the lodgings and so forth. For that very reason...
In the *Madhavanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "Having excluded even the precincts of the monastery, as one does for a village, the measurement should be taken between the two throws of a clod.
"Five hundred bow-lengths" means the measure of five hundred bows when shot by a master archer.
"It blocks the path here and there" means it blocks small paths in various places. "A thief of the ascetic practices" (*dhutaṅgacora*).
By this, he demonstrates the absence of the fulfillment of the factors for this training rule as well.
"Deemed dangerous" means they are recognized as such by seeing places where thieves have settled and so forth;
"where a powerful danger is present" means that because one sees people who have been killed, plundered, or maimed by thieves, it is said that a powerful danger is present.
The meaning: By the phrase "If [he goes] during the later part of the day," etc., he clarifies the very same meaning stated previously by way of contrast (*byatirekamukhena*).
For, having specified that very measure already stated in the passage beginning with "wherever for alms," etc., he shows it here.
Regarding the phrase "only where there is danger and fear": whether it be dangerous or fearful, it is indeed permissible.

In the Pāḷi, by the statement: “If there should arise some reason for that bhikkhu to be separated from that robe-cloth, he may be separated from it for a maximum of six nights,” this refers to a case where a bhikkhu has deposited his robe-cloth within an inhabited area while residing in a monastery;
when there is a necessity to go elsewhere, being separated from the robe outside the monastery for six nights [is permitted].
It is permitted. For it is stated that being separated from one’s robes for six nights applies to a place other than the dwelling site, not to one staying in that very monastery.

And by this [rule], it is said: “Having again entered the village boundary—if the lodging is in the eastern direction from the alms-village, and he has gone to the western direction,” and so forth. For this very reason, it is also stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*:
Regarding the phrase “if he should live apart from it for longer than that,” the meaning stated here is:

“if he should cause the seventh dawn to rise while staying in that same lodging for more than six nights. However, the venerable teacher Buddhadatta has stated this very same meaning even more clearly. For he said:
“If a bhikkhu lives in the forest having made a certain village his alms resort,
it is permitted for him to remain in that village for one month.
For one living elsewhere, a maximum of six nights is prescribed.”
"This is its underlying intention; what was hidden has now been made clear.
Because it was stated, "In Kosambī, a certain bhikkhu was ill," it is said that "the authorization for those from Kosambī (kosambaka-sammuti) was permitted.
The authorization for a bhikkhu from Kosambī is the "authorization for those from Kosambī. "Having come to the lodging" refers specifically to the monastery where he had resided.
Because it was spoken with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*), it is not permissible to cause the dawn to rise in another monastery even within that same village precinct.
"Having stayed" means having caused the dawn to rise. Because the place he had gone to was too far away, it is said: "by one who is unable to do so.
"Right there" means in that very place where he had gone.
The commentary on the training rule concerning suspicion is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning what has been set aside. 657–659.
Regarding the tenth [rule], "a portion set aside specifically for oneself": this refers to a separate portion that has been designated and set apart in one's own house.
"Give me one, give him one"—because it must be undertaken with such a single statement, it is said, "one should undertake [it] together.
"Ghee and so forth have been brought for you" means ghee and so forth have been brought for your sake.
Even though he knows they have been digested, if he requests them according to the stated method, it is said that he has requested what belongs to them alone; thus he spoke.
—“Give some to me as well,” he says; it is permissible.
660. “It is not even permissible to place flowers [on the stupa]”—this was said with reference to what has already been offered.
However, if one takes a flower that was offered at one cetiya and offers it at another cetiya, it is permissible. “Having seen what remains” refers to the leftovers.
Having seen [the food] being held and standing [there], [one says]: "Do not give it to this dog; give it to that one.

This is [an offense] only when the food has been formally dedicated (*pariṇata*). However, if it is given after having relinquished it to an animal, it is permissible to drive that [animal] away and have another eat it. By the phrase "Where shall we give it?
and so forth, an exemption from offense (*anāpatti*) is shown in the Canon in one way; yet, even if one has not asked in such a manner, if the food has not been formally dedicated...
"This may be given wherever one wishes, provided that one knows 'this' [is what is being offered]"—so it is stated in all three *gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
Regarding the phrase "give it where you wish," because it is said "according to your own preference," one is permitted to have it given wherever one desires.
This is according to the very method set forth in the *Pāḷi*: "wherever your gift [is to be given]," and so forth.
By way of method: the state of being dedicated to the Saṅgha, knowing that [dedication], and one’s own act of dedication—these are the three factors here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning dedication is finished.
The third chapter, the Chapter on Bowls, is concluded.
Thus ends the explanation of the *Nissaggiya* [offenses] in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, a commentary on the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The second part is completed.
